body: Armenia Armenia Courts Central Asia As TRIPP Corridor Takes Shape By Zamira Eshanova and RFE/RL's Kyrgyz Service September 06, 2026 13:34 CET Armenia Courts Central Asia As TRIPP Corridor Takes Shape Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian speaks at an SCO summit in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, on September 1. Armenia is courting Central Asia as it intensifies efforts to break ground on an ambitious trade corridor named after US President Donald Trump -- the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP. Part of a peace deal between Yerevan and Baku, the planned corridor would run across Armenian territory, linking Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave while opening a new east-west trade artery bypassing Russia and Iran. The proposed plan has the backing of Washington, but has riled Moscow and Tehran, two countries under heavy Western sanctions. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian has in recent weeks pushed for the involvement of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. But both countries, observers say, are wary of angering Russia, a key political and economic player in Central Asia. Pashinian discussed TRIPP with the leaders of Azerbaijan and India as well representatives from the United States during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek on September 1. SEE ALSO: Bypassing The Kremlin: Armenia And Azerbaijan Expand Trade, Testing Russia's Grip On August 27, Pashinian confirmed to RFE/RL’s Armenian Service that he had discussed Kazakhstan’s possible participation in TRIPP during a recent phone call with Kazkah President Qasym-Zhomart Tokaev. “We discussed this issue in relation to Kazakhstan and the TRIPP project. Various countries are now showing interest,” Pashinian said, without elaborating. Kyrgyz official Daniyar Amangeldiev told RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service that the government had yet to receive an official proposal. Public Rollout While the participation of potential regional partners remains uncertain, Armenia and the United States are moving ahead with plans to publicly launch the project. On September 1, they launched the official TRIPP Armenia Facebook page , jointly managed by the Armenian Foreign Ministry and US Embassy in Yerevan. On the same day, US and Armenian officials met in Armenia’s province of Syunik, where the 43-kilometer-long corridor is planned, to discuss the project and its potential economic benefits. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian (left) meets with US President Donald Trump in Egypt in late 2025. The United States owns 74 percent of the project, with Armenia retaining the rest. Washington has committed an initial $145 million. Pashinian has called TRIPP a “multibillion-dollar project.” TRIPP was approved by the Armenian government in July. The Constitutional Court is expected to rule on it on September 15 before it goes to parliament for a final vote. Washington has pledged to help secure additional financing from public and private investors, although no new investors or funds have been announced. For landlocked Armenia, the project is seen as a way to end its economic isolation and become a regional transport hub. SEE ALSO: Armenia Wants In On Asia-Europe Trade. Russian Rail Control Stands In The Way. Unveiled as part of the US-mediated peace process following Armenia's war with Azerbaijan over its breakaway region of Nagorno-Karabakh, TRIPP envisages rail and road infrastructure, possible oil and gas pipelines, and fiber-optic and electricity ventures. Since Azerbaijan regained control over Karabakh in a lightening offensive in September 2023, Armenia has shifted its geopolitical orientation, distancing itself from longtime ally Moscow and aligning more closely with the West. Bishkek, Astana 'Curiously Muted' Kazakhstan has publicly expressed interest in participating in TRIPP. TRIPP would complement the Middle Corridor, an emerging 6,500-kilometer-long trade route, bypassing Russia, that connects China to Europe through Central Asia and the Caucasus. TRIPP would provide onward connectivity from Azerbaijan through Armenia and Nakhchivan to Turkey and Europe. Kyrgyz officials have also presented TRIPP as a potential extension of the country’s transport links to Europe. “Our railway would reach Baku, which would also open a direct route for us to Turkey... It is a new opportunity,” Kyrgyzstan’s ambassador to the United States, Edil Baisalov, told RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service. Still, neither Bishkek nor Astana has publicly committed to participating in TRIPP. Kyrgyz political analyst Emilbek Dzhuraev said both countries have been “curiously muted.” SEE ALSO: Russia Uses Economic Chokehold To Counter Armenia's Westward Tilt “While both of them have had positive exchanges with the US, their SCO partners -- Iran in particular, but also Russia -- do not welcome TRIPP, and therefore, probably, they are hesitant at jumping on this opportunity,” Dzhuraev said. Russia, he added, may be the biggest factor behind their caution, given Moscow’s increasingly tense relations with Pashinian’s government. “Russia has a still greater stake in this -- given its collapsing hold on Armenia -- and hence, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan would not be cheered on by Russia to join TRIPP,” he said. summary: Armenia is stepping up efforts to pull Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan into an ambitious trade corridor named after US President Donald Trump. While Bishkek has shown enthusiasm and Astana has voiced support, neither has so far committed to the project.
title: Armenia Courts Central Asia As TRIPP Corridor Takes Shape

body: Features 'Shanghai' Grouping At 25: Rifts, Rivalries, And A Show Of Unity By Zamira Eshanova and RFE/RL's Kyrgyz Service August 31, 2026 21:12 CET 'Shanghai' Grouping At 25: Rifts, Rivalries, And A Show Of Unity Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on August 31 on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek. With a summit in Bishkek, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) is turning 25 at a moment of extraordinary tension that touches directly on many of the increasingly sprawling regional group's members. Iran is at war with the United States, Russia's war on Ukraine continues to rage with no sign of a let-up, China faces mounting US pressure over trade, and nuclear-armed foes India and Pakistan sit together despite deep rivalry, just to name a few. The four Central Asian members -- host country Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan -- are regional players but also the objects of various nations seeking to increase their sway, including China, Russia, India, and the United States, which is not a member of the SCO. SEE ALSO: Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit In an interview with the People's Daily, the newspaper of the Central Committee of China's Communist Party, SCO Secretary-General Nurlan Yermekbaev of Kazakhstan touted the "Shanghai spirit," which he said involves mutual trust, respect, and benefit, among other qualities he asserted make the group appealing to the so-called Global South. But behind these "shared values" are deep differences, with members using the SCO platform to pursue their own, often competing agendas. Each member "has its own distinct position, and the major powers have views that differ from one another," Kyrgyz political analyst Emil Juraev said. China and India "have differing positions on many issues, and there are also areas of dispute between them," Juraev said. "Russia is trying to exert influence on the world and...continues its war without stopping it. In addition, there is Iran. Everyone is waiting to see what Iran will do." Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shake hands during a meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Bishkek on August 31. The 26th annual SCO summit marks 25 years since it was established by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan. India, Pakistan, Iran, and Belarus are now members, and along with observer states and dialogue partners it represents nearly half of the world's population and roughly a quarter of the global economy. "Bishkek has become a world capital today," a local paper proclaimed on August 31 as leaders gathered for bilateral meetings on the eve of the formal summit. The September 1 meeting is expected to produce a Bishkek Declaration marking the anniversary along with thematic statements and decisions covering security, the economy, transport, environmental protection, artificial intelligence, and cultural and humanitarian cooperation. Past gatherings have produced no momentous decisions, however, and for members large and small it may be more about show than substance. Despite deep differences within the organization, the SCO gives its members and observers a platform to appear together on the international stage and project the weight of a larger collective, said Reid Standish, a nonresident research fellow at the Central European Institute of Asian Studies and a former RFE/RL correspondent. "It may not have major policy achievements to its name and it can be hamstrung by its internal rivalries, but the SCO still clearly serves a purpose in bringing these leaders together in a forum that isn't dominated by Western powers," he said. "The SCO's leaders clearly attach meaning to this, otherwise they would not be attending." China is the SCO's most influential member, and its economic weight has put Beijing at the center of mounting international pressure over trade. SEE ALSO: What If China Doesn't Play Ball? US Sanctions Campaign Faces Its Biggest Test Ahead of an August 31 meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors halfway around the world in Asheville, North Carolina, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he would encourage members to rethink their trade with China, calling Beijing's roughly $1.2 trillion global trade surplus unsustainable. Last week, Bessent urged countries to cut ties with Iran as part of an effort to " sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone." For Iran, the signal it hopes the SCO summit will send is that it is not alone. "In the confrontation between Iran and America, we should expect stronger statements here, statements about Western influence and pressure or a declaration expressing disagreement with the processes in Iran or saying something along the lines of, 'You are doing the wrong thing,'" Kyrgyz political analyst Chynara Esengul said. Likewise Russia, which is under increasingly tight Western sanctions over its war against Ukraine. In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin on suspicion of war crimes over the illegal transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia. For China, Standish said, SCO meetings "serve a useful purpose in providing important optics to the world that key global decisions can be reached without the presence of Western leaders." summary: The Shanghai Cooperation Organization turns 25 at a moment of extraordinary tension embroiling several of the regional security group’s most prominent members. For China, Russia, Iran, and others, it may be less about substance than a show of influence and independence in the face of the West.
title: 'Shanghai' Grouping At 25: Rifts, Rivalries, And A Show Of Unity

body: Features Central Asia Seeks Open Borders, But Security Fears Get In The Way By Sarah Ashcroft and RFE/RL's Kyrgyz Service August 30, 2026 14:44 CET Central Asia Seeks Open Borders, But Security Fears Get In The Way Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google An archive photo captures the natural beauty of the Pamir mountains in Tajikistan. Bermet Tursalieva takes hikers through the mountains of her native Kyrgyzstan and says that while the tourism business is looking up, what she really needs is for Central Asia's onerous border controls to lighten up a little. "If we cooperate with tour operators in neighboring countries and strengthen regional integration, ethnotourism could develop even further. In that case, we could organize ethnic tours across Central Asia," she told RFE/RL's Kyrgyz Service recently. Tursalieva might take heart from recent political initiatives by Central Asian leaders to ease frontier checks for tourists. But the region's powerful security services and deep-rooted authoritarian instincts have put the block on such moves in the past. Traveling The Silk Road In recent years, Central Asia has become a hotspot for Western tourists looking for a holiday off the beaten track . From ancient Silk Road architecture to stunning mountain trekking, the region has something for everyone. SEE ALSO: The Making Of The World Nomad Games Social media hashtags like #dadlore and #sidequest have become inundated with videos of young people camping in yurts and riding horses across the steppe while bespoke, all-inclusive tour guides cater to those looking for a more comfortable, curated experience. However, a major hitch remains for Western tourists in the form of difficulties traveling between countries once they arrive. Due to the high cost and long travel time for tourists, the appeal of visiting multiple countries on one trip is clear. "People who come here usually want to visit two or three 'stations' at the same time," Kazakhstan tourism expert Yerkin Tikenov told RFE/RL. "Central Asia is located far from the world's major tourist centers, and it takes a long time to get to the region. It's logical that a tourist...wants to see a lot in a short period of time." Embed share Ruins Of Ancient Buddhist Temple Set To Open In Kyrgyzstan by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:06 0:00 This idea is not only appealing to tourists but to locals like Tursalieva working in the sector. "From Osh (in Kyrgyzstan), they could enter Uzbekistan or travel through Batken into Tajikistan. The village of Zardaly in Batken is itself a tourist attraction. There are also historical sites and mausoleums in Uzbekistan's Andijan region and in Samarkand," she said. "Tajikistan offers its own cultural attractions, while Kazakhstan is known for its traditional healers. We would like to showcase all of these destinations," Tursalieva added. Bermet Tursalieva However, non-uniform visa systems and disorganized border controls across the region mean this is easier said than done. Despite many Central Asian countries adopting a visa-free regime for foreign tourists, the process of obtaining a stamp in and out of each country at the border causes long lines. Dealing with different rules and permits complicates things further. For example, visiting Tajikistan's eastern Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Region -- which makes up nearly half of the country -- requires a permit even if you can travel to the country visa-free. Additional permits that can only be obtained inside the country are also necessary to visit the Zorkul and Sarez lakes. SEE ALSO: Ancient Central Asian Language Dying Off As Villagers Leave For Better Life This lengthy process, alongside the multiple checks that foreign tourists must undergo, provides significant complications to those hoping to visit some of the country's most beautiful landscapes. A unified visa system requiring just one application and a streamlined process at the border would reduce these obstacles. 'An Asian Schengen' The appeal of such a system is not lost on Central Asian governments. At an informal summit of regional leaders on July 31, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov pushed for collaboration on a unified visa system. In fact, this is not a new idea. It was first proposed by Kazakhstan in 2018, with the idea that an EU-style " Asian Schengen " would allow foreigners to travel freely between Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan. But progress has been slow along a path littered with obstacles. Only in 2025 was a treaty delineating the long-disputed trilateral border finally signed between Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. The head of the Tourism Development Agency in Kyrgyzstan, Eduard Kubatov, told RFE/RL that work was under way on building a unified travel system. "It will strengthen Central Asia's economic, social, and cultural integration and facilitate safe border crossings. Now we are negotiating with Uzbekistan; they are ready to support. We are also negotiating with Kazakhstan and Tajikistan," he said. SEE ALSO: Kyrgyzstan And Tajikistan's Border Agreement: Deal Of The Century? Tourism has been growing in recent years, albeit from a relatively low baseline. According to the World Travel and Tourism Council's June 2026 Central Asia Travel and Tourism Economic Impact Research, the total contribution of travel and tourism to Central Asian GDP grew from $6.7 billion in 2020 to $20.1 billion in 2025. Tursalieva has also noted development in the mountains where she leads tours. "A year ago, the situation was different in Besh-Tash, in Talas (in northwestern Kyrgyzstan). Within a year, there was visible progress. The conditions of the dormitories and services have improved, and the quality of food has improved," she said. But in a region where authoritarian rulers like to keep a lid on people's movements -- and where there are serious concerns about terrorism and smuggling -- the economic incentive to boost tourism has not proved enough to open borders. "While presidents say 'yes, yes' verbally, law enforcement and intelligence agencies ...seem reluctant to do so," Tikenov said. SEE ALSO: Hormuz Crisis Has Supercharged The Middle Corridor Trade Route Luca Anceschi, professor of Eurasian studies at the University of Glasgow, pointed out in an interview with RFE/RL that only Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan are members of the Eurasian Union, allowing for citizens to move freely between the countries. Without the free movement of Central Asian citizens themselves, a unified tourist visa is unthinkable, he said: "Such a system would have to be applied equally, for Central Asians and non-Central Asians." Central Asian security expert Edward Lemon was also skeptical. "Turkmenistan is unlikely to join such a scheme," told RFE/RL. "It remains one of the world's most closed countries and is very difficult to enter. Tajikistan also uses border security as the reason for making it relatively difficult to visit." Despite official attitudes toward tourism in the country shifting in early 2025 with the introduction of an e-visa system, tourists to Turkmenistan have described harsh restrictions on photography and movement within the country. Visa applications are often arbitrarily denied, and both locals and tourism industry insiders are yet to notice an increase in tourists since the changes. summary: Central Asia has lots to attract tourists but it’s difficult getting around. Efforts to make it easier for tourists to cross borders have been proposed -- but there are substantial obstacles.
title: Central Asia Seeks Open Borders, But Security Fears Get In The Way

body: News Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote By Zamira Eshanova August 24, 2026 17:36 CET Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Members of a local electoral commission count ballots at a polling station during parliamentary elections in Almaty, southeastern Kazakhstan, on August 23. Four months ago, the Adilet party did not exist. Today, it dominates Kazakhstan’s political landscape, following an election in which it gained 71.17 percent of the vote according to results announced on August 24. The vote marks a further tightening of President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev's grip on power -- and was roundly criticized by international election observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). “The 23 August early parliamentary elections, while technically well prepared, took place in an environment lacking political pluralism. Political choice was reduced by the lack of distinct political alternatives, with all contesting parties supporting the incumbent President’s policies,” an OSCE statement said. In the August 24 statement , issued a day after the vote itself, the OSCE reported misuse of public resources, including public-sector employees being mobilized to attend campaign events, and concluded that Adilet had "an undue advantage that blurred the line between state and party.” The OSCE noted that independent candidates had been excluded from the election, a factor which “limited political participation and electoral competitiveness.” Observers also cast doubt on the results themselves, stating that discrepancies between what they saw at polling stations and official turnout data “raised questions about the integrity of the voter turnout reporting and the counting process.” OSCE missions have made similar criticisms of all previous elections held in Kazakhstan since it became independent after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, noting a lack of genuine political competition in an authoritarian country dominated for decades by presidents Nursultan Nazarbaev (1991-2019) and his successor, Toqaev. SEE ALSO: Kazakh Voters Appear To Approve Controversial Changes That Critics Say May Concentrate President's Power When Adilet was formed, in April, it absorbed the ruling party that had dominated Kazakhstan during and since the Nazarbaev era. Its stated aim is to implement Toqaev's policies and it will now comfortably control Kazakhstan's new unicameral parliament, the Kurultai. Adilet’s vote share was more than eleven times that of its nearest rival. The election was the first since constitutional changes rammed through by Toqaev earlier this year to switch from a previous bicameral structure. Media Pressure Before the Vote The election took place amid reports of pressure on independent activists and media. Almaty-based civil activist Asset Abishev said police blocked access to his home on August 23, which he described as interference with his right to vote. Another activist, Nurbol Arterkhan, who is under probation and subject to electronic monitoring, said he was repeatedly required to report to probation officials on election day and that police later visited his home. SEE ALSO: Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, five prominent journalists have been jailed or convicted since mid-July, while criminal cases have been opened against two others. Several have also been barred from practicing journalism. Media freedom was another major concern in the OSCE assessment. “Long-standing concerns about arrests and pressure on independent journalists generate pervasive self-censorship,” it noted in its statement. Sevilay Celenk, who headed a team of observers from the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), also raised the issue. “Without an inclusive, credible, and pluralistic media environment, political participation and representation are fundamentally limited, especially during elections,” Celenk said. Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Follow us Facebook X (Twitter) Youtube Instagram Follow us Print Zamira Eshanova Zamira Eshanova is a correspondent for RFE/RL's Uzbek Service. This item is part of News Kazakhstan
summary: A party formed just four months ago has swept Kazakhstan’s parliamentary election, tightening President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev’s grip on power amid international criticism over a lack of political competition, media pressure, and questions about the vote count.
title: Election Observers Say Kazakh President's Party Had 'Undue Advantage' As It Grabs 70 Percent Of Vote

body: News Voting Over In Kazakh Election Amid Opposition Exclusion, Media Pressure By Zamira Eshanova and RFE/RL's Kazakh Service August 23, 2026 08:44 CET Voting Over In Kazakh Election Amid Opposition Exclusion, Media Pressure Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Voters cast their balots at a polling station during a snap parliamentary election in Almaty, Kazakhstan, on August 23. Kazakhstan has elected its new, unicameral parliament in a tightly controlled process following changes to the country's constitution, with genuine opposition groups excluded from the race. Seven state-vetted parties contested the election, while opposition groups were denied the status of political parties under legislation used to exclude them. The Central Election Commission said 72.15% of the more than 12.6 million voters on the electoral register had cast ballots by 6 p.m. local time. Preliminary results are expected on August 24. President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev, whose reform agenda paved the way for the creation of the new unicameral parliament, cast his ballot at a polling station in Astana, calling the election an "important historic event" for Kazakhstan. He said the vote was only the beginning of a broader reform effort. Asked at the polling station whether he plans to seek another presidential term, Toqaev said it was too early to discuss the issue. His comments come after constitutional changes that have opened a legal path for him to seek another seven-year term. SEE ALSO: Is Political Opposition Still Possible In Central Asia? Toqaev also said there would be changes to the government following the election, without providing details. Under Kazakhstan's new constitutional system, the formation of a new parliament is expected to be followed by the resignation and re-formation of the government. The election took place amid reports of pressure on independent activists and media. Almaty-based civil activist Asset Abishev said police blocked access to his home on August 23, which he described as interference with his right to vote. Police did not immediately comment on the allegation. Another activist, Nurbol Arterkhan, who is under probation and subject to electronic monitoring, said he was repeatedly required to report to probation officials on election day and that police later visited his home. Arterkhan has previously faced prosecution over statements critical of the authorities. The restrictions extended to independent election monitoring. Under the election-monitoring rules, domestic nongovernmental groups receiving direct or indirect foreign funding cannot observe inside polling stations. This has left independent Kazakh watchdogs outside the official monitoring process. The authorities say 777 foreign observers are accredited, many representing regional organizations including the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). The SCO said its observers had recorded no violations or complaints during the first half of voting on August 23. The SCO mission said it would issue its final assessment after polling, with a news conference scheduled for August 24. The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), whose interim report noted the absence of genuine opposition parties and independent candidates and concerns over restrictions on political expression, is also observing the vote. SEE ALSO: Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote More than 70 parliamentarians and staff from around 30 countries were deployed as part of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly observation mission, its 13th election observation mission in Kazakhstan since 1994. The OSCE has criticized all of the elections held in this period, noting a lack of genuine political competition in an authoritarian country dominated for decades by presidents Nursultan Nazarbaev (1991-2019) and his successor as head of state, Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev. The vote also took place amid pressure on independent media. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, five prominent journalists have been jailed or convicted since mid-July, while criminal cases have been opened against two others. Several have also been barred from practicing journalism. The CEC is expected to release preliminary results on August 24, with final results due within seven days. Separately, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) will present its preliminary findings on August 24. The vote follows constitutional changes approved in a March referendum that replaced the previous bicameral parliament with a single chamber, the Kurultai. The Adilet party, which absorbed the former ruling party’s political structures as a new vehicle for the post-Nazarbaev era, is expected to dominate the first Kurultai. A nationwide poll by the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development put the party at 70.2 percent support, positioning it to further cement Toqaev's grip on power. summary: Voting is under way in elections for Kazakhstan's new, unicameral parliament, but opposition groups have been excluded from the group in a tightly controlled process that follows contentious changes to the country's constitution.
title: Voting Over In Kazakh Election Amid Opposition Exclusion, Media Pressure

body: Kazakhstan Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote By RFE/RL's Kazakh Service August 21, 2026 15:29 CET Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Journalists in Kazakhstan face growing legal and online restrictions, press freedom groups say. (file photo) Independent journalists and government critics in Kazakhstan are facing growing pressure ahead of parliamentary elections this weekend, rights groups say, pointing to criminal investigations, detentions, travel restrictions, and court-ordered bans on journalism. The vote on August 23 will elect the first members of the Kurultai, a new unicameral parliament that replaces Kazakhstan’s two-chamber legislature under constitutional changes approved in a March referendum. President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev has portrayed the changes as political modernization. Critics say they have further concentrated power in the presidency, raising questions about the environment in which the first Kurultai election will take place. Adilet (Justice), a party founded in May and led by Toqaev’s former presidential administration chief, is heavily favored to win , with the latest national poll putting its support at 70.2 percent. The party absorbed the former ruling Amanat party and inherited its nationwide political network, leading critics to portray it as a rebranding of the pro-Toqaev political establishment. In an assessment last month of the upcoming vote, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights said people interviewed by its mission had raised concerns about a “growing intolerance of criticism by the authorities, resulting in increasing pressure and sanctions.” They said this has contributed to “self-censorship and reduced civic participation.” Kazakh President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev (file photo) On August 14, Civil Rights Defenders and eight other human rights and press freedom organizations warned of what they called a “broader, longer-term pattern” of politically motivated charges, online restrictions, and other forms of harassment and intimidation against government critics. The organizations highlighted four recent cases. Independent journalist and government critic Dinara Yegubaeva faces a criminal investigation following a July 31 traffic accident involving her car and a cyclist. Rights groups say the case was initially treated as an administrative matter. Authorities have also barred her from leaving Kazakhstan. Journalist and editor Lukpan Akhmedyarov is under investigation after sharing a Ukrainian government list of Kazakh citizens alleged to be fighting for Russia in Ukraine. Authorities accuse him of knowingly spreading false information. He was also barred from leaving Kazakhstan on August 3. Journalist Aleksandra Alyokhova, known by her pen name Sentsova, was convicted on August 3 of publishing private information about a person involved in a dispute at an Almaty bazaar. She received a three-year suspended prison sentence and was also barred from practicing journalism for three years. Rights groups say the information had previously been made public on a Telegram channel. Azamat Omarov (file photo) Political commentator Azamat Omarov, who runs the current affairs YouTube channel Akhual Segodnya, has been held in pretrial detention since July 18 on suspicion of inciting social, national, racial and religious discord. His lawyer says the case concerns videos containing satire and criticism of the authorities. Government Denies Crackdown The Kazakh government rejects allegations that it is suppressing legitimate journalism and criticism. Culture and Information Minister Aida Balaeva said on August 17 that the government does not block the social media accounts of journalists or media outlets. “The state is not interested in such actions or in restricting freedom of speech and opinion,” she said. “Combating unlawful content must not lead to unjustified restrictions...” Several recent court cases, however, have resulted in journalists being barred from their profession. KazTAG editor in chief Amir Qasenov On July 31, an Almaty court sentenced Amir Qasenov, editor in chief of KazTAG, an independent Kazakh news agency, to one year and three months of restricted freedom after convicting him of knowingly disseminating false information in articles about Freedom Finance, one of Kazakhstan’s largest brokerage firms. He was also banned from practicing journalism for five years. KazTAG’s general director Aset Mataev was convicted of failing to properly perform his managerial duties and of hooliganism in connection with a separate altercation in March. He received the same restricted-freedom sentence and three-year journalism ban. Both men denied the charges . Human rights activist Yevgeny Zhovtis said such restrictions have implications beyond professional journalism because bloggers and ordinary citizens also publish information and opinions online. “The approach here is not merely a ban on journalistic activity; its scope is much broader,” he said. “It amounts to depriving a person of their civil rights, specifically their freedom to express their opinion.” SEE ALSO: CPJ Expresses Concerns Over Kazakhstan's New Media Accreditation Rules Diana Okremova, director of Kazakhstan’s Legal Media Center, said bans on journalism were “completely incompatible” with democratic principles and Kazakhstan’s human-rights commitments. Another prominent independent journalist has been given a similar professional ban -- along with a lengthy prison sentence. On August 18, an Almaty court sentenced Gulnar Bazhkenova, former editor in chief of the news outlet Orda.kz, to eight years in prison and barred her from journalism and other activities for five years. Bazhkenova, who had been under house arrest since December, faced multiple charges, including repeatedly disseminating information that authorities claimed she knew to be false. She denied all the charges against her. Digital Restrictions Mount Press freedom monitors say the pressure has also increasingly moved online . RFE/RL’s Kazakh Service and Azattyq Asia, its Russian-language unit covering Central Asia, became difficult to access in Kazakhstan in May after RFE/RL published an investigation examining links between relatives of Toqaev and VD Stroy-Engineering, a recipient of large state contracts. Kazakh authorities denied involvement. Network measurements, however, found evidence consistent with deliberate restrictions on access. SEE ALSO: Access To RFE/RL Kazakh Websites Mysteriously 'Throttled' After Investigative Story The Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) has separately documented what it described as fraudulent copyright complaints targeting RFE/RL content, including political coverage and investigations involving people allegedly linked to Kazakhstan’s political elite. Nazira Darimbet, head of the Adil Soz press freedom foundation, said online restrictions intensified around the March constitutional referendum, eased afterward, and have risen again ahead of the Kurultai election. “Sometimes we cannot even keep up,” she said. “This one is being blocked, that one is being blocked. Complaints are being filed against YouTube videos, and [journalists’ accounts] are being flagged for blocking.” The government denies responsibility for blocking journalists’ accounts. The August 23 vote will be the first nationwide election held under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional framework. SEE ALSO: Kazakh President Seeks Tighter Grip On Power With New Constitution The new constitution replaces the Senate and lower-house Mazhilis with the Kurultai and creates the post of vice president. The president appoints the vice president with parliamentary consent and continues to control key senior appointments. For T
summary: Independent journalists and government critics in Kazakhstan face mounting pressure ahead of the country’s first parliamentary elections following a controversial constitutional overhaul that critics say has strengthened the president’s power.
title: Criminal Cases, Travel Bans: Pressure Mounts On Kazakh Journalists Ahead Of Parliamentary Vote

body: Ukraine As Ukrainian Strikes Hit Hard, Moscow Seeks Deeper Defense Ties With Central Asia By Zamira Eshanova August 18, 2026 20:57 CET As Ukrainian Strikes Hit Hard, Moscow Seeks Deeper Defense Ties With Central Asia Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian President Vladimir Putin (right), Kazakh President Qasym-Zhomart Tokaev (center), and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoev attend a military parade in Moscow. (file photo) Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed directives to amend military-technical cooperation agreements with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, potentially opening the door to deeper defense ties with the two Central Asian states. As Western sanctions and Ukrainian long-range strikes strain Russia's military industry, the move may signal that Moscow is seeking to relocate parts of its military-industrial base to reduce its vulnerability to attack. After Putin signed the directives last month, the Kremlin has not said what changes it is seeking to the agreements, which cover the supply and upkeep of weapons and military equipment and other forms of defense cooperation. Since the agreement with Kazakhstan entered into force in 2015 following its initial signing in Moscow in 2013, Astana has acquired a range of Russian military equipment including fighter jets, helicopters, and air defense systems. Similarly, the 2016 agreement with Uzbekistan expanded military-technical cooperation between the two countries, with Tashkent acquiring Russian attack helicopters, armored personnel carriers, and tactical drones. 'The Kremlin Is In A Difficult Position' Yermek Seytbattalov, a Kazakh military analyst specializing in defense and security issues, said the timing reflects growing international pressure on Moscow. "I believe the Kremlin is in a difficult position," Seytbattalov said. "The 21st package of [EU] sanctions is on the horizon. There have been no notable successes on the battlefield...and at the same time the European Union and the United States...are increasing the level of assistance to Ukraine." According to Seytbattalov, another source of pressure comes from Ukraine's enhanced long-range drone campaign, which he said is disrupting Russia's domestic military supply chain and highlighting Moscow's need to establish production and repair facilities farther from the front. "This can be qualified as an attempt to bring stability to the Russian military-industrial complex by expanding its base into neighboring countries that are located outside of combat zones," Seytbattalov said. SEE ALSO: Kazakhs Weigh Hosting Russian Retailers Against Ukraine Neutrality Geographic distance from Russia would be a strategic advantage, Derek Bisaccio, a military analyst at Forecast International, told Azattyq Asia , RFE/RL's Russian unit covering Central Asia. "Anything they can get operating on the territory of another country will only complicate operations for Ukraine. I think Ukraine has certainly become bolder in its operations, but they will not want to launch drone strikes on Kazakh territory. That would be regarded there as a serious escalation, and that is not something the Ukrainians would want to do. I think Russia knows this," he said. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan currently host key facilities that provide maintenance and modernization for Russian military equipment. Key sites include Kazakhstan's Semey Engineering, which works on armored vehicles, and the Aviation Repair Plant in Almaty, which specializes in helicopter overhauls. Uzbekistan's Chirchik Aircraft Repair Plant also services Soviet-designed military aircraft. Soviet Collapse Following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia sought to preserve its military influence over the newly independent Central Asian states through bilateral agreements and the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), established in 1992. The bloc has helped keep the region's militaries tied to Moscow through joint exercises, arms sales, and military-technical cooperation, while serving as a Russia-led counterweight to NATO in the post-Soviet space. The military relationships of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan with Russia are closely intertwined with the CSTO. Uzbekistan has more strategic autonomy since exiting the alliance in 2012 to manage its military relationship with Moscow strictly through bilateral agreements. Military analyst Seytbattalov said Moscow may now be seeking to move beyond its traditional role as a supplier of military equipment and spare parts. "Under the existing agreements, Moscow may have been dissatisfied with the concept of one-way cooperation. In other words, it sells weapons and military equipment, as well as spare parts for their repair and limited modernization, to CSTO member states, while they are expected only to pay and comply with the rules by refraining from purchasing other types of weapons from countries outside the CSTO." SEE ALSO: Central Asia's Fuel Crisis: The Cost Of Russian Dependence And Short-Term Thinking What isn't clear is whether countries in Central Asia -- particularly Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan -- even desire enhanced and reciprocal military ties with Russia. Kazakhstan's Defense Ministry, responding to an RFE/RL inquiry about the military-technical agreement with Russia, said such matters remain under review by the relevant state authorities and declined to discuss the substance of the proposed amendments. The ministry added that any agreements or protocols ultimately adopted would be implemented "in strict accordance with the legislation of the Republic of Kazakhstan." Uzbekistan's Defense Ministry did not respond to RFE/RL's request for comment. Hidden Agenda? Pavel Baev, a political scientist and research professor at the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO), questions whether Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have much reason to deepen military-technical ties with Moscow, particularly with Ukraine's growing ability to penetrate Russian air defenses and strike military, industrial, and energy infrastructure deep inside the country. Ukrainian long-range strike capabilities have expanded substantially during the war, with Kyiv now able to reach targets hundreds or even more than 1,000 kilometers from the front. "The fact of the matter is that something has already changed dramatically. Russian air defense systems have proven to be an epic fail, so for the neighbors, cooperation in this sphere now makes little sense," he said. SEE ALSO: Central Asia Emerges As Strategic Energy Player Amid Oil Crisis Baev added that Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan could simply refuse to reopen the agreements or prolong negotiations. "Nuances can be many, but a plain signal that they see no need in renegotiating is entirely possible. The interesting question is whether they can coordinate a joint response," he said. He added that delaying negotiations would be easier if Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan acted together. Asked whether accommodating Moscow's demands could expose Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to potential Western sanctions, Baev said that could be part of the Kremlin's calculation. "That may be a hidden agenda in Putin's instruction, and he may try to pull them apart by playing on the difference, as Kazakhstan is a CSTO member," Baev said. "It is, however, entirely in their interests, as well as in their power, to break his not-very-clever plan." summary: As the war in Ukraine drags on, the Kremlin is looking beyond its borders for help sustaining its military machine. Russian President Vladimir Putin has recently ordered negotiations to revise military cooperation agreements with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
title: As Ukrainian Strikes Hit Hard, Moscow Seeks Deeper Defense Ties With Central Asia

body: Kazakhstan The Horrors Of Aktas Mental Hospital: Inside Kazakhstan's Secretive Asylum By RFE/RL's Kazakh Service August 18, 2026 12:46 CET The Horrors Of Aktas Mental Hospital: Inside Kazakhstan's Secretive Asylum Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Secret videos allege abuse at Kazakhstan's only high-security psychiatric hospital. The Republican Psychiatric Hospital with Intense Observation stands in the isolated settlement of Aktas, about 40 kilometers northeast of Almaty. The only Kazakh high-security psychiatric facility of its kind, the heavily fortified compound sits on the western edge of a sprawling industrial mining and quarry complex. According to the country's Health Ministry, more than 80 percent of patients at the institution have committed "grave crimes against others" and are being held under a court-ordered compulsory medical regime. Until now, little information has been publicly available about what happens behind the guarded walls of the Aktas hospital. But recently, a former patient leaked multiple videos on social media, sparking widespread discussion. The footage, consisting of secretly recorded interviews, was subsequently shared with Azattyq, RFE/RL's Kazakh Service. Some videos have been published on social media. Some of the videos obtained by Azattyq are new. Embed share Tied To Beds, Forcibly Injected: Secret Videos Allege Abuse At Kazakh Psychiatric Hospital by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:29 0:00 The former patient who provided the footage asked Azattyq not to disclose his name, while most of those he interviewed identified themselves in the recordings. He said he was a patient at the hospital from 2022 until February this year and that the footage was recorded in 2025–2026. RFE/RL was unable to independently verify the dates on which the footage was recorded. One after another, the patients interviewed in the videos described remarkably similar experiences of what they said they had been forced to endure. One of the patients, Ruslan Kemelov, said he was tied to a bed for refusing an order from hospital staff and was subsequently given an injection against his will. Asked what had prompted the restraint, he answered simply: "I refused to wash the sink." The hospital declined to comment on Kemelov's individual case, citing medical confidentiality. Other former patients described similar experiences. Former patient Samat Sattarov described the effects of being forced to take an antipsychotic drug, including being restrained afterward. "After decanoate, a person can neither walk, nor sit, nor lie down normally. Your whole body is in a state of torment. Imagine: I lay tied to a bed for 10 days." Another patient, Alisher Karimov, described how frequently he was subjected to these injections. SEE ALSO: Family Seeks Answers After Prominent Kazakh Writer Disappears In Xinjiang "Six injections a day -- I received 60 injections in 10 days. What's even worse is that they tie you to the bed. You lie there tied up for 10 whole days and cannot move. They don't even untie you to let you go to the toilet. You have to relieve yourself where you are." Sattarov said he believes such treatment is intended to frighten patients into submission. "After all these 'executions,' a person completely loses the desire to live. You can no longer think normally; you become like a vegetable." Involuntary detention on mental health grounds, according to rights groups, should only be possible in exceptional circumstances clearly defined in law, based on a determination by qualified health-care professionals that a person poses a serious and imminent risk to themselves or to a third party. Human rights activist Elena Semenova, who received some of the videos, said the accounts described by patients warrant serious investigation. "This is the suppression of a person's will, instilling fear in them in order to achieve a desired result, to make them perform certain actions. That is torture." The patients who spoke in the video interviews described more than just physical restraint. They said they were routinely forced to perform manual labor to keep the facility running and that being discharged was extremely difficult. According to their accounts, full obedience to staff was the only way to secure release. One patient, filmed washing toilets with his bare hands, was asked why he was doing it. He answered simply: "For discharge." When asked whether staff explicitly told him he would not be released if he refused, he replied: "Yes, yes." Another patient described being ordered to work at a garbage dump where waste was handled entirely by patients. "If you say you won't go, they put you in the observation ward and give you injections." Former employees verified the accounts. "They make them wash toilets and sinks. They force them," said Baizhan Sagyndykov, a former hospital staff member. "If patients say anything about wanting to defend their rights, they threaten them, saying, 'I'll tie you up, I'll put you on injections,' and that they will take other measures as well. I'm telling you this based on what I personally witnessed." Despite the videos and reports, the hospital denied the forced-labor allegations, saying patients do not perform employees' duties and that cleaning, kitchen work, and maintenance are carried out by staff. (screenshot) Another former employee, Nagima Nurbekova, said patients who could barely walk were made to perform such work and were tied up and given injections if they objected. In response to an inquiry from Azattyq, the hospital denied the forced-labor allegations, saying patients do not perform employees' duties and that cleaning, kitchen work, and maintenance are carried out by staff. The hospital's director, Dulatbek Dauylbekov, also rejected the suggestion that restraints are used as punishment. "Physical restraint measures are used only when there are medical indications and are not used as punishment or disciplinary measures," Dauylbekov stated, maintaining that restraint is a last resort utilized only if there is a direct threat of violence. Ward No. 9 Some of the most serious allegations involve Ward No. 9. Patients and former staff describe it as one of the harshest departments in the institution. Former patient Alexey Alekseev described seeing a fellow patient, Yuri Prikhodchenko, repeatedly restrained and heavily medicated there. "For 10 days, the person is forced to relieve himself where he is because they do not untie him at all. He experiences terrible torment. I am speaking about this openly because I went through it myself." Another patient, Timur Nauanov, also mentioned Prikhodchenko. "Prikhodchenko is currently in the ninth ward, the tuberculosis ward, although he does not have tuberculosis. They put him there deliberately because he began openly speaking about his rights and freedoms. I am afraid for my health and my life because there have been cases of patients dying, and not just once." In an official response to Azattyq, the hospital's director denied that such a ward currently exists, even though patients described its exact location in detail. Contrary to the director's statement, Kazakhstan's sanitary authorities confirmed that the institution has a 60-bed ward for patients with tuberculosis, as well as an isolation room for people suspected of having the disease. The hospital not only denied the existence of Ward No. 9; it also refused to provide information about patients said to be held there, citing medical confidentiality, even to their families. Prikhodchenko's mother, Olga Petrova, told Azattyq that she had repeatedly struggled to get through to the hospital and was often unable to see her son. summary: A former patient has leaked multiple videos about conditions at a high-security psychiatric hospital in Kazakhstan, sparking widespread discussion about what happens behind its guarded walls.
title: The Horrors Of Aktas Mental Hospital: Inside Kazakhstan's Secretive Asylum

body: Russia 'Organized Slavery': Russia's Tighter Migrant Rules Could Hit Central Asian Workers, Worsen Shortages By Azattyq Asia August 16, 2026 14:34 CET Listen 7 min This audio is automated Learn more 'Organized Slavery': Russia's Tighter Migrant Rules Could Hit Central Asian Workers, Worsen Shortages Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google About 3 million foreigners were working in Russia at the beginning of 2026, many of them from Central Asian countries. (file photo) Russia is proposing an overhaul of its system for recruiting foreign workers beginning in 2027, tying migrants to specific employers, jobs, and regions in a move authorities say will give the state greater control over labor migration. But the plan is already drawing concern from migration experts and businesses. They warn that tighter restrictions could drive migrant workers into informal employment and further worsen workforce shortages in a country that relies heavily on foreign labor. The four-year experiment, scheduled to run from January 1, 2027, through the end of 2030, would cover 87 Russian regions, excluding Moscow and the Moscow region. Russian authorities estimate that more than 1.7 million foreign workers could be affected, including large numbers from Central Asia. The new system would move away from the “work-patent” mechanism that has been the main route to legal employment for migrants from visa-free countries such as Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. In 2025, foreigners obtained about 2.3 million Russian work patents, according to Interior Ministry figures. That represented more than 40 percent of all foreigners in Russia and almost 77 percent of officially employed foreign workers. SEE ALSO: Central Asian Schoolchildren Caught Up In Russia's Crackdown On Migrants Russia remains heavily dependent on foreign labor. About 3 million foreigners were officially working in the country at the beginning of 2026, while the total number of foreign nationals in Russia, including migrants’ family members, exceeded 5.7 million, according to the ministry. Under the proposed system, migrants would arrive in Russia already matched with a particular employer and vacancy. A new information system would maintain registries of employers and foreign workers and match workers with jobs based on regional labor-market needs. The system would also expand the amount of information authorities collect on migrants before they enter Russia. In addition to photographs and fingerprints, migrants would undergo mandatory genomic registration and medical examinations. 'No Rights For The Migrant' For migrants, however, the biggest change could be the loss of freedom to change jobs. Under the proposed rules, once in Russia, workers recruited through the new system would not be allowed to work for a different employer, in a different profession, or outside the region specified in the registry until their employment contracts expire. SEE ALSO: Russia's Migrant Crackdown Expands With Mandatory Mobile Tracking Violating those rules could result in removal from the foreign-worker registry and an obligation to leave Russia. Such workers could then only reenter the system and regain the ability to work in Russia after a year. “During my nearly 15 years in Russia, I have always stayed in the same city, but I changed my work several times with different private construction companies, depending on the money and conditions they offered,” Sarvar, a Tajik worker in the Russian city of Surgut, told RFE/RL. “I don’t know much about this plan yet, but I fear that if my employer knows that I can’t easily change my job, it would be difficult for me to negotiate my salary or other things.” A Russian traffic policeman checks the documents of guest workers from Central Asia. (file photo) Valentina Chupik, a human-rights advocate who heads Tong Jahoni, an organization that assists migrants, said the restrictions could leave workers particularly vulnerable to abusive employers. “There will be no rights for the migrant. He will be firmly attached to the employer,” Chupik said, describing the proposed system as “organized slavery.” The government says the new model is intended to make migration more transparent and reduce illegal employment by giving authorities more information about workers before they arrive. It also says the model is intended to increase employers’ responsibilities. Divided Opinion The proposed changes have divided migration experts. Mikhail Burda, head of the Center for Migration Studies at the Moscow-based Tsargrad Institute, argues that the country will remain attractive because of the size of its labor market and its established ties with Central Asia. “Targeted organized recruitment should become the only possible procedure for temporary employment in Russia for mass migration,” Burda said. “The formula ‘come, work, leave’ should be implemented in its absolute sense, without reservations or exceptions.” SEE ALSO: Thousands Of Central Asians Enlisted To Fight Russia's War In Ukraine Through 'Coercion, Enticements' Karimjon Yorov, a Tajik migration expert, takes a sharply different view. He said the additional procedures and restrictions could make it harder for Central Asian workers to enter Russia. “I can say with confidence that there is nothing good in it,” Yorov said. “Unfortunately, the consequences will be bad...for all migrants.” Yorov warned that the new recruitment system could create opportunities for corruption if intermediaries begin charging migrants for access to jobs or recruitment lists. He recalled that when work permits cost 1,000 to 2,000 rubles ($12-$24 at current exchange rates), they were sometimes resold for 20,000 to 50,000 rubles ($240-$600). Russia’s business community is also worried about the potential consequences. The Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs has warned the government that tying migrants to a single employer could push some workers out of the formal economy. The group wants migrants to be allowed to work for multiple employers and for the process of changing jobs to be made easier. The business group has also proposed delaying the experiment from 2027 to 2028 and introducing a two-year transition period during which the new system would operate alongside existing patent and work-permit mechanisms. Moscow has begun reviewing its agreements with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, two major sources of migrant labor, on organized recruitment. Yorov told RFE/RL that Tajikistan has begun preparing for the new system, with centers being established to prepare prospective migrants and conduct medical examinations, fingerprinting, and photography. Written by Farangis Najibullah based on reporting by Azattyq Asia. 'Organized Slavery': Russia's Tighter Migrant Rules Could Hit Central Asian Workers, Worsen Shortages Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Follow us Facebook X (Twitter) Youtube Instagram Follow us Print Azattyq Asia Azattyq Asia is RFE/RL's Russian unit covering Central Asia. summary: Russia is proposing an overhaul of its foreign-worker recruitment system in 2027, tying migrants to specific employers, jobs, and regions. Experts warn that tighter rules could worsen labor shortages and push more migrants into informal employment.
title: 'Organized Slavery': Russia's Tighter Migrant Rules Could Hit Central Asian Workers, Worsen Shortages

body: News Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit By RFE/RL August 31, 2026 00:43 CET Listen 6 min This audio is automated Learn more Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian President Vladimir Putin (right) and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shake hands during a meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek on August 31. Facing increasing confrontations with the West, Russian President Vladimir Putin is looking eastward to restore his country's standing in the region at a major summit in Bishkek, the Kyrgyz capital. It comes at a time of increased difficulties for the Kremlin leader, with Russia's economy in tatters due to Western sanctions and Ukrainian drone strikes, ally Iran battered in war, and the leaders of former client states such as Syria and Venezuela ousted amid a muted Moscow response. Putin is set to hold bilateral meetings with at least nine world leaders, including Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian, starting on August 31 on the sidelines of the two-day Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), which is celebrating its 25th anniversary. SEE ALSO: Aggressive Recruiters Are Rounding Up Russians To Fight In Ukraine. In One Town, They're Pushing Back On the first day, the Russian leader met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Xi focused on bilateral issues and only discussed the war in Ukraine "marginally...essentially there was no discussion." Western nations have called on China to use its influence to pressure the Kremlin into ending its war on Ukraine. Russia's Interfax news agency reported Modi told Putin that India supported "every peace effort" to end the war in Ukraine, without providing further details. Putin is also expected to hold bilateral sessions with leaders of non-SCO nations, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian, who has angered the Kremlin by seeking closer ties to the West for his small Caucasus nation. United Front Putin and Xi have often used SCO gatherings to put up a united front against Western influence in the region. Xi arrived late on August 30 and held his first meeting with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, who will serve as host of the summit. Along with Russia, Iran, India, and China, the SCO grouping consists of Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan. Not all members are allies, of course, with nuclear powers Pakistan and India often on the brink of war with each other. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi greet each other on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek on August 31. The organization began as the "Shanghai Five" in 1996 but began expanding to other regional nations starting in 2001. Moscow and Tehran are both under crippling Western sanctions -- Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and Iran for a multitude of issues, including its support for extremist activity in the Middle East and its alleged pursuit of a nuclear weapon. Kyiv and the West have demanded Iran cease from providing deadly Shahed drones to Russia for use in the Ukraine war, while US officials told RFE/RL that Russia is providing Iran with targeting information to attack US troops and military assets in the Middle East, confirming a Washington Post report . 'Key Subjects' Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said "one of the key subjects" in the talks between Putin and Pezeshkian will be the Middle East crisis. "You know how relevant this meeting is in light of the current uneasy atmosphere in the Middle East and the situation surrounding Iran," he added. Also on the agenda will be the $25 billion agreement signed by Tehran with Russia's state nuclear company Rosatom to build four nuclear power plants in Iran. Leaders of SCO nations attend the 2025 summit in the Chinese city of Tianjin. Naser al-Tamimi, a UK-based analyst and founder of MidEast Strategia, wrote on X that the SCO can help largely isolated Iran, "but only to a point." "The SCO offers Iran broader political cover, helps reduce its international isolation, and expands opportunities for trade and settlements in yuan, rubles, and other national currencies. In doing so, it can modestly reduce Tehran's dependence on the Western financial system." "But the SCO is not an economic shield against US sanctions. It lacks a fully developed alternative financial architecture, provides no reliable protection for major banks and companies exposed to secondary sanctions, and cannot compel China or India to absorb high economic costs on Iran’s behalf." Potentially Tense Armenian Meeting Along with Turkey, other nonmember nations and others participating and observing will include Armenia, Azerbaijan, UN chief Antonio Guterres, and heads of several Moscow-oriented international organizations. Putin is scheduled to meet Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian, whose country has long been an ally of Russia but which has angered Moscow by seeking to move closer to the West. SEE ALSO: Mobilization Migration: Is There An Uptick In Russians Fleeing Amid Fears Of A New Draft? Tensions heightened between the two countries after Armenian police on August 25 arrested former President Robert Kocharian, now leader of the country's second-largest opposition party, amid accusations of corruption-related offenses. Kocharian, 71, served as Armenia's president between 1998 and 2008. He currently leads the Armenia Alliance, which is considered pro-Moscow and finished third in recent parliamentary elections in June. Yerevan has also angered Moscow by expressing its ambition to eventually join the European Union. SEE ALSO: Former Armenian President Arrested On Corruption Charges "We will insist that Armenia cannot aspire for EU membership while hugely benefiting from cooperation within the European Economic Union (EEU)," said Ushakov, referring to the five-member trade bloc that also includes Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan. Following the Bishkek event, Putin is scheduled to travel to Vladivostok for the Eastern Economic Forum on Russia's Pacific coast from September 1-4. He is also set to meet with leaders of several other countries there, including the Indonesian president and Mongolian prime minister. summary: Facing increasing confrontations with the West, Russian President Vladimir Putin looks eastward to restore his country's standing in the region at a major summit in Bishkek, the Kyrgyz capital.
title: Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit

body: Russia Mobilization Migration: Is There An Uptick In Russians Fleeing Amid Fears Of A New Draft? By Ray Furlong , Robert Zargaryan , Sandro Jupalakiani and Zamira Kozhobaeva August 21, 2026 14:46 CET Mobilization Migration: Is There An Uptick In Russians Fleeing Amid Fears Of A New Draft? Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Sergei Rasokhin talking to RFE/RL's Armenian Service, August 7, 2026 Sergei Rasokhin says he spent two years in hiding before finally escaping military service in Russia and recently making it to safety in Armenia. The country took in many Russians dodging the draft in 2022-23 and now, amid growing fears of a new mobilization in Russia to boost a military depleted by the war on Ukraine, there are some indications that the numbers of Russians coming to Armenia are again rising. There have also been recent signs of this in other countries that saw an influx of Russians in 2022-23, but the evidence is patchy and sometimes conflicting. SEE ALSO: 'No Way Out': Russia Sends Badly Wounded Men Back Into Battle In Ukraine In any case, if the Kremlin decides to announce a new wave of mobilization, it may wait until after parliamentary elections next month -- meaning those hoping to avoid it still have time. Two Years In Hiding Rasokhin told his story to RFE/RL’s Armenian Service from the safety of Yerevan, home to a thriving community of Russians who have fled the increasingly repressive environment in their homeland under President Vladimir Putin in recent years. He said his life changed completely two years ago when, to deal with financial problems, he voluntarily signed a contract to join the Russian Army. He was told he would serve as an auto mechanic -- but soon learned he’d been tricked. “The sergeant laughed at me. He said: ‘You were deceived. They will take you to the front line with 95 percent certainty. Don’t hope for anything else,’” Rasokhin said. Rasokhin said he ran away from his unit and spent two years on the run, moving on from one location to another every few months, until he was eventually captured by military police. SEE ALSO: Russia Scrambles To Recruit Enough Men For Ukraine War. Now It’s Also Forcing Them. Instead of taking up arms, Rasokhin said he preferred to stand trial, even though he knew that deserters face up to 15 years in prison. Awaiting trial, he decided to buy a train ticket to Belarus. “[People] advised me to buy a ticket in cash an hour before departure, so that they wouldn’t have time to check the details. When I was at the ticket office, a man in an armed forces uniform came and took some papers. As I understood it, it was the list of passengers with tickets. And I hadn't bought one yet at that point, so maybe that saved me," he said. Rasokhin said he hoped his story would inspire other Russians to know that there are ways to get out of the country and avoid military service. What Do The Numbers Show? Official statistics show an uptick of Russians entering Armenia. Following the declaration of mobilization in September 2022, more than 500,000 Russians came to Armenia on tourist visas in the first six months of 2023. Every year after, the numbers fell, reaching nearly 340,000 last year. But between January and June this year they’re up again -- at some 417,000 people. Of course, this by itself does not prove an exodus. People, especially tourists, come and go. Another indicator is how these numbers compare. Embed share Russian Vehicles Flock To Georgian Border Following Partial Military Mobilization by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:59 0:00 From January to May 2026, the number of Russian citizens arriving in Armenia was 7,000 higher than the number leaving. An outlier compared to statistics for previous years, this is a fairly large number given that, according to official data from December last year, the total of Russian citizens with Armenian residence permits was 43,000 people. An increase in people staying in Armenia would put pressure on the housing markets, and there’s anecdotal evidence of this. Back in July, an independent Russian media outlet, Vyorstka , cited real estate agents in Yerevan talking of a sharp increase in demand from Russians. This was confirmed by real estate agents that spoke to RFE/RL’s Armenian Service, though most declined to be quoted. One agent, who agreed to identified by his first name, Gevorg, said: “Based on my impression and my local statistics -- there is about a 30 percent increase in prices. Up to a 50 percent jump in the case of rentals.” It was, he said, “very similar to 2022.” The change in market conditions is doubly interesting given that it reverses a previous trend, identified by another independent Russian outlet, The Insider , in July. “By 2025, the rental market had stabilized. Experts note a 30 percent decline in rates compared to the peak at the start of the full-scale war,” it said. In other words, it appears the market is again on a sharp upward curve -- possibly driven or partly-driven by new arrivals from Russia. What About Other Countries? Back in 2022-23, Russians were also fleeing to other countries. Dramatic drone footage revealed enormous lines of traffic at the border with Georgia, for example. On August 18, official Russian data made headlines by reporting that more than 20,000 people had crossed the main crossing into Georgia on a single day. It added that a “similar dynamic” had been observed for several days. This "significantly exceeds the data for the same period in previous years," it said. The Georgian authorities denied the Russian claim, however. In a statement on August 19, it said some 7,900 citizens had used the crossing to enter Georgia in 24 hours beginning at 9 a.m. on August 18. SEE ALSO: 'The Country Is In Trouble. When Will You Return?': Russians Fleeing To Georgia Share Their Experiences Of Getting Out There may be some discrepancy on what 24-hour period the two datasets refer to, but in any case the situation is unclear. When RFE/RL’s Georgian Service visited the border crossing on August 20, they saw no evidence of mass traffic jams or an exodus of fleeing Russians. "I came in 2022, and back then people were waiting for days. Today, when we went through, there were only three or four cars ahead of us on the Russian side," one young Russian woman said after driving across the border. There have also been anecdotal reports from Central Asia of dual-nationals returning from Russia due to fears of an imminent military draft. RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service spoke to a woman who declined to be identified for security reasons. She lived in Russia for more than 20 years, gaining citizenship for herself and her children. “When I heard that there would be a mass mobilization in the fall, the first thing I thought about was my son, who was already in his 20s, and we returned to our homeland,” she said. SEE ALSO: Anti-War Russians Abroad Fear Kremlin Covertly Pressuring Hosts To Send Them Back A representative of a Kyrgyz diaspora group in Russia, who could not be named for security reasons, said cases like this were on the rise. "Kyrgyz people are leaving Russia for other places, including Kyrgyzstan, due to various pressures. There is also development and job creation in Kyrgyzstan, so many people are leaving for there,” he said. “Recently, when an acquaintance of mine with Russian citizenship was leaving for Kyrgyzstan, he was warned at the border that ‘if you don't come back, your house and property here will be confiscated.’ Some of them, even if they have citizenship, say they won't come back. They sell their houses and leave," he added. But, he said, other dual nationals were staying, having been rejected for military service in the previous mobilization for health or other reasons.
