summary: Armenia and other countries bordering Russia took in many Russians dodging the draft in 2022-23 and now, amid growing fears of a new mobilization to boost a military depleted by the war on Ukraine, there are some indications that the numbers of Russians coming to Armenia are again rising.
title: Mobilization Migration: Is There An Uptick In Russians Fleeing Amid Fears Of A New Draft?

body: News Taliban Official Killed As Violence Flares In Northern Afghanistan By RFE/RL's Radio Azadi and RFE/RL's Tajik Service August 14, 2026 13:15 CET Taliban Official Killed As Violence Flares In Northern Afghanistan Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Armed Taliban fighters parade atop humvee vehicles in Kabul in 2022. A senior Taliban official has been assassinated in Afghanistan’s northeastern province of Badakhshan, where violence has flared in recent weeks. The killing on August 13 came amid ongoing clashes between Taliban fighters and a dissident commander in Badakhshan’s Nusai district, located along the border with Tajikistan. Vast and mountainous, Badakhshan has witnessed a spate of attacks in recent weeks. Experts say anti-Taliban armed groups are feeding off ethnic tensions, disputes over control of resources, and local grievances against the Taliban. SEE ALSO: Spate Of Attacks In Northern Afghanistan Pose Test For Taliban Habibur Rahman Mansur, mayor of the provincial capital, Faizabad, was killed on August 13 after his vehicle was targeted by a bomb, sources told RFE/RL’s Radio Azadi. The attack was claimed by the National Resistance Front, an armed opposition group. It came just weeks after another Taliban official was gunned down in Badakhshan. Zabihullah Amiri, head of the provincial information and culture department, was killed by two men on motorbikes on July 28, the Taliban said. The attack was claimed by the Islamic State-Khorasan (IS-K) extremist group, which has posed the biggest threat to the Taliban since it seized power in 2021 after the withdrawal international forces. Mansur’s killing came amid ongoing clashes between the Taliban and fighters loyal to dissident commander Juma Khan Fateh. Sources told Radio Azadi that the Taliban has deployed additional fighters and helicopters to Nusai. One of the helicopters was shot down by Fateh’s fighters, sources in Darvoz, the district in Tajikistan bordering Nusai, told RFE/RL’s Tajik Service. A 21-year-old woman in Darvoz was struck and killed by a stray bullet, according to Tajik authorities. Tajikistan’s Foreign Ministry sent a note of protest to the Taliban and called on the group to “take effective measures to prevent the recurrence of such incidents.” Embed share Under Taliban Rule, Pregnancy Brings Deadly Risks To Afghan Women by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:30 0:00 Dispute Over Resources During the 1990s, Badakhshan was a bastion of resistance to the rule of the Taliban. The province is predominantly made up of ethnic Tajiks. The Taliban is a mostly Pashtun militant group dominated by clerics that previously ruled Afghanistan from 1996 until 2001, when its regime collapsed following the US-led invasion. Since returning to power in 2021, it has monopolized authority and sidelined many of the country's ethnic and religious groups as well as political factions. Badakhshan is also rich in natural resources, including gold, silver, and semiprecious stones. The extraction of those minerals has intensified in recent years, and the Taliban's cash-strapped and unrecognized government has sought to centralize control over mining revenues. The move has fueled local resentment and infighting among Taliban commanders. Several small armed groups have waged a low-level insurgency against the Taliban, carrying out sporadic hit-and-run attacks as well as the assassination of Taliban officials. Experts say the groups have not yet shown that they can recruit on a large scale, maintain dependable supply lines, unify their various fronts, or govern territory after capturing it. body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan's Saida Mirziyoeva Gains New Powers, Fueling Succession Questions By Farangis Najibullah and Khiromon Baqozoda August 22, 2026 11:09 CET Listen 7 min This audio is automated Learn more Uzbekistan's Saida Mirziyoeva Gains New Powers, Fueling Succession Questions Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Saida Mirziyoeva (file photo) When Saida Mirziyoeva entered Uzbekistan's government in 2019, she was largely unknown and had no previous political experience. Seven years later, the eldest daughter of President Shavkat Mirziyoev has become one of the most powerful people in the country and a figure increasingly discussed as a possible successor to her father. A law signed by Mirziyoev on August 14 has given that speculation a new dimension by formally expanding the powers of the Presidential Administration, which Mirziyoeva, 41, heads. Under the law, the head of the administration -- the president's chief of staff -- becomes deputy chair of the Security Council, which is headed by the president and coordinates the country's security, law enforcement and military structures. Mirziyoeva will also organize and coordinate the activities of the council's members. Alisher Ilhomov, a London-based Central Asia analyst, said the change is particularly significant because control over the security apparatus is one of the main pillars of the president's power. "She was already de facto the No. 2 person in the country after the president, but her position was not strongly regulated by law. Now a legal foundation has been created that allows her to concentrate power and control over the security agencies," Ilhomov said. The new powers are the latest step in a rapid political rise that has repeatedly fueled speculation that Mirziyoev could be preparing his daughter for the presidency. Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoev (fourth from right) and members of his family pose while voting in a presidential election in July 2023. Mirziyoev, 69, won a third term in a tightly scripted election in 2023, while being awarded 87 percent of the vote. The same year, he engineered a constitutional overhaul that extended the presidential term to seven years and gave him the right to run again in 2030, meaning he could rule until 2037. Mirziyoeva joined the government in April 2019 as deputy head of the Agency for Information and Mass Communications, a position that also made her a deputy presidential adviser. SEE ALSO: Uzbekistan's Increasingly Influential First Daughter Seen As Successor To President Mirziyoev In 2020, she became deputy chair of the supervisory board of the Public Foundation for Support and Development of National Mass Media. In November 2022, she was appointed head of the Communications and Information Policy Department in the Presidential Administration, placing her at the center of the government's media and public relations strategy. Then, in August 2023, Mirziyoeva was appointed first assistant to the president, effectively becoming the second highest-ranking official in the Presidential Administration after the president. At the time, independent Uzbek journalist Jahongir Muhammad described her rise as "meteoric." "A literally unknown person got the second-highest post in Uzbekistan out of the blue," he said. High-Profile Responsibilities In June 2025, Mirziyoev restored the position of head of the Presidential Administration and appointed his daughter to the post, further consolidating her position at the center of the government. Saida Mirziyoeva and Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin in Moscow in May 2025 Mirziyoeva has since taken on additional high-profile responsibilities. In November 2025, she was appointed Uzbek co-chair of the newly established American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council. The appointment gave Mirziyoeva a prominent role in managing a major channel of Uzbekistan's economic relations with the United States. There has been no official indication that Mirziyoeva is being prepared to succeed her father. But her expanding role has also revived comparisons with Gulnara Karimova, the daughter of Islam Karimov, who was Uzbekistan's president from 1990, before the Soviet Union's collapse, until his death in 2016. SEE ALSO: Gulnara Karimova Enjoying 'Special Treatment' In Uzbek Prison, Former Inmate Says Karimova was once viewed as a possible successor to her father before falling out with him and eventually being imprisoned. But unlike Karimova, Mirziyoeva has steadily accumulated formal government positions. Sweeping Authority The latest law goes further by giving the office Mirziyoeva heads sweeping authority over government bodies and state institutions. The Presidential Administration can monitor and coordinate the work of government agencies and regional authorities, evaluate officials, issue instructions, and make proposals on domestic and foreign policy. It has also now acquired a role in coordinating the work of law enforcement and security structures. The law has drawn particular attention for its broad immunity provisions. Some senior Presidential Administration officials will retain immunity for life after leaving office, while other managerial officials will retain it for five years. The protections extend to their homes, vehicles, correspondence, and electronic data, and place significant restrictions on criminal investigations and other procedural measures against them. Mirziyoeva during a visit to Uzbekistan's Andijon region in June. Shukhrat Latipov, a journalist with the independent Uzbek outlet Gazeta.uz, questioned the breadth of the immunity provisions in the new law, writing on Telegram that they raised questions that required additional public explanation. "I don't know whether employees and heads of other presidential administrations around the world have such guarantees," Latipov wrote. Latipov also questioned how quickly the law was adopted. The lower legislative house approved it on August 6, the Senate on August 7, and Mirziyoev signed it on August 14, a remarkably short period for legislation of this significance, Latipov noted. For Ilhomov, however, the most consequential change is the formal role Mirziyoeva now has in the security structures. SEE ALSO: A New Uzbek Princess? The Growing Stature Of The President's Daughter Raises Eyebrows In Uzbekistan He said the new law potentially puts her in a position to help control the security agencies that are central to maintaining political power. That does not necessarily mean Mirziyoev is preparing to hand over the presidency anytime soon, or to tip his daughter as his chosen successor when his current term ends in 2030. Ilhomov said the new arrangement should instead be viewed as a kind of backup system, a way to ensure that a trusted figure can maintain control of the state if unexpected developments prevent Mirziyoev from doing so. "It is being done in case of a possible change of power under some extraordinary circumstances," Ilhomov said. Uzbekistan's Saida Mirziyoeva Gains New Powers, Fueling Succession Questions Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Follow us Facebook X (Twitter) Youtube Instagram Follow us Print Farangis Najibullah Farangis Najibullah is a senior correspondent for RFE/RL who has reported on a wide range of topics from Central Asia, including the impact of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on the region. She has extensively covered efforts by Central Asian states to repatriate and reintegrate their citizens who joined Islamic State in Syria and Iraq. Khiromon Baqozoda Khiromon Baqozoda is a senior correspondent for RFE/RL's Tajik Service in Prague. summary: A new law expanding the powers of Uzbekistan’s Presidential Administration has further elevated Saida Mirziyoeva, the president’s daughter, within the country’s political hierarchy. It gives her a role in the Security Council and has fueled fresh speculation about Uzbekistan’s eventual succession.
title: Uzbekistan's Saida Mirziyoeva Gains New Powers, Fueling Succession Questions

body: News Trump Tells Kyiv To Stop Attacks On Russian Diesel As Moscow's Drones Strike Near Polish Border By RFE/RL September 13, 2026 12:26 CET Updated September 13, 2026 21:03 CET Trump Tells Kyiv To Stop Attacks On Russian Diesel As Moscow's Drones Strike Near Polish Border Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters aboard Air Force One on his return to the United States following a visit to Ireland. US President Donald Trump has called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure amid Russia's relentless attacks across Ukraine, including near the Polish border. "There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel," Trump told reporters on September 13 during his visit to Ireland. "You have to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," he said. Trump's comment came a week after his envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, had visited Kyiv and Moscow in the latest US-mediated diplomatic effort to bring the wartime capitals closer to a negotiated agreement. While all sides have called the talks "substantial," the dynamics on the front line have not changed, with Russia continuing to attack Ukraine and hitting its civilian, logistics, and energy infrastructure as the cold weather sets in. Ukraine, meanwhile, has continued to respond, targeting energy and military sites inside Russia with its long-range drone attacks. Kyiv has been calling the effort "long-range sanctions" as it seeks to curb Moscow's energy profits and force it to negotiate. Since the beginning of the summer, Ukrainian drone strikes have caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia and stoked discontent among its citizens, who were disconnected from the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year. SEE ALSO: Ukraine's Refinery Attacks Force Russia To Turn Abroad To Process Its Oil Ukraine Warns Russia 'Knocking On NATO's Door' With the latest diplomatic efforts yielding no practical easing of tensions on the battlefield, two Russian drone strikes hit near the Polish border early on September 13. The first strike hit a petrol station near the Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine, in the latter's Volyn region. No casualties were reported. The second, also in Volyn, struck the locomotive of a passenger train just two kilometers from the Polish border, Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, reported. According to Oleksandr Shevchenko, a local transportation official, the train was traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw. As Ukrzaliznytsia said that a threat-monitoring group was able to warn the train's crew of the attack in advance, no casualties were reported. Video footage spread over Ukrainian social media showed people running from the blast at the railway station. Embed share Tusk Says Poland On High Alert After Russian Strikes Near Ukraine's Western Border by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:47 0:00 Separately, Ukrzaliznytsia said that "quite possibly," the original target of the drone strike could have been the "diplomatic train," which carried top European officials, including former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson. It added that former CIA Director David Petraeus was aboard another train at the time. Petraeus told The New York Times that he could hear Russian drones above and then an explosion, leading to the immediate evacuation of passengers. "For those who have not been under fire, this was terrifying...This is the act of a truly barbaric leader trying to terrorize Ukrainian civilians," Petraeus said. As the incidents occurred, air-raid alerts were issued in several eastern districts of Poland. While there were no reports of violations of Polish airspace, Jacek Goryszewski, spokesman for the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces, said the "threat to Poland was real." In separate incidents on September 13, Romanian authorities reported a drone entering the country, and Lithuania called on residents in the capital and neighboring regions to preventively seek shelter after issuing an alert of possible drone sighting. The country's main airport in Vilnius was shut down and NATO jets were scrambled. The alert was called off within an hour. "Russia's barbaric strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn are not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X on September 13. "This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO." He urged European leaders to "throw the full weight" of sanctions against Russia. SEE ALSO: Russian Strikes Kill 9 Across Ukraine, As Zelenskyy Offers To Meet Putin At Miami G20 Earlier this month, Germany officially blamed an incident on Moscow in which explosive-laden drones interrupted flights at Leipzig Airport. At the time, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that "Europeans are faced with a hard truth that this is the new normal." "It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every single day, laying down their lives to keep this aggression from expanding," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram on September 13. "Russian terrorism is a shared threat to many, but it can and must be defeated right here in Ukraine," he added. According to Zelenskyy, a total of 2,100 drones, 1,700 gliding bombs, and 73 missiles were launched at targets across Ukraine in the past week. Ukrainian authorities said that elsewhere in Ukraine, the latest Russian attacks had also targeted the country's western regions of Ivano-Frankivsk, Ternopil, and Lviv, as well as the war-torn eastern Donetsk region and the key southern region of Odesa. SEE ALSO: Ukrainian Soldier Honored For Rescue In 'Kill Zone' Regional authorities in the Odesa region said nine people had been injured after a drone struck several residential buildings. A warehouse in the region was also reportedly targeted. Meanwhile, in the region's capital city of Odesa, rescuers have completed work at the site of the drone strike on a 25-story residential building on the night of September 12. Two people were killed and more than 20 injured in that attack. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that its overnight strikes targeted "logistics centers through which military cargo is delivered and distributed, as well as energy facilities that support their operation." The ministry also reported strikes on railway infrastructure in western Ukraine. Russia denies targeting civilian areas despite widespread evidence of such attacks that have killed thousands of people since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. We provide what many people cannot get locally: uncensored news, responsible discussion, and open debate. This item is part of News Russia Ukraine Europe
summary: Two Russian drone strikes hit near the Polish border early on September 13, Ukrainian authorities have reported, attacks that Kyiv said was Moscow “knocking on the doors of the EU and NATO” and urged further sanctions.
title: Ukraine Warns Putin 'Knocking On NATO's Door' After Russian Drones Hit Sites Near Polish Border

(file photo) Iran live Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount September 11, 2026 07:15 CET Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google As the conflict in the Persian Gulf continues to impact and shape the region, journalists from RFE/RL's Central Newsroom and Iranian service, Radio Farda, deliver ongoing updates and analysis. Key Takeaways Oil prices surged to a four-month high on September 11 amid fears of prolonged supply disruptions and renewed inflation. US President Donald Trump said he had no regrets about going to war with Iran despite the conflict's potential impact on November's midterm elections Gulf Arab foreign ministers are expected to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi in Oman next week as regional powers seek support for a temporary arrangement to restore commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian arrived in New Delhi on September 11 for a BRICS summit, with the escalating Middle East conflict expected to feature prominently. Several US military aircraft were damaged in Iranian missile strikes on a base in Jordan housing American soldiers, according to reports. New posts 14:24 Houthis Reach Strategic Island On Key Red Sea Shipping Route Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels have reached the strategic island of Perim, also known as Mayyun, in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, potentially strengthening their grip on one of the world's most important shipping routes, according to Yemeni government sources. Four government sources told Reuters on September 11 that Houthi forces had reached the island, while the German dpa news agency cited a Yemeni government source as saying the group had taken control of it. Reuters reported that forces loyal to Yemen's internationally recognized government had withdrawn from Perim. AFP cited an unnamed Yemeni military official as saying the Houthis now control the country's entire Red Sea coast. All territory that had been under government control "on the western coast has fallen" following the Houthis' seizure of Perim and the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands, AFP quoted the military official as saying. Perim, or Mayyun, sits at the southern entrance to the Bab al-Mandab, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and a crucial route for trade and energy shipments between Asia and Europe via the Suez Canal. The waterway's strategic importance has grown sharply since the Iran war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, another of the world's key energy chokepoints. The Houthi advance follows the group's reported capture of the Red Sea port of Mocha on September 10. Government sources also reported Houthi advances on the mainland and other islands in the strait. The developments raise the prospect of disruptions to shipping through the Red Sea at a time when Saudi Arabia has become increasingly reliant on the route for oil exports because of conflict-related restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz. Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share 11:54 Iranian President Arrives In New Delhi For BRICS Summit Amid Gulf Crisis Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian (center right) arrives to attend a BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 11. Iranian President Masud Pezeshkian arrived in the Indian capital, New Delhi, on September 11 to join the leaders of BRICS countries for a summit, with the escalating Middle East conflict expected to feature prominently on the agenda. BRICS, a grouping of major emerging markets and developing countries, takes its name from Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. It expanded from five to 11 members in 2024 and 2025, adding Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Making his first visit to India since taking office in 2024, Pezeshkian is scheduled to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Iran's IRNA state news agency reported. The two-day BRICS Leaders' Summit begins on September 12 and is expected to bring together Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, among other leaders. Iran, which joined BRICS in 2024, is directly involved in the conflict, while fellow member the UAE has faced Iranian missile attacks and taken measures against Tehran. The UAE suspended all trade and financial transactions with Iran in August following the attacks, underscoring growing tensions within BRICS as the summit convenes amid the deepening regional crisis. The UAE is expected to be represented by Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. With reporting by AFP and Reuters Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share 09:14 Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount Oil prices surged to a four-month high on September 11 as escalating threats to two of the world's key energy shipping routes fueled fears of prolonged supply disruptions and renewed inflation. Brent crude touched $109.97 a barrel after jumping more than 6 percent a day earlier, before falling back. The benchmark was still on track for a weekly price gain of about 11 percent. Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain restricted as the United States and Iran trade attacks, while the reported seizure of Yemen's Red Sea port of Mocha by Iran-aligned Houthi rebels has raised concerns over shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The oil rally intensified inflation concerns across global markets, pushing government bond yields sharply higher as investors increased bets on further interest-rate hikes. JPMorgan analysts now expect eight of nine developed-market central banks to raise interest rates by the end of the year as policymakers contend with persistent inflation and rising commodity prices. With reporting by Reuters Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share 08:18 Gulf States, Iran Plan Talks On Hormuz Shipping Deal, FT Reports Foreign ministers from Persian Gulf Arab states are expected to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi in Oman next week as regional powers seek support for a temporary arrangement to restore commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times reported . The meeting, an Omani initiative, is scheduled for September 14 in the coastal city of Salalah, according to two people briefed on the matter cited by the FT. One of the people said details were still being finalized, but that a number of states had confirmed their participation and the meeting was expected to go ahead. Oman and Iran have been negotiating a temporary arrangement under which ships would enter the strait through Iranian waters and mostly exit through Omani territory. Diplomats cautioned, however, that a US-Iran agreement would ultimately be needed for the waterway to fully reopen. One person briefed on the talks told the FT that Iran and Oman hoped to get GCC backing and use it to press Washington to lift its blockade of Iranian ports. Gulf states, meanwhile, want to ensure that any arrangement is temporary and allows vessels to enter and leave. The diplomatic push comes after a short-lived US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed in June unraveled amid disputes over shipping through Hormuz. Washington has told mediators it wants any new agreement to also address Iran's nuclear program, while Tehran is demanding concessions including an end to the blockade and permission to resume oil

body: News Russian Strikes Kill 9 Across Ukraine, As Zelenskyy Offers To Meet Putin At Miami G20 By RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service September 13, 2026 00:06 CET Listen 6 min This audio is automated Learn more Russian Strikes Kill 9 Across Ukraine, As Zelenskyy Offers To Meet Putin At Miami G20 Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Aftermath of a Russian strike on a residential building in the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa on September 12. KYIV-- Russia continued to pound the Ukrainian civilian population, killing at least nine people in attacks throughout the country, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeated he'd be willing to meet Russia's Vladimir Putin at the upcoming G20 summit -- something the Kremlin called "impossible." Russia has intensified air strikes throughout Ukraine over the past two months, with the Kremlin hitting power plants and other infrastructure as the potentially brutal winter months loom on the horizon. Civilian deaths were reported in several cities and regions on September 12 as Ukraine struggles to secure its population amid a shortage of air defense weapons badly needed to intercept high-speed Russian missile. SEE ALSO: US House Set To Take Up Russia Sanctions Bill Amid Fight Over Trump Tariff Powers In Kramatorsk in Ukraine's Donetsk region, the city of some 150,000 people -- which has been under Russian military pressure for months -- local authorities said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people in three incidents over a 90-minute period. "These are not ⁠military targets," the city council said in a statement. "They are ordinary civilian cars. People were going about their business." Vitaliy Bunechko, governor of Ukraine's Zhytomyr region west of Kyiv, said a Russian strike hit a grocery store, killing two people in the town of Zvyahel. Ivan Fedorov, governor of Zaporizhzhia region, said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other communities. Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryviy Rih's military administration, said two people had been killed in overnight attacks on the city by drones and missiles. SEE ALSO: Zelenskyy Says Latest Russian Missile And Drone Attacks Targeted Civilian Sites Across Ukraine Russia’s military claimed its forces targeted Ukrainian steel maker Zaporizhstal in Zaporizhzhia, an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro, and several plants in Kryviy Rih. The claims could not independently be verified. In response to Russian attacks, Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses, often deep inside Russia, causing acute energy shortages throughout the country, while both sides have targeted each others' shipping in and around the Black Sea. Zelenskyy Willing To Meet In Miami In a interview with German broadcaster Deutsche Welle released on September 12, Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet with Putin for peace talks at the December 14-15 Group 0f 20 (G20) gathering in Miami. "Yes, of course," he said when asked about a meeting. "We have to come. We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions. It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter. Results matter." The Kremlin immediately rejected Zelenskyy's offer. "It is impossible," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told AFP, repeating Russia’s demand that such a face-to-face meeting could only take place in Moscow. "There is a readiness to meet him in Moscow," said Peskov, who noted that it has not been decided yet whether Putin will attend the G20 gathering. SEE ALSO: Hundreds Of Russian Teens Face Terrorism Charges As Wartime Crackdown Intensifies Zelenskyy has long rejected the possibility of meeting in Moscow at a time when his country is facing a full-scale invasion by Russian forces. “He can come to Kyiv," Zelenskyy told ABC News in reference to Putin. "I can't go to Moscow when my country's under missiles, under attack, each day. I can't go to the capital of this terrorist." Washington is attempting to kick-start long-stalled talks on Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv last week, while US President Donald Trump and Putin have conducted phone talks in recent days. In the Deutsche Welle interview, which took place on September 11 while he was in Canada, Zelenskyy said Witkoff and Kushner's visit was a "good signal" and that it was important the two had made a trip to Kyiv as well as Moscow. SEE ALSO: Exclusive: A Secluded Russian Island May Hold Bioweapons Secrets Zelensky has said he he plans to meet Trump in late September, although details have not been confirmed. Trilateral Talks Meanwhile, a top Ukrainian official suggested US-Russia-Ukraine talks could resume as early as next month. Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian presidential office, said a new round of trilateral talks on ending the war may take place in October. Speaking to the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on the sidelines of the Yalta European Security forum in Kyiv, Budanov said Ukraine is preparing for a new meeting in the trilateral format, but he did not provide details. Earlier, Budanov told The New York Times that the negotiation process would likely intensify after Russia's State Duma elections on September 18–20 and the US midterm elections on November 3. The last direct talks between Russia and Ukraine came in February in Switzerland, with the US acting as mediator and with Budanov being a part of the Ukrainian delegation. body: Ukraine Interview: Ex-Envoy Stefanishyna Sheds Light On US-Ukraine Diplomacy Amid Corruption Probe By RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service and Vlasta Lazur September 12, 2026 15:48 CET Interview: Ex-Envoy Stefanishyna Sheds Light On US-Ukraine Diplomacy Amid Corruption Probe Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Ukraine's Former Ambassador to the United States Olha Stefanishyna speaks with RFE/RL in Kyiv on September 8. KYIV -- Olha Stefanishyna has held three prominent jobs under President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over the past six years, most recently as Ukraine's ambassador to the United States. Ahead of renewed US diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war on Ukraine, Stefanishyna resigned in early August after serving less than a year in Washington. Her departure came just days before Ukraine's main anti-graft agencies, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), formally notified her that she was suspected of illegal enrichment and failure to declare assets. With Zelenskyy yet to appoint a new ambassador to the United States, Stefanishyna, in an interview with RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service, discussed her decision to resign and the dynamics between Kyiv and Washington amid Russia's full-scale invasion, now in its fifth year. 'Russia's Narrative Has Not Changed' RFE/RL: We are speaking shortly after [US President Donald Trump's] representatives [Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner] visited Ukraine.... [Witkoff] has been to Moscow many times; this time they were in Kyiv for the first time. I assume you also worked on this visit when you were ambassador, because it was postponed for several months. How do you assess this visit in the short-term perspective? Olha Stefanishyna: [...] The most important element is simply that they came. The event itself is the fact that they came and made it all the way to Kyiv.... [...] We can see that the narrative coming from Russia has not changed at all since last year. Remember last year, [US Army Secretary] Dan Driscoll came here and brought us 28 points, saying: "The winter will be difficult. Ukraine will not survive this winter. It is better to negotiate now than in six months. In six months, Ukraine will be in terrible shape; its energy infrastructure will have been destroyed...[Russia] will capture the Donbas." It's the same old story. A year ago, this looked so realistic to the Pentagon, the White House, the US president, and the negotiators that they were almost panicked about taking responsibility for what would happen if Ukraine fell.... But we survived the winter. We stabilized the situation on the front, and the war has been shifted onto the enemy's territory. What do we see now? The negotiators have returned from Moscow.... And essentially, the narrative is the same. And in the eyes of the [US] negotiators, I am sure this weakens Russia. Because today, we have cards that we did not have back when President Trump spoke with President Zelenskyy [at the White House in February 2025]. Putin calls Trump and asks him to call Zelenskyy to make sure he doesn't attack Moscow and Red Square on May 9. You see, we already have our own levers of influence. Over the past year, we have shown that, despite limited resources, restrictions on weapons supplies, and enormous political pressure, including pressure from the United States, we not only survived the winter, but Ukrainians also stood their ground.... We managed to show an entirely new reality on the battlefield and we have brought the war onto the enemy's territory through our long-range strikes. SEE ALSO: US Renews Ukraine Peace Push, But Former Ambassadors See No Breakthrough Did Washington Ask Kyiv To Halt Attacks Against Russian Oil Terminals? RFE/RL: In Washington, how often did you receive requests from government representatives asking Ukraine not to attack [Russia's] oil terminals, Novorossiisk -- anything that could drive up energy prices or be unfavorable for the US government? Stefanishyna: Never regarding any strikes, except for strikes that targeted either vessels belonging to [US oil giants] Chevron and Exxon or infrastructure at the port of Novorossiisk. I have longstanding and good relations with Kazakhstan. I was in contact with the Kazakh ambassador. So, on the one hand, there is an understanding of the situation. On the other hand, this is a major revenue-generating sector for Kazakhstan and a direct matter of US economic interest. Both the Kazakhs and Exxon and Chevron have made it clear they understand Ukraine's position, but they also understand their mistake was creating a situation in which there was no alternative route. In other words, there is no quick alternative to shutting down this terminal and establishing some kind of alternative routes. But the Russians...knowing this as well, moved their military capabilities as close as possible to the commercial infrastructure. In the end, I figured out how this could be resolved. There is now a mechanism for working with the companies that makes it possible to avoid incidents like those we saw. We can see that, despite the fact that long-range [Ukrainian strikes] reach different parts of the world and Russia, they do not reach Chevron and Exxon vessels. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Olha Stefanishyna meet in Kyiv in July 2025. RFE/RL: Were you working on this solution while you were in Washington? Stefanishyna: I was called directly to the White House, urgently. It's quite a moment when you're summoned to the White House at a high level and you don't know why. I thought through a lot of different possibilities. I thought it could be about the war, peace, perhaps some kind of decision -- maybe a license for Patriot [air-defense missiles], maybe the Lindsey Graham bill, or perhaps President Trump would come to Kyiv. I had all sorts of thoughts running through my head. Then I arrived and heard that this concerned the sovereign interests of the United States.... The first, official, message was that, while there is an understanding of Ukraine's objectives in carrying out certain military operations, regardless of how those operations are assessed they result in events that directly harm the economic and sovereign interests of the United States. In other words, they said we should keep this in mind when we do something. And the second [message] was a call to develop a mechanism that would prevent this from happening. Ukraine's Corruption Scandals Through A US Lens RFE/RL: [...] Your [term as ambassador] coincided with a period when [Ukraine] was rocked by corruption scandals, most notably Mindichgate . A lot happened here in a relatively short period, from the fall of 2025 to the spring of 2026. First, [Zelenskyy's former chief of staff] Andriy Yermak was formally suspected of a crime.... A number of ministers were also formally suspected of crimes...A lot of people were implicated. And all of this was happening while you were working in Washington.... What did you get asked about most often? [...] Stefanishyna: US politics is the politics of a mature society. We all understand and can see from the congresspeople and senators who come to Ukraine that...these are people who have been in politics for 30, 40, 50 years. So they've seen it all. These changes of ministers don't particularly concern them. I'll say two things. First, the case involving Andriy Yermak was obviously a very big story in the United States because for many years Andriy was the person handling the US track.... In other words, he was actually the person who would pick up the phone and call Secretary [of State Marco] Rubio, and Rubio would speak with him. When events like these happen, of course, there were a lot of questions. And some of the communications that prosecutors decided to publish didn't exactly help matters either, about Veronika Feng Shui.... RFE/RL: That's about t
summary: Olha Stefanishyna has served in three key government positions in Ukraine over the past six years, most recently as ambassador to the United States. In an interview with RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service, she discusses US-Ukraine ties and her decision to resign days before a corruption probe.
title: Interview: Ex-Envoy Stefanishyna Sheds Light On US-Ukraine Diplomacy Amid Corruption Probe

body: Afghanistan Washington Warns US Companies Over Dealing With Taliban-Ruled Afghanistan By RFE/RL's Radio Azadi September 12, 2026 11:02 CET Washington Warns US Companies Over Dealing With Taliban-Ruled Afghanistan Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Zalmay Khalilzad (back row, center) attends the signing of an oil and gas deal with senior Taliban officials in Kabul on September 7. The US State Department has urged American companies to exercise extreme caution when considering business transactions with Taliban-ruled Afghanistan after a former US official attended the signing of a deal between a Saudi energy group and the hard-line authorities. A US State Department spokesperson, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed the warning to RFE/RL, adding that private companies interested in doing business in Afghanistan should ensure their transactions comply with applicable US laws and regulations as the Taliban is on the list of Designated Global Terrorist Groups (SDGT). SEE ALSO: Washington Distances Itself From Former Envoy's Taliban Meetings Ahead Of 9/11 Anniversary The warning comes after a visit to Afghanistan earlier this week by Zalmay Khalilzad, who was US special envoy to Afghanistan from 2018 to 2021. Khalilzad was in Kabul on September 7 for the signing of a Saudi oil and gas deal and he also met with the Taliban's foreign minister, Amir Khan Muttaqi. The trip, which came on the eve of the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terror attacks, raised eyebrows as the United States does not recognize the Taliban as the legitimate government of Afghanistan. Washington has distanced itself from Khalilzad's trip, with a State Department spokesman telling RFE/RL that "Khalilzad is not a US government employee. As such, he does not represent the United States government." According to the US Treasury Department, US citizens and companies generally do not have the right to engage in any transactions, payments, contracts, services, or financial cooperation with individuals and entities on this list. Treasury added that non-US individuals and companies that conduct certain transactions with these groups may themselves be subject to US sanctions and civil or criminal penalties. The Taliban's Mines and Petroleum Ministry, which signed the initial $200 million contract with the Saudi company Delta International Energy, says it includes the Kashk-Tirpol oil field located between Herat and Badghis in western Afghanistan. According to the ministry, the deal covers oil and gas exploration across some 23,000 square kilometers of territory of the oil field in western Afghanistan, including a proposed 700-kilometer gas pipeline. SEE ALSO: 25 Years After 9/11, Could Afghanistan Again Become A Launchpad For Global Terror? Delta International Energy is a Saudi company that invests and engages in business in the Middle East and other markets. The Taliban, which retook power in 2021, is considered one of the most repressive regimes in the world. The international community has blacklisted Taliban leaders and cut off the group from the global financial system. In recent months it has sought to reverse its isolation, seeking both foreign investment and international legitimacy. Russia is the only country that has formally recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan's legitimate government. Several countries -- including China, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan -- maintain diplomatic, trade, and economic ties with the Taliban without officially recognizing its government. In June, Taliban officials for the first time held talks in Brussels on the repatriation of Afghans despite sharp criticism from rights groups that said the European Union was legitimizing the hard-line group, which has been accused of severely curtailing the basic rights of Afghans, especially of women. body: News Zelenskyy Says Latest Russian Missile And Drone Attacks Targeted Civilian Sites Across Ukraine By RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service September 12, 2026 10:51 CET Updated September 12, 2026 11:30 CET Listen 5 min This audio is automated Learn more Zelenskyy Says Latest Russian Missile And Drone Attacks Targeted Civilian Sites Across Ukraine Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A resident stands outside a damaged apartment building following a Russian attack on the Ukrainian city of Odesa, on the Black Sea coast, early on September 12. A fresh round of Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least three people and wounded dozens of others over the past 24 hours, Ukraine's president said on September 12, adding that the strikes targeted civilian sites and infrastructure across the country. "Since the night, there have been virtually constant strikes on our cities and communities," Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media. "Ten regions were under Russian strikes last night, and Russian attack drones are still flying in many of them." Two people were killed and six others were wounded by a Shahed-type drone strike on residential buildings in the Zaporizhzhia region, he said, adding that a missile attack on "critical infrastructure" in Kryviy Rih killed one person and injured three others. In Odesa, 37 people were injured when a high-rise residential building was hit by Russian missile overnight, and rescue operations were under way at the site. The search continued for two people that were unaccounted for, Zelenskyy said. Earlier, local officials in Odesa said that a 25-story residential building had been damaged, with apartments on the 21st through 23rd floors catching fire. The upper floors were destroyed. Three other residential buildings were also damaged in Odesa, officials said. SEE ALSO: US House Set To Take Up Russia Sanctions Bill Amid Fight Over Trump Tariff Powers Ukraine's Air Force said Russia attacked the country with ballistic and cruise missiles and 129 attack drones, including jet-powered Shahed-type drones. It said Ukrainian air defenses had destroyed or suppressed 110 of the targets. The air force said strikes were recorded in 20 locations across the country and falling debris in four others. It said the Odesa region was the most affected. The attacks came a day after Russian strikes killed at least six people in Zaporizhzhia and other parts of Ukraine, as Moscow and Kyiv have traded strikes on logistics, energy, and other economic infrastructure in recent weeks. SEE ALSO: The Kremlin Tries A New Weapon For Its War: The Relics Of A 14th-Century Saint Russia's Defense Ministry claimed on September 12 that Russian forces had hit the Zaporizhstal steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, as well as an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro and several facilities in Kryviy Rih, including the Northern Iron Ore Beneficiation Works complex. The ministry also said its forces had struck two cargo vessels overnight in the Ukrainian Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, according to Russia's Interfax news agency. The claims cannot be independently verified. The attacks followed a deadly Russian assault on Zaporizhzhia on September 11, when one person was killed, according to Ukrainian officials. Russia also struck other parts of Ukraine that day, including Kyiv, where attacks on two petrol stations killed two people and wounded at least 12. Embed share 'Save Him!' RFE/RL Captures Chaos After Russian Strike On Ukrainian Shops by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:44 0:00 Russia has intensified its air campaign against Ukraine in recent weeks, including repeated attacks with faster jet-powered drones. The strikes have increasingly hit logistics and economic targets as fighting along the front line has largely stalled. On September 10, Russian strikes killed five people in the southeastern industrial city of Pavlohrad and also hit a petrol station in Kyiv and a sunflower-oil facility operated by US-based Bunge in Dnipro. Ukraine Strikes Economic, Industrial Targets Ukraine has also stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russian economic and industrial targets. On September 12, Ukrainian drones struck industrial facilities in Russia's Samara region, Interfax reported, citing regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev. He did not specify which facilities were targeted or the extent of the damage. Ukraine's military said it had struck the Togliattikauchuk plant, one of Russia's largest producers of synthetic rubber, in the city of Togliatti, causing a fire. The Ukrainian General Staff said the plant produces synthetic rubber and fuel additives used in fuel for Russian missiles. The claim could not be independently verified. The mayor of Togliatti said several residential buildings were damaged and one person was injured. Russia's Defense Ministry said it had downed 230 Ukrainian drones overnight over more than a dozen Russian regions, as well as over Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014. In a separate attack, four commercial properties were set ablaze in the southern Russian city of Taganrog, local officials said. body: News US House Set To Take Up Russia Sanctions Bill Amid Fight Over Trump Tariff Powers By Alex Raufoglu September 11, 2026 22:26 CET US House Set To Take Up Russia Sanctions Bill Amid Fight Over Trump Tariff Powers Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US Congress members on the floor of the House of Representatives at the US Capitol in Washington in July 2025. WASHINGTON -- The US House of Representatives is preparing to take up legislation next week that is intended to impose tougher economic pressure on Russia, setting up what could be a heated fight between Republicans and Democrats over how far Congress should go in expanding President Donald Trump's tariff powers. The Senate passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on August 7 by an overwhelming 86-11 vote. The bill targets Russian officials and institutions as well as the "shadow fleet" of vessels that enable Moscow to evade sanctions on oil deliveries, a key source of revenue for the economy and the war against Ukraine. It gives the US president the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from major purchasers of Russian oil and gas and countries deemed to be involved in sanctions evasion. It would also extend the existing Iran Sanctions Act for five years. The House Rules Committee is scheduled to meet on September 14 to consider the legislation , according to House leadership. A senior Republican congressional aide told RFE/RL that Republicans believe they have the votes to advance it. "We're fine. The numbers are there if the bill gets through Rules on Monday," the aide said. SEE ALSO: Ukraine Sees Russian-Iranian Sanctions Networks Converging As US Targets Tankers House Speaker Mike Johnson (Republican-Louisiana) has called for bipartisan support for the legislation. But Democrats are pushing back, arguing the measure's tariff provisions give Trump excessive authority while failing to require the administration to impose sanctions on Russia. "House Democrats are rock solid in our support for Ukraine, but the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act would do more harm than good," Representatives Gregory Meeks of New York, Don Beyer of Virginia, and Richard Neal of Massachusetts said in a joint statement . They said the bill would "dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia," warning the provisions could raise prices for Americans and undermine support for Ukraine. The bill enables the president to impose the sanctions involved but does not force him to do so. "We need a bipartisan bill that holds Russia accountable without risking higher costs for the American people," Neal said separately. Democrats say they want a bipartisan, bicameral negotiation over the legislation, which was negotiated and overwhelmingly approved in the Senate. They also argue that Trump already has broad authority to sanction Russian companies, individuals, and vessels financing the war. Despite the House Democrats' opposition, Republicans are seeking to move the bill through regular order, meaning Johnson will need strong support among lawmakers from his party to clear the procedural hurdles before the House can vote on final passage. The legislation's supporters say the tariff authority is precisely what gives the measure its potential force. Ukrainian sanctions official Vladyslav Vlasiuk told RFE/RL that tariffs could strengthen the impact of sanctions. "Tariffs are a powerful way to amplify the impact of sanctions," Vlasiuk said. "Swift passage of the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act is needed, along with other decisive measures to further increase pressure on the aggressor." SEE ALSO: Ukraine 'Optimistic' On Russia Sanctions Bill But Obstacles Loom Ukraine's diplomatic representatives in Washington have also urged lawmakers not to let disagreements over the bill's details derail its passage. At a September 10 briefing hosted by the Bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus, Ukraine's charge d'affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, acknowledged that major decisions require compromise but argued that the legislation would give Washington another tool for pressuring Moscow. "What message will it send to Ukrainians, and what message will it send to Russia if this does not pass?" Sienik asked. He said Russia continues to generate substantial revenues from oil and gas while producing weapons and recruiting soldiers for the war. Sienik urged lawmakers to "finish what" Graham, a longtime Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July, started. "Sanctions need to be imposed now. Sanctions must be strong," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X on September 11. "This is a tool the United States has to deprive Russia of its ability to finance the war against Ukraine every day." He added that "during a war, it is sometimes better to make a not-so-perfect decision than to do nothing." Zelenskyy called on Congress to pass the Graham bill and also urged Trump to take stronger executive action. body: Iran Anthropic Disrupts Iran’s Use Of Claude To Spread Propaganda, Spy On Dissidents By Frud Bezhan September 11, 2026 17:41 CET Anthropic Disrupts Iran’s Use Of Claude To Spread Propaganda, Spy On Dissidents Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Anthropic said it has disrupted attempts by Iran, China, and other countries from using its artificial intelligence (AI) models to disseminate state propaganda and spy on ethnic minorities and dissidents. That is according to the AI company’s latest threat intelligence report issued on September 11, which covers incidents from December 2025 to August. The report also said criminals, state institutions, and scientists, including in Russia and China, were using AI models like Claude and Gemini to design missiles and bombs as well as create deadly pathogens. SEE ALSO: Oil Hits 4-Month High As Hormuz, Red Sea Risks Mount 'Cognitive Warfare' Anthropic named several Iranian state institutions it said were using its AI models to shape public opinion inside and outside the country. The entities include the Islamic Culture and Communications Organization, which operates under the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance and oversees Iran's official cultural diplomacy and international relations abroad; the Islamic Propaganda Office, a religious organization; and the Islamic Propaganda Organization, a religious and cultural group. Anthropic accused the institutions of running “cognitive warfare” campaigns and promoting narratives created by the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, the elite branch of Iran’s armed forces that plays a prominent role in politics and the economy. “In each case, the operation relied on Claude to build campaign plans, doctrine manuals, persona systems, target databases, and ministerial planning documentation,” said Anthropic’s report. “Using the model in this manner allowed them to generate complex organizational frameworks and assets that would otherwise have required a fully staffed program office to produce.” In one case, the Islamic Culture and Communications Organization used Claude to “complete organizational plans” for the state funeral of slain Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei that took place from July 3-9, Anthropic said. SEE ALSO: From Russia With Expertise: Iranian Students Return Home With Potentially Deadly Knowledge Of Drones, AI, And More Recruitment Tool Anthropic also said it disrupted an “influence operation” by the Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK), an exiled opposition group that seeks to overthrow the Islamic republic and that Tehran regards as a terrorist organization. The operation, the AI company said, “used a shared AI agent to impersonate real people and recruit inside Iran.” “The operation successfully scraped over 500 social media channels to build detailed profiles of individuals inside Iran,” the report said. “They then grouped these targets by city, age, occupation, political alignment, and arrest history likely to help them tailor their messages to the specific audiences.” Surveillance Operations Anthropic said it also disrupted operations by state actors, including Iran, that used Claude to “build, run, and otherwise facilitate surveillance operations.” In one case, Iran-based actors used Claude to build and deploy a malicious Firefox extension that harvested users’ identities from social media networks, the AI company said. In another case, an Iranian actor used Claude to analyze hundreds of thousands of social media posts and chose 39 opposition accounts to monitor. “The operators were state-aligned organizations that targeted the same diaspora and dissident communities these regimes have historically targeted,” Anthropic said. Previously, he was the Regional Desk Editor for the Near East, with a primary focus on Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. As a correspondent, he reported from Afghanistan, Turkey, Kosovo, and Western Europe. This item is part of News Iran Russia
summary: Anthropic said it has disrupted attempts by Iran to use its artificial intelligence (AI) models to disseminate state propaganda and spy on ethnic minorities and dissidents.

body: Iran What Houthi Gains In Yemen Mean For The Iran War By Kian Sharifi September 11, 2026 15:16 CET What Houthi Gains In Yemen Mean For The Iran War Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Fighters loyal to the Houthi march during a rally to recruit more fighters in Sanaa on September 10. Iran’s hold on the Strait of Hormuz gave it significant leverage over a much more powerful United States for months. But that grip is loosening, even if global energy markets have yet to reflect it. Now another global transport chokepoint is emerging as a potential front in the conflict, hundreds of kilometers away, on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula. The Iran-aligned Houthis' capture of the Red Sea port city of Mocha and their reported advance toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait have suddenly given Yemen a new significance in the wider war. The timing is particularly consequential for Saudi Arabia. With shipping through Hormuz disrupted, Riyadh has increasingly relied on routes through the Red Sea to move its oil to global markets. Saudi seaborne crude exports through Bab al-Mandab were reportedly eight times higher between March and mid-July than during the same period last year. SEE ALSO: Next Flashpoint In Iran War? The Bab Al-Mandab Strait Off Yemen's Coast A Houthi presence close to the strait therefore offers the group a potentially powerful means of threatening Saudi interests and gives Iran another source of leverage over regional energy flows and global shipping. This, in addition to Houthi strikes this week on Saudi energy infrastructure, “has contributed to a further increase in oil prices, which has been Tehran’s aim all along,” said Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group. “One can therefore expect these developments to further embolden Tehran to stick to its demands and adopt an even more defiant posture vis-a-vis the United States,” he told RFE/RL. SEE ALSO: Yemen's Houthis Grow Bolder Despite US Bombing Campaign The Houthi resurgence also underscores the limits of the US campaign against the group. Despite weeks of intensive American air strikes targeting Houthi leadership, weapons, and military infrastructure last year, the group has retained the capacity to mount a major ground offensive and threaten key maritime routes. But that does not necessarily mean Tehran ordered the Houthi offensive. An Iranian Ally, Not A Proxy The Houthis are closely aligned with Iran and have received extensive Iranian weapons, training, intelligence, and technical assistance. Iranian personnel have also reportedly helped guide Houthi military operations. But portraying the group as simply an Iranian proxy risks missing what makes the current situation so complicated. “I have always seen the Houthis’ relationship with Iran as a strategic partnership, and that is even more the case now than before,” Azizi said. The Houthi movement has its own leadership, interests, ideology, and calculations. It emerged from Yemen's own political and sectarian conflicts long before the current confrontation between Iran and the United States. The group has repeatedly demonstrated that it is capable of making decisions independently of Tehran, even when those decisions ultimately serve Iranian strategic interests. SEE ALSO: US Lawmakers Examine Growing Russia, China Ties To Iran-Backed Houthis Despite Iranian patronage over the years, the Houthis “have their own local and, increasingly, regional ambitions, and they see themselves as a regional power in their own right,” according to Azizi. The Houthi movement’s rise in stature comes as Lebanese Hezbollah, a once-powerful Iranian partner, has suffered significant setbacks as Israel continues to dismantle its infrastructure in southern Lebanon. “In this context, the Houthi advances could boost morale among supporters of the Islamic republic inside Iran as well as across its regional network,” Azizi argued. “They could also help offset the broader weakening of Iran’s network of influence in the region.” The Houthis Advance, Iran Gains Iran does not necessarily need to control the Houthis for the group to function as a powerful source of Iranian leverage. If the Houthis consolidate their gains along Yemen's western coast, Tehran could benefit from pressure on Bab al-Mandab without having to directly close another international waterway. SEE ALSO: Reopening Hormuz Strait Easier Than Restoring Confidence, Naval Analyst Tallis Says For the Houthis, meanwhile, the war offers its own opportunities. The collapse of the Yemeni government's defensive line around Mocha gives the group a chance to expand its territorial and military position on the Red Sea coast while strengthening its regional standing. Any threat to shipping can simultaneously serve Houthi objectives in Yemen and Iran's broader confrontation with Washington and its regional partners. “The fact is that, at the current moment, both sides see a benefit in coordination and simultaneous escalation,” Azizi said. He added that the Houthi advances spare Iran from having to directly engage Saudi Arabia, while Houthi disruption of shipping through Bab al-Mandab and attacks on Saudi energy facilities “would not have had the same impact they have now if the Strait of Hormuz had not already been under pressure from Iran.” It also presents Saudi Arabia and the United States with a difficult choice. A major military response could push Yemen from a parallel conflict into an active theater of the Iran war, potentially provoking further Houthi attacks against Saudi territory and infrastructure. But allowing the Houthis to consolidate their position risks leaving a movement hostile to Riyadh in a stronger position near one of the world's key maritime chokepoints. The dilemma is particularly acute because the United States is already trying to manage a conflict whose economic consequences extend well beyond the Middle East. Disruptions to oil supplies and shipping have pushed up energy and transportation costs, threatening to fuel inflation and further strain an already fragile global economy. The significance of developments in Yemen, therefore, is not simply that the Houthis have captured another strategic city. It is that the war may be creating a second maritime pressure point at a moment when the first, the Strait of Hormuz, has become central to the global economy. He got his start in journalism at the Financial Tribune, an English-language newspaper published in Tehran, where he worked as an editor. He then moved to BBC Monitoring, where he led a team of journalists who closely watched media trends and analyzed key developments in Iran and the wider region.
