body: Credit: Kyrgyz Presidential Administration / Facebook Subscribe for ads-free reading China’s growing efforts to increase control over the Turkic states of Central Asia was the dominant, if little discussed, outcome of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan on September 1. Beijing wants its relationship with the Central Asian states to be one of vassals thankful for China’s “protection” and economic integration. The recent summit produced the 25th anniversary Bishkek Declaration and 27 other documents , which claimed they would strengthen mechanisms for security, countering terrorism and organized crime, and promised new transport lines and logistics. On its face, the Central Asian states are promised infrastructure, technology and diplomatic engagement. But beneath those promises is guaranteed deeper dependence on Chinese capital, standards, and security concepts. China successfully got Muslim-majority states (including Iran, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan) to sign onto documents clearly aimed at China’s own Turkic Muslim populations. The SCO endorsement of combatting “ terrorism, separatism, and extremism ” was China-sponsored and indisputably about Uyghurs. Under this pretext, the institutional capacity that enables surveillance, intelligence exchange, and political labeling of Uyghurs is being expanded. Sadly, China’s economic leverage and coercion means the public support that these Muslim-majority states provide to Muslim communities globally is absent when it comes to China. The Central Asian states should ponder carefully when Beijing uses the security vocabulary noted in the Bishkek Declaration. China’s decade-long ethnic cleansing campaign in Xinjiang, also referred to as East Turkestan, demonstrates what happens when cultural difference is reclassified as a security problem. Religious behavior can be labelled extremism. Cultural autonomy can be called separatism. Overseas relationships of Uyghurs with Turkic states have tended to attract suspicion. Language, memory, and identity become objects of political management. ASPI’s Xinjiang Data Project has documented mass detention, surveillance, forced labor and political re-education. ASPI’s Cultural Erasure research estimated that around 16,000 of Xinjiang’s 24,000 mosques had been damaged or destroyed, alongside extensive damage to Islamic shrines and other sacred sites central to regional Turkic history. Arguments that Beijing is only concerned about its “ internal affairs” are blind to China’s foreign policy. Beijing’s formula of combating the “three evils” – terrorism, separatism, and extremism – was incorporated into the SCO establishment document signed in June 2001, and that vocabulary has been institutionalized across Eurasia. That should matter in the Muslim-majority Turkic states of Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkiye. During Xi’s visit to Kyrgyzstan, Bishkek explicitly reaffirmed support for China on Xinjiang-related issues while agreeing to deepen law-enforcement, counterterrorism, and information-security cooperation. China and Uzbekistan have made similar commitments. Uyghur, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, and other Turkic identities do not end at borders. Families, languages, religious traditions, and diaspora communities extend across the region. When governments repeat Beijing’s anti-separatist language without qualification, they risk allowing legitimate concern for fellow Turkic communities to be recast as interference or subversion. China’s July 2026 Law on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress contains a provision on extraterritoriality (Article 63) that authorizes Chinese authorities to pursue organizations and individuals outside of China’s borders. China’s recent technological advancements increase the risks that might have been assessed in 2001 by the SCO founding nations (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan) as unlikely to cross borders. Some Chinese tech companies expanding across Central Asia have developed important capabilities within the same security ecosystem used to monitor and suppress Uyghurs and other Turkic peoples in the region. iFLYTEK worked with China’s Ministry of Public Security on voiceprint systems and supplied voice-recognition technology used by Xinjiang police. It has since established a Central Asian presence in Tashkent offering multilingual AI services. Technical documentation from Dahua policing systems described functions including “ real-time Uyghur warnings ” and identification of Uyghur attributes. Dahua disputes allegations that it intentionally designed systems for ethnic targeting. But its technology demonstrates how ostensibly neutral surveillance platforms can be adapted for ethnicity-based policing. Dahua systems are already present in Central Asian security environments. Genomics raises an equally serious question of sovereignty. BGI has established sequencing capabilities in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan and has discussed combining AI with large-scale genomic data in Central Asia. Those laboratory platforms are likely to be connected and operate on Beijing’s cyber cloud, in collaboration with companies such as Huawei . But genomic information is permanent, sensitive, and strategically valuable. The Central Asian states should know where samples are processed, where data is stored, who can access it, and whether it can leave national jurisdiction. The same scrutiny should apply to natural resources. Chinese entities are expanding into geological exploration, mining, and processing across Kazakhstan , Uzbekistan , Turkmenistan , Tajikistan , and Kyrgyzstan . Joint surveys can give Chinese partners detailed knowledge of strategic mineral deposits long before extraction begins. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway will bring genuine commercial benefits, but it will also strengthen Beijing’s overland supply chains and reduce China’s dependence on vulnerable maritime routes. The answer for the Central Asian SCO members is not decoupling from China as there is a genuine need for infrastructure, capital, technology, and markets to boost living standards. But blindly accepting and complying with Beijing’s demands is also not what a sovereign state should aim for. The Russian invasion of Ukraine has heightened anxiety across the former Soviet republics and encouraged Central Asian states to diversify their external relationships, including by moving closer to Beijing. But that strategic realignment should not proceed without regard to China’s human rights in general and to Xinjiang specifically. The experience of Uyghurs and other Turkic peoples under Chinese rule offers a stark warning about the political costs that can accompany deeper dependence on Beijing. Turkic governments should distinguish violent terrorism from peaceful political advocacy, religious practice, and diaspora activity. They should scrutinize Chinese surveillance and AI systems, protect biometric and genomic data, retain sovereign control over strategic geological information, and strengthen protections against transnational repression. The SCO may serve legitimate Central Asian interests, but it should not become the vehicle through which Beijing’s definitions of security, political loyalty, and ethnic identity become normalized across the Turkic world. body: Lava spews from Anak Krakatau, a volcano in the Sunda Strait between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra, during an eruption on Oct. 20, 2018. Credit: Wikimedia Commons/Adhari Arief Subscribe for ads-free reading Indonesia reopened five airports early this morning, after a volcanic eruption over the weekend forced them to suspend operations for two days. Anak Krakatau, which is located on a small island in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra, began erupting late on Friday and remained active for around 25 hours . The eruption threw up black plumes of volcanic ash that were carried by the wind over the skies of the capital, Jakarta, which lies around 150 kilometers to the east, and across Lampung province in the southern part of Sumatra. This forced the closure of eight airports, including two servicing Jakarta. As the BBC reported , “snaking queues had formed at the departure halls in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.” Indonesian officials said yesterday that 2,961 flights were disrupted , leaving around 341,000 people stranded. In a statement today, Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said that Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, the capital’s primary airport, resumed operations this morning after wind blew the ash away from the ⁠vicinity, Reuters reported . Four other airports, including a smaller one in Jakarta and another in the neighboring city of Bandung, also reopened today. Two airports remain closed, while one resumed operations yesterday. Dudy told reporters that authorities would now need to confirm the airworthiness of the 178 aircraft that were at Soekarno-Hatta during the closure. “Perhaps it’ll ⁠take some little extra time to prepare the planes,” he said. It has been sporadically active for much of the last decade, and an eruption in 2018 caused a devastating tsunami that killed hundreds of people and displaced tens of thousands. body: A massive flood in the Bhotekoshi River affected riverbanks and nearby houses in Nuwakot, Nepal, causing widespread damage to homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure in the area, Aug. 28, 2026. Credit: Shutterstock Subscribe for ads-free reading Nepal’s recent floods, which have killed at least 1,280 people while over 5,600 are still missing as of this writing, rank among the country’s worst natural disasters. Preliminary estimates put economic losses at $2.56 billion. But the disaster’s consequences will extend far beyond the immediate human and economic toll. It has also undermined the efforts of successive post-2015 governments to achieve more geopolitical balance, largely through the development of new transport, trade and transit facilities with China. As a landlocked country wedged between India and China, Nepal has long sought to preserve its strategic autonomy by balancing the influence of its two neighbors. For a variety of reasons, India, which surrounds the country on three sides, has blockaded its open border with Nepal three times since 1969 — most recently in 2015. That year, Nepal promulgated a new constitution that had failed to address India’s concerns. At other times, New Delhi has openly meddled in Nepali politics. To reduce that vulnerability to Indian pressure, Nepali rulers have felt the need to increase engagement with China, the northern neighbor. After the 2015 blockade, the then-K.P. Sharma Oli government signed a slew of agreements with China to establish new trade and transit links. As part of the process, a significant investment was made to upgrade the Kerung border point (known as Gyirong on the Chinese side) into an all-weather international crossing . Much of China-Nepal trade has gradually shifted to Kerung from Tatopani, the previous main artery of bilateral trade that was badly damaged by the 2015 earthquakes. Unfortunately, the recent floods literally washed away much of the investment around Kerung. There is not even a trace of the customs buildings and customs yards — on either side of the border. After the flooding of the Kerung border, China has also shut down Tatopani, citing possible landslides on the Nepali side. (Beijing has also long been wary of the possible use of the Tatopani route by “Free Tibet” activists.) All cross-border traffic has been diverted to Korala, the third international border crossing between Nepal and China. But Korala is not an easy crossing , nor is there much in terms of cross-border trade infrastructure. Besides these three, the three other designated points for Nepal-China trade are minuscule and limited to handling local trade. In the big picture, Nepal’s trade with China, which was already limited, will be further restricted after the floods. India is Nepal’s largest trade partner, with China coming in at a distant second. The floods will exacerbate an already troubling imbalance. But Kathmandu’s options are limited. Rebuilding Kerung or upgrading Korala to handle more traffic will require a lot of time and money. Shipping goods from China is an option, but a costly one. The country’s dependence on India will thus further increase. Besides the prospect of some Indian goods replacing Chinese ones in Nepali markets, Nepal will now have to use Indian ports to import even vital supplies from China. With the floods knocking out around 10 percent of Nepal’s electricity-generation capacity , the energy dependence on India could go up too. The Rasuwa floods will strengthen the argument that geography leaves Nepal with no realistic substitute for India as its principal commercial and transit partner, with China serving mainly as a supplementary option. And as India’s commercial clout increases in Nepal, so will its strategic sway. Nepal, after all, shares a long, flat open border with India and the two countries are bound together by cultural and family ties. Nepali Prime Minister Balen Shah had already complicated Nepal’s external relations with his unconventional approach, initially avoiding individual meetings with foreign envoys and senior visiting officials. Beijing, with whom Nepal will now have to work closely to rebuild damaged infrastructure along the border, was particularly displeased at what it saw as the Nepal government’s repeated failures to uphold the “One China” policy . Yet rebuilding Nepal’s northern connectivity could itself have geopolitical consequences. Kathmandu will need Chinese technical and financial assistance to restore damaged border infrastructure. China will also be averse to involving other countries in reconstruction in the sensitive region. The floods could therefore produce a peculiar form of dual dependence: greater reliance on India for immediate trade and transit, even as Nepal turns to China to rebuild the infrastructure needed to reduce that very reliance. For the 36-year-old Nepali prime minister, this creates a separate political dilemma. Shah will have to rely more on India for trade and connectivity while also being under pressure to maintain a safe distance from New Delhi — in keeping with the wishes of core nationalist constituencies. The mountainous trade routes to China have long been vulnerable to landslides and earthquakes, limiting the northern neighbor’s viability as a trade and transit alternative to India. The recent disaster has highlighted this weakness like never before. The floods will not change Nepal’s need to balance India and China. body: A humanoid service robot as a cashier in an automated convenience store selling drinks in Shanghai, China, Nov. 28, 2025. Credit: Shutterstock Subscribe for ads-free reading As China’s President Xi Jinping prepares to travel to Washington, D.C. on September 24 , his approach will reflect not only the specific items on his agenda, but also broader geopolitical transformations currently underway. These revolutions-in-progress create both enormous opportunities for China and hazards for it, and the international community, to navigate. Reinforcing advances currently underway in “big data,” artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous systems, and robotics are rapidly transforming both economic and military dynamics , with radical implications for political systems and the global balance of power . Latin America and the rest of the developing world will be a battleground, a beneficiary, and a victim in that enormous and chaotic change. Although the future cannot be predicted with certainty, one reasonable outcome of the current confluence of trends is a world that is far more violent, less democratic, and more dominated by China. That future could emerge more rapidly than most traditional analysts expect. Here’s how such traumatic and revolutionary change could occur, and what it could mean for the United States, Latin America, and the world. The Coming AI-Robotics Revolution Within the next decade, developments arising out of the synergy between artificial intelligence and robotics will likely present non-human alternatives to a wide variety of both white-collar and blue-collar, skilled and unskilled labor, transforming a far broader range of work, far more rapidly than occurred in last century’s industrial revolution . The amortized cost of industrial robots is already less in many cases than employing a human to do the task. Mass-produced Chinese robots from companies like Unitree and UBTech can be ordered for as little as $5,000 , with many industrial capable units costing only $20,000-$50,000 . At that price, such a robot, capable of replacing three shifts of factory workers, costs only a few months of the human wages its use would save. As with personal computers in the 1990s, those costs will only come down, and the sophistication of hardware, firmware, and AI-powered “control” mechanisms will only improve, as robotic systems are deployed at scale in an increasingly broad range of tasks. What makes the current revolution even more transformational is that increasingly capable AI tools, whether virtual or embodied, have the capability to replace humans not only in factory work, but also in domestic and service work, as well as white collar tasks. This is particularly the case in technical areas, such as computer programming , legal work, medical technicians, and administrative support staff, among others. It is highly likely, as Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, has said, that the nature of work will change from human beings doing things to directing and supervising AI and robotic systems in such tasks. Yet it is highly unlikely that the number of “supervisory” jobs created in the new AI-robotic economy, combined with new kinds of work supporting or complementing that economy, will fully offset those human jobs rendered economically non-competitive. The World Economic Forum estimates that current developments could displace 92 million jobs by 2030 alone. Moreover, the speed of the onset of the new tech economy, and the inherent difficulty of human beings adapting to new types of skills in new places, will significantly and rapidly expand what 19th century philosopher Thomas Robert Malthus once chillingly referred to as a “ redundant population .” As with the industrial revolution, the AI-robotics revolution will also likely expand socioeconomic inequality between those owning, implementing, and managing the structures of the new AI-robotics economy, and those whose jobs are replaced, or sectors whose wages are decreased, by competition with new AI and robotic alternatives. Those effects will be particularly acute among populations already increasingly discontent with democratic political systems ’ dysfunction and inability to address contemporary challenges. The responses of different political systems to such pressures will likely reflect a combination of two impulses: compensation and repression. Some governments will create or expand social “safety nets” to retrain, relocate, or at least mitigate the suffering of those displaced. Other governments – or in some cases, the same ones – will use instruments of state repression against those who react to the stresses caused by such economic displacement through descent into common criminality, or alternatively, violent protest and terrorism. Ironically, the tools for monitoring and controlling population’s movements, finances, and other aspects of their livelihood are also being greatly strengthened by advances in AI, access to “big data,” and other technologies. As AI puts significant pressures on democratic political systems and market economies, it will also play an ever-more-important role in the distribution, and ultimately, allocation, of resources for populations. Even today, AI is being used in operational management and logistics for both firms and governments. AI could actually mitigate some of the distortions and inefficiencies historically associated with government-led economic systems, most eloquently argued in 1945 by Friedrick Hayek . AI may thus help China and other authoritarian governments outcompete democratic free market systems by helping their performance, as well as their repressive capabilities, even as technology disruption dramatically expands stresses on democracies and market-based systems. In tandem with such economic and political transformation, the aforementioned technology advances are also accelerating a revolution in military affairs . AI-enabled autonomous systems will increasingly replace manned ones in the air, on and under the ground, and in and under the water. They will be increasingly coordinated by AI-enabled battle and logistics management systems, whose ability to rapidly identify patterns and consider the outcome of numerous response scenarios will give them significant advantages over “human-in the loop” systems. At the same time, the new technologies will give middle powers, small states, and even resource-rich non-state criminal and terrorist groups the ability to defy and extort much larger actors, as Iran has done to the United States with its drone and missile systems. China’s AI Strategy In the context of such transformations, China’s current strategy is particularly alarming, and potentially transformational. On one hand, as seen previously in other technologies such as electric vehicles, Beijing has dedicated significant resources to dominating developments in AI and robotics. Repeating a tried-and-true blueprint, China has significantly invested in basic and applied research , protected and subsidized key enabling technology sectors , and leveraged China’s enormous captive internal market , in order to develop commercial products that could dominate in the global arena. In the present case, China is seeking to lead the world on AI by developing efficient, open-weight models such as Kimi K3, Deep Seek V4, and Qwen 3.8 , even where its companies do not have access to the highest performance chips such as Nvidia Vera Rubin and Blackwell . While Chinese models are still modestly inferior to frontier Western models such as Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, ChatGPT 6 Astra, and Grok flagship, over the long term, the open-source nature of China’s models and their ability to function with lower performance chips positions them to dominate global markets such as those of Latin America, Africa, and developing Asia, even if they are excluded from the United States and Europe. Following a path similar to its approach to dominating other sectors of the global e

body: Soldiers pose for a photo with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Adampur Air Force Base in Punjab on May 13, 2025, following Operation Sindoor. Credit: Prime Minister Office of India Subscribe for ads-free reading Some incidents in world history not only leave deep scars on the soul of a nation but alter the nation’s trajectory irreversibly. The terror attack of September 11, 2001 was one such incident. A perfectly normal morning turned into a horrific nightmare when 19 al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, two of which crashed into the Twin Towers in New York and one into the Pentagon building outside of Washington, D.C. The Twin Towers came crashing down and the result was a death count of almost 3,000. The resultant national outrage and anger led to the United States leading its most extensive military mission since the Vietnam War, chasing al-Qaida and its leader Osama bin Laden into Afghanistan. In a military campaign lasting almost 20 years, al-Qaida was largely neutralized and Osama bin Laden was eventually tracked and killed in Pakistan on May 2, 2011. The 9/11 attacks led to profound changes in the United States as well, especially in matters of internal security. There was a clear mandate that no matter what, there cannot be another 9/11 type of incident on the American mainland ever again. In the Indian context however, it took decades of terror attacks before India similarly said, “no more.” Thanks to a policy crafted by Pakistan in the early 1990s to “ bleed India through a thousand cuts ” with cross-border terrorism, India endured a large number of terror attacks and losses, especially in Kashmir. But then one terror incident shook India like never before. The terror attack in Pahalgam on April 22, 2025 killed 26 innocent civilians in a popular tourist spot in Kashmir. The attack was launched by terrorists belonging to The Resistance Force, an offshoot of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT). The anger and outrage in India were magnified many times over as the victims – all men – were specifically identified by their religion (Hindu, except for one Christian and one local Muslim who tried to intervene). The men were also shot dead in front of their wives. The resultant military operation, Operation Sindoor, launched by India into Pakistan on May 7, made clear India’s new resolve against terrorism. While these two incidents – 9/11 and the Pahalgam attack – were separated by almost 24 years, they are united by two nations’ expressed resolve to fight terror to the ends of the Earth. But as the Pahalgam attack sadly showed, the war against terror has not been won. Al-Qaida may not be a force to reckon with in the form it was 25 years ago and it may no longer have leaders like Osama bin Laden who could attract and ideologically indoctrinate youth to join. But many smaller offshoots of al-Qaida still operate across the globe. In the Indian context, while LeT and other Pakistan-based terror groups may have been dealt a punishing blow by India, inputs from Pakistan indicate that there is a strong resolve to revive these groups. Therefore, the fight against terror isn’t over yet. It is therefore important to examine how terror is changing form and how nations are constantly evolving their strategies to stay ahead of the curve to counter and neutralize such threats before they manifest. The Evolution of Terror Over the past 25 years, the form terrorism has changed, as have the type of instruments used to carry out terror attacks. Naturally, the strategies to tackle terror have evolved as well. Unlike big terror groups like al-Qaida or the Islamic State (IS) in the past, terror groups have now morphed into smaller and more autonomous groups. Lone wolf attacks are now becoming the norm and technologies like drones, cyber, and even artificial intelligence are being used by terror groups. Indirect attacks like cyberattacks on key energy and banking infrastructure are complementing high-impact physical attacks on the population. Hierarchical organizations and organized training camps are increasingly giving way to more fluid structures, which operate through affiliations and franchises, encrypted communications, cryptocurrencies, social media, and loosely connected cells. Campaigns seeking territorial control like the IS in Iraq and Syria are being replaced by terror campaigns to disrupt social cohesion within a country and bleed nations financially. And, accordingly, strategies to fight terror by countries too are evolving rapidly. Counterterrorism has evolved from a predominantly military campaign into a much broader strategy incorporating multiple instruments of state power like intelligence, financial surveillance, border control, cyber monitoring, deradicalization, and international cooperation. When military action is taken, it takes the form of precision operations through cutting-edge standoff weapon platforms. The India Context The fight against terror in India had a frustrating beginning. In most cases, the response to terrorist attacks was limited to sectoral military operations, tightening border controls, and issuing warnings to Pakistan. In some cases, it also led to cutting off diplomatic ties for some time. The first such terror attack was the hijacking of Air India’s flight IC-814 on December 24, 1999, just a few months after the Kargil war. With very few options then and increasing public pressure, India agreed to release two Pakistan-based terrorists, Ahmed Omar Shiekh and Masood Azhar, in exchange for over 160 civilian hostages. Massod Azhar went on to establish Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM), the Pakistan-based terrorist group that later launched a terror attack on the Indian Parliament on December 13, 2001. Caught by surprise, India ordered a full-scale military mobilization under Operation Parakaram, but it ultimately ended without a bullet being fired. The 26/11 Mumbai terror attack in 2008 was a milestone in many ways. Widely considered as India’s 9/11 moment, it brought global attention to India’s war against terror. Although once again India did not end up punishing Pakistan for the attack, it did lead to a major security review and structural changes. The National Investigative Agency (NIA) was formed as a result, with sweeping powers on matters of internal national security. The NIA is now functioning as the central counterterrorism law enforcement agency in India. The mandate of fighting terror expanded to include stronger intelligence coordination, tighter coastal security and border surveillance, specialized forces to fight terror, and cooperation between central and state agencies. The overall responsibility for coastal security was placed under the Indian Navy. Tracking and monitoring terror finance too became a key instrument in the fight against terror. The Multi Agency Center, which was established in December 2001 as a part of the key recommendations of the Kargil Review Committee, also became a key coordination platform for intelligence exchange and cooperation against terror. However, most of India’s anti-terrorism measures remained passive, reactive, and preventive. The Kinetic Strategy It was only after 2014, when the Modi government came to power, that the intent to deliver a decisive response to any act of terror grew firm. Counterterrorism operations in Kashmir were given a new momentum and measures to block infiltration across the Line of Control were strengthened. A terror attack on September 18, 2016 by JeM terrorists against an army camp in Uri, Kashmir, led to the first cross-border surgical strikes by the Indian Army, which destroyed multiple terrorist camps and infrastructure in Pakistan. It was not only a strong reply to the terror attack but also signaled a major shift in India’s strategic policy and rules of engagement regarding cross-border terrorism. While it did deter Pakistan to some extent, it did not end its terror campaign. On February 14, 2019, JeM terrorists unleashed ano
title: From 9/11 to Pahalgam: India’s Evolving Strategy in the Global War on Terror

body: Credit: Shutterstock/AI generated image Subscribe for ads-free reading Since emerging from its self-imposed COVID-19 isolation, North Korea has closed a number of its diplomatic missions overseas while reshaping others. The government has concentrated on relationships it sees as strategically useful, focusing heavily on deepening ties with Russia , its burgeoning relations with Belarus , and, most recently, the rekindling of engagement with China . Yet, amid this diplomatic retrenchment, one unexpected country has received particular outreach and attention from the Kim Jong Un regime: Nicaragua. At a time when North Korea is restructuring its foreign relationships, its decision to court Nicaragua stands out, both for its geographic position and the fact that it came at the invitation of the Kim regime. While the two countries seem like natural partners given the nature of their authoritarian systems of government and long-standing history, the outreach is nevertheless a notable deviation from North Korea’s baseline behavior. Ultimately it could signal increased cooperation between the two countries as well a new trajectory for North Korea’s foreign policy designs going forward, one that exists outside China’s and Russia’s immediate orbit. Background on the Nicaragua-North Korea relationship North Korea’s relationship with Nicaragua has ebbed and flowed with changes in Managua’s government. Pyongyang avoided diplomatic relations with the U.S.-backed Nicaraguan government until 1979, when the Sandinista National Liberation Front took power. At the time, the Kim regime’s connections to the Sandinistas largely ran through its Cuban partner, although North Korea had reportedly provided military training to the group’s personnel in the lead-up to the revolution. Bilateral engagement between the two countries peaked in the 1980s. This included North Korean military assistance with the delivery of four patrol vessels valued at $8 million , as well as mutual diplomatic support. In 1986, Daniel Ortega, the Sandinista leader and then president of Nicaragua, traveled to Pyongyang for a first-of-its-kind summit between the two nations. Nicaragua followed this up with a show of solidarity by deciding to boycott the 1988 Olympics hosted in Seoul. Bilateral ties cooled after the Sandinistas fell out of power in 1990. This eventually led to the closure of the North Korean embassy in Managua in 1995. It was not until Ortega returned to power in 2006 that the two governments reestablished diplomatic relations. But it would still take another decade before the next notable development. In January 2017, a North Korean delegation headed by Choe Ryong Hae – one of Kim Jong Un’s top officials – attended the inauguration of Daniel Ortega for his third term as president of Nicaragua. There, the two governments lauded nearly 40 years of friendship and mutual diplomatic support. However, the practical depth of the relationship remained shallow. In 2017, North Korea’s exports to Nicaragua were reportedly worth just $1.8 million, while reciprocal trade was minimal. There were no indications of military cooperation, and diplomatic engagement remained surface-level. Beyond the ceremonial nature of Choe Ryong Hae’s visit, there was little indication that the relationship was poised to deepen. North Korea’s Post-COVID Reset The COVID-19 pandemic marked a substantial turning point for North Korean foreign relations. The border lockdowns and restrictions on movement of overseas personnel sharply curtailed diplomatic activities. All but a handful of embassies in Pyongyang closed owing to movement restrictions and resource depletion, reducing contact between foreign diplomats and North Korea government officials. This self-imposed isolation enabled the Kim regime to reset its policy designs going forward. The Eighth Party Congress in January 2021 produced a five-year policy roadmap for North Korea. The implications for foreign policy began to manifest when emerging from the COVID-19 lockdown period. As North Korea began reopening in 2023, evidence of this restructuring of foreign partnerships became increasingly visible. Pyongyang closed its embassies in Angola (2023), Bangladesh (2023), Democratic Republic of the Congo (2023), Guinea (2023), Libya (2024), Nepal (2023), Senegal (2023), Spain (2023), Syria (2024), and Uganda (2023). Although North Korea’s government did not give a specific reason for these closures, it signaled a reallocation of resources that went toward other relationships it wished to cultivate further. North Korea opened additional consulates in Russia, pursued deeper engagement with Belarus – culminating with Alexander Lukashenko’s March 2026 visit – and, curiously, invited Nicaragua to open an embassy in Pyongyang. Courting Nicaragua In July 2023, the Kim regime sent a delegation to Nicaragua to propose that Managua set up an embassy in the North Korean capital. Pyongyang’s state media did not publicize the initiative; rather, it was the Nicaraguan government that revealed the invitation. Within a year, Managua had inaugurated its diplomatic mission in Pyongyang and presented ambassadorial credentials to the North Korean government . Since then, North Korea has increasingly referenced Nicaragua in its state media reporting. In the official news wire service, KCNA, Nicaragua has been the subject of 12 reports so far in 2026, after 15 in 2025 and eight in 2024. This compares to only two in 2023. There are still unanswered questions as to why Pyongyang extended this outreach. Does North Korea see potential for trade (arms or otherwise)? Is Pyongyang seeking to expand its own work in the region? Part of the answer may lie in Cuba, a longtime partner of both governments. At the same time that North Korea was seeking to advance ties with the Nicaraguan government, South Korea was moving to normalize diplomatic relations with Cuba. Cuba had long maintained close ties with the North while keeping its distance from South Korea, but that changed in February 2024 when Havana and Seoul formalized ties. This move was a diplomatic setback for Pyongyang, which had up to that point maintained its third-largest embassy in Havana (behind Moscow and Beijing) . In essence, Seoul’s encroachment in Cuba marked the potential weakening of a key regional partnership for the Kim regime. Notably, Nicaragua closed its embassy in South Korea in April 2024. Although Managua cited budget constraints as its reason for the closure, the timing was notable: it came just two months after the Cuba-South Korea normalization of relations and amid Pyongyang’s continued courtship of Nicaragua. Whether the events were connected, however, remains unclear. But finding a regional partner is only part of the equation. Other Central American countries maintain friendly relations with North Korea, raising the question of what makes Nicaragua stand out for Pyongyang. In practice, North Korea’s preferred relationships have been with those countries that satisfy three prerequisites. First, they are looser in their adherence to the rules-based international order. Second, they are not closely aligned with the United States, South Korea, or their allies and partners. Third, the country lacks something that North Korea can provide, giving Pyongyang a potential source of leverage. Nicaragua satisfies those three criteria. The United States strongly opposes the Sandinista government, and Nicaragua no longer maintains a diplomatic mission in Seoul. Further, Nicaragua’s traditional security relationships with Cuba and Venezuela have become less reliable, creating potential space for another source of military equipment or training. Managua’s Interests in Pyongyang From Managua’s perspective, North Korea offers a like-minded partner with a similarly personalized, family-centric political system. This is in part why Nicaragua has earned the moniker the “North Korea of Latin America.” For governments run by families like th

body: Privacy Cookie policy Tue 1 Jul 2025 08.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jump to Introduction 1. What is a cookie? 2. First-party and third-party cookies 3. How do we use cookies? 4. What types of cookies do we use? 5. How long do cookies last? 6. How do we use cookies for advertising? 7. How do third parties use cookies for advertising? 8. How can you control advertising cookies? 9. How to manage cookies at the Guardian? 10. Useful links 11. Changes to this cookie policy Introduction This is the cookie policy for Guardian News & Media Limited (collectively referred to as “Guardian”, “we”, “us” or “our” in this policy), our site theguardian.com, and our associated apps (“our sites”). Some of our other sites and services have their own cookie policies, which will be relevant to you when you are using those sites and services. 1. What is a cookie? A cookie is a small file that contains letters and numbers that is downloaded to your device when you visit a website. It is sent to your browser and stored on your computer’s hard drive, tablet or mobile device. When you visit our sites it can allow us to recognise and remember you. Technologies similar to cookies Technologies that store or access information on a user’s device are similar to cookies and are also covered by this policy. These technologies may include: Device fingerprinting – using a set of information without relying on cookies in order to identify a particular device. For this purpose where you are resident in Australia, our partner Ipsos Iris may collect your IP address, monitor settings, type of browser and operating system to create a unique serial number which constitutes a digital “fingerprint”. Local storage – storage of data in the local device’s cache, for example to load content quicker. Pixels – a small pixel graphic which is used to track user behaviour, site conversions etc. Scripts – small computer programs embedded within websites that give them extra functionality but may access user devices. In this policy we call all cookies and similar technologies “ cookies ”, for ease. 2. First-party and third-party cookies There are different types of cookies: First-party cookies – cookies that are set by or on behalf of the Guardian when you use our site. Third-party cookies – cookies that are set by parties or organisations other than the Guardian when you use our site. Some Guardian web pages may also contain content from or link to other sites which may set their own cookies. If you share a link to a Guardian page, the service you share it on may set a cookie on your browser. 3. How do we use cookies? We use cookies in a range of ways to improve your experience on our sites, including: Keeping you signed in. Delivering content to you. Showing you journalism that is relevant to you. Providing a better reading experience for signed in readers and readers with a guest account, including tailored messaging, remembering your preferences across devices and showing you Guardian products and services that are relevant to you. Understanding how you use our site, for instance, how long you stay on a page or which article you read next. Reminding you to complete online registration. Processing payments and refunds. Monitoring how users interact with pages on our site to identify and remedy technical issues. Working with partners to deliver relevant advertising to you. In the next sections, we explain in more detail how cookies on our site may be useful, as well as when and where you can control them. 4. What types of cookies do we use? We use four types of cookies: Strictly Necessary – These cookies are essential to provide you with services you have requested, which means they cannot be switched off through the “Privacy settings” link. For example, strictly necessary cookies make it possible for you to stay logged into your Guardian account and make comments. If you set your browser to block these cookies, then these functions and services will not work for you. In particular, we won’t be able to save your preferences about cookies. Performance – These cookies measure how often you visit our sites and how you use them. We use this information to get a better sense of how you engage with our journalism and to improve our sites so that you have a better experience. For example, we collect information about which of our pages are most frequently visited, and by which types of users. Functionality – These cookies are used to recognise you and remember your preferences or settings when you return to our site so that we can provide you with a more personalised experience. For example, if you are based in the UK, we will remember this and make sure that you receive the UK homepage when you visit our site, rather than the US or Australia homepage. Advertising – These cookies are used to collect information about your visit to our site, including the content you have viewed, the links you have followed and information about your browser, device and your IP address. We have set out more details on our use of advertising cookies below. 5. How long do cookies last? Session cookies – These cookies only last as long as your online session and expire when you close your browser (e.g. Chrome or Safari). Persistent cookies – These cookies stay on your device after your browser has been closed and last for a time specified in the cookie (but not longer than 13 months). We use these cookies when we need to remember you for more than one browsing session, for instance to remember your preferences from one visit to the next. 6. How do we use cookies for advertising? If you accept cookies, as you browse our site, we will place cookies on your device. Some cookies are for advertising, so we can understand what sorts of pages you read and are interested in viewing. We can then display advertising on your browser based on these interests. For instance, if you have been reading a lot of food articles, you may be shown more adverts for food. Our apps integrate third-party software that provides us with information about how the app is used and what content you have viewed for the purposes of online advertising and analytics. It uses cookies from some of the providers listed in our “Privacy settings”, that can be found in the footer of every page on our site. We sometimes use information such as your IP address, browser type and identifiers generated by third parties for advertising, and also sometimes share these with others for advertising purposes. We also allow other organisations to use cookies and other technologies to help us analyse how our site is being used, measure the number of visitors to the site, and display advertising. 7. How do third parties use cookies for advertising? With your consent we share and receive online data collected through cookies with our advertising partners. This means that when you are on another website, you may be shown advertising based on your browsing patterns on our site. We may also show you advertising on our site based on your browsing patterns on other sites that we have obtained from our advertising partners. Online retargeting is another form of online advertising that allows us and some of our advertising partners to show you advertising based on your browsing patterns and interactions with other sites. The use of cookies may mean that when you are on another site, you may be shown advertising based on what you have looked at on our site. For example, if you have visited the website of an online clothes shop, you may start seeing adverts from that same shopping site displaying special offers or showing you the products you were browsing. This allows companies to advertise to you if you leave their website without making a purchase. We require that all our contractual partners treat your personal data with a similar level of respect that we would provide. body: ‘Feminists argued that the tradition of using “she” to describe ships was anachronistic and “perpetuat[ed] the patriarchal view” while naval enthusiasts claimed it was “political correctness gone mad”.’ Photograph: Stewart Sutton/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘Feminists argued that the tradition of using “she” to describe ships was anachronistic and “perpetuat[ed] the patriarchal view” while naval enthusiasts claimed it was “political correctness gone mad”.’ Photograph: Stewart Sutton/Getty Images Language This article is more than 7 years old Language wars: the 19 greatest linguistic spats of all time This article is more than 7 years old Words are ever evolving – but not without controversy. From creative applications of an apostrophe to the overuse of literally, what makes you rage? David Shariatmadari Mon 17 Jun 2019 11.12 EDT Last modified on Tue 18 Jun 2019 05.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hat is it about language that gets people so hot under the collar? That drives them to spend hours arguing with strangers on the internet, to go around correcting misspelt signs in the dead of night, or even to threaten acts of violence? The languages we speak are central to our sense of self, so it is not surprising that their finer points can become a battleground. Passionate feelings about what’s right and wrong extend from the use of “disinterested” to what gay people are allowed to call themselves. Here are some of the most memorable rows, spats and controversies. Apostrophe catastrophe A so-called “grammar vigilante” has been correcting shop fronts in Bristol, England, for more than a decade. His pet peeve is the confusion of plain old plurals with possessives, which in English are usually marked by an apostrophe followed by an S. Confronted with a sign advertising “Amy’s Nail’s”, he will obliterate the second apostrophe with a sticker. Addressing the potentially illegal nature of his mission in a BBC report , he said: “It’s more of a crime that the apostrophe is wrong in the first place”. Linguist Rob Drummond disagrees : “Fetishising the apostrophe as if its rules are set in stone,” he writes, “and then fostering an environment in which it is acceptable to take pleasure in uncovering other people’s linguistic insecurities is not OK.” Are you really disinterested? Use this word at your own risk. If what you want to say is “lacking in interest” then brace yourself, because there’s an army of people who will point out that it should be “uninterested”, and that “disinterested” must mean “impartial”. They are sticklers for what they regard as the correct meaning, and have taken up columnist William Safire’s command to “rear up and rage, rage against the dying of an enlightening distinction”. The problem is that if a word is more frequently used to mean one thing than another, then that’s effectively what it means: you can’t fight a linguistic consensus. The news for pedants gets worse, however. The OED tells us that the use of “disinterested” to mean not interested or unconcerned has been around since at least the 17th century, used by no less a stylist than the poet John Donne. View image in fullscreen English and Maori versions of the Treaty of Waitangi had important differences. Photograph: Ian Paterson/Alamy Stock Photo Shipshape and patriarchal “It is an insult to a generation of sailors ... a ship is like a mother.” An incensed Admiral Lord West was speaking earlier this year about the Scottish Maritime Museum’s decision to stop using “she” to describe ships and boats on its information signs. The move, made after the female pronouns were scratched out by persons unknown, provoked a furious debate, with feminists arguing that the tradition was anachronistic and “perpetuat[ed] the patriarchal view” while naval enthusiasts claimed it was “political correctness gone mad”. Unlike English, many languages force speakers to assign a gender to inanimate objects, and there is evidence that it influences the way they think about them. For example, “bridge” is feminine in German and masculine in Spanish. When asked by researchers to pick words they associated with it, German speakers chose adjectives like “beautiful”, “elegant”, “pretty” and “slender” and the Spanish speakers chose “big”, “strong”, “sturdy” and “towering”. ‘Nucular’ war The fact that we used to make fun of George W Bush for his malapropisms seems quaint these days. But it was worrying to many of us at the time that the man in charge of the world’s most powerful nuclear arsenal didn’t seem to be able to pronounce it right. He said “ nucular ” and it was one more black mark against his intelligence. But this syllable-flip is in fact a fairly common linguistic process called metathesis. All English speakers live with the results of historic metatheses that caught on: horse used to be “hros” and bird used to be “brid”. Trumped by language Now we have far greater opportunities for ridicule in Donald Trump, whose multisyllabic manglings have become world famous: “ covfefe ” anyone? But acting as a linguistic irritant appears to be a family trait. Journalist Eve Peyser has kept tabs on words the president’s daughter Ivanka seemed to misuse in public pronouncements, and they included relative (“my husband keeps incredibly long hours, so I try to keep mine on a relative basis”), otherwise (“Cuddling my little nephew Luke, the best part of an otherwise incredible day!”) and “indeniably” (“Indeniably it’s very expensive to raise children”). When commas change history Let’s just hope none of the Trump family gets to rewrite the US constitution, because it’s there that linguistic quirks get really serious. Its precise wording, even punctuation, has been endlessly scrutinised, sometimes with life-and-death consequences. The second amendment states that: “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” The comma after the word “arms” has been used to argue that the framers of the constitution believed the right of an individual to own a gun was more important than collective self-defence. That interpretation ultimately resulted in the striking down of some Washington DC gun controls, which had been among the strictest in the nation. ‘Please return the word “gay”’ The word used to refer to gay people has been controversial in several languages, not least English, where people railed against the co-option of the term until quite recently. In 1990 an anonymous journalist wrote a piece for Newsweek headlined “Please return the word ‘gay’”. “It is of the least possible concern to me what homosexuals do with one another in the privacy of their homes ... But I want the word ‘gay’ back. ‘Gay’ used to be an extremely useful word. It showed up frequently in poetry and prose – Shakespeare used it 12 times.” Fast forward 30-odd years and a similar row is playing out in China, where the word tongzhi , whose literal meaning is “comrade” increasingly only has one interpretation. That didn’t stop the Contemporary Chinese Dictionary from prudishly refusing to list its common connotation, with one compiler telling the BBC they “did not want to draw attention to its more colloquial meaning”. The Ebonics controversy In 1996 the school board of Oakland, California, decided to recognise the dialect of many of its African American pupils, which it called “Ebonics”, as a language. It would henceforth be used to “facilitate their acquisition and mastery of English-language skills”. The move became a major flashpoint in the US culture wars after being attacked by commentators across the country. Then Clinton aide Rahm Emanuel labelled it “a big mistake” and black leaders weighed in, too, with Jesse Jackson writing “in Oakland some madness has erupted over making slang talk a second language”. body: Listen (2 mins) Save Share Kazakhstan’s Tokayev appoints longtime adviser as vice president on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev attends the Supreme Eurasian Economic Union summit in Astana, Kazakhstan, Friday, May 29, 2026 [Alexander Kazakov/Kremlin Pool Photo via AP] By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters Published On 31 Aug 2026 31 Aug 2026 Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has appointed longtime adviser Erlan Karin as vice president, the office created under a new constitution adopted earlier this year. The move on Monday makes Karin, who has served as a top ⁠⁠aide to Tokayev since taking over the presidency in 2019, first in line to succeed him as leader of the Central Asian country. Tokayev described Karin as an experienced public servant with extensive knowledge of state governance, local media reported. “He has worked in the system of public administration for many years. One can say that he is a person of broad outlook, with rich experience and a true patriot,” Tokayev was quoted as saying. The 50-year-old has a background in “counter-terrorism” and has ⁠⁠positioned himself as a key figure in promoting Tokayev’s ideology, which he has dubbed “New Kazakhstan”. Tokayev also proposed reappointing Olzhas Bektenov as prime minister, a position ⁠⁠he has held since 2024. Both appointments were swiftly approved by parliament, which is dominated ⁠⁠by the pro-Tokayev Adilet party. Tokayev, 73, is eligible to run for another seven-year term as president under the new constitution, according to Kazakhstan’s supreme court. His current term ends in 2029. presidents are otherwise limited to a single term in office under Kazakh basic law. Tokayev, a ⁠⁠former Soviet diplomat and top United Nations official, took office as the chosen successor of Nursultan Nazarbayev, Kazakhstan’s founding president, who ruled from 1991 to 2019. Advertisement Tokayev broke from his predecessor, whom he had served as prime minister and foreign minister, in 2022 after a bout of nationwide unrest that left hundreds dead and which he cast as a coup attempt by Nazarbayev-era figures. Kazakhstan is a major exporter of energy and minerals, including uranium for nuclear power, and maintains warm ties with Russia, the West and China.
title: Kazakhstan’s Tokayev appoints longtime adviser as vice president

body: Listen (7 mins) Save Share Ukraine’s offensive against Russia causes petrol panic across Central Asia on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Cossacks keep order at a petrol station and prevent conflicts due to fuel shortages in the Russian Black Sea resort of Anapa, July 8, 2026 [Sergey Pivovarov/Reuters] By Mansur Mirovalev Published On 24 Aug 2026 24 Aug 2026 A Russian woman explained on camera what made her and a smiling, bearded man next to her drive to a petrol station in Kazakhstan. “Simply to fill the tank,” she said in a viral video that explains new terms in today’s Russia: “fuel tourism” and “gas hunting”. For most of this year, swarms of Ukrainian drones have been burning down Russian oil refineries and fuel depots from annexed Crimea to the Baltic to western Siberia, causing sky-high plumes of putrid smoke. As Russian President Vladimir Putin refuses to resume peace talks, claiming that his forces “advance in all directions”, tens of millions of Russians face fuel shortages and hours-long queues at petrol stations – with occasional shouting and fist fights. And those living in regions bordering Kazakhstan – including a string of urban centres along the Volga River, Russia’s most densely populated region – drive to Central Asia’s most oil-rich nation, often hundreds of kilometres, just to fill up. Even though in late May the Kazakh government banned petrol exports, border guards report thwarting hundreds of attempts to smuggle fuel back to Russia in canisters, makeshift fuel tanks – or in giant fuel trucks. But some industrious smugglers still make their way across the world’s second-longest land border that stretches 7,644km (4,750 miles) across the barren steppe, according to people interviewed for this article. “There’s total contraband along the border,” Timur, a businessman in Almaty, Kazakhstan’s capital, told Al Jazeera. He withheld his last name for safety reasons. Advertisement Even though Kazakhstan boasts three giant, Soviet-era oil refineries, fuel prices in Kazakhstan increased by 15.6 percent this year, the UlusMedia website reported on July 10 . Only one of Kazakhstan’s neighbours, Turkmenistan, has large hydrocarbon reserves, but its autocratic leaders isolated the country from the rest of the region in the 1990s. ‘Deficit here for a long time’ Other Central Asian nations feel the ripple effect too – especially Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, resource-poor, mountainous nations that used to get up to 90 percent of their petrol from Russia. “They’ve been hurt the most,” Galiya Ibragimova, a Moldova-based expert on Central Asia with Carnegie Politika, which is headquartered in Berlin, told Al Jazeera. Kyrgyzstan is a member of the Eurasian Economic Union, the free trade bloc of five former Soviet nations dominated by Russia and the Kremlin’s political decisions. Tajikistan is not a member of the group, but it bought discounted Russian fuel as “payment for political loyalty, not because Putin is so kind”, Ibragimova said. A key source of petrol for Central Asia was Russia’s largest refinery in the city of Omsk in southwestern Siberia. But it stopped operating after Ukrainian drone attacks in early July that damaged a crude distillation unit. Around that time, Kyrgyzstan began regulating petrol prices and asked other ex-Soviet nations for help to “ensure sustainable fuel supplies”. Kyrgyz experts predict long-term problems at Russian refineries will take months or even years to fix. “Equipment for oil refineries is not a delivery from an online shop or a supermarket,” Kyrgyz energy expert Olzhas Baydildinov said in televised remarks. “The deficit that has come is here for a long time.” The Kyrgyz government pledged to “provide at least a half” of Kyrgyzstan’s needs – but only after modernising the nation’s largest refinery, deputy energy minister Nasipbek Kerimov said in early July. He did not specify how long it would take. By the middle of this month, Kyrgyz authorities said they had spent about $11.4m to subsidise petrol prices. China’s help in drilling Tajikistan is especially vulnerable because domestic oil processing amounts to 0.5 percent of petrol consumed there. Drivers already face fuel shortages and limits of 20 litres per car at some petrol stations. “There are problems both in the [processing of oil] and in logistics,” deputy energy minister Daler Juma said in early July, when announcing that the government had amassed fuel reserves that would last “at least 60 days”. Advertisement In mid-August, he travelled to Tehran and signed a deal to provide 2.5 million tonnes of oil, petrol and diesel from Iran. With the help of experts from the giant state-owned China National Petroleum Corporation, Tajikistan has intensified the search for prospective oil fields. By the end of this year, they are due to submit a report on seismic reconnaissance, a method of quickly assessing potential oil reserves. “Then, we will decide where we can start drilling,” Tajikistan’s chief geologist, Ilhomjon Oymukhammadzoda, told a news conference in early July. Uzbekistan’s ‘reserves’ for winter Both Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan used to resell Russian petrol to neighbouring Uzbekistan, the regional economic powerhouse with a population of almost 39 million and half a dozen car manufacturing companies. As Uzbekistan processes its own oil into petrol satisfying about two-thirds of its needs, the rest usually comes from Russia. But the new shortages have forced the government to start amassing a strategic reserve. “We have a separate plan for the fall and winter, we’ve created enough reserves. I can say with confidence that we have enough reserves for two or three months,” deputy energy minister, Umid Mamadaminov, said early last month. Meanwhile, many Uzbek drivers are happy they switched their engines to run on compressed natural gas – even though huge gas tanks take up most of the boot. “I switched 15 years ago, saved a lot of money,” Azamat Tolipov, a taxi driver in the Uzbek capital, Tashkent, told Al Jazeera. Regional governments are trying to find new sources of oil and gas, but the United States and Israeli war on Iran drives global prices up. “Central Asian nations will convulsively look for new suppliers, but considering what’s going on in the Strait of Hormuz , even if they find an alternative, it will be more expensive,” analyst Ibragimova predicted. Beijing seems to be the only power to benefit from the fuel crisis as sales of Chinese-made electric cars skyrocketed even before it unfolded. Electric car sales in Kazakhstan alone grew 36 times between 2022 and 2025, said the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, a Berlin-based think tank in last year’s report titled: “China has flooded Central Asia with electric cars”.

body: Listen (3 mins) Save Share Kazakhstan’s newly formed pro-government party wins parliamentary election on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Electoral commission staff in Almaty count parliamentary election votes after polling stations closed after Sunday's election [Pavel Mikheyev/Reuters] By AFP and Reuters Published On 24 Aug 2026 24 Aug 2026 Kazakhstan’s pro-government Adilet party won more than 71 percent of the vote in Sunday’s parliamentary election , said the electoral commission in a result likely to consolidate the power of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev . Announcing the results on Monday, the commission said that four other blocs also entered parliament: the pro-business Respublika and Ak Zhol parties, the centre-left Nationwide Social Democratic Party and the Auyl party, which represents rural voters. According to the commission, 74 percent of eligible voters cast ballots to choose the new 145-member, single-chamber parliament, called the Kurultai. Approximately 12.6 million of the 20 million population were eligible to vote. Adilet was founded in the Central Asian nation earlier this year and is led by Tokayev’s top aides. Shortly after its inception, it absorbed the previous ruling party, Amanat. All four other parties entering parliament are also seen as broadly supportive of Tokayev’s administration. Sunday’s election was triggered by a new constitution adopted earlier this year, which streamlined parliament from two chambers into one. Kazakhstan’s Supreme Court ruled last month that the new constitution allows Tokayev to run for a new seven-year term. Officials say that the structural change aims to give parliament more weight in political decision-making. Previously, it was confined to a largely auxiliary role under a system that concentrated power in the presidency. A former Soviet diplomat and top United Nations official, Tokayev has led Central Asia’s largest economy since 2019, maintaining warm relations with the West, Russia and China. Advertisement Tokayev has also championed a reform programme called “Just Kazakhstan”. The initiative followed riots in 2022 when 238 people were killed as cost-of-living protests escalated. The 73-year-old president said he is trying to move away from the legacy of his authoritarian predecessor, Nursultan Nazarbayev , who ruled for three decades after the collapse of the Soviet Union. Tokayev originally took office as the chosen successor of Nazarbayev, Kazakhstan’s founding president, who governed from 1991 to 2019. While voting in the capital, Astana, Tokayev told journalists it was too early to say whether he would seek another term. He also said that he would name his choice for vice president, the newly created office under the new constitution, within the next seven to 10 days, adding that it would be a “well-known” person.

body: Listen (2 mins) Save Share Polls close in Kazakhstan parliamentary elections; vote count under way on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google People vote at a polling station during snap parliamentary elections in Almaty, Kazakhstan, on August 23, 2026 [Pavel Mikheyev/Reuters] By AFP and Reuters Published On 23 Aug 2026 23 Aug 2026 Polls have closed in Kazakhstan’s snap parliamentary elections, which are expected to further strengthen the power of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. Voting concluded on Sunday at 8pm (03:00 GMT), and Central Election Commission officials began counting ballots. According to the commission, 74 percent of about 12 million eligible voters cast their votes to choose a new single-chamber, 145-member parliament called the Kurultai. The pro-Tokayev Adilet party is widely predicted to win an overwhelming majority, according to The Associated Press news agency, and several smaller parties loyal to Tokayev are also expected to enter parliament. Sunday’s vote was the culmination of a constitutional overhaul that Tokayev initiated in March when 87 percent of voters supported a referendum to abolish Kazakhstan’s upper house in favour of a unicameral parliament. Officials said the change would give parliament more weight in political decision-making, having previously been confined to a mostly auxiliary role. However, only seven state-approved parties, all loyal to Tokayev, have been allowed to put forth candidates. The constitutional changes also reset term limits to allow Tokayev to run again in 2029. He has led the Central Asian country since 2019. The 73-year-old was the chosen successor of longtime leader Nursultan Nazarbayev , who ruled for almost 30 years from the 1990s. But Tokayev broke with his predecessor amid cost-of-living protests in 2022 that led to the deaths of 238 people and has since touted a reform agenda called “Just Kazakhstan”. Advertisement The election came at a difficult economic moment for Kazakhstan as inflation hit 10.2 percent in February and tax hikes have fuelled public discontent. The vote also took place against a backdrop of intensifying crackdowns on media freedom. Media organisations have urged Tokayev to drop criminal charges against several journalists under house arrest and to revise legislation to ensure media freedom. Authorities have opened roughly 10 criminal cases against independent journalists and popular bloggers. A former Soviet state, Kazakhstan balances relations with China, Europe and Russia, and Tokayev has had to navigate recent tensions over Moscow’s war with Ukraine. Kazakhstan is oil-rich and produces about 2 percent of the world’s daily supply, mostly exporting to European countries through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium to Russia’s port of Novorossiysk. Tokayev, who has sought to maintain a delicate balance between Moscow and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over the war in Ukraine, has justified the constitutional changes by citing the need for rapid decision-making in a fast-changing world.
title: Polls close in Kazakhstan parliamentary elections; vote count under way

body: Listen (7 mins) Save Share Kazakhstan parliamentary elections begin: What’s at stake? on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google A woman casts her ballot at a polling station during early parliamentary elections in Almaty, Kazakhstan [Vladimir Tretyakov/AP Photo] By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters Published On 23 Aug 2026 23 Aug 2026 | Updated: 23 Aug 2026 10:35 AM (GMT) Updated: 23 Aug 2026 10:35 AM (GMT) Voting is under way in Kazakhstan for a snap parliamentary election that is expected to strengthen President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s rule over the country. The last parliamentary elections were in 2023. The election comes just weeks after Kazakhstan, a nation of 21 million that borders Russia and China, revamped its legislative system by introducing constitutional changes and shifting from a dual-chamber parliament to a single-chamber one as it seeks to assert itself as a major democratic power in Central Asia. How does the election process work and what’s at stake? Here’s what we know: When is the election happening? Elections for the 145 seats of the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral legislature, is taking place on Sunday. To enter government, parties must receive at least 5 percent of the overall vote. Before July 1, when Kazakhstan’s new constitutional system came into effect, the parliament was bicameral, with the Mazhilis (lower house) and Senate (upper house). On the day the new system came into effect, President Tokayev signed a decree calling the snap election. According to national media outlet Astana Times, under the previous system, “legislation passed through the Mazhilis before moving to the Senate. Under the new model, the Kurultai concentrates legislative consideration, and adopted laws are then sent to the President.” Under the new constitutional system, presidents will only be permitted to serve a single, seven-year term. However, when his current, second term as president is up, Tokayev will be able to run for a third seven-year term of office, since the introduction of the new legislature resets his time in office. Advertisement He won the last presidential election, in 2022, with more than 80 percent of the vote, having run largely unchallenged, as all five of his competitors were unknowns. International observers will attend the parliamentary election on Sunday. The OSCE Parliamentary Assembly announced last week that nearly 80 parliamentarians and staff from about 30 countries would be deployed to observe the election. Pedestrians walk past an electronic screen promoting the Adilet (Justice) party before Kazakhstan’s upcoming parliamentary election in Almaty, Kazakhstan, August 17, 2026 [Pavel Mikheyev/Reuters] Who is contesting in this year’s election? Seven political parties are fielding candidates in this year’s elections. These include the newly formed Adilet party, Auyl, Aq Jol, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party, Baytaq, and Respublica. Amanat, the party that has dominated Kazakh politics under various names since the 1990s, officially voted to dissolve itself into Adilet – which means “Justice” – a new party led by top aides to Tokayev, in June this year, largely to distance itself from Amanat’s former leader, the previous President Nursultan Nazarbayev. Nazarbayev , who was once close to Tokayev and considered his mentor, was the country’s president from 1991 to 2019. While he led economic modernisation of the country, his rule was defined by corruption, civil unrest and authoritarianism. He was elected president five times in widely criticised votes. In the run-up to the election on Sunday, Adilet has been running on the campaign message of “Just Kazakhstan”, pledging to raise household incomes, strengthen the country’s economy and improve public services, infrastructure and digitalisation. Around Almaty, Kazakhstan’s largest city, election posters – mostly in support of Adilet – have been ubiquitous for weeks, the Reuters news agency reported. Opinion polls suggest the new party is likely to win a large majority of the vote, with a number of smaller opposition parties, which analysts also consider broadly loyal to Tokayev, also likely to enter parliament. The Aq Jol Democratic Party is running on a campaign pledging support for entrepreneurship, while the Auyl party is advocating for stronger rural communities and the Baytaq Green Party is campaigning on the environment. Kazakh political analyst Rustam Burnashev told Reuters that while this snap election offers Tokayev a chance to remove figures associated with his predecessor, Nazarbayev, from the political stage, major reform of the political system is unlikely. Advertisement Despite the new Adilet party having been formed to distance itself from Nazarbayev’s legacy, analysts say little is likely to change materially. “All the parliamentary candidates are known,” Burnashev said. “Nor can one say that the parliament itself will be a transformative one.” Although Kazakhstan has enjoyed rapid economic growth in recent years, tax rises and inflation have hit living standards. Atapsha, a fruit seller who declined to give his full name, told Reuters that he would cast a vote, but without any particular expectations. “I am 73 years old. I’ve been waiting for things to get better for 73 years, but so far, nothing has really worked out. Still, I hope that this year things will finally improve.” What’s at stake? In 2022, Tokayev launched the “New Kazakhstan” package of reforms for the political system. A referendum was held on the legislative changes, which came in in July. Analysts say the upcoming elections will determine if the country’s new leaders can adhere to the renewed unicameral legislature and uphold its foreign policy. Besides these changes in the country’s legislative makeup, the elections come at a time when Astana is trying to showcase itself as a democracy and key power in Central Asia. To this end, Tokayev has focused on revamping the country’s infrastructure and economy and expanding ties with both China and the European Union. The country has also been beefing up relations with the United States in recent years. Last November, Kazakhstan signed a $4.2bn agreement with the US locomotive parts maker Wabtec. According to the US Department of Commerce, the deal will provide Kazakhstan with 300 kits to build locomotives for the Kazakh national rail company, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy. US President Donald Trump took to Truth Social to trumpet the deal, referring to it as “the largest Railroad Equipment Purchase in History”. Traditionally close to Russia, the country has preferred to play a neutral role in Moscow’s war on Ukraine and has called for peace. It has also offered itself as a venue for peace talks in the US-Iran war. In an article published in April by the Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs at Harvard Kennedy School, Nargis Kassenova wrote: “Kazakhstan has begun positioning itself as a middle power.” According to the Bureau of National Statistics, Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product (GDP) increased by 6.5 percent to about US$335bn in 2025 compared with last year, using the consumption method of calculations. “While a ‘lightweight’ by conventional standards, it has assets that make it significant for the rest of the world. Its geostrategic location at the heart of Eurasia makes it both an important connector and buffer between Europe, Russia, the Middle East, South Asia, and East Asia. It is also a regional leader in Central Asia,” she wrote.
