body: Frequently Asked Questions on OCCRP’s Funding and Editorial Policies | OCCRP About About Us Our Team Board of Directors Our Global Network Annual Reports Impact Awards OCCRP Under Attack Support Us Frequently Asked Questions on OCCRP’s Funding and Editorial Policies Where does OCCRP get its money? We are a donor-funded nonprofit organization. The breakdown of our donors changes every year, but typically we received funding from governmental donors, including from the UK, Sweden, Denmark, and New Zealand, as well as a number of private foundations that support investigative journalism and private individuals. In total, we have around 50 separate grants from these donors. We are always working on diversifying our sources of funding in order to remain financially stable. A few years ago, we launched the “Accomplice” membership program as part of this effort. Transparency is important to us, and our annual reports, audits, and 990 nonprofit tax forms are all available online. We have a four-star rating from Charity Navigator , which ranks U.S.-based nonprofits on their financial accountability and transparency, and a platinum seal of transparency from Candid/Guide Star, a similar organization. If you’d like to learn more, here are some publicly available sources of information on our donors and finances: Our recent annual reports and financial statements Our 990 forms and audits on ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer A list of our donors What does OCCRP do with this funding? In addition to our editorial work, which includes collaborating with local journalists to produce and publish investigations, we also provide our network with research and data support. This includes access to a team of experienced cross-border researchers who can help journalists anywhere in the world track down corporate records or land titles half a world away. We also provide our network, and other journalists in need, with digital and physical security support. Over the years, we’ve also helped independent investigative journalists in countries like Russia, Serbia, Romania, Solomon Islands, Georgia, and Slovenia set up their own media organizations. We provide support, resources, experience, and encouragement, but our partners are independent of OCCRP and make their own editorial decisions. A large proportion of the money we received from donors is also “passed through” OCCRP and distributed to local media organizations that might have trouble getting larger grants on their own. How does OCCRP decide what stories to publish? OCCRP is a network of journalists who live in every corner of the world. Compared to traditional media outlets, we are very decentralized, and most of our investigations come from local partners who bring us the stories they feel are important to tell. Their ideas are then developed in collaboration with a team of editors who work globally. Some of our stories also come from large data leaks, which we are well-equipped to work with thanks to our investigative data platform Aleph, or from human sources who come to us with tips and information about wrongdoing. Sometimes our central editorial team also decides to pursue stories or projects on topics we have special expertise in. When a reporter in our network wants us to publish a story, we assess it along several lines. We look at whether the story uncovers wrongdoing, breaks new ground, matters to citizens and is in the public interest, and has the potential to be impactful or important, either locally or internationally. We prioritize stories that uncover significant wrongdoing, particularly related to corruption, organized crime, and their nexus with political power. Because our investigations cover very serious issues, we also need to make sure that we can prove our claims — through documentary evidence whenever possible. Our editors strive to ensure that every story we publish meets high standards of proof, fairness, and clarity. What OCCRP does not do is tell partners what to publish. Even though OCCRP may provide money for a story, our partners always have the right to run their own stories from their own perspective. This diversity of viewpoints makes the content of our network stronger. Can you run a story if you don’t have a donation for it? Absolutely — and, in fact, we do not accept donations to do specific stories or projects. The process works the other way around: Our editorial team comes up with projects and story ideas, and after they are published, administrative staff members determine how to charge these stories against grants we have received. Since stories are assigned to grants retrospectively, journalists working on them do not know who paid for the work. Does OCCRP accept US government money? In the past we have, but as of mid-2025, OCCRP has minimal U.S. government money. A decision by the current U.S. administration ended most foreign assistance in early 2025, including funding for almost all media work. This included the closure of all but three of our U.S. grants, which we expect will close soon. OCCRP has sued the U.S. Department of State and the Trump administration for the illegal closure of the grants. We did not do this in order to maintain our funding — we understood the current U.S. administration would not continue to support the important work we do — but because we saw this decision as illegal. Under the U.S. Constitution, what the government spends is decided by Congress and not the executive branch. We are obligated by ethical practices to speak out when illegal actions occur. The case is ongoing. Do OCCRP’s donors have any influence over editorial policy? No. Just like a traditional newspaper, which maintains a strict “firewall” between its advertising and editorial departments, we have a division between staff who handle donations and those who produce the journalism. Donors never have access to editorial meetings or any aspect of our editorial process, nor do they have input into what stories we publish. We also guarantee our editorial independence by adding written language into relevant grant agreements that explicitly states we will retain complete editorial control over our work. Here is what that looks like: A clause from a multi-year grant from USAID to OCCRP in 2022. A clause from a multi-year grant from USAID to OCCRP in 2022. How can I find out more about your funding? OCCRP discloses all of our donors publicly. Here are some ways in which we do it. We provide financial statements in our annual reports, available on our website. This is an extract from our most recent report, from 2023. We provide financial statements in our annual reports, available on our website. This is an extract from our most recent report, from 2023. An excerpt from our 2022 annual report, showing how we list our donors. An excerpt from our 2022 annual report, showing how we list our donors. We break down our individual grants in annual audit reports, which are publicly available here . This shows grants we received in 2023. We break down our individual grants in annual audit reports, which are publicly available here . This shows grants we received in 2023. Do donations come with conditions for what you can and cannot write about? No. OCCRP only takes funding on the condition that we exercise complete editorial independence. You can read our donation acceptance policy here . We do apply for some geographically or thematically focused grants, meaning that the work must be completed in a specific country or region or broad theme. We pursue these grants only when their terms align with our mission, and when we are already trying to expand our work in these areas. All donors, both governmental and private, have areas of interest, and this will always be a limitation of grant-supported organizations. This is why OCCRP also raises what is known as “core funding,” which gives us funds we can use for any purpose, including reporting on countries not specifically funded by a major donor. Becau
title: Funding and Editorial Policies

body: Gift and Donation Acceptance Policy | OCCRP About About Us Our Team Board of Directors Our Global Network Annual Reports Impact Awards OCCRP Under Attack Support Us Gift and Donation Acceptance Policy The Journalism Development Network, doing business as the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), a U.S.-registered 501(c)(3) tax exempt corporation, solicits and accepts gifts from sources that support the advancement of our core mission, including: our core work; relevant projects; our member centers; the long-term sustainability of the organization. Sources of Funding Donations and other forms of support will generally be accepted from individuals, foundations, charitable organizations, educational organizations, governments, and corporations. Donations are subject to limitations and OCCRP reserves the right to decline any donation that it believes will threaten or undermine our mission. OCCRP seeks to be transparent with its funding and will err on the side of disclosing donors. OCCRP reserves the right to decline any gift. For example, we do not accept funds: from elected officials, political parties, or candidates seeking public office; that may have been illegally obtained; that could otherwise pose a conflict of interest to the organization; that could otherwise cause reputational damage to the organization; that could in any way compromise our editorial or operational independence. Editorial Independence In all cases, OCCRP retains complete editorial independence and never promises specific stories, nor do we accept funds for specific stories or funds that require donor approval of stories. OCCRP retains full discretion, independence, and authority over our editorial content and policy on all projects. Our news judgments are based solely on matters of newsworthiness, public interest, and journalism principles and not on the basis of donor support. Accepting support does not constitute an endorsement of the activities of our donors. Donors are not aware of specific stories the newsroom is working on, do not review them before publication, and have no influence over findings. Public Disclosure OCCRP is dedicated to making transparent its sources of funding and, as a matter of practice, publicly discloses its donors. Our standard practice is to cite all institutional donors and support on our website and in our annual report and tax statements. Individual donations equaling more than two percent of our annual operating budget will also be included in our annual report; all individual donations over $5,000 must be disclosed to U.S. tax authorities. The Internal Revenue Service redacts all donor identifying information before making tax returns publicly available. Due to the sensitive nature of our work exposing organized crime and corruption, we also recognize that certain supporters may need to give anonymously. Anonymous gifts from individuals and donor-advised funds for unrestricted support will be accepted if they are less than two percent of OCCRP's annual operating budget. Anonymous gifts above this amount will be considered on a case-by-case basis. Should OCCRP receive a gift that violates this policy and is unable to return it, OCCRP will make a contribution to a charitable organization for an amount that exceeds the policy. Definitions Gifts are defined as cash donations or in-kind contributions. OCCRP will calculate a fair market price for in-kind contributions. Gifts include unrestricted support and gifts designated for broad categories of work or restricted editorial coverage. OCCRP is required to ensure that all gifts meet the benchmark of charitable and education support for tax deductibility. Sources of gifts may include individuals, donor-advised funds with clear and transparent origins, foundations, governments, corporations, and anonymous donors up to 1 percent of annual expenses per calendar year. Grants to External Organizations In agreement with the donor, OCCRP can subgrant and pass through funds to member centers, individual journalists, and partner organizations. The process for sub-granting funds to organizations is as follows: JDN transfers funds to third parties, being individuals or legal entities, by way of grants, sub-grants, sub-contracts (in some cases) or other financial support (“forwarding of funds”). Sub-grants (also known as sub-awards), are usually for third parties charged with meeting all or a set of grant project deliverables directly, over and above merely providing related services. Sub-contracts are usually for specific services, products, or tangible deliverables. Beneficiary Agreements are usually for core support or development. Personal Data Security OCCRP will not sell, rent, or share the personal or contact information of donors with any other individuals or organizations. Contact information will be used only to update the donor on OCCRP activities and initiatives, send information on fundraising campaigns, and express appreciation for the donor's support. OCCRP does not store payment information: Credit card numbers and expiration dates are not kept on paper or electronically. OCCRP's intent is to comply with the regulations and laws regarding donations of the states in which it operates. Although all software is carefully vetted, OCCRP is not responsible for any actions or behaviors of third-party payment processors. Crypto Assets The IRS classifies cryptocurrencies as property, so cryptocurrency donations to 501(c)(3) charities receive the same tax treatment as stocks. Donating cryptocurrency is a non-taxable event, meaning you do not owe capital gains tax on the appreciated amount and can deduct it on your taxes. Please contact your tax or financial adviser for more information. Cryptocurrency may be sold immediately or held as an asset as decided by OCCRP financial policy. OCCRP can only accept anonymous donations of cryptocurrency amounting to less than two percent of its annual expenses per calendar year. Anonymous donations of cryptocurrency are not tax deductible. Adopted by the Board of Directors on December 14, 2021. Support fearless reporting. Unlock crucial insights. Donate Your donation powers investigations that expose organized crime and corruption worldwide. As a supporter, you’ll also gain access to events and insights only available to our donors. Give today and get the inside take. Donate

Aid and Policy Podcasts 8 September 2026 Rethinking Humanitarianism | The rise of privatised aid: A conversation with Fogbow Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email GENEVA Our editors’ weekly take on humanitarian news, trends, and developments from around the globe. On our radar UK leads 12 countries in announcing major shift on Israeli settlements Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced a major shift in UK policy toward Israel, recognising Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as illegal, and condemning the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians by “settler terrorists”. In a speech to parliament on 8 September, Miliband said the UK would ban goods from Israeli settlements, sanction companies and individuals involved in settlement expansion, and refuse to export weapons to Israel that support the occupation. Eleven other countries – including Canada, France, Ireland, Spain, and Sweden – joined the UK in announcing similar moves. Some Palestinians in the West Bank – where settlement expansion and violence have spiralled – cautiously welcomed the announcement as a good though belated step. Others preferred to reserve judgement to gauge its real impact. The UK and other Western governments have long been accused of inertia, if not complicity, when it comes to Israel’s actions in the West Bank and the war on Gaza. Miliband did touch on Gaza, stating the UK’s support for the case brought by South Africa at the International Court of Justice that accused Israel of genocide. But there were few other specifics, other than calling for the full implementation of US President Donald Trump’s stalled 20-point peace plan. Sudan’s chemical weapons programme revealed The Sudanese military ran an alleged chemical weapons programme in 2024 for use against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), according to an intelligence dossier reviewed by the New York Times and Washington Post . Chlorine gas cylinders were reportedly sourced from global markets and from a water treatment plant in a Sudanese city, where they had been donated by aid groups to stem cholera outbreaks. It is unclear how often the munitions were deployed, though the alleged programme appears to have ended last year after the US determined that chemical weapons had been used and imposed sanctions. France 24 also reported their use . The New York Times and Washington Post received the dossier from an unnamed Middle Eastern intelligence agency, which Le Monde and Middle East Eye reported was Israeli. Israel is an ally of the UAE, the RSF’s main backer, and has held meetings with senior RSF officials during the war. Both the RSF and the Israeli government have carried out genocide crimes, according to human rights investigators. Lebanon civilians killed as Israel escalates bombing Israel says it has destroyed a network of Hezbollah tunnels in south Lebanon, in a blast so heavy it triggered a 4.1 magnitude tremor . While Defence Minister Israel Katz said the move “completes the achievement of operational control” over the area, the escalation in attacks has destroyed homes and killed civilians. On 7 September alone, 12 people were reportedly killed in strikes on a residential building and a vehicle. The recent wave of attacks has forced around 20,000 people to flee the district of Nabatieh, including people who were able to return home after a June agreement between Lebanon and Israel that led to a decrease in fighting and bombing – but certainly not an end. “The last few days are a devastating reminder that a reduction in widespread attacks is not the same as safety,” Maureen Philippon, Lebanon country director for the Norwegian Refugee Council said in a statement . “Children are being killed in their homes, health facilities are being hit, and communities that have already endured months of displacement remain exposed to near-daily hostilities.” Yemenis forced to flee as battles rage Yemen’s Houthi rebels have seized the Red Sea port city of Mokha and an island in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, consolidating their control over the shipping route to the Red Sea. The Houthis, who control much of north Yemen, say they only plan to target ships coming from Saudi Arabia. The kingdom has relied heavily on the Bab al-Mandeb strait to export oil since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The strategic port is not the only place in Yemen where the Houthis and government-allied forces are fighting anew. There are battles in al-Jawf, which lies between Houthi and government-controlled regions, as well as in Taiz . Aid groups have pointed out that the renewed violence has displaced 46,000 people in just a week , with entire villages emptying and Yemen’s already strained health system coming under serious pressure. The state we’re in: a humanitarian system in retreat What a difference four years makes. When research outfit ALNAP issued its last State of the Humanitarian System report in 2022 , the COVID-19 pandemic was easing, organisations were expanding, and aid budgets were peaking . Fast forward to today, and the mood has turned dire. A “generational funding collapse” has forced the system into retreat, states the latest version of the landmark report, published on 10 September . The indicators are stark: 64 million fewer people are receiving aid, there’s no safety net for those left behind, and funding has plummeted by at least 30%. The process of picking and choosing who gets help – often called “ prioritisation ” in the UN-coordinated system – means people have to be increasingly desperate before aid can step in, yet the aid they receive is often not what they want. Despite the tectonic shift forced on today’s sector, some things sound achingly similar. Years-old promises to shift power, both reports highlight , are happening far too slowly. In 2022, it was a warning to improve amid rising costs, soaring needs, and worsening access. In 2026, it’s a missed opportunity for a system at the breaking point. Opening the door to the benefits of migration in Africa Migration stirs populist sentiments worldwide. In Africa, that’s currently playing out in Kenya (see below) and South Africa, with xenophobia usually a proxy for domestic policy failure . In South Africa, where GDP per capita has not increased for over 20 years, it’s easier to scapegoat migrants than fix the problem. Yet the evidence shows migration delivers economic growth, and the continent’s future will be shaped, in part, by the movement of people, skills, and labour, a recent Out of Africa podcast by CSIS-Africa suggests. Harnessing the benefits will take vision and policy commitment . Twelve million young Africans enter the labour market each year, but only three million formal jobs are created. The kneejerk reaction is to shut the door to “foreigners”. Yet the development potential of migration can be leveraged by: upskilling ; matching those skills to local opportunities ; and clearing away the obstacles to legal employment. Much is being made of the African Continental Free Trade Area and the push for deeper regional integration. But that shouldn’t just be about the free movement of goods but also a more liberal regime for people. body: Home Asia Iran Related stories Conflict Feature 3 September 2026 Lives on hold: Young Iranians watch their futures slip away Media and culture Podcasts 7 July 2026 Decolonise How? | Lessons on media ethics from the Middle East Series Decolonise How? When disasters and humanitarian emergencies unfold, the narratives that follow shape public perception, policy, and response. More of this in-depth coverage Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email Lisbon On 24 July, The New Humanitarian (TNH) published an Instagram post recapping the third round of the war waged by the US against Iran. It named four American soldiers who had been killed in Iranian airstrikes in Iraq and Jordan. Missing from the post were the Iranians: 55 people killed in US strikes since 27 June and hundreds injured. Why was this remarkable? Because TNH is not just any media outlet. It calls itself a “mission-driven, impact-seeking, decolonial organisation” and has made decolonising its journalism a strategic priority . Such claims create expectations. Not one to stay silent, I raised this omission in the comments section, asking rather bluntly whether TNH considered Iranian casualties not worth mentioning. To its credit, TNH responded immediately, deleting the post within minutes and replacing it with one captioned : “Edited, Iranian casualties added to slide 2.” The omission was probably not deliberate, but that is precisely why it matters. Nobody had to decide that Iranian deaths were unworthy of mention. Four American soldiers registered immediately, 55 Iranians did not. Adding them corrected the post, but it did not explain how a country with a population of over 90 million people under attack could initially be overlooked. If this can happen in a decolonial newsroom committed to centering people affected by crises, what should we expect from organisations without that commitment? Iran is a textbook example of a country that is hyper-visible while its people are rendered invisible. I choose this example, not just because I’m Iranian-American, but because Iran is everywhere in the news: nuclear weapons, sanctions, security threats, regime change, and the never-ending Strait of Hormuz saga. Yet, Iranians are harder to find: civilians, political prisoners, journalists, women, queer and minoritised people, aid workers, Afghan migrants and refugees – people surviving and dying because of decisions they never made. That invisibility matters far beyond whether a decolonial newsroom acknowledges deaths caused by an imperial power: When Trump threatens the annihilation of Iranian civilisation, the silence from media and humanitarian organisations makes these threats politically viable. The silence is therefore consequential. The Iranian people are doubly invisible as a population caught between imperial violence and domestic repression, a bind that shapes what gets reported and funded. The Islamic Republic has become interchangeable with its population, erasing the population’s agency. After successive rounds of aggression by the United States and Israel, Iran has been exalted as the last bastion against imperialism. The dilemma is that though Iran is rightly aggrieved under international law, the Islamic Republic is also an autocratic theocracy that arrests and executes its own citizens daily. The right sees only a regime to be overthrown, presenting the violent, illegal war as liberation. Trump’s own rhetoric already embodies this logic of annihilation recast as liberation. In doing so, it usurps Iranians’ role as authors of their own future. Parts of the left demand a choice between condemning imperialist violence and condemning the regime, as if the two cannot coexist. Kamran Matin and Somayeh Rostampoor call this campism. It protects states, not people. Iran’s right to resist imperialist aggression is real, and so is the war being fought against it. That is not in dispute. What campism does is take that one legitimate fact and use it to bury another: in this case, that this is a regime with a long record of authoritarian repression now using the war to deepen it. Campism recasts anyone resisting the regime as a foreign plot rather than a popular uprising, erasing the fact that they are the same people risking their lives against both the war and the regime. Both positions narrow the stories journalists tell, the statements humanitarian leaders make, and the suffering donors will fund. Iranians disappear when they cannot fit neatly into either political camp. Whose suffering is funded? Visibility is not just a backdrop to humanitarian response; it is a determinant of it. Money follows attention, shaped by three actors: media deciding what counts as a story, humanitarian organisations deciding what counts as a crisis worth naming, and politicians deciding which victims are convenient to grieve. Iran’s underfunding is what happens when all three fail at once. Attention does not mechanically dictate funding decisions , bureaucratic priorities and government interests shape them too; but it determines which crises get named as crises in the first place, and that naming is where the failure begins. The scale should have made failure impossible: Iran has endured four rounds of war in just over a year. The 12-day air war in June 2025 killed more than 1,000 people. The second, beginning on 28 February 2026, killed nearly 3,500 people and injured more than 32,000. Millions fled, almost 150,000 civilian buildings were damaged. Two further rounds of US strikes have killed dozens more. During the most recent, a US missile struck a wedding in Kuhestak , killing four civilians and injuring dozens, including children. Humanitarian leaders should defend the universality of aid, not allow donor politics determine whose suffering is recognised or funded. At least nine Iranian Red Crescent Society staff and volunteers have been killed. I work in a sector that regularly insists aid workers are not targets, yet I recall no outrage over these nine colleagues. The contrast with responses elsewhere was flagrant: the same erasure that produced the TNH slide, now at sectoral scale. International media was present in Iran throughout the strikes – filing, verifying, present on the ground. And even there, Iranian deaths still went uncounted. In Gaza, they aren’t present at all – barred from entering, while Palestinian journalists reporting the same deaths aren’t treated as credible enough to confirm them on their own. That exposes “we can’t confirm the casualties” as a hollow excuse: The only source treated as trustworthy is absent from Gaza and proved unreliable in Iran even when it was there. Humanitarian leadership followed the same pattern of delay and euphemism. Tom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, made his first (and so far only) public statement on Iran on 15 April 2026, after two wars had passed. It announced $12 million from the UN’s emergency fund . It said infrastructure had been destroyed and services disrupted, but it did not say by whom, nor whose lives were lost, nor that aid workers had been killed – the passive language made military violence sound like a natural disaster. Fletcher is representative, not an outlier. Many of the humanitarian system’s largest donors are also waging or supporting the war against Iran. Humanitarian leaders should defend the universality of aid, not allow donor politics determine whose suffering is recognised or funded. Politicians complete the circuit: They protect suffering that fits their alliances. Iranian civilians killed by US and Israeli strikes are inconvenient for governments allied with one or both; those imprisoned by their own state are inconvenient for anyone whose politics require a tidy narrative of resistance. Both categories need a political sponsor to be seen. Neither has one. The funding record shows what these three compounded failures look like in dollars. The

Humanitarian finance Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email GENEVA Norwegian People’s Aid will turn down millions in US government funding due to wide-reaching restrictions on reproductive health and equity, the mine action group announced, in a rare example of a humanitarian organisation publicly rejecting US cash. The decision could affect 40% of NPA’s de-mining budget and 1,700 jobs, and will have “major consequences” for the organisation, NPA said. Few humanitarian groups have spoken publicly about the so-called “global gag rules” since the Trump administration expanded the discriminatory restrictions this year . The regulations, known as the Mexico City policy, handcuff organisations receiving US cash even if potentially banned work is paid for in separate budgets by other donors. Over decades, the US has repeatedly rescinded then reinstated the global gag rule as the government lurches between Democrat and Republican-led administrations. “I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years.” Previous versions have tried to block organisations that receive US health funding from providing or promoting abortion care as part of family planning – even if the money came from other sources. This year, the Trump administration has expanded the rules to cover almost all foreign aid including humanitarian funding, and to target gender identity and diversity, equity, and inclusion. “We see that a more rights-based approach is being challenged globally,” Gry Ballestad, NPA’s director of policy and communications, said in an interview. “And I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years.” The restrictions affecting NPA cover funding from the US State Department’s Office of Weapons Removal and Abatement. Critics say the global gag rules are an attempt to co-opt international aid along US ideological lines. The US made drastic cuts to humanitarian budgets when it dismantled its aid programme last year, which could lead to millions of deaths, a study published in The Lancet estimated. But other governments are also cutting back – leaving the US as a top humanitarian donor that can shape how and where the system works by sheer volume. For example, the US has earmarked some $3.75 billion to UN-run pooled funds – roughly 83% of total funds so far, and $3.6 billion more than the next largest donor. It has also promised hundreds of millions more directly to UN agencies like the World Food Programme and UNICEF, or non-governmental organisations like World Vision . The initial $2 billion to UN pooled funds was signed just before the global gag rule’s new restrictions came into effect. Ballestad spoke to The New Humanitarian about NPA’s decision, its consequences, and what this moment means for the wider humanitarian and development sectors. This interview was edited for length and clarity. The New Humanitarian: Can you describe the decision-making process: What were the considerations? Gry Ballestad: It’s been a difficult decision given the implications, the programmes it affects around the world, the size of the funding, all the people that will be losing their jobs, and the impact on the ground. It’s been a very difficult decision to take. In [2026], the big change for us was that now the requirements are not just for the American funding – not just the mine action programmes funded by the State Department, but it would affect also all our other activities and programmes... This would put limitations on everything we do – not just the American funding. When we started working with the Americans, these were not the requirements we signed on to – actually, quite the opposite. For a long time, it’s been a requirement that we do take into consideration equal opportunities and all these things that are now a problem. We see that now, with the change in the requirements, and looking at our core values and principles, that it’s such a big change that we cannot accept it. Because there’s a change in the regulation, we would basically have to change our core values, our activities – really, who we are. NPA is not just working on mine action. We are the humanitarian solidarity organisation of the labour movement. That’s our origin. Our core values are very much linked to the labour movement. They’re very close to us still. Basically, we would have to change who we are. We would have to change our core values. We have a big programme in Norway that’s working on search-and-rescue activities, but also integration activities. For example, today we had the launch of our new anti-racism guidelines for our members, and other organisations, on how to work on anti-racism. We have local chapters all over the country, and they are very much involved in integration and anti-racism activities. We couldn’t do that. It would affect what we do also in Norway together with our partners around the world. And it’s not something we can accept. It’s beyond the American funding. It would affect who we are, how we operate. Of course, we can’t change our identity and all of our activities because one of our donors changed their requirements. The New Humanitarian: I think what people might not understand is how far the global gag rule reaches. Ballestad: It’s very broad. For us, it’s very much about who we are. What are the core values of an organisation like NPA? The first paragraph of our principles ... says “Norwegian People’s Aid’s values are based on equal rights for all regardless of gender, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, functional ability, and social status. Norwegian People's Aid is an anti-racist organisation.” That’s the first paragraph. So already there, we’re in trouble. What’s the game-changer this time: The [US] requirements that came out in [2025] were similar, but they were only for American-funded activities. This time, it would cover all of what we do. You can’t compensate for what you can’t do with American funding with other funding. It would affect who we are, how we operate. Of course, we can’t change our identity and all of our activities because one of our donors changed their requirements. It’s basically about our political freedom. The New Humanitarian: Many mine action programmes have focused on recruiting women as de-miners. Is something like that – the US would consider that to be non-compliant? Ballestad: Yes. When we advertise, for example, sometimes we encourage women to apply so that we can have more of a gender balance in, for example, our management positions. This, we wouldn’t be allowed to do. And we do that for everything. That’s part of our HR policies. There’s a lot of levels that we would have to change. We can’t accept it. Of course, Americans set their requirements for their funding. But we have to assess if this is something we can accept to remain true to our foundational values. The New Humanitarian: Looking at the entire aid sector, why do you think it’s important that NPA made this decision? What’s the significance of it? Ballestad: In the bigger picture, we see that a more rights-based approach is being challenged globally. And I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years. It costs, if you stand up for rights. And I think it’s the time to do so. It’s a slippery slope... Currently, these are the rights we’re discussing. You don’t know what’s next. When do you put your foot down? Edited by Andrew Gully. Read

body: Related stories Aid and Policy Cheat Sheet 11 September 2026 UK condemns “settler terrorists”, Sudan’s chemical weapons exposed, and Yemen’s war escalates Aid and Policy Interview 10 September 2026 “When do you put your foot down?” Why this de-mining group is rejecting US funding Aid and Policy Podcasts 8 September 2026 Rethinking Humanitarianism | The rise of privatised aid: A conversation with Fogbow Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email Editor’s note: This episode was made in collaboration with Start Network as part of a series that explores what really drives change in the humanitarian system, and what it tells us about future efforts to transform the system for the better. In the previous collaborative episode between Rethinking Humanitarianism and Start Network , Fogbow CEO Brook Jerue questioned why the aid sector was so “infatuated” and critical of his company – a small private American firm delivering aid in high‐conflict contexts like South Sudan and Gaza. In this follow‐up episode, host Tammam Aloudat speaks with Beatrice Lindstrom – co‐author of a recent policy brief on the rise of privatised, militarised, and politicised aid actors – to situate Fogbow within the larger context of these emerging operators, and to examine why their growing "subsumption" of professional humanitarian roles deserves closer scrutiny. Lindstrom, who is also a human rights lawyer and a senior clinical instructor at Harvard Law’s International Human Rights Clinic, warns that we may be sliding towards a future where “aid-for-profit” becomes normalised at the risk of harming affected communities. She draws distinctions between firms like Fogbow and entities such as the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, whose US‐Israeli‐backed activities were linked to Israel’s killing of thousands of aid seekers . Yet, she argues, they share structural features that matter: corporate structures and incentives, close relationships with states that are parties to conflict, and approaches that risk turning aid into an instrument of military and political strategy. A central concern for Lindstrom is the ambiguous nature of these companies, which “seem to be asking to be held to corporate transparency standards rather than humanitarian ones”. That mix, she says, creates “a grey zone of accountability” in which people in crisis – and the public funding much of the response – lack clear information on who is calling the shots, whose interests are being served, and what safeguards exist when those interests clash. Lindstrom links this shift to “massive defunding” of professional aid organisations and a deliberate policy turn by major donors like the United States. This is embracing “a philosophy around aid that is entirely instrumentalised to serve American interests, and where private actors are named as core actors to carry out that plan”. While private actors have long been in the humanitarian space, Lindstrom says the sector is “on the cusp of a broader trend” where aid-for-profit models risk becoming increasingly accepted and entrenched, “and I think that that's exactly why it's so critical that we scrutinise these actors adequately right now, before they are legitimised”. Lindstrom says traditional NGOs also fall short, especially on accountability to affected people, but insists that this cannot be a reason to abandon core principles. “I don't think we're disproportionately focused on for-profit companies here, but rather that this conversation now needs to be applied to these new actors in the same way that it's been applied to nonprofit organisations,” she says. “We all share a responsibility to fight for a model of aid grounded in needs and rights, and kept at arm’s length from politics.” Guests Beatrice Lindstrom, senior clinical instructor at Harvard Law School's International Human Rights Clinic; co-author of "The New Humanitarian Actors: Politicization, Corporatization, and Militarization in the Aid Sector” Read more Rethinking Humanitarianism | The rise of privatised aid: A conversation with Fogbow The New Humanitarian Actors: Politicization, Corporatization, & Militarization in the Aid Sector The problem with emergency aid’s growing reliance on corporations Subscribe on Spotify , Apple , Google , Stitcher , or YouTube , or search “The New Humanitarian” in your favourite podcast app. Got a question or feedback? Email [email protected] or have your say on Twitter using the hashtag #RethinkingHumanitarianism. Transcript | Will aid-for-hire become the new normal? Beatrice Lindstrom They seem to be asking to be held to corporate transparency standards rather than humanitarian ones, and that the funding sources are largely not disclosed. [...] And I think ultimately my concern here is that this combination can create sort of a grey zone of accountability, because they can present themselves as mission-driven when it's convenient, but also as a commercial actor when it's advantageous [...] and in a humanitarian context, that ambiguity matters because people in crisis, and the public that is funding much of this work, they deserve clarity about whose interests are being served, and what safeguards exist when those interests conflict. [Music] Tammam Aloudat Welcome to this special edition of the Rethinking Humanitarianism podcast, in collaboration with Start Network. In this series, we explore what really drives change in the humanitarian system. Christina Bennett And what it tells us about future efforts to transform it for the better. In this episode, we'll look at a future scenario where aid becomes increasingly politicised, privatised, and militarised. Tammam Aloudat From The New Humanitarian, I’m Tammam Aloudat. Christina Bennett And from Start Network, I'm Christina Bennett. Tammam Aloudat Christina, last week we talked to Brooke Jerue from Fogbow about private corporations acting as aid organisations or as part of the aid landscape. It was an interesting conversation, and I think we do, we did need to elaborate on that further, didn't we? Christina Bennett Yeah, I think it was really important to put that conversation with Fogbow into context, and I think the conversation with Beatrice has done that. I think she did a really good job of zooming out from the implications of what that conversation might mean for the future of aid. Tammam Aloudat Yeah. Christina Bennett For me, it isn't a question of whether aid can be delivered efficiently. I think the conversation with Fogbow demonstrated that, you know, there are organisations that are able to do things very quickly, very efficiently, very cost effectively, and getting aid on the ground or getting aid to people. But it begs the question: Is the efficient delivery aid enough? And is it,if efficiency comes at the expense of, you know, the principles, the practices, the standards that we have held dear for so long, is it worth it? Tammam Aloudat And as well as the accountability and transparency that we take for granted, and that isn't binding for corporate entities. Is it principled? Is it not having unintended harm? Is it not causing political cost to this very people we're trying to aid? But also, there is another point: Brooke insisted that they are unique, and for example, not like other militarised organisations like the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, which was very problematic the year before. And I think what Beatrice helps us see is the range of actors that might be included in this privatised aid space that goes beyond just the particular case we interviewed last week. Christina Bennett I think we can agree that we need to look at these new aid models more carefully. That, you know, privatised, militarised aid, like the type of aid that Fogbow has is delivering, needs further scrutiny, needs time for us to really understand the implications of what that style of aid delivery looks like before we normalize it, because normalising it at t

Read the first report here . MAIDUGURI, Nigeria Mamman Nur, the senior cleric of Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), had tried to escape detention by his own comrades twice before – he knew this failed third attempt was likely his death sentence. The influential ideologue had been a leading figure in Nigeria’s insurgent jihadist movement for more than two decades. He had been one of the closest aides to Boko Haram’s deceased founder, Mohammed Yusuf, was a key link to Islamic State-Central, and for a time was popularly thought of as ISWAP’s leader. But the tall, charismatic teacher was now undone. He had been accused of secret contact with the Nigerian government through an initiative known as the “Swiss process”, which was exploring a path to dialogue and regarded Nur as a possible interlocutor . To ISWAP’s governing Shura council, this was treason. With the blessing of IS-Central, Nur was detained while the council debated what to do. In September 2018, he was sentenced to death and publicly shot by the head of the amniya , ISWAP’s secret police. Nur’s fate exposed the central problem facing any attempt to negotiate with Nigeria’s jihadists: Can a movement that treats dialogue as treason ever be persuaded to make peace? Nearly eight years later, a reported ceasefire between the government and Boko Haram suggests that, however tentatively, the answer may be changing. Can you make peace with jihadists? After 17 years of war and close to 350,000 indirect civilian deaths , the conflict in Nigeria’s northeast is stalemated. Yet behind the scenes there has been a long if faltering attempt by the Nigerian government to find a negotiated breakthrough to the jihadist insurgency. The idea of negotiations with “Boko Haram” – officially Jama’at Ahl al Sunna li Da’wa wal Jihad (JAS) – and ISWAP, its offshoot and rival, sharply divides Nigeria. The government officially says there can be no talks with groups legally proscribed as terrorist organisations, even though a three-month ceasefire with JAS, agreed in June, seems to be holding . The New Humanitarian has spoken to security officials, diplomats, mediators, and former jihadist fighters – protecting their anonymity so they could speak freely – to explore the potential of that dialogue process. Is there a path to a sustainable peace with extremist groups that reject the legitimacy of the Nigerian state, its secular constitution, and world view? “Both sides believe a settlement is possible,” a diplomat with knowledge of the chronology of the dialogue process told The New Humanitarian. “For all parties, a non-kinetic [military] approach is intellectually acceptable.” Military operations alone rarely resolves insurgencies. Political settlements, where they are possible, are more likely to produce lasting peace. But governments tend to exceptionalise jihadist groups and publicly shun the idea of dialogue with people typically characterised as irredeemably violent. These groups’ perceived maximalist ideological demands are seen as obstacles to peace – the spiritual and sacred regarded as incompatible with the give and take of political bargaining. Yet Islamist ideology is not monolithic . Extremist groups are political actors that shape and are shaped by their environments. Supposed “red lines” over political demands can also fade over time. In Egypt, Gama’a al Islamiya carried out armed attacks for two decades before it renounced violence and stood in elections in 2011. And more recently, in Syria, Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham transformed from an al-Qaeda franchise into the dominant force behind a transitional government. However, the cell-like structures of jihadist groups, legal prohibitions, histories of distrust, and the difficulty of building domestic political consensus all weigh on the timing and incentives for peace talks. Negotiations demand patience, political will, and good intelligence networks, said the diplomat. Nigeria has struggled on all three fronts. Successive governments have also avoided confronting the grievances driving the northeastern conflict or properly understanding their opponents. The traditional establishment approach has been to “settle” troublemakers, buying them off with money and positions. But JAS and ISWAP have been different: ideological foes not seeking a financial reward or patronage. “Peace can be possible, but it needs trust and sincerity,” a former ISWAP commander who surrendered to the authorities last year, told The New Humanitarian. “The problem is that up until now, nobody has sat with [JAS/ISWAP] to understand them. A close observer of the Nigerian conflict was more sceptical. “The record shows that jihadist groups, like other insurgent groups, can engage in negotiations, at least preliminary or limited ones, when they are under pressure,” he noted. However, there are fewer examples of longer-term political solutions. Talking about talks The insurgency, which began in northeastern Maiduguri in 2009, was still growing when President Goodluck Jonathan was elected two years later. A southern Christian, his poll victory sparked riots in several predominantly Muslim northern cities in a controversy over whether he should have stood. For some in his administration it was proof of a conspiracy : that JAS was manufactured by aggrieved northern elites to undermine Jonathan’s rule. In the early days of the conflict, mediation efforts were largely privately led. Former president Olusegun Obasanjo made the first attempt in 2011, followed by Sheikh Ibrahim Datti Ahmad, the respected president of the National Supreme Council of Sharia. Both ended almost as soon as they had begun – with each side blaming the other. Demands by JAS were basic: the release of detained wives and colleagues, the rebuilding of homes and buildings destroyed by the security forces in Maiduguri, the payment of compensation to families of members killed, and the prosecution of the policemen responsible for the assassination of Yusuf, the movement’s founder. They have not included larger ideological goals. Splits and rivalries: A timeline of Boko Haram/ISWAP discord Boko Haram began as an ultra-conservative religious movement in the early 2000s in Maiduguri under a young cleric, Mohammed Yusuf. It tapped into a radical zeitgeist that appealed across classes – condemning so-called “Western values” and celebrating 500 years of Islamic learning and empire in Nigeria’s northeast. Initially, Yusuf resisted calling for jihad, but as tensions with the authorities increased, he launched an urban insurrection in July 2009. It was quickly crushed, and Yusuf was extrajudicially killed by the police. Abubakar Shekau, his deputy, took over as imam. A wave of bombings, kidnappings, and the overrunning of towns had the army on the backfoot, and rural Borno emptied as people were displaced from their homes. Shekau declared allegiance to so-called Islamic State in 2015 and the group was renamed Islamic State of West Africa Province (ISWAP). In 2016, ISWAP split. Dissident commanders led by Abu Musa al-Barnawi and cleric Mamman Nur accused Shekau of despotism and condemned his use of “takfir” – the death penalty for infidels – against rural civilians. Bitter factional fighting followed, but the dissidents managed to establish themselves in the Lake Chad region and win the blessing of IS-Central. body: Home Asia Nepal Related stories Environment and Disasters Analysis 1 September 2026 The Himalayan disaster Nepal could not see coming Environment and Disasters Investigations 2 December 2021 How Bangladesh is beating the odds on climate disaster deaths Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email DAKAR Rajendra Dawadi had to make a decision in an instant. Warned that floodwaters were racing towards his school in Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, the headmaster had no way of knowing how much time he had, nor whether the floodwaters would reach his school. He did not hesitate and evacuated more than 900 students and 16 staff to higher ground. Approximately 13 minutes later, a wall of water, mud, and debris swept through the area, destroying the school. Dawadi acted before he knew for certain what was coming. His calculation was simple. If the warning proved wrong, his students would miss a day of school . If it was right and he did nothing, hundreds of children could die. The instinct to act while there is still time, despite uncertainty, is at the heart of anticipatory action. Investing ahead of known risks has been shown to save lives and reduce losses . But acting ahead requires accepting that some forecasts will never provide complete certainty, and that waiting to act can carry far higher consequences. Nepal shows what formal systems can and cannot do Nepal is hardly a newcomer to acting ahead of disasters. The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology introduced the flood early warning system in the 1990s, combining both high-tech river level monitoring stations with simpler community-based systems for detecting rising waters and disseminating warnings. In 2022, the government held the first national dialogue on anticipatory action, and this year endorsed a national policy. Humanitarian organisations have been experimenting with anticipatory approaches for more than a decade , releasing pre-arranged emergency funding at least twice for flood response. The August disaster , however, fell outside of the mainly weather-related monsoon flooding that these mechanisms were designed to anticipate and warn against. A huge section of glacier and surrounding bedrock collapsed high in Tibet , sending ice, rock, and debris into the river system and generating a catastrophic flood that travelled nearly 100 kilometres downstream. Automatic monitoring stations along the upper Bhotekoshi River were meant to detect rising water and alert communities downstream, but the flood moved so quickly that monitoring stations inside Nepal were destroyed before they could transmit a warning. The community-level river gauges that gradually measured river behaviour were also too slow for a flood travelling at an average speed of 193 kilometres per hour . Some of these limitations were already understood. A 2023 review of Nepal’s anticipatory action experience raised concerns about the reliability of forecasts and called for greater flexibility to combine scientific triggers with human judgement and changing conditions on the ground. A later study in 2025 found their early warning messaging system frequently did not prompt the necessary actions to save lives and protect assets. What happened at Dawadi’s school shows why this matters. The warning that saved Dawadi’s students did not come through the formal monitoring or early warning system. A relative upstream called the school accountant. Teachers received calls from family and friends. A parent arrived to collect her child. Dawadi ordered the evacuation. Teachers, parents, and others then helped get the children uphill. Many others were not so fortunate. Elsewhere along the flood’s path, people had almost no time to react . Forecasting and early warning technology remain essential, but they have to be matched by readiness at the community level – evacuation plans, trusted communication networks, prepared local institutions and people able to act when information arrives. Those community connections are part of the infrastructure of disaster readiness. I saw their importance when I lived in Japan and studied how the country prepares for disasters in 2019. Japan is famous for its enormous investment in seawalls, flood defences, earthquake-resistant buildings and sophisticated warning systems. But some of its most important investments are far simpler . Children learn about disaster risk from kindergarten. Communities practise evacuations. Families are encouraged to have a go-bag ready at all times. Residents identify neighbours who may need help. Survivors share their experiences with communities facing similar hazards. Japan also shows the limits of relying too heavily on infrastructure and more formal warning systems. During severe 2018 flooding in Mabi , a district in western Japan situated near two rivers, embankments were overwhelmed and mobile-phone warnings failed to reach some of the elderly people most at risk. Research after the Mabi flood and the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and Tsunami found that some residents delayed evacuating because they believed physical defences would protect them . Forecasting and early warning technology remain essential, but they have to be matched by readiness at the community level – evacuation plans, trusted communication networks, prepared local institutions and people able to act when information arrives. These investments may be less visible than satellites, monitoring stations or dams, but they can determine whether a warning actually saves a life. Schools are an important part of that community readiness. My research on education and anticipatory action with the Geneva Global Hub for Education in Emergencies in 2025 * found much the same thing that Dawadi’s experience demonstrates: Schools can play a critical role in turning early warnings into action. They reach children and families every day, while teachers are often trusted community leaders who can communicate risks, organise evacuations, and connect formal warning systems with local knowledge. Disaster education also gives children knowledge they take home and carry into adulthood, strengthening the ability of entire communities to respond to future crises. Governments, donors, and aid agencies must become more comfortable spending money before they can be certain a crisis will unfold as forecast. Scientists are still grappling with how to predict rock-ice avalanches like the one in Nepal. But as glacial flooding increases as a result of global warming , they warn that these events are expected to be more common around the world. Anticipatory approaches and funding will need to adapt to include these emerging risks while investing more in the local institutions and relationships that can turn warnings into action. Yet humanitarian financing still runs overwhelmingly in the opposite direction. Ninety-nine percent of international humanitarian funding still flows after disasters happen and only about 12% of total anticipatory action funding between 2022 and 2023 involved those organisations closest to communities. In a time of collapsing budgets and hyper-prioritisation, it is urgent to rethink whether scarce resources are being deployed where – and when – they can have the greatest effect. Some actions may prove unnecessary. Sometimes, supplies will be moved for a flood that changes course. Cash may be released ahead of a drought that proves less severe than expected. Schools may close for storms that never arrive. That does not make those decisions bad ones. Governments, donors, and aid agencies must become more comfortable spending money before they can be certain a crisis will unfold as forecast. The cost of acting unnecessarily can be far smaller than the cost of acting too late. Dawadi understood that tradeoff. *This article was revised on 10 September 2026 to show that the research was published in 2025, rather than 2024 as originally stated. Sha

Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email When private companies employ former military personnel and work with controversial political actors in the name of humanitarian aid, should they still follow humanitarian principles? And who holds them accountable? These were some of the questions that animated an impassioned conversation between Fogbow CEO Brook Jerue and host Tammam Aloudat. The latest collaborative episode between Rethinking Humanitarianism and Start Network tackles the rise of privatised, militarised, and politicised players in the humanitarian landscape. “We are abiding by the same principles that everybody else is abiding by,” says Jerue, who argues that traditional humanitarian agencies also have ex-military in their fold, and that being a corporation allows them to deliver life-saving aid where others can’t. Fogbow is an American firm that says it specialises in logistics – enabling access in tough environments. It counts former World Food Programme boss David Beasley as an adviser. So far, its work in humanitarian emergencies has mostly consisted of small air drops and truck deliveries in highly complex conflict zones in South Sudan, Sudan, and Gaza. Critics say companies like Fogbow could be part of a new wave of private actors willing to take on projects that instrumentalise aid and serve the interests of particular governments – and that bypass traditional aid agencies that insist on following humanitarian principles. Some say Fogbow’s operations could compromise humanitarian principles , have aided a party to the conflict in South Sudan, and could put aid recipients at risk . Jerue disputes these claims, distinguishing Fogbow from players like the controversial Gaza Humanitarian Foundation , and instead painting a picture of a company using its military know-how to do what UN agencies can’t, and whose shareholders are willing to break even “because they just want to be a part of something that is bigger than themselves”. “The reason why we can operate where we operate is because we're a private entity, because we're small and agile... if you turn into another WFP, you're just going to run into the same bureaucracy and problems they have,” says Jerue. Guests Brook Jerue, CEO of Fogbow Key moments [06:31] – What makes Fogbow different from traditional humanitarian actors? [15:09] – The Gaza maritime corridor and US backing [18:47] – “I don't think you can operate in a vacuum without political or economic pressure on any aid” [38:41] – “We’re a private company. We’re not an NGO [45:57] – Fogbow’s finances [51:06] – Did people refuse aid airdropped by Fogbow in South Sudan? [56:50] – “Why is everybody so infatuated with Fogbow?” Read more Fogbow operations in South Sudan and beyond raise red flags for faltering aid system US Gaza pier to close after costing $230m for a day’s worth of aid The problem with emergency aid’s growing reliance on corporations Subscribe on Spotify , Apple , Google , Stitcher , or YouTube , or search “The New Humanitarian” in your favourite podcast app. Got a question or feedback? We just abiding by the same principles that everybody else is abiding by. [...] There's a reason why we've been able to do what we do, and is I think it's more because we're an outsider coming in. And honestly, we get a lot of flack because we're an outsider coming in. [...] I don't understand why we get this blowback for helping people, you know, that are on the cusp of starving to death." Tammam Aloudat Welcome to this special edition of the Rethinking Humanitarianism podcast, in collaboration with Start Network. In this series, we explore what really drives change in the humanitarian system Christina Bennett And what it tells us about the future, and what it tells us about future efforts to transform it for the better. In this episode, we'll look at a future scenario where aid becomes increasingly politicised, privatised, and militarised. Tammam Aloudat From The New Humanitarian, I’m Tammam Aloudat. Christina Bennett And from Start Network, I'm Christina Bennett. Tammam Aloudat So, Christina, this was an interesting and quite long conversation. Christina Bennett I was really, really sorry I couldn't co-moderate this one with you, in part because I did moderate the other episode we did on sort of the changing face of aid, and that was much more about how we were looking at aid from the ground up. How grassroots aid is transforming the way aid is delivered in so many ways, and you know, that was an example of how volunteer organisations, grassroots organisations, organisations from within communities, are adapting to the new sort of political and financial realities of what aid is. And what we heard in that episode was a lot of underlying themes around aid based on solidarity with people suffering, and even things like joy being an important byproduct of aid, alongside life-saving assistance, alongside survival, alongside addressing needs. Tammam Aloudat This was entirely different. This is a very outsider view to aid, and it is by a corporation. So, I spoke to Brook Jerue from Fogbow. It is a private American company that is quite new to the humanitarian space. They have mostly dropped aid in conflict zones and Fogbow has stirred up controversy because of some of those projects, specifically in Gaza and South Sudan. And to our listeners, I’d strongly encourage them to read the New Humanitarian’s reporting on Fogbow. In it, they will read that critics have alleged that Fogbow doesn’t adhere to humanitarian principles and has used aid to serve the political and military interests of governments and political actors in these contexts. As we will hear in this interview, Fogbow strongly disputes that. Listeners will see it is a long episode, but I think it's worth listening to the whole thing because it goes into ups and downs. Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email Editor’s note: This is the first in a series of reports exploring the feasibility of dialogue as a path to peace in Africa’s protracted civil conflicts. MAIDUGURI, Nigeria A ceasefire agreement with the jihadist group Boko Haram has been in effect for the past three months and is expected to be extended, but has not been previously reported publicly, The New Humanitarian has learned. The agreement is linked to hostage negotiations that secured the release in June of 360 civilians abducted by the group from Ngoshe village, in the foothills of the Mandara mountains on the border with Cameroon. The mass kidnapping occurred in March during a Boko Haram attack on a nearby army base. Three people with contacts among Boko Haram members, some of them senior figures, independently told The New Humanitarian that a truce had been in effect since June and was likely to be extended for a further 40 days. Communities in the Ngoshe area – regular victims of Boko Haram predation – say attacks have stopped since the ceasefire, according to two of the sources. The deal that freed the villagers also reportedly included a ransom payment of five billion naira ($3.7 million) by the government, a transaction Abuja has denied amid controversy over the alleged misappropriation of some of the money. The New Humanitarian reached out to spokespeople for the government, defence headquarters, and the army to verify reports of a ceasefire, but received no reply prior to publishing. What remains unclear is the longer-term significance of any agreement. “It could be just a temporary, tactical ceasefire that benefits both sides, but doesn’t really affect the trajectory of the war,” said conflict researcher Malik Samuel. “I don’t think it’s a step towards a sustainable peace settlement.” The deal does not involve so-called Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), an offshoot and rival to Boko Haram, based on the islands of Lake Chad and a rural swathe of northeastern Borno State. Clashes have continued between the two groups. After 17 years of a war that has indirectly cost close to 350,000 civilian lives, the idea of negotiations with Boko Haram – officially Jama’at Ahl al Sunna li Da’wa wal Jihad (JAS) – and other armed groups sharply divides Nigerians. Those living closest to the conflict tend to be far more supportive of dialogue than the rest of the country. However, the government’s public position is an emphatic rejection of talks with a group legally proscribed as a terrorist organisation. President Bola Tinubu has instead announced the beefing up of an overstretched army – an initiative related to elections early next year in which public safety will be a key issue. The promised 30,000 new recruits and four extra divisions will provide the “teeth that are needed to defeat terrorism and banditry”, Tinubu said in July. Nevertheless, behind the scenes, “the government seems very interested in having a dialogue with Boko Haram, perhaps realising a military response alone is inadequate to resolving the problem,” noted Samuel. When rebels rule: ISWAP’s formula for winning support in Nigeria’s northeast The jihadist group poses more than a military challenge to the Nigerian government – its hearts and minds campaign is also a political threat. “Both sides believe a settlement is possible” Since the Boko Haram insurgency began in 2009, there has been a long if faltering history of under the radar dialogue approaches, according to security officials, diplomats, and mediators, who spoke to The New Humanitarian on the condition of anonymity so they could talk freely. “Both sides believe a settlement is possible,” a diplomat with knowledge of the chronology of contacts told The New Humanitarian. “For all parties, a non-kinetic [military] approach is intellectually acceptable. But they still believe that by improving their military situations they can influence those negotiations.” Those talks have been led on the government’s side by the Office of the National Security Advisor and the spy agency, the Department of State Services. They have repeatedly failed, typically scuppered by spoilers within the government and military, forcing the parties to rebuild confidence each time. Historically, “we’ve negotiated a couple of ceasefires but they couldn’t be maintained,” said a government security official with knowledge of the dialogue process. “The last hudna [armistice] was in the 2022/2023 period but it also collapsed.” The current agreement may suffer the same fate. Two sources who told The New Humanitarian about the deal warned that Boko Haram may be using the ceasefire to strengthen its position, potentially by moving “equipment” into the Mandera mountains. Can dialogue with jihadist groups bring peace to the Sahel? Warfighting has only deepened wounds, hardened divides, and fuelled new insurgencies – a rethink is long overdue. Who’s who Boko Haram is headed by Ibrahim Bakura Doro , the overall commander and imam (religious leader), based on the islands on the northern section of Lake Chad, on the Niger Republic border. Boko Haram has three factions , all of which have sworn allegiance to Bakura: Darul Gazwa, operating in southeastern Borno and headed by Alhai Kale; the Sadiku group of Abubakar Sadiku Saidu, active around north-central Nigeria; and the Ali Ngulde faction, which carried out the Ngoshe kidnappings. The success of the ceasefire depends on whether Bakura, from his Lake Chad base thousands of kilometres away, can yoke the three other Boko Haram commanders into a sustainable deal. Rival ISWAP is operationally and organisationally distinct from Boko Haram, its jihadist cousin. While Boko Haram survives on looting and extorting civilians – a practice known as fey'u – plundering is banned by ISWAP. Boko Haram is also more locally focused whereas ISWAP – among the most active of so-called Islamic State-Central’s franchises – is loyal to the transnational “caliphate”, which effectively hands IS-Central veto power over any dialogue initiative, according to people familiar with the group. “ISWAP needs buy-in from IS. They make the final decision,” a rehabilitated former ISWAP commander told The New Humanitarian. “But Bakura needs money, you can make a deal with him.” Splits and rivalries: A timeline of Boko Haram/ISWAP discord Boko Haram began as an ultra-conservative religious movement in the early 2000s in Maiduguri under a young cleric, Mohammed Yusuf. It tapped into a radical zeitgeist that appealed across classes – condemning so-called “Western values” and celebrating 500 years of Islamic learning and empire in Nigeria’s northeast. Initially, Yusuf resisted calling for jihad, but as tensions with the authorities increased, he launched an urban insurrection in July 2009. It was quickly crushed, and Yusuf was extrajudicially killed by the police. Abubakar Shekau, his deputy, took over as imam. A wave of bombings, kidnappings, and the overrunning of towns had the army on the backfoot, and rural Borno emptied as people were displaced from their homes. Shekau declared allegiance to so-called Islamic State in 2015 and the group was renamed Islamic State of West Africa Province (ISWAP). In 2016, ISWAP split. Dissident commanders led by Abu Musa al-Barnawi and cleric Mamman Nur accused Shekau of despotism and condemned his use of “takfir” – the death penalty for infidels – against rural civilians. Bitter factional fighting followed, but the dissidents managed to establish themselves in the Lake Chad region and win the blessing of IS-Central.
