title: OSCE expands access to its technical guidance on the physical security of critical infrastructure: Release of official Turkmen version

body: Women, Water Management and Conflict Prevention — Phase III Project Update OSCE Supports Sustainable Water Management and Regional Co-operation at the 4th High-Level International Conference on the International Decade for Action “Water for Sustainable Development” (2018–2028) Issued on: 1 June 2026 Issued by: Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities From 25 to 28 May 2026, the OSCE actively participated in the Fourth High-Level International Conference on the International Decade for Action “Water for Sustainable Development”, 2018–2028, held within the framework of the Dushanbe Water Process, as part of preparations for its contribution to the 2026 UN Water Conference. Through its participation in several official sessions, the OSCE contributed to discussions on how countries can strengthen co-operation under increasing climate stress, while reinforcing the importance of linking policy dialogue with the lived realities of communities that depend on shared water resources. Water insecurity, compounded by the impacts of climate change and unequal access to resources, continues to affect communities across the OSCE region, particularly in shared river basins where co-operation is essential for sustainable water management and resilience. Ahead of the Conference, the Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities (OCEEA) organized a three-day regional workshop, “Promoting Collaboration over Shared Water: Concepts and Approaches for Building Trust and Co-operation” in partnership with the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH) and with support from the Regional Environmental Centre for Central Asia. The regional workshop brought together women water professionals and young experts from across Central Asia to develop practical recommendations for strengthening co-operation focused on stronger data sharing, more effective communication, and more inclusive decision-making in transboundary water management. These recommendations were presented during a reception marking UNU-INWEH’s 30th anniversary, highlighting the work of the Women in Water Diplomacy Network. The discussions underscored a shared message: sustainable water security depends on inclusive participation and shared responsibility. During the Conference itself, the OSCE contributed to multiple sessions, including the opening plenary and several policy dialogues. On 25 May, it co-hosted the Youth Water Forum with the Government of Tajikistan, represented by the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources of the Republic of Tajikistan. Young participants called for stronger and more meaningful involvement in global water decision-making, and their outcome statement will help inform future policy processes. The same day, the OSCE contributed to the Women Water Forum, which underscored the importance of co-operation on water and glaciers and reinforced the value of inclusive approaches to shared environmental challenges. Together, these engagements demonstrated that water diplomacy is ultimately about people—building trust and fostering more secure and resilient societies. At the interactive dialogue on “Water for People,” Bakyt Dzhusupov, Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities**,** delivered an “ignite speech” emphasizing the foundations of effective water co-operation and noted: “Water co-operation across borders depends on transparency, dialogue, trust, and strong institutions that can manage shared resources peacefully. Climate change is intensifying these challenges, with droughts, floods, and shifting rainfall patterns exposing and deepening existing vulnerabilities, especially in fragile contexts. This reinforces that water governance is not only a development issue, but also a matter of peace and stability. Building resilient societies requires more than technical solutions alone.” The Conference served as an important platform for strengthening partnerships, mobilizing collective action, and advancing the implementation of the UN Water Action Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, while providing an opportunity to reflect on priorities for the post-2030 framework. These activities were implemented under the OSCE extra-budgetary project “ Women, Water Management and Conflict Prevention – Phase III ,” funded by Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland, and Finland. body: News News Item New protocol brings faster access to identity, rights, and services for all Issued on: 28 April 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Skopje Fields of work: Human rights , Roma and Sinti North Macedonia is a global champion in ending statelessness. The country introduces measures to prevent future cases. The OSCE Mission to Skopje, jointly with the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Health promoted a new Protocol on Procedures for Statelessness. The Protocol sets clear steps for institutions to work together to prevent new cases, because not having a legal identity means not being able to see a doctor, go to school, or access basic services. The event brought together representatives from key institutions, civil society organizations, and professionals who work directly with people at risk of statelessness. It also recognized the efforts of frontline staff who helped resolve real-life cases and improve co-ordination between institutions. “This is about real people and real lives. This Protocol helps ensure that every child born is registered, every person is recognized, and everyone can access their basic rights.”, said the Head of the OSCE Mission in to Skopje, Ambassador Kilian Wahl. The initiative sustains recent progress. Already by mid-2025, North Macedonia had resolved all known cases linked to the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, granting citizenship to 317 people. However, challenges remain, especially for children born to parents without regulated legal status. A recent pilot effort showed how co-operation can make a difference. In one case, institutions worked together to ensure that both a mother and her newborn received personal documents and access to healthcare, quickly and effectively. The new Protocol aims to make such solutions standard practice. The OSCE Mission continues to support national authorities and partners in preventing and reducing statelessness, ensuring that everyone can enjoy their fundamental rights and that no one is left behind. title: New protocol brings faster access to identity, rights, and services for all

body: News News Item From invisibility to equality: Advancing Roma inclusion through legal identity in North Macedonia Issued on: 8 April 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Skopje Fields of work: National minority issues , Roma and Sinti , Tolerance and non-discrimination On 8 April 2026, partners gathered at the Assembly of the Republic of North Macedonia to mark International Roma Day and focus on a simple but essential idea: inclusion starts with being recognized. “Today, we stand here, in the house of democracy, united around a value greater than any policy, any party, and any daily interest. The value of human dignity,” said Prime Minster Hristijan Mickoski. “Behind every statistic there is a person. Behind every number, a story. And behind every challenge, a hope waiting to be recognized and supported.” Under the theme “From Invisibility to Equality,” discussions centred on legal identity, the key that enables access to education, healthcare, employment, and social protection. “Legal identity may sound technical. But in reality, it is what makes a person visible to the State. And without that visibility, access to rights remains out of reach,” said Edward Anderson, the Mission’s Head of Public Safety and Community Outreach Department. This is where practical work is making a difference. With support from the OSCE Mission to Skopje, around 750 people who previously lacked legal identity have been able to register and access their rights, while all known statelessness cases linked to the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia have been resolved. In 2025 alone, mobile legal aid initiatives supported by the Mission helped around 300 Roma individuals obtain documents and access social protection, thereby bringing services directly to communities and reducing administrative barriers. Looking ahead, the focus is shifting to prevention. In 2026, the Mission will support the development of a Protocol on Statelessness to strengthen implementation of legislation and improve co-ordination between institutions. Working together with institutions and communities, these efforts are helping ensure that no one remains invisible, and that inclusion becomes a reality. title: From invisibility to equality: Advancing Roma inclusion through legal identity in North Macedonia

body: News News Item OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Christophe Kamp on first official visit to Georgia Issued on: 7 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Fields of work: Conflict prevention and resolution , Human rights , National minority issues , Tolerance and non-discrimination , Education , Gender equality , Women, peace and security , Youth OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Christophe Kamp visited Georgia from 31 August to 4 September 2026. During his visit, Kamp travelled to the municipality of Marneuli and to the city of Batumi. He also joined a European Union Monitoring Mission in Georgia patrol on the Administrative Boundary Line. In Tbilisi, the High Commissioner met with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Affairs Minister Maka Botchorishvili, Education, Science and Youth Minister Givi Mikanadze, State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality Tea Akhvlediani, Public Defender Levan Ioseliani, and members of the Government and the parliament. Kamp also engaged with representatives of the international community, minority representatives and civil society organizations. In Batumi and Marneuli, Kamp met with local and regional authorities, community leaders, as well as teachers and directors of minority-language schools. He also had the opportunity to exchange with members of minority-led civil society organizations working to foster inter-community dialogue and strengthen the effective participation of national minorities in public life. His interlocutors underlined the important contribution of mother tongue-based multilingual education (MLE) in facilitating opportunities for persons belonging to national minorities while also helping to preserve communities' identities. They also discussed ways in which this contribution could be further recognized and supported. The High Commissioner noted that his office had supported the development of mother-tongue based MLE in Georgia at policy and implementation level for more than two decades. During his visit, the High Commissioner also exchanged views on the legal and institutional framework supporting the integration of Georgia's diverse society. In his meetings, Kamp discussed the importance of meaningful consultation of communities at all levels of government, as well as the effective participation of national minorities in political and public life. He also discussed the situation of conflict-affected populations. The visit was an opportunity for the High Commissioner to exchange with a broad range of stakeholders on social cohesion and inter-community relationships in Georgia, based on the office’s previous long-term engagement in the country. body: News News Item Public broadcasters must not amplify the glorification of convicted war criminals Issued on: 7 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina , OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media Fields of work: Human rights , Rule of law SARAJEVO/VIENNA, 07 September 2026 - The OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina and the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media express serious concern regarding RTRS’s direct live transmission of a commemoration at which speakers repeatedly glorified Ratko Mladić. His convictions for genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war were upheld on appeal in 2021, as was his sentence of life imprisonment. Reporting on events of legitimate public interest is an essential part of media freedom and editorial independence. While reporting on events of public interest falls within the media’s editorial remit, particular concern arises given that content glorifying a convicted war criminal was amplified without adequate editorial context or reference to judicially established facts. Public service broadcasters have a particular responsibility to provide accurate, impartial and properly contextualized journalism. The Mission recalls that Article 145a(6) of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina criminalizes the glorification of persons sentenced by final judgment for such crimes. Whether the broadcast may have breached criminal law is for the competent justice institutions to determine. Separately, the Mission and the Representative call on the Communications Regulatory Agency to assess the coverage promptly and independently, including under Articles 4(8), 5 and 7 of the CRA Code on Programme Content, and to respond proportionately to any violation established. Respect for judicially established facts and for the dignity of victims and survivors is fundamental to responsible journalism, reconciliation and lasting peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Any media coverage of the forthcoming funeral should accordingly be accurate, properly contextualized and consistent with applicable professional and ethical standards.
title: Public broadcasters must not amplify the glorification of convicted war criminals

body: News News Item OSCE calls for safeguarding BHRT’s independence and functioning ahead of elections Issued on: 6 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina Fields of work: Media freedom and development SARAJEVO, 06 September 2026 - The OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina (Mission) calls on all relevant authorities to respect and implement binding court decisions, safeguard judicial independence and ensure the functioning and independence of BHRT ahead of the elections. Public service broadcasters play a particularly important role during elections by providing citizens with reliable information needed to make informed decisions. Beyond the immediate measures needed to ensure BHRT’s continued functioning, a sustainable long-term framework for public service broadcasting is necessary, with strong safeguards for its independence. The Mission also calls on all public officials, candidates and political parties to respect media freedom and provide an enabling environment for journalists to work freely and independently during the election period.
title: OSCE calls for safeguarding BHRT’s independence and functioning ahead of elections

body: News News Item OSCE supports evidence-based basin planning through stakeholder consultations and data verification in Kazakhstan Issued on: 4 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Astana From 26 July to 4 August 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Astana, in partnership with the Information and Analytical Center for Water Resources under the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, supported a series of consultations with basin inspections and other water-sector stakeholders in the Aral-Syrdarya, Zhaiyk-Caspian and Yertis basins. The consultations formed part of Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to develop basin plans and a General Plan for integrated water resources management based on accurate, up-to-date and jointly verified data. The consultations brought together more than 100 representatives of basin inspections, branches of the Republican State Enterprise (RSE) “Kazvodkhoz” and RSE “Kazhydromet”, local executive bodies, water-user organizations, and scientific and research institutions. Conducted by a team of three water specialists (two women and one man), the meetings took place from 26 to 29 July in Kyzylorda, from 30 to 31 July in Aktau, and from 2 to 4 August in Semey and Oskemen. Participants worked to verify baseline data, align projected water balances with local investment and development plans, and identify measures for inclusion in the basin plans. The consultations combined technical review with field observation. Participants examined water-use limits, the accuracy of water accounting and metering, the condition of hydraulic infrastructure and irrigation canals, transportation losses, and the fulfilment of transboundary commitments. Discussions also addressed the functioning of basin councils, the participation of water users and the public, and the availability and quality of data required for basin planning. Field visits to key water infrastructure and water-use facilities enabled participants to connect the planning process with conditions on the ground. Working directly with the expert team, representatives of the basin inspections also reconciled discrepancies between primary reporting data and previously prepared analytical materials. This included correcting data on water-supply sources and transboundary inflows in the three basins, strengthening the basis for calculating water balances under current and future demand scenarios. The consultations also highlighted priorities for continued investment in canal rehabilitation, water-saving technologies and monitoring networks. By bringing together national authorities, basin inspections, water users and other stakeholders to verify data and jointly identify priorities, the consultations strengthened the evidentiary basis for Kazakhstan’s basin plans and General Plan for integrated water resources management. The initiative supports the country’s long-term efforts to strengthen water security, transboundary co-operation and sustainable water governance, in line with OSCE commitments and international good practices. body: In support of strengthening capacities of Ukrainian authorities in preventing and combating illicit trafficking in weapons, ammunition and explosives in all its aspects News Item OSCE provides server equipment to strengthen Ukraine’s border security and counter illicit weapons trafficking Issued on: 3 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Secretariat Extra-Budgetary Support Programme for Ukraine Fields of work: Arms control In August 2026, the OSCE provided the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine (SBGS) with server equipment to strengthen its criminal analysis and operative-search activities against illicit trafficking in firearms and other cross-border threats. The donated equipment will enhance the capacity of SBGS criminal analysis units to process, store and exchange information, ensuring more reliable and resilient operative-search measures in line with the law enforcement mandate of the agency. This assistance package builds directly on the OSCE’s earlier support to SBGS through the provision of specialized software and relevant training. “Criminal networks constantly adapt their methods, and our analytical capabilities must evolve for adequate response. The analytical software provided by the OSCE previously gave our specialists powerful tools, and the server infrastructure we are receiving now will allow us to use those tools more effectively and at a greater scale. Together, this support will amplify our ability to identify links, detect patterns, and anticipate criminal threats, helping us turn information into actionable intelligence and more effectively disrupt organized cross-border crime,” said a representative of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine during the handover event. The procurement and donation of the equipment were carried out under the OSCE extrabudgetary project “ In Support of Strengthening Capacities of Ukrainian Authorities in Preventing and Combating Illicit Trafficking in Weapons, Ammunition and Explosives in All Its Aspects ”, funded by the European Union, Finland, France, Germany, and Poland.
title: OSCE provides server equipment to strengthen Ukraine’s border security and counter illicit weapons trafficking

body: News News Item Electoral Integrity and Public Confidence at the Heart of the 2026 General Elections Issued on: 3 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina Fields of work: Elections SARAJEVO, 3 September 2026 – With Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 2026 General Elections approaching, the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina and Civil Society BiH today brought together election officials, civil society, media, academia and international partners to discuss new election technologies, electoral integrity and the importance of a peaceful and democratic election campaign. The conference , “What Can We Expect from the 2026 Elections? New Electoral Technologies, Election Integrity, and a Democratic Election Campaign,” takes place one day before the official campaign begins and one month ahead of Election Day on 4 October. For the first time, the General Elections will involve biometric voter identification and authentication, as well as ballot scanners and electronic transmission of election results. The Mission has worked closely with the Central Election Commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina (CEC BiH) in supporting preparations for the introduction of these technologies, alongside its broader support for electoral integrity and voter education. “These new technologies will make the electoral process more accurate, transparent and efficient, but it is not just technology alone that builds public confidence in election results,” said Ambassador Rick Holtzapple, Head of the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina. “Confidence also depends on how elections are administered, observed, reported and explained to voters. All those involved, institutions, political parties, observers, civil society and the media, have a responsibility to contribute to an electoral process that citizens can trust.” "Despite strong support from international organizations and individual global powers for electoral integrity, democratic campaigning, and the building of a democratic society, and, to a certain extent, the introduction of new technologies, the responsibility for the integrity of the electoral process lies primarily with the politicians. They must demonstrate whether they are all finally committed to progress, democracy, and the European path, or if some still wish to continue with the undemocratic and corrupt practices of the past," said Laura Bošnjak, Project Manager of Civil Society BiH. "It is the citizens who elect them; therefore, those citizens must recognize serious platforms, turn out to vote in the largest possible numbers, and decide to whom they will entrust their future and what that future will look like. Participants also discussed the responsibility of political parties to conduct a peaceful, constructive and substantive campaign focused on issues affecting citizens, rather than divisive rhetoric and narratives that heighten ethno-national tensions. Particular attention was given to the participation of first-time voters and to the importance of accurate voter information about the new voting procedures. The OSCE Mission to BiH and Civil Society BiH call on all eligible citizens to exercise their right to vote on 4 October 2026, to seek information from reliable sources and to reject divisive rhetoric and misinformation. They also call on political parties and candidates to offer voters a peaceful, issue-based campaign focused on concrete solutions and the future of all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
title: Electoral Integrity and Public Confidence at the Heart of the 2026 General Elections

body: Stories Story From Tokyo to Prague: Bridging continents through Europe’s living legacy Date: 2 July 2026 Source: OSCE Documentation Centre in Prague Copied Why does a renowned Professor from Tokyo travel over 9,000 kilometres to a quiet archive in Prague? For Professor Takeshi Yuasa, the answer lies in the pursuit of historical truths found only in the records of the OSCE Documentation Centre in Prague . The Centre is the guardian of the Organization’s institutional memory, preserving the diplomatic milestones that have shaped European security and co-operation since the Helsinki Final Act was signed in 1975. The Centre is more than a library; it is a bridge connecting researchers to the past through its archives, and to the present through the living witnesses who shaped European security. Tracing European security from Tokyo to Prague Professor Yuasa, an expert in Russian Studies and International Relations from Sophia University in Japan, arrived in Prague for a two-month mission: the OSCE Documentation Centre's Researcher-in-Residence programme . Since its launch in 1998, the programme has welcomed over 300 researchers and academics to the CSCE CSCE Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe and OSCE archival collections, offering scholars a front-row seat to nearly three decades of institutional history. As the first researcher of 2026, Professor Yuasa set out to decode the "trial-and-error process regarding the construction of regional security architecture in Europe,” as he says. He focused on the OSCE Security Model discussions of the mid-1990s and the subsequent Corfu Process, and how participating States navigated these frameworks to maintain regional stability. But would the archives alone answer his questions, or would the Centre open a door to the living history behind them? Papers and documents scattered in the air with a blue tint, against a light background. Decoding the archives The answer lies in the Centre’s rich collections, paired with the dedicated assistance offered to every Researcher-in-Residence. "From start to end, the archival assistant's guidance was essential,” Professor Yuasa shares. ”While the database and orientation are user-friendly, the collection is so rich that without assistance, I could not have worked effectively here." The archives are vast, but never navigated alone. That guidance soon led Professor Yuasa to a discovery he hadn't expected. " Have you ever heard of the 'Food for Thought' documents? I encountered this phrase for the first time in the Prague archives." He described these informal papers, used to stimulate discussion and propose new perspectives among participating States. "I felt very lucky to have the chance to touch history through these documents," he said. These were an invitation to think alongside the original diplomats, tracing the earliest ideas that would eventually redefine the security discussions. A bridge beyond Europe Turning archival fingerprints into real dialogue Deeper in the conference and plenary records, one name recurred: former Director of the OSCE Conflict Prevention Centre, Ambassador Herbert Salber, whose efforts to foster dialogue among participating States left a clear mark on the discussions. In one document, Salber posed a question that struck a chord: "What can we do concretely to turn ideas into actual practice?" Professor Yuasa shared his discovery with Ambassador Halka Kaiserova, Head of the Documentation Centre, who connected him with the right contacts. What followed was a facilitated informal meeting in Germany. "When I arrived in Prague for the Researcher-in-Residence programme, I had no expectation to travel to Germany or reach out to such an important figure. I didn't know I would find such a completely new point of view. Catching this chance was a great insight for my research — it was a true surprise for me," he added. A bridge beyond Europe Professor Yuasa's work with the Researcher-in-Residence built a bridge between research, security, and diplomacy, one that reaches beyond Europe. As an Asian Partner for Co-operation, Japan’s connection to the Centre shows how this support extends across continents to foster a shared vision of peace and security. Reflecting on this transformative experience, the Professor shared: "Now, my dreams have come true, and I am quite satisfied with the opportunity to work here at the Documentation Centre in Prague,” he emphasized. His experience is the latest in nearly three decades of the Centre’s contribution to global scholarship, a legacy of countless books, dissertations, and research papers that keep the OSCE's mission at the forefront of academic inquiry. As Professor Yuasa returns to Sophia University in Tokyo, the history he uncovered in Prague will continue to inform his research, proof that the Centre is not just an archive but an engine of the OSCE's visibility and intellectual leadership. title: From Tokyo to Prague: Bridging continents through Europe’s living legacy

body: Stories Story Roots of resilience: the OSCE’s three dimensional approach to security Date: 2 July 2026 Source: OSCE Secretariat Copied Imagine this. One country strikes another, hitting a major power plant in the capital. Overnight, the military situation shifts, troops mobilize, ready to retaliate. It doesn’t stop at the front line. Electricity and heating collapse across the region. Water pumps shut down. Farms can’t irrigate. Entire supply chains grind to a halt. Hospitals switch to emergency generators — then run out of fuel. Families flee as basic services fail. This situation is more than hypothetical. It highlights how an armed conflict is never just a military event. It is simultaneously a political crisis, an economic shock, an environmental hazard, and a human‐rights emergency. This is the basis on which the OSCE was built. Its work spans three areas: politico-military, economic and environmental, and human. These are known as the three dimensions of security, where if something goes wrong, everything can go wrong. The historical roots of the OSCE approach The OSCE’s three areas of security grew out of a simple but radical idea: security is never just military. When 35 states signed the Helsinki Final Act in 1975, they challenged Cold War-thinking by organizing their commitments into three baskets — political‐military stability, economic and environmental co-operation, and protecting human rights. The Helsinki process treated security as something woven through every part of society. A border incident could destabilise markets. A polluted river could inflame political tensions. A human‐rights violation could trigger unrest that spills across borders. Over the following decades, as the Conference on Security and Co‐operation in Europe (CSCE) evolved into the OSCE, these baskets – now dimensions - became the Organization’s operating system. They shaped its dedicated institutions, its field operations, its monitoring tools, and its diplomatic culture. They also proved prescient: the post‐Cold War era brought exactly the kind of multidimensional crises the Helsinki signatories had anticipated. Politico-military dimension of security Politico-Military: The frontline against escalation The politico‐military dimension — the OSCE’s first dimension — is the Organization’s frontline against escalation. It is where the OSCE works on hard security: military transparency, risk reduction, and preventing misunderstandings from turning into crises. But its scope is broader than military de‐escalation alone. It also includes border security, from preventing the trafficking of humans, drugs, and weapons to training border officials to detect forged documents and identify cross‐border criminal activity. On the ground, the OSCE also works directly with states to stop the illicit trafficking of small arms and light weapons— securing vulnerable depots, destroying excess stockpiles, and reducing the risk that weapons leak into criminal or extremist networks. Economic-environmental dimension of security Economic-Environmental: Resilience as a security imperative The economic and environmental dimension recognizes that instability doesn’t only come from armed conflict — it can come from failing institutions, environmental crises, and financial systems that can be exploited in seconds. This means strengthening anti‐corruption systems so public funds aren’t siphoned off by criminal networks. It means helping governments improve energy security so a single cyberattack or pipeline failure doesn’t paralyze an entire region. It means supporting water management in drought‐prone areas, improving disaster‐risk reduction, and building the capacity of institutions that keep societies functioning under pressure. It also tackles new security risks linked to modern finance, from digital assets that make it easier to move money anonymously to weak rules that let corruption, trafficking, and organized crime grow. This second dimension is about making societies resilient and ensuring that when pressure builds, institutions hold, services continue, and communities are protected from the kinds of shocks that can destabilize entire regions. Human dimension of security Human: Protecting rights to protect stability The human dimension is about ensuring that people have rights they can rely on, institutions they can trust, and a voice in shaping their societies. When institutions weaken and conflict intensifies, rights erode. Journalists are silenced. Courts stop functioning. Minorities face discrimination. Civil society loses space. Communities become polarized, tensions escalate, and violence becomes more likely. The third dimension is where the OSCE supports protecting human rights, rule of law, and democratic institutions. It includes the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights election observation missions, which help ensure that political processes are transparent and accountable. This dimension also encompasses monitoring media freedom, supporting civil society, and helping states strengthen protections for minorities and vulnerable groups. A strength, not just a mandate The OSCE’s three dimensions reflect a simple truth: security is inseparable from the societies that uphold it. When politico-military security is reinforced by resilient economies, when environmental risks are matched by strong governance, and when human rights are protected without compromise, societies become harder to destabilize. Today, the three dimensions remain the backbone of the OSCE. They are not simply historical artefacts, but real-life tools that reflect how conflict and crises actually unfold. This comprehensive approach is not just the OSCE’s mandate. It is its strength and unique character. body: 02/09/2026 Report Thailand en fr th VALERIA MONGELLI / ANADOLU / ANADOLU VIA AFP A new report published by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and its member organisation Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) sheds light on the severe human rights impacts of the enforcement of Article 112 of Thailand’s Criminal Code (lèse-majesté) since the country’s latest military coup in May 2014. Bangkok, Paris, 2 September 2026. The report, titled " The unsayable - Q&A on Thailand’s lèse-majesté" , answers 15 frequently asked questions about Article 112 and its implications for human rights, civic space, the media, and democratic development in Thailand. " The evidence of the serious human rights violation linked to the enforcement of Article 112 is overwhelming and causes great damage to Thailand’s international standing. Reform of Article 112 is long overdue and efforts by Thai civil society to peacefully campaign for such changes should be commended and protected, " said FIDH Vice-President Teppei Ono. Statistics about lèse-majesté reflect the severity and scope of the human rights violations linked to the enforcement of Article 112. Between May 2014 and July 2026, at least 461 individuals were prosecuted under Article 112, with at least 199 receiving prison sentences. The 10 longest prison sentences imposed under Article 112 averaged approximately 30 years and six months, with the longest sentence reaching 50 years. At least 21 children were prosecuted under Article 112, with the youngest one aged 14. As of July 2026, 29 individuals remained detained under Article 112. Of these, 12 were detained pending trial or appeal, while the judgments for the remaining 17 had become final. Among those behind bars is prominent pro-democracy activist and human rights lawyer Arnon Nampa, who has accumulated a prison term of over 31 years stemming from 11 lèse-majesté convictions for his speeches and online posts that called for monarchy reform. Three additional lèse-majesté cases remain pending. At the international level, all the relevant key United Nations (UN) human rights mechanisms have consistently expressed their concerns over various aspects of the enforcement of Article 112 and declared it incompatible with Thailand’s human rights obligations under international law. Many states also expressed growing concern over the issue of lèse-majesté during Thailand’s Universal Periodic Review (UPR). Thailand’s fourth UPR is scheduled for 9 November 2026. FIDH and TLHR call on states to use Thailand’s fourth UPR to raise their concerns over the ongoing abuse of Article 112 and make recommendations to the Thai government to bring this provision into line with international law. FIDH and TLHR also urge Thai authorities to establish a moratorium on new lèse-majesté prosecutions and to immediately release all those who are being deprived of their liberty under Article 112. body: 31/08/2026 Press release Democratic Republic of Congo en es fr Belgium Corruption NICOLAS MAETERLINCK / BELGA MAG / BELGA VIA AFP For the first time, a Belgian company will have to answer in court over allegations that it bribed foreign public officials. Congolese citizens, supported by a coalition of organisations, have joined the proceedings as civil parties before the Belgian courts. Part of the money paid for passports has allegedly been channelled to a relative of former Congolese President Joseph Kabila. The civil parties hope that justice will now be served in this case, which has been ongoing for nine years, and concerns the alleged embezzlement of US$60 million. Kinshasa, Brussels, 31 August 2026. The civil parties welcome the decision handed down this morning by the Brussels Council Chamber today to refer the 14 defendants in the Semlex case to the criminal court. They will have to answer allegations of bribery of foreign public officials, money laundering and tax fraud in connection with the contract for Congolese biometric passports. Semlex, the company that produced the Democratic Republic of Congo’s (DRC) biometric passports between 2015 and 2025, is the first Belgian company to be referred to a Belgian criminal court over alleged foreign bribery, with the prospect of the case being examined on its merits. In May 2020, 51 Congolese citizens brought a civil action before the Belgian courts with the support of the coalition Le Congo n’est pas à vendre (Congo Is Not For Sale). They were joined by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the Human Rights League (LDH), UNIS, Transparency International and Transparency International Belgium, all of which joined the proceedings as civil parties in this landmark case. The civil parties commend the work of the investigators who, over nearly nine years, traced bank transactions, analysed hundreds of emails and electronic messages, interviewed numerous witnesses and suspects, and carried out letters rogatory in the DRC and the United Arab Emirates, where several of the companies involved were registered. This is one of the most thorough investigations ever conducted in Belgium into allegations of international corruption. A US$60 million case The accused are alleged to have set up a large-scale corruption scheme centred on the biometric passport contract. According to documents reported in the press, for every passport sold for US$185, US$60 was allegedly channeled to LRPS Ltd, a Dubai-based company believed to be linked to a close associate of former DRC President Joseph Kabila. The scheme is alleged to have resulted in the diversion of nearly US$60 million. For the civil parties, this case concerns, above all, the Congolese people. " We paid $185 for our passports, before learning from the press that some of that money had allegedly been used to bribe members of the political elite. We have a right to know where our money went. This trial will finally shed light on the matter " said Fred Bauma, Congolese citizen acting as a civil claimant . " It is hoped that this case will also shed light on responsibilities at the Congolese level, which could lead to further legal action in the DRC, so that all those responsible in this case are held to account for their actions before the competent courts ", said Jean-Claude Katende, Vice-President of the FIDH and President of the African Association for the Defence of Human Rights (ASADHO) . This decision also marks a significant step forward for the Belgian justice system. Despite its commitments under the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention and the United Nations Convention against Corruption , the country has been criticised on several occasions for its inadequate enforcement of laws against the bribery of foreign public officials. This trial will be a major test of its ability to uphold these commitments. " For far too long, Belgium has fallen short of its commitments to combat international corruption. This referral to court is historic: it demonstrates that a Belgian company can be held to account for serious alleged acts of corruption committed abroad " said Transparency International Belgium . The signatory organisations stress that those brought before the court are presumed innocent. They hope that the trial will establish responsibility and send a clear message: Belgian companies must be held to account for their actions, including when alleged acts of corruption are committed abroad. body: 12/08/2026 Statement Chad en es fr International Criminal Court (ICC) JORIS BOLOMEY / AFP The announcement by Chadian authorities of their decision to withdraw from the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC) marks a worrying setback for the fight against impunity for the most serious crimes and for victims’ rights. Chad’s commitment to international justice is called into question at a time when the international justice system is facing growing attacks and when state cooperation is more essential than ever. N’Djamena, 12 August 2026. On 27 July 2026, the Government of the Republic of Chad decided to withdraw from the Rome Statute of the ICC. The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the Chadian League for Human Rights (LTDH), the Chadian Association for the Promotion and Defense of Human Rights (ATPDH), and the Public Interest Law Center (PILC) express their profound indignation and condemn this decision. The Rome Statute does not replace national courts; it operates on the basis of complementarity, stepping in when national courts lack the capacity or willingness to investigate and prosecute the most serious crimes. Withdrawal does not strengthen the ability of national courts to deliver justice; instead, it deprives victims of an alternative path to obtaining it. Chad’s withdrawal represents a further setback for the global fight against impunity and for victims’ rights, at a time when the Court is facing unprecedented attacks, including the U.S. government’s campaign to dismantle the ICC . Chad’s announcement does not, however, carry immediate legal consequences. Article 127 of the Rome Statute governs the effects of such a withdrawal: it takes effect only one year after written notification to the UN Secretary-General , in this case, on 27 July 2027. Moreover, withdrawal does not release the State concerned from obligations incurred while it was a party to the Statute, including the obligation to cooperate with the Court on investigations and criminal proceedings already underway before the withdrawal takes effect, and it does not affect investigations or proceedings the Court had already opened before that date. Chad’s withdrawal, should it go forward, therefore cannot erase the past or prevent the Court from exercising jurisdiction over crimes committed before it takes effect. Chad’s announcement comes amid a growing challenge to international criminal justice and the ICC. The three member States of the Alliance of Sahel States (Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger) also recently announced their withdrawal from the ICC. Those withdrawals will take effect on 18 June 2027 for Niger, and 24 June 2027 for Burkina Faso and Mali. African States nonetheless played an essential role in the creation of the Court in 1998, ratifying the Rome Statute in large numbers and even referring certain domestic situations to the Court’s jurisdiction. That commitment gave victims of the most serious crimes an international ally when justice could not be obtained at the national level. Chad’s announced withdrawal runs counter to this history of African leadership, leaving victims with fewer means of obtaining justice. While the ICC has in the past been criticised for the selectivity of the cases it opens and for what was seen as excessive focus on Africa, the Court has progressively worked to strengthen the universality of its mandate, extending its work well beyond the African continent, with ongoing investigations and cases in Afghanistan, Bangladesh/Myanmar, Palestine, Ukraine, Venezuela, and the Philippines. The recent arrest of former President Rodrigo Duterte demonstrated that no region and no senior official is beyond the reach of justice. This universality strengthens the Court’s legitimacy but also makes it more vulnerable to political attacks. The organisations call on Chadian authorities to reverse their decision to withdraw from the ICC and to reaffirm their commitment to the Rome Statute and to international justice. As Chad hosts several hundred thousand refugees from Darfur, many of whom have suffered serious violations of international humanitarian and human rights law, this announcement sends an alarming signal to victims. Victims of the most serious international crimes must not be the first casualties of States’ political choices. When national courts are unable or unwilling to deliver justice, the ICC remains an essential mechanism of last resort to guarantee victims’ right to truth, justice, and reparation. At a time when serious human rights violations persist in many parts of the world, States should be strengthening international mechanisms against impunity, not distancing themselves from them. FIDH, LTDH, ATPDH, and PILC reaffirm their determination to continue, alongside the whole of Chadian and international civil society, the fight against impunity and for justice, victims’ dignity, and respect for human rights in Chad. body: 10/09/2026 Report Ecuador en es fr Human Rights Defenders Antonella Calle International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and six international organisations denounce the climate of repression and militarisation in Ecuador. A new report, prepared following a visit to Ecuador, includes on-the-ground interviews with various communities, human rights defenders, local authorities, and representatives of the international community. Quito, September 10, 2026. Following an observation visit conducted in March 2026, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), within the framework of the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, Front Line Defenders (FLD), CIVICUS: Global Alliance for Citizen Participation, 11.11.11 – Coalition for International Solidarity, the Association of Human Rights Lawyers, Judges, and Prosecutors of Latin America and the Caribbean (Asociación de Abogadas, Abogados, Jueces y Fiscales de Derechos Humanos de América Latina y el Caribe – AJUFIDH), Peace Brigades International (PBI), and the World Rainforest Movement (WRM) are publishing a joint report today that warns of the rapid deterioration of the human rights and environmental situation in Ecuador. Against a backdrop marked by the militarisation of public security, the weakening of the rule of law, and a growing link between extractive conflicts and the securitisation of territories, the report, in spanish only, " Ataques y criminalización contra la sociedad civil en un contexto de militarización y extractivismo en Ecuador " presents the following findings. Setback in the Rule of Law Since March 2024, the government has repeatedly imposed states of emergency, declared internal armed conflict, and expanded the role of the Armed Forces in public safety, thereby normalising exceptional measures that have failed to reduce public insecurity in the country. On the contrary, the number of violent deaths has reached historic highs, and serious human rights violations are being reported in militarized areas, with disproportionate impacts on Indigenous peoples, Afrodescendant communities, and rural campesino communities. " Ecuador stands at a crossroads: either it strengthens the rule of law or it deepens the crisis. Exceptional measures cannot become the new normal, and socioenvironmental conflicts cannot be resolved through the militarisation of territories. A security policy in the country must address the multidimensional causes of violence and must adhere to international law, " states Soraya Gutierrez, Secretary General of the FIDH. Institutional Weakening The organisations note attacks on the Constitutional Court, challenges to judicial independence, delays in the administration of justice, and in the enforcement of court rulings, as well as an insufficient response from the Defensoría del Pueblo (Ombudsman’s Office / People’s Advocate Office) to the criminalisation and freezing of bank accounts of human rights defenders and civil society organisations. In this regard, César Sivo, president of AJUFIDH , states that " judicial independence is non-negotiable: without autonomous powers, the rule of law vanishes and justice becomes a mirage ". Criminalisation of Protest and Shrinking of Civic Space The report identifies patterns of violent repression against peaceful protests led by Indigenous movements, including criminalisation, stigmatisation, and the persecutory use of administrative, financial, and legal measures against human rights defenders and civil society organisations. " We observed a concerning and accelerating deterioration of civic space. The violent repression of the 2025 national strike, coupled with the increase in threats and attacks against journalists, as well as regulatory obstacles to the operation of civil society organisations, create an increasingly hostile environment for the exercise of civic freedoms, " emphasised Eduardo Marenco, Advocacy Officer for the Americas at CIVICUS. Attacks on Human Rights and Environmental Defenders, Civil Society Organisations and Social Movements The visit documents an alarming rate of violence and attacks against human rights and environmental defenders and civil society organisations, with particular attention to cases of criminalization, while the State fails to acknowledge the scale of this problem and adopt robust and effective measures to prevent these violations and protect defenders. " Defending human rights and nature is not a crime, as Ecuador’s own Constitution recognises. The criminalisation, stigmatisation, and attacks against defenders in Ecuador must cease immediately. The State has an obligation to protect those who defend the rights of their communities, not to persecute them, " says Álvaro Gómez del Valle, Advocacy Lead for the Americas at Front Line Defenders. The Rise of Extractivism Far from being a mere sectoral economic policy, extractivism—which spans the mining, oil, agro-industrial, fishing, and hydroelectric sectors—emerges as a web of regulatory, institutional, and security decisions that favor its expansion in the name of economic growth and investment stability in the country. This dynamic occurs at the expense of guarantees of participation, protection of rights, and compliance with democratic and judicial decisions, without respecting Ecuador’s international human rights obligations, which ultimately affect community governance, livelihoods, and the ability of communities to make free and informed decisions regarding their own territories. Regarding this serious issue, Carla Moscoso, Coordinator for the Andean Region of 11.11.11 , notes that " What is at stake is who decides on the territories, which ways of life are protected, and who bears the social and environmental costs of the conflicts, in the face of certain perspectives or categories such as ‘national interest,’ ‘strategic security,’ or ‘strategic sectors’ ." Among their urgent recommendations, the organisations urge the Ecuadorian government to: – align security policies with the principles of legality, necessity, and proportionality, with civilian and judicial oversight over the use of force; – guarantee the independence of public authorities; – put an end to the stigmatisation and criminalisation of protesters, individuals, and organisations defending human and nature rights; – protect human rights and nature defenders and groups through comprehensive policies that incorporate a gender and intercultural perspective; – respect the free, prior, and informed consent of communities affected by extractive projects. At the same time, the organisations call on the international community to: – not normalise the erosion of human rights as a cost of security policies and economic development initiatives; – strengthen monitoring and support for human rights defenders and civil society organisations. " The international community cannot look the other way. Ecuador needs strong support to protect those who defend rights. Our organisations will remain vigilant through international oversight and will closely monitor the human rights situation in the country ," emphasised the signatory organisations. body: 21/08/2026 Statement Japan en es fr Death Penalty MAKOTO KONDO / YOMIURI / THE YOMIURI SHIMBUN VIA AFP The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and its member organisation Center for Prisoners’ Rights (CPR) strongly condemn the latest execution in Japan–the first carried out under Sanae Takaichi, who has been Prime Minister since 21 October 2025. Paris, Tokyo, 21 August 2026 . Sunao Takami, a 58-year-old man convicted of killing five people in a pachinko parlor arson in Osaka in 2009, was executed by hanging at Osaka Detention House today. In 2011, a six-member jury and a panel of three judges rejected the defense’s argument that Takami was mentally ill at the time of the crime. In Japan’s recent history, there have been executions of death row inmates with suspected mental illnesses. Today’s execution is the sixth since 2020 and the first since June 2025. There are currently 100 prisoners (including six women) on death row. FIDH and CPR urge the government to take concrete steps towards the abolition of the death penalty, by implementing the recommendations that States and United Nations (UN) human rights mechanisms have made for many years. These recommendations include: the declaration of an official moratorium on the use of the death penalty; the ratification of the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; the commutation of all death sentences to prison terms; and the alignment of conditions for death row inmates to international standards. FIDH and CPR also urge the Japanese government to abstain in the upcoming UN General Assembly’s biennial resolution on a moratorium on the use of the death penalty. Japan has consistently voted against such resolution in the past. FIDH, a founding member of the World Coalition Against the Death Penalty (WCADP) and a member of its Steering Committee, and CPR, a member of the WCADP, oppose the death penalty for all crimes and in all circumstances. body: 28/08/2026 Statement India en fr United Nations FIDH The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) welcomes the findings and recommendations made by the United Nations (UN) Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) related to India. FIDH urges the Indian authorities to fully implement the CERD’s recommendations without delay, particularly regarding comprehensively criminalising discrimination and hate crimes, and ensuring accountability for perpetrators of related human rights violations. Paris, 28 August 2026 . On 25 August 2026, the UN CERD released its findings and recommendations (known as " Concluding Observations ") concerning India, following the review of the country’s combined 20th and 21st periodic reports on the implementation of the International Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (ICERD), which took place on 11 and 12 August 2026 in Geneva. The CERD monitors the implementation of the ICERD’s provisions by state parties, including India. Some of the CERD’s Concluding Observations reflected information presented by FIDH and partners in two joint reports submitted to the CERD as part of its review of India. For example, the CERD expressed concern over gaps in the Indian legislative framework, including the lack of a comprehensive definition of racial discrimination and the failure to explicitly criminalise all acts of racist hate speech and hate crimes. It also expressed concerns about " reports of widespread racial discrimination, including hate crimes and hate speech " including by politicians. The CERD called on the Indian government to review the legislative framework to address these gaps, and to take effective measures to increase accountability for hate speech and hate crimes. The CERD was " gravely concerned " by reports of widespread human rights violations against ethnic and ethno-religious groups, Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, and non-citizens, including extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detentions, torture, and sexual violence. It called on the Indian authorities to ensure that perpetrators are prosecuted and held accountable. With regards to civic space, the CERD raised concerns over the use of laws such as the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA), the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA) and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) to stifle the rights to freedom of expression and association, and to silence human rights defenders, including those working to defend the rights of minorities. It recommended that the authorities review those laws and ensure an enabling environment for civil society. The CERD also expressed concerns about, and made recommendations to address, the specific situations for Dalits, Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, nomadic and semi-nomadic tribes, domestic workers, and migrants and asylum seekers. The CERD noted in particular its concerns relating to the deportation and forcible returns of Rohingya asylum seekers, as well as the use of hate speech by politicians and other public figures targeting Rohingya and Bengali-speaking Muslims. Finally, the CERD made recommendations related to the right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion, the right to health, and the National Register of Citizens and Citizenship Amendment Act. body: 13/08/2026 Press release Guinea - Conakry en es fr PATRICK MEINHARDT / AFP In Guinea, Bienvenu Lamah, one of those accused in the 28 September 2009 massacres, has been promoted to the rank of brigadier general of the national gendarmerie by a decree issued by President Mamadi Doumbouya, despite the extremely serious charges against him. The Guinean regime must abandon this promotion, as civil parties have appealed his acquittal and a new trial is due to take place. For the civil parties, this promotion is deeply regrettable and amounts to the authorities normalising the massacres committed on 28 September 2009, which were nonetheless classified as crimes against humanity by the Guinean judiciary itself. 13 August 2026. Complicity in murder, rape, and assault occasioning actual bodily harm; abductions; unlawful detention; obstruction of assistance to victims. The charges against Bienvenu Lamah paint a chilling picture of a man who has been promoted to the rank of brigadier general of the national gendarmerie by decree of President Mamadi Doumbouya, only a few days after his acquittal . This promotion comes as the civil parties have appealed against this ruling by the Dixinn Criminal Court. The Kaléyah military training centre, where Bienvenu Lamah was serving at the time, is said to have been the starting point for groups of " recruits in training " involved in the violations committed on 28 September 2009 at the stadium of the same name, which left 156 people dead, over a thousand injured, and saw more than 100 women raped. The prosecution had argued for the defendant’s responsibility and sought a ten-year prison sentence, calling for the acts to be reclassified as crimes against humanity. " Given the charges that still stand against Bienvenu Lamah, since we have appealed the ruling acquitting him, his promotion to the rank of brigadier general of the Guinean national gendarmerie is an affront to the civil parties and amounts to normalising the violence of 28 September 2009 ", said Drissa Traoré, Secretary-General of FIDH and lawyer for the civil parties in the Conakry trial . " By promoting one of those allegedly responsible for the massacres of 28 September 2009, President Mamadi Doumbouya has chosen to reward, even before the judicial process has concluded, a person accused of acts classified as crimes against humanity. This sends a bad signal to all victims, and indeed to all Guineans, and runs counter to the rule of law and human dignity ", said Alpha Amadou DS Bah, President of the Guinean Organisation for the Defence of Human and Civil Rights (OGDH) and coordinating lawyer for the group of lawyers representing the civil parties . " We observe that at Bienvenu Lamah’s trial, the victims were listened to without being heard. Their harrowing accounts left no doubt as to the defendant’s direct involvement in the worst violations committed on 28 September and in the days that followed. His promotion, after his acquittal, is felt as a deep wound and a further injustice for all those still waiting for recognition and justice ", said Asmaou Diallo, founder and President of the Association of Victims, Relatives and Friends of 28 September 2009 (AVIPA) . The appeal concerning Bienvenu Lamah is one of three appeals currently under way, lodged by the civil parties, to which the judicial authorities have yet to give any concrete response. body: FIDH - International Federation for Human Rights reposted this Truth Hounds 3,442 followers 3d Report this post On 9 September, Truth Hounds, together with FIDH - International Federation for Human Rights , organised and held a side event as part of the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council ( #UNHRC ), focusing on #Russia ’s use of predatory recruitment practices to replenish the ranks of its armed forces. The event brought together 42 participants, including representatives of 12 State delegations accredited to the UN. The event featured a strong and diverse panel comprising Ilia Nuzov , Head of Eastern Europe and Central Asia Desk (FIDH); Andrii Latsyba , Legal Counsel (Truth Hounds); Dr. Katarina Schwarz , UN Special Rapporteur on Contemporary Forms of Slavery and Trafficking in Persons; and H.E. Mr. Yevhenii Tsymbaliuk, Permanent Representative of Ukraine to the UN Office and other International Organizations in Geneva, who delivered the closing remarks. The panel also included Rosemary Tollo, Journalist and Researcher of the Russian Recruitment in African countries and a Truth Hounds partner in documenting predatory recruitment practices, as well as Jelena Aparac, former Chair of the UN Working Group on the use of mercenaries, global expert in governance, risk, and accountability in conflict-affected and high-risk environments. Jelena Aparac previously participated in the presentation of the Truth Hounds and FIDH report in April 2026. The participation of diplomatic representatives, UN experts and independent researchers provided an important opportunity to bring documented evidence of Russia’s recruitment practices to the attention of key international stakeholders and strengthen advocacy on this issue within the UN human rights system. “Russia's predatory recruitment, which in many cases may amount to human trafficking, continues and is expanding. Since the report's publication in April 2026, we have already observed new trends that were previously difficult to identify, in particular the large-scale recruitment in Peru and Southeast Asia,” said Andrii Latsyba, Legal Counsel at Truth Hounds. The event formed part of Truth Hounds’ broader advocacy efforts aimed at drawing international attention to Russia’s systematic recruitment of foreign nationals, as well as the coercive and deceptive practices used to carry it out. Truth Hounds continues to monitor the geographical scope of Russia’s recruitment efforts and expand its network of journalists, researchers and civil society representatives working on this issue in different countries. In the coming months, Truth Hounds and its partners plan to continue their advocacy efforts at other international and intergovernmental platforms in Europe and beyond. 26 Like Comment Share

body: Share The OMCT works with 200 member organisations to end torture and ill-treatment, assist victims, and protect human rights defenders at risk wherever they are. Together, we make up the largest global group actively standing up to torture in over 90 countries. We work to protect the most vulnerable members of our societies, including women, children, indigenous peoples, migrants and other marginalized communities. To achieve this, we advocate with governments to change or implement their laws and policies, we help victims seek justice and strive to hold perpetrators to account. Because torture can never be tolerated, and human dignity is not negotiable.
title: Who we are

body: What is torture? Share Torture is the intentional destruction of a human being by another. The methods by which severe pain and suffering are inflicted vary, but they all have the same objective: to break a person, erase them as an individual, and deny they are human. Most of the time, torture evokes physical suffering, such as beatings or electrical shocks, and sexual abuse, such as rape and sexual humiliation. Inhuman conditions in detention, including severe overcrowding and total lack of hygiene, or the denial of medical care, can also amount to torture or other ill-treatment. But it is important to stress that psychological torture can inflict equal levels of pain. This is the case for example with sleep deprivation, prolonged solitary confinement, or with the person being threatened that someone they love will be tortured or killed. Breaking bodies ultimately aims at destroying minds. Torture victims suffer of course in their flesh. The humiliation and shame they feel as a result of what they endured also cause great damage and are difficult to heal. Torture obliterates trust in others and reconnecting that bond to society is critical to start rebuilding the survivor’s life and avoid trauma in future generations. When torture is widespread, the whole community can be profoundly affected. Torture and other ill-treatment keep happening worldwide, to varying degrees – from rare to systematic, depending on the country, and are often left unpunished. Because the effects of torture and other forms of ill-treatment are so utterly devastating, these practices are among a handful that have been universally banned. The prohibition of torture, just like the prohibition of slavery, is legally called ius cogens. This means that, even if a State is not a party to one of several treaties that specifically ban torture and other ill-treatment, it must not resort to it, and not tolerate that anyone carries it out on its territory. From a legal standpoint, acts of torture must be investigated, prosecuted and perpetrators must be punished. The victims have the right to benefit from remedies and reparation, including rehabilitation. The reality is very different. Torture and other ill-treatment keep happening worldwide, to varying degrees – from rare to systematic, depending on the country, and are often left unpunished. Precise statistics are impossible to establish, because torture is overwhelmingly a crime of darkness, but very large numbers of people are victims every year. For the past two decades, public perception has often equated torture with the fight against terrorism. The reality is that torture can happen to anyone. The victims are most often the poor, marginalized groups, members of ethnic or religious minorities, those without power or any form of social protection. Even children are tortured or otherwise ill-treated, particularly in settings of deprivation of liberty, which takes a particularly heavy toll on them. Officials, including the police, prey on all these people in secret and without fear of punishment. Torture is linked to corruption, to the reliance on forced confessions, and to authoritarian governments instilling fear to entrench their power. TAKE ACTION ON TORTURE Find out how you can help by being loud, sharing the facts and never backing down. Click here The 1984 Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman, or Degrading Treatment or Punishment defines the perpetrators as people in an official capacity. Article 1 states: For the purposes of this Convention, the term "torture" means any act by which severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted on a person for such purposes as obtaining from him or a third person information or a confession, punishing him for an act he or a third person has committed or is suspected of having committed, or intimidating or coercing him or a third person, or for any reason based on discrimination of any kind, when such pain or suffering is inflicted by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity. It does not include pain or suffering arising only from, inherent in or incidental to lawful sanctions. Since then, the UN Committee Against Torture and regional human rights courts have interpreted this definition, by finding that a State is responsible for acts committed by individuals acting in a private capacity if the State fails to exercise due diligence to prevent, investigate, prosecute and punish such acts. This is for example the case when the authorities refuse to prosecute a private individual who has inflicted severe harm, including rape, on a woman. In such a situation, the State is complicit or otherwise responsible for consenting or acquiescing to the violence.

body: Our Coalitions Share OMCT works hand in hand with member organisations of the global SOS-Torture Network . In addition to this key collaboration, OMCT is part of several coalitions, including the United Against Torture Consortium (UATC), ProtectDefenders.eu (PD.EU), and the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders. Together, these partnerships ensure that no defender or victim stands alone. They allow us to multiply the reach and impact of our work: combining expertise, pooling resources, and building the collective pressure that no single actor could generate alone. They embody our core conviction that only a strong, globally connected anti-torture movement can turn the tide. The United Against Torture Consortium (UATC) The United Against Torture Consortium brings together OMCT alongside APT, FIACAT, IRCT, OMEGA and REDRESS — six organisations united in their commitment to eradicating torture. The Consortium channels EU funding into the capacity building of local actors, movement building, advocacy, victim support, accountability work, and crisis response. The Consortium demonstrates how organisations with complementary mandates — covering prevention, protection, accountability, and rehabilitation — can join forces to generate a greater systemic impact. ProtectDefenders.eu (PD.EU) ProtectDefenders.eu is the European Union Human Rights Defenders mechanism, led by a consortium of 12 NGOs. Operating a permanent, round-the-clock helpdesk, it provides urgent support to defenders in danger — including emergency grants, temporary relocation, and organisational strengthening for local groups in hostile contexts. OMCT participates in this consortium, contributing its global network and anti-torture expertise to ensure that defenders targeted for their work receive timely and effective protection. The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders Launched in 1997 by OMCT and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the Observatory is a collaboration built on both organisations' global networks. Its strategy encompasses prevention and early warning, direct assistance to defenders at risk, capacity building, and advocacy at the United Nations and regional bodies across Africa, the Americas, and Europe.

body: Nothing can replace action on the ground. The SOS-Torture Network is at the heart of the OMCT and is the currently the most important global network striving to put an end to torture and protect human rights defenders. At the outset, in 1985, it was composed of 48 non-governmental organisations (NGOs). Today, its over 200 members work in over 90 countries all over the world. The members are highly diverse in terms of their size, composition, resources and specific modes of action. What they have in common are their commitment to document cases of torture, help victims, seek justice, advocate legal and policy reforms and protect human rights defenders. Why become a member? learn more How to become a member learn more Our Member Directory Get to know our members from around the world Our member directory OMCT actions within the Network follows three principles: OMCT seeks to respect the originality and action methods of each NGO member in the Network. It believes that the information received from these organisations reflects the reality on the ground in all its complexity, and integrates the local NGO’s strategic approach and cultural background. OMCT’s “modus operandi” completes and reinforces action on the ground, without ever trying to replace it.
