body: Bishkek, Sept. 10, 2026. /Kabar/. A roundtable on the role of women in promoting good-neighborliness and sustainable development between Kyrgyzstan and China was held in Bishkek on Thursday. The event brought together representatives of government agencies, the diplomatic corps, business and academic communities, women's organizations and entrepreneurs from Kyrgyzstan and China. Chinese Ambassador to Kyrgyzstan Liu Jiangping said cooperation between women has become an important part of relations between the two countries. According to her, the All-China Women's Federation and the Congress of Women of Kyrgyzstan have maintained close cooperation for many years. The Chinese Embassy also supports projects aimed at expanding opportunities for Kyrgyz women, including computer courses, vocational training and the provision of equipment to women's crisis centers. This year, as part of the SCO Women's Forum, the All-China Women's Federation and the Congress of Women of Kyrgyzstan also launched a Kyrgyz-Chinese beauty salon project. Chinese specialists visited Kyrgyzstan to share their professional skills and experience with local women. Liu Jiangping noted that China pays particular attention to women's development. More than 99.9% of school-age girls in China attend school, while about 27 million women study at higher educational institutions, accounting for 50.8% of all university students. President of the Congress of Sinologists of Kyrgyzstan Kanaiym Baktygulova said women's cooperation is becoming an increasingly important component of Kyrgyz-Chinese relations. She highlighted prospects for creating new women's business networks between Kyrgyzstan and China, implementing joint educational and digital programs, and developing cooperation in e-commerce, tourism, creative industries and light industry. “Supporting women is not only a social task. It is an investment in the economic future of the country,” Baktygulova said. The roundtable also presented regional projects of the Congress of Women of Kyrgyzstan, including branches of the Kyrgyz-Chinese Digitalization Center for Women in Batken, Jalal-Abad, Naryn and Issyk-Kul regions, as well as sewing centers in Jalal-Abad and Batken regions. As part of the event, the Congress of Women of the Kyrgyz Republic presented sewing machines to the Kyrgyz Council of Craftsmen and the Dinar Brand KG ethnic studio on a grant basis. Honorary members of the Congress were also awarded medals for leadership, labor valor and exemplary motherhood. Participants discussed prospects for further expanding Kyrgyz-Chinese cooperation, developing joint economic and humanitarian initiatives, introducing innovations and digital technologies, supporting women's entrepreneurship, and strengthening the role of women in public diplomacy. Following the roundtable, participants developed proposals and recommendations aimed at further strengthening the partnership, implementing joint initiatives, and promoting friendship, peace and good-neighborly relations between Kyrgyzstan and China. Print

body: Kyrgyzstan Airports Bishkek, Aug. 25, 2026. /Kabar/. In connection with the SCO Summit and the World Nomad Games, Manas International Airport will switch to a special operating regime on August 31 and September 1, 2026. To ensure the reception and servicing of aircraft carrying heads of state and official delegations, temporary restrictions on the arrival and departure of scheduled passenger flights will be introduced during the daytime. On August 31, the restrictions will be in effect from 9:00 AM to 8:00 PM. During this period, passenger flight arrivals and departures will be temporarily restricted due to the arrival of summit participants. On September 1, the airport will continue to operate under a special regime. Restrictions on passenger flights will be in effect from 10:00 AM to 10:00 PM. Kyrgyzstan Airports is currently conducting the necessary coordination and information work with airlines. Carriers are advised to adjust their schedules in advance: reschedule individual flights to available time slots or cancel them if necessary. Manas International Airport will not completely cease operations. At night, outside of the restricted periods, the airport will continue to handle passenger flights. Kyrgyzstan Airports asks passengers planning travel on August 31 and September 1 to closely monitor the current schedule, check the status of their flight directly with the airline in advance, and take into account possible changes to departure and arrival times. The temporary restrictions are necessary to ensure security and organize the reception of official delegations during the summit. Kyrgyzstan Airports apologizes for any inconvenience this may cause and asks passengers for their understanding regarding the temporary changes to airport operations. Print

body: Bishkek, July 27, 2026 /Kabar/. The State Civil Aviation Agency is strengthening its requirements for the quality of passenger service and is introducing a mandatory ban on overbooking for all airlines operating flights through Kyrgyz airports and cooperating with Kyrgyzstan. This decision to protect passenger rights, improve the quality of aviation service, and prevent the denial of carriage to passengers with confirmed air tickets. Overbooking is the practice of an airline selling more tickets than the number of seats on board an aircraft. Despite the prevalence of this practice in a number of countries, it often results in violation of passenger rights, as passengers are forced to wait for their next flight, change their plans, and incur additional expenses. In this regard, all airlines operating through airports in Kyrgyzstan are required to eliminate the practice of overbooking passenger seats and ensure that the number of tickets sold corresponds to the actual capacity of the aircraft. In the event of a forced aircraft substitution with a smaller capacity, the carrier is obligated to offer passengers a choice: a voluntary change of travel conditions only with the customer's consent, transfer to the next available flight, or a full refund of the ticket price. Airlines are instructed to promptly bring their internal sales procedures into compliance with the new requirements and conduct staff training. Print
title: State Civil Aviation Agency bans overbooking on Kyrgyz flights 27 July 2026 1563

body: Kabar As part of their comprehensive strategic partnership, Kyrgyzstan and China are developing a multi-level system of cooperation aimed at strengthening regional ties and enhancing the effectiveness of interaction both bilaterally and within multilateral formats. In this context, experts view Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Bishkek during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit as an important political event that will align the development of bilateral relations with broader efforts to strengthen cooperation across the Eurasian space. While the key areas of cooperation supported by both sides are being advanced at the diplomatic level, the practical details of major infrastructure projects designed to create new drivers of economic growth are being worked out directly between the countries involved. One of the most significant examples is the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway. The project is expected to become a key element of efficient regional logistics, providing a shorter transport corridor connecting trade routes across the SCO space. Experts say the launch of this high-capacity transcontinental highway will change the geopolitical landscape of Central Asia and influence the development logic of many countries both within the Eurasian continent and beyond. Therefore, the topic of the project's practical implementation and accelerating its implementation will be central to the talks between Sadyr Zhaparov and Xi Jinping. Political scientists compare the expected effect to the arrival of a full-flowing river in arid lands. The economy will flourish thanks to a transport artery that will feed stranded factories and plants, opening up opportunities for them to purchase raw materials and technology, and freely ship finished products to previously inaccessible markets. Public and political figure, historian Zainidin Kurmanov, speaks of a transition to a new coordinate system, where new infrastructure projects serve the goals of shared development, where economies do not compete with each other but, by complementing each other, allow for the growth of the potential of a common development space. "This, of course, has profound implications, both geopolitical and economic, as we are entering a crucial phase of implementing the 'One Belt, One Road' strategy. This strategy is intended not only for China, Europe, and Asia, but also for other continents. This is a very important global project. Therefore, Xi Jinping's visit and the SCO summit, with 20 heads of state coming to Bishkek, share a common goal: improving and strengthening relations with the region surrounding China, including Russia, India, Central Asia, Europe, and so on. Kyrgyzstan is the focus of China's current policy as a strategic partner, and the implementation of this project is given serious importance. And for our country, as President Sadyr Zhaparov said, the railway will become a second Kumtor, perhaps even more significant in scale, impact, and economic potential. Kyrgyzstan is breaking its geopolitical deadlock and gaining access to the seas and oceans, becoming an extremely important point that is integrated into the global concept of new development. We are becoming a focal point for the interests of major partners, a hub for the development of a new world. It's a mistake to think that the road through Kyrgyzstan is just part of a median corridor to the Caspian; it will have a direct connection with the transport infrastructure of Russia and other countries. First and foremost, this is an SCO project, and this corridor will serve the interests of the organization's partners, who will ensure its full capacity. We've maintained high growth rates for several years now; this year, GDP is growing by more than 11%. This is an excellent trend, but it won't last forever; we can't lose momentum now. Therefore, while there is the opportunity and the willingness of friendly countries to support our development, we should certainly take advantage of this, in a positive way, of course, by advancing our national interests and economically integrating with our partners," expert Zainidin Kurmanov said. Political scientist Sheradil Baktygulov noted that, thanks to the efforts of the heads of state, relations between Kyrgyzstan and China have reached an unprecedented level. Sadyr Zhaparov and Xi Jinping have built pragmatic and good-neighborly relations that are beneficial to both sides and serve national interests. "In recent years, bilateral cooperation has demonstrated excellent results. Among these is a remarkable leap in economic and trade development. China has become Kyrgyzstan's largest trading partner. Bilateral trade turnover reached $27.2 billion in 2025, a 19.8% increase from the previous year. China and Kyrgyzstan aim to increase trade turnover to $45 billion over the next four years. This goal is ambitious but achievable. These figures reflect revenues to the country's budget, which will be used to pay salaries, pensions, and benefits, as well as to build schools, hospitals, internal roads, and so on. Both sides firmly support each other on issues affecting their core interests. For example, Kyrgyzstan firmly supports the "one China" principle, and China supports Kyrgyzstan's territorial integrity and national sovereignty. The flagship China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway project is moving forward rapidly. The modernization of the irrigation system, supported by China, is addressing the water supply issues of millions of Kyrgyzstanis. It's also worth noting that cooperation between Kyrgyzstan and China has expanded beyond traditional trade and economic interactions to new areas such as renewable energy, artificial intelligence, and the digital economy. "From large-scale highway construction to small-scale waste-to-energy projects, this cooperation is gaining momentum and ensuring the long-term sustainable development of Kyrgyzstan and the entire Central Asian region," said Sheradil Baktygulov. Furthermore, the political scientist noted that China is sharing its technologies. China built and launched Kyrgyzstan's first large-scale solar power plant in the city of Kemin, which provides energy to 30,000 households. In Bishkek, a waste-to-energy plant generates electricity from waste. In terms of technology, it's a thermal power plant, but it burns waste rather than coal or gas. This means that cooperation in the energy sector has broad prospects. And this applies not only to the development of renewable energy sources or investments in hydroelectric power plants. Just recently, an agreement was signed on fuel supplies to Kyrgyzstan, and agreements were reached with China on the construction of oil refineries and oil exploration and production. New technologies are changing our country's economic model. We are transitioning from a re-export model to a manufacturing one. This means that high-value-added industries are being created in Kyrgyzstan. In simple terms, the country will earn more. Another important aspect is the agreement on joint management of border crossing points, the number of which, as we see, is increasing. This means the introduction of a "single window," where border and customs services from Kyrgyzstan and China, located in the same building, will simultaneously monitor the crossing of goods. This will speed up the process of goods clearance and have a positive impact on trade volumes. Ultimately, our citizens will receive the goods they need more quickly, businesses will receive additional dividends, and the state will generate additional revenue by reducing "black" and "gray" imports. Political scientists say Kyrgyzstan is becoming a key logistics hub in the heart of the Eurasian continent. This is the result of diplomatic engagement with friendly countries, the development of fundamentally new relations within the SCO, and the strengthening of ties with close partners. body: Kabar Trade, investment, and railways: State of Kyrgyz-Chinese Relations Relations between Kyrgyzstan and China have reached a new level in recent years, reflected not only in intensified political dialogue but also in the implementation of concrete projects in trade, investment, transport, energy, agriculture, technology, and education. Today, bilateral cooperation extends beyond trade and focuses on expanding transport and logistics capacity, developing production and exports, strengthening energy potential, introducing digital technologies, and training skilled personnel. Trade between Kyrgyzstan and China According to the National Statistics Committee, from January to May 2026, the total foreign trade turnover between Kyrgyzstan and China amounted to $2.09 billion. China remains the country's largest trading partner, accounting for 32.1% of its total foreign trade. During the same period, Kyrgyzstan's exports to China reached $73.7 million. Kyrgyzstan's imports from China totaled $1,935.9 million. Investments: Production and new projects China is the largest non-CIS investor in Kyrgyzstan's economy. In the first quarter of 2026, direct investment from China to Kyrgyzstan amounted to $ 80,154,400. This figure increased by 20.9% compared to the same period last year and accounted for more than one-fifth of the total foreign capital inflow into the country. Chinese investment plays a significant role in Kyrgyzstan’s economy, spanning the mining, manufacturing, energy, and infrastructure sectors. A number of major enterprises and industrial projects have been implemented in the country with Chinese investment. Among them is Altynken LLC, which is developing the Taldy-Bulak Levoberezhny gold deposit, one of the largest joint investment projects between Kyrgyzstan and China. In the industrial sector, the ORIS NPZ oil refinery was launched in 2024 as part of Kyrgyz-Chinese cooperation. A total of 255 million soms was invested in the project, and the facility is currently operating at full capacity. In addition, a waste-to-energy plant has been built in Bishkek, processing municipal waste while generating electricity. Economist Iskender Sharsheyev told Kabar News Agency that cooperation with China is opening up new opportunities for Kyrgyzstan in trade, investment, infrastructure, manufacturing, energy, and transit. "Relations between Kyrgyzstan and China have risen to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership in a new era. According to Chinese customs statistics, trade turnover between the two countries reached a record high in 2024, exceeding $22 billion. China is one of Kyrgyzstan's main trade and investment partners. This creates conditions for the entry of affordable goods from China and the entry of Kyrgyz agricultural products, including organic produce, into the Chinese market," the economist said. Railway: An opportunity for Kyrgyzstan to become a transit country One of the largest cooperation projects between Kyrgyzstan and China is the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway. The section within Kyrgyzstan is approximately 304 km long. This railway will transform Kyrgyzstan into part of a new transport link between China and Central Asia. "The largest infrastructure cooperation project is the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway. Its construction was symbolically launched at the end of 2024, after which it entered its active phase. This railway is expected to transform Kyrgyzstan into a major transit hub between China, Central Asia, and Europe, reducing cargo delivery times to 7-8 days. Annual transit revenue could reach approximately $200 million. Enterprises and logistics centers such as At-Bashy and Manas will be established along the route, and new jobs will be created," Sharsheyev said. It is worth noting that the possibility of establishing a freight transfer station and logistics center in the Makmal area is currently under consideration. Cargo will not only transit through Kyrgyzstan but will also create demand for storage, sorting, processing, packaging, and other logistics services. President Sadyr Zhaparov, in a recent interview with journalist Ali Toktakunov, noted that the launch of the railway would generate significant budget revenues from cargo transit. The head of state described the railway as a long-term investment project for Kyrgyzstan, calling it “a second Kumtor.” Energy: A key prerequisite for production The operation of new factories, logistics centers, and enterprises directly depends on a stable electricity supply. Energy is considered a separate area of cooperation with China. For example, agreements have been signed and projects are being implemented with Chinese companies to build large solar power plants in the country. Specifically, investment projects to build solar power plants are currently underway in the Ak-Tatyr rural municipality of the Batken district and in the Ak-Turpak rural municipality of the Kadamjay district. Ak-Turpak Solar Power Plant: This plant is being jointly built by States Technology Co., Limited, and San Energy Co., in accordance with an agreement signed in Suzhou, China. The total capacity is 250 MW. Preparatory and construction work is currently underway, with full commissioning scheduled for 2027. The Ak-Tatyr solar power plant is being implemented by CECEP Solar Energy Co., Ltd., one of China's largest state-owned corporations. The first phase of this plant, with a total capacity of 600 MW (200 MW), is scheduled to begin operation in September 2026. Construction is currently nearing completion. Both plants are separate facilities being built with direct Chinese investment to ensure energy independence for the Batken region. Technology and the digital economy Technology is a new area of cooperation with China. During President Sadyr Zhaparov's state visit to China in 2025, the Ministry of Digital Development signed two memorandums with the Chinese side, creating new opportunities for technological development and digital transformation in the country. China's experience in artificial intelligence, digital payments, telecommunications, and e-commerce is of great importance to Kyrgyzstan. For example, in 2025, a memorandum was signed between the Kyrgyz Elcard system and the Chinese international digital payments platform Alipay+. As part of this partnership, in May of this year, Interbank Processing Center CJSC (Elcard), together with Alipay+, launched international QR payments for users in Kyrgyzstan. As a result, Elcard Mobile users now have the ability to make payments abroad. This project was implemented as part of digital infrastructure development and aims to simplify payments for tourists and entrepreneurs. Education - a long-term capital of cooperation Education is another important area of Kyrgyz-Chinese cooperation. For the 2025–2026 academic year, the Chinese side offered 125 scholarships under the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region program and 15 scholarships under the Sichuan Province program. According to the Ministry of Science, Higher Education and Innovation, China has also allocated 15 government scholarships to Kyrgyz citizens. In particular, a competition was announced for undergraduate, language training, master’s, and doctoral programs at Chinese universities for the 2026–2027 academic year. These initiatives are being implemented as part of bilateral cooperation in education, providing Kyrgyz citizens with opportunities to study at Chinese educational institutions. The scholarships cover tuition fees, dormitory accommodation, monthly stipends, and health insurance. All of these measures are being implemented as part of the two countries' cooperation in education, and Kyrgyz citizens are receiving scholarships for study at Chinese educational institutions. These scholarships also cover tuition fees, dormitory accommodation, stipend payments, and health insurance. body: Bishkek, Feb. 19, 2026. /Kabar/. On February 18, the Chairman of the Central Election Commission, Tynchtyk Shainazarov, met with the European Parliament delegation for relations with Central Asia, led by President Giussi Princi. According to the CEC, the meeting was attended by Ambassador Rémi Duflo, EU Head, as well as members of the delegation – representatives of Italy, Finland, Germany, France, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria. Shainazarov emphasized that Kyrgyzstan and the Central Election Commission remain open to constructive dialogue and cooperation with European countries. He recalled that parliamentary elections were held in the country on November 30, 2025, to which international observers were invited. A total of 778 observers participated in monitoring the election process, including 374 representatives of OSCE missions. The head of the Central Election Commission noted that the parliamentary corps of the 8th convocation of Kyrgyz Parliament is now fully formed and comprises 90 deputies. Four more deputies were awarded their mandates today. According to him, the updated electoral system has ensured gender equality and expanded opportunities for citizens to exercise their active suffrage, including through remote voting. The use of modern technologies has minimized violations such as ballot stuffing and so-called "carousel voting." Princi noted that the representative composition of the delegation demonstrates the European Parliament's strong interest in strengthening cooperation and developing the partnership between Europe and Kyrgyzstan. She emphasized that the electoral process in the country is perceived as transparent and fair, and expressed interest in the practical aspects of implementing the new electoral system. Print
title: Kyrgyz CEC, European Parliament discuss electoral reforms of Kyrgyzstan 19 February 2026 11231

body: Kabar Agency Bishkek, Feb. 9, 2026. /Kabar/. Central Election Commission has published the list of voters for the re-election of deputies of the Jogorku Kenesh in multi-mandate constituency No. 13. According to the Central Election Commission, the list of voters was compiled by the state institution "Kyzmat" based on the data contained in the Unified State Register of Population. The list of voters will be posted at 94 polling stations. According to it, there are 161,344 voters, of whom: men - 80,3418, or 49.84 percent; women - 80,926, or 50.16 percent. A voter can check his/her name on the list until February 18, 2026: by calling the short numbers 1255 or 119; at the polling station; from the website "tizme.gov.kg"; It is worth noting that the re-election in the district is scheduled for March 1. body: Kabar Agency Bishkek, Feb. 9, 2026. /Kabar/. Today, the campaigning for the re-election of deputies of the Jogorku Kenesh in multi-mandate electoral district No. 13 has begun, Central Election Commission reports. According to the information, since the upcoming elections are being re-held in electoral district No. 13, the period of the general election process has been reduced by one third. Accordingly, the election campaign will last for 20 days. Specifically, from February 9, 2026 to February 28, 2026, at 08:00. Central Election Commission registered a total of 25 candidates to participate in the early elections, 15 of whom are men and 10 are women. Three candidates were deregistered based on their applications. Starting from February 9, 2026, candidates, political parties and other interested citizens have the right to carry out activities aimed at encouraging voters to vote for or against specific candidates, as well as free and comprehensive discussion of candidates' election programs. The main requirement in this case is that all forms and methods of campaign activities must comply with the requirements of election legislation. The re-election in the district is scheduled for March 1. Print

body: The high-level talks between Kyrgyzstan and Pakistan, held in Cholpon-Ata, are a logical continuation of the country's leadership's multi-vector foreign policy. Economist Nurgul Akimova stated in her interview with Kabar news agency. Pakistan is one of the world's leading economies in a number of areas, and has experience in resolving serious international disputes. What does Pakistani leader's visit to Kyrgyzstan indicate? Bishkek has traditionally built close relations with Russia, China, and the CIS countries. The restoration of relations with Pakistan suggests that Kyrgyzstan is accessing South Asia through this country. These negotiations are a logical continuation of the country's leadership's multi-vector foreign policy. Pakistan is known to maintain an independent foreign policy position. Furthermore, it has nuclear power. The country has served as a key mediator between Iran and the United States and is an important regional player. Kyrgyzstan, in turn, currently chairs the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and is strengthening its political clout. I am confident that the agreements reached in December 2025 will be formalized in July 2026. What are the key aspects of economic cooperation between Kyrgyzstan and Pakistan? First and foremost, for Kyrgyzstan, this is an opportunity to gain access to the sea. Pakistan could become an alternative to dependence on ports in China, Russia, or Iran. Furthermore, this country, with a population of approximately 250 million, is a member of the Economic Cooperation Organization. This is a beneficial partnership for us. I'd also like to highlight the potential revenues in the energy sector. As part of the CASA-1000 project, Kyrgyzstan will be able to export excess electricity. I believe the projected revenue for both countries is over $250 million. How are Kyrgyz exporters currently accessing South Asian markets? Currently, Kyrgyz businesses ship goods south by road. Logistically, there's the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor from Kashgar to Karachi. However, it's not a rail corridor—transportation is carried out only by road. As is well known, the volume of Kyrgyz goods is still very small. Furthermore, the route to Karachi remains too long, and transit is expensive. Will China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway project solve this problem in future? If the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway starts to operate, an alternative and cheaper route will emerge. This will increase trade turnover and boost freight traffic. Once completed, transport flow and trade volume will increase. However, until construction is complete, it's premature to discuss logistics and access to the sea, since, as noted, the infrastructure is still underdeveloped. Most importantly, in addition to trade with the CIS countries and China, opportunities for developing alternative economic directions will open up. If Kyrgyzstan and Pakistan demonstrate political will, this will boost economic development and attract investment. Talks with the President of Pakistan indicate that an important political step has already been taken. Thank you for the interview! Print
title: Kyrgyzstan and Pakistan's political will to expand economic opportunities 8 July 2026 2484

body: Kabar The Cabinet of Ministers has submitted for public discussion a draft resolution on granting the status of specially protected natural areas to glaciers and snow-capped regions of Kyrgyzstan. This document establishes the rules for accounting, monitoring, protection and effective use of glaciers, and aims to develop a unified, systematic approach to their conservation. Almaz Musaev, Deputy Minister of Natural Resources, Ecology and Technical Supervision told Kabar about the impact of climate change on the country's main natural wealth, glaciers, and the lives of the people, as well as the measures being taken by the state. — Mr. Musaev, can you tell us about the measures being taken in Kyrgyzstan in connection with climate change? — First of all, I would like to touch upon the fact that President Sadyr Zhaparov raised the issue of the impact of mountainous regions at UN, resulting the adoption of Five-Year Plan for the Development of Mountainous Regions (2023-2027). A special Roadmap sets the tasks of economic development of mountainous regions, implementation of climate change adaptation measures, and protection of natural ecosystems. For example, these include measures such as growing plants that are suitable for the conditions, introducing water conservation technologies. The relevant ministries and state institutions are working on the basis of this Roadmap. Climate change has shown us that mountains, which used to be rich in water, clean air, comfortable and safe, are the most vulnerable. Unfortunately, with climate change, mountainous areas are at risk of being exposed to completely different impacts. Glaciers are melting rapidly, and climate disasters and risks are increasing. With climate change, the areas of diseases and insects that were previously confined to warm regions are also changing. This is a big challenge for the health sector. As part of the five-year anniversary of the development of mountain regions, we plan to hold the “Bishkek+25” Global Mountain Summit in 2027 and once again draw the attention of the world. — What specific projects has Ministry of Natural Resources, Ecology and Technical Supervision introduced ahead of the “Bishkek+25” Mountain Summit, taking into account climate change? — The development of mountain regions by our country and raising the problems of mountaineers at the global level have given a great impetus to the international community. After the call was issued, international organizations are eager to come and work with projects. This can be said to be Kyrgyzstan’s political determination and focus on specific programs. For example, the FAO is implementing a project to increase forest areas as part of climate change adaptation measures. This large-scale pilot project is being implemented in Ak-Talaa, Toguz-Toro, Uzgen, and Suzak districts in collaboration with local forestry, aiyl okmotu (local administration), and specially protected areas. In addition, World Bank started projects on clean air in cities. Adaptation Fund project is also being implemented to prevent pasture degradation, transition livestock from quantity to quality, to breed livestock, and improve seed quality. With climate change, changes are also occurring in wild biodiversity. Wild animal migration routes are changing, and diseases are becoming more prevalent. Projects are underway to preserve the snow leopard and snow leopard ecosystem. By the way, the global conservation initiative “30x30” was launched, which aims to preserve 30 percent of all land and water resources on the planet by 2030. Kyrgyzstan also accepted the challenge, and today the number of specially protected areas has reached about 13 percent. We are working with partners to reach 30 percent by 2030. As you know new climate conditions are affecting glaciers. What measures is the ministry taking to protect them? — Today, in order to protect glaciers, the law “On Specially Protected Natural Areas” was amended, and all glaciers were included in the category of specially protected areas. Also, draft resolution was submitted for public discussion, which provides for all the conditions for how to count glaciers, who will monitor them, and how to protect them. — Meanwhile, there are cases of wild animals descending from high mountains. What does it mean? — The situation varies depending on the species of wild animals. First, they are descending in search of food. Second, since the areas around the city have been improved, they may be looking for grazing land. And the number of some species of wild animals has increased. In addition, there are animals are coming down. For example, we can mention the mountain goats in the Chui region. Previously, they inhabited only high-mountainous areas. — Is this a positive development? — On the one hand, it is a pleasant sight. On the other hand, with climate change, the habitats of animals are changing. We need to study this situation in depth. Because in some places, anthropogenic impacts may be so strong that wild animals are forced to migrate. — Thank you for the interview! Print
title: Glaciers in Kyrgyzstan to be specially protected area 22 June 2026 1983

body: Kabar Poaching in Issyk-Kul has been reduced by 99%, and in the coming years, the region plans to completely resolve the garbage problem and conduct a large-scale study of the lake's ecosystem. Kylychbek Tentimishev, head of the Issyk-Kul regional administration of the Ministry of Natural Resources, Ecology, and Technical Supervision, spoke about the current environmental situation and future plans for preserving Issyk-Kul Lake in an exclusive interview with Kabar. — Every year, fishing nets are recovered from the bottom of Issyk-Kul. What matters first: preventing illegal poachers or removing those nets that have been lying over the years? — Presidential Decree No. 131 is currently in effect, clearly stating the need to clean up the lake and ensure its sustainable development. As part of this, a systematic campaign against poaching nets has been underway throughout the Issyk-Kul region for three to four years. Last year, the Ministry of Natural Resources, Ecology, and Technical Supervision removed 47,000 meters of old fishing nets from the lake. In the first five months of this year, 30,000 meters of nets have already been removed. This year, we have intensified our efforts thanks to the arrival of new equipment and three new boats. The ministry currently has six or seven boats in operation. Besides us, the Ministry of Emergency Situations, the environmental police, and the tourism police are also involved in net removal. Around 25 boats from various agencies are working on the lake at any given time. We've practically eliminated new nets. Poaching in Issyk-Kul has been virtually eradicated. Previously, illegal nets were set all over the lake, but now they're gone. We estimate that poaching has been reduced by 99%. Residents started to understand that this isn't right. A fishing culture has emerged, the Kyrgyz Fishing Sports Federation was created, and even former poachers have begun helping to remove the nets themselves. The cleanup effort will continue on an ongoing basis. — Is it possible to completely get rid old and illegal fishing nets, or is this a permanent task for environmental services? — Of course, it is. We're working towards it. Technology is constantly evolving. We're already using underwater drones that descend to depths of 200 meters and detect fishing nets, after which relevant services will remove. We also have a map of the areas where cleanup is taking place. However, the lake's peculiarity is such that during storms, nets that remain under a layer of silt can rise again and be washed ashore, where we collect them. Despite the work being done, old nets are still on the bottom. There will be no new nets, as the import of synthetic fishing nets into the republic is completely prohibited. — In recent years, restrictions on the use of plastic bags have been implemented in the region. What do you think, have these measures actually covered the Issyk-Kul region, and can we talk about a complete transition to alternative packaging, or is plastic still used in certain segments? — As of today, large retail chains and hypermarkets in the Issyk-Kul region have already banned the use of plastic bags and disposable plastic tableware. Smaller stores are gradually joining this trend. At first, we conduct preventative measures, then we start practicing penalties. But the issue isn't just about punishment. We need to change people's minds so that everyone understands their responsibility for preserving nature. Alternatives, paper bags, fabric totes, and shoppers are available in the market. Unfortunately, we understand that polyethylene is cheaper and convenient for storing bulk goods for retail outlets. People are used to receiving these bags for free, but now they have to pay for a paper bag or shopper. Therefore, people need to be convinced, and this process is gradually underway. However, plastic remains a major component of household waste. During inspections of landfills and waste collection facilities, we see that a significant portion of waste consists of plastic bags and plastic packaging. However, starting in 2027, the distribution and sale of plastic bags throughout Kyrgyzstan will be completely banned, in accordance with Law No. 177. Accordingly, their import into the Issyk-Kul region will also be stopped. Customs posts will not allow plastic bags to pass through. Thus, the country will no longer use polyethylene, which has been damaging the environment. — Which areas around Issyk-Kul remain most vulnerable to pollution today, despite the operation of treatment facilities? —Issyk-Kul region currently bears the greatest burden, as it is the largest region receives the majority of tourists. Most of the tourist infrastructure is concentrated here. At the same time, tourism is also actively developing in other areas of the region. Guesthouses, resorts, and yurt camps are being built, and mountain tourism is developing. This contributes to economic development, but also requires adherence to strict environmental requirements. — What are the main areas of further environmental measures planned for the region in the near future, and what will be the focus of strengthening monitoring? — We will continue to combat poaching and clean up the lake of old nets. In addition, two waste plants are being built in Balykchy and Karakol with the participation of Chinese investors, similar to the facility in Bishkek. The Karakol plant is scheduled to begin accepting waste in late 2026 or early 2027. A waste recycling and sorting facility is also operating in Karakol. These two new waste plants will completely solve the waste problem in the Issyk-Kul region. They will also generate electricity. Another important area is reducing the number of illegal dumps. Previously, there were approximately 88 landfills and dumps in the region. Currently, 11 landfills are officially operating, although the actual situation does not always correspond exactly to the statistics. However, we are aiming to have no more than ten large facilities in operation, which will make monitoring easier. We also plan to conduct a global scientific study of the Issyk-Kul ecosystem. We are currently establishing a permanent research team. In the future, the Ministry of Natural Resources will establish hydrographic stations at Issyk-Kul Lake and the rivers flowing into it. These stations will measure precipitation, the biochemical composition of the water, and monitor the substances entering the lake. In the Issyk-Kul region, the Ministry of Natural Resources will conduct a comprehensive series of activities aimed at studying forests, glaciers, and the impact of agriculture on the environment. Print
title: Major environmental reset underway in Issyk-Kul lake 11 June 2026 2409

body: Your browser does not support the video tag Kabar Agency Kabar Director of Chon-Kemin Nature Park, Adilbek Kasmaliev: -In fact, Chon-Kemin State Nature Park was established on August 13, 1997. Its main purpose is to protect ecologically valuable areas and preserve nature. The park is home to large numbers of deer, including maral and roe deer. Their populations have been increasing in recent years. Hunters are only permitted to deal with wolves that attack livestock in village areas, and only with official authorization. However, hunting is completely prohibited within our protected nature park, and no one is allowed to enter the park carrying a gun. Where do these animals come from? - They come down to the water to drink and visit natural salt licks. We install one or two camera traps along the trails leading to these areas, because that's where the animals pass by, allowing us to capture and identify them on camera. For example, when we monitor snow leopards, we already know the routes they usually use. They move through rocky areas and have their own regular trails. We install camera traps on rocks or pine trees along those routes, carefully hiding them and making sure they leave no human scent. After that, we check the results about three months later. Print
title: Photo trap captures animals in Chon-Kemin park 6 July 2026 1530

body: Your browser does not support the video tag Kabar Agency Kabar Taigans help protect livestock from wolves that cause major losses. These are not ordinary puppies. They are Kyrgyz Taigans. Every sprint and sharp turn made by these eight-month-old dogs is part of their training. In the past, our ancestors trained hunting dogs using live prey, but today Taigans are trained with specially prepared hides. Erkin Iskender uulu, Taigan breeder: We train young puppies this way to develop their speed and hunting skills. In the past, our ancestors used to train them on wild animals. Today, in order to protect wildlife, we train them using hides. The Taigan is a heritage passed down to us from our ancestors. Erkin Iskender uulu lives in a mountainous area at an altitude of 2,200 metres above sea level. Here, encounters with wolves and jackals are common, and attacks by predators can cause significant losses to livestock owners. For this reason, Taigans are not only valued as a cultural heritage and hunting companion, but also play an important role in protecting livestock from predators. Erkin Iskender uulu, Taigan breeder: We raise livestock, so we need Taigans. There are many wolves and jackals in this area. In a single winter, they can kill 15–16 head of livestock. When you calculate the losses, they can amount to millions of soms. Taigans help us protect our animals from these predators. At Erkin’s yard, there are currently seven Taigans. He has already given three of them to his younger brothers. Erkin Iskender uulu, Taigan breeder: From a very young age, Taigans sould be raised alongside sheep and goats. Otherwise, they may chase and even bite livestock when the animals start running. Such incidents have happened before. Taigans have a very strong bite, which is why proper training and socialization are essential from an early age. The Kyrgyz Taigan has its own unique qualities. Breeders pay attention to its body structure, speed, courage, and hunting abilities. To keep his dogs in top condition, Erkin feeds them meat throughout the year, regardless of the season, purchasing it himself and ensuring they receive proper care and nutrition. Erkin Iskender uulu, Taigan breeder: I mostly feed them raw meat, even with the skin on. We also prepare jarma, a traditional Kyrgyz barley drink, and give them milk. I bring the meat from the district center, which is about forty kilometers away. My wife often jokes that I take better care of my Taigans than I do of her. The Kyrgyz Taigan has not lost its importance even today. However, Erkin believes that greater efforts are needed to preserve this valuable breed and ensure that it is passed on to future generations. Erkin Iskender uulu, Taigan breeder: I would not say that the Kyrgyz Taigan is being neglected. However, stronger support would certainly help. In Kazakhstan, they are being showcased at international exhibitions and even promoted for UNESCO recognition. If more competitions and events were organized here, more young people would take an interest in Taigans and their preservation. Since ancient times, the revered Taigans have served as helpers to herders and companions to hunters. They are an ancient and valuable breed of animals. Print
title: Taigan, Kyrgyzstan's ancient and valuable breed 24 June 2026 2072

body: Talas, Sept. 8, 2026 /Kabar/. The President’s Akylman Lyceum, a specialized educational institution for gifted children, will open its doors in Kyrgyzstan’s Talas city on September 11. The opening ceremony will be attended by the President of the Kyrgyz Republic Sadyr Zhaparov. The new lyceum was established as part of the country’s efforts to develop the intellectual, scientific and creative potential of talented young people and create opportunities for their academic and personal growth. The lyceum in Talas has a capacity of 920 students and is equipped with modern facilities designed to provide students with comfortable conditions for learning and development. The complex also includes a dormitory for students from different regions of the country. The construction of the educational institution is being carried out with the support of the President of the Kyrgyz Republic and with sponsorship from Gazprom Kyrgyzstan. Education at the Akylman Lyceum will be free of charge. Admission is based on a competitive selection process, and students from across Kyrgyzstan are eligible to apply. Arstanbek Sekishov, Director of the President’s Akylman Lyceum in Talas told Kabar News Agency that preparations for the opening are currently underway. He noted that this year, 96 students from all regions of the country have successfully passed the entrance selection and will begin their studies at the Talas lyceum. “Students living in the dormitory will receive three meals a day and will have access to extracurricular clubs and activities in the evenings,” he added. According to Sekishov, the feature of the institution is to combine high academic standards with strong national values. “Our main distinctive feature is that we place a strong emphasis on national values while providing education based on international standards,” Sekishov said. The lyceum will focus particularly on STEM-related subjects, with classes taught in English. The school has recruited qualified teachers through a competitive selection process. The Akylman Lyceum is designed not only to support students’ academic achievements but also to help develop well-rounded individuals with strong intellectual, scientific and creative potential. The opening of the Talas lyceum is part of a wider national effort to expand educational opportunities for gifted children. The Talas lyceum will become the second President’s Akylman Lyceum in Kyrgyzstan. The first such institution was opened in Issyk-Kul Region in 2023. Print
title: Kyrgyzstan's Talas opens new educational hub for gifted children 8 September 2026 21

body: A team of American cowboys proved to be the unlikely stars of this year's World Nomad Games in Kyrgyzstan. Vyacheslav Oseledko/AFP/Getty Images Kabar It’s 4 p.m. on day two of the World Nomad Games, and eight horses are converging on a small patch of dirt. The riders elbow, kick and flail while USA team captain Ladd Howell leans off his saddle towards the ground, clenching a whip in his teeth as he grabs for the 70-pound headless goat carcass below. Goat in hand, Howell gallops off towards the goal, kicking up an oppressive cloud of dust while the crowd roars in approval. “The legendary USA captain Ladd Howell takes the lead,” booms the Kyrgyz announcer. “Ladd! Ladd!” But just before Howell reaches his destination, a Kyrgyz player collides directly with his horse, knocking him off his path and snatching the goat away. Horses swarm, the flat blue of Issyk-Kul Lake behind them. This is Kok-Boru, the national sport of Kyrgyzstan beloved across Central Asia for its unrelenting intensity and spectacular display of horsemanship. Few outside of the region have heard of Kok-Boru, but there is a small group of self-described Christian cowboys from the US who can’t get enough. A group of nine ranchers and rodeo men, most from Utah, have made the 6,600-mile journey to Kyrgyzstan’s largest resort town, Cholpon-ata. Taking two weeks away from their families and ranches and together spending nearly $100,000 to cover travel, gear and stipends, the men are competing in Kok-Boru’s most elite level: the World Nomad Games. The Americans have shown up for the Games since 2014, though despite 12 years and five tournaments, they have yet to win a match. They keep coming back anyway. Stuffed goat carcass Kok-Boru is somewhat akin to polo, but instead of knocking around a ball, the athletes try to pick up a stuffed goat carcass from the ground and throw it into a goal, called a taikazan. This game has been a staple across Central Asia for millennia. Originally played with a dead wolf — slain after feeding on local cattle — the epic equestrian sport has evolved with the people of the region. “It’s one of the most important elements of our culture, especially the traditional part of our culture, because our ancestors have played this game for many centuries,” said Kyrgyz Nomad Games volunteer Jantai Saparbekov. “It symbolizes our traditions being passed from generation to generation.” UNESCO has recognized the sport on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, describing it as a fusion of Kyrgyz culture, history, and identity. In practice, it is dusty, immensely physical (for horses and men alike), and, quite frankly, unforgiving for foreigners who did not grow up playing the sport. Several Kyrgyz players make it their full-time job, competing professionally in national leagues. The game has started to expand its reach. Notably, Netflix’s popular “Home Game” series , released in 2020, featured an episode on Kok-Boru, introducing many international audiences to the sport for the first time. The Olympics, these Games are not. These Games are six days of cultural, athletic and intellectual competitions rooted in Central Asian nomadic heritage — a heritage that goes back 4,000 years according to Kyrgyz political scientist Arzuu Sheranova. The lifestyle lives on; in a country where only about 35% of citizens reside in cities, many still live somewhat migratory existences. A sporting time capsule The week honors a past that is still very much present, and the appeal has spread far beyond Central Asia: around 3,000 athletes from 112 countries turned up. At any given moment, an eight-on-eight tug-of-war game could be happening between India and Pakistan, a Russian man could be struggling to hoist an 1,300-pound stuffed camel down a track, and an Australian woman could be shooting a bow and arrow from horseback. “These are sports that they’ve been doing and have remained unchanged for thousands of years. They still do it out of pride of their culture,” said USA Kok-Boru player Nick Willert. The informality runs deeper than the events. Athletes underwent no performance drug testing at the Games, and the World Anti-Doping Agency confirmed the World Nomad Games are not a signatory to the World Anti-Doping Code. The main venue, the Kyrchyn Gorge, is located about an hour and a half from downtown Cholpon-Ata and feels like entering the deep Kyrgyz mountains. A vast open field tucked between snow-capped peaks, the gorge serves as home to several sports, a mud-built castle turned into a local food bazaar, and fields of yurts. Participating countries got to host their own expositions; the American yurt featured a cutout of George Washington, US history trivia and cornhole. Yurt-style tents and a mud-built fortress provided the venue for the Games. Pavel Mikheyev/Reuters The Games are as much — if not more — about culture and costume as they are about sport. On top of over 600 cultural events throughout the week, teams were instructed to don “traditional wear” for the Opening Ceremony, meaning Iranians dressed as Persian Immortals, Mongolians as Mongol warriors, and Americans as ... cowboys. “It feels like a Central Asian Renaissance Fair,” said Connor Ryan, a fan from Boston. While it may be tempting to dismiss them as just good fun, the Nomad Games have played a pivotal role in Kyrgyzstan’s effort to reclaim and revive its history, which was long buried under several hundred years of Chinese and Soviet control. “The event itself has contributed to nation-building through a revival of the nomadic values and traditions. It is very explicit in the Kyrgyz rise of ethno-fashion, or dressing in traditional garb in everyday life, which has mushroomed following the first Games in 2014,” explained Sheranova. There is also an undeniable element of soft power strategy at play. The Games overlapped with high-profile diplomatic summits in the region, drawing Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian to attend the opening ceremony. US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Ambassador Sergio Gor also attended. With an upcoming election, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov is sending a clear message to his citizens and the world: Kyrgyzstan has global presence. The American cowboys A record 52 American athletes showed up to compete this year, but the scene stealers are the men of USA Kok-Boru. They range in age from 25 to 50, with one of the players also a grandfather. “We’re just some Midwest guys,” said Howell. “Our real purpose in being here is that when the Games are over, people will know the culture in the US is amazing and authentic. After they meet us here with our cowboy hats, we want them to remember, ‘Hey, the cowboys are good guys.’” Howell, a cattle rancher and religious Mormon, speaks fluent Russian thanks to a church mission in his late teens that placed him in St. Petersburg. His language skills propel him into the role of team translator and ambassador (Russian is one of Kyrgyzstan’s two national languages). Howell returned to the US in 2013 and subsequently heard about Kok-Boru through friends in the Utah rodeo circuit. Six of the players are fellow Mormons, recruited by Howell over the years. “We stand for our country, for our families, for cowboy culture, and definitely for our religion,” said Howell. “We believe strongly in Jesus, so I know bringing these guys over here, there’s no worries about anyone doing anything wrong. Everyone is seriously great ambassadors of America, the church, families, everything.” On top of being connected by religion, everyone on the team has spent their life on ranches or working with horses. “These guys are a different breed,” said USA Kok-Boru physiotherapist Hayden Hilke. “They’ve all been riding horses their whole lives. body: Bishkek, Sept. 8, 2026. /Kabar/. Scholars and experts from 23 countries called for a unified professional effort to preserve the diversity of nomadic cultural heritage, strengthen intercultural dialogue, and ensure the living continuity of traditions for future generations, the organizers said following the International Scientific and Practical Conference "Cultural Heritage of the World's Nomadic Peoples: Preservation, Study, and Development." The conference was held on September 3–4 at the Chyngyz Aitmatov Cultural and Ethnographic Center "Rukh Ordo" in Cholpon-Ata as part of Section 3 of the International Scientific and Practical Conference "Nomadic Civilizations: Heritage, Paradigms, and Prospects" of the 6th World Nomad Games. The conference was organized by the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, and Innovation of the Kyrgyz Republic. The event was held in both offline and online formats in Kyrgyz, Russian, and English. Representatives of the scientific and professional communities from various countries expressed interest in the conference. Over 100 applications were received. Forty-three scholars from 23 countries participated in the in-person work, and another 20 scholars presented their papers remotely. Experts from Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan, Turkey, the United Kingdom, Slovenia, the United States, Canada, New Zealand, China, India, Pakistan, Japan, Mongolia, Greece, Italy, Hungary, Ghana, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Russia, France, and other countries participated in the scientific discussions. The focus was on the preservation and development of traditional music, epic and storytelling art, crafts, musical instruments, oral traditions, and other forms of cultural heritage of nomadic peoples in the modern world. One of the key topics was the "ustad-shakirt" system—a traditional form of knowledge and performance skill transmission from master to apprentice. Participants emphasized that cultural heritage cannot be preserved solely in museums, books, and archives. In their view, tradition remains alive when knowledge, skills, and mastery are directly transmitted to future generations through education, practice, performance, and creativity. As part of the conference, scholars who are also representatives of traditional music held master classes for guests and participants. In particular, Japanese professor of traditional culture and performer Miho Yamaji led a master class on the koto, a traditional Japanese 13-string instrument. Chinese representatives Wang Jianxin and Li Fengyun introduced participants to traditional musical instruments, including the ancient guqin zither, the xiao and dizi bamboo flutes, and the xun ocarina. The Chinese masters performed pieces from the classical repertoire. Indian participant Manikat Rachana held a master class on traditional dance during the conference. The scholars paid special attention to modern technology. Discussions included the creation of digital archives and databases, audio and video recording of traditional art, and the use of modern research methods and artificial intelligence. Participants also noted the need to combine the use of new technologies with a respectful attitude toward the cultural context, as well as respect for the copyrights and collective rights and interests of tradition bearers. International cooperation was another area of focus. Participants proposed expanding joint research and scientific expeditions, academic and educational exchanges, programs for young scientists and performers, international summer schools and master classes, as well as joint projects between universities, conservatories, research centers, archives, and cultural institutions. Following the work of Section 3, the participants' research papers were further disseminated. Fifteen papers were included in the international scientific collection "Nomadic Civilizations: Heritage, Paradigms, and Prospects" published by the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, and Innovation of the Kyrgyz Republic. Another 64 scientific articles were published in a special issue of the Bulletin of the Arabaev Kyrgyz State University and the International Eurasian University. Following the conference, a resolution was adopted outlining the main areas for further joint work between the international scientific and cultural communities. These included the development of an international scientific platform for the study of traditional culture, the creation of digital archives and databases, support for outstanding traditional art practitioners, the development of a master-student system, the training of young researchers and educators, the use of modern technologies for the study and documentation of cultural heritage, the expansion of international scientific and educational exchange, and the development of cultural diplomacy. Participants also advocated for the development of international inter-institutional projects capable of uniting the scientific potential of universities, conservatories, academic and research centers, archives, and cultural institutions from different countries. The work of the section became part of the scientific program of the International Festival of Traditional Music. Print
title: Scientists from 23 countries call for joint efforts to preserve cultural heritage of nomadic peoples 8 September 2026 31

body: www Kabar US President Donald Trump said late Wednesday that the United States has become the world’s largest oil producer, excluding Venezuela’s vast reserves, which the US recently added to its stockpile, Anadolu reported. Speaking at a rally in Dallas, Texas, Trump hailed an energy agreement involving Venezuela’s estimated 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, calling it potentially “the biggest deal in the history of our country.” “Now we’re the biggest in the world, and that’s without Venezuela, which we’ve just added to our little stockpile,” he said. The White House announced the details of the energy deal, under which North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) would grant the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital a 35% equity stake in its corporate parent at no cost to US taxpayers. The US State Department would also have the right to purchase 20% of production at cost. The White House said NABEP had secured 100-year concessions covering 17 oil fields, while Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez had previously described the agreement as a 25-year deal. The pact is expected to generate $200 billion in royalties and taxes over its first 25 years, according to the White House, with funds earmarked for Venezuela’s reconstruction and social development. Print

body: OTS Kabar On 9 September 2026, Ambassador Kubanychbek Omuraliev, the Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), delivered a keynote speech at the 2nd Meeting of the Turkic Green Finance Council. In his address Ambassador Omuraliev highlighted the gathering as a vital step in advancing shared commitments to green and sustainable finance across the Turkic World. Recalling the Council’s establishment initiated by President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and formalized via the Memorandum of Understanding signed at the 11th OTS Summit in Bishkek, he commended national and regional progress and noted the expanding scope of multilateral economic cooperation. Ambassador Omuraliev emphasized that the Council must serve as an active, year-round mechanism to turn policy into bankable, practical projects and measurable outcomes, urging the establishment of a regional green project database and actionable work programs for a resilient, low-carbon future. Organized on the margins of the Astana Finance Days platform, the second meeting gathered heads and representatives of financial regulators, ministries of economy and finance, and stock exchanges from OTS Member States and Observers. The aim of the event was to build upon the foundations established at the inaugural session, deepen regional cooperation in sustainable finance, and identify concrete measures to mobilize green investment. Participants focused on setting measurable targets, expanding the pipeline of eligible green projects, enhancing data and expertise sharing, and strengthening the integration of capital markets across the OTS region. At the end of the meeting the sides signed a Communiqué affirming their commitment to sustainable green development guided by the principles of the Turkic Green Vision, as well as further development cooperation in the area of green finance. Print
title: 2nd meeting of Turkic Green Finance Council convened in Astana 9 September 2026 11

body: OTS Kabar Kubanychbek Omuraliev, Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), met with Arfiya Eri, Parliamentary Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs of Japan, on 10 August 2026 at the OTS Secretariat in Istanbul. During the meeting, Secretary General Omuraliev shared information on the activities and priorities of the OTS, highlighting the Organization’s growing role as a platform for regional cooperation, connectivity and dialogue across the Turkic World and the wider Eurasian region. Secretary General Omuraliev underlined the increasing economic and strategic importance of the OTS region, situated at the crossroads of major transport, trade and energy routes connecting Asia and Europe. In this context, he emphasized the opportunities offered by the Trans-Caspian International East-West Middle Corridor and the potential for closer cooperation with Japan in connectivity, infrastructure, technology and sustainable development. Vice-Minister Eri highlighted the longstanding relations between Japan and the OTS countries and reaffirmed Japan’s interest in further strengthening its engagement with the Turkic World. She emphasized Japan’s values-based approach to international cooperation, underlining the importance of dialogue, mutual respect, the rule of law and a free and open international order. She also expressed Japan’s interest in advancing mutually beneficial cooperation with the countries of the region, particularly in the areas of economic development, connectivity, innovation, digital transformation and green transition. The sides exchanged views on regional developments and discussed prospects for further strengthening cooperation between the OTS and Japan, including within the OTS+ format. In this context, they explored opportunities for enhanced interaction in such areas as trade and investment, energy, transport and connectivity, digitalization and innovation, green transformation, education, and people-to-people contacts. The meeting concluded with the sides expressing their readiness to maintain contacts and continue exploring concrete opportunities for mutually beneficial cooperation between the Organization of Turkic States and Japan. body: Society Uncategorized World AI could destroy humanity within a decade, Anthropic researcher warns Who will keep technology under control? asia+ 11.09.2026 17:07 Telegram Facebook WhatsApp Copy URL Artificial intelligence could “destroy all of humanity” within the next decade, with the risk of such a scenario estimated at around 10%, according to Evan Hubinger, an AI safety researcher at Anthropic, as reported by the BBC’s Russian Service . In a post on X , Hubinger said the risks posed by currently existing AI models remain small. However, he warned that the rapid development of AI could lead to new models becoming highly autonomous and eventually posing an existential threat to humanity. His comments came amid reports by the Financial Times that Anthropic had not given the UK’s AI Safety Institute (AISI) access to its latest AI model. AISI is one of the organizations responsible for assessing risks associated with artificial intelligence. The BBC contacted Anthropic for comment. Hubinger did not provide details about how AI systems could potentially threaten humanity. His comments came in response to a post by Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who left Anthropic this week after previously working at OpenAI. “None of these companies are behaving responsibly,” Coxon wrote, explaining his decision to leave Anthropic. “Soon these will be systems that surpass human intelligence and are capable of hacking anything, revolutionizing any field overnight, and gaining real power and resources,” he added. The BBC also contacted OpenAI for comment. The UK government declined to comment on reports that AISI had not been granted access to Anthropic’s latest model. A Cabinet spokesperson said British authorities “continue to work closely with industry partners, including Anthropic, and to work on improving the safety of AI models.” Neil Lawrence, a professor at the University of Cambridge, told BBC Radio 4’s Today program that the United States was increasingly stepping back from cooperation with other countries and international organizations on AI. “In my view, this is not surprising, given that in the US, artificial intelligence is perceived primarily in the context of a race with China and there is a growing lean toward isolationism; it is quite likely that the (US) administration is in favor of reducing cooperation with some allies,” he said. ‘AI poses an existential threat to humanity’ Hubinger’s post, which received more than 10 million views, said that researchers at Anthropic “genuinely believe” AI poses an existential threat to humanity. “I believe Anthropic is doing everything it can, but we don’t yet have a plan for solving the problem of aligning superintelligence’s goals with human values, and we are not moving in that direction,” he wrote. Hubinger specializes in AI alignment, a field focused on ensuring that AI systems operate in ways consistent with human values and intentions. A number of leading AI researchers have warned that current efforts to address these risks may be falling short. Several incidents reported this summer involved AI agents and autonomous systems being used to carry out cyberattacks. OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have disclosed information about hacking incidents involving their AI tools. In its August safety report, Anthropic assessed as low the risk that its AI models could stop following the instructions of organizations using them and instead interfere with their systems or exploit them for their own purposes. The company also rated as low the risk that its models could independently conduct research and development that might cause “catastrophic harm” to an organization. However, Anthropic said its experts were now “less confident in this assessment” than previously. “We are seeing early signs of a potential acceleration (of developments in this direction),” the report said. Growing warnings from AI leaders Leading figures in artificial intelligence have warned about the potential security risks of the technology for years. The heads of OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic publicly raised such concerns as early as 2023. In recent weeks, however, the warnings have become more urgent as evidence has emerged that companies may be struggling to maintain control over increasingly capable AI systems. In early September, Jakub Pachocki, who leads the development of advanced models at OpenAI, called for “extreme caution” over the pace of AI progress. He said additional intervention may be needed to ensure that “humans retain control (over AI) in the future.” In recent months, senior industry figures, including Anthropic executives Dario Amodei and Jared Kaplan, have also called for slowing the development of new AI models. An open letter signed by 1,300 AI company employees calls on the US government to “support international efforts to develop the technical and governance tools needed to regulate the pace of development of new artificial int elligence systems.” Join us on social media! body: Economics Politics News Migrants contributed 321 billion rubles to Russia’s budgets in 18 months: Interior Ministry According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the share of legal labor migration is growing in Russia. asia+ 11.09.2026 16:13 Telegram Facebook WhatsApp Copy URL Migration-related revenues to Russia’s federal and regional budgets reached 321 billion rubles (about $4 billion) over the past 18 months, up 30% from the previous period, according to Russia’s Interior Ministry. First Deputy Interior Minister Andrei Kikot, who heads the ministry’s Service for Citizenship and Registration of Foreign Nationals, presented the figures during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, according to the Kremlin . “Somewhere around 60 billion goes to the federal budget, and over 250 or 260 billion goes to regional budgets. But, as I understand it, primarily from patents?” Putin asked. Kikot confirmed that the bulk of the revenue comes from payments related to labor migrants’ patents. According to Kikot, around 9 million foreign nationals enter Russia each year for various purposes. At any given time, 6–6.5 million foreigners are in the country, including about 3 million labor migrants , 1.7 million family members and around 1 million people in other categories, such as tourists, students and private visitors. He also reported that the share of legal labor migration has increased from 45% to 50% , calling the trend “a good indicator.” Kikot said that in the first half of 2026, the number of registered crimes committed by foreign nationals in Russia fell by 40% . New rules for migrants’ families Kikot also discussed measures being introduced under Russia’s State Migration Policy Concept, adopted last year. One of its goals is to reduce the number of non-working family members of labor migrants living in Russia. According to Kikot, their number has already declined by 20% from the previously reported 1.7 million. He attributed the decline partly to new requirements for children of foreign nationals seeking to attend Russian schools, including a Russian-language proficiency test . A federal law initiated by the migration service will also take effect on January 1, 2027 . It provides for employed foreign nationals to pay additional taxes for each non-working family member residing with them in Russia. Russia considers organized recruitment of foreign workers Another migration-service initiative is a bill that would introduce a system of organized recruitment of foreign workers . The proposal is currently being reviewed by the Russian government. Under the existing system, foreign nationals can travel to Russia independently and seek employment after arrival. Under the proposed model, an employer would apply to the migration service, which would select workers through a designated operator, arrange their entry and documentation, and then assign them to the employer. The draft would require medium-sized and large companies using the system to provide recruited workers with specialized accommodation and transportation to and from their workplaces . The proposed model is designed around a closed “home–work–home” system. Once an employment contract expires, the worker would be returned to their home country in an organized manner. Meanwhile, according to some estimates, labor migrants make a significant contribution to Russia’s economy and public finances, accounting for an estimated 7% to 8% of annual GDP and generating hundreds of billions of rubles in taxes and other fees.
