title: Uzbekistan and India agree to elevate relations to comprehensive strategic partnership.

body: Photo: Press service of president of Uzbekistan Uzbekistan, Singapore discuss Strategic and Innovation Partnership Program Uzbekistan and Singapore may adopt a Strategic and Innovation Partnership Program focusing on investments, technology transfer, public administration and human capital. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and former prime minister of Singapore Lee Hsien Loong discussed this at talks in Tashkent. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 29 August 2026, 21:09 Politics Uzbekistan and Singapore are discussing the development of a joint medium-term Strategic and Innovation Partnership Program. It will focus on trade, investment, technology transfer, modernization of public administration, human capital development, digitalization and other areas. The issue was discussed on Friday during a meeting between president Shavkat Mirziyoyev and a Singaporean delegation led by senior minister Lee Hsien Loong, who served as prime minister from 2004 to 2024, the press service of the president of Uzbekistan announced . The two sides noted growing trade turnover and an increase in the number of joint ventures. Singaporean investments in Uzbekistan have reportedly reached around $2 billion. Advertising on Gazeta The two sides also discussed using Singapore’s experience in developing special economic zones, the Tashkent International Financial Center and digital banking in Uzbekistan. They welcomed Uzbekistan’s recent accession to the Singapore Convention on Mediation, a 2018 United Nations treaty that allows commercial settlement agreements to be enforced quickly across different countries. According to the Singapore government, Lee Hsien Loong is visiting Uzbekistan from 27 to 31 August. This is his first visit to Central Asia. Before arriving in Uzbekistan, he led a delegation to Kazakhstan. During his visit, Lee is expected to address the Senate. The Singaporean delegation is also scheduled to visit Samarkand. Mirziyoyev and Lee Hsien Loong previously held talks in January 2023, when Lee was prime minister, during Mirziyoyev’s state visit to Singapore. At the time, the two sides identified five key areas for cooperation: developing human capital and training highly qualified specialists for public administration; involving Singapore in Uzbekistan’s privatization processes; introducing advanced green technologies and digital solutions; developing urban infrastructure and communications; supporting investment and expanding bilateral trade. The two sides also agreed to establish the Uzbek-Singapore Investment Company an with authorized capital of $500 million. title: Uzbekistan, Singapore discuss Strategic and Innovation Partnership Program

body: Parks Tau and Laziz Kudratov. Photo: Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade Uzbekistan, South Africa to begin work on preferential trade agreement Uzbekistan and South Africa will begin work on preferential trade and investment protection agreement and establish an intergovernmental commission. In the autumn, around 50 Uzbek companies are expected to travel to Johannesburg as part of a business mission. O‘zbek tilida Ўзбек тилида На русском языке 29 August 2026, 21:07 Economy Uzbekistan and South Africa agreed to begin work on a preferential trade agreement. This was discussed on 26 August by Uzbekistan’s minister of investment, industry and trade Laziz Kudratov and South Africa’s minister of trade, industry and competition Parks Tau during a video conference. The agreement could involve reducing or removing duties on certain categories of goods, making bilateral trade easier. The countries have not yet specified which goods could receive preferential treatment. The sides also plan to establish an intergovernmental commission and prepare an investment protection agreement. They discussed joint projects and technology exchanges in the chemical and mining industries. In the autumn, around 50 Uzbek companies are expected to travel to Johannesburg as part of a business mission, where they will meet with South African businesses. Advertising on Gazeta The ministers also outlined cooperation plans for 2026−2027 and agreed to continue developing specific projects. In July, Uzbekistan’s ambassador Ashraf Khodjaev discussed simplifying visa procedures and the possibility of introducing visa-free travel with representatives from Ethiopia and South Africa. Trade turnover between Uzbekistan and South Africa reached $7.5 million in January-July, more than three times the $2.3 million recorded during the same period last year. body: Photo: Press service of the president President announces seven national programs for Uzbekistan in coming years President of Uzbekistan announced seven national programs covering education, healthcare, economy, environment, rule of law, mahallas (neighborhoods) and foreign policy. The plans include school preparation for all six-year-olds, vocational training for 1 million young people and more. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 29 August 2026, 09:20 Politics Seven national programs will be implemented in Uzbekistan in the coming years, covering education, healthcare, the economy, the environment, the rule of law, mahalla (neighborhood) development and foreign policy. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced the plans on 28 August during a ceremony marking the 35th anniversary of the country’s independence. “The next ten years will be a period of national revival for us. And we can achieve this only through the intellect, hard work and unity of our people,” the president said. Education and professions of the future Advertising on Gazeta The first national program will focus on turning knowledge and skills into the “main capital” for the country’s further development. “I constantly say this: education, education, teacher, teacher. Therefore, the first national program will be aimed at turning knowledge and skills into the main capital of our further development,” Shavkat Mirziyoyev said. The authorities intend to quickly increase the share of six-year-old children attending preparatory classes to 100% while maintaining incentives for the opening of private kindergartens. All schools are planned to be fully covered by international knowledge-assessment programs, while international educational standards will be introduced in technical colleges. The authorities aim to increase the number of young people receiving training in high-paying professions to 1 million. “In other words, in New Uzbekistan, not a single young man or woman will remain without a profession,” the president said. The government also aims to place at least 10 universities in Uzbekistan ranked among the world’s top 1,000 universities. Health and longevity The second program will focus on public health and increasing life expectancy. Over the next five years, government health spending is planned to reach 5% of GDP. In healthcare, the authorities intend to place greater emphasis on prevention and shift to a model focused on preserving health. State health insurance is expected to cover all households in the country. “In healthcare, by strengthening prevention, we will shift to a model focused on preserving health. State health insurance will cover all households in the country,” Mirziyoyev said. To develop specialized medicine, the authorities also plan to attract at least five leading global clinics to Uzbekistan. High-tech economy The third national program envisages transitioning the economy toward a model based on high technology and high labor productivity. Over the next ten years, the government plans to attract $450 billion in foreign investment, while by 2030 it aims to grow the economy to $300 billion , up from the previously planned $240 billion. In industry, the authorities expect to create 2 million high-income jobs. Startups, venture financing and artificial intelligence will be among the priorities. The government also plans to create an ecosystem to help small businesses grow into medium-sized companies, and medium-sized enterprises develop into large companies and corporations. “As a result, over the next ten years, GDP per capita will exceed $10,000,” the head of state said. Water, environment and green spaces The fourth program will focus on changing attitudes toward water and nature. Over the next five years, the authorities intend to bring the share of agricultural land using water-saving technologies to 100%. The nationwide Yashil Makon (Green Space) movement is also planned to enter a new phase. “Green spaces around schools, kindergartens, hospitals and apartment buildings will be protected as an inviolable public asset,” the head of state said. The authorities also intend to increase the share of green areas in district and city centers to 30%. “We will definitely achieve this,” Mirziyoyev said. Judicial independence and rule of law The fifth national program will focus on strengthening the independence of the judiciary and making the rule of law a shared value. Legal education is planned to be organized under a unified system starting from school. The president also pledged to continue reforms aimed at strengthening legal protections for citizens and entrepreneurs. The authorities intend to step up the fight against cybercrime, drug addiction and human trafficking. According to the president, the fight against the shadow economy, organized crime and violations of the rights of women and children should also enter a new phase. Mahalla as the “customer” of development The sixth national program will focus on the role of the mahallas (neighborhoods). “The mood of our people, the well-being of families, the dreams and aspirations of young people and the initiative of entrepreneurs are manifested first and foremost in the mahalla,” Shavkat Mirziyoyev said. According to him, the mahalla should become the “main customer of society’s development”. The approach to developing government programs is expected to change: district budgets, investment programs and infrastructure projects should be developed based on the needs of mahallas. “Most importantly, the demands and needs of citizens and the well-being of the mahalla will be defined as the main criterion. And, of course, we will implement this criterion in consultation with the people,” the president said. Peaceful foreign policy and economic diplomacy The seventh program will focus on strengthening Uzbekistan’s role as a “country of peace and friendship” built on tolerance. The president noted that representatives of more than 130 nationalities and ethnic groups live in the country, while 16 religious denominations are represented there. “Interethnic harmony and religious tolerance are the golden fund of our people, their invaluable wealth,” he said. Uzbekistan will continue pursuing an open, pragmatic and peaceful foreign policy. According to Mirziyoyev, Uzbekistan has established diplomatic relations with nearly 170 countries. “To turn Uzbekistan into an important center of international diplomacy, we will continue to pursue a multi-vector, measured and balanced foreign policy,” the president said. Economic diplomacy will remain one of the priorities. In 2027−2029, Uzbekistan will chair the Non-Aligned Movement for the first time. Uzbekistan will continue its constructive approach toward Afghanistan. In conclusion, the president said: “Today, we are stronger than yesterday. God willing, tomorrow we will be even stronger than today... If the people and the state unite around a common goal and act selflessly, there is no peak that cannot be conquered.” Subscribe to our Telegram channel Gazeta 4 827 # 35th anniversary of independence # shavkat mirziyoyev
title: President announces seven national programs for Uzbekistan in coming years

body: Photo: Benedict Tufnell / World Rowing Historic gold: Uzbekistan’s rowers become world champions in Amsterdam (+video) Shahzod Nurmatov and Sobir Safaroliyev won gold in the men’s lightweight double sculls at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam. Uzbekistan’s crew finished the final in 6:21.93, ahead of Germany and the US, marking the country’s first-ever medal at the senior World Rowing Championships. На русском языке Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida 28 August 2026, 12:25 Sport Uzbekistan’s rowers Shahzod Nurmatov and Sobir Safaraliyev won gold in the men’s lightweight double sculls (LM2x) at the 2026 World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam. It is Uzbekistan’s first-ever medal at the senior World Rowing Championships. In the final, Uzbekistan’s crew posted a time of 6:21.93. Germany’s Naveen Alexander Shah and Maximilian Ruehling took silver in 6:23.87, while the United States' Jamie Copus and Sean Richardson won bronze with a time of 6:27.45. Advertising on Gazeta Nurmatov and Safaraliyev took the lead from the start. They were about two seconds ahead at the 500-meter mark, with their advantage growing to around six seconds by the 1,500-meter mark. In the final quarter of the race, reigning U23 world champions Shah and Ruehling managed to close the gap, but Uzbekistan’s crew held on to first place. India also challenged for third place for much of the race, but the US crew overtook them in the closing stages. India finished fourth, followed by the Netherlands in fifth and Brazil in sixth. World Rowing noted that Uzbekistan’s athletes have won medals at youth world championships and World Cup events in recent years, but Uzbekistan had never previously won a medal at the senior World Championships. Nurmatov highlighted the historic significance of the achievement for Uzbekistan: “This is the first medal for Uzbekistan. The competition was exciting and intense. We dedicate this medal to the 35th anniversary of Uzbekistan’s independence. Because this is history — it’s the first time in history. Our coach helped us a lot.” The 2026 World Rowing Championships are being held in Amsterdam from 24 to 30 August . body: Photo: Lennart Ootes / Grand Chess Tour Javokhir Sindarov to play against Carlsen and other stars in Global Chess League Uzbekistan’s grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov will lead FYERS American Gambits as an Icon in the Global Chess League in Bengaluru. Carlsen, Anand and Firouzja will also compete. The league will be part of Sindarov’s preparation for the Chess Olympiad and World Championship match. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 28 August 2026, 10:51 Sport Javokhir Sindarov will compete in the fourth season of the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League , one of the world’s largest franchise-based chess leagues. The tournament, featuring Magnus Carlsen, Viswanathan Anand, Alireza Firouzja, Ian Nepomniachtchi and other leading players, will take place in Bengaluru, India, from 3 to 13 September. Sindarov’s international tournaments, preparation and work with coaches are supported by the National Bank of Uzbekistan . Sindarov will represent FYERS American Gambits and, for the first time in his GCL career, will play the team’s top board — the Icon board, reserved for franchise leaders. In the previous three seasons, Uzbekistan’s grandmaster represented three different teams: UpGrad Mumba Masters, Triveni Continental Kings and Ganges Grandmasters. For the 20-year-old Sindarov, the Bengaluru tournament will be another event in a packed season ahead of the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand and his World Championship match against reigning champion Gukesh Dommaraju. Advertising on Gazeta The two future opponents have taken fundamentally different approaches to preparation: Gukesh opted not to participate in the Global Chess League or the Grand Chess Tour, while Sindarov continues to play regularly in major tournaments. In an interview with The Indian Express, Sindarov explained that he still lacks experience playing consistently against the world’s elite. “I became a top chess player only this year. I was a 2700-rated player, but that doesn’t really count as being a top player. But Gukesh has been a top-10 player for more than three years now, so he has a lot of experience playing against the best in the world,” he said. According to the grandmaster, this is why he tries to take advantage of almost every opportunity to compete in a strong field. “I enjoy playing against top chess players. I want to feel more comfortable in high-level tournaments before the World Championship match, and that’s why I’ve been playing so many events,” Sindarov said. In recent months, Sindarov’s tournament schedule has taken him to Goa, Mumbai, Doha, Wijk aan Zee, Cyprus, Warsaw, Bucharest, Hong Kong, Charlotte, Miami and St. Louis. After Bengaluru, he is expected to return to Uzbekistan, where the World Chess Olympiad will be held in Samarkand. Sindarov also expects to face the strongest version of Gukesh in their World Championship match. “I've played a lot against him, and I know he can play incredibly well. If he’s in his top form, like we saw in 2024, anything can happen in the match. So I am preparing for his best form.” How the Global Chess League works The Global Chess League is a joint project of FIDE and Indian technology company Tech Mahindra. Organizers describe it as the first major official franchise-based chess league. Unlike traditional individual tournaments, six clubs compete, each fielding a fixed team. Each franchise consists of: one Icon — the team leader; two Superstar Men; two Superstar Women; one young player in the Prodigy category. Men and women compete on the same team, with all six games in a team match taking place simultaneously. Each franchise plays 10 matches in a double round-robin format — twice against every opponent. The colors are reversed in the second meeting between the teams. The top two teams after the round-robin stage advance to the final. One of the GCL’s key features is its scoring system, which rewards more aggressive play with the black pieces. A win with Black earns four game points, a win with White earns three, while a draw gives one point to each side. The team with more game points across the six boards receives three match points; if the teams are tied, they receive one match point each. According to ChessBase, games in the fourth season will have a 20-minute time control, with a two-second increment starting from move 40. This time control, combined with the unusual scoring system, can produce situations where the outcome of an entire match can change within minutes because of the result on a single board. The total prize pool for the 2026 Global Chess League is $1 million. Half of that amount — $500,000 — will be distributed according to the teams' final standings: the champion receives $250,000, the runner-up $125,000, the third-place team $75,000 and the fourth-place team $50,000. Another $450,000 will be distributed among all teams proportionally to the number of game points they score throughout the tournament. An additional $50,000 will go to the league winner. Thus, prize money depends not only on the final standings but also on the results of individual games. According to the schedule, Sindarov could face each of the other franchise leaders twice. American Gambits will face Carlsen’s team on 7 and 11 September at 18:00 Tashkent time. The matches against Anand’s team are scheduled for 5 September at 15:00 and 8 September at 19:30, while Firouzja’s team will face American Gambits on 5 and 9 September at 19:30. Sindarov told The Indian Express that the format requires players to consider not only their own position but also the situation across the entire match. “In team events, you understand when you need to take a risk, when you need to play slowly... But GCL is a different kind of tournament. There are six boards, different time controls and the scoring is completely different. If Black wins, they get four points; if White wins, three. It’s a unique format.” At the same time, Sindarov said that during the game itself, he tries not to get distracted by his teammates' results. “In team tournaments, you always need to think about your own chessboard, but of course you also need to help your teammates. You need to motivate them, support them. I like being a team player, but when it comes to the game, you need to focus only on your own game.” Sindarov to lead American Gambits The FYERS American Gambits lineup this season is: Icon — Javokhir Sindarov (Uzbekistan); Superstar Men — Daniil Dubov and Nihal Sarin; Superstar Women — Bibisara Assaubayeva and Sara Khadem; Prodigy — Marc’Andria Maurizzi; Coach — Srinath Narayanan. In August, former Spain and Barcelona footballer Gerard Piqué became a strategic shareholder in American Gambits. The franchise’s co-owners also include former India cricketer Ravichandran Ashwin. Sindarov’s move to the Icon board reflects his rapid rise over the past year. Last season, he played on the men’s Superstar board for Ganges Grandmasters and was the second-highest-scoring player in the entire league, behind Firouzja. Sindarov scored 24 game points, winning seven games. Sindarov will now face the leaders of the other teams. His potential opponents on the first board include Carlsen, Firouzja, Nepomniachtchi, Anand and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave. Sindarov is particularly looking forward to a possible encounter with Carlsen. The tournament will also be notable for the Indian chess community, as Gukesh’s upcoming World Championship opponent will compete in India shortly before their title match. Carlsen, Anand, Firouzja: who else will play in the league Alpine SG Pipers will be led by former world champion and longtime world No. 1 Magnus Carlsen, who returns to the Global Chess League after missing last season. He will be joined by Anish Giri, Vidit Gujrathi, Koneru Humpy, Divya Deshmukh and reigning world rapid champion Volodar Murzin. Alpine Pipers enter the season as the defending champions , having defeated Triveni Continental Kings in the 2025 final. However, the club’s lineup has changed signif
title: Javokhir Sindarov to play against Carlsen and other stars in Global Chess League

body: Photo: Uzbekistan 24 264 people granted citizenship of Uzbekistan ahead of Independence Day President Shavkat Mirziyoyev signed a decree granting citizenship of Uzbekistan to 264 people. Some said they had waited decades for citizenship. Since 2016, around 26,000 people have been granted citizenship, while none received citizenship between 2007 and 2016. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 27 August 2026, 14:54 Society Ahead of the 35th anniversary of Uzbekistan’s independence, president Shavkat Mirziyoyev signed a decree granting citizenship of Uzbekistan to 264 people, Uzbekistan 24 TV channel reported . Khursanoy Jumaboyeva, who was born in Tajikistan, said she has lived in Tashkent region for 26 years. “I moved in 2000. For many years, I could not travel to Tajikistan. When my mother died, I could not be there to see her off on her final journey,” she said. Advertising on Gazeta Another interviewee, Robiya Kahhorova, said she had waited 40 years for citizenship. Otabek Rasulov said being without citizenship had been difficult: “For 10 years, we carried around ‘Form 4'... They told us we would be granted citizenship. One evening, I came home from work, and my nephew ran up to me and said, ‘Uncle, there’s news.'” Of the 264 people granted citizenship, 90 live in Surkhandarya region. After Uzbekistan declared independence, 482 stateless people were granted citizenship between 1991 and 2007. No citizenship was granted between 2007 and 2016. Since 2016, when the country’s president changed, around 26,000 people have been granted citizenship of Uzbekistan. In addition, more than 60,000 people have been recognized as citizens of Uzbekistan following the introduction of the citizenship recognition procedure. Mirziyoyev’s first decree granting citizenship was issued in December 2016 and covered 179 people. In 2017, 10 decrees granted citizenship to 1,064 people. In 2018, 15 decrees granted citizenship to 2,759 stateless people. In 2019, 25 decrees were reported to have granted citizenship to 5,441 people. body: Marius Dan. Photo: Central Bank Economic growth and AI to sharply increase electricity demand in Uzbekistan — Franklin Templeton Economic growth, digitalization and AI are expected to sharply increase electricity demand in Uzbekistan, Franklin Templeton representative Marius Dan said. Tariff liberalization, RAB regulation and faster legal reforms are needed to ensure timely investment in the power grid, he noted. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 27 August 2026, 14:50 Economy Economic growth, digitalization and the development of AI are expected to significantly increase electricity demand in Uzbekistan, said Marius Dan, CEO for Central Asia at Templeton Global Investments, specialized investment division within Franklin Templeton. He added that tariff liberalization, full implementation of the regulated asset base (RAB) regulation and a clearer legislative framework are needed to attract international capital to the country’s energy sector and ensure timely investment in generation and power grids, he noted. Franklin Templeton manages Uzbekistan’s National Investment Fund (UzNIF), which, among others, holds stakes in five energy companies — Uzbekhydroenergo (40%), National Power Grid of Uzbekistan (40%), Regional Electric Networks (40%), Thermal Power Plants (25%) and Hududgazta’minot (40%). Speaking at the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum in Tashkent on 24 August, Dan said the development of AI, the digital economy and the population would put increasing pressure on Uzbekistan’s energy infrastructure. “Ultimately, all of this will run on electricity. As the National Investment Fund, we have assets in the energy sector and want to make sure our companies are ready for this. That means significant capital investment in distribution networks, generation, transmission and transport infrastructure,” Dan said. According to Dan, one of the fund’s priorities is preparing its portfolio companies to raise funds on international markets to fund these investments. Advertising on Gazeta He stressed that regulatory reforms in the energy sector are also necessary, including electricity tariff liberalization and the full implementation of the RAB methodology for transmission and distribution networks. This, he said, would give energy companies sufficient incentives to continue investing in infrastructure. Dan noted that the need for investment is becoming more pressing amid economic and population growth and continued digitalization. Asked whether the energy system would be able to adapt to rising demand while simultaneously increasing capital investment and reforming tariffs and regulation, Dan said much would depend on how quickly the government moves forward with legislative reforms. “There is a lot to be done, and much also depends on the government’s willingness to accelerate the adoption of the necessary legislative framework that will create incentives for these companies,” he said. Private capital has already been attracted to Uzbekistan’s energy sector through power purchase agreements (PPAs), Dan noted. However, state-owned energy companies also need to become more attractive to investors and improve their ability to raise financing. “Steps have already been taken this year, particularly with the initial implementation of the RAB mechanism, but significantly more clarity should be provided by the end of this year — at least that is what we hope for from the fund’s perspective. This will determine how much capital these companies can raise and subsequently invest in the networks to meet growing demand on time,” he said. “The last thing we want is to face an electricity shortage or problems with its transmission and distribution,” Dan added. In May, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Economy and Finance announced plans to introduce RAB methodology for calculating electricity and gas tariffs. Under the system, tariffs are calculated not only based on a company’s current costs but also on the value of its regulated assets, such as networks, equipment, substations and gas pipelines. The ministry projected that the new methodology would increase the price of electricity generation by around 9%, transmission costs by 30%, electricity distribution costs by around 10% and natural gas distribution costs by around 23%. These figures refer to individual stages of the supply chain rather than directly to household tariffs. Some costs of electricity and gas generation, transmission and distribution that exceed tariffs set for end consumers are expected to be covered by the state budget. For a company that has taken regional electricity networks under its management, RAB regulation could provide a mechanism for recovering investments through the tariff system. Investments in network repairs, new transformers, digital metering, loss reduction and improved supply reliability could be included in the regulated asset base if deemed justified and effective by the regulator. The company could then receive a regulated return on those investments, potentially through WACC, which the Ministry of Economy and Finance has indicated could be set at 14−16% after tax, depending on the company. In October 2025, managing director and partner at Boston Consulting Group (BCG) Igor Alekseev said that the introduction of tariffs based on the RAB methodology is planned for 2027−2028. body: Timur Ishmetov. Photo: Central Bank External shocks have yet to directly affect Uzbekistan — Central Bank chief Global oil and food price increases have yet to directly affect Uzbekistan, Central Bank chief Timur Ishmetov said. The regulator is monitoring possible second-round effects and is ready to act if inflation continues to decline or if upside risks materialize, he noted. O‘zbek tilida Ўзбек тилида На русском языке 26 August 2026, 11:42 Economy Uzbekistan’s Central Bank must be prepared to respond both to a further slowdown in inflation and to rising inflation risks, Central Bank chief Timur Ishmetov said at the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum in Tashkent on 24 August, Gazeta correspondent reported. “The work of a central bank is always associated with risks. They are always present. If there were no risks, perhaps a central bank would not be needed at all,” Ishmetov said. He noted that the global economy was operating amid continued uncertainty and a large number of external shocks. “Therefore, I think we need to move from simply managing risks to being better prepared for persistent shocks and uncertainty. We need to focus on resilience,” the Central Bank chief said. Advertising on Gazeta To make the financial system more resilient, the Central Bank plans to build up its financial buffers and strengthen financial stability, he said. “All these external shocks, especially what is happening now with oil and food prices, have not yet directly affected Uzbekistan, but we are closely monitoring the situation,” Ishmetov said. At the same time, the regulator is assessing the risk of so-called second-round effects, when an external shock spreads through the economy through costs, expectations and domestic prices. “Therefore, the Central Bank must be ready to act in both directions — regardless of whether inflation continues to decline or upside risks materialize. We must be ready to act decisively in both directions and, in any case, continue to fulfill our mandate,” Ishmetov said. Uzbekistan’s fuel imports fell sharply in June following high import volumes in April and May. Gasoline imports were higher than a year earlier but one-third lower than in May, while diesel imports fell nearly 19-fold and kerosene imports fell by 12.5-fold. The average import cost of gasoline and kerosene continued to rise. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), aviation fuel prices rose sharply in early 2026 as tensions around Iran escalated and supplies through the Strait of Hormuz were disrupted. By the end of May, prices had fallen from their April peaks but remained well above late-February levels. body: Photo: Shohruh Haydarov / Gazeta Tashkent proposes starting workday at hokimiyats at 8:00 Tashkent hokimiyat proposed shifting municipal and district hokimiyats, departments and subordinate units to an 8:00—17:00 schedule. Under the proposal, the working day would start at 8:00 instead of 9:00 and end at 17:00 instead of 18:00, the capital’s hokimiyat press service said . body: Illustration: Eldos Fazylbekov / Gazeta “Bring someone sighted!”: How an internal notary regulation outweighed the law in Uzbekistan People with visual impairments face systematic discrimination when accessing notary services in Uzbekistan. Notaries refuse to accept legally recognised facsimile signatures. Dilmurad Yusupov and Abdullo Abdukhalilov call for the system to be changed in an op-ed for Gazeta. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 16 August 2026, 13:56 Columns Society On July 24, Abdullo, who has had a visual impairment since birth with disability Group I, visited a notary office in the Yashnabad district of Tashkent with his son. He needed to issue a simple power of attorney authorising another person to receive a bank card. However, instead of receiving a public service, he ran into a bureaucratic wall and blatant discrimination based on disability. The notary refused to process the documents, categorically stating that this required bringing a representative from the Society of the Blind of Uzbekistan . The attempt to resolve the situation on the spot led to even greater absurdity. During a phone call to the Notary Chamber, its employee asked a completely unethical question: “Have you been blind since birth, or did you acquire the disability?” Upon learning that Abdullo had been blind since birth, she confirmed the previously stated requirement to find a mediator from the Society of the Blind. It turns out that if the visual impairment is acquired, there is no need to summon a representative from the Society of the Blind. This logic-defying regulation makes the situation even more absurd. Unfortunately, this case is not the mistake of a single notary but a systemic problem faced by all people with visual impairments. Today, state regulations effectively turn legally capable, independent citizens into second-class people , depriving them of the right to manage their own lives. The Law Permits, but the Regulation Prohibits People with visual impairments are full-fledged and legally competent citizens. They bear full responsibility for their actions. To enable them to sign documents independently, a facsimile -a specially made stamp that replaces a handwritten signature-is used all over the world. Advertising on Gazeta In Uzbekistan, this right is clearly established in Article 29 of the Law “On the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.” The law explicitly states that the facsimile signature of a person with a disability is recognised as an official signature and carries legal force. However, in practice, notaries ignore this law. They refer to their internal departmental regulation (paragraph 9 of the 2019 Ministry of Justice regulation on the procedure for performing notarial acts ), which categorically prohibits accepting documents with a facsimile signature. A gross legal conflict arises: a subordinate act of an individual ministry is somehow placed above the law and the Constitution of the Republic of Uzbekistan. According to the Law ‘On Normative Legal Acts' , departmental regulations are subordinate acts and under no circumstances can they contradict laws. The internal regulation of the Ministry of Justice, being a subordinate departmental act, has no right to cancel or restrict the effect of the Law ‘On the Rights of Persons with Disabilities', which permits the use of a facsimile. By applying the regulation instead of the law, notaries directly violate Article 15 of the Constitution, which recognises the unconditional supremacy of the laws. The absurdity of forced ‘intermediaries' To bypass its own ban on facsimiles, the notarial regulation (paragraph 8) offers visually impaired people a humiliating solution. Another person (a ‘proxy') must sign the document on behalf of the person with a visual impairment in the presence of a notary, under video recording. At the same time, for some reason, notaries persistently demand that blind people bring representatives specifically from the Society of the Blind. There is no logic whatsoever in this requirement. Firstly, the majority of employees at the Society of the Blind are themselves blind; how can they act as a sighted proxy? And if a representative who also has a visual impairment comes to the notary as a proxy, will their rights also be infringed? Secondly, by no means all people with visual impairments are members of this organisation. A state service should not depend on whether a person is a member of any NGO or not. This artificially creates a dependency of the blind person on third parties. Why should the Society of the Blind be the only possible intermediary between notaries and blind citizens? In which normative legal documents is such a role for the Society of the Blind enshrined? And why can only a representative of one specific organisation act as a proxy for a blind person? After all, a person with a visual impairment must have the choice of their trusted representative-whether it be a legal entity or a natural person. Or, overall, to do without any intermediaries when receiving notarial services. All these questions remain open... Moreover, by imposing the proxy services of a specific organisation, notaries directly violate the Law ‘On Non-Governmental Non-Profit Organisations' . Part 3 of Article 18 of the law clearly states: “The requirement to indicate in official documents membership or participation in the activities of a particular non-governmental non-profit organisation is not permitted. The affiliation or non-affiliation of citizens with an NGO cannot serve as a basis for restricting their rights and freedoms.” It turns out that by refusing service without a representative of the Society of the Blind, the notary system illegally restricts the rights of citizens with visual impairments. Justice Ministry’s response: “You have misunderstood everything” The Tashkent City Department of Justice sent an official response to Abdullo’s appeal to the President’s virtual reception regarding this incident. In the letter signed by the Deputy Head of the Department, J. Khudoyorov, the agency fully justifies the notary’s actions. In its response, the department refers to the Administrative Regulation (approved by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 726 of 2020). According to the document, when a blind person applies, the presence of a ‘typhlo-interpreter' is required, whose credentials must be confirmed by a power of attorney and an official identity card issued exclusively by the Society of the Blind of Uzbekistan. The response concludes by stating that the notary was simply explaining the regulation, and the citizen ‘incorrectly understood this as discrimination'. This response raises more questions than it answers and exposes the striking incompetence of the system. Firstly, such a profession as a ‘typhlo-interpreter' simply does not officially exist in Uzbekistan. There are audio describers (specialists who describe visual sequences for the blind). Where is a blind citizen supposed to find a specialist of a non-existent profession? Secondly, the Society of the Blind has no legal authority, mechanisms, or educational facilities to train, certify, or issue identity cards to any ‘typhlo-interpreters'. Thirdly, the regulation itself (No. 726), referred to by the officials, is written with the grossest logical errors and without the slightest understanding of the specifics of disability. The document indicates that a ‘typhlo-interpreter' is not needed if the notary knows how to work with a certain ‘device intended for a blind citizen'. Exactly what kind of device is meant is not specified. Is it a Braille display? A screen reader programme (JAWS, NVDA)? A dictaphone? The wording ‘if the notary knows how to work with the device' ( moslama bilan ishlay olsa ) dooms the norm to failure from the outset. Not a single notary in the country undergoes training in working with special typhlotechnical aids. Moreover, the regulation absurdly links this mythical device with the possi
title: “Bring someone sighted!”: How an internal notary regulation outweighed the law in Uzbekistan

body: Vozinha. Photo: Yevgeny Sorochin / Gazeta FIFA WC 2026: How 40-year-old Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha became the tournament’s breakout star The World Cup turned Vozinha into one of the tournament’s biggest sensations. He played his most important matches past the age of 40, and his story moved millions of people around the world. Gazeta tells player’s journey to global recognition through Yevgeny Sorochin’s photographs. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 3 August 2026, 20:16 Sport One day, almost no one outside your home country knows your name. A few days later, every camera at the world’s biggest sporting event is pointed on you. In the age of social media, that transformation can occur almost overnight — and that is exactly what happened to Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha, aged 40. A handful of matches was all it took for millions of followers across the world to discover him. Gazeta tells the story of a goalkeeper whose life has always been inseparable from football, seen through the lens of our photograpther Yevgeny Sorochin, who covered Cape Verde’s Round of 32 match against Argentina at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. This article was produced with the support of Uzbekistan Airways. “He had Maradona right there” Vozinha’s real name is Josimar José Évora Dias. He was born on June 3, 1986, in Mindelo, one of the largest cities in Cape Verde, an island nation in the Atlantic Ocean with a population of under one million. For most of his club career, he played for little-known teams in Cape Verde, Angola, Moldova, Portugal, Cyprus, and Slovakia. Advertising on Gazeta Vozinha is the second most capped player in Cape Verde’s national team history. He represented the national side at five major international tournaments: the Africa Cup of Nations in 2013, 2015, 2021, and 2023, and the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Although football fans know the Cape Verde goalkeeper as Vozinha, his father originally intended to name him after the famous Argentine forward Jorge Valdano, the 1986 World Cup winner who scored one of Argentina’s three goals in the final against West Germany. When registering the child, however, José Pedro was informed that foreign names could not be given to children in Cape Verde. He named his son Josimar instead, after Brazilian defender Josimar Pereira of the 1980s, whose name fitted the country’s Portuguese-language naming tradition without issue. A few days before Cape Verde’s World Cup debut, FIFA contacted Valdano and told him the story. The former Argentine forward had known nothing of it, and was genuinely moved to hear it. “Forty years after playing at the 1986 World Cup, I’m playing vicariously at World Cup 2026, through Vozinha. It came as a huge surprise to me. Initially, I was a bit confused. Why did his father think of me? He had Maradona right there! ” Valdano said. Vozinha’s nickname also has its roots in his childhood. While his mother was occupied with work and his father was serving in the military, the boy was raised by his grandparents. He spent much of his time playing football with older children. “I used to take quite a few knocks, and whenever I couldn’t get my own back, I’d go home angry and sulking,” said Vozinha in an interview in 2014. “They would tease me, saying I was going to complain to my grandparents.” In Portuguese, vozinha is a diminutive of avó (grandmother), carrying the sense of grandmother’s boy. Two years later, after Cape Verde’s World Cup debut and historic draw with Spain, Vozinha dedicated the result to his grandparents. “I'm so grateful to my parents and grandparents, who are now shining down on me from above... If they were still alive today, they would be very proud of their grandson. That’s why it meant so much to me. It’s something Cape Verdeans have dreamed of their whole lives,” he said. “We came here to fight” The match against Spain — one of the tournament favourites — ended in a goalless draw. For Cape Verde, making their World Cup debut, it was a historic result. When the final whistle sounded at the stadium in Atlanta, celebrations broke out: thousands of supporters who had backed the team for all 90 minutes embraced, danced, and made no effort to hide their emotions. Neutral spectators joined in too. The hero of the game was 40-year-old Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha. After the final whistle, he could not hold back his tears. “I cried because I grew up with my grandparents and unfortunately they were not here; they died a few years ago... I also cried because my mum didn’t manage to be here because of the visa. Because of the money we had to pay for the visa, we didn’t manage to [get it done] on time. I would like her to be here,” Vozinha said after being named player of the match. “Everyone thought that we came here just to enjoy the World Cup... but we are here to compete, and we are here to fight for our country ,” he added. Vozinha notes that he came to professional football relatively late, after the age of 25, when he joined Angolan club Progresso in 2012. “I thought about leaving but I continued because of this dream. This is for everyone. I was named man of the match but this is for all of my teammates because without them nothing would be possible. I will continue to work for Cape Verde and for the people,” goalkeeper promised. After the Spain match, Vozinha’s following grew at extraordinary speed. Within the first 24 hours, his Instagram account went from around 50,000 followers to nearly 10 million. By the end of the World Cup, that figure had reached 29.4 million. “Делить поле с Месси — это мечта” If the Spain match introduced Vozinha to the world, the games that followed confirmed that the draw against one of the tournament favourites was no coincidence or pure luck. The goalkeeper who had kept out La Roja helped Cape Verde complete the group stage unbeaten — after Spain, the team drew with Uruguay and Saudi Arabia. In the expanded World Cup format, the top two teams from each group advanced to the knockout stage, along with the eight best third-placed sides. Across all 12 groups, only Senegal and Cape Verde managed to reach the round of 32 with just three points — made possible by the fact that Cape Verde had not lost a single group stage match. On July 4, Cape Verde faced Argentina in the Round of 32. Before the match, Vozinha made no secret of his excitement at the prospect of facing Lionel Messi. “He is the greatest footballer of all time. Sharing the pitch with Messi is a dream, and one day I will proudly tell my children that I played against him. I know it is almost impossible to stop him, but I will give everything I have to make sure he does not score against me,” he said. За более чем 120 минут игры против Аргентины Возинья совершил семь сейвов. Несмотря на поражение со счётом 2:3, Кабо-Верде, дебютировавшая на чемпионате мира, дала бой будущим финалистам и чемпионам турнира. В матче отличился и Лионель Месси, однако ещё четыре его удара парировал Возинья. Зрителям особенно запомнился момент во втором тайме, когда голкипер отбил мяч, закрученный капитаном “альбиселесте” в противоположный угол ворот. После матча Возинья рассказал о разговоре с Лионелем Месси, который, по его словам, навсегда останется в его памяти. “После игры я подошёл к Месси. Он обнял меня и сказал: „Ты великолепен. Твой народ должен тобой гордиться“. Для меня это было невероятно. Услышать такие слова от Лео Месси значит очень многое. Я поблагодарил его и ответил: „Спасибо, Лео. Ты лучший“”, — рассказал голкипер. Career After the World Cup, Vozinha found himself at the centre of global attention, yet for most of his career he had played far from the top European leagues. He began at clubs in his home city of Mindelo, representing Batuque until 2011 before moving to Mindelense . In 2012, Vozinha signed for Angolan club Progresso do Sambizanga , where he spent three seasons. Then he returned briefly to Mindelense before moving to Moldova in 2015 to join Chisinau-based club Zimbru . A year later, Vo
title: FIFA WC 2026: How 40-year-old Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha became the tournament’s breakout star

body: Photo: Yevgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta Photos: Lionel Messi’s final World Cup. What does “MessiMania” look like? This World Cup was likely the last for Argentina’s legendary captain. Backed by passionate supporters, he delivered one of his finest tournaments. Here is a look at Leo’s play through the lens of Gazeta photojournalist Evgeniy Sorochin, captured at the Argentina vs Cape Verde Round of 32 match. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 27 July 2026, 11:44 ЧМ-2026 Sport Spain were crowned world champions after defeating Argentina 1−0 in the final, denying Lionel Messi the chance to win a second consecutive title with the Albiceleste. One of the greatest footballers of his generation, Messi likely played his final World Cup match on July 19 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. We suggest to look back at the Round of 32 match between Argentina and Cape Verde, covered by Gazeta photojournalist Evgeniy Sorochin. His photographs capture the key moments of the game, Messi himself in the iconic number 10 shirt, and the emotions of Argentine supporters for whom he has long become the symbol of an entire footballing era. This article was produced with the support of Uzbekistan Airways. Advertising on Gazeta For Argentine supporters, choosing a shirt is either very complicated or very simple — fans not wearing the number 10 are a rare sight. Try finding even three supporters in this photograph who chose a different number. While many supporters continue to compare Messi to Diego Maradona, Argentinians take pride in the fact that their country gave the world both of football’s greatest wizards of the ball. The scale of MessiMania in the Argentine stands is impossible to miss. When Argentina take to the pitch, supporters' eyes are fixed on Lionel Messi, and camera lenses follow his every move. Among those keeping a close eye on Messi is David Beckham, who was in attendance with his family. The former England captain is a co-owner of Inter Miami, the club where the Argentine currently plays. “Альбиселесте” на каждый свой матч так эффектно выходили во главе с Лео, что все говорили о своеобразной ауре команды. “Если вы это видите, значит, готовьтесь проигрывать” , — писали в футбольных пабликах. Every time the Albiceleste took to the pitch led by Messi, the entrance was so striking that people spoke of a kind of aura surrounding the team. “If you are seeing this, you had better prepare to lose,” football pages wrote. Even opponents respect and admire Messi. Cape Verde captain Ryan Mendes, despite winning the pre-match coin toss, still deferred to the Argentine and gave him the first choice. During the match, opponents also try to stay as close to him as possible — though no longer out of a desire to be near a legend, but to deny Argentina’s captain any space. Without question, all free kicks and corners are entrusted to Lionel, who has demonstrated his mastery repeatedly throughout his career. After the match in Miami, our photojournalist admitted that Messi’s performance had not particularly impressed him. For much of the game, the Argentine simply walked around the pitch, engaging in play only in brief moments. He has already been dubbed the “tournament's biggest pedestrian”. By some counts, the captain spends 63% of his playing time walking. Yet the moment he spots space or an opportunity to play a pass, he makes the right decision instantly and extracts the maximum from every moment of involvement. Even at this “pedestrian” pace, the Argentine captain scored eight goals and provided four assists at this World Cup, becoming the all-time leading assist provider in tournament history. With his 21st World Cup goal, Messi surpassed the record of German striker Miroslav Klose, who had long held the record as the tournament’s all-time top scorer with 16 goals. However, French forward Kylian Mbappé ultimately finished ahead of him, netting his 22nd World Cup goal across three tournaments. Still, in what was likely his final World Cup match, Leo was unable to help Argentina retain the title and left the stadium defeated. But Argentine supporters never stopped cheering for their hero, not even for a moment. In the final in New York, as Spain captain Rodri was presented with the tournament’s best player award, Argentine fans chanted just one name in unison — Messi! This article was produced with the support of Uzbekistan Airways. Subscribe to our Telegram channel Gazeta 6 943 # football # lionel messi # world cup 2026
title: Photos: Lionel Messi’s final World Cup. What does “MessiMania” look like?

body: Photo: Karel Balas 10 buildings of Tashkent modernism added to UNESCO World Heritage List Ten landmarks of Tashkent’s modernist architecture have been added to the UNESCO World Heritage List. The newly inscribed sites include the Pearl residential building, the Peoples' Friendship Palace, the State Circus, Chorsu Market, Kosmonavtlar Metro Station, the Sun Heliocomplex and more. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 26 July 2026, 20:12 Culture Ten landmarks of Tashkent’s modernist architecture have been added to the UNESCO World Heritage List of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). The decision was adopted on Sunday during the 48th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee, held in Busan, Republic of Korea, from 19 to 29 July. The session was attended by a delegation from the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation and the National Commission of Uzbekistan for UNESCO. Among 30 new nominations considered for inscription, the committee reviewed Uzbekistan’s nomination , “Tashkent Modernist Architecture: Modernity and Tradition in Central Asia”. The nomination comprises ten outstanding examples of late twentieth-century modernist architecture, representing diverse public, cultural, residential and engineering structures. Inscribed sites All photographs by Karel Balas. Images provided by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation. Advertising on Gazeta Pearl Residential Building (1975−1985). State Museum of the History of Uzbekistan (1968−1970). Peoples' Friendship Palace (late 1970s-1981). State Museum of Arts of Uzbekistan (1967−1974). Tashkent State Circus (1965−1975) . Central Exhibition Hall of the Academy of Arts (1972−1974). Palace of Arts, Panoramic Cinema (formerly Alisher Navoi Cinema Palace) (1962−1964). Chorsu Market (Chorsu Bazaar) (1983−1990) . Kosmonavtlar Metro Station (1982−1984) . Sun Heliocomplex in Tashkent region (1981−1987) . Chairperson of the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation and head of the National Commission for UNESCO Gayane Umerova said: “The inscription of these sites on the World Heritage List restores an important chapter of Uzbekistan’s modern architectural history to the international context of 20th-century heritage and the global modernist movement.” “These buildings demonstrate how Tashkent used architecture to shape public life, collective identity and visions of the future. UNESCO recognition also carries a long-term responsibility — to preserve these buildings with the highest professional standards, ensure they remain an integral part of the city’s life and pass knowledge about them on to future generations,” she added. Head of the Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva stated : “This recognition celebrates not only the value of individual buildings but an entire era, when a new image of Tashkent emerged after the earthquake, successfully combining modern architecture with the traditions of Central Asia and the characteristics of our climate. It is a major achievement for Uzbekistan and an important step toward preserving our architectural heritage for future generations.” Prior to this inscription, the UNESCO World Heritage List included 1,248 sites in 170 countries. Uzbekistan had five cultural and two natural World Heritage sites. According to the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation, this sixth inscription is the country’s first national property to be added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 25 years. Uzbekistan has also become the first country in Central Asia and the CIS to have 20th-century modernist architecture inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. It joins a small group of just over ten countries worldwide whose modernist architectural heritage has received this prestigious international designation. The UNESCO World Heritage Committee is the governing body of the 1972 Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage. It serves as the principal international forum for considering matters related to the protection of World Heritage sites, evaluating their state of conservation and deciding on new nominations submitted by states parties to the convention. In addition to the 30 new nominations , the committee is also reviewing proposals concerning three existing World Heritage sites and assessing the state of conservation of 147 listed properties. title: 10 buildings of Tashkent modernism added to UNESCO World Heritage List

body: Erik Ahlström Photo: Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation “The cleanest cities are not where people clean the most, but where they litter the least.” Founder of plogging Erik Ahlström on litter as a new normal, community clean-ups and leading by example Plogging, picking up litter while running, was invented in Sweden in 2016. Its founder, Erik Ahlström, spoke with Gazeta about how a simple habit became a global movement and why picking up “someone else’s” litter should never be a cause for shame. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 20 July 2026, 18:43 Society In 2016, Erik Ahlström went for a run through Stockholm with a trash bag in his hands. That was the beginning of a movement that today exists in more than 50 countries. The name plogging (Plogga) was coined by co-founder Karina Svensson, combining the Swedish plocka upp (to pick up) and the English word jogging . In June this year, Erik Ahlström came to Tashkent as eco-ambassador of the Samarkand Marathon race series, organized by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF). Gazeta journalist met with him to find out how one Swedish man’s simple habit grew into a global movement and what it takes for cleanliness to become part of everyday life. “It's not my trash, and not yours, but this is our planet” Before plogging, Erik was well known in the world of trail running. For more than 30 years, he organised sports events in Sweden, founding the alpine ski race Kebnekaise Classic, the multisport race Åre Extreme Challenge, the 24-hour ultramarathon Sweden Sky Race, and others. Advertising on Gazeta “I've been organising events for 30 years — running, multi-sport, ski touring. I know how it works. And I wanted to give something back to nature, because I’ve spent so much time in it ,” he says. His habit of picking up litter started back in Åre, a small ski resort in northern Sweden, where he lived for about 20 years. While walking his son to school, he would pick up whatever lay on the ground. He gradually began organising group clean-ups, and over 20 years, the town noticeably changed. When he moved to Stockholm, a city of two million, the contrast was striking. “The new normal was trash everywhere,” he recalls. Photo: Plogga. Photo: Plogga. In Stockholm, Erik continued going out on runs with a bag — this time with friends. “It became like a treasure hunt. We were running, laughing, and having fun. Others saw us and said they wanted to join in,” he shares. One day, he photographed his “catch” and posted it on social media. The post sparked interest; people in the comments joked and suggested names for the new sport. The idea began to gain momentum, with major sports brands getting on board. Soon, foreign TV channels came to film reports about the new movement, dozens of local groups appeared across Sweden, and the plogging gradually spread beyond the country’s borders. Photo: Plogga. Photo: Plogga. The main obstacle in plogging, according to its founder, is not physical fitness but stigma. In many cultures, picking up litter, especially someone else’s, is considered shameful. “Almost everywhere you find this feeling — in some religions, some cultures. It’s not my job, it’s someone else’s job. But if you start doing it with a smile and you inform people about what you’re doing, you will break the stigma. And if you do it in groups, it becomes easier as well.” He himself felt uncomfortable back in 2016, but the desire to make the city cleaner was stronger. “It's not my trash and not your trash. Somebody else threw it. But the planet is ours,” he says. Plogging has been taken up by major brands, for example, Ericsson. Ahlström believes there is more to it than just image. Photo: Plogga / Instagram. Photo: Plogga / Instagram. “Ericsson has been doing this globally. I’ve been travelling around, meeting their teams in Bogota, Mexico City, and Delhi. They’re really, really engaged. And as a Swedish company, they’re proud to stand behind a Swedish activity,” he explains. However, not every story is like that. Once, while running a plogging session with a large tech company in Sweden, he opened their fridge in the office. “It was full of single-use plastic, mugs, and food on demand. It felt really strange, like there was no real engagement. It was only for CSR. They had some money to spend on it, so it happened,” he recalls. Litter creates litter According to Ahlström, the problem of waste exists in every country he has visited. But what surprises him most is that in countries without a well-developed recycling system, people are sometimes more engaged than in places where the infrastructure already exists. In India, where Erik spent three weeks, a centralised waste management system is almost non-existent. But in some villages, people have started separating organic waste from the rest and composting it on site. According to Ahlström, it works: food waste goes back into the ground rather than being mixed with everything else. Photo: Humrahi Studio. Photo: Humrahi Studio. Photo: Humrahi Studio. Photo: Humrahi Studio. A similar story comes from Zimbabwe. Locals would gather on the beach at six in the morning, dancing, celebrating. Together with ploggers, they cleaned a shore covered in plastic. “They didn’t understand the difference between a plastic bottle and a coconut shell. For them it was all the same. But after that clean-up, people came back to the beach on their own, with scythes and sticks. Knowledge changed behaviour,” says Ahlström. In Japan, the approach is different. There are no street bins at all. When people buy a bottle of water, they know they will take it home and sort it. In Ahlström's words, they are buying not just the contents, but the entire life cycle of the product. Photo: Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation. Photo: Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation. Uzbekistan has its own tradition — hashar , community clean-ups during which residents come together to tidy up yards, streets and neighbourhoods. It might seem that if people are willing to do this, the problem should solve itself. But Ahlström draws a line between a one-off event and a daily habit. He says that willingness alone is not enough. What is needed is education, personal responsibility, and constantly visible examples. As an example, Erik points to New York in the 1980s. Crime was rampant, and the subway was dirty and unsafe. Rather than relying solely on increased policing, the subway management focused on maintaining order: workers washed graffiti off carriages every day, repaired seats, and replaced broken lights. No train left the depot dirty. Gradually, the crime situation improved, and residents began to take pride in their city. This experience is often linked to the broken windows theory: if one broken window is not replaced, soon none will be left intact. Disorder breeds disorder, and cleanliness breeds cleanliness. Photo: Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation. Erik describes Tashkent as one of the cleanest cities among the 46 countries he has visited, but acknowledges that the bins here are too small and fill up quickly. People leave bags beside them, and then the wind and birds scatter the litter. He says infrastructure matters, but what needs to change first is people’s behaviour. “The cleanest places are not necessarily those with the biggest clean-ups. These are the places where fewer people litter in the first place,” he assures. Illustrative photo: Iskandar Mirzakhmedov / Gazeta. Illustrative photo: Iskandar Mirzakhmedov / Gazeta. Illustrative photo: Iskandar Mirzakhmedov / Gazeta. Plogging in Uzbekistan After arriving in Uzbekistan, Ahlström went for a run with the Tashkent Ploggers community. Participants moved in a chain: some picked up bottles, others removed their caps, and others sorted the waste into different bags. After the Bukhara Night Race, the same approach yielded 16 kilograms of plastic, which was sent to a local
title: “The cleanest cities are not where people clean the most, but where they litter the least.” Founder of plogging Erik Ahlström on litter as a new normal, community clean-ups and leading by example

body: Photo: Shuhrat Latipov / Gazeta US dollar exchange rate in Uzbekistan falls to lowest level since August 2023 The official US dollar exchange rate fell to 11,778.52 soums, its lowest level since the August 2023 devaluation. The soum has strengthened by approximately 1.9% against the dollar in August, in line with the global trend of a weaker US currency, economist Mirkomil Kholboev said. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 26 August 2026, 09:24 Economy The official US dollar exchange rate in Uzbekistan fell to 11,778.52 soums on 26 August, reaching its lowest level since the sharp depreciation of the soum in August 2023. According to the Central Bank, the dollar fell by 39.55 soums following Tuesday’s trading session. This was the fourth new low for the dollar in the past month . Dynamics of the US dollar exchange rate against the soum since the beginning of 2026. Source: Central Bank / Gazeta Advertising on Gazeta At commercial banks, the dollar is mostly being sold for 11,840−11,875 soums. Economist Mirkomil Kholboev said the soum’s strengthening has accelerated noticeably in August. From the beginning of the year through the end of July, the soum had weakened by just 0.01% against the dollar. In August alone, however, it has strengthened by approximately 1.9%. Kholboev noted that the strengthening of the soum was also taking place amid a broader global trend of the US dollar weakening against several major currencies. However, there is not yet enough data to assess the impact of several domestic factors that may have contributed to the soum’s appreciation. These include August exports, particularly gold exports amid rising global gold prices, investment inflows, remittances and external borrowing. During the first half of the year, individuals sold $12.3 billion worth of foreign currency to banks, 35% more than a year earlier. Purchases of foreign currency by individuals rose by 26% to $6.8 billion. Households' foreign-currency sales to banks exceeded their purchases by around $5.5 billion during the first half of the year. A year earlier, the difference was $3.7 billion. Households remain major net sellers of foreign currency. The share of their net foreign-currency supply in total foreign-exchange market turnover increased from 26% in the first half of 2025 to 29% in January-June 2026. The IMF previously reclassified Uzbekistan’s de facto exchange-rate system from “crawl-like” to “floating”. Photo: Central Bank Uzbekistan aims for 5% inflation, WTO accession and reduced state role — deputy prime minister Uzbekistan aims to reduce inflation to 5% in 2027, keep the budget deficit below 3% of GDP and secure an investment-grade credit rating. The government also plans to complete the country’s accession to the WTO and reduce the state’s role in the economy, deputy prime minister Jamshid Kuchkarov said. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 25 August 2026, 09:23 Economy Uzbekistan plans to secure an investment-grade sovereign credit rating, complete its accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO) and further reduce the state’s presence in the economy in the coming years, deputy prime minister Jamshid Kuchkarov said on 24 August. He made the remarks at the opening of the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum in Tashkent, Gazeta 's correspondent reported. Kuchkarov said the development of financial technologies, attracting private capital and introducing new financial instruments are among Uzbekistan’s economic policy priorities. Advertising on Gazeta “Successful development of any sector, including fintech, ultimately depends on stable and favorable macroeconomic conditions that provide a foundation for sustainable growth and investment,” Kuchkarov said. The deputy prime minister noted that Uzbekistan’s economy has grown by an average of 6−7% annually over the past decade. Over that period, GDP tripled from around $60 billion to $180 billion, he said. GDP per capita also increased from approximately $1,900 to $4,600, bringing Uzbekistan closer to the ranks of upper-middle-income countries. Kuchkarov said inflation has fallen to single-digit levels after several years of double-digit inflation. “This year, inflation is expected to be around 6.5%, and our goal is to reach the target rate of 5% next year,” he said. External public debt remains at around 27% of GDP. “Maintaining fiscal discipline is a fundamental principle for us. In recent years, we have kept the budget deficit below 3% of GDP,” Kuchkarov said. He also pointed to improvements in international assessments of Uzbekistan’s economy, upgrades to Uzbekistan’s sovereign credit ratings and increased foreign direct investment. Investment-grade rating, WTO accession and reduced state role Kuchkarov said the government plans to maintain a “favorable and predictable environment” for investors and market participants over the next decade. “We will take all necessary measures to bring inflation down to the target level, maintain fiscal discipline and keep public debt at a reasonable and sustainable level,” he said. Another government goal is to secure an investment-grade sovereign credit rating for Uzbekistan. “We will work toward achieving an investment-grade sovereign credit rating, completing Uzbekistan’s accession to the World Trade Organization, further reducing the state’s presence in the economy and continuing market reforms,” Kuchkarov said. He said these measures should strengthen the role of the private sector, deepen Uzbekistan’s integration into the global economy and expand opportunities for local and foreign investors. “A system where technology reduces barriers” As part of its structural reforms, the government plans to develop a modern, competitive and inclusive financial system that is integrated into the global economy, Kuchkarov said. “It should be a system where technology reduces barriers, innovation is encouraged and trust is protected,” he said. The deputy prime minister also highlighted plans to strengthen regional and international cooperation and connectivity. According to Kuchkarov, fintech development can support economic growth through faster movement and allocation of capital, greater access to financial services and more efficient use of financial resources. “We are confident that the important proposals and initiatives put forward during this forum will lead to significant practical outcomes and create new opportunities for cooperation in the years ahead,” he said. body: Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta Law on Enterprise Uzbekistan International Digital Technology Center signed. Details President signed the constitutional law establishing the Enterprise Uzbekistan International Digital Technology Center in Tashkent. Located within IT Park, the center will allow major technology companies to operate under a special legal framework that will remain in effect until 2100. На русском языке 21 August 2026, 21:11 Economy President Shavkat Mirziyoyev signed the constitutional law On the International Digital Technology Center (Enterprise Uzbekistan, website ). The law will enter into force in six months, on 21 January 2027. The law aims to create a special jurisdiction for attracting investment in digital technologies, facilitate the development and commercialization of innovations and promote the export of services. The special legal framework will remain in effect until the end of 2100. The president will determine the boundaries of the center. The special legal framework may cover: the development, implementation and commercialization of digital technologies, services and products; investment activities and the export of services; experimental testing of digital technologies; civil and economic proceedings; labor and employment; foreign-exchange operations; financial and banking activities; customs; government services; intellectual property protection. In certain cases, the framework may also apply to projects carried out by center participants outside its main territory. Advertising on Gazeta The center will have a special framework for applying legislation. It will include the Constitution, the constitutional law itself, decisions of the president and the Supervisory Board and, where necessary, English and Welsh common law and principles of equity. According to Enterprise Uzbekistan, the center is a technology jurisdiction for global big tech companies and will be located within IT Park in Tashkent. Enterprise Uzbekistan emphasized that the center was not primarily about tax incentives, but about the special legal framework as a whole, which would allow major technology companies to operate directly from Uzbekistan. President will chair the center’s council The president of Uzbekistan will approve the composition of the center’s Supervisory Board and serve as its chair. The board will set the center’s strategic development priorities and approve key rules governing its special legal framework. English will be the center’s official working language. All decisions of the Supervisory Board and the center’s administration will be published in English. Four categories of investors The center’s participants will include residents and investors. The law defines four categories of investors: institutional, infrastructure, startup and resident investors. Different requirements, operating conditions and support measures may be established for each category. Investors will have the right to independently determine the amount, types, forms and areas of their investments and freely dispose of income generated from investment activities within the special legal framework. The assets, investments and property of center participants will be protected from confiscation, nationalization, expropriation and seizure. Exceptions include final decisions of the Tashkent International Commercial Court, as well as measures related to combating money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions-related restrictions. Tax and customs benefits The center’s authorities, participants and their employees will be exempt from taxes and fees established by Uzbekistan’s tax legislation, except for VAT, corporate income tax and personal income tax. The center’s authorities and participants will also be exempt from VAT and customs duties when importing equipment, components, software, materials and samples used for the production of digital technologies, activities within the regulatory sandbox and the operation of the center. Regulatory sandbox A regulatory sandbox will be introduced to test innovative technologies, products and services. It will operate for up to 12 months, unless the board sets a different period. Participants may be temporarily exempted from certain legal requirements and licensing and permitting procedures while working within the sandbox. They will also have access to the center’s infrastructure, including research laboratories. Center participants will be able to obtain banking, investment, venture capital, insurance, payment and other financial services through accredited partners. With the Central Bank’s approval, branches of foreign banks may also operate within the center. Special rules for personal data The center may establish special rules for accessing and protecting personal data. The law also contains provisions on cloud technologies. The center may set rules for storing and reusing information using cloud technologies. At the same time, measures must be taken to protect data from unauthorized access, alteration, destruction or dissemination. Requirements for storing information must also take international security standards into account. The law separately regulates the protection of intellectual property rights. Special labor rules Employment relations within the center will be governed by the constitutional law, Uzbekistan’s labor legislation and decisions of the center. Special rules for organizing work may also be introduced. Foreign workers will be subject to a separate procedure. Within established quotas, they may be exempt from the requirement to obtain confirmation of their right to work in Uzbekistan. Entry, visa and registration procedures for foreign specialists will also be subject to the special legal framework. AI and education The constitutional law also establishes rules for activities involving artificial intelligence. Center participants will be able to develop and test AI technologies. When developing or testing solutions that could directly or indirectly affect human rights and freedoms, they must take measures to protect those rights and legitimate interests. The law also requires participants to assess risks, prevent discrimination and comply with Uzbekistan’s international obligations. Educational institutions will be able to implement programs in line with the center’s requirements. The use of educational programs and standards from foreign countries and international organizations will also be permitted. Disputes will be handled by Tashkent International Commercial Court The law establishes a separate framework for resolving disputes arising under the special legal framework. The Tashkent International Commercial Court will have jurisdiction over economic, civil, corporate and labor disputes related to the activities of center participants, among other matters. The court will also hear disputes concerning decisions by the center’s authorities, property relations, liquidation, reorganization, insolvency and bankruptcy of participants, as well as other cases provided for by law. For violations of the center’s rules, its administration may issue written warnings, impose financial sanctions, temporarily restrict activities, suspend benefits or ultimately terminate a participant’s status.
