body: Photo: Sabina Amangeldina / ALMA What Bill Viola is known for and why his exhibition at the Almaty Museum of Arts is not to be missed The ALMA is hosting the first retrospective exhibition of Bill Viola (1951−2024) in Central Asia. He is one of the most significant artists in the history of video art, a pioneer who elevated the moving image to the level of classical art. Gazeta explains why this is an event worth traveling for. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 11 July 2026, 15:30 Culture The opening of Bill Viola’s retrospective at the Almaty Museum of Arts (ALMA) is a historic moment. His work has never been shown in Central Asia before. The closest it came to the region was his solo exhibition at the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts in Moscow in 2021 — his first in Russia. For decades, this most influential video artist of the late 20th and early 21st century exhibited at the world’s leading cultural institutions, including MoMA in New York, the National Gallery and Tate Modern in London, the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, the Grand Palais in Paris, and many others. Kazakhstan joined that list thanks to the Almaty Museum of Arts, which opened in September last year. The museum’s founders, Nurlan Smagulov and Madina Smagulоva , acquired Viola’s original installation Stations (1994) for one of its four Artist Rooms , giving Almaty audiences their first encounter with his work. Nine months later, the ALMA team presented their first major international exhibition project. A retrospective titled The Space of Time is dedicated to the memory of the artist, who passed away in 2024. Advertising on Gazeta Photo: Sabina Amangeldina / ALMA. “We [founders of the museum] had dreamed of bringing an international exhibition of the highest caliber to Almaty. Bill Viola was a global figure. In 2017, I traveled with my family to Liège, Belgium, to see his exhibition, and even then we began thinking about how important it would be to make an encounter with world-class video art possible in Almaty too. I hope this retrospective will draw visitors from China, Azerbaijan, Russia, Uzbekistan, and countries around the world to see Bill Viola’s work in person. Being able to give everyone access to his art speaks to the museum’s core mission: to integrate Kazakhstan into the global art world. It matters deeply to us that local and Central Asian artists find inspiration here and go on to create great work that we can one day bring to audiences abroad. That exchange is crucial to everything we do,” said Nurlan Smagulоv at the opening. (left to right) Kira Perov, Meruert Kaliyeva, Umut Shayakhmetova, Nurlan Smagulоv. Photo: Yevgeniy Novikov / ALMA. The exhibition was organized by the Almaty museum with the support of Halyk Bank and in collaboration with Bill Viola Studio, led by the artist’s wife and long-time collaborator, Kira Perov, who also served as curator of the project. It brings together 18 works, ranging from large-scale immersive installations to more contained video pieces, created by the artist over 36 years (from 1977 to 2013). They are displayed in the impressive Uly Dala hall, with its 12-meter ceilings. Tristan’s Ascension (2005). Over 40 days, the combined technical teams of ALMA and Bill Viola Studio transformed more than 1,000 square meters into a mystical, dimly lit labyrinth. It consists of installation rooms and corridors, which exhibition coordinator Dayana Vafina describes as liminal, or transitional, spaces. They are designed to slow visitors down, giving them time to reflect on what they have seen as they move through the exhibition. “Each work demands attention and an open mind. You cannot rush from one to the next. The exhibition leads you through this space of time, unfolding gradually,” says Vafina. Photo: Sabina Amangeldina / ALMA. The installation process, she notes, was highly complex. The works require a wide range of equipment, from CRT monitors to projection panels and LCD screens. Certain sculptural elements, including Heaven and Earth (1992) and Incrementation (1996), were fabricated and installed by specialists from 235 media , a leading German studio in exhibition design and media technology. The variety of technical approaches makes it possible to trace how media technology evolved over nearly four decades and how the way we experience images changed along with it. Viola’s video installations grew increasingly ambitious in scale, while the screen itself ceased to be a flat surface, acquiring an almost tangible depth that pulls the viewer in. Heaven and Earth (1992). Photo: Sabina Amangeldina / ALMA. Photo: Sabina Amangeldina / ALMA. Sound plays an equally important role. Many of the works have their own voice within the labyrinth: the sound of water, nature, whispers, the noise of a city. Together, they become part of the exhibition’s architecture, filling a space that feels liminal, dreamlike, and charged with life. Photo: Sabina Amangeldina / ALMA. One distinctive feature of Bill Viola’s exhibitions, including this retrospective, is the absence of explanatory texts beside the works . This is a deliberate choice of an artist and his studio. Viola, who spent much of his life studying and reflecting on religions, spiritual practices, and rituals from around the world, believed that description alone cannot lead to understanding. It only sets boundaries. What mattered to him was speaking through sensation, allowing viewers to experience what he experienced while making the work. For Viola, experience is a form of knowledge. He shares his discoveries and leaves viewers free to make their own. The only thing that matters is whether the encounter has transformed them, whether it has turned them inward and offered a new way of seeing the world. The Raft (2004). Photo: Sabina Amangeldina / ALMA. The themes Viola addresses through his work are fundamental: life and death, rebirth, self-awareness, the nature of time, and human emotion. He is unflinchingly honest. Rather than replacing genuine experience with spectacle, everything shown on screen actually happened. To create the powerful video installation Fire Woman (2005), a pool was built inside an aircraft hangar, into which a lone woman falls, arms outstretched, alongside a real wall of fire. Fire Woman (2005). In his earlier works, Viola frequently filmed himself, his newborn son, and his aging mother. One of the most powerful installations in the exhibition is Incrementation (1996), in essence, a self-portrait. A monitor mounted on the wall displays a black-and-white image of the artist, while a red LED counter beside it registers each of his breaths. By the day before the exhibition opened, the count had passed four million. Viola calculated that a person takes approximately 900 million breaths over 85 years of life. He did not live to that age — he died at 73. But his digital self continues to breathe. Incrementation (1996). Photo: Yevgeniy Novikov / ALMA. In his search for meaning in the fundamental themes of human existence, Viola frequently turned to art history. Works inspired by the old masters allowed him to continue the traditions of classical painting. One of them he identified as time, calling it “the great hidden tradition.” “Art historians often miss this: time and the unfolding of consciousness. The movement of consciousness is the real subject of many old master paintings. Although they contain an eternal moment of still image, a static object, they are all really about movement. (...) When I look at this as a video artist, my respect for the old masters only increases. In the form they practiced it, painting had something in common with Zen. Imagine someone comes to you and says: ‘You have only one frame to depict the flow of time. Which one do you choose?' I have 54,000 frames in a 30-minute video; they had one. And whose way of understanding time is better?” Viola told curator John G. Hanhardt in an interview published in the exhibition catalogue. The Water Po

body: Photo: Mirolim Isajonov / Gazeta Inside “Rise of the Conqueror (Amir Timur)”: How movie was made The crew of the film “Rise of the Conqueror (Amir Timur)” shared details about the project. “We are proud to finally be telling the story of our ancestors ourselves, through our own perspective and in our own voice,” executive producer and co-screenwriter Behruz Hamzayev said. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 18 April 2026, 10:40 Culture The “Rise of the Conqueror (Amir Timur)” movie had its world premiere on 2 April, with releases across more than 120 countries and theatrical screenings in 30 of them. The film follows a young Amir Timur (ruler, founder of Timurid dynasty, also known as Tamerlane) as he pursues power in the aftermath of a grave injury and profound personal loss. It is set in the mid-14th century, during a period of political fragmentation along the Silk Road that followed the collapse of the Mongol Empire. The production was a collaboration between international companies Mystery Box, 7SABER, and BWG Production. Executive producer and co-screenwriter Behruz Hamzayev said distribution rights had been sold to more than 120 countries, with the film’s potential audience estimated at over 250 million viewers. Advertising on Gazeta “For many people, it has been a source of deep pain to have their history narrated by outsiders,” Hamzayev said. “We are proud to finally be telling the story of our ancestors ourselves, through our own perspective and in our own voice.” A scene from the movie. Director Jacob Schwartz said the production crew worked closely with Uzbek historians and cultural consultants from start to finish, with the screenplay drawing on primary historical sources, including the “Institutes of Timur”. “I think we did our best to try to make the film as historically accurate as possible,” he said. “Obviously, we are trying to tell a very unique story, and we had to try to figure out a way to structure it. Whether it was historically accurate — that is for audiences to decide.” Filming took place across Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. One of the production’s defining commitments was to shoot entirely on location, forgoing studio sets and CGI altogether. Around 530 people worked on set each day, rising to 800 during battle sequences A scene from the movie. The most demanding of those sequences — and Schwartz’s greatest challenge as a director — was the “Battle in the Mud,” the only engagement in Timur’s military career that ended in defeat. The battle pitted Timur and his ally Emir Husayn against the Moghulistan khan Ilyas-Khoja, and the production spared little effort in recreating it. With an insufficient number of trained horses available in Uzbekistan, the entire sequence was relocated to Kazakhstan. Filming lasted four days, with the fire service of the Almaty region brought in to help simulate rainfall — tens of tonnes of water were used each day to achieve the effect. A scene from the movie. The leading role was taken by Danish actor Christian Mortensen, who also served as a producer on the project. Mortensen and director Jacob Schwartz have collaborated for two decades, and the film represented the fulfillment of a long-held ambition for both. “We have dreamed of telling different stories, whether it is George Washington in the United States, one of our revolutionary heroes, or your revolutionary hero, Amir Timur. And the goal was always to humanize these people who seem larger than life. But what I found over the time of filming in Khiva, in Toprakala, in Almaty, I did not find the legend. I found the man. And then I found a reason why the man was willing to sacrifice so much. And the reason are you, the people and the culture of Central Asia,” Mortensen said. Christian Mortensen. The role of Emir Husayn was brought to life by Mahesh Jadu, known to international audiences through the series “The Witcher and Marco Polo”. Asked whether historical drama demanded a different approach from fantasy, he questioned the premise. “When you play any character, you have to look for the truth of who you’re playing and what the performance is all about. So sometimes when you’re playing a character that is from a real story, you have to find the magic in it, and then when you’re playing a character that is about fantasy and magic, you have to find the truth in it. So for me, it’s sometimes two sides of the same coin,” actor shared. Mahesh Jadu. Joshua Jo, who portrayed the antagonist Ilyas-Khoja, drew on his background in voice acting to develop a distinct vocal quality for the character. The scene that left the deepest impression on him was a tense chess match with Mortensen’s character. To ensure the sequence appeared convincing on screen, both actors spent two weeks studying the game before filming began. Joshua Jo. Jo also reflected with evident warmth on his time in Uzbekistan. Early in the production, 65-year-old Uzbek actor Maruf Atadjanov cooked plov for the entire crew of thirty people. When Jo addressed him as “sir” the following morning, Atadjanov declined the formality. “There is no need for that,” he said. “Call me dada” — the word for father. Jo said it was the most generous gesture he had received from a senior colleague in his professional career. title: Inside “Rise of the Conqueror (Amir Timur)”: How movie was made

body: Photo: Art and Culture Development Foundation Who will perform at 10th International Jazz Festival in Tashkent The 10th International Jazz Festival will be held at the open-air venue of the Palace of International Forums Uzbekistan in Tashkent from 28 April to 12 May. The lineup includes performances by Leonid Agutin and Therr Maitz, Stanley Clarke, Kurt Elling and Jazzirama. Admission is free. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 15 April 2026, 12:23 Culture The 10th International Jazz Festival will be held in Tashkent from 28 April to 12 May, the press service of Art and Culture Development Foundation of Uzbekistan announced . The events will take place at the open-air venue of the Palace of International Forums Uzbekistan. Admission to all concerts is free. The festival is set to feature performances by Leonid Agutin and Therr Maitz, Stanley Clarke, Kurt Elling, as well as other international and local artists. “Jazz has united people around the world for decades and remains an important part of cultural exchange and mutual understanding. UNESCO views jazz as a powerful tool for promoting peace, dialogue and mutual respect between cultures,” the foundation noted. Festival program 28 April , 19:30 — Stanley Clarke; Advertising on Gazeta 29 April , 19:30 — Myles Sanko; 30 April , 19:30 — Fonograf. 1 May , 19:30 — Leonid Agutin & Therr Maitz. 2 May 19:00 — East Band & Skyband (Uspensky Music School); 19:30 — Anush Band; 3 May, 19:30 — Gunhild Carling; 4 May, 19:30 — Incognito. 5 May 19:00 — Jazapella (Embassy of Romania); 20:00 — Kurt Elling Quartet. 6 May , 19:30 — Tigran Hamasyan. 7 May , 19:30 — GoGo Penguin. 8 May 19:00 — Jazzkent; 19:30 — Sound Travel Jazz Quartet. 9 May, 19:30 — Sylvain Gontard (Yamaha Artist) with the National Symphony Orchestra of Uzbekistan (conductor — Alibek Kabdurakhmanov). 10 May, 19:30 — Ayo Trio (Embassy of Israel). 11 May, 19:30 — Big Band of the Batyr Zakirov National Institute of Pop Arts (conductors — Mominjon Olimov, Igor Budyukov). 12 May, 19:30 — Jazzirama and leading soloists of Uzbekistan. body: Photo: CCA Center for Contemporary Arts Tashkent to open after historic renovation The Center for Contemporary Arts Tashkent will open this March. It will become the country’s first permanent space for contemporary art and research. Housed in a renovated industrial building dating back to 1912, the venue was redesigned by French architects. Admission to the center will be free. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 19 January 2026, 11:10 Culture The Center for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA) will officially open on 21 March. The institution is housed in a former industrial building constructed in 1912, which once served as Tashkent’s first diesel power station prior to the revolution. Founded in 2019, the CCA operated on a trial basis before closing for renovation in 2021, with completion initially planned for 2023. The concept of the renewed space was presented as a scale model by the French architectural firm Studio KO at Art Basel Paris in October 2025. Advertising on Gazeta According to Uzbekistan’s Art and Culture Development Foundation, the CCA will become the country’s first permanently operating center dedicated to contemporary art, research and public engagement. It is also expected to serve as a platform for artistic residencies, internships, and educational initiatives. The CCA will run a year-round program led by artistic director and chief curator Dr Sara Raza, focusing on supporting Uzbek art, hosting international exhibitions in Tashkent, and promoting local artists on the global stage. “When we first envisioned the center, it was important to me that the space be open to everyone and serve as a place for inspiration, dialogue, and opportunity, as well as a meeting point for the city’s community,” said Gayane Umerova, chairperson of Uzbekistan’s Art and Culture Development Foundation. The building will house a library, workshops, and a café. Admission will be free. Program at the CCA 21 March — 30 June | Hikmah . Curator: Dr Sara Raza The exhibition’s title translates from Uzbek as “ wisdom .” Hikmah will be the first exhibition in the newly opened space, presenting works created in dialogue with the building and its architecture. The exhibition will feature new works by Muhannad Shono (Saudi Arabia), Nari Ward (USA), Shohrukh Rakhimov (Uzbekistan), and Tarik Kiswanson (Sweden/France). It will also include a work by Nadia Kaabi-Linke (Tunisia) from the Guggenheim Museum collection, works by Kimsooja (South Korea) and Ali Cherri (USA), as well as pieces from the I. V. Savitsky State Museum of Art by Vladimir Pan, Daribay Saipov, and Bakhtiyar Saipov. May — November — Vyacheslav Akhunov: Instruments of the Mind . Curator: Dr Sara Raza. Venue: Palazzo Franchetti, Venice The CCA will present an exhibition by Vyacheslav Akhunov, one of the leading figures of Uzbek modernism, as part of the parallel program of the 61st International Art Exhibition of the Venice Biennale. September — Kabakov: The Centre for Cosmic Energy. Guest curator: Zelfira Tregulova This site-specific solo exhibition will transform the center into a “living laboratory of art and speculative parafictions”. Public events and educational programs 21−23 March — Navruz Gala and Festival The festival will feature performances, live music, gastronomic events, film screenings, poetry, and storytelling. “The program draws on numerology, cosmology, and symbolic systems characteristic of the cultures of Central and West Asia, as well as other regions,” the foundation noted. April — Architectural Association Visiting School Uzbekistan (First Cohort) In partnership with the Architectural Association in London, the CCA will launch a three-year Visiting School program (2026−2028), bringing together architecture and urban studies students, young architects, researchers, artists, and curators. The collaboration aims to advance research into traditional architectural thinking in Uzbekistan while supporting the next generation of Uzbek architects. The program will result in a shared body of research, annual exhibitions and public programs. 21 June — 9 August — Tashkent Summer Days Tashkent Summer Days is a seven-week arts festival organized in collaboration with Invisible Island Studio, founded in 2023 by Tashkent-based photographer Hassan Kubanbaev and creative producer Misha Kuzhel. The festival will span all districts of Tashkent and several makhallas, drawing inspiration from historic urban celebrations and film programs of the past. December — Tashkent Film Encounters Film festival aims at reviving the legacy of the Tashkent International Film Festival (1968−1988), once regarded as one of the world’s key platforms for global cinema. title: Center for Contemporary Arts Tashkent to open after historic renovation

body: Photo: Yevgeny Sorochin / Gazeta Exploring the universal landscape: Ural Tansykbayev on display in Tashkent The exhibition marking 120th anniversary of Ural Tansykbayev opened at the NBU Gallery, bringing together 124 paintings and graphics. As Gazeta’s reviewer Dmitry Povarov observes, Tansykbayev continues to stand out as an artist who bridges the local and the universal dimensions of art. На русском языке 14 November 2025, 11:47 Culture The exhibition “Ural Tansykbayev. To the 120th Anniversary of His Birth” opened in September at the Art Gallery of Uzbekistan (NBU). It continues the retrospective project first presented at the Abylkhan Kasteyev State Museum of Art in Almaty, Kazakhstan from March to June. The ambitious scope of the project, organized by the Art and Culture Development Foundation of Uzbekistan, is evident right from the start. A panel listing all participants welcomes visitors at the entrance. Chaired by Saida Mirziyoyeva, aead of Administration of the President of Uzbekistan, the committee underscores that this is no ordinary museum retrospective. Instead, the exhibition positions Tansykbayev as a cultural symbol of national stature, embedded within the broader narrative of world art. The exhibition features works from the collections of four museums: The State Art Museum of Karakalpakstan named after Igor Savitsky, the State Museum of Arts of Uzbekistan, the House-Museum of Ural Tansykbayev, and the A. Kasteev State Museum of Arts of Kazakhstan. According to organizers, a significant number of the paintings are being shown to the public for the first time. Advertising on Gazeta “Tansykbayev embodies a truth I have always believed in — that a true artist, even in the most challenging situations, finds a way to pursue what he believes he is meant to do,” curator Zelfira Tregulova, former director of the Tretyakov Gallery, told journalists. Zelfira Tregulova. Photo: Yevgeny Sorochin / Gazeta. This statement reveals the essence of the artist’s creative journey from his early academic experiments to the pursuit of a personal visual system and rhythm. In 1928, Tansykbayev first saw in Moscow the paintings of Cézanne, Matisse, and Gauguin. The experience made such a lasting impression that it can already be noticed in his early works. The Uzbek Girl (1928) and Portrait of an Uzbek (1934) maintain the figure as the conceptual center, while color evolves from a mere supporting role into an independent expressive medium. From the mid-1930s onward, the figure in Tansykbayev’s paintings began to dissolve into the surrounding space. Works such as Crimson Autumn (1931) and The Road (1935) mark the moment when the landscape no longer functions as a simple background but transforms into a stage where lines and colors play the leading roles. The World War II marked a profound turning point in Tansykbaev’s career. In 1942, he was sent to the front as part of a delegation from Uzbekistan. His series of wartime works reveals the artist’s shift toward a complex tonal painting, where subtle shades of gray, brown, and muted green replace the bold palette of earlier works. In these canvases, art becomes a means to convey the war, transforming catastrophe into a language of form and light. In the postwar years, this experience became integrated into a new vision. By the 1950s, he had returned to landscape painting, now with a different focus on intricate details and the expressive power of color. At the Mines of Soviet Uzbekistan (1960) demonstrates how an industrial subject can be read not only as a documentary account but also as a philosophical commentary on the encounter between humanity and nature. “In my opinion, Tansykbayev stands out as the most compelling voice of the Thaw-era landscape,” Tregulova notes. Indeed, it is in this genre that he reaches true philosophical depth. His paintings are not solely depictions of ethnographic color; they explore rhythm and vibration and capture the timeless essence of the natural world. “This is an example of how an artist can be intensely engaged in seeking his own path, reflecting the spirit of his time, and yet remaining utterly honest,” Tregulova explained to Gazeta , responding to a question about the exhibition’s relevance for contemporary audiences. In today’s context, as landscape painting once more becomes a space to explore ecological and human interventions, Tansykbayev’s works — though he passed away in 1974 — remain remarkably relevant. More importantly, he captures not the fleeting moment, but the eternal. It is this vision of Central Asia that transcends regional boundaries to become a universal language of painting. And it is what makes this meticulously organized anniversary exhibition an event of international scale. The exhibition at the NBU Gallery is about more than just color’s aesthetic appeal. It also serves as a reminder that painting in the mid-20th century did not need to strike a pose, issue declarations, or chase trends. Perhaps this is why Tansykbayev’s canvases remain strikingly alive today, like letters discovered by accident, offering unexpected insights into oneself. Visitors can experience this journey u ntil November 20 , with the gallery open from 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM daily. Originally in Russian; translated and edited for clarity. body: Javokhir Sindarov. Photo: Lennart Ootes / Grand Chess Tour Javokhir Sindarov finishes third at Sinquefield Cup in USA Javokhir Sindarov finished third at the Sinquefield Cup after a strong finish to the tournament. After failing to win any of his first six games, he won two in a row and entered the final round with a chance to win. He scored 5 points out of 9, missing the Grand Chess Tour final by 0.5 points. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 20 August 2026, 16:49 Sport Uzbekistan’s grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov finished third at the 2026 Sinquefield Cup in St. Louis, Missouri, USA, scoring 5 points out of 9. From second-round loss to fight for first place The Sinquefield Cup was held as a round-robin tournament featuring 10 grandmasters. The prize fund was $475,000. The tournament was the fifth and final stage of the Grand Chess Tour, a prestigious international series, with the top four players in the overall standings qualified for the final. Sindarov fell just 0.5 points short of qualifying. Sindarov began the tournament with a draw against Levon Aronian. He gained an advantage in an opposite-colored bishop endgame, but was unable to convert it. According to Chess.com, Sindarov considered the position with two extra pawns to be winning and was surprised by the chess engine’s evaluation. Advertising on Gazeta In the second round, he suffered his only defeat of the tournament, losing to Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa. The Indian grandmaster won a pawn endgame after 95 moves. After the game, Praggnanandhaa described their games as uncompromising, noting that they “almost never draw” because both players try to fight until the very end. Photo: Lennart Ootes / Grand Chess Tour Sindarov’s next four games ended in draws against Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Anish Giri, Sam Sevian and Fabiano Caruana. In his fifth-round game against Sevian, Sindarov attempted to test the American’s opening preparation, but Sevian handled it confidently. “I'm not happy with my play. Probably, today wasn’t the best choice of opening,” Sindarov said after the game. One of the key encounters in the sixth round was Sindarov’s game against Caruana, the world No. 2. The American gained a dangerous passed pawn, but Sindarov carefully exchanged queens and secured a draw. After six rounds, Sindarov had 2.5 points — five draws, one loss and no wins. Two consecutive victories The turning point came in the seventh round. Sindarov needed to beat German grandmaster Vincent Keymer with Black to keep his hopes of reaching the Grand Chess Tour final alive. He chose the Benko Gambit. “If I lose, I will learn something, but maybe if I win I will get some chances,” Sindarov said, explaining his choice of the risky opening. At one point, Keymer gained the advantage, but the German eventually entered a bishop endgame with opposite-colored bishops. The position was objectively defensible, but Keymer made a mistake under time pressure. Sindarov secured his first win of the tournament, moving to 3.5 points. Photo: Lennart Ootes/Grand Chess Tour In the eighth round, Sindarov defeated Jorden van Foreest to claim his second consecutive victory. On the sixth move, he sacrificed a pawn, gained positional compensation and eventually converted his advantage. “When everyone is tired, I show my level!” Sindarov joked after the game. In just two rounds, he climbed from the lower half of the standings into the group of contenders for the title. As Chess.com noted, just three days earlier Sindarov had been third from last, while before the final round he still had theoretical chances of winning the entire Sinquefield Cup. To do so, he needed to beat Wesley So with Black. “I think Wesley will ‘kill' the game, but we’ll see. If I were in his position, I would do the same,” Sindarov said ahead of the decisive game. Photo: Lennart Ootes/Grand Chess Tour Half point short of tiebreak In the final round, Sindarov employed the King’s Indian Defense against So. However, on move 11 he played the d5 break and opted for simplification instead of continuing the fight from a slightly worse position. The game ended in a draw. So and Praggnanandhaa remained tied at 5.5 points after the classical portion. The winner was decided in a tiebreak: the two rapid games ended in draws, while a draw in the Armageddon gave the title to So, who had the black pieces. So received $87,500. Across his nine classical games, Sindarov recorded two wins, six draws and one loss, scoring 5 points. The Sinquefield Cup was particularly important for qualification for the Grand Chess Tour final. Before the tournament, Sindarov was fifth in the overall standings with 20.5 points, just half a point behind Keymer. Earlier in St. Louis, Sindarov had finished second at the Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz, behind only Praggnanandhaa. Following the Sinquefield Cup, Praggnanandhaa, So, Caruana and Keymer qualified for the Grand Chess Tour final. Sindarov fell 0.5 points short of the top four. This year, 20-year-old Sindarov has already achieved the biggest achievement of his career. In April, he won the FIDE Candidates Tournament, earning the right to challenge reigning world champion for the world title.Gukesh Dommaraju In September, Sindarov will also compete in the fourth season of the Global Chess League, a team league created by FIDE and Tech Mahindra. The tournament will take place in Bengaluru from 3 to 13 September. Six teams of six players will compete, with matches played in rapid format across six boards. Sindarov will play on first board for FYERS American Gambits. Subscribe to our Telegram channel Gazeta 4 790 # chess # grand chess tour # javokhir sindarov # sinquefield cup
title: Javokhir Sindarov finishes third at Sinquefield Cup in USA

body: Photo: Мадина Аъзам / Gazeta Uzbekistan’s first world boxing champion Rufat Riskiyev dies at 76 Uzbekistan’s first world boxing champion and 1976 Olympic silver medalist Rufat Riskiyev, known as the “Tashkent Tiger”, has died at the age of 76. He was seriously ill in recent years, the Boxing Federation said. На русском языке Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida 15 August 2026, 12:04 Sport Uzbekistan’s first world boxing champion and 1976 Olympic silver medalist Rufat Riskiyev has died at the age of 76 after being seriously ill in recent years, the Boxing Federation said . Riskiyev was born in Oqqorgon in 1949 into a family of a doctor. He began boxing at the age of 12 under the guidance of renowned coach Sidney Jackson. At 14, he joined the Tashkent sports society Burevestnik. From 1966, he trained under another prominent coach Boris Granatkin. Riskiyev made history in 1974 as the first boxer from Uzbekistan to win a world championship. At the inaugural World Amateur Boxing Championships in Havana, he won gold in the 75 kg category while representing the Soviet Union. The International Boxing Association (IBA) later referred to him as the “Tashkent Tiger”. Two years later, Riskiyev won a silver medal at the 1976 Olympic Games in Montreal. He was the only Soviet boxer to reach the final, where he faced American boxer Michael Spinks. Riskiyev also won the Soviet championship four times, in 1972 and from 1974 to 1976. In 1974, he was awarded the title of Honored Master of Sport of the USSR. According to the IBA, he fought 189 bouts and won 174. Advertising on Gazeta After ending his boxing career, Riskiyev appeared in several films and later worked as a boxing referee. In 1997, he joined the refereeing section of the World Boxing Association (WBA) and became the first internationally certified professional boxing referee in Central Asia. In 2020, Riskiyev was awarded the Dostlik (Friendship) order of Uzbekistan. Since 2019, an award bearing his name has been presented to the best boxer at the Uzbekistan Boxing Championships. In 2016, he underwent surgery that resulted in the amputation of part of his right leg. Subscribe to our Telegram channel Gazeta 4 624 # boxing # rufat riskiyev

body: Photo: Lennart Ootes / Grand Chess Tour Javokhir Sindarov moves closer to Grand Chess Tour Final after finishing second in St. Louis Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov finished second at the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz, placing runner-up in both the rapid and blitz events. He earned 22 points and moved up to fifth in the Grand Chess Tour standings, just 0.5 points outside the qualification spots for the Grand Chess Tour Final. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 9 August 2026, 09:06 Sport Uzbekistan’s grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov finished runner-up at the Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz, the fourth event of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour, after placing second in both the rapid and blitz events to score 22 points overall. The tournament was held from 2−6 August and consisted of nine rapid games and 18 blitz games. Rapid games awarded 2 points for a win and 1 for a draw, while blitz followed the traditional scoring system of 1 point for a win and 0.5 point for a draw. The event featured a $200,000 prize fund. Runner-Up in both rapid and blitz Photo: Lennart Ootes/Grand Chess Tour. Advertising on Gazeta After nine rounds of rapid, Sindarov scored 11 points to finish second. India’s Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa led with 12 points, while American Wesley So was third with 10. Sindarov’s rapid performance rating was 2739, compared to his pre-tournament rapid rating of 2730. He entered the blitz portion just one point behind the leader. In the first nine blitz rounds, Sindarov scored 5.5/9, maintaining second place. His strongest stretch came between rounds four and six, when he defeated Fabiano Caruana, Awonder Liang and Leinier Domínguez in succession. One of the key games of the first day of blitz came against Praggnanandhaa. Sindarov won a pawn and, according to Chess.com, reached a winning position, but an inaccuracy in the pawn endgame allowed his opponent to escape with a draw. A victory would have reduced the gap to just half a point. “I saw I’m winning [with] any move,” Sindarov later explained after the game. After the first blitz round robin, Praggnanandhaa led the overall standings with 18 points, followed by Sindarov on 16.5 and So on 15. Photo: Lennart Ootes/Grand Chess Tour. On the second day of blitz, Sindarov again scored 5.5/9. After drawing with Aronian, he defeated Jorden van Foreest and Vincent Keymer in consecutive rounds. Although he later lost to Caruana, he bounced back by defeating Anish Giri. At one point, Sindarov closed the gap to the tournament leader to just half a point. The tournament’s decisive game came in the penultimate, 17th round, when Sindarov faced Praggnanandhaa. Despite being a pawn up, Sindarov was unable to convert the advantage, and the draw secured the Indian grandmaster’s tournament victory with one round to spare. Sindarov finished the event by drawing with So. In the final blitz standings, Praggnanandhaa scored 11.5 points, Sindarov 11, So 10.5 and Aronian 10. Sindarov recorded five wins, two losses and 11 draws in blitz. His performance rating of 2749 was the second-best of the tournament, behind only Praggnanandhaa’s 2771. He also gained nine rating points in blitz during the event. Overall standings Praggnanandhaa won the tournament with 23.5 points (12 in rapid and 11.5 in blitz). Sindarov finished second on 22 points (11+11), while So placed third with 20.5. Levon Aronian finished fourth with 19 points. They were followed by Domínguez, Caruana and van Foreest, all on 17 points. Giri scored 15.5, Keymer 14.5 and Liang 14. Praggnanandhaa earned the $50,000 winner’s prize, while Sindarov received $40,000, So $30,000 and Aronian $20,000. This marked Praggnanandhaa’s second Grand Chess Tour event victory, having previously won in Bucharest in May 2025. After the tournament, the Indian grandmaster praised Sindarov’s resilience. “When you see the score... everything looks smooth, but it wasn’t the case. It was crazy. I mean, kudos to Javokhir, he kept the fight to the end.” Sindarov, meanwhile, said he had learned from his loss to Caruana and was generally satisfied with his performance. “Sometimes, playing really well is not enough. You need to be lucky.” Half a step away from the Grand Chess Tour Final The result in St. Louis significantly strengthened Sindarov’s chances of qualifying for the Grand Chess Tour Final. His runner-up finish earned him 10 tour points, lifting him to fifth place in the overall Grand Chess Tour standings with 20.5 points after four events. Caruana leads the standings with 25 points, followed by Praggnanandhaa on 24.5 and So on 23.5. Keymer currently occupies the fourth and final qualifying spot with 21 points. Sindarov now sits just 0.5 points outside the qualification places. One last chance Grand Chess Tour points are awarded as follows: 13 points for first place, 10 for second, 8 for third, followed by 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 for the remaining places. If players tie for a position, the corresponding points are combined and shared equally. The top four players in the overall standings will qualify for the Grand Chess Tour Final. The first-placed player will face the fourth-placed player, while the second-placed player will meet the third-placed player. The decisive event will be the Sinquefield Cup, held in St. Louis from 10−20 August. The classical tournament will serve as the fifth and final event of the Grand Chess Tour season. To qualify for the final in his debut Grand Chess Tour season, Sindarov must finish ahead of Keymer in the overall standings. The Grand Chess Tour Final is scheduled for 22−27 August in St. Louis and will feature a $450,000 prize fund, including $200,000 for the champion. title: Javokhir Sindarov moves closer to Grand Chess Tour Final after finishing second in St. Louis

body: Behruz Karimov against Colombia at the World Cup. Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta Uzbekistan defender Behruz Karimov joins Swiss club Lugano Uzbekistan national team defender Behruz Karimov (19) joined Swiss club Lugano. At the 2026 FIFA World Cup, one of Asia’s most promising young footballers started in Uzbekistan’s matches against Colombia and Portugal. На русском языке Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida 9 August 2026, 09:04 Sport The 19-year-old Uzbekistan defender Behruz Karimov signed a contract with Swiss club Lugano, the Uzbekistan Football Association said . Karimov, born on 7 August 2007, began his football career at the Odil Junior academy before joining Tashkent-based Olympic. In February 2025, he moved to Termez-based Surkhon. The right-back quickly established himself in the Uzbekistan league and earned a call-up to the national team. At the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Karimov started in Uzbekistan’s matches against Colombia and Portugal. Karimov is also considered one of Asia’s most promising young footballers. According to the CIES Football Observatory, which assessed the performances of players under 19 over the past season against their peers in the same position, Karimov ranked second among Asian players. Founded in 1908, Lugano is one of Switzerland’s oldest football clubs. The team has won the Swiss Super League three times and the Swiss Cup four times. Advertising on Gazeta Lugano finished third in the 2025/26 Swiss Super League, recording 19 wins, 10 draws and nine defeats in 38 matches to collect 67 points. The result earned Lugano a place in the UEFA Conference League qualifying rounds. Earlier, another Uzbekistan national team defender, 22-year-old Jakhongir Urozov, joined Russian club Rubin Kazan. His former club Dinamo Samarkand said he had joined the Kazan side on loan until the end of 2026, with an option to buy. Urozov’s contract with Dinamo runs until the end of 2027. Urozov joined Dinamo in 2024 and made 55 official appearances over three seasons, scoring one goal. His performances for the club earned him a call-up to the Uzbekistan national team. At the 2026 FIFA World Cup, he featured in matches against Colombia and DR Congo. body: Javokhir Sindarov. Photo: Lennart Ootes / Grand Chess Tour Javokhir Sindarov finishes second in St. Louis rapid event, remains unbeaten Uzbekistan’s grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov finished second in the rapid section of the St. Louis Rapid & Blitz, scoring 11 points from a possible 18. He remained unbeaten in all nine rounds and trails leader Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa of India by one point ahead of the blitz. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 6 August 2026, 10:57 Sport Uzbekistan’s grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov finished second in the rapid section of the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz , the final rapid and blitz event of the elite Grand Chess Tour series. After nine rounds, Sindarov scored 11 points, one point behind tournament leader Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa of India. American grandmaster Wesley So placed third with 10 points. In the rapid section, a win was worth two points and a draw one point. Sindarov recorded two wins and seven draws, remaining unbeaten in all nine games. Day 1: Victory over Van Foreest Three rounds were played on the opening day. Sindarov began with a draw against Anish Giri. He had promising winning chances in the first game, but his advantage disappeared in a heavy-piece endgame. Advertising on Gazeta He then drew with Vincent Keymer. At one point, Sindarov found himself in serious trouble but managed to save the position under severe time pressure. His first victory came in Round 3 against Jorden van Foreest, where he converted an endgame featuring opposite-colored bishops and rooks. After the first day, Sindarov had 4 points out of 6, sharing second place with Wesley So, one point behind Praggnanandhaa. “In general I’m happy I finished +1 because the second game [against Keymer] was tricky. At some moment I’m just losing, but in time trouble I managed to survive the position,” Sindarov said. Photo: Lennart Ootes/Grand Chess Tour Day 2: Three hard-fought draws On the second day, Sindarov faced Praggnanandhaa, Levon Aronian and Fabiano Caruana. In Round 4, Praggnanandhaa trapped Sindarov’s bishop in the opening and gained an extra piece. However, Sindarov created complications and managed to save what appeared to be a lost position. Against Aronian in Round 5, Sindarov enjoyed a significant advantage and came close to victory. The position later swung in Aronian’s favor before the game ended in a draw by repetition. After the game, Sindarov showed Aronian the winning line he had missed. “You have to forget about it after the game, but it’s not easy,” Sindarov said about the missed opportunity. In Round 6, he defended an inferior position against Caruana. After sacrificing the exchange, Sindarov found several precise defensive moves to prevent the American from converting his advantage. After six rounds, Sindarov had 7 points, sitting in second place, two points behind Praggnanandhaa. Photo: Lennart Ootes/Grand Chess Tour Day 3: Victory over Liang secures second place Sindarov opened the final day of the rapid event with another draw against Giri. In Round 8, he defeated American grandmaster Awonder Liang by steadily putting pressure on his opponent’s isolated pawns. After 24...g6, Black was left with four isolated pawns, weaknesses that Sindarov eventually converted into a win. He finished the rapid section with a draw against Keymer in the final round, completing the tournament undefeated. Although Praggnanandhaa lost to Van Foreest in Round 9, he retained first place with 12 points. Sindarov finished second with 11, while Wesley So took third with 10. “I think the US is better than Warsaw, but tomorrow is a tough day. We’ll see, hopefully I’ll try to get more points,” Sindarov said. 18 blitz games remain The tournament now enters the blitz section, where players will compete in a double round-robin of 18 games. Unlike the rapid event, each win is worth one point, while a draw earns half a point. The first nine blitz rounds are scheduled to begin on 5 August at 22:10 Tashkent time, with Sindarov facing Aronian in the opening round. The tournament runs from 2−6 August and features 10 grandmasters competing for a $200,000 prize fund, with $50,000 awarded to the overall winner. body: Photo: Gazeta Kyrgyzstan proposes unified visa for Central Asian countries Following a border agreement with Tajikistan, president of Kyrgyzstan proposed a visa-free regime among Central Asian countries and a unified regional visa for foreigners. The Silk Road visa project is being discussed in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan since 2018 but has yet to be implemented. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 16 March 2025, 13:23 World President of Kyrgyzstan Sadyr Japarov proposed that Central Asian countries establish a visa-free regime among themselves and introduce a unified visa for foreign nationals, similar to the Schengen visa. “Central Asian countries should begin the process of implementing a visa-free regime with each other and introduce a single visa for foreign visitors, allowing them to travel freely across the region, similar to the Schengen visa,” Japarov wrote on his Facebook page on 13 March following the signing of a state border agreement with president of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon. The idea of a Silk Road Visa was first introduced in 2018 when Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan signed agreements on mutual recognition of visa regimes for Silk Road countries. At the time, Uzbekistan noted that Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan were interested in the joint visa, while Turkmenistan was still considering its prospects. Kazakhstan also proposed including Azerbaijan and Turkey in the project. Advertising on Gazeta In 2020, reports suggested that the agreement was close to completion, but the COVID-19 pandemic delayed progress, and some unresolved issues remained for participating countries to negotiate. By 2022, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan were still discussing the Asian Schengen project, working on regulations defining the visa’s status and the legal framework required for implementation. Japarov also highlighted that resolving the long-standing border issue between Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, which remained unsettled for 101 years since 1924, was a significant milestone for the entire Central Asian region. “Now we can say that all countries in the region have finally resolved their border disputes. From this moment, eternal peace was established in Central Asia,” he emphasized. The signed border agreement is set to be presented for ratification in Jogorku Kenesh (Kyrgyzstan's parliament) on 19 March. “It is undoubtedly difficult for our citizens to leave the transferred lands, as this is their homeland, the resting place of their ancestors. The same feelings are shared by Tajik villagers whose settlements became part of Kyrgyzstan. It is a painful process for both sides. However, when resolving state border issues, the interests of individual villages cannot take precedence — the interests of the entire state must come first,” Japarov stated. He also explained that aside from Dostuk village, several houses situated in a checkerboard pattern along the border were also relocated to ensure a straight demarcation line, which is essential for efficient border control in the future. “Over the past 30 years, border conflicts claimed the lives of thousands of citizens on both sides,” Japarov said, vowing that the government would support the resettled citizens. “We will provide them with modern homes offering significantly better living conditions,” he promised. body: Photo: sledcom.ru Citizen of Uzbekistan detained in Moscow on suspicion of killing Russian general Russia’s Investigative Committee announced the arrest of a citizen of Uzbekistan for a terrorist attack in Moscow that killed general Igor Kirillov and his assistant. Authorities claim the suspect confessed during interrogation to being “recruited by Ukrainian intelligence services”. На русском языке Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida 19 December 2024, 12:09 World The Investigative Committee of Russia (ICR) announced the arrest of a suspect in connection with a terrorist attack in Moscow that killed the head of the Russian Armed Forces' Radiation, Chemical and Biological Defense Troops Igor Kirillov and his assistant Ilya Polikarpov. According to the ICR, the suspect, born in 1995, is a citizen of Uzbekistan whose name has not been disclosed. However, Telegram channel Baza identified him as Ahmad Kurbanov. During interrogation, the suspect allegedly admitted to being “recruited by Ukrainian intelligence services”, the ICR stated. Advertising on Gazeta “Following their instructions, he arrived in Moscow and obtained a homemade explosive device. He placed it on an electric scooter parked near the entrance of the residential building where Igor Kirillov lived. To monitor the serviceman’s residence, he rented a car-sharing vehicle equipped with a surveillance camera. Footage from this camera was streamed live to the organizers of the attack in Dnipro. Once the servicemen were seen exiting the building, the explosive device was remotely detonated,” the Investigative Committee said. A video of the suspect’s interrogation has also surfaced on social media. The ICR alleges the suspect was promised $100,000 and relocation to a European country in exchange for carrying out the attack. The Russian Interior Ministry said the suspect was apprehended in the village of Chornoye, near the city of Balashikha in Moscow region. The embassy of Uzbekistan in Moscow said it had established contact with the Russian law-enforcement bodies and was clarifying the information about the detained. General Igor Kirillov and Ilya Polikarpov were killed in the explosion on 17 December while leaving their residence on Ryazansky Prospekt in Moscow. Investigators say the explosive device was concealed in the electric scooter near the building’s entrance. The ICR opened criminal cases on charges of murder, terrorism and the illegal circulation of explosives. Reuters and The New York Times , citing sources in Ukrainian intelligence, reported that the assassination of Kirillov was orchestrated by Security Service of Ukraine (SSU). A day before his death, the SSU accused Kirillov in absentia of being responsible for the mass use of chemical weapons against Ukrainian forces. body: Photo: Freedom House Freedom House: Democracy Score in Central Asia continues to decline Democratic performance in Central Europe and Central Asia continues to decline, with the war in Ukraine and other conflicts having hastened geopolitical shifts in the region, Freedom House reports. Uzbekistan’s democracy level is rated at 1.18 out of 7 points. O‘zbek tilida Ўзбек тилида На русском языке 16 April 2024, 20:53 World A persistent decline in democratic performance in Central Europe and Central Asia for the past 20 years was revealed in the annual report “Nations in Transit 2024” by Freedom House, the international human rights organization. The report covers 29 countries in the region. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh, and other events in recent years “have accelerated a geopolitical reordering in the region, with countries sorting themselves into two opposing blocs: those committed to a liberal, democratic order and those that violently reject it”, the report stated. Over the past year, 10 countries in the region suffered declines in Democracy Score, while just five earned improvements. Experts attribute the region’s “failure” in consolidating democracy to authoritarian and anti-democratic leaders. Freedom House classified Democracy Scores in Azerbaijan, Belarus, Russia and all Central Asian countries as “Consolidated Authoritarian Regimes” . Among the “Hybrid Regime” countries are Armenia, Georgia, Hungary, Moldova, Ukraine and others, totalling 11 states. Advertising on Gazeta The “Semi-Consolidated Democracies” category encompassed 10 countries, including Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland. Freedom House notes that all eight countries in the “Consolidated Authoritarian Regimes” category continued to “lead the race to the bottom” over the past year. Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, which “previously scored one the less repressive end of the authoritarian range, now fit the broader Central Asian trend of authoritarian consolidation,” according to the organization. Uzbekistan received a Democracy Score of 1.18 out of a possible 7 points in Freedom House’s assessment. Last year’s score was at 1.21 points. Kyrgyzstan’s Democracy Scores decreased to 1.64 points (from 1.68), while Kazakhstan’s dropped to 1.29 (from 1.32). Tajikistan and Turkmenistan received Scores of 1.04 points and 1 point respectively. Belarus scored 1.11, while Russia and Azerbaijan scored 1.07 points each. Among the highest scorers in the region, Estonia led with a score of 6, followed by Latvia and Slovenia, each with a score of 5.79. Ukraine’s democratic development was rated at 3.43, followed by Armenia at 3.07 and Georgia at 3.04. In March, Freedom House published its annual freedom rating, with Uzbekistan scoring 12 out of a possible 100 points. All Central Asian countries were classified as “not free”. body: Photo: Evgeny Sorochin / Gazeta.uz Uzbekistan ranks 106th in Human Development Index Uzbekistan has dropped one position to 106th out of 193 in the latest UN Human Development Index. The country remains categorized among those with high HDI. O‘zbek tilida Ўзбек тилида На русском языке 15 March 2024, 18:14 World Uzbekistan has been positioned as 106th out of 193 countries and territories worldwide in the latest Human Development Index (HDI) report prepared by the United Nations Development Program (UNDP). The data covers the year 2022, indicating a decline of one position compared to the previous year’s ranking. Countries were evaluated on three key indicators of human development — life expectancy at birth, mean years of schooling and gross national income per capita. Uzbekistan maintains an average life expectancy of 71.7 years, a duration of education of 12 years and a gross income per capita of $8,056. Advertising on Gazeta With an HDI score of 0.727 in 2022, Uzbekistan keeps its status in the high HDI category, positioned between Egypt and Vietnam. In the Central Asian region, Kazakhstan secured the 67th spot, Turkmenistan the 94th, Kyrgyzstan the 117th, and Tajikistan the 126th place in the rankings. The top-ranked country on the index was Switzerland, with a score of 0.967, followed by Norway and Iceland. Hong Kong and Denmark also secured positions in the top five. Inequality and the “paradox of democracy” The latest UNDP report on human development, titled “Breaking the gridlock: Reimagining cooperation in a polarized world”, forecasts that the HDI will reach record levels in 2023, following sharp declines in 2020 and 2021. “But this progress is deeply uneven. Rich countries are experiencing record-high levels of human development while half of the world’s poorest countries remain below their pre-crisis level of progress,” the report read. Head of UNDP Achim Steiner noted the currently reversed trend of steadily reducing inequalities between wealthy and poor nations. “Despite our deeply interconnected global societies, we are falling short. We must leverage our interdependence as well as our capacities to address our shared and existential challenges and ensure people’s aspirations are met,” he said. The report argues that advancing international collective action is hindered by an emerging “democracy paradox”. According to data analyzed in the report, while 9 in 10 people worldwide endorse democracy, over half of global survey respondents express support for leaders that may undermine it by bypassing fundamental rules of the democratic process. Half of people surveyed worldwide report having no or limited control over their lives, and over two-thirds believe they have little influence on their government’s decisions. Experts refer to political polarization as a growing concern with global repercussions. It is fuelling inward-turning policy approaches — starkly at odds with the global cooperation needed to address urgent issues like the decarbonization of our economies, misuse of digital technologies and conflict, according to the authors of the report. The report cites research indicating that countries with populist governments have lower GDP growth rates. Fifteen years after a populist government assumes office, the GDP per capita is found to be 10% lower than it might under a non-populist government scenario. body: Photo: Sergey Lantyukhov / news.ru Russia’s MIA suggests imposing new restrictions on illegal migrants Russia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs proposed to introduce a controlled stay regime for illegal migrants, along with a number of bans and restrictions. Those appearing in the register will not be able to drive, transfer money or get married. 28 November 2023, 17:37 World Russia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA) proposed to introduce a controlled stay regime for illegal migrants, which provides for a number of prohibitions and restrictions for them. TASS reported this news with reference to MIA’s draft law. “Controlled stay is a legal regime applied [...] to a foreign citizen staying in the Russian Federation and has no legal grounds for stay (residence) in the Russian Federation or who has knowingly provided false information or documents in the course of migrants' registration,” the agency quotes an excerpt from the document. According to the document, a foreign citizen is considered to be in the regime of a controlled stay from the date of entering personal information in the register. The grounds for this may be: expiration of the term of temporary stay, temporary residence permit, residence permit; illegal border crossing; annulment of visa, refugee status or temporary asylum, citizenship. Those under control are obliged to inform about their whereabouts, change of place of stay, date, place and route of planned independent departure from Russia. In case of violation, they can be deported. Advertising on Gazeta At the same time, foreigners will have the right to request the reasons justifying applicability of the controlled stay regime to them. They will also be able to appeal against the actions or omissions of officials. The bill sets consequential limitations on those to whom such a regime applies. These are: a ban on state registration of legal entities and individual entrepreneurs; a ban on the purchase and sale of real estate, vehicles and self-propelled machines; a ban on placing real estate on the country’s cadastral registration; a ban on state registration of vehicles; a ban on driving a car, a possible denial in taking licensure examinations and replacement of driving licenses. In addition, Russia’s MIA proposes to restrict illegal migrants from opening bank accounts, transferring money and marrying . According to MIA, innovations will help to identify illegal migrants and “remove” them from the territory of Russia. Now in Russia there are 6.4 million foreign citizens. Most of them arrived to the country for working purposes, the head of the main department of MIA on migration Valentina Kazakova has reported earlier. In 2022, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan were listed as the three leaders in terms of the inflow of migrant workers to Russia.
