body: Photo: UNDP Op-Ed. Environmental sustainability is not only about protecting nature Environmental sustainability is not only about protecting nature, UNDP Resident Representative Akiko Fujii writes in her op-ed. It depends on building strong institutions, resilient landscapes, ensuring green growth, empowering local communities and developing regional cooperation. На русском языке 31 May 2026, 16:21 Columns Society Author: Akiko Fujii, UNDP Resident Representative As Samarkand hosts the Eighth Assembly of the Global Environment Facility (GEF) alongside ECO EXPO Central Asia 2026, Uzbekistan is emerging not only as a venue for global environmental dialogue, but increasingly as a contributor to regional and global solutions. This moment reflects the growing recognition that the region can become a platform for innovation, resilience, and partnership at a time when climate change, biodiversity loss, land degradation, and pollution are reshaping economies and societies worldwide. Three decades of partnership For the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), this year’s GEF Assembly carries special significance. Since Uzbekistan joined the GEF partnership in 1995, the Government of Uzbekistan has been advancing the country’s commitments under the Rio Conventions on climate change, biodiversity and desertification, as well as the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants. For more than three decades, UNDP and the GEF have worked alongside the Government of Uzbekistan, National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, national institutions, academia, civil society organizations, and local communities to help advance environmental sustainability and climate resilience agenda through a broad portfolio of over 20 initiatives worth more than $40 million. Over the years, this tripartite partnership has evolved far beyond individual projects. Together, we have worked to address interconnected challenges ranging from biodiversity loss and land degradation to climate change and environmental pollution, as well as to build systems, knowledge, and partnerships that connect environmental action with people’s livelihoods, economic opportunity, and long-term development. Advertising on Gazeta Photo: UNDP. The results of this cooperation can be seen across the country. From restoring ecosystems in the Aral Sea region and conserving globally significant biodiversity, to advancing sustainable urban transport, expanding access to renewable energy solutions, and supporting environmentally sound management of chemicals and waste, GEF-supported initiatives have helped demonstrate how environmental action can also generate economic and social benefits. Few places symbolize both environmental tragedy and resilience more powerfully than the Aral Sea region. Once one of the world’s largest inland seas, the Aral Sea became a global symbol of ecological collapse. Yet the region is also increasingly becoming a place of innovation and restoration. Through the GEF-supported Aral Sea Wetlands Project, implemented by UNDP together with the National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, efforts are underway to restore wetlands, strengthen sustainable water and land management, conserve biodiversity, and support climate-resilient livelihoods across the Lower Amudarya basin. These integrated approaches recognize a simple but critical reality: restoring ecosystems is inseparable from strengthening communities and improving resilience for future generations. Photo: UNDP. Beyond wetland restoration, the initiative has helped strengthen integrated water resources management through ecological flow assessments and improved planning tools, while supporting the restoration of degraded landscapes through saxaul planting on six thousand hectares. At the same time, biodiversity conservation efforts are being strengthened across protected areas covering more than four million hectares through improved management approaches and monitoring systems. The lessons emerging from the Aral Sea region are increasingly relevant beyond the region. For example, another joint initiative of the National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, UNDP, the GEF, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) EcoLand will support the restoration and conservation of landscapes and ecosystems in other regions of Uzbekistan. Across the whole Central Asia, climate pressures, land degradation, and water stress are creating shared environmental risks that require shared responses. Environmental sustainability also depends on strong institutions and effective governance systems. This is particularly important in the area of chemicals and waste management, where countries continue to face complex technical, regulatory, and financial challenges. A new joint initiative of the Government of Uzbekistan, the GEF and UNDP on the implementation of the Stockholm Convention in Uzbekistan represents an important step toward strengthening the sound management of hazardous chemicals and waste. The initiative focuses not only on reducing the risks associated with persistent organic pollutants, but also on strengthening monitoring systems, laboratory capacity, institutional coordination, and long-term regulatory frameworks. Such work may often remain less visible than large infrastructure projects, yet it is essential for protecting ecosystems, public health, and future generations. Protecting nature as an economic imperative At the same time, one of the most important environmental conversations globally is increasingly centered on finance. Protecting nature is no longer seen solely as an environmental issue. It is also an economic imperative. Through the Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN), UNDP has worked with governments around the world to help identify financing solutions for biodiversity and ecosystem restoration. In Uzbekistan, this cooperation is now entering a new phase through the launch of a Biodiversity Finance academic module jointly developed with the Central Asian Green University, based on the BIOFIN methodology. This effort reflects a broader shift taking place globally and nationally: the recognition that future economists, financiers, policymakers, and business leaders must understand the value of ecosystems and integrate nature into financial and development decision-making. Building a green future will require not only technology and investment, but also new skills, new knowledge, and a new generation of professionals capable of linking finance with sustainability. Lasting progress depends on people Yet perhaps one of the most powerful lessons over the years is that environmental transformation cannot be achieved through institutions alone. Lasting progress depends on people. Photo: GEF SGP. For nearly two decades, the GEF Small Grants Programme (SGP) in Uzbekistan has demonstrated how locally led solutions can generate tangible environmental, social, and economic benefits. From biodiversity conservation and sustainable agriculture to renewable energy and land restoration, community organizations and civil society actors across the country have shown that local innovation can become a powerful driver of resilience and sustainable development. As Uzbekistan and UNDP launch the next operational phase of the GEF SGP , the focus is not only on supporting grassroots initiatives, but also on strengthening the role of communities , local knowledge, and civil society in shaping the country’s green transition, contributing to the implementation of the Uzbekistan’s new targets of the National Biodiversity Strategy, fully aligned with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF). This broader transition is increasingly positioning Uzbekistan as an active participant in regional and global environmental dialogue. The country’s environmental agenda today is no longer defined solely by addressing past crises. It is increasingly focused on building resilient landscapes, strengthening gree
title: Op-Ed. Environmental sustainability is not only about protecting nature

body: Dr Hans Kluge. Photo: WHO Op-ed: Aral Sea region cannot heal until its people do The outcome and success of the Astana Regional Ecological Summit will be judged not by the declarations signed, but by whether a child born in the Aral Sea region in 2030 is healthier than one born today, Dr Hans Henri P. Kluge, WHO Regional Director for Europe, writes in his op-ed. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 22 April 2026, 06:00 Columns Politics Op-ed by Dr Hans Henri P. Kluge, World Health Organization’s Regional Director for Europe, for the Regional Ecological Summit opening in Astana, Kazakhstan, on 22 April. No recovery plan for the Aral Sea region can truly succeed if it does not help the people living there become healthier. As leaders from across Central Asia and beyond gather in Astana for the Regional Ecological Summit, this is an important opportunity to recognize this fundamental truth and match it with the commitment and resources needed to make it a reality. For decades, much of the response to the Aral Sea crisis has focused on environmental remediation, while the health burden on local communities remained at the margins of investment and attention. Women and children bear the heaviest burden. Over the past 10 years, anemia has remained significantly higher in the Aral Sea region than nationally — 2.5 times higher among children and 2.7 times higher among women. Among pregnant women, the burden is even more severe, with anemia affecting 77%. Recent evidence points to high rates of endocrine and gynecological disorders among women living closest to the ecological catastrophe zone, including early menopause, infertility, and perinatal losses. Thyroid-related disorders are also widespread: 12% of women were found to have diffuse goiter, 32% had raised anti‐thyroid peroxidase antibodies — an indicator of impaired thyroid function — and 2−3% were diagnosed with overt hypothyroidism. Children, meanwhile, face elevated risks of developmental abnormalities, chronic respiratory illness, and anemia. Advertising on Gazeta These are not isolated findings — they are patterns sustained across generations, shaped by daily exposure to toxic dust, contaminated water, degraded soils, and industrial pollutants that have defined this landscape for half a century and reduced access to healthy diets. Over the past few years, climate change, resulting in higher temperatures that in turn accelerate evaporation from the Aral Sea, has amplified these effects. The people of this region don’t need to be told about any of this. They are living it. What is still needed is a sustained and coordinated response that places people’s health at the center of recovery and treats it as one of the clearest measures of whether recovery is working. The Initiative for a Healthy Future in the Aral Sea Region is designed to change that. It grew from a request by the Ministers of Health of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan for WHO support in assessing the crisis' health impact. Through a package of workstreams, the Initiative seeks to make health a leading driver of Aral Sea recovery efforts with countries, partners, and donors. This initiative will strengthen surveillance and monitoring systems to map health risks, identify exposure hotspots, and track causal pathways between environmental conditions and disease. It will support reforms to drinking water safety, air quality management, and school environments. It will invest in health systems capable of recognizing and managing diseases directly linked to environmental exposure — including the reproductive and developmental conditions that have been under-resourced for far too long. By building early warning systems for dust storms, strengthening action on extreme heat, and improving water safety, the initiative will help protect communities before dangers intensify. None of this can be done by one country alone. Dust storms do not stop at borders. Water scarcity, biodiversity loss, and climate impacts do not respect political boundaries. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have recognized this. The memorandum of understanding they plan to sign in Astana is an important step forward, reflecting a commitment to regional cooperation rather than parallel national efforts. The recent establishment of an Interdisciplinary Working Group between these two countries is another important sign of growing shared responsibility. The lessons of the Aral Sea should also help guide action on the shrinking Caspian Sea, including through a better understanding of its environmental and potential health impacts. In this spirit, Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan will sign a joint statement during the Summit, reinforcing their commitment to coordinated action. Regional cooperation is not a technical detail — it is essential to protect public health and to make the most effective use of available resources. Convened at the initiative of Kazakhstan’s President, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the Summit is intended to serve as a regional platform for dialogue and cooperation on climate and broader environmental challenges. It offers an important opportunity to build on the political will already shown by Central Asian governments and bring together national, regional, local, and international partners around sustained technical and financial support. The outcome and success of the Astana Summit will be judged not by the declarations signed, but by whether a child born in the Aral Sea region in 2030 is healthier than one born today. That is the only measure that matters. Subscribe to our Telegram channel Gazeta 14 980 # aral sea # hans kluge # op-ed # who
title: Op-ed: Aral Sea region cannot heal until its people do

body: Regina Maria Castillo. Photo: UNICEF Girls' empowerment begins with protection. Op-ed by UNICEF Representative in Uzbekistan International Women’s Day is meant to celebrate girls and women. But it’s also a moment for a harder question: how do our societies actually treat girls and women every other day of the year? Op-ed by Regina Maria Castillo, UNICEF Representative in Uzbekistan. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 8 March 2026, 11:04 Columns Society Op-ed by Regina Maria Castillo, United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) Representative in Uzbekistan. Globally, International Women’s Day is meant to celebrate girls and women — gestures of respect, love and appreciation that are important and heartfelt. But it’s also a moment for a harder question: how do our societies actually treat girls and women every other day of the year? In my years as UNICEF Representative in Uzbekistan, I have seen that the commemorations to celebrate girls and women are indeed matched by political will, policy frameworks and concrete rubric and actions to protect and empower them. This year I write this piece just five days after another important decree came into force here — a reminder that progress is possible when commitment is turned into action. Advertising on Gazeta On 3 March, the Presidential Decree “On additional organizational and legal measures to strengthen the protection of the rights of women and children, as well as prevent cases of harassment and violence against them,” was adopted. UNICEF warmly congratulates the Government of Uzbekistan for its strong commitment to better protect girls and women, reflected in the latest Presidential Decree. This matters because protecting girls and women is not a side issue. It is central to national progress. No country can fully thrive when women live with violence, when girls face pressure into child or early marriage, or when adolescent pregnancy cuts short education and opportunity. For UNICEF, the message is simple: girls' empowerment begins with protection. A girl who is safe is more likely to stay in school, stay healthy, and build the skills and confidence she needs for adult life. A young woman who can access support without fear or stigma is better able to continue her education, participate in society and contribute to her family, community and country. That is why this Decree is so important. Its focus on prevention, stronger coordination and improved support systems reflects an essential truth: violence, coercion and harmful practices are not private matters. They are public challenges with lifelong consequences. They limit potential, deepen inequality and weaken communities. This is especially clear when we consider the impact of pregnancy in the teenage years, an area touched on by the decree. Adolescent pregnancy can derail a girl’s education, narrow her choices and increase health risks for both mother and child. Too often, it is linked to child marriage, unequal power dynamics, poor access to information, and weak support systems. Preventing teenage pregnancy — and ensuring that girls who do become pregnant are protected, supported and able to continue learning — must be part of any effort to empower girls. In Uzbekistan, comprehensive prevalence data on all forms of violence against women and girls are not yet fully available. But the absence of complete data must not impede action. If anything, it is a reminder that stronger prevention, identification and response systems are needed. And global evidence leaves no room for complacency. UNICEF estimates that 1 in 4 children worldwide — around 610 million — live with mothers who have experienced intimate partner violence in the past year. UNICEF also estimates that 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 every year. Behind every number is a child whose safety, well-being and future are at risk. That is why the real value of this Presidential Decree lies not only in what it says, but in what it makes possible. It can help shift the national response from reacting after harm occurs to preventing harm before it takes hold. That is the right ambition and the right direction. UNICEF also welcomes the Decree’s emphasis on strengthening families and promoting family life free from violence. Prevention works best when it starts early: when parents and caregivers have support, when communities recognize warning signs, and when social norms reinforce respect, equality and non-violence. As UNICEF, we look forward to contributing to these efforts, including through support for the development and rollout of the “Happy Family” Programme. This is an important opportunity to promote evidence-based approaches, strengthen the capacity of frontline workers, and reach adolescents, young couples, parents and communities where girls may face heightened risks of violence, early marriage and teenage pregnancy. But laws and programmes alone are not enough. Implementation will be everything. Progress depends on trained professionals, survivor-centred services, sustained financing, and systems that are accessible to women and girls in every part of the country, from Tashkent to Termez, from Fergana Valley to Karakalpakstan. It also depends on listening to girls, to women, and to the people working closest to families every day. On this International Women’s Day, Uzbekistan and its leadership at the highest level, is taking bold steps to protect women and girls. While the world seems to be falling apart, it is fulfilling to see that this country is moving forward towards greater protection of women and girls. Because every girl deserves to grow up safely. Every woman deserves to live free from violence and discrimination. And every adolescent girl deserves a future defined by hope and opportunity — not by fear, child marriage or pregnancy in the teenage years. When women and girls are protected, empowered and heard, everyone benefits. Subscribe to our Telegram channel Regina Maria Castillo 16 118 # regina maria castillo # unicef # women and children
title: Girls' empowerment begins with protection. Op-ed by UNICEF Representative in Uzbekistan

body: Dr Asheena Khalakdina, WHO Representative and Head of Office in Uzbekistan. Photo: WHO / Andreas Beck Every two minutes a woman dies from cervical cancer. We must act now Cervical cancer is one of the few cancers that is fully preventable, detectable and treatable when caught early. On the first World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day, Dr Asheena Khalakdina, WHO Representative in Uzbekistan, writes that cervical cancer can be eliminated within our lifetime. 18 November 2025, 15:20 Columns Society This Monday, 17 November, the world marked the first-ever World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day, designated by the 78 th World Health Assembly. For the first time in history, countries are observing a global health day dedicated to eliminating cancer — united under the call: “Act Now: Eliminate Cervical Cancer” to build on existing progress and accelerate impact. A preventable and curable cancer, and an unequal burden Cervical cancer is one of the few cancers that is fully preventable, detectable and treatable when caught early. Yet, it remains the 4 th most common cancer among women globally, with 660,000 new cases in 2022. In the same year, 350,000 deaths were caused by cervical cancer. Tragically 94% of these deaths occurred in low- and middle-income countries, where access to vaccination, screening, and treatment services remains limited. These deaths are linked also to risk factors such as social and economic determinants, including gender bias and poverty. The burden falls heavily on families. Cervical cancer disproportionately affects younger women, and as a result, globally 1 in 5 children who lose their mother to cancer lose her to cervical cancer. The consequence is not only medical, but social, emotional, and economic. In Uzbekistan cancer remains a major public health concern. According to the 2022 Global Cancer Observatory by the International Agency for Research, in Uzbekistan cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women and accounted for over 2,000 new cancers in women. Sadly, approximately 1,585 women died from cervical cancer in the same year. Arofat’s story: why early detection matters Photo: WHO / Andreas Beck. Advertising on Gazeta Last year WHO published the story of Arofat Marakhimova , a school nurse from Tashkent region whose life was changed by a single HPV test. When the clinic called with her results, she was afraid. The diagnosis felt overwhelming. But early detection through an HPV pilot programme launched by WHO, UNFPA, IARC, and the embassy of France meant her condition was identified early, when treatment is most effective. Arofat is one of the many women who participated in the pilot programme in Tashkent region and Karakalpakstan, which aimed to reach more than 56,000 women with HPV screening. Stories like Arofat’s laid the foundation for Uzbekistan’s first HPV-based national screening programme, which started in 2025. A global plan and Uzbekistan’s progress The encouraging news is that the world has a plan. Proven, cost-effective interventions exist to prevent, screen for, and treat cervical cancer. In 2020, all 194 WHO Member States agreed to eliminate cervical cancer — the first global commitment to eliminate a cancer. WHO launched the Global strategy to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem. The strategy calls on all countries to reach the 90−70−90 targets by 2030: 90% of girls fully vaccinated with HPV vaccine by age 15; 70% of women screened with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45; 90% of women with cervical disease receiving treatment. Through modelling, some interim benefits of achieving 90−70−90 shows 300,000 cervical cancer deaths averted by 2030. Uzbekistan is taking decisive steps towards cervical cancer elimination. HPV vaccination According to the Ministry of Health, 94% of girls aged 12−14 have received the first dose of HPV vaccine. This is one of the highest rates in the region — and a powerful step toward protecting the next generation. Early detection and screening programs Demonstrating strong political commitment to address the cancer burden including cervical cancer, the government of Uzbekistan secured a loan from the Islamic Development Bank to support the expansion and enhancement of oncology services in the country. The government has partnered with WHO through an agreement to strengthen access to safe, high-quality oncology services. WHO continues to provide technical expertise and assistance for strengthening prevention, early diagnosis and treatment services for cervical cancer. WHO has supported the update of national clinical guidelines and protocols for cervical cancer prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, ensuring alignment with WHO recommendations and international standards. WHO further provided technical support for an HPV testing pilot in Chirchik district which demonstrated the feasibility of implementing screening at the primary care level, with 5,600 women screened. Thirty-five providers have been trained to deliver cervical cancer screening at the primary care level through strengthening of knowledge, communication to women and community, and understanding referral pathways for women with complex cervical disease. Twenty-four laboratory staff have been trained to ensure they are well-informed about HPV test processing, operational procedures, communication of results to women. Eighty specialists (nurses, medical technologists, cytotechnologists, and pathologists) trained to interpret cytology and biopsy samples improving the accuracy of diagnosing precancerous and malignant cervical lesions and ensure the rational use of colposcopy and treatment resources. Photo: WHO / Andreas Beck. Closing the gaps: what must happen next While we celebrate the significant strides made, missed opportunities for diagnosis and treatment should be addressed with a more integrated approach. To make the change, cervical cancer services need to be integrated throughout the life course, linked with maternal health, family planning and primary care to leverage the opportunities of other programs within the health system. I would like to leave you with these key messages: Cervical cancer can be prevented and treated when detected early; This requires interventions from vaccination to treatment; Addressing sociocultural barriers is essential; and Strong partnerships and collaboration are critical. Cervical cancer elimination is not an aspiration. It is achievable within our lifetime. With every girl received HPV vaccination and every woman screened, diagnosed and treated, Uzbekistan moves one step closer to this historic milestone. We all must ACT . Governments act. Youth act. Communities act. Survivors act. Will you? title: Every two minutes a woman dies from cervical cancer. We must act now

body: Photo: SCO Summit press center Opinion. What will “SCO in action” look like? In the 30th year of SCO’s existence, observers continue to raise questions about its specific goals and objectives. Expert Temur Umarov writes that this uncertainty might be considered as flexibility allowing the organization to remain relevant and attract new members amid global uncertainty. 1 September 2025, 02:46 Columns Politics The latest summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), which took place in Tianjin, China, as usual, draws significant international attention. This summit is special: it was the 25th in a row, the 5th held on Chinese territory (the most influential participant and one of the founding states) and it brings together almost 30 leaders of world countries and international organizations. Next year the SCO will turn 30 — it was founded as the Shanghai Five in 1996 and transformed into the SCO in 2001. However, experts are still asking questions about the organization’s tasks and objectives. Opinions range from “it is a club of interests” to “a NATO-like alliance”, or even “a new UN”. The organization itself cannot but be aware that its declared and real identities do not coincide. Therefore, as if answering the question “What does the SCO actually do?”, the summit in Tianjin is being held under the slogan “SCO in action”. Temur Umarov, expert of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin, in this op-ed tries to answer this question. Identity No1. Declared According to the SCO charter , its main goals include strengthening mutual trust and good-neighborly relations among member states; promoting effective cooperation in political, trade and economic, scientific and technical and cultural spheres, as well as in education, energy, transport, tourism, environmental protection and others. Advertising on Gazeta In addition, its tasks include jointly ensuring and maintaining peace, security and stability in the region, as well as advancing the creation of a democratic, just and rational new international political and economic order. Official SCO documents also mention the principle of the Shanghai Spirit, which implies mutual trust and mutual benefit, equality, respect for cultural diversity, maintaining non-aligned status, and the principle of consensus in decision-making. The SCO’s often cited “achievement” is being the largest regional organization: its member states cover almost one-third of the world’s territory, are home to more than 40% of the world’s population, and account for a quarter of global GDP. At the same time, the SCO is constantly expanding. Over the past decade, India, Pakistan, Iran and Belarus joined the organization, and another 14 countries are dialogue partners. Along with observer states and candidates for observer status, this formed the SCO Plus format. Identity No2. Real The SCO was especially effective at the very beginning of its existence, when it was created as the Shanghai Five in 1996, successfully resolving territorial issues between China and its neighboring post-Soviet states. It then transformed into a regional structure for cooperation between China and Russia in the post-Soviet space, and after Uzbekistan joined, it became the full-fledged SCO. Within the SCO, its own institutions emerged, which appear quite impressive: the SCO Business Council unites representatives of business communities, the Interbank Consortium finances investment projects and the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) in Tashkent deals with anti-terrorism activities. RATS, which conducts joint military exercises, can be called the organization’s most active structure. The existence of these institutions within such a diverse organization helps build bridges between various agencies of different countries, which otherwise would not be able to interact. Hence the value of the SCO: it is not just a large platform with regular meetings, but also a safe space — a place where there are no countries inclined to point out each other’s domestic political problems. Identity No3. Hidden As is often the case with large intergovernmental organizations, they lack subjectivity and largely reflect the positions of their members. Given the diverse composition of countries that disagree on many issues, the SCO is forced to be extremely cautious in its public activities. Nevertheless, this does not prevent different countries from trying to use the organization for their own purposes. For example, Russia repeatedly hoped to secure SCO support for its foreign policy ventures. In 2008, then-president Dmitry Medvedev raised the issue of South Ossetia’s independence, in 2014 the Russian agenda included recognition of Crimea and in 2022 Moscow wanted to achieve a unified SCO position on UN votes concerning the war in Ukraine. Moscow also periodically tries to promote its ideological vision of a new SCO mission, but its current ideology does not align with the foreign policy priorities of other member states. Before the 2022 SCO summit in Samarkand, official Tashkent specifically refuted Russian journalists' claims that “the SCO is Russia’s answer to NATO”. China uses the SCO to promote its discursive power, which can be seen in the joint documents adopted by the organization. They contain terms rooted in Chinese Communist Party documents, such as “community of common destiny”. At one time, Beijing tried to turn the SCO into a working structure for realizing its ambitions in Central Asia, but Russia consistently blocked China’s two main proposals: creating a development bank and a free trade zone. As a result, Beijing began to act independently. Other countries showcase their participation in the SCO as proof of their involvement in global politics and lack of international isolation (for example, Iran, Belarus and Afghanistan as an observer). For India, the SCO can serve as an alternative platform that strengthens its negotiating position with the West. For the Central Asian states, particularly Uzbekistan, the SCO is important for several reasons. First, the countries of the region were at the origins of this organization, and there are not many major international structures founded by them. Second, the SCO is a valuable geopolitical platform, as it spans Eurasia, whose core is Central Asia. Third, it provides a unique opportunity to establish contacts with the leadership of different countries at all possible governmental levels, and with the right approach, SCO summits can serve as an excellent occasion to deepen bilateral relations. Identity No4. Future The immediate future of the SCO appears to lie in its continued expansion and strengthening of its role as a platform for multilateral negotiations, rather than as a rigid military or economic bloc. Countries continue to join the organization because membership does not impose serious obligations and allows them to pursue narrow national interests. The SCO’s vagueness is not a flaw but a key feature, in some ways reflecting the broader trend in contemporary international relations. More and more countries are moving away from rigid unions and alliances to avoid additional responsibility for the behavior of other states, even if their bilateral relations are closer than ever. Examples can be found even among traditional Western alliances. NATO, considered the model of a military alliance, is now seen as an outdated format even within the United States. New American initiatives — QUAD (the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue between Australia, India, the US and Japan) and AUKUS (a military-political format between Australia, the UK and the US) — no longer contain commitments as strict as, for example, NATO’s article 5. This same flexibility is characteristic of the SCO. China, as the main driving force, is not eager to make its activities more concrete, because in a constantly changing geopolitical environment this could become a limitation. Thus, the SCO remains a strategic asset precisely because of i

body: Photo: Presidential Press Service Addressing the 22 million young citizens of Uzbekistan, the president underscored the collective responsibility of state officials, ranging from ministers and governors to school directors, to ensure no youth is left behind. He called for a more rigorous approach to supporting language learning, vocational training, sports, and the incubation of innovative startups. The president highlighted the significant strides made by Uzbek youth on the global stage, bolstered by expanded state opportunities: Academic excellence: Students have secured 66 gold, 147 silver, and 221 bronze medals at international science Olympiads in recent years. Global education: Over 500 Uzbek students are currently enrolled in prestigious Ivy League institutions such as Harvard, Yale, Princeton, Columbia, and Cornell, while more than 3,500 are studying at Top–100 ranked universities worldwide. Entrepreneurial reach: 63 startup projects initiated by Uzbek youth have successfully entered international markets, including the USA, South Korea, the UK, and the UAE. Sports mastery: Young athletes have brought home a total of 720 gold, 671 silver, and 854 bronze medals from international arenas. "It brings us great pride that Uzbekistan has been declared the fastest-growing country in the Global Youth Development Index," President Mirziyoyev remarked, noting that young entrepreneurs now account for 35% of the country’s business sector. The president announced that Tashkent will become the headquarters for the Global Youth Movement for Peace this year. Furthermore, Uzbekistan is set to host several major international events, including: The 12th Global Conference of Young Parliamentarians in Samarkand. The "Take Off" International Startup Summit. The 46th World Chess Olympiad. To combat emerging global threats to the mindset of the younger generation, the president mandated a transition to a new system of engagement. Every Thursday has been officially designated as "Youth Day" across all ministries, agencies, and regional administrations. On these days, responsible officials are required to visit neighborhoods, schools, and technical colleges to listen to youth concerns directly. Governors have been tasked with developing youth-oriented trade and service projects, providing grants for startups, and organizing competitions for the best young farmers, industrialists, and creators.

body: Fabian Sommer / dpa / dpa Picture-Alliance via AFP The AMMC, a strategic state-owned enterprise slated for a partial initial public offering (IPO) in late 2025, awarded contracts exceeding $200 million to 10 foreign companies. The findings raise serious questions regarding transparency and the legitimacy of the procurement process at one of Uzbekistan’s largest industrial assets. "Dormant" British firms winning multi-million dollar contracts Two UK-registered entities, Lemixton Solutions and Golders Business, secured contracts worth approximately $35.5 million despite officially reporting themselves as "dormant" to British authorities. Under UK law, dormant companies are prohibited from engaging in commercial activities or financial transactions without a valid reason. Lemixton Solutions: Since 2022, this firm won at least 56 tenders worth $22.5 million. It has only one employee, no official website, and no physical office in Uzbekistan. Golders Business: This company won contracts totaling $13 million and made over 100 deliveries, yet consistently filed financial reports as a non-trading entity. When OCCRP journalists began inquiring about these firms in December 2025, "urgent and strange" backdated changes appeared in the UK Companies House registry. Initially owned by British nominees, the records were amended to show Grigory Khvan as the person with significant control since 2018. However, by January 2026, the records were changed again to transfer ownership to Felipe Guerrero, a Colombian citizen, also backdated to 2018. Allegations of forged signatures The investigation revealed that electronic signatures of MoreGroup employees (a UK accounting firm) appeared on at least 13 AMMC contracts. Wendy Mary Ann Conroy, whose facsimile signature appears on $6.2 million worth of Lemixton contracts, was removed as a controlling person just days before the latest contract was signed. Furthermore, Ruairi Laughlin-McCann, a former MoreGroup employee, discovered his signature on $1.4 million worth of Golders Business contracts. He told OCCRP he had no involvement with the firm for five years and had "absolutely not signed" the documents. He has since reported the matter to the City of London Police and the UK Serious Fraud Office.
title: Economy OCCRP uncovers $200 million shadow network in AMMC procurement tenders

body: Фото: Kun.uz Who needs an international passport An international passport is required for all citizens of Uzbekistan traveling abroad. There are no exceptions based on the purpose of travel or the visa regime — the document is needed for both visa-required and visa-free countries. Uzbekistan issues only biometric international passports. Their validity depends on age: for adults — 10 years; for children — 5 years. Each child receives their own passport; children cannot be added to a parent’s passport. Where to apply for an international passport Applications can be submitted in two places: at Public Service Centers; at the migration and citizenship departments of the internal affairs bodies (passport desk). Both options are legally equivalent. The place of submission does not depend on the travel purpose or destination country. International passports are issued under a unified procedure for all applicants. The applicant must be physically present to submit the documents and undergo mandatory procedures, including biometric data collection. How to submit an application You can fill out the application online in advance through the government services portal or complete it in person at a Public Service Center or passport office. Regardless of the chosen method, the applicant must visit the authority in person to finalize the procedure. During the in-person visit: documents are accepted and verified; the application is completed in the system; a photograph is taken and fingerprints are collected. Personal presence is mandatory because the passport is a biometric document. Fully remote submission or submission via a representative is not allowed. The order of service and waiting time depend on the specific location and workload, but this does not affect the production time.
title: Society How to get an international passport in Uzbekistan

body: Photo: Mobiuz According to Mobiuz, hackers managed to gain unauthorized access to one of the company’s test servers but failed to breach the main server where subscribers’ personal and financial data are stored. In an official statement, the operator said that unauthorized access to a test server not connected to the company’s core systems was detected during routine security monitoring in February. “One of the company’s test servers, which was not connected to the main systems, was accessed without authorization. The server was subsequently isolated, allowing the incident to be contained,” the statement said. The company stressed that systems storing subscribers’ personal and financial information are located in a fully protected environment. No signs of intrusion into those systems were detected. “Services were not disrupted, and customers’ personal data were not leaked,” Mobiuz said. Mobiuz added that it is conducting a detailed investigation in cooperation with the relevant authorities and is taking additional measures to strengthen the protection of its information systems. The incident comes amid broader cybersecurity concerns in Uzbekistan. In early February, the country’s electronic government systems were also targeted in a cyberattack. Digital Technologies Minister Sherzod Shermatov stated that the information systems of three government agencies had been partially compromised. However, he clarified that, contrary to online claims of 15 million affected individuals, data relating to approximately 60,000 Uzbek citizens had been stolen.
title: Society Mobiuz confirms cyberattack, rules out customer data leak

body: Photo: Press Service of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev The project is being implemented under a Presidential Decree dated July 1, 2025. President Mirziyoyev laid the foundation stone for the museum last August. The President reviewed major construction and installation work at the site, including foundation work and engineering infrastructure development. Mirziyoyev said the museum would become an important cultural space showcasing the country's rich history and culture, as well as the people's goals and aspirations. Renowned Japanese architect Tadao Ando designed the museum's architecture, while German design firm Atelier Brückner developed the exhibition concept, both drawing on leading international practices. The museum will span 3.9 hectares and have a total floor area of more than 40,000 square meters, with a three-story main building and a two-level underground section. Sixty percent of the museum's space will support educational and research activities, including exhibition halls, an extensive library, restoration laboratories, and conference halls. Restaurants and children's playgrounds will also serve families and young visitors. The museum will accommodate up to 3,500 visitors at a time and display around 10,000 historical and artistic exhibits. Once complete, the building will form a unified architectural ensemble with the Abulkasim Madrasah, the Peoples' Friendship Palace and the National Park. The museum would cooperate with leading cultural institutions worldwide, including the Louver in France, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in the United States, and the British Museum, to organize joint exhibitions.

body: Photo: Xalq Banki On September 9, Forbes published its first World’s Top Performing Banks 2026 ranking. It includes 500 banks from 89 countries. Xalq Banki ranked 142nd in Tier 6 , which covers banks with assets ranging from $3 billion to $10 billion. It is important to clarify that this is not a 142nd-place ranking among all banks worldwide. Forbes first divided the banks into six groups based on asset size, so that large global banks would not be compared directly with significantly smaller financial institutions. This is not the Forbes ranking based on customer surveys Forbes already has a separate ranking called World’s Best Banks . It is based primarily on customer surveys, with respondents rating their banks on satisfaction, trust, service quality, digital services and other factors. World’s Top Performing Banks takes a different approach. Forbes and research firm Statista used banks’ financial data, information from major data providers including S&P Capital IQ, the results of their own research, and information submitted by banks to verify the accuracy of their figures. To qualify for the ranking, a bank had to have more than $3 billion in assets, publish audited financial statements and have comparable data available for at least three consecutive years. Forbes noted that when 2025 financial statements were available, it used the most recent financial year; otherwise, it used 2024. The banks were then evaluated across four areas:

body: International brands investing at least $50 million will be offered ready-to-use buildings with infrastructure. Photo: Press Service of the President Shavkat Mirziyoyev reviewed proposals aimed at developing the electrical engineering industry and supporting the production of competitive products. The presidential press service reports . During the presentation, officials noted that there are “a number of issues that need to be addressed.” Some companies face a shortage of collateral needed to obtain loans to replenish working capital. There is also a need for more convenient mechanisms to purchase raw materials through the exchange and for expanded guarantees to attract global brands. To address these issues, new financial support mechanisms for the industry have been proposed. Under the proposal, electrical equipment manufacturers would pay 25% of the cost when purchasing copper raw materials, while the remaining 75% would be covered by Uzsanoatexport. Businesses would repay the funds within 90 days at an interest rate of up to 6% per year. A total of $50 million will be allocated to finance copper purchases. Advertising on Spot When issuing loans, banks will be able to accept alternative forms of collateral, including export contracts and insurance policies. Part of loans provided in Uzbek soums and foreign currencies for investment projects will be compensated over three years. International electrical engineering brands that invest at least $50 million in Uzbekistan’s economy will receive tax incentives. They will also be offered ready-to-use buildings with infrastructure for setting up production facilities. Tax and customs incentives for the electrical engineering industry may be extended until 2030. Support for local companies in related sectors is also expected to be expanded. To boost exports, the government plans to establish trade warehouses in foreign markets, simplify the certification of electrical appliances and facilitate their exports. Opportunities to expand exports of integrated technological solutions to the markets of Afghanistan, Mongolia, Kazakhstan and Iraq were also discussed. Another initiative involves establishing a Research and Innovation Center for the Fourth Industrial Revolution. It will focus on digital modeling, localization and testing of new products, prototype development and engineering services. The president instructed responsible officials to take measures to increase added value in the electrical engineering sector. The goal is to develop the production of high-tech goods and ensure integration into global value chains. body: The total amount raised across four deals was $359,000, while the figures for two rounds were not disclosed. Photo: Yevgeniy Sorochin / Spot In August, six startups from Uzbekistan closed early-stage investment rounds. Spot was informed about this by venture data platform Stanbase . The total amount of funding raised across the four rounds for which details were disclosed was $359,000. The amounts of two other deals were not disclosed. The largest disclosed round was raised by Prestige Club, a B2B platform that integrates travel services into banking and fintech applications. Yoshlar Ventures invested $150,000 in the startup, with the deal announced on August 17. Second was corporate training service Osnova, which received $124,000 from UC Ventures in a pre-seed round. Advertising on Spot Rounding out the top three was Bitimchi AI, which raised $45,000 from undisclosed business angels. The platform provides automated preparation of contracts and invoices, forecasts the tax implications of transactions, analyzes incoming documents for potential risks and checks counterparties. Another $40,000 went to DriveX, a project developing modular off-road vehicle platforms. The company develops modules mounted on basic chassis for mountain tourism, cargo transportation in difficult conditions and rescue services. DriveX raised $25,000 from Yoshlar Ventures and $15,000 from Turin Polytechnic University. OCBC Bank Photo: Bloomberg Forbes, in partnership with market research firm Statista, has published its first ranking of the World’s Top Performing Banks, based on objective financial data rather than customer surveys. The ranking evaluates banks across four key areas: profitability, growth and earnings quality, capital and funding resilience, and asset quality and efficiency. Eligible banks were required to be licensed deposit-taking institutions with more than $3 billion in assets, publish audited financial statements and provide at least three consecutive years of financial data. Banks were divided into six tiers based on total assets, ranging from global banks with more than $500 billion in assets to small banks with $3−10 billion. In total, 500 banks from 89 countries were included in the 2026 ranking. OCBC Bank took the top position among global banks , followed by DBS Group. body: ABB acquired a total of 51 million ordinary shares at a single price of 32,281.28 soums per share. Photo: Evgeny Sorochin / Spot The International Bank of Azerbaijan (ABB) has acquired a 51% controlling stake in private joint-stock commercial bank Davr Bank. The total value of the transaction, recorded on the Republican Stock Exchange “Toshkent”, amounted to 1.646 trillion soums (about $140 million). According to stock exchange data, the transaction was structured and completed on September 10 through a series of six consecutive deals. In total, ABB purchased 51 million ordinary shares at a single price of 32,281.28 soums per share. On August 23, the completion of ABB’s acquisition of a stake in Davr Bank was announced . The deal was mentioned in a video about joint projects shown during a meeting between Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Advertising on Spot The leaders of Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan then took part in an online ceremony to open and lay the foundations for Azerbaijani investment projects in Uzbekistan. Davr Bank was among three projects launched at the ceremony. Speaking to the media, Aliyev said that “a leading Azerbaijani bank has entered the Uzbek market”. A day earlier, Azerbaijani Economy Minister Mikayil Jabbarov announced ABB’s entry into Uzbekistan’s banking market at the 4th Forum of Regions of Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan in Tashkent. “Today, an agreement will be signed with ABB, the largest bank in Azerbaijan and the entire South Caucasus region, marking the bank’s entry into the Uzbek market through a partnership and the acquisition of a stake in Davr Bank”, the Azerbaijani minister said. Jabbarov expressed gratitude to Shavkat Mirziyoyev, the regulator, the Central Bank and the government of Uzbekistan for creating a favorable investment environment and supporting the implementation of the project. On August 27, the Tashkent Stock Exchange announced the resumption of trading in Davr Bank ordinary shares, 5.5 years after they were removed from the exchange’s quotation list. The securities, with the code UZ7050240009, were included in the list under the ticker DRBK. Trading began on August 28. What is known about the deal In May, it became known that in the second half of the year, the state-owned International Bank of Azerbaijan planned to acquire Uzbekistan’s Davr Bank and begin operations in the Uzbek market. The Azerbaijani state bank intended to acquire a 51% stake in Davr Bank for $100 million. In June, Davr Bank shareholders approved the continuation of negotiations with ABB over the possible sale of a 51% stake in the bank. According to the Unified State Register of Enterprises and Organizations, private joint-stock commercial bank Davr Bank was registered in September 2001. Its founders are several individuals. The largest stake, 46.9%, belongs to Lutfulla Khayrullaevich Ubaev, Chairman of the bank’s Supervisory Board. Another 13.5% of the shares are held by Mahfuza Abdumalikovna Ubaeva, who has the same surname. The bank is headed by Abdumajid Abduakhitovich Samadov. body: Shares in major universities and specialized medical centers are planned to be sold to private investors. Photo: Ilya Semendeev / Spot Land plots are planned to be offered for auction as “ready-made packages” with construction permits. This is stipulated in President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s decree dated August 28 on reducing the state’s participation in the economy and accelerating privatization. According to the decree , Uzbekistan is introducing a practice of temporarily retaining the right to “special state participation” (a “golden share”) during the privatization of large and strategic enterprises. It will be applied based on special presidential resolutions. The right to “special state participation” will be used to “protect national security, social stability and the interests of the population,” with mandatory disclosure before the privatization process begins. Large higher education institutions and specialized medical centers will be transformed into business entities. Private investors will be involved in their activities, including through the sale of shares at public auctions. Advertising on Spot Starting from October 1, the registration of rights to shares in companies where the state holds more than 50% will be handled by the Central Securities Depository. The new procedure will also apply to their subsidiaries. From the same date, the establishment of new state institutions in sectors with a “developed competitive environment” without state-budget funding will be prohibited. Exceptions will apply to institutions operating in the defense and security sectors, as well as cases specified in presidential resolutions. All non-core structures of state-owned companies that have the status of institutions will be reorganized, separated from their parent companies and put up for auction. By December 1, state institutions engaged in commercial activities must be transformed into business entities. This requirement does not apply to organizations performing tasks unrelated to administrative, social, cultural or commercial activities. body: Uzbekistan proposed joint production of automotive and industrial components with Serbian companies, including Gosa FOM. Shavkat Mirziyoyev and President of the Republic of Serbia Aleksandar Vučić took part in a joint business forum. The President’s press service reported this. More than 200 officials and business representatives from the two countries, as well as heads of leading industrial and trading companies, took part in the event. Serbian companies including Galenika, AbelaPharm, Gosa FOM, YUMCO and Luss Textile were represented. The two sides set a goal of increasing bilateral trade severalfold by expanding the range of products supplied between the countries and simplifying customs procedures. To develop industrial cooperation, a joint action plan for 2026−2028 was adopted. Advertising on Spot According to a report by Uzbekistan 24 TV, Shavkat Mirziyoyev identified five key areas for developing cooperation with Serbia: mechanical engineering and electrical engineering, pharmaceuticals, light industry, agriculture and food processing, as well as the digital economy. The President expressed Uzbekistan’s readiness to create favorable investment and business conditions for Serbian companies and provide practical support in implementing every joint project. Mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering Mechanical engineering and electrical engineering were identified as the first priority areas. Mirziyoyev said Uzbekistan and Serbia have significant potential for cooperation in the automotive industry. The President noted that the two countries currently produce nearly 500,000 vehicles annually in cooperation with General Motors, Volkswagen, Kia and BYD. He also highlighted that Uzbekistan exports electrical engineering products to more than 70 countries. Uzbekistan proposed that Serbian companies jointly produce automotive and industrial spare parts, components, equipment, transformers and automation systems. The President specifically highlighted opportunities for cooperation with Gosa FOM. “We see great prospects for cooperation with Gosa FOM in this area. I would like to emphasize once again that we will create all the necessary conditions for working together”, Shavkat Mirziyoyev said. Pharmaceuticals Pharmaceuticals were identified as the second priority area. Uzbekistan’s pharmaceutical market is worth around $3 billion. Mirziyoyev called on Serbian companies to become more actively involved in the Uzbek market, emphasizing that the goal is not simply to increase imports of medicines. The President noted Serbia’s extensive experience in the sector and proposed moving from pharmaceutical trade to technology transfer by establishing joint ventures and launching localized production of pharmaceutical products. “We have created a very good foundation for this. A pharmaceutical cluster has been established, and all the necessary conditions are in place for foreign partners. I assure you that we will do everything possible for Serbian companies. We see great potential for cooperation with Serbian companies such as Galenika and AbelaPharm”, the President said. Light industry Light industry was identified as the third priority area. It was noted that Uzbekistan produces more than 4.5 million tonnes of raw cotton annually, a significant volume for Central Asia. Uzbekistan has developed a full value chain from raw materials to finished products, while textile products are exported to more than 75 countries. The country therefore proposed combining Uzbekistan’s production capabilities with the expertise of Serbian companies to implement joint projects in clothing and textile manufacturing. Negotiations are currently underway with YUMCO and Luss Textile on localizing production in Uzbekistan. The President noted that many companies are interested in cooperation in this area. Agriculture and food processing The fourth priority area covers agriculture and food processing. The parties noted Uzbekistan’s large agricultural base and sizeable consumer market. The country ranks among the world’s top 10 exporters of cherries, peaches, plums and apricots. Mirziyoyev described Serbia’s experience in breeding, seed production and agricultural technologies as important for Uzbekistan. Agreements have been reached with the Institute of Field and Vegetable Crops in Novi Sad on developing horticulture. “We need scientific technologies and experience. Serbia has them. If you come to Uzbekistan, we will create all the necessary conditions for you. This will be a mutually beneficial partnership. We invite our partners to implement joint projects in growing and processing agricultural raw materials and producing export-oriented products”, the President said. The President expressed Uzbekistan’s readiness to establish a joint agro-cluster, noting the country’s extensive experience in this area. Digital economy The fifth priority area is the digital economy. The President noted that Serbia has developed a strong IT sector and a cluster focused on training highly qualified specialists. Uzbekistan’s IT industry is also developing rapidly, with exports of IT services exceeding $1 billion in a short period. “We have ambitious goals and a strong foundation”, Shavkat Mirziyoyev said. The International Information and Communication Technologies Week will be held in Tashkent on September 22−25. A dedicated business forum for Serbian companies is planned as part of the event. According to the President, this will create new opportunities for joint projects in software development and artificial intelligence. Mirziyoyev stressed the importance of strengthening political trust through joint ventures, investment, technology and new jobs. Following talks with Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić, he announced that a decision had been made to open a special diplomatic mission of Uzbekistan in Belgrade. Diplomats are expected to be sent to Serbia as early as next week. The two sides also agreed to accelerate the process of launching direct flights between the two countries. The President noted that the new air links would help increase bilateral trade. Shavkat Mirziyoyev expressed confidence that the business forum would mark a new stage in practical business cooperation between Uzbekistan and Serbia. “I wish you success, peace and prosperity. Our historic visit has taken place, and we are very pleased with its results. We look forward to welcoming you to Uzbekistan. We are determined to ensure the active participation of Serbian companies in the Uzbek market. This is a large and sizeable market in Central Asia”, the President concluded. body: In May, the former deputy transport minister was elected Secretary General of TRACECA. His position remains vacant. Photo: Ministry of Transport Jasurbek Choriyev has officially left his position as Deputy Minister of Transport of Uzbekistan, according to the ministry’s website. The Transport Ministry’s leadership section now lists only three officials: Minister Ilhom Mahkamov, First Deputy Minister Mamanbiy Omarov and Deputy Minister Ilhomjon Abdugafarov. The position of second deputy minister, previously held by Jasurbek Choriyev, remains vacant. In mid-May, at the 18th meeting of the TRACECA Intergovernmental Commission in Astana, Jasurbek Choriyev was elected Secretary General of TRACECA as Uzbekistan’s candidate. His name was no longer mentioned in the Transport Ministry’s official channels after May 21, although he continued to be listed among the ministry’s leadership. Advertising on Spot According to Spot, after being elected Secretary General of TRACECA, Jasurbek Choriyev effectively stopped performing his duties as deputy transport minister, as the two positions cannot be held simultaneously. However, no official order on his dismissal had been published until recently, which is why Choriyev continued to appear on the ministry’s leadership page. TRACECA is an international cooperation program between the European Union and partner countries aimed at developing the Europe-Caucasus-Asia transport corridor. Organizationally, TRACECA is an intergovernmental commission. The Secretary General of TRACECA serves as the chief executive of its permanent Secretariat. He is elected by the Intergovernmental Commission and is responsible for the overall management of its work. Who is Jasurbek Choriyev? Jasurbek Choriyev Ergashovich was born in 1978 in Denau district of Surkhandarya region. He studied at the University of World Economy and Diplomacy, the University of Colorado Boulder and the Tashkent State Aviation Institute. He began his career at the Chkalov Aviation Production Association and later held senior positions at foreign airlines. Choriyev joined Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Transport in 2019. Since August 2020, he had served as Deputy Minister of Transport, overseeing the aviation and railway sectors. body: The sale of Turonbank will take into account the recommendations of international consultants and the bank’s readiness for privatization. Photo: Turonbank In 2026−2027, state-owned stakes and shares in 62 enterprises are planned to be offered for public auction. The list was approved by a presidential decree “On additional measures to reduce the state’s participation in the economy and accelerate privatization processes” dated August 28. The document is in the possession of the editorial team. The decree provides that the number of stakes put up for sale and the disposal of assets may be adjusted if the legal and organizational form of an enterprise changes. If an enterprise’s capital includes stakes in companies with a predominant state share, they will be offered for sale as a single package. Where necessary, and with the approval of the Presidential Administration, the Agency for Management of State Assets (AMSA) will be able to determine the procedure for transferring assets of state-owned enterprises to the agency. In particular, the assets may remain with the enterprises until a buyer is identified, or the enterprises may be entrusted with managing the assets on behalf of AUGA. Advertising on Spot When organizations within business companies are transformed into LLCs, their property will be inventoried, while the charter capital will be set at the amount of the existing charter capital based on the latest balance sheet submitted to the tax authorities, without a valuation of the assets. The list of enterprises and the size of the state’s stakes in them may be amended or removed by a decision of AMSA with the approval of the Presidential Administration. A separate procedure for transferring assets to AUGA has been established for commercial banks. Assets will be transferred using reserves created by banks to cover potential losses or proceeds from their sale, after deducting the costs of putting them up for sale and completing the transaction. If the sale price exceeds the book value, the bank will receive the amount corresponding to the residual value. The transfer of assets must also take into account covenants attached to issued bonds, loans obtained from foreign financial institutions and banks, as well as statutory requirements regarding the size of charter capital. Separate conditions have been established for certain assets. The privatization of the state’s stake in Turonbank’s charter capital will be carried out by the Ministry of Economy and Finance, taking into account the conclusions of international consultants and the bank’s readiness for privatization. State stakes in the International Cooperation Centre and Uzexpocentre will be sold with the approval of the Presidential Administration, taking into account the concepts of projects being implemented on their sites and the terms of sale. Meanwhile, the state’s 0.001% stake in Trustbank may be offered for sale without a valuation, based on the stock exchange quotation price. If there is no quotation, the value will be determined proportionally to the company’s net assets. The terms and procedure for selling state stakes in enterprises under local government authorities will be proposed by local authorities and established by AUGA. Proceeds remaining after the sale, minus valuation and transaction costs, will be transferred to the respective local budgets. body: The government plans to sell stakes in 84 companies and 1,242 real estate assets, while also easing installment payment terms. Shavkat Mirziyoyev signed a decree on August 28 introducing new mechanisms for the privatization of state assets, the Agency for Management of State Assets reported . The presidential decree (UP-177) provides for new measures to reduce the state’s presence in the economy, make it easier for investors to participate, and expand opportunities for the private sector. The document approves a new privatization program covering real estate, land plots and stakes in companies. The total value of the assets to be put up for auction amounts to UZS 100 trillion. By the end of the year, proceeds from their sale are expected to reach at least UZS 14 trillion. As part of the program, buyers will be offered government stakes in 84 companies. Investors will also be able to purchase 1,242 real estate properties and land plots with a total area of around 8,000 hectares for business and urban development projects. Advertising on Spot A total of 85 state-owned or state-participated enterprises are planned to be liquidated or reorganized. The 84 assets that were not sold previously will be put up for auction again with a starting price of UZS 1 million. The decree also introduces new sale mechanisms based on proposals from businesses. The down payment required for purchases will be reduced from the current 35% to 15%, while no interest will be charged on the remaining amount. Additional incentives will be provided for large transactions. Buyers will be eligible for a 25% discount if they pay the full value of an asset within six months of signing the sale agreement, instead of one month. The terms for interest-free instalment payments will also be extended. Investors who pay 35% of the lot’s value within three months will be allowed to pay the remaining amount over five years. If 50% of the price is paid within six months, the remaining amount can be paid over seven years. If an asset is not sold within three months of being put up for sale, its price will be gradually reduced. In addition, a “hybrid auction” mechanism will be introduced, allowing the price to be lowered and raised during the bidding process. The new mechanisms and incentives will apply to both state-owned assets and assets held on the balance sheets of banks with state ownership. The decree also addresses ways to increase the investment attractiveness of land plots. They will be sold on a “ready-to-use package” basis, with permits and technical conditions for connecting to utility networks prepared in advance. In addition, major state universities and specialized medical centres are planned to be gradually commercialized. body: The reserves increased by $7.2 billion over the month, with gold rising 15.7% in value while foreign currency reserves fell 13.3%. Photo: Bloomberg International reserves of Uzbekistan continued to grow in August, according to data from the Central Bank. As of September 1, the country’s total international reserves stood at $72.13 billion, the highest level since February . The figure increased by $7.78 billion (+12.1%) over the month, with the main increase driven by higher gold prices and a rise in the physical volume of gold reserves. The value of gold held in the Central Bank’s reserves reached $64.92 billion, up $8.8 billion (+15.69%). At the same time, the physical volume of gold increased to 14.11 million troy ounces (around 438.8 tonnes), compared with 13.85 million ounces a month earlier. At the beginning of August, gold was trading at around $4,000 per troy ounce. During the first half of the month, however, prices began to rise rapidly. After August 5, the price of the precious metal reached peak levels, approaching $4,700 per ounce. By the end of the month, the market underwent a moderate correction, with the price settling at around $4,450 per ounce. Advertising on Spot The foreign currency component of the reserves stood at $6.64 billion at the end of August, down $1.01 billion (-13.29%) from the previous month. Cash and deposits held with other banks fell by 17.3% to $4.87 billion. This included $1.09 billion (-10.56%) held with central banks of other countries and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), as well as $3.77 billion (-19.1%) held with foreign commercial banks. Meanwhile, the volume of foreign securities on the Central Bank’s balance sheet remained virtually unchanged at $1.76 billion (+0.2%) at the end of August. However, their share of total reserves fell to 2.45%, compared with 2.74% a month earlier, amid growth in the overall volume of assets. body: The high-speed train will begin operating between Bukhara and Tashkent on September 14, with services in the reverse direction starting September 15. body: The Central Bank chairman reaffirmed Uzbekistan’s commitment to a floating exchange rate. “We don’t need anyone to teach us not to repeat these mistakes,” he said. Uzbekistan intends to maintain a floating exchange rate regime and does not plan to return to intervening in the currency’s formation. Central Bank chairman Timur Ishmetov said this in an interview with the Financial Times. According to him, when assessing the risks associated with foreign capital inflows, the structure of investments should be taken into account. In particular, Uzbekistan should place greater emphasis on foreign direct investment (FDI), especially long-term investment, rather than borrowing. Ishmetov also outlined the Central Bank’s position on the exchange rate. He said the country has had negative experience with attempts to manage the exchange rate and does not intend to repeat those mistakes. “We are committed to a floating exchange rate. We have our own bad experience of playing with the exchange rate. We don’t need anyone to teach us not to repeat these mistakes”, he emphasized. According to the Central Bank chief, the transition to a floating exchange rate was the result of reforms carried out over many years, lasting around a decade. Therefore, the regulator does not intend to “play with” the exchange rate anymore or abandon the chosen regime. Timur Ishmetov. Photo: Screenshot At the same time, Ishmetov highlighted several areas that should contribute to greater economic resilience. “We should focus more on foreign direct investment rather than borrowing, pay more attention to the national currency and economic development”, he said. According to him, economic growth should be driven not only by external borrowing but also by increasing domestic revenues. body: He noted that the Central Bank and government are working on the supply side to mitigate inflationary risks. Uzbekistan needs to shift its focus from forecasting risks to strengthening economic resilience as external shocks become a permanent factor, Central Bank Chairman Timur Ishmetov said in an interview with the Financial Times. According to Ishmetov, during the early years of reforms, Uzbekistan was mainly focused on addressing domestic challenges. However, after the COVID-19 pandemic, the country faced a series of external shocks, including various conflicts, making uncertainty the new normal. “If previously we focused on risk management and forecasting, trying to understand where risks might emerge, now we probably need to pay more attention to resilience”, Ishmetov said. In his view, instead of trying to predict the source of the next shock, Uzbekistan should assume that external shocks will continue to occur and strengthen the economy’s ability to withstand them. External shocks and inflation Ishmetov also discussed the impact of external factors on inflation. He said that rising global oil and food prices cannot be fully contained through monetary policy alone. Advertising on Spot The Central Bank and government are therefore considering various supply-side measures, including finding alternative logistics routes and developing domestic production of certain goods. “It's not about monetary or fiscal policy, but about the availability of these goods. We need to understand how to ensure supply — by finding alternative logistics or, where possible, producing these goods domestically”, Ishmetov said. At the same time, price stability remains the Central Bank’s main priority. Ishmetov stressed that the regulator is ready to respond if upside inflation risks materialize, but does not intend to react automatically to every change in global markets. According to him, the Central Bank will base its decisions on economic data and assess whether external shocks are actually beginning to affect Uzbekistan’s economy. If such risks materialize, the regulator will be prepared to maintain its current tight monetary policy.
