body: China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Law is Already Harming Uyghurs - Uyghur Human Rights Project Skip to content China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Law is Already Harming Uyghurs August 6, 2026 | The Diplomat | Omer Kanat China’s new Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress has been in effect for more than one month. Beijing claims the law will foster cohesion and protect the rights of minorities. In reality, it is already doing the opposite. One month in, the law is already harming Uyghurs and other ethnic groups and dissidents. Governments must take decisive action to challenge the law and protect diaspora communities before it is too late. As numerous sources have warned , the new law codifies a dramatic shift away from even the promise of regional autonomy, instead embedding Xi Jinping’s campaign of forced assimilation into nearly every facet of government and public life. In doing so, the law violates China’s own constitution. For Uyghurs, this is not new. In 2017, a Chinese official summarized the government’s strategy toward Uyghurs: “Break their lineage, break their roots, break their connections, and break their origins.” Since then, Chinese authorities have systematically dismantled Uyghur social, cultural, and religious life in what the United States government and numerous national parliaments have formally recognized as genocide and crimes against humanity. The indoctrination Uyghurs faced in internment camps, where authorities sought to replace Islam and Uyghur identity with loyalty to the CCP, is now imposed in daily life across the Uyghur homeland of East Turkestan. What has changed is this: Government actions that could once be described as regional campaigns are now embedded in national legislation. These restrictions will become easier to expand and harder to challenge. The new law makes schools, religious institutions, all levels of government, and even families responsible for instilling and enforcing the CCP’s definition of “ethnic unity.” It requires parents to “educate and guide minors to love the Chinese Communist Party,” replaces bilingual education with Mandarin beginning in preschool, and requires religious institutions to persist in the “Sinicization” of religion. In other words, all children must be raised to love the CCP, all languages must give way to Mandarin, and any faith is permitted only when reshaped to serve the state. The law’s effects are already visible. Videos on Chinese social media show Uyghur-language signs being removed from city streets and replaced with Chinese. Uyghurs are unable to resist, or even express sadness, as CCP cadres watch. Any negative reaction can be labeled resistance to “ethnic unity,” placing a person at risk of interrogation, detention, and arrest. Just three days after the law took effect, two Uyghur sisters and their mother were reportedly arrested for sending merchandise to another sister in Turkiye. They were accused of “supporting terrorism” for helping with her business. While it is not new for authorities to penalize Uyghurs for contacting family abroad, the ethnic unity law gives an already abusive system an even broader vocabulary with which to characterize normal family ties, cultural expression, and overseas contact as threats to national unity. The danger also extends to individuals beyond China’s borders. As many have warned , Article 63 of the law declares that organizations and individuals overseas can be pursued for activities Beijing claims undermine ethnic unity or create ethnic division. Chinese officials have openly defended the government’s claimed authority to target people abroad under this provision, creating yet another pretext for transnational repression against Uyghurs, Tibetans, Southern Mongolians, and other diaspora groups or dissidents. This too is already taking effect. In Kazakhstan, Uyghurs and others with ties to East Turkestan report “feeling the pressure” since the law’s enactment. Dolkun Isa – a prominent Uyghur activist, former president of the World Uyghur Congress, and German citizen – was recently detained and deported from Morocco while traveling to attend a religious freedom conference. Such cases demonstrate how China uses its influence to pressure other governments to restrict or intimidate Uyghurs on its behalf. The claim that overseas individuals may face legal responsibility for “undermining ethnic unity” should alarm every government. Uyghurs, Tibetans, Hong Kongers, Falun Gong practitioners, Chinese dissidents, and Taiwanese advocates should not have to wonder whether exercising their freedoms abroad will place themselves or their relatives in danger. The international response has been inadequate thus far, limited to statements rather than actionable commitments. U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk called for the law’s repeal. Eight U.N. special rapporteurs for human rights expressed serious concern. The European Parliament urged China to repeal the law, and the European Union and Taiwan warned about its extraterritorial reach. Australian officials reportedly raised concerns with their Chinese counterparts. The United States in particular has been noticeably quiet, as the Trump administration has yet to take a public stance. A State Department spokesperson called the measure “problematic,” and members of Congress urged a stronger response, but informal remarks and congressional statements are not enough. Governments, including the United States, should issue clear public condemnations, demand the law’s repeal, and make clear that China has no jurisdiction over lawful speech in other countries. Furthermore, governments should coordinate to protect diaspora communities from the transnational repression the law enables. To do so here in the U.S., Congress should pass the Uyghur Policy Act of 2025 and Transnational Repression Policy Act . The damage caused by China’s ethnic unity law is no longer hypothetical. Governments must respond with urgency before forced assimilation and transnational repression become even more deeply entrenched. Read the op-ed in The Diplomat : https://thediplomat.com/2026/08/chinas-ethnic-unity-law-is-already-harming-uyghurs/ Tweets by UyghurProject
title: China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Law is Already Harming Uyghurs

body: Australia’s door is still open to goods made with Uyghur forced labour - Uyghur Human Rights Project Skip to content Australia’s door is still open to goods made with Uyghur forced labour July 8, 2026 | The Strategist | By Elijah Pockell-Wilson Australia is leaving its market exposed to goods tied to Uyghur forced labour. As the United States and European Union move to block such goods, countries with weaker import controls risk becoming destination markets for products facing tougher scrutiny elsewhere. For Australia, this risk is not theoretical; it’s happening now. In my report for the Uyghur Human Rights Project, published last month, I found that in 2024, Australia imported about US$4.82 billion (A$6.95 billion) in goods from China from high-risk sectors linked to the forced labour of Uyghurs. These figures do not show that every good in the high-risk sectors identified in the report – including cotton textiles and apparel, solar inputs, aluminum and chemical products – was made using forced labour. Rather, they show Australia’s exposure to sectors where forced-labour risk is well documented and independent verification remains difficult. Since 2017, Chinese authorities have arbitrarily detained large numbers of Uyghurs and other Turkic peoples in ‘vocational education and training’ facilities , alongside broader patterns of detention and imprisonment in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. This repression has also extended into the region’s economy through state-directed labour transfer programs and restrictions that make independent supply-chain verification extremely difficult. The region remains central to Chinese cotton, textile, solar, and industrial supply chains that feed into ordinary consumer goods, clean energy and industrial materials. While not every product in these sectors is tainted, they are at a high risk of involving Uyghur forced labour, and Australia lacks a reliable system to distinguish goods made with forced labour from those that are not. Australia’s current laws do not meet the scale of the problem. The Modern Slavery Act requires covered companies to report on supply chain risks but does not require them to remove high-risk goods from their supply chains. The act also does not create a forced-labour import ban. Reporting can expose risk, but it can’t stop a shipment from entering the country. This gap in enforcement places responsibility on companies rather than relevant government authorities. Some companies may investigate risk seriously. Others may not. Either way, Australians should not have to depend on voluntary action to know whether everyday goods they buy and use are linked to slavery. In 2025, the Australian Uyghur Tangritagh Women’s Association brought a case against department store chain Kmart Australia. The association, which filed a lawsuit under consumer protection law, alleges that Kmart may have misled consumers about its exposure to forced-labour risk and is seeking disclosure of its supply-chain information. Kmart says it opposes slavery in all forms, including forced labour. ‘Our modern slavery risks are assessed as part of an ongoing and overarching human rights risk management process,’ the retailer adds. The association’s lawsuit points to a larger problem in Australia’s modern slavery framework. Importers bringing in goods from high-risk sectors should be required to provide credible evidence that their products are not linked to forced labour. Customs authorities should have the power to stop goods when the evidence is weak. This would shift responsibility away from consumers and onto the companies and agencies best placed to identify forced-labour risk before goods reach the Australian market. Without these measures, Australia will remain out of step with larger markets that are moving towards stronger import controls. The US has adopted a stronger import control system through the Uyghur Forced Labor Protection Act. The EU is also moving towards a ban on forced labour. These larger markets are beginning to treat forced-labour risk as something to stop at the border, not just something for companies to report. If Australia doesn’t strengthen its own laws, goods facing tougher scrutiny in the US and Europe may be redirected onto Australian shelves. My report describes this trend as ‘redirected risk.’ Stronger enforcement in one market does not automatically remove forced-labour goods from global supply chains. It can push risk towards markets where imports face less scrutiny. Japan similarly faces this exposure, as the report shows. Australia has recognised this risk but has not built a system strong enough to address it. Australian Anti-Slavery Commissioner Chris Evans has warned that the current system is too weak. Evans has backed stronger laws, including mandatory due diligence and high-risk declarations, so companies must act on modern slavery risks rather than simply reporting them. Australia should close this gap by adopting a forced-labour import ban, strengthening customs powers and requiring importers to trace goods in high-risk sectors. Australia should also work with its global trading partners, including the US, through information-sharing on high-risk sectors and importers. Disclosure can reveal exposure to forced labour. It cannot, by itself, stop it. If Australia wants to keep goods made with Uyghur forced labour out of Australian homes, businesses and supply chains, it must give border authorities the tools to act. Read the op-ed in The Strategist : https://www.aspistrategist.org.au/australias-door-is-still-open-to-goods-made-with-uyghur-forced-labour/ Tweets by UyghurProject
title: Australia’s door is still open to goods made with Uyghur forced labour

body: China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Cup: Football and Assimilation in the Uyghur Region - Uyghur Human Rights Project Skip to content China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Cup: Football and Assimilation in the Uyghur Region June 30, 2026 | The Diplomat | By Henryk Szadziewski The FIFA World Cup 2026 in the United States, Mexico, and Canada has captured the global imagination through open play, star players, fan diversity, and state-of-the-art stadiums. Few events attract attention quite like a World Cup, drawing worldwide television audiences at all hours of the day and night. Yet football’s showcase tournament is rarely free from controversy. This World Cup has generated criticism over travel restrictions , eye-watering ticket prices , and commercial pressures that have reshaped the game. Less visible are protests directed at corporate actors, such as Aramco and Mytel , linking FIFA to states with dismal human rights records. The World Cup has long been used by malign governments seeking legitimacy and international prestige. Benito Mussolini recognized the propaganda value of the tournament when Italy hosted the 1934 World Cup, presenting fascist Italy as modern, disciplined, and successful. During Argentina’s 1978 World Cup, General Jorge Rafael Videla’s military dictatorship projected an image of national unity while political prisoners were tortured and disappeared only miles from tournament venues. More recently, Russia’s hosting of the 2018 World Cup and Qatar’s of the 2022 tournament demonstrated how major football events can help soften international criticism and cultivate favorable narratives. Much of the discussion surrounding “sportswashing” focuses on international competition. Yet domestic tournaments can serve a similar function. The Chinese government’s promotion of football in the Uyghur Region provides an example of how local sporting events can be mobilized to distract from ongoing human rights violations while advancing the state’s political objectives. Since 2017, the Chinese state has been implicated in a range of human rights abuses targeting Uyghurs and other Turkic peoples, including mass internment , state-sponsored forced labor , widespread surveillance , cultural destruction , and forced sterilization . The Uyghur Tribunal concluded that these policies amounted to genocide, while the United Nations found that they may constitute crimes against humanity. As international scrutiny intensified, Beijing gradually shifted its messaging. Rather than defending its crackdown, officials began presenting those same policies as responsible for creating a stable region now open to visitors and investors. Uyghurs increasingly appeared in state narratives as grateful beneficiaries of development and modernization. International hotel chains and travel companies participated in building a regional tourism industry, while social media influencers amplified images of hospitality and prosperity, ignoring the context of repression. Sporting events became an important part of this effort. Winter sports , rally races , and other competitions helped normalize conditions and redirect attention away from allegations of atrocity crimes. The Assimilation Cup Football has now become one of the most visible components of China’s shift in messaging. Chinese state media is promoting the 2026 Tongxin Cup Xinjiang Super League as the first region-wide amateur football competition. Fourteen prefecture-level teams are competing in a tournament running from May through August. The extensive state media coverage emphasized large crowds , inexpensive tickets , and grassroots participation . The league is also marketed as an economic driver , with prefecture governments promoting football tourism , cultural performances , merchandise , and local branding campaigns. These initiatives fit the sportswashing aim to distract from human rights abuses and cultivate favorable narratives. Yet the political messaging surrounding the Tongxin Cup reveals something else. The competition’s name, “Tongxin” (同心) – translated as “one heart” or “united as one” – carries strong associations with Chinese Communist Party (CCP) discourse on “ethnic unity.” State media consistently frame the Tongxin Cup as bringing players and spectators from “all ethnic groups” together, while the tournament’s pomegranate-themed mascots, Tongtong and Xinxin, draw directly on CCP narratives of ethnic unity. The pomegranate branding is a direct reference to Xi Jinping’s comment that China’s ethnic groups should be “closely united like the seeds of a pomegranate.” As such, the political messaging of the Tongxin Cup is closely aligned with state policies to reshape ethnic identity in the region. Adopted in March this year, the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress requires state institutions, schools, media organizations, and businesses to promote a shared national identity over distinct ethnic identities. The law expands Mandarin-language education, encourages greater “interethnic integration,” and institutionalizes campaigns promoting national unity. Consequently, national identity is understood as Han culture, and the decades-long process of Uyghur cultural loss is codified under law. Within this framework, football becomes a vehicle for reinforcing assimilation and erasing diversity. It is no coincidence that the law comes into effect on July 1, 2026, in the midst of Tongxin Cup games. Football as a Tool of Control The use of domestic football competitions for political purposes is hardly unique to China. Across different political systems and eras, authoritarian governments have used domestic football to manufacture consent, project legitimacy, and divert attention from repression. Francisco Franco renamed Spain’s historic Copa del Rey as the Copa del Generalísimo between 1939 and 1976, turning football into an affirmation of his regime. China’s use of football in the Uyghur Region fits within this tradition. The strategy is particularly effective because football is as popular in Uyghur society as it is in countries such as Spain. However, for many years, football provided a means of expressing dissatisfaction with Chinese rule among Uyghurs. Support for whichever national team happened to be playing against China became a common form of resistance among some Uyghur fans. Furthermore, football became a means of independent organization. In the mid-1990s, Uyghurs in Ghulja responded to unemployment and substance abuse among young people by reviving the meshrep , a traditional community gathering, to offer mutual support and moral guidance. Meshrep leaders organized a 16-team football league to provide healthy activities for marginalized Uyghur youth. Chinese authorities shut down the tournament, deployed tanks onto football pitches, and removed goalposts to prevent matches from taking place. The suppression of meshrep activities became one of the grievances that contributed to the February 1997 Ghulja protests and subsequent massacre of Uyghur demonstrators by Chinese security forces. The lesson learned by the Chinese state was not that football could strengthen communities. It was that football could become a focus of resistance and generate social networks beyond state control. Today, football is encouraged , but only under official supervision. The state promotes participation and funds facilities , provided that football serves state objectives rather than community autonomy. Football thrives in the Uyghur diaspora, with initiatives like the establishment of the East Turkistan national team, which competes in non-FIFA international tournaments, as well as the playing of the “ Uyghur World Cup ” and amateur competitions organized by diaspora communities in countries such as the United States , Australia and Turkiye . However, these initiatives operate on shoestring budgets. Their significance lies in the ability of communities in exile to organize themselves and maintain language, culture, and communal ties despit
title: China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Cup: Football and Assimilation in the Uyghur Region

body: SVG Commentary Aug 28, 2026 Türkiye Today Mr. Trump, Take the Golden Road to Samarkand Ken Moriyasu Senior Fellow Ken Moriyasu Commentary Caption Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on April 10, 2025. (Getty Images) Bishkek is about to become the most consequential piece of diplomatic real estate in Eurasia. Over three days, Kyrgyzstan's capital will host Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and, notably, only a U.S. special envoy. The imbalance is hard to miss. Xi Jinping arrives on Aug. 30 for a state visit, during which he will also play a leading role in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization's (SCO) annual summit, while Washington sends a senior envoy to watch folk games. On Aug. 31, SCO members and guests will pour into the city, including Putin, Erdogan, Modi, Iranian President Masood Pezeshkian and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. The main SCO summit and a parallel SCO-Plus gathering will be held on Sept. 1. Meanwhile, Aug. 31 is Kyrgyzstan’s Independence Day, marked by the opening of Bishkek Arena and the World Nomadic Games. It is this event that Gor, President Donald Trump’s highly active envoy, is set to attend. Gor's presence will ensure that Washington is not entirely absent from the diplomatic spotlight. He is also expected to hold separate meetings with Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and host President Sadyr Japarov, according to a diplomatic source. Center of new global competition Central Asia is emerging as a new battleground in great-power competition, because both the United States and China need the region to reduce their vulnerabilities to each other. China needs Eurasian energy and transport corridors to reduce its exposure to maritime chokepoints which could be blocked by the U.S. Navy in a contingency over Taiwan. The United States needs the region’s critical minerals to reduce its dependence on China. Amid the newly found focus on the region, Central Asian governments are doubling down on multi-vector foreign policy: relationships in every direction. Kazakhstan, which borders both Russia and China, has just held a fresh round of elections, following constitutional reform, to strengthen political stability at home. The goal is to make decision-making more agile in a less predictable global environment. The memory of January 2022 , when political unrest forced Tokayev to call in the Russia-led CSTO, remains a stark reminder of how domestic instability can quickly create foreign dependence. While Russia is consumed by the war in Ukraine, China sees an opportunity to expand its influence in Central Asia. The United States cannot afford to be absent as Beijing deepens its position in the heart of Eurasia. This week in Bishkek, China will have the upper hand: Xi will attend as head of state, while Washington sends only an envoy. Trump should change that next year. Trump-like merchants He has a chance to become the first sitting U.S. president to visit Central Asia. The groundwork is already being laid. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is scheduled to travel to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on Oct. 18 and 19 to meet Central Asian counterparts for a C5+1 meeting, according to Central Asian sources. Astana, Kazakhstan's capital, and Tashkent, Uzbekistan's capital, would be logical destinations for Trump, paying tribute to Central Asia's largest economy and most populous nation, respectively. But Samarkand, the ancient Silk Road crossroads, could offer the ideal photo op. The turquoise domes of Registan Square belong to madrassas, or Islamic schools, not mosques. Standing before them would signal an American president paying respect to the Islamic world's contributions to human knowledge, such as algebra, algorithms, astronomy and celestial mapping. For centuries, merchants traded with whoever arrived. Trump would feel right at home. None of the five Central Asian countries is rated “Free” by Freedom House . But they sit atop enormous reserves of oil, gas, uranium and critical minerals. Trump in Samarkand would show an American president arriving not to lecture, wage war or demand allegiance, but to do business. The United States does not need to dominate Central Asia. It just needs to make sure no other power does. As Beijing seeks to reduce its dependence on maritime chokepoints, the old Silk Road is again becoming strategically important. More than a century ago, British poet James Elroy Flecker wrote: "For lust of knowing what should not be known, we take the Golden Road to Samarkand ." Next year, the president of the United States should take that road. Beijing will be watching. Read in Türkiye Today. Enjoyed this analysis? title: Mr. Trump, Take the Golden Road to Samarkand

body: SVG Commentary Aug 25, 2026 Washington Post I Was a US Diplomat for 20 Years. Now I See How the Iran War Could Be Won. The best outcome for core US interests is the collapse of the regime. Ludovic Hood Senior Fellow, Center for Peace and Security in the Middle East Ludovic Hood Commentary Caption An Iranian national flag waves on a street in downtown Tehran, Iran, on August 23, 2026. (Getty Images) On Monday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the Trump administration’s planned “economic D-Day” for Iran: a patient campaign to financially strangle the regime in Tehran. The plan calls for full-throttle enforcement of U.S. sanctions and discreet yet hard-nosed diplomatic engagement with Beijing and other actors who facilitate illicit trade and cash flows with Iran. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime,” Bessent declared . President Donald Trump is right to resort to an intensive economic pressure campaign, backed by the implicit threat of renewed kinetic action. The regime and Iran’s economy have taken a beating, compounding the country’s preexisting woes. Moreover, talks are likely to continue to sputter. Twenty years of experience as an American diplomat has made me realize that no amount of diplomatic ingenuity can contain Iran. The United States should keep pushing until it gets the best outcome for American interests, the region and the Iranian people: the shattering of the illegitimate regime in Tehran. Iran’s rulers have outmaneuvered a succession of U.S. administrations. Jimmy Carter’s presidency foundered over the Iran hostage crisis ; Ronald Reagan took out half of Iran’s navy in Operation Praying Mantis but his legacy was tarnished by the Iran-contra scandal; George W. Bush declared Iran part of an “axis of evil” without ever confronting it directly; and Barack Obama subordinated much of his foreign policy to a quixotic bid to negotiate the regime into moderation. At each turn, Iran’s rulers proved clever opponents willing to suffer military losses and risk economic catastrophe in order to maintain their grip on power. I was sent to Kuwait for my first State Department assignment, arriving in 2007 at the peak of Iraq’s bloody civil war and the onset of Gen. David H. Petraeus’s “ surge .” The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps drove much of the violence, building death squads and militias and arming them with IEDs that killed and injured hundreds of U.S. servicemembers . The U.S. ambassador to Iraq, Ryan Crocker, engaged Iranian officials in the first public, formal talks since 1979, but Tehran stalled and kept killing. My subsequent tour in Bahrain coincided with the onset of the Arab Spring protests in 2010. Popular grievances fueled the demonstrations, but Iran exploited the situation, pouring fuel on sectarian tensions that reverberated through the region. Gulf rulers seized on fears of Iranian interference to justify the Saudi-led intervention that put an end to the protests. From 2011-13, I coordinated State Department policy for Lebanon — a country hollowed out by decades of Iranian meddling and hostage to Tehran’s shadow war against Israel. Billions of dollars of IRGC backing meant Hezbollah outgunned Lebanon’s national army and possessed an arsenal of about 60,000 rockets and missiles aimed at Israeli towns and cities. As President Bashar al-Assad’s murderous repression led to civil war in neighboring Syria, Iran in 2013 dispatched Hezbollah and other regional militias to shore up the Assad regime — fueling a conflict that led to over half a million deaths . During my next assignment as the “Iran watcher” in Paris, I was privy to the Obama administration’s determined — and at times desperate — effort to sign a nuclear accord with Tehran. Iran’s negotiators were (and remain) savvy and cunning interlocutors who extracted U.S. concessions that concerned our French counterparts. My experiences in Paris and the Persian Gulf made me see the logic of Trump’s exit from the nuclear agreement and, during postings in Qatar and in the White House on the staff of Vice President Mike Pence, I witnessed the benefits of the president’s “maximum pressure” campaign. However, a variety of diplomatic considerations tempered the efficacy of the campaign and the policy failed to yield to new talks, let alone a comprehensive deal. Uranium enrichment and missile production carried on. Iran continued to sow havoc in the region. The mullahs might not have orchestrated Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attacks , but IRGC know-how and hundreds of millions of dollars of funding over two decades enabled the rampage across southern Israel that killed more than 1,200 people, including 46 Americans. The Hamas attack marked an inflection point in the Middle East’s evolution: It ended tentative moves by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and others to improve relations with Israel, and it transformed long-standing tensions in the Levant and Persian Gulf into inexorable and overlapping cycles of violence. Earlier in my career, in 2008, Saudi Arabia’s King Abdullah urged U.S. officials to “ cut off the head of the snake ” by attacking Iran’s nuclear program. The more I learned about the region, the more I agreed with the king’s characterization: The regime in Tehran bears overwhelming responsibility for the mayhem and misery in the Middle East since 1979, and its hold on power is a dire threat to regional stability. The current showdown in the region is an inevitable result of the Iranian regime’s efforts to dominate the region through bullying, blackmail and terror. Iran’s rulers have shown time and again they will not accede to an arrangement that constrains their hegemonic aspirations. The best outcome for the region — and for core U.S. interests — is the regime’s collapse. The Islamic republic is in terminal decline: Iran’s economy is in free fall, its leadership is in disarray, and the government does not have legitimacy with the people. A patient, sustained campaign of economic and military pressure, coupled with hard-nosed diplomacy supported by our regional partners, can strike a mortal blow to a regime that grows more brittle with each passing day. Donate Hudson Institute’s Center for Defense Concepts and Technology examines the evolving field of military competition and the implications of emerging technologies for defense strategy, military operations, capability development, and acquisition. The center focuses on a comprehensive view: connecting strategy with new operational concepts; assessing the weapons and systems needed to implement new concepts; and evaluating the necessary commitment of resources. The center’s experts are focusing their initial research on the growing centrality of information and decision-making in military operations. US and allied militaries face great power and regional adversaries with improving capabilities and geographic advantages. Deterring and defeating aggression by these competitors will require military concepts that emphasize maneuver warfare and decision superiority rather than the attrition-focused approaches of the post-Cold War era. Tools and processes for harnessing and exploiting information will likely form the foundation of twenty-first century military superiority in the same way that chemistry, physics, and material sciences built the capabilities needed during twentieth century conflicts. Hudson Institute’s Center for Peace and Security in the Middle East studies the security threats to America and its allies arising from the Middle East and situates the region within the global great power competition in which the United States is engaged. Russia and China are using Iran—America’s long-time enemy and the leading state-sponsor of global terrorism—to weaken American leadership and threaten its allies, Israel first and foremost among them. Despite these facts, Washington’s foreign policy establishment is once again pursuing a policy of appeasement toward the Islamic Republic and fails to grasp Iran’s role in the broader great power contest. To remain the dominant player in the region and protect American interests, the United States must forge an alliance, with Israel at its center, dedicated preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and defeating Iranian forces and proxies, while also countering Russia’s and China’s attempts to expand their spheres of influence. Director Brigham McCown Senior Fellow and Director, Initiative on American Energy Security bmccown@hudson.org Media Inquiries press@hudson.org Follow: Support Support critical programs like Hudson's Initiative on American Energy Security. Donate International events have brought into acute focus the intrinsic relationship between energy security, economic security, and national security. They have also highlighted the degree to which dramatic shifts in US policy and, too often, the failure to consider the full and long-term implications of those policies have undermined an American strategic asset—abundant energy resources. Economic growth and prosperity will need affordable energy, even as remarkable improvements in technology and energy efficiency occur. National security requires secure access to multiple energy sources and raw materials—in particular, the United States needs these resources to project power globally to protect US and allied interests. Market access to the quantities and types of energy, when and where needed, along with the security and resiliency of energy systems require thoughtful and sustained long-term capital investments in production, distribution infrastructure, storage, and research and development—all of which require a predictable and stable policy environment. The Hudson initiative is conducting a comprehensive assessment of energy policies and practices leading to constructive policies that prioritize energy security, economic security, and national security—balanced with a realistic path to transition to a larger role for renewable energy sources. body: SVG Commentary Aug 28, 2026 First Breakfast Getting Creative About the Munitions Crisis Mike Gallagher Distinguished Fellow Nadia Schadlow Senior Fellow Mike Gallagher & Nadia Schadlow Commentary Caption Mortar shells move along a conveyor at General Dynamics in Scranton, Pennsylvania, on August 20, 2026. (Getty Images) First Breakfast asked several experts, “If you had free reign to fix America’s munitions bottleneck, what would you propose?” Below are responses from Mike Gallagher and Nadia Schadlow. Mike Gallagher: Stop Lighting Money on Fire The Pentagon is rightly rushing to spend every single one of its Congressionally appropriated dollars before the end of the fiscal year. If it succeeds, it will avoid a self-inflicted problem that has had a disastrous impact on our deterrent posture. In the last decade, the Pentagon has lost more than $125 billion because of an outdated budgeting process that requires any unspent, Congressionally appropriated dollars to be returned to the Treasury. In other words, billions of budgeted dollars have been allowed to simply vanish instead of being used to replenish munitions stockpiles, procure new technology, or invest into our defense industrial base. The FIRES Act I introduced as a member of Congress fixes that. Rather than let this appropriated but unspent money disappear, the FIRES Act puts these dollars into a special fund that the Secretary of War could use to fund Congressionally mandated priorities. This could go a long way toward supporting priorities that may prove decisive in a Pacific conflict. The first of these: Deputy Secretary Feinberg’s efforts to ramp munitions production via multi-year purchases. The second: scaling the manufacturing and deployment of autonomous capabilities that can turn China’s coastal waters into a hellscape. The third: funding advanced energetics such as CL-20 in existing systems to extend both their range and destructive power. The Pentagon has rightly identified munitions production and autonomy as key to preventing or winning war in the Pacific. But funding it sufficiently and in time remains a challenge. The FIRES Act gives the Secretary of War the flexibility and authority needed to fund enduring priorities at the speed of relevance, making us safer without budgeting another dime of taxpayer dollars. Nadia Schadlow: It’s Not Easy, But It’s Not Rocket Science In the category of “kind of simple” (recognizing that simple and the Pentagon are something of an oxymoron), there are some basic steps that could help avoid repeating past mistakes. Start by taking stock of recent efforts to support new entrants and expand capacity in the energetics space: What was funded? What actually got built? What new capacity came online? What worked, what didn’t, and why? This is not a “gotcha” exercise. It is a way to learn from recent investments and inform the next round. For example, in 2024 the Department of Defense awarded $192.5 million to seven companies under the Defense Production Act to expand domestic production of 22 chemicals used in defense systems, including critical energetic precursors and other materials such as oxidizers and magnesium. What resulted? Which projects delivered the capacity they promised? Which did not? And why? Read in First Breakfast. Enjoyed this analysis? body: SVG Commentary Aug 14, 2026 Arab News US Today Lacks Meaningful Leverage in Afghanistan Luke Coffey Senior Fellow, Center on Europe and Eurasia Luke Coffey Commentary Caption Taliban security personnel stand guard atop armored Humvees along a road in the Green Zone area in Kabul on August 12, 2026. (Getty Images) The fifth anniversary of the Taliban’s takeover of Afghanistan falls on Saturday. Yet, in Washington, one could be forgiven for barely noticing the occasion. Hindsight offers clarity and foreign policy should be no exception. The decision to withdraw all US forces from Afghanistan, and the way it was carried out, looks worse today than it did at the time. Perhaps this explains why few in Washington want to revisit it. Afghanistan was a bipartisan debacle. During his first term, President Donald Trump was determined to end America’s “forever wars.” His administration negotiated directly with the Taliban and signed the February 2020 Doha agreement, under which foreign forces were to leave Afghanistan by May 2021. When President Joe Biden entered office, he postponed the deadline by a few months but otherwise continued down the path set by his predecessor. Dislike of the Afghan mission was perhaps the one thing that united Trump and Biden. Biden had long opposed a large US presence there. During the Obama administration’s 2009 Afghanistan review, then-Vice President Biden argued for a smaller mission focused on counterterrorism. Meanwhile, others such as then-Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Defense Secretary Robert Gates and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Adm. Mike Mullen instead supported a surge-style approach like the strategy that had proved effective in Iraq. When Biden entered the White House in January 2021, only 2,500 US troops remained in Afghanistan. America continued to provide critical funding and support to Afghan security forces, including air support. American casualties during this period were minimal, while the financial burden of the military mission, in relative terms, was near its lowest level in almost two decades. The irony is that Biden inherited something close to the limited footprint he had advocated for years earlier. Yet he chose complete withdrawal. Biden later argued that his hands were tied by Trump’s agreement with the Taliban. That was never convincing. His administration reversed or discarded many Trump-era policies. It could have changed course in Afghanistan as well. It chose not to. The fall of Kabul in the summer of 2021 was not inevitable. No one should pretend that 2,500 American troops, allied forces and continued financial support were enough to bring every corner of Afghanistan under Kabul’s control. But their presence did prevent the Taliban from taking over the whole country, as it later did. The departure from Bagram Airfield in the middle of the night in early July 2021 served as the beginning of the disaster soon to unfold. But it did not have to be this way. And the Taliban takeover was not guaranteed that summer. Despite years of offensives and almost two decades of fighting, the Taliban had never been able to seize and hold a single provincial capital for any extended period. After the US departure from Bagram, however, the Taliban began capturing provincial capitals in rapid succession. Zaranj, the first provincial capital to fall, was captured on Aug. 6. Kabul fell on Aug. 15. Within weeks, a 20-year Western effort had collapsed. The consequences did not end at Afghanistan’s borders. In August 2021, the world watched desperate Afghans cling to departing aircraft as the US scrambled to evacuate Kabul. Only six months later, Russian tanks crossed into Ukraine. America’s adversaries saw disorder and indecision. Allies questioned American resolve. Vladimir Putin’s decision to invade had many causes, but the perception of US weakness almost certainly informed his timing. The road to Kyiv, in that sense, first passed through Kabul. Afghanistan has also again become a concern for transnational terrorism. UN reporting warns about the presence of Al-Qaeda, Daesh, Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan and other Central Asian extremist organizations operating from Afghanistan. Whatever the Taliban claim about preventing Afghan territory from threatening other countries, the concentration of such groups should concern the region. Taliban rule has also contributed to worsening relations with Pakistan. Islamabad accuses the Taliban authorities of harboring Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan militants responsible for attacks against Pakistani security forces and government targets. Against the backdrop of the Pakistan-India rivalry — and New Delhi’s growing engagement with the Taliban — the potential for wider regional instability should not be dismissed. The greatest tragedy, however, is borne by ordinary Afghans. Humanitarian needs remain enormous. Taliban restrictions have complicated international assistance. Natural disasters, economic isolation and declining donor attention have compounded the suffering. Girls remain barred from secondary and higher education, women face sweeping restrictions on public life, and religious and ethnic minorities continue to live under pressure. The US, after investing lives, treasure and two decades of effort in Afghanistan, now lacks meaningful leverage inside the country. Many Afghans who worked alongside Americans remain displaced or uncertain about their futures. Terrorist networks remain active. Russia, China and regional powers have expanded their engagement while Washington’s influence has diminished. Five years later, policymakers should acknowledge what went wrong. Afghanistan before 2021 was deeply flawed. There were serious problems with corruption in the government. The security situation remained stable but fragile. And no one on either side could credibly claim victory. But it is equally difficult to argue that today’s Afghanistan better serves American interests. Next month, the US will mark the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, which were planned by Al-Qaeda from its sanctuary provided by the Taliban. A quarter of a century later, the Taliban controls more of Afghanistan than it did on Sept. 11, 2001. That fact alone should force reflection. Leaving Afghanistan in the manner the US did was a strategic mistake. It weakened America’s position, abandoned hard-earned leverage, emboldened adversaries and exposed Afghans to a brutal regime. This could all have been avoided. Read in Arab News. Enjoyed this analysis? Subscribe to Hudson’s newsletters to stay up to date with our latest content. Email See more subscription options Foreign Policy Terrorism Politics and Government
title: US Today Lacks Meaningful Leverage in Afghanistan

body: SVG Reports Aug 4, 2026 New Initiatives at the DoW’s Office of Industrial Base Growth The Arsenal Papers | No. 1 — Less Process, More Power Nadia Schadlow Senior Fellow Michael Dressler Research Associate Nadia Schadlow & Michael Dressler Reports Caption A production line of the Glide, a high-altitude glider that delivers munitions across thousands of miles, is seen at the defense tech startup Mach Industries in Huntington Beach, California, on September 11, 2025. (Getty Images) View PDF The authors would like to thank Matthew Florance, Thianna Chisholm, Philip Dackiw, and Naveen Wineland for their excellent research support. Introduction Revitalizing and expanding the United States defense industrial base (DIB) is a top priority for the second Trump administration, which recognizes that “American national power depends on a strong industrial sector capable of meeting both peacetime and wartime production demands.” [1] In line with this assessment, the 2026 National Defense Strategy (NDS) set the goal of making the United States “the world’s premier arsenal, one that can produce not only for ourselves but also for our allies and partners at scale, rapidly, and at the highest levels of quality.” [2] The Department of War (DoW) has been driving this effort by implementing long-overdue reforms across the national security ecosystem. Yet much of this important work is happening out of the public eye. As a result, interested individuals often have difficulty understanding the purpose of key reforms and cannot appreciate the progress taking place. The Arsenal Papers seek to highlight these key policy developments and reforms in the defense industrial sector and explain their significance. The objective is to foster a better understanding of how DoW is working to increase warfighting readiness, supply chain resilience, and the nation’s ability to rapidly scale defense production in response to emerging global threats. The reports will not cover all of the DoW’s efforts, which would be unrealistic. Rather, they will be episodic explainers drawn from Hudson Institute’s conversations with key policy officials. The first in this series focuses on initiatives underway at the Office of Industrial Base Growth (IBG). The office’s inaugural head is Deputy Assistant Secretary of War (DASW) for Industrial Base Growth James Mismash, who is also the director of the DoW Office of Small Business Programs. DASW Mismash and his team are pursuing multiple initiatives to foster greater participation in the US defense marketplace. IBG is involved in several interrelated initiatives. It operates the LYNX platform, which supports the burgeoning Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network (CRMN); these initiatives assist new entrants into the DIB. The office is also leading efforts to put the long-running 1260H List into practice by implementing Section 805 of the Fiscal Year (FY) 2024 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) and Section 851 of the FY 2025 NDAA; these efforts are focused on reducing reliance on China. This report examines the purpose of these tools and how IBG uses them to advance the pool of new entrants into the DIB and the administration’s goals for American industry. Specifically, it explores how LYNX and CRMN can be used cooperatively to expand the US DIB by raising the visibility of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), giving them direct paths into the defense marketplace, and enabling them to make their extensive industrial capacity available to the DoW. It also explores how the 1260H List is increasing the transparency of US critical supply chains and how Section 805 and Section 851 aim to gradually eliminate the United States’ material dependence on China by improving cooperation with domestic manufacturers. Background: The Office of Industrial Base Growth DoW established IBG in January 2026 as part of a growing push within the federal government over the last several years to revitalize and restructure the US DIB. This was a priority for the first Trump administration, which issued Executive Order (EO) 13806, “Assessing and Strengthening the Manufacturing and Defense Industrial Base and Supply Chain Resiliency of the United States.” This order mandated an in-depth review of US manufacturing capacity and supply chain resiliency. [3] The report resulting from this EO, published in 2018, identified a wide array of weaknesses across the American defense industrial sector, which successive administrations have sought to remedy. The second Trump administration is working to revitalize production capabilities, partly by encouraging the entry of new participants into the defense sector through both new and existing mechanisms, including Defense Production Act Title III and the financial incentives it provides, as well as authorities such as loans and purchase-offtake agreements, in addition to newly developed platforms such as LYNX that aim to simplify the acquisition process. The administration has also signaled this intention through national strategy documents. The 2025 National Security Strategy (NSS) noted the need to “innovate powerful defenses at low cost” and “re-shore our defense industrial supply chains.” [4] Similarly, the 2026 NDS called for a “national mobilization” to “bolster our organic sustainment capabilities, grow nontraditional vendors, and partner with traditional DIB vendors.” [5] The prime contractors that have come to dominate the DIB cannot completely meet these objectives. While established defense companies remain crucial to US national security, their organizational complexity and incentive structures often make them far less effective at rapidly innovating, producing, and surging production. To promote these outcomes at scale, it is essential to create pathways for emerging firms with novel technologies to enter the defense marketplace. Reshoring the American defense industrial supply chain will require a broader ecosystem of domestic producers comprising a range of companies with different areas of expertise—including highly specialized entities and larger and smaller commercial enterprises. Commercial entities of all sizes and specialties, working together across the DIB, could comprise a diverse defense manufacturing ecosystem to fulfill US production needs in peace or in war. This view motivated the DoW to create IBG. [6] Previously, the DoW Office of Small Business Programs (OSBP), established in 1978, sought to increase small enterprises’ participation in defense programs, [7] and its mandates and programs were separate from the Pentagon’s interactions with larger, established manufacturers. This segregated approach led to a systemic disconnect in the department’s engagement with industry, limiting its ability to implement a national industrial strategy that would truly revitalize the DIB. The 2025 NSS, however, made clear that expanding the DIB required cultivating new entrants of all sizes, including larger commercial firms that could contribute to national reindustrialization efforts. [8] The creation of the new office and its subsumption of OSBP constitute DoW’s first steps toward putting this understanding into practice. IBG: Expanding and Strengthening the Defense Industrial Base As DoW has officially explained, IBG is the umbrella organization for efforts focused on “expanding and strengthening the defense industrial base through vendor growth and supplier maturity.” [9] In addition to broadening recruitment efforts beyond small businesses, IBG is focused on actively helping new entrants, mid-tier firms, and non-traditional contractors succeed in the defense ecosystem. By helping firms secure their first government contract—an objective OSBP has historically undertaken—the office hopes to further identify and secure long-term industrial capacity to meet pressing US defense needs. These changes position IBG at the intersection of four important questions: 1. How can the federal government help more firms enter, compete,
title: New Initiatives at the DoW’s Office of Industrial Base Growth

body: SVG Reports Aug 20, 2026 Hudson Institute A Test Case for US Resolve: Securing the Release of Uyghur Doctor Gulshan Abbas Olivia Enos Senior Fellow Olivia Enos Reports Caption Rushan Abbas holds a photo of her sister, Uyghur doctor Gulshan Abbas, who is detained in China, during the “No Deals Without Freedom” protest at Lafayette Park on May 11, 2026, in Washington, DC. (Getty Images) View Full PDF In September 2018, Dr. Gulshan Abbas, a 64-year-old doctor with no history of political activism, was disappeared from her hometown of Urumqi, the capital of the Uyghur Autonomous Region, during a state-sponsored mass arrest. [1] Her disappearance came mere days after her sister, Rushan Abbas, spoke at a Hudson Institute event on the Chinese government’s ongoing atrocities against Uyghurs. [2] Within six months of her disappearance, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) sentenced Dr. Abbas to 20 years in prison on fabricated charges of “participating in a terrorist organization” as well as “aiding terrorist activities” and “gathering a crowd to disrupt social order.” [3] She remains behind bars. The case of Dr. Abbas has long been a priority for the United States, partly because she has more than 24 family members who are American citizens. The government recognizes that her case is unique in that she was detained because her American relative exercised her right to free speech. On July 4 of this year, Chinese pastor Ezra Jin Mingri, who was detained with other pastors and associates of Zion Church, arrived in the United States after the Trump administration secured his release. [4] His safe arrival on the 250th anniversary of US independence was an unmitigated victory for freedom and indicated that the CCP may be willing to release political prisoners before President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the White House in September. [5] The United States should insist on the release of political prisoners across China before rolling out the red carpet for Xi. [6] Washington should also consider Pastor Jin’s release to be just the beginning of its efforts to secure political prisoners’ freedom, especially as his release happened shortly after Chinese authorities detained Burmese-American academic Min Zin in June of this year. [7] The administration should focus on the release of Dr. Abbas and other high-priority political prisoners before the September meeting. By obtaining the release of Abbas, the eight remaining Zion Church associates, and Hong Kong pro-democracy advocate Jimmy Lai, the US would not merely demonstrate its benevolence but would also signal its strength. America has the upper hand in negotiations. Economically, China needs the US more than the US needs China. [8] In addition, visiting the US would be a privilege for Xi. Washington should condition the visit on the release of several priority political prisoners, including Dr. Abbas. Why Abbas’s Release Matters for US Interests While every political prisoner has inherent value as an individual, Dr. Abbas’s case is unique because it overlaps with several issues of concern to the United States: Her detention has direct implications for her American relatives. Not only is she a peaceful, 64-year-old doctor with no history of political activism, but Dr. Abbas also has 24 American citizen family members, including her two brothers and a sister, as well as her two daughters and a number of grandchildren. Many of them have directly advocated at the highest levels of the US government to secure the release of their mother, sister, and grandmother. What started as an act of transnational repression against adult American citizens is now impacting innocent American children, including Dr. Abbas’s grandchildren who have never been able to hug their grandmother. The US has a history of prioritizing American citizens in its advocacy, and in this case, she has dozens of American citizen family members who are demonstrably harmed by her ongoing detention. Her detention has implications for free speech in the United States. The timing of Dr. Abbas’s arrest and initial detention clearly demonstrates that the Chinese government was retaliating against her sister’s outspokenness on the plight of the Uyghur people. This is one of the clearest-cut cases of transnational repression—where the CCP commits crimes against individuals who speak out against the party beyond the country’s borders. Rushan Abbas, like any American, has the right to freedom of speech; her remarks should never have led to her sister’s detention and sentencing. A strong US stance in support of Dr. Abbas would signal American commitment to defending free speech. Her detention has implications for US efforts to counter forced labor across China. Abbas has been detained since 2018, first in a political “reeducation” camp and later in a prison adjacent to a factory where, given the CCP’s long history of “reeducation” through forced labor, she likely was subjected to this practice. Marco Rubio, while serving in the Senate, was the lead sponsor of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act. The administration continues to view forced labor as an issue of concern, as demonstrated by its recent imposition of Section 301 tariffs, which it implemented, in part, on forced labor grounds. [9] Her detention has implications for US efforts to advance religious freedom. Dr. Abbas is a Uyghur Muslim. The CCP has wrongfully labeled Uyghurs a threat on the basis of their faith and used that as justification for its ongoing genocide and crimes against humanity. Dr. Abbas is one of the 1.8 million Uyghurs who have been detained inside China’s vast system of political reeducation camps, a clear example of the price Uyghurs pay for the ongoing atrocity crimes the CCP continues to carry out. [10] During the previous Trump administration, the US became the first country to formally issue a determination that Uyghurs face genocide and crimes against humanity, and now the president has the opportunity to act on that determination by securing Dr. Abbas’s freedom. [11] Failing to prioritize her release would have implications for issues of increasing importance to the US government and signal weakness to Xi. Dr. Abbas has been detained for nearly eight years and has served nearly half of her 20-year sentence. [12] She suffers from serious health conditions, including high blood pressure, severe osteoporosis that often leads to immobilization, and an eye condition that requires annual monitoring to prevent permanent blindness. [13] Given her age, her health, and the amount of time she has served, the CCP could easily release her. The Way Forward Ongoing negotiations between Trump and Xi have created an opportunity to win the release of Gulshan Abbas and other political prisoners. It is past time for the US government to make good on promises to prioritize Dr. Abbas’s case and secure her release. Her case is well-known: a bipartisan, bicameral congressional resolution passed in May 2026 that called for the release of high-priority political prisoners included her and several others, including Pastor Jin. [14] (Pastor Jin’s case set a precedent for prioritizing the release of political prisoners who are not US citizens but have family members who are.) Speaker of the House Mike Johnson invited Dr. Abbas’s daughter, Ziba Murat, to the State of the Union address earlier this year as a special guest. [15] Heads of state and secretaries of state have met with Dr. Abbas’s family and expressed a commitment to securing her release, and her daughter and sister have spoken at the United Nations on her behalf. Yet despite her fame, diplomats have made little progress in securing her release. President Trump could change this if he raised her case by name in negotiations with Xi. The US government should do the following: Press for Dr. Abbas’s release. Before Xi’s White House visit, President Trump should demand that China release Dr. Abbas and ensure she is reunited
title: A Test Case for US Resolve: Securing the Release of Uyghur Doctor Gulshan Abbas

body: SVG Commentary Sep 11, 2026 Law and Liberty What We Remember Twenty-five years after 9/11, Americans may once again need to call on the strength we found in their aftermath. John P. Walters President and CEO John P. Walters Commentary Caption An unidentified man with a face mask walks on an ash-covered street near Ground Zero after the collapse of the Twin Towers on September 11, 2001, in New York City. (Getty Images) Rereading the 9/11 Commission Report triggers a flood of memories for anyone over 30. The “just-the-facts” description of the attacks brings back the agony and heartbreak of that terrible day and the days following as we searched desperately for the victims and then laid them to rest. Looking back, the Report’s recommendations seem a bit underwhelming and even naïve (for example, reorganizing the committee structure of Congress). Some of them were implemented, and others were not. Some were better ideas than others. They were not nearly enough, however. With the experience of 25 years, what should the 9/11 attacks and their aftermath teach us today? First, the attacks might make us wonder if the notion of a divided America is more superficial and circumstantial than it seems. Under the sudden threat of terrorism, America united. We were all embattled brothers and sisters. Our common ideals almost instantly came to the fore as a wellspring of strength and unity. And we were inspired by the heroic acts of some of the victims and the first responders. Before the attacks, George W. Bush won a divisive election so close it required a Supreme Court decision to settle the result. Bitterness and division lingered, prompting such comments as, “He’s not my president.” But when President Bush spoke to a Joint Session of Congress on September 20 and when he walked alone to the mound in a packed Yankee Stadium on October 30, 2001, and threw a strike to start Game 3 of the World Series, he was everyone’s president. He was the undisputed leader of a united America. The enemy sought to make us afraid, divided, and weak. They failed spectacularly. Americans—and our enemies today —should reflect on this lesson from 9/11. Such intense unity could not—and did not—last, of course. Political differences are the stuff of American democracy. As the Founders explained, they are the natural result of freedom, self-interest, and political ambition. The terrorist attacks of 9/11 did not keep us from eventually returning to normal. But the second crucial lesson of 9/11 is that this did not matter in the decisive sense. As my friend Tod Lindberg recently reminded us in the pages of Commentary , we won the Global War on Terror even as we debated and disagreed about the means and ends. We still changed our routines, reduced vulnerabilities, and transformed our military, intelligence, and law enforcement institutions to fight terror. The result, as Lindberg notes, is, “There aren’t many terrorist groups of global reach left in business. That’s impressive in its own right,” even though “the question is whether we can maintain our vigilance.” At times, we may have won ugly, but we won—there were no more successful mass-casualty attacks. We created a new normal to preserve that victory and indeed our liberty. Every 9/11 we should remember, with the deepest gratitude, those who sacrificed for this victory and those on the front lines who sustain it each day. The third lesson from 9/11 is embedded in how we won. After examining the vulnerabilities of our free and open nation and recognizing that ruthless homicidal enemies cannot be stopped with defensive and deterrence methods alone, America changed the rules and took the fight to them. Many still do not like preemption or a global policy of “finding, fixing, and finishing” those at war with America. But we faced the reality of the threat, and we did what had to be done. Republican and Democrat administrations alike achieved this. We deprived our enemies of financial resources and arrested many of those who could be apprehended. Most of all, however, we deployed old and new techniques to kill the worst, in large numbers. We hear the mocking phrase, “You cannot win playing whack-a-mole.” Actually, we did. If you find and isolate or eliminate an enemy’s key leaders and fighters, you weaken that enemy. This works as a strategic policy only if you can find, fix, and finish enough of the enemy’s critical personnel, at a pace sufficient to degrade and ultimately collapse its offensive capacity. This is not “body count” or “dumb whack-a-mole.” How we won is what we need to remember most this 9/11. Why? Because we are going to have to do it again. We may not have to go to war the same way against today’s enemies as we did against Al-Qaeda in 2001, but they must be confronted with the same resolve and many of the same tactics. Those who seek to collapse the American-led order are powerful, sophisticated, and united. They use criminal and terrorist proxies as well as large arsenals of state-of-the-art weapons. They are already using some of them—in Ukraine, in the Indo-Pacific, in Europe, and even within the United States. Information warfare, cyberattacks, probing by drones, and the subversion of institutions are only part of the ongoing attacks. As we saw on 9/11, terrorism breaks the rules. It kills and harms not as an unavoidable excess in war, but as a fundamental goal. This thinking—call it the strategic immorality of terrorism—makes all means of inflicting harm welcome tools. Twenty-five years later, individuals associated with the regimes of Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin continue to embrace this morality. Their militaries have published and celebrated documents that portray victory in war as requiring the breaking of existing moral constraints. The goal is to use our self-imposed, civilized limitations as a strategic weapon against us and our allies. These arguments within Putin’s military explicitly include the use of nuclear weapons to create and then use fear. Iran and North Korea similarly anchored their highest hopes on such weapons. Moreover, Putin has kidnapped Ukrainian children and regularly uses terror strikes on civilian targets. Putin uses banned chemical weapons in ground combat in Ukraine , and he has notoriously killed enemies, sometimes using dangerous poisons . We also know that Xi and Putin are pursuing military research on biological pathogens that are now becoming targetable to specific populations and individuals. Today, our enemies in Putin’s Russia, Xi’s Chinese Communist Party, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and Kim Jong Un’s North Korea are more dangerous than the terrorists of 9/11. They are seeking and testing means of attack in all domains, from the heavens to the depths of the sea and from inside our bodies and minds. Their sophistication makes it difficult to track all evolving threats and develop countermeasures. The wars in Ukraine and Iran are a form of preemption, even as Putin and Iran’s leaders probe for new means of attack for strategic advantage. These wars are weakening dangerous enemies . Is America more ready than it was on September 10, 2001? Yes, I think it is. But is it ready enough ? On the morning of 9/11, we knew Osama bin Laden and Al-Qaeda were going to strike the United States, but we did not know precisely when and how—we could not stop those attacks, and we followed rules that made Americans victims. Now we know better. May our leaders use that knowledge in the face of today’s enemies and may the American people support such leadership. The anniversary of 9/11 is also an occasion to reflect on the words of Victor Davis Hanson in his book Carnage and Culture : Western civilization has given mankind the only economic system that works, a rationalist tradition that alone allows us material and technological progress, the sole political structure that ensures the freedom of the individual, a system of ethics and a religion that brings out the best in humankind—and t
title: What We Remember

body: SVG Commentary Sep 11, 2026 Hudson Institute Twenty-Five Years after 9/11: A Morning I Shall Never Forget Ludovic Hood Senior Fellow, Center for Peace and Security in the Middle East Ludovic Hood Commentary Caption People walk up a ramp from FDR Drive as they evacuate from Lower Manhattan in the wake of the terrorist attacks in New York City on September 11, 2001. (Getty Images) At 8:46 a.m. on September 11, 2001, I was standing on the platform at Canal Street in lower Manhattan, awaiting the downtown express train. A loud boom sounded through the tunnels, causing other straphangers to look up quizzically before returning to their newspapers. I later realized the noise was American Airlines Flight 11 crashing into the North Tower. At about 8:55 a.m., I walked up and out of the Wall Street subway station. High above me, papers fluttered in the clear sky. I initially thought it was a publicity stunt associated with an initial public offering at the New York Stock Exchange. At 9:03 a.m., I stepped out of my usual bagel shop and looked west. At that moment, I heard a loud roar and then saw a flash of orange on an airplane, United Airlines Flight 175, right before it crashed into the upper floors of the South Tower. Seconds later, scores of people came running toward me, and I stepped back into the shop. By 9:15 a.m., I was standing about a block away from the World Trade Center, looking up at the two towers. The impact sites were so high up that it was hard to comprehend the size of the fires. People around me speculated that radar issues caused two Cessnas to fly into the towers. More grimly, others talked about people jumping out of the North Tower. By about 9:30 a.m., I grew concerned that I couldn’t reach my brother on his cell phone. He typically used the World Trade Center subway stop to commute to his office nearby. Nearly all cell networks were overloaded. At about 9:42 a.m., people around me said the Pentagon had been hit and that other New York City sites might be under attack. I started to walk to my office on Exchange Place. By 9:58 a.m., I was in my 34th-floor office at 20 Exchange Place. My brother, with whom I had finally spoken, came out of the elevator and joined me in the common area. At 9:59 a.m., a colleague yelled, “The tower’s collapsing!” We ran to the window. Thirty stories beneath us, a massive cloud of dust rushed toward the foot of the building and then raced up toward us. Within seconds, it reached our floor, and the blue sky disappeared. At about 10:20 a.m., we walked out of the building into the gently swirling dust. Someone in the lobby had ripped up a shirt, and we covered our faces with the strips of cloth. My brother and I started to walk toward the South Street Seaport. At 10:28 a.m., we heard a distant roar and, after a minute, the dust around us became more intense. The North Tower had collapsed. My brother and I then spent the next hour or so walking up the side of the FDR Drive. We were too spooked to head back into the heart of downtown, given reports of additional attacks. I recall bumming cigarettes from strangers along the way—our hands were shaking. My main recollection from that day and the days that followed is a sense of both sadness and togetherness. I had lived in Manhattan for much of the prior decade—I loved the city. The murder of 3,000 people was unfathomable. At the same time, New York City residents and commuters had a common bond—you felt the solidarity everywhere in those early weeks. The nihilistic ideology that led to the September 11 attacks persists. It has killed thousands of people in suicide bombings, terrorist attacks, and wars in countries across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. America exhausted itself trying to fight it. Some Middle Eastern governments understand the dire threat this ideology poses, but it feels like many Western politicians do not or will not, out of fear of being offensive. I look at the foreign policy priorities of New York City’s mayor and the United Kingdom’s new prime minister, for example, and I can only shake my head in disbelief. Enjoyed this analysis?
