body: Getting a Security Clearance Doesn't Have to Be So Intimidating: Q&A with Sina Beaghley Commentary Sep 9, 2026 Photo by Panya7/Getty Images Sina Beaghley has worked for years to solve a problem that could keep good candidates from considering government service. Intelligence officers, members of the military, and other key government employees and contractors have to undergo security screening. The process can be difficult and time-consuming. A few clicks on the internet, and prospective candidates can find countless stories of people stuck in security-clearance limbo. Yet the government has made big strides in modernizing and improving the process. Beaghley , a senior international and defense researcher at RAND, has provided much of the research underpinning that effort. She and her research teams have also developed plain-English guidance to make the process less intimidating. Do applicants need to report past marijuana use? Yes. Will seeking treatment for a mental health concern automatically disqualify them from a federal position? No. Beaghley came to RAND from the National Security Council staff, where she led the security review following a massive leak of classified documents in 2013 by then-contractor Edward Snowden. She has also worked at the National Counterterrorism Center, the Pentagon, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Treasury Department. What's at stake in efforts to improve the security clearance process? This is really about recruiting and retaining the best candidates for government service, especially those who can be trusted with federal security clearances. These are the people the government needs to execute its missions. But if the clearance process is too cumbersome, it's going to discourage them from even applying. It can also cause confusion, which opens the door to a lot of misinformation when people turn to the internet for advice. Subscribe to the Policy Currents newsletter Email Subscribe What are some of the most common examples of misinformation you've found? People think that things like student debt or foreign travel will disqualify them from getting a job that requires a federal clearance. But the reality is that there are very few issues that automatically disqualify someone. When there are concerns, what the government looks for is mitigating factors. So maybe you had a drug problem, but you sought treatment and haven't touched drugs for years. That's something where the government will have to decide: Is this person a risk? Or have they mitigated the problem, and we can trust them? Another big misperception is with dual citizenship . We found a really widespread perception that dual citizens can't get a security clearance. One hundred percent not true. In fact, the U.S. government wants people who have foreign experience and expertise in some of these key national security positions. They can make the government more effective in executing international policy. But they do, clearly, need to display loyalty to the United States. Where would you make changes? The government has been working for years now to improve this process, and it's done a lot already. But it's not all the way there yet . You ask almost anyone who's gotten a security clearance, and unless they've never traveled, have no foreign contacts—have absolutely no reportable situations—they're going to have stories about how long it took or how difficult it was. At RAND, we've really focused on improving the experience for applicants. So, for example, putting everything in plain language so people can understand it. Making sure the instructions are consistent across agencies. The idea is to improve recruitment and retention, and that requires people who are willing to go through the process. The process can't be such a nightmare that people don't even want to embark on it. The reality is that there are very few issues that automatically disqualify someone. What advice would you give someone considering a job that requires vetting? My best advice: Be honest. Most issues have mitigating factors that the government will look at. But if you're not honest, then the issue becomes your personal conduct. The government will say, “You weren't honest here, so how can we expect you to be honest in the future?” And then, don't let the process intimidate you. Understand that it's not necessarily going to be the quickest and easiest process, but there are resources out there that can help. Our RAND team developed a toolkit that includes a step-by-step guide so people know what to expect. It has tips for completing the vetting questionnaire ( PDF ) , section by section, explaining what to include and what not to include. And we tried, as much as possible, to put it all into plain English. You've been through the process a few times. What was your experience like? I was actually just updating my security clearance as I was writing our most recent report on this. And I had to call a support hotline twice and ask for help because parts of the process were so unclear. And that's for me, who's supposed to be an expert here! Fortunately, someone did answer my questions and helped me make sure I was providing the correct information. So that's progress in improving the applicant experience, and I'll take that! body: What the Record Shows on Corporate Veteran Support George Zuo , Jeffrey B. Wenger Research Summary Published Sep 9, 2026 Download PDF Share on LinkedIn Share on X Share on Facebook Email Photo by Flashizzle/peopleimages.com / Adobe Stock Large corporations have the scale and reach to shape veterans’ transitions into civilian careers, and many publicly commit to hiring and supporting veterans. Focusing on Standard and Poor’s 500 (S&P 500) firms, RAND researchers analyzed publicly available data on what companies say about veteran support, how their foundations give to veteran causes, and the extent to which federal contractors hire protected veterans. Here's what the data shows: What companies say about veteran support only weakly aligns with how they give and hire. Companies with stronger veteran messaging do not consistently direct more foundation giving to veteran causes or report higher protected veteran hiring rates, and these companies rarely report verifiable retention or advancement outcomes. Corporate foundations direct little of their grantmaking to veteran causes. Veteran-related grants account for less than 1 percent of observed S&P 500 foundation giving, and most active corporate foundations direct no grant dollars to veteran causes. Protected veteran hiring at S&P 500 contractor establishments remained below the national planning benchmark for federal contractors. In the 2025 hiring cycle, protected veterans accounted for 2.4 percent of new hires, compared with the 5.1 percent national benchmark. More military-related federal business does not reliably translate into stronger observable veteran support. Industries with greater military-related contract exposure do not consistently disclose more, give more, or hire more veterans. The broader diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) retreat may have spilled over to veteran disclosures and programs. High-quality veteran disclosures fell sharply in 2025 and the first half of 2026 amid increased federal scrutiny of private-sector DEI, even though federal protections and obligations for veteran hiring remained. Case studies suggest that some firms had housed veteran programs alongside other DEI activities and drew on the same staff and resources. Public data capture veteran hiring far better than they capture retention or advancement. Federally required contractor reports provide standardized head counts and new-hire counts for protected veterans at federal contractors, but these reports do not track whether veterans stay or advance. Corporate disclosures almost never voluntarily provide that information. These findings highlight the limits of the public record and do not provide a complete assessment of any company’s veteran programs. The full report outlines federal policy options for strengthening disclosures to provide a fuller view of veteran hiring, retention, advancement, and investment. body: When Disaster Strikes, Could AI Help? Q&A with Jessica Jensen Commentary Sep 2, 2026 Evacuations in the Ravenswood neighborhood due to flooding after days of heavy rain in Indianapolis, Indiana, August 15, 2026 Photo by Michelle Pemberton/USA Today via Reuters When disaster strikes, the public sees the most visible parts of the response: evacuations, first responders, rescue operations, and recovery efforts. But behind the scenes is a much larger network of people working to help communities manage through chaos. That job is getting harder. Disasters are more frequent, more severe, and more costly. Pressure is mounting on emergency managers and the organizations that support them. In a new RAND study supported by the Markle Foundation as part of the AI for Disasters and Emergencies Initiative (AIDE) , senior policy researcher Jessica Jensen and her RAND colleagues examined how artificial intelligence could help carry some of that burden. Over more than two decades, Jensen has helped emergency management rethink how communities prepare for, respond to, and recover from increasingly complex disasters. Now, she is exploring how AI could help a field that's already stretched thin adapt to even greater demands. What could AI realistically help emergency managers do—and how could that improve outcomes for communities? AI can help with prediction and modeling, including when events are likely to occur and how severe impacts may be. It can also help bring together data from different groups, so people better understand what is happening during a disaster. If AI is used well, it can help communities get the right help at the right time without inefficiency or duplicated effort, ultimately saving lives. Before disasters happen, emergency managers spend a lot of time on routine work like preparing plans, creating outreach materials, and managing grants. AI can speed up much of that work. That allows emergency managers to spend less time behind their desks and more time doing important public-facing work—helping people prepare, building community relationships, and focusing on the things that lessen disaster impacts. If AI is used well, it can help communities get the right help at the right time without inefficiency or duplicated effort, ultimately saving lives. Your team identified more than 1,000 AI-enabled products relevant to emergency management. What do these tools do, and what surprised you about your findings? We were shocked by the number of tools out there. We thought we might find dozens. Instead, we found 1,179. A lot of them support response. They support situational awareness, hazard monitoring, damage assessment, information sharing, and more. But the market is uneven, with more tools for response than for preparedness or recovery. A big challenge facing emergency managers is that many of the products are very narrow. For example, many offer one piece of insight, but they do not connect different information streams or help create a fuller picture. That creates what we call a stacking problem. People would need to use multiple tools and would have to connect them. The products also tend not to facilitate interorganizational coordination, a hallmark of emergency management task areas. What are the biggest barriers to using these tools—and what will it take for emergency management to adopt them more widely? As we found, it's not that the tools do not exist. It is whether organizations have the capacity to evaluate them, buy them, integrate them, and keep using them over time. A lot of these products require technical expertise. Often, you need someone with an IT background to set the tool up and provide ongoing support. Many jurisdictions don't have that kind of staffing. Many products also require internet connectivity, which can become an issue during response. A significant number depend on another product to work. And pricing is often hard to find—which makes procurement difficult. Then you add privacy or cyber concerns, and the reality is that many offices are already stretched thin. One issue by itself may be manageable, but taken together, they can be overwhelming. This is also where there is room for progress. Technology companies can design products more specifically for this field and prioritize transparency on pricing, access, and technical requirements—which will drive better adoption. Policymakers can make decisions about governance, procurement, and funding that make adoption easier. And emergency managers can build more familiarity with what these tools can do and where their limits are. Subscribe to the Policy Currents newsletter Email Subscribe In your research, what role did large language models (LLMs) and AI chatbots play in emergency management today? We found they could be especially useful for administrative and communication tasks in emergency management. They can help summarize reports, draft materials, translate information, and process large amounts of text more efficiently. Those kinds of general-purpose tools stood out as one place the field may be able to realize benefits quickly, since they have broad capabilities, are user-friendly, and already available to some jurisdictions. For more complex emergency management tasks, though, there is still more research and real-world testing that needs to be done to determine LLMs effectiveness. This study was supported by the Markle Foundation's AI for Disasters + Emergencies (AIDE) Initiative. How critical is philanthropic support in a fast-moving area like this? One of the most important things philanthropies can do is bring together technology companies, the user community, and the researchers developing the underlying technologies, and facilitate conversations about how to balance everyone's interests. That convening role—and the ability to sustain those conversations—can make the difference between tools that sound promising and tools that actually help communities. That is exactly what the AIDE Initiative is doing—bringing the right people together to explore how AI can better support disaster preparedness, response, and recovery. The AIDE Initiative is bringing the right people together to explore how AI can better support disaster preparedness, response, and recovery. You've dedicated your career to emergency management. What's kept you in the field so long? I've known I wanted to serve this field since I was 14. Around that time, a regular at the restaurant where I worked would talk about his job helping communities and organizations recover after disasters. What stayed with me was how many different people and systems have to come together to help a community heal. Now, years later, this work feels even more meaningful. There is an incredible opportunity in emergency management to keep evolving the practice to better serve communities. And I care deeply about the people who do this work. They are hardworking, passionate, and committed—even when resources are scarce and the demands keep growing. In a world of increasing disasters and rising impacts, that work matters enormously. It's what keeps me going. body: The use of artificial intelligence in biology offers great promise but could also endanger global health and national security. In this report, the authors develop a layered mitigation strategy that is robust against a variety of threat scenarios. The authors examine the strengths and weaknesses of a network of nine mitigations, describe areas of mutual reinforcement, and propose next steps for decisionmakers. Building a Defense-in-Depth Biosecurity Strategy for the AI Era Steph Guerra , Aurelia Attal-Juncqua , John P. Tarangelo , Casey Aveggio , Katie Dammer , David Glickstein Research Published Aug 18, 2026 Download PDF Additional Downloads Includes Infographic: Considerations for Policymakers; Infographic: Considerations for Industry; Infographic: Strategy Overview Share on LinkedIn Share on X Share on Facebook Email The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and biology offers great promise for medicine and public health, including the potential to yield transformative societal benefits. Yet this same convergence could introduce serious global health and national security risks. As capabilities continue to advance, AI-enabled biotechnology might lower the technical, operational, and motivational barriers to creating biological weapons. It might also enable high-consequence attacks involving enhanced or novel pathogens. The dual-use nature of biotechnology requires proactive mitigation measures to counter these threats. In this report, the authors develop a defense-in-depth mitigation strategy that is robust, complementary, and deployable across a wide variety of threat scenarios. To create the strategy, the authors assessed the capabilities of various actor types across different steps of the bioweapon-development pathway prior to an attack, from ideation to weaponization. They also examined how different mitigations could add friction to primary milestones that nefarious actors must bypass to successfully execute an attack using AI-enabled biological weapons. The authors describe a network of nine mitigations, each with their own strengths and weaknesses and areas of mutual reinforcement, and propose next steps for how decisionmakers in the public and private sectors can work collaboratively to advance this strategy. Key Takeaways Different threat actors require different prevention mechanisms. Resource-constrained individuals might be thwarted at material or information access chokepoints. However, technologically sophisticated or well-resourced groups, such as state actors, might be immune to access controls and therefore require deterrence through elevated perceived costs and a degraded expected utility of attack. Prevention must evolve beyond access controls alone. Although restricting dual-use information and materials remains necessary, determined actors with sufficient resources can circumvent these barriers. An effective strategy, therefore, requires a complementary detection architecture that identifies and disrupts misuse patterns in digital and physical domains before they culminate in harm, shifting the paradigm from denial to integrated monitoring and early response. Aggregate signals matter. Threat actors operating across multiple nodes of the AI-biology ecosystem—probing different models, querying multiple synthesis providers, sourcing materials from separate vendors—produce signals that appear ambiguous when observed individually but form identifiable patterns of concern when analyzed collectively. Realizing this aggregate value requires centralized information-sharing infrastructure that no entity can provide alone. Invest early. Implementing this strategy’s mitigations will require investments in new research, institutional adaptation, legal clarification, and international coordination. Waiting until more-advanced biological threats are undeniable will be waiting too long. body: Modernizing Department of the Air Force Training and Education Approaches Leveraging Stackable Certificates for Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Technologies Kelly Piazza , Kelly Atkinson , Nelson Lim Expert Insights Published Aug 11, 2026 Download PDF Share on LinkedIn Share on X Share on Facebook Email The U.S. Department of the Air Force (DAF) is balancing (1) the demands of strategic competition and ongoing conflict with (2) the constraints of a workforce that is consistently tasked to do more with less. In this context, the DAF needs to adopt innovative approaches and strengthen its technological capabilities to prepare its personnel for the challenges of strategic competition and future warfare. As warfare becomes increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), autonomy, cyber capabilities, and data-driven operations, the DAF may consider treating technological fluency as a core element of force readiness. RAND Project AIR FORCE researchers have identified stackable certificate programs in AI and advanced technologies as a potential way to build these skills over time in critical missions and career fields and to modernize existing professional military education curricula. They describe how such programs might be leveraged to the DAF’s benefit. body: Tomorrow's Victory and the Army of the Future: Forecasting the Next Steps in Ukraine's Military Evolution Commentary Sep 3, 2026 Ukrainian soldiers practice operating a ground-based drone (UGV) during a training session at the 10th Corps’ drone school, Kharkiv Photo by Frederic Petry/Hans Lucas/Reuters By Jacob Parakilas and Oliver Gill Amidst a changing strategic context which has seen Russian fortunes recede from their high water mark, Ukraine’s armed forces are facing another inflection point. The Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) of 2026 bear little resemblance to the army which faced Russia's initial seizure of Crimea, the force which fought Russian-backed separatists in Donbas from 2014–2022, and even the force that turned back Russia’s attempt to decapitate Ukraine in February 2022. That army, which just over a decade ago was still defined by its Soviet legacy, has emerged today as something new: a hybrid force, in which legacy organisational structures and Soviet-era kit work alongside imported doctrines, arms from Western partners, and increasingly domestically produced equipment and experimental methods. But like the war itself, that force has not reached a static final form. It remains a work in progress , adapting to circumstance as Ukraine continues to defend its sovereignty against Russian aggression. The question we ask here is: if Ukraine’s armed forces are a substantial evolution relative to the beginning of the war, what form will they take on next? The choice facing Ukraine's forces is far from a binary between East and West. As the full-scale war enters its fifth year, with its character still changing, the AFU continues to be tasked with building, deploying, and improving its existing capabilities while simultaneously developing innovative organisational structures, tactics, and doctrine to use them most effectively. Two camps have emerged into view this last month, each associated with a senior official whose disputes became highly public and controversial. A traditionalist camp, personified by recently relieved Chief of the General Staff Oleksandr Syrskyi, highlights the way in which Ukraine’s forces succeeded in holding the frontline against a materially and numerically superior adversary with an often-overlooked reliance on traditional tactics and weapons ( PDF ) . A reformist camp, symbolised by equally recently dismissed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, champions technological superiority and suggests more fundamental restructuring to better leverage novel weapons, unconventional tactics, and reformed procurement practices favouring decentralisation, SMEs, and increased transparency. Put simply, this reflects a struggle of the old guard against the next generation. One could interpret the dismissal of the senior figures in both camps as a sign that Ukraine’s leadership is trying to find a middle path, but the fundamental questions of how to continue the AFU’s evolution in the face of ongoing Russian assaults is unlikely to disappear. And as General Syrskyi’s successor Mykhailo Drapatyi assumes the role of Chief of the General Staff of the AFU, it is worth first questioning the validity of this framing. The distinction between Old and New, static and manoeuvrable, traditional and novel, is perhaps an oversimplification. The public rivalry between General Syrskyi and Fedorov cannot be viewed simply as a difference of opinion on military management, divorced from the political and cultural context from which both men have emerged. For the future of the AFU, it is far more useful to view these two sides as a contest between theories of victory and governance — and about what kind of force posture and approach to military management best achieves that end goal. If Ukraine’s armed forces are a substantial evolution relative to the beginning of the war, what form will they take on next? The Unmanned Systems Forces: The Command of the Future? Within the AFU, the Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) stand out as a source of pride for their technological and technical mastery of asymmetric warfare with attritable, adaptable tools ( PDF ) . The USF make up just two percent of the military’s personnel strength yet are responsible for roughly 30 percent of Russian losses , having irrevocably changed the character of the battlefield. Converting the AFU into a vehicle for a massively expanded USF is one possibility. That said, the remaining 98 percent of personnel (what might be termed the "traditional army") are just as essential, still accounting for the remaining 70 percent of Russian losses. To achieve full effect, hold the line, and sustain Ukraine's valiant defence over the past four years, both the “traditional” and “novel” camps have had to work together, regardless of friction, every step of the way. This is not as outlandish as it might seem at first blush. After all, it was under General Syrskyi's tenure that the world's first Unmanned Systems Force was codified as a branch of the armed forces . But what would be the implications of either camp—the Traditionalists or the Technologists—taking the lead on the AFU’s future? To structure this discussion, we consider four areas of potential change: unit structure, training, recruitment, and procurement. And for the purposes of this thought exercise, our assumption is a relatively steady state over the next two years, with no ceasefire and a constant level of ongoing hostilities with Russia. Subscribe to the Policy Currents newsletter Email Subscribe Scenario One: Traditionalist Retrenchment In this scenario, the General Staff fend off radical transformation while continuing an approach of large-scale but selective integration of emerging technologies. Doing so has preserved interoperability with NATO, avoiding the unknown vulnerabilities that radical restructuring might introduce, and leant into a narrative of battlefield success and national effort to keep the ranks filled with volunteers. Unit Structure Over the course of the full-scale war, traditionalists have consistently favoured fielding the maximum number of brigades . As fresh recruits complete basic training, they continue to be more or less evenly distributed across all active units, rather than being preferentially assigned to higher-performing or more combat-effective formations. Despite efforts to centralise command and control into a Corps structure , the AFU has continued to centralise decision-making at the General Staff level. As in previous years, brigades subordinated to this new corps structure remain non-contiguous across the frontline — a complicating factor that has continued to require constant intervention from the General Staff. Training Structures Under General Syrskyi's tenure, General Basic Military Training was extended from 30 to 51 days for standard entry into the Ground Forces . Under this regime, all soldiers are first trained as infantrymen, only later being potentially trained as Uncrewed Systems (UxS) operators. Given the prevalence of Russian infiltration tactics , and the subsequent risk of finding themselves in direct small-arms engagements, this approach persists. Moreover, despite Technologist aspirations toward full battlefield automation , human spotters and ground troops have remained essential for taking and holding positions. Centralised training ensures all personnel master foundational soldiering skills, enabling tactical movement and combined-arms discipline. In this scenario, technical expertise has remained a specialist force enhancer rather than the central organising principle of individual training. Recruitment In a war of attrition, with frontline ground forces bearing the cost of holding the line, waves of mobilisation have continued to be key to maintaining a viable force. As training structures continue to emphasise infantry skillsets, voluntary recruitment, which was already struggling to meet demand, has become increasingly inadequate. body: Not All ‘Magic’ Mushrooms Are the Same Commentary Aug 31, 2026 Photo by Robin Verhoef/Getty Images By Michelle Priest and Beau Kilmer This commentary was originally published by San Francisco Chronicle on August 29, 2026. Mushrooms are everywhere in California—literally and figuratively. Some are edible, some are psychoactive, some are toxic. And in the case of Amanita muscaria mushrooms, they can be all three. You may not yet have heard of Amanita muscaria , also called “fly agaric,” but you certainly have seen images of it. The orange-, yellow- or red-capped mushroom with white spots is in everything from “Alice in Wonderland” to Super Mario video games. In our recent RAND report on the use of psychedelics , we estimated that about 3.5 million American adults used Amanita muscaria in 2025, compared with 11 million who reported using psychoactive psilocybin mushrooms. Psilocybin mushrooms and Amanita muscaria are not the same. Given the growing popularity of so-called “magic” mushrooms for recreational and therapeutic use, as well as possible confusion between these different mushrooms, policymakers and health officials should not ignore health concerns related to Amanita muscaria . This is especially true because of the media attention psilocybin has received. Emerging clinical research has shown promise in using psilocybin for treating a variety of mental health ailments. Yet despite growing public interest, psilocybin has not been approved as a medicine by the Food and Drug Administration and remains illegal under federal law. Federal prohibition has not stopped some states and localities from moving ahead. In addition to three states legalizing supervised psilocybin use, more than 30 cities and counties have “deprioritized” the enforcement of certain offenses related to psychedelics, including psilocybin. About 3.5 million American adults used Amanita muscaria in 2025, compared with 11 million who reported using psychoactive psilocybin mushrooms. Oakland was an early mover in this space. In 2019, the City Council passed a resolution making the investigation and arrest of adults “for planting, cultivating, purchasing, transporting, distributing, engaging in practices with, and/or possessing” psilocybin mushrooms and other naturally occurring psychedelics one of the lowest priorities for local law enforcement. But not all psychedelic mushrooms are the same. Unlike the vast majority ( PDF ) of mushrooms containing psilocybin, Amanita muscaria can be quite toxic . If not properly prepared, effects can include nausea and vomiting, with more severe cases involving seizures, coma and, in extremely rare instances, death . Most people who use Amanita muscaria do not run into problems, but a recent international review highlighted some troubling anecdotes. In one case report , an older couple was rushed to the hospital after consuming Amanita muscaria . They both went into severe comas, and one had a seizure, in addition to other serious symptoms. Thankfully, after intensive medical treatment, each made a full recovery. The main active compound in Amanita muscaria is muscimol, which acts primarily on neurotransmitters in the brain. The most common self-reported effects are an intoxicated feeling similar to alcohol, sleepiness (sometimes with altered dreams), and relaxation. Others report that it can help reduce substance use or alleviate anxiety, but no clinical trials have confirmed these health claims . Subscribe to the Policy Currents newsletter Email Subscribe The mushroom is not hard to find. Amanita muscaria grows in many parts of the country. The California State Parks Foundation website even features a picture of it growing in Salt Point State Park in Sonoma County. It is also sold in unregulated gummies, chocolates, and other products. And, yes, people report using it to microdose, too. Amanita muscaria is not illegal under the federal Controlled Substances Act. And only one state, Louisiana, prohibits it. A 2024 assessment by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration ( PDF ) found that it is not safe to eat or add to food, but minimal action has been taken to get these products out of brick-and-mortar and online shops. Given its risk profile and legal status, there are concerns about unregulated products advertising with images of Amanita muscaria or claims that they contain it. These products may contain Amanita muscaria , or they may not. They may also contain a mix of other unregulated intoxicants that can be harmful. A 2026 review from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention identified 180 cases of severe illness in 34 states associated with eating mushroom-containing products, including some that contained compounds from Amanita muscaria and psilocybin mushrooms along with other substances. The California Department of Public Health has also raised concerns about the substances that are in widely available mushroom products. The popularity and accessibility of Amanita muscaria suggests public health agencies should step up education campaigns that highlight their specific risks. State and federal policymakers have many options when it comes to Amanita muscaria and products claiming to contain it, and each has unique costs and benefits . For example, prohibition is an option, although enforcing the law against those foraging for mushrooms would be difficult. Jurisdictions could also allow adults to grow and possess Amanita muscaria but prohibit retail sales, as Colorado has done with psilocybin mushrooms and some other nature-based psychedelics. If states decide to regulate production and sales, they’ll confront many decisions around child-proof packaging requirements, product testing, marketing restrictions, taxes, and how these products can be sold. Regardless of any legal or regulatory changes, the popularity and accessibility of Amanita muscaria suggests public health agencies should step up education campaigns that highlight their specific risks . Not all mind-altering mushrooms are the same. In the current environment, consumers need to know that what they are buying is unregulated and may contain other harmful products. Although Amanita muscaria isn’t as popular as psilocybin, it’s time for policy and public health conversations to include the other magic mushroom. body: Mirror Life Is Theoretical. The Danger Is Anything But. Commentary Aug 31, 2026 Image by Ake Puttisarn/Getty Images By Nidhi Kalra This commentary was originally published by the Washington Post on August 31, 2026. “This includes creation of mirror organisms.” These six bland words appear as a footnote in the White House policy for “Stopping High-Risk Life Sciences Research” ( PDF ) released in July—but they shouldn't be treated like one. If you've never heard of mirror life—the more commonly used term for mirror organisms—there's a good reason: It doesn't exist. But this sci-fi-sounding form of life could theoretically be built out of biological molecules that are mirror images of the ones that exist naturally. The idea emerges from the fact that nearly all biomolecules in nature have a kind of handedness—all DNA, for example, is built from right-handed sugars, and all proteins are made from left-handed amino acids. Thus, it's possible to imagine—and maybe even create—a living organism made of mirror-image counterparts to natural biomolecules. The first would probably be mirror bacteria. That may not sound like reason for alarm. But scientists warn that mirror bacteria could devastate most life on earth. In 2024, dozens of them issued an urgent call to prevent mirror bacteria from ever being created, saying, “We cannot rule out a scenario in which a mirror bacterium acts as an invasive species across many ecosystems, causing pervasive lethal infections in a substantial fraction of plant and animal species, including humans.” Yet we are edging closer to the threshold of mirror life. Over the past decade, biologists have engineered specialized tools for replicating and assembling mirror-image biomolecules. These tools could have some uses: For example, medicines made from mirror biomolecules could evade the processes that normally break them down, so treatments based on them might be longer-lasting than treatments based on regular biomolecules. Certain advances could also become stepping stones toward mirror bacteria, and that's where the danger lurks. But certain advances could also become stepping stones toward mirror bacteria, and that's where the danger lurks. Mirror bacteria might not be recognized by the things—immune systems, enzymes and other predator microorganisms—that keep normal bacteria in check. Outside of a lab, it might spread out of control, which is why no one should ever create it. The good news is that the breakthroughs required to make mirror life are probably 10 to 30 years away , and very few scientists are even equipped to make the attempt. If the world's leading scientists desist, they will effectively deny the means to everyone else. So here's the call to action: As Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet in September to explore areas of cooperation, they should put prevention of mirror life on the agenda. If the two leaders seek a topic of global importance they can agree on, surely this is it. Mirror life is a shared existential risk with no credible upside for either country. Instead, they can lay a foundation for universal restraint. A first step would be for the two countries to articulate a shared belief that there should be boundaries between acceptable and unacceptable research in this field. They could produce joint ethical standards for researchers, plus issue public statements that make it clear that mirror life is not a legitimate area of scientific pursuit. Deciding exactly where to draw boundaries regarding mirror life research should involve collaborative discussions. The goals should be to determine when potentially beneficial early research steps onto a slippery slope. As Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet in September to explore areas of cooperation, they should put prevention of mirror life on the agenda. For instance, some scientists have suggested that the mirror version of a ribosome—the machinery in cells that makes proteins—could make it easier to produce mirror proteins for medical use. But a mirror ribosome would also be a huge step toward creating mirror life. Instead, the United States and China might agree to prohibit the development of mirror ribosomes and work together on other ways to make mirror proteins. This should lead to formal agreements not to pursue mirror life, along with jointly establishing economic and logistical barriers to its creation. Some will dismiss hopes of such cooperation between strategic competitors as gross naiveté. But history has shown that cooperation among rivals is possible when the stakes are high enough. In 1967, in the depths of Cold War animosity, the United States and the Soviet Union together championed the Intensified Smallpox Eradication Program. With joint leadership—money, logistics, and more than a billion Soviet vaccine doses—smallpox was successfully eradicated worldwide in 1980. Beijing and Washington can take inspiration from this example to protect the entire biosphere. It's rare to meet a moment when the risks of a scientific breakthrough are so clear. More typically, it's too early to tell or too late to fix. With mirror life, scientists have given world leaders both the foresight and the time to address the danger. What's needed isn't alarm but action to ensure that mirror life remains just a footnote in human history—and not its final chapter. body: OpenAI Says ChatGPT Is Safer for Teens. Now It Needs to Show Proof. Commentary Aug 27, 2026 Photo by Amfer75/Getty Images By Ryan K. McBain This commentary was originally published by Los Angeles Times on August 27, 2026. Last week, OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT for Teens , a new user experience crafted to help young people “learn, think critically, deepen understanding, and use AI with confidence.” Maybe most importantly, OpenAI vowed that it would place any users its system “estimates” to be under 18 into the system “automatically.” For nearly a year, parents have been able to link their children's ChatGPT accounts to their own, restricting features, setting quiet hours, and receiving alerts in high-risk situations. Those parental controls remain available, but account linking is still voluntary: The invitation must be accepted, and either party can sever the connection. ChatGPT for Teens sets a different default. When a user reports being age 13 to 17, or when OpenAI's system predicts that an account belongs to someone under 18, teen protections are automatically applied without waiting for a parent to activate them. This shift matters because nearly 60 percent of U.S. teens now use ChatGPT, according to Pew, even though parents often have no idea what their children are discussing. In a nationally representative survey my RAND colleagues and I conducted last year, we found that nearly 1 in 5 Americans ages 12 to 21 —about 8.2 million young people—reported using an AI chatbot for mental health advice. Nearly two-thirds hadn't told anyone. A parent who never learns a conversation is occurring cannot be expected to activate safeguards around it. Automatic protections at least have a chance to reach that user. Sixty percent of U.S. teens now use ChatGPT even though parents often have no idea what their children are discussing. Independent testing conducted with Common Sense Media and Stanford Medicine before the launch of ChatGPT for Teens last week illustrates what can go wrong. Widely used AI chatbots missed warning signs that emerged gradually over longer conversations; in one test, ChatGPT advised a tester posing as a teen to conceal cuts and scars from self-harm rather than directing the teen toward help. OpenAI's new protections aim to prevent such failures. For users placed in the teen experience, these protections include tighter boundaries around conversations involving self-harm and eating disorders, graphic violence, and sexual or romantic role-play. OpenAI says ChatGPT for Teens will not encourage emotional dependence nor pretend to have feelings or position itself as a substitute for human relationships. It also adds study tools, homework reminders, prompts to take breaks, and warnings before a teenager uploads a potentially sensitive image. This is an improvement over making parents find and activate a safety menu. But automatic protections for teens rests on an unforgiving premise: that OpenAI can find them. The company says its age-prediction system will consider signals including the subjects an account discusses, times of day it's active, usage patterns, and how long the account has existed. But in materials released during the launch, OpenAI did not publish the figure that matters most: What proportion of actual teens does it identify? Roblox, the online gaming platform popular with children, offers a cautionary example. To use the included chat feature, players have to pass an age check—usually through an AI-powered face scan. Reports surfaced earlier this year of adults classified as children and children as adults. A Wired investigation found users had fooled the scan using avatars and even a photo of Kurt Cobain; one boy drew wrinkles and stubble in marker and was placed in the 21-plus category. The details were comical, but the consequences were not: A marker-drawn beard could become a passport into the adult category and out of the protections meant to safeguard children. Subscribe to the Policy Currents newsletter Email Subscribe Correctly identifying teens is only the first test. The second is determining just how safe ChatGPT for Teens responses truly are. OpenAI has made a welcome start by publishing evaluations in areas including self-harm, eating disorders, and sexual content. But it has released the scores without sharing its actual methods: Its report does not include the prompts, the number of cases, or the detailed instructions used to judge the answers. Parents should not have to inspect those materials, but a third party should be able to determine whether such self-reported results deserve parents' confidence. Instagram illustrates a different problem: the gulf between activating a safety feature and proving it works. Meta, which on Wednesday agreed to pay $17 billion and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to settle claims filed by 47 states, introduced Teen Accounts in 2024, automatically placing identified teens into restrictive settings. It later announced that Instagram had 54 million active teen accounts and that 97 percent of users age 13 to 15 remained in the protections. Those figures measured scale and retention, not effectiveness. They also did not reveal how many teens Instagram missed, or how much harm the settings prevented. When outside researchers later tested ( PDF ) 47 of Instagram's announced safety features, they judged only eight as fully functional. Reuters confirmed some of the report's findings in its own tests. For instance, a teen account could view eating disorder content by searching “skinnythighs” without the space between words. Meta disputed the report and said teens placed in its protections saw less sensitive content, unwanted contact, and late-night use. Both can be true: Meta's system may reduce those harms but also have significant failure points. The public still does not know how much protection Instagram Teen Accounts actually provide, because the data needed to answer that question remains inside Meta. The tech industry has arrived at a convenient arrangement, where its assurances are public, but its evidence is not. The tech industry has arrived at a convenient arrangement, where its assurances are public, but its evidence is not. The lesson is not that automatic protections are futile. It is that even ambitious efforts can fall short, and the public needs a way to discover when they do. OpenAI says it will “measure and publish what we are learning.” That promise needs a protocol and a timetable. OpenAI needs to publish a clear evaluation plan that answers three basic questions: Does the system reliably identify teens, including those who try to evade it? Does ChatGPT for Teens respond more safely in real-world conversations, compared to before the rollout? And does the teen experience change what its younger users actually do—for instance, curbing prolonged use or making those in distress more likely to seek human help? These results can be reported in aggregate without exposing private conversations, but OpenAI should disclose whether outcomes differ across groups and allow independent researchers and regulators to verify them. That would allow the public to judge the product by what it accomplishes, not what it promises. OpenAI deserves credit for moving a core set of protections from voluntary to default. Other AI companies whose products are used by teens should follow its lead by adopting comparable protections. That said, last week's launch is akin to a ribbon-cutting ceremony for a building that has yet to pass safety inspection. The question now is whether OpenAI will open its doors to independent inspectors and let the public see what they find. body: Politics & Diplomacy Freedom and Prosperity Do countries need freedom to achieve prosperity? Do democracies or autocracies have the better answers for the aspirations of their people? With the goal of increasing the prosperity of the poor and marginalized, the Atlantic Council is seeking to answer these defining questions and explore the relationship between freedom and prosperity in developing and developed nations. The Freedom and Prosperity Center aims to increase the prosperity of the poor and marginalized in developing countries and to explore the nature of the relationship between freedom and prosperity in both developing and developed nations. body: Africa South & Central Africa Democratic Republic of the Congo The largest Sub-Saharan African country by area, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is resource rich and home to some of the world’s largest deposits of rare earth minerals, but the vast majority of the population lives in extreme poverty. Governance is a perennial challenge, but President Kabila’s 2019 exit has cautiously raised hopes for democratic reform. The country has historically struggled with conflict, violence, and disease, a concern for the international community given DRC’s central location and numerous neighbors. body: Africa East Africa Spanning from Sudan in the north to Tanzania in the south and centered around the strategic Horn of Africa, East Africa is a gateway to the Arabian Peninsula and the Indian Ocean. East Africa includes a diversity of states, ranging from the relatively successful developmental models of Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Kenya to the weak conflict-prone examples of South Sudan and Somalia. Playing host to the African Union and several other regional organizations, East Africa is a critical area with both high hopes for growth and demands for stability. body: Africa North and West Africa North and West Africa encompasses a geographically diverse expanse from Morocco to Nigeria, and from the Sahel to the Atlantic coast. The region is home to renowned African civilizations while indelibly tied to Arab empires and European colonization. Security remains a burden for many, but the region has also produced some of Africa’s most compelling democratic success stories in recent years. body: Europe & Eurasia Eastern Europe The Caucasus Named for the mountain range between southern Russia, and northern Turkey and Iran, the Caucasus is home to the nations of Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia. Since their independence in 1991, these nations have faced frozen conflicts which have hampered development and have given Russia and Turkey means to exert and maintain influence. While all three nations have made progress toward democracy and a free market in varying degrees, corruption, human rights violations, and conflict still hinder efforts to improve regional security. body: Middle East Stretching from the Western Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean, the Middle East continues to be a region struggling with violent conflict, political repression, and poor development. Geographic priorities Argentina Argentina plays a key role in the economic landscape of the Americas, with strong potential for deeper integration with the United States. AALAC promotes policies that support Argentina’s fiscal resilience and strengthen bilateral economic cooperation. Brazil As Latin America’s largest economy, Brazil is central to regional economic stability and geopolitics. AALAC advances a forward-looking US-Brazil agenda by fostering strategic dialogue and promoting sustainable, innovation-driven cooperation across trade, energy, and agriculture. Caribbean The Caribbean is among the world’s most vulnerable regions, exposed to climate-induced disasters, economic shocks, and shifting geopolitical dynamics. The Caribbean Initiative raises awareness about regional priorities and deepens US and global engagement across issues such as energy security, financial inclusion, and economic competitiveness. Central America A secure and prosperous Central America is vital to US national and economic interests. AALAC advances strategic engagement that strengthens supply chains, attracts investment, and supports democratic governance as pillars for long-term regional prosperity. Colombia Colombia and the United States share a longstanding partnership rooted in security, development, and commercial ties. AALAC advances understanding of issues critical to US interests and works to ensure that Colombia can serve as a vital US ally in South America for decades to come. Mexico As the United States’ top trading partner, Mexico plays a notable role in advancing investment and cross-border commerce. AALAC supports engagement to strengthen commercial ties, address shared security challenges, and align opportunities to incentivize productive investment. Venezuela Following the US removal of Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela stands at a pivotal moment after years of economic mismanagement, cronyism, and democratic erosion. AALAC is seizing this moment to usher in a Venezuela where people overcome economic paralysis, live without fear of the state, and freely choose their leaders. body: Digital Forensic Research Lab The Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab (DFRLab) has operationalized the study of disinformation by exposing falsehoods and fake news, documenting human rights abuses, and building digital resilience worldwide. Research Policy Digital Sherlocks Explore the program Check out DFRLab.org Sign up for The Source newsletter Like the DFRLab on Facebook Follow the DFRLab on Twitter Follow the DFRLab on Instagram Cyber Statecraft Initiative Democracy & Tech Initiative The Digital Forensic Research Lab (DFRLab) is a first of its kind organization with technical and policy expertise on disinformation, connective technologies, democracy, and the future of digital rights. Incubated at the Atlantic Council in 2016, the DFRLab has conducted over 1,000 investigations exposing influence operations and emerging digital threats worldwide. With a team rooted in diverse regional expertise and subject-matter knowledge, the DFRLab works to promote digital resilience, defend democratic institutions, and ensure that objective fact remains central to public discourse in an increasingly contested information space. Read the DFRLab’s latest case studies, learn about our initiatives, and more at DFRLab.org visit dfrlab.org STAY CONNECTED Receive the latest research, along with discussions about disinformation and tech issues. ABOUT US The Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab is building the world’s leading hub of digital forensic analysts (#DigitalSherlocks). Digital Forensic Research lab At the Atlantic Council’s DFRLab, our mission is: To identify, expose, and explain disinformation where and when it occurs using open source research; to promote objective truth as a foundation of government for and by people; to protect democratic institutions and norms from those who would seek to undermine them in the digital engagement space. To create a new model of expertise adapted for impact and real-world results. body: Eurasia Center The Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center promotes policies that secure vital American interests by strengthening stability, opposing aggression by US adversaries, and supporting democratic values and economic opportunities from Eastern Europe to the South Caucasus to Russia to Central Asia. About us Events Blogs Videos Explore the program The Power Vertical Timely commentary & analysis In-depth research & reports In the News Insight & Impact Eurasia Congressional Fellowship Ukraine in Europe Initiative Putin's endgame: The stakes beyond Ukraine stay updated Signup to receive the latest on events, news, and publications for all of Eurasia. our regions in focus Ukraine Ukraine is the Eurasia Center’s main focus because Russia’s war threatens the vital interests of the United States and its allies. The outcome of the war will determine Ukraine’s future and Europe’s as well. Ukraine’s on-and-off efforts to reform are another area of great attention. Since the 2014 Maidan Revolution, Ukraine has made notable, if uneven, progress toward reform that must continue even as it fights off Moscow’s massive invasion. Russia Russia under Vladimir Putin violently menaces its neighbors and seeks to tear down the US-led global order. But the Kremlin aggression of today need not preclude a more peaceful and prosperous tomorrow. While Putin’s regime tries to paint US policy—and Eurasia Center activity—as anti-Russian, the Center’s efforts are based on the understanding that defeating Kremlin aggression in Ukraine will be positive not just for Ukraine, Europe, and the United States, but also for Russia itself. The Caucasus Named for the mountain range between southern Russia and northern Turkey and Iran, the South Caucasus is home to the nations of Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia. This geopolitically complex region has the potential to be a crossroads of global commerce. The Eurasia Center supports efforts for a just peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan and works to help prevent further democratic backsliding by Georgia’s increasingly authoritarian leadership. Central Asia The Central Asian republics—Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan —are located at the nexus of Russia, China, South Asia, and the Middle East. Growing dynamism in the region may provide openings for greater freedom and prosperity. It is in US interests that this region not fall under the outsized influence of either China or Russia. The Eurasia Center regularly hosts leaders from Central Asia for expert discussions and high-level events. Belarus When Belarusian dictator Alyaksandr Lukashenka attempted to steal the 2020 presidential election, he inadvertently set off a national movement in Belarus toward greater freedom and self-determination that persists today. The Center has reported actively on the efforts of the Belarusian opposition, led by Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, and provided a premier platform to keep Belarus on the agenda in Washington. Moldova Moldova has moved fitfully toward an open society and market economy while Moscow has supported separatists in the region of Transnistria. But, its European Union candidacy may herald a better integrated future. The Eurasia Center’s Moldova programming actively promotes the country’s democratic and European future. Regions in focus European Union Growing from its start as the European Coal and Steel Community, the European Union has risen as a key actor and norm-setter in areas as diverse as trade, energy security, digital policy, and defense. In an era of great power competition, the United States has a national interest in the EU reinvigorating faith in the European project. France The United States’ oldest ally, France is a key strategic partner for Washington. France remains a key country to watch for the future of the European project as it pursues a vision for a more integrated, cohesive European Union. Germany Germany is a key player in the transatlantic relationship and in Europe. The US-German relationship has been the backbone of the international order for seven decades, and a strong transatlantic community and rules-based order relies on close US-German cooperation. Poland Poland is a major actor within NATO and the European Union, a growing economic powerhouse, and an influential regional leader. With increased Russian aggression, foreign influence campaigns, and a rise of populism, the United states needs to continue investing in the relationship with a key ally. United Kingdom The United Kingdom is a long-time friend and ally of the United States. Despite wrestling with internal challenges, the UK plays an important leadership role in the international system as a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, a NATO leader, and the bridge between Europe and the United States on issues of defense, security, sanctions, and trade. The Western Balkans The Balkans are enjoying a period of relative stability after decades of turmoil. US and European engagement are as necessary as ever to stabilize the fragile peace of the 1990s and build further Euro-Atlantic political and economic integration. Issues in focus Transatlantic Digital Marketplace Initiative The Transatlantic Digital Marketplace Initiative seeks to foster greater US-EU understanding and collaboration on digital policy matters and build tangible cooperation in this fast-growing area of the transatlantic economy. Three Seas Initiative Programming The Atlantic Council strives to promote a Europe undivided, free, and prosperous through its support of the Three Seas Initiative. The Initiative seeks to bolster investment in Central and Eastern European transportation, energy, and digital infrastructure to improve regional connectivity and bolster development. Transform Europe Initiative Based on the lessons of the Kremlin’s war on Ukraine, the Transform Europe Initiative aims to strengthen European security against petro-aggression, climate change, and weaponized corruption. The initiative aids in the development of structural reforms and expedited but practical solutions that promote Europe’s decarbonization and defenses against transnational kleptocracy networks. . body: GeoTech Center Shaping the future of technology and data to advance society. About Us Explore the program AI Connect GeoTech Cues GeoTech Commission Reports Events Follow us on X Mission The Atlantic Council GeoTech Center has a mission to shape the future of technology and data to advance society. Vision and Purpose Technological advances are transforming lives across the globe—and the accelerating pace at which emerging technologies are being developed and deployed can lead to unanticipated outcomes. The GeoTech Center is working to identify and communicate what is required so that emerging technologies can enter use widely across the globe for public benefit, while identifying and mitigating potential societal and geopolitical risks. The Center thereby serves as an essential bridge between technologists and national as well as international policymakers, bringing together subject matter experts, thought leaders, and decision-makers through purposeful convenings to consider the broader societal, economic, and geopolitical implications of new and emerging technologies; leverage technology to solve global challenges; and develop actionable tech policy, partnerships, and programs. The Atlantic Council GeoTech Center seeks to provide policymakers and technologists with diverse stakeholder perspectives on “tech for good” and pragmatic approaches to the geopolitics of technological change. Pillars of Work Tech cooperation: Building global partnerships The GeoTech Center’s work to advance government-to-government and industry-to-government relationships focused on technology frameworks, standards, and measures that protect shared interests and mitigate risks globally. Tech competition: Defining leadership in the tech landscape The GeoTech Center’s engagement with government policies, investment decisions, and regulatory frameworks and pathways for secure and strategic international tech competition. Tech innovation: Shaping the future The GeoTech Center’s forward-looking insight on the secure and principled use of pioneering emerging technologies that can enhance global stability. The Atlantic Council Technology Programs comprises five existing efforts—the Digital Forensic Research Lab (DFRLab), the GeoTech Center, the Cyber Statecraft Initiative, the Democracy + Tech Initiative, and the Capacity Building Initiative. These operations work together to address the geopolitical implications of technology and provide policymakers and global stakeholders necessary research, insights, and convenings to address challenges around global technology and ensure its responsible advancement. learn more Reports and Issue Briefs Issue Brief Jul 7, 2026 India’s AI playbook: From talent incubator to AI leader By Trisha Ray India’s AI talent ecosystem is rapidly growing but faces structural gaps. body: Millennium Leadership Program For over sixty years, the Atlantic Council has convened global leaders to address our world’s most pressing challenges. As a central pillar of this legacy, the Millennium Leadership Program (MLP) launched in 2015 to connect and empower the next-generation of international changemakers who will shape the twenty-first century. The MLP currently hosts three programs: The Millennium Fellowship, the Millennium Leadership Intensive, and the European Leadership Accelerator. Global Leadership Forum The Millennium Fellowship Millennium Leadership Intensive About the Millennium Leadership Program Since its inception, the Atlantic Council’s Millennium Leadership Program (MLP) has focused on building a vibrant community of leaders who transform bold ideas into action. Through its programming, the MLP equips global professionals across diverse industries with the tools to elevate their leadership and expand their impact. Participants gain access to a global network of exceptional peers, engage with world leaders through global study tours, participate in dynamic leadership development experiences, and lead the debate on key issues. Explore Ou r programs Millenium fellows and alumni Study tour reflections Stay connected The Millennium Leadership Program is built on three core pillars: leadership, community, and impact. These pillars are woven into every aspect of programming, enabling participants to grow both personally and professionally while contributing to a larger global community. Together, they equip leaders to address today’s challenges and shape a more equitable, prosperous future. Through the MLP, leaders gain tools to enhance their leadership skills, amplify their ability to drive meaningful change, and build strong, supportive networks. The MLP boasts a robust and active alumni network, ensuring participants stay connected and engaged after completing the program. “The Millennium Fellowship connects the internal to the interpersonal, and ultimately to the international. What binds us together as fellows is a commitment to lead from a place of hope .” — Karim Farishta , Director of Intergovernmental Affairs, Office of the Secretary of Defense (Millennium Fellowship 2023) Current Programs Millennium Fellowship The MLP’s flagship program brings together thirty-five exceptional rising leaders from diverse sectors for a transformative nine-month fellowship. Fellows both contribute to and benefit from the Atlantic Council’s expertise, participating in world-class leadership training, personalized coaching, and tailored growth assessments. The program features an in-person study tour, where fellows engage directly with senior decision-makers tackling today’s pressing global challenges. Explore Millennium Leadership Intensive (MLI) MLI offers a dynamic, three-month program for leading professionals eager to connect and enhance their leadership capabilities. The program focuses on the complexities of the Middle East, combining in-depth leadership training, expert engagement, and an immersive study tour to the region. Participants will refine their ability to lead effectively in a rapidly evolving global landscape. Explore Young Global Professionals Program (YGP) The YGP Program is a paid internship that offers current students and recent graduates hands-on experience across the Atlantic Council’s sixteen programs and centers. Jointly facilitated by the MLP and HR teams, the program is designed to prepare the next generation of young global leaders. YGP participants benefit from tailored career development sessions and opportunities to network with leading professionals within the Council. Explore Global Leadership Forum The Global Leadership Forum brings together Millennium Leadership Program alumni, Atlantic Council experts, and partners for dialogue on the challenges shaping leadership. Explore Past Programs Millennium Leadership Summit In September 2024, the Millennium Leadership Program celebrated its tenth anniversary by hosting the inaugural Millennium Leadership Summit, uniting its global network for the first time. The Summit brought together members of MLP’s expansive network, allowing alumni and current Fellows, to connect and collaborate with each other. Explore European Leadership Accelerator (ELA) This five-month leadership accelerator brings together a select cohort of rising European leaders at the forefront of the digital and green transition. ELA provides unparalleled opportunities to collaborate, engage leading experts, and drive impact. Explore Climate Leadership Program The Climate Leadership Program is a unique community accelerator for climate finance leaders across the USA, China, European Union, and African Union. The program provides established professionals in the intersection of climate and finance an opportunity to supercharge their leadership toolkits and develop networks to lead future climate change mitigation efforts through effective and equitable financial architecture. Explore In their own words 2024 ELI Participant Reflections from Israel and Palestinian territories Study Tour The participants of the Executive Leadership Intensive explored the local and regional implications of the ongoing conflict in Gaza and gleaned lessons that they can apply in their home countries. 2023 Fellow Reflections from Taiwan Study Tour Global leaders cannot sit idly by as the world order faces increasing threats; instead, they will need to be proactive to secure the future. The 2023 cohort of Millennium fellows traveled to Taiwan for their study tour, meeting with government officials, private sector innovators, and civil society groups to discuss the challenges leaders contend with today. Climate Leadership Program: Lessons From Ghana After successful action planning in Ghana, Climate Leadership Program participants are ready to take on a pressing issue in climate investment. How our fellowship prepared us for a world of challenges Members of the 2021 Millennium Fellowship came away with vast and diverse insights, but some lessons stood out above the rest. body: Rafik Hariri Center & Middle East Programs The Rafik Hariri Center and Middle East Programs are leading the way in providing a forum for informing and galvanizing the transatlantic community to shape a stable and prosperous Middle East and North Africa. We have been at the vanguard of promoting peace and security and unlocking the region’s economic and human potential through the ideas we publish, the solutions we generate, and the communities we influence. Initiatives Analysis Events Team Our Mission Advancing security through stability is a core American and European priority in the Middle East. As the region undergoes significant political and socioeconomic change, the Council’s Middle East programming provides a forum for informing and galvanizing the transatlantic community to work together to address the range of challenges and support opportunities for growth in the region. The Atlantic Council examines key trends and current events in the Middle East through the lens of a cadre of DC-based and regional experts, providing timely analysis and policy recommendations for the United States, its allied governments, and the broader policy community. Our work on the Middle East focuses on two broad themes: building peace and security and unlocking the region’s largely untapped human potential. The breadth of our work on this critical region spans several initiatives and centers at the Council. We have dedicated programs that address both security issues and economic and human development challenges focused on Iraq, Iran, North Africa, and Syria with in-house experts tracking the latest developments and crafting recommendations for transatlantic and regional policy makers. Our inspiration The Atlantic Council’s work on social, economic and human development issues in the Middle East honors the legacy of Rafik Hariri and his life’s mission to unlock the human and economic potential of the Arab world. The Atlantic Council’s work on Middle East security honors the legacy of Brent Scowcroft and his tireless efforts to build a new security architecture for the region. Stay Connected Follow us on social media Our Initiatives Iraq Initiative The Iraq Initiative is driving policy-oriented programs and analysis that advance Iraq’s stability and sovereignty, regional integration, and democratic and economic development. It also aims to promote a strengthened US-Iraq partnership. MENA Futures Lab The MENA Futures Lab, a flagship initiative of the Rafik Hariri Center for the Middle East, is dedicated to harnessing innovation, entrepreneurship, and human capital to build a more prosperous future for the Middle East. Perspectives on North Africa The North Africa Initiative at the Atlantic Council’s Rafik Hariri Center for the Middle East analyzes the strategic, political, and economic importance of the region for the United States and its allies. Since the 2011 Arab Spring uprisings, North Africa has undergone political and economic transformations that have impacted stability and security in the region. With its geographic crossroad between Europe, Africa, and the Middle East, North Africa continues to be an integral partner in addressing shared interests and concerns. Project for Middle East Integration The Project for Middle East Integration is helping policymakers leverage a dynamic moment to foster greater political and economic integration between all the countries of the Middle East. Realign for Palestine The Realign for Palestine project is committed to challenging violent extremism, divisive narratives, and hatred by elevating common-sense approaches through policy and action. Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative The Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative (SMESI) provides fresh insights into core US national security interests by leveraging its expertise, networks, and on-the-ground programs to develop holistic assessments on the future of the most pressing political and security challenges in the Middle East. Strategic Litigation Project The Strategic Litigation Project injects fresh thinking into how government and practitioners can apply legal tools to advance human rights and accountability around the world. Syria Project Our work on Syria sheds light on the ongoing struggle of Syrians to fulfill their desire for democratic self-governance as the United States and the international community grapple with the aftermath of a devastating civil war, millions of refugees across the Middle East and Europe, and ongoing security and political challenges spilling over Syria’s borders. Transatlantic Project The Rafik Hariri Center’s Transatlantic Project aims at strengthening US-European cooperation on the most critical opportunities and challenges facing the Middle East and North Africa.
