body: Tashkent’s Islamic Civilization Media Forum: Why Matters? Tashkent’s Islamic Civilization Media Forum and Uzbekistan’s Cultural Diplomacy Image generated with the support of artificial intelligence Executive Intelligence Snapshot The Islamic Civilisation International Media Forum in Tashkent forms part of Uzbekistan’s cultural diplomacy and supports its effort to strengthen its position as an influential Central Asian actor while promoting the region’s Islamic heritage and broadening its international partnerships. Uzbekistan is simultaneously expanding Islamic finance and international investment channels, creating an economic dimension to its wider outreach to Muslim-majority states and international investors. The forum as the recent law on Islamic banking confirm Tashkent’s attempt to combine cultural diplomacy, international visibility and economic diversification to strengthen its regional standing. Context From 24 to 29 August 2029 , Tashkent hosts the International Media Forum “Islamic Civilization: A New Look – New Discoveries” brings together media organisations, journalists, academics, experts and communications specialists from abroad and Uzbekistan. The programme addresses the preservation of historical heritage, the dissemination of the scientific achievements of Islamic civilisation and new formats for reaching international audiences through television, documentary production and digital platforms. The forum also has an operational media component. The Islamic Civilization Centre cooperates with international media organisations, including Euronews and the BBC, on documentaries, television projects and special programmes concerning Uzbekistan’s history and culture. The initiative consequently extends beyond domestic cultural promotion and seeks to place Uzbekistan and Central Asia within international media narratives concerning Islamic civilisation. Uzbekistan is also developing Islamic finance and expanding its international investment channels. Indeed, on 27 March 2026 , President Shavkat Mirziyoyev signed a landmark law establishing a legal framework for Islamic banking in Uzbekistan to allow and ease the establishment of Islamic banks and the development of sukuk-related mechanisms. These measures are intended to attract additional investment and deposits and form part of a wider effort to increase foreign investment and develop Tashkent as an international financial centre. Why Does It Matter? The forum provides Uzbekistan with a platform to present itself as a Central Asian centre for the study, preservation and international promotion of Islamic civilisation. Tashkent’s approach places greater emphasis on historical heritage, scientific achievement, education and culture. This allows Uzbekistan to promote its own national and regional identity while engaging Muslim-majority countries through a cultural rather than primarily religious or political agenda. The initiative also supports Uzbekistan’s effort to diversify its external partnerships. International media cooperation expands its diplomatic and reputational reach, while Islamic finance can create additional channels for engagement with investors and financial institutions from Muslim-majority countries. The two strands operate in different policy domains, but together they broaden the instruments through which Tashkent can strengthen external relationships. The regional objective is particularly relevant. Uzbekistan seeks greater influence in Central Asia and greater freedom to manage its external relationships. The forum contributes to this objective by positioning Tashkent as a venue for international engagement with Islamic civilisation and by linking Central Asian heritage to global audiences. Thanks to initiatives such as the forum Uzbekistan is broadening its international engagement and developing additional channels through which it can project influence and attract cooperation. Outlook The most likely near-term development is continued use of cultural and media initiatives to increase Uzbekistan’s international visibility and reinforce Tashkent’s position as a Central Asian hub for Islamic heritage and international dialogue. The strategic significance of the forum will increase if media partnerships produce sustained international content and if cultural initiatives generate additional institutional or economic cooperation. The main indicator to monitor is whether cultural diplomacy produces measurable diversification in Uzbekistan’s external partnerships. Increased participation by Gulf and other Muslim-majority institutions, new media agreements, investment commitments and the expansion of Islamic financial activity would strengthen the assessment that Tashkent is linking cultural outreach with broader diplomatic and economic diversification. body: Aliyev Visit to Tashkent and Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan Relations President Aliyev’s State Visit to Tashkent and Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan Strategic Alliance Executive Intelligence Snapshot This report evaluates the strategic consolidation of bilateral ties between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan following the August 2026 signing of the Treaty on Eternal Friendship in Tashkent and Ilham Aliyev’s state visit to Tashkent. The bilateral agenda focuses on scaling annual trade turnover to 1 billion US dollars by 2030, enhancing Trans-Caspian transit logistics, and deepening joint investment mechanisms. These developments strengthen non-energy commercial transit across Eurasia while reducing geographical constraints for doubly landlocked Uzbekistan. Context On 23-24 August 2026 , Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev paid an official visit to Tashkent and met with Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. At the third council meeting in Tashkent, both heads of state signed the Treaty on Eternal Friendship alongside agreements to increase trade turnover to 1 billion US dollars by 2030, establish city-twinning partnerships, and coordinate foreign ministry programs. Under the treaty, both states commit to non-participation in alliances hostile to the other’s sovereignty and prohibit third-party state usage of their territories against either signee. Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan established diplomatic relations in 1995, but bilateral ties have accelerated considerably in recent years. The two governments have gradually expanded cooperation from political and cultural relations into investment, transport, energy, industry and other sectors. A major step was taken in August 2024 , when President Ilham Aliyev visited Uzbekistan and the two countries signed the Treaty on Allied Relations . The agreement elevated bilateral relations to an alliance and strengthened the legal and political framework for cooperation. The first meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council was also held during the visit, creating a mechanism for the two presidents to regularly review bilateral projects and establish new priorities. The second meeting of the Council was held in Baku in July 2025 during President Mirziyoyev’s state visit to Azerbaijan. The two sides reviewed cooperation in areas including transport, energy, agriculture, culture and investment, while also adopting a roadmap for implementing the Treaty on Allied Relations for 2025–2029. The third meeting occurred in August 2026 in Tashkent therefore represents the continuation of an institutional process. Economic relations have also developed rapidly. According to President Aliyev’s August 2026 interview with Uzbekistan’s national news agency, bilateral trade reached $795 million in 2025 , more than three times the previous year’s level. During January–May 2026, trade turnover increased by a further 33 percent compared with the same period of 2025. Investment cooperation has been supported by the Azerbaijan–Uzbekistan Investment Company , established with $500 million in authorized capital. The company provides a mechanism for financing joint projects and has identified areas such as manufacturing, transport, energy, logistics, healthcare, IT and education as potential investment sectors. Why Does It Matter? The development of Azerbaijan–Uzbekistan relations should be viewed within the broader transformation of Central Asian connectivity . Uzbekistan is Central Asia’s most populous country and occupies a central geographical position within the region. However, it is also doubly landlocked, meaning that access to global markets depends heavily on transport routes through neighbouring countries. Azerbaijan , located on the western side of the Caspian Sea, offers Uzbekistan an alternative and even more reliable connection toward the South Caucasus, Turkey and Europe. This makes transport cooperation one of the most strategically significant elements of the bilateral relationship. According to President Aliyev, transit transportation between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan increased by 6.7% in 2025, reaching 1.4 million tons. During the first half of 2026, transit volumes increased by another 12.2% compared with the same period of the previous year. These figures are particularly relevant to the development of the Middle Corridor , which connects China and Central Asia with the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, the South Caucasus and Europe. Uzbekistan’s developing railway connections with China, including the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway , could eventually complement the Middle Corridor and provide a more interconnected network linking East Asia with European markets. For Azerbaijan, stronger economic ties with Tashkent increase its relevance as a gateway between Central Asia and Europe. For Uzbekistan, the relationship provides another route for exports, imports and investment beyond its immediate neighbourhood. This mutual interest gives the transport partnership a strategic foundation. Energy cooperation is developing as well. In 2025, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan established the Green Corridor Union . The initiative emerged from the strategic partnership agreement on green energy signed by the three countries during COP29 in Baku in November 2024. Baku and Tashkent also cooperate within the Organisation of Turkic States and have supported stronger economic, transport and cultural connections among Turkic countries. Azerbaijan’s participation in the Consultative Meetings of the Heads of State of Central Asia has further connected Baku with regional discussions traditionally cantered on the five Central Asian states. Outlook President Ilham Aliyev’s August 23–24 state visit will further strengthen the institutional and strategic foundations of Azerbaijan–Uzbekistan relations. The third meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council provides an opportunity to advance existing agreements and identify new areas for cooperation. The Azerbaijan–Uzbekistan partnership constitutes a permanent structural component of Central Asian and South Caucasus connectivity . Institutional oversight by the Supreme Interstate Council maintains alignment on political, transit, and financial objectives. Operational risks persist around cross-border coordination . Sustained growth depends on aligning multi-country customs procedures, expanding Caspian port capacity, and securing infrastructure capital for cross-border power transmission. Primary scenarios indicate a continued rise in Middle Corridor cargo volumes, expanded joint industrial investments, and accelerated energy trade linking Central Asia through the Caspian region directly to European markets. * Cover image : The meeting between the President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and the President of Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev (Credits: President.az, CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons) Written by Adkhamjon Janobiddinov Independent Researcher. Economics student at the College of Wooster, independent researcher and journalist focusing on Central Asia. His articles have been published in more than 50 countries of the world. Through his publications, Adkhamjon aims to contribute to a better understanding of the Central Asian region around the world. body: Russia-Indonesia Military-Technical Cooperation Russia-Indonesia Military-Technical Cooperation Confirms Moscow’s Strategy in the Asia-Pacific Image generated using artificial intelligence technology Executive Intelligence Snapshot This report assesses the strategic and economic implications of deepening military-technical co-operation between the Russian Federation and the Republic of Indonesia. Recent bilateral naval exercises, expanding commercial trade, and official diplomatic engagements highlight Moscow’s sustained focus on expanding its strategic posture in South-East Asia. Strategic risk centres on regional political friction with Western allies, secondary sanctions exposure, and potential disruptions to maritime security corridors. Context On 17 August 2026 , Russian President Vladimir Putin sent a congratulatory telegram in honour of Indonesia’s Independence Day in which he affirmed that Russia and Indonesia are strengthening bilateral ties to bolster regional and global security. Previously, on 16 August 2026 , in an interview for the Russian media RIA Novosti, Russian Ambassador to Indonesia Sergei Tolchenov confirmed that bilateral military-technical co-operation remains active and ongoing, while explicitly denying reports regarding the construction of a Russian air force base in eastern Indonesia, accusing the West of “hysteria.” Tolchenov’s statements followed Australian concerns regarding expanding relations between Moscow and Jakarta and rumours of a potential Russian military footprint in the country. Irrespective of these claims, Moscow and Jakarta have demonstrably enhanced their military co-operation; in July 2026, the Russian Navy and the Indonesian Navy conducted the joint “Orruda-2026” naval exercises off Vladivostok in the Sea of Japan/East Sea. Furthermore, Indonesian authorities confirmed a standing invitation for President Putin to conduct an official state visit to Indonesia. On economic tracks , the Russian-Indonesian bilateral trade volume reached approximately 4.8 to 5.1 billion US dollars , recording over 20% growth year-on-year. The two nations are finalising the ratification of the Indonesia-Eurasian Economic Union Free Trade Agreement , aimed at significantly expanding market access, energy transactions, industrial manufacturing, and critical commodity trades including Russian wheat, fertilizers, crude oil, and Indonesian palm oil. Why Does It Matter? Moscow seeks to secure non-Western strategic partnerships and maintain arms export channels in the Indo-Pacific region. Russia’s growing military and economic co-operation with Indonesia forms an integral component of the Kremlin’s broader strategy in the Asia-Pacific, specifically targeting ASEAN member states to establish a persistent regional presence, as demonstrated by the Russia-ASEAN Summit held in Kazan in June 2026. The Kremlin’s strategic imperatives include countering Western diplomatic isolation, establishing strategic influence across critical maritime routes, and also challenging the Chinese regional strategy. Furthermore, Moscow aims to offset Washington’s presence in the Asia-Pacific by promoting bilateral relations with ASEAN members and exploiting ongoing US military commitments in the Persian Gulf against Iran, which are diverting and straining US Navy capabilities . Indonesia maintains a non-aligned foreign policy posture, utilising relations with major global powers to balance regional influence and ensure sovereign strategic autonomy. Security friction arises from Australian defence anxieties regarding northern maritime approaches, increasing diplomatic tension within regional security groupings such as AUKUS and ASEAN. Outlook In the short term , it is highly likely that Russia and Indonesia will continue expanding bilateral security and economic engagement through scheduled high-level visits, the implementation of free trade frameworks, and joint defence activities. In this context, Moscow will continue leveraging its defence industry to target South-East Asian markets (such as Indonesia) to preserve export capacity. Western regional partners will likely increase intelligence monitoring and diplomatic pressure on ASEAN members regarding defence procurement and broader co-operation with Moscow. In the medium term , driven in part by the heightened deployment of the US Navy in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, the Asia-Pacific region will likely witness increased activity by regional powers such as the Russian Federation and the People’s Republic of China. This trend may elevate geopolitical friction along major maritime corridors, introducing incremental security risks and operational constraints for commercial logistics across South-East Asian shipping routes. body: Syria–Russia Agreement Defines Moscow’s Military Presence Syria–Russia Memorandum Restructures Moscow’s Military Presence in the Middle East Executive Intelligence Snapshot Syria and Russia have signed a memorandum that will reorganise Moscow’s military presence on the Syrian coast after approximately 18 months of negotiations. Damascus will assume management of Khmeimim Airport and the fourth commercial berth at Tartous, while Russian military facilities will be converted into joint training and qualification centres within three months. The agreement gives Syria greater control over strategic civilian infrastructure but does not establish a complete Russian military withdrawal. The immediate economic relevance lies in the transfer of port and airport facilities into Syrian administration, although the sources provide no evidence yet of a material change in trade, investment, fiscal revenues or financial markets. Background On 9 August 2026 , the Syrian Foreign Ministry announced that Damascus and Moscow had reached a memorandum governing Russia’s future presence on the Syrian coast. The agreement follows approximately 18 months of negotiations . Under its terms, Syria will take management of facilities designated for civilian use, including Khmeimim Airport and the fourth commercial berth at Tartous Port . These facilities will be gradually integrated into Syrian civilian administration. The military facilities at Khmeimim and Tartous will no longer operate under their previous arrangement as Russian military bases. The two governments agreed to convert them into joint training and qualification centres . The transition should take no more than three months, after which the new arrangements will enter into force. The available sources do not specify the number of Russian personnel that will remain, the military equipment permitted at the facilities, Russian access rights, or the operational restrictions that will apply after the transition. The memorandum consequently establishes a change in the status of the facilities without establishing the final scale of Russia’s military capability in Syria. Why Does It Matter? For Syria , the agreement increases state control over infrastructure previously associated with Russia’s military presence because of the cooperation that Moscow had with the former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. Control of Khmeimim Airport and the fourth commercial berth at Tartous gives the Syrian authorities direct responsibility for facilities that can serve civilian purposes. The arrangement also allows Damascus to reduce the previous military status of Russian facilities without terminating the bilateral relationship. For Russia , the memorandum preserves a formal military relationship with Syria through joint training centres. The agreement does not demonstrate that Russia has abandoned Khmeimim and Tartous. It does, however, remove the previous designation and places the future operation of the facilities within a jointly defined arrangement. The political significance lies in the change in control and the impact that this agreement can have on Russia’s logistics operations in the MENA region . Damascus has secured control of civilian facilities while keeping Moscow engaged in a military relationship. This reduces the likelihood of an abrupt rupture in bilateral ties and gives both governments a mechanism for changing the previous arrangement through negotiation. The principal security risk is uncertainty during implementation . The three-month transition creates a defined period in which the practical implications of the new arrangement will become clearer. Reaching an agreement with Moscow supports Damascus’s strategy of diversifying its foreign partnerships and avoiding alignment with a single external bloc. Continued military cooperation with Russia could also provide terrorist and jihadist organisations with additional material for anti-government propaganda, particularly the Islamic State , which has portrayed al-Sharaa’s government as corrupt and subordinate to foreign powers. Russian military cooperation could reinforce such narratives by allowing jihadist groups to depict the government as dependent on an external power. Outlook The most likely near-term development is implementation of the memorandum within the stated three-month period. The decisive indicators will be the transfer of civilian management, the formal conversion of the military facilities and the practical rules governing Russian personnel and equipment. A managed reduction in Moscow’s military role would strengthen Damascus’s control over strategic infrastructure while preserving a bilateral security relationship. A more substantial Russian withdrawal would produce a larger change in the security arrangement than the memorandum itself currently confirms. A third outcome would involve Russia retaining a substantial operational presence under the joint-centre designation. Such an outcome would make the change primarily institutional rather than a major reduction in Russian military capability. * Cover Image : Russia President Vladimir Putin and Syria President Ahmed al-Sharaa in the Kremlin (Credits: Kremlin.ru, CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons) Written by SpecialEurasia OSINT Team A specialised analytical unit dedicated to open-source intelligence collection and geopolitical forecasting. body: Iran’s Rare-Earth Potential and the US-China Competition Iran’s Emerging Rare Earth Potential and the US-China Critical Minerals Competition Image generated with the support of artificial intelligence technology. Executive Intelligence Snapshot Iran has identified more than 20 new areas with potential rare-earth deposits and has made their exploration a national priority. Although these discoveries do not yet constitute significant production capacity, they increase the country’s relevance to the growing US-China competition over critical minerals, in which control of reserves, processing capabilities and supply-chain infrastructure is becoming a strategic objective. Context Iran’s Geological Survey and Exploration Organisation (GSI), together with the Iranian Mining and Mining Industries Development and Renovation Organization (IMIDRO), identified potential rare-earth elements in more than 20 prospective areas across East and West Azerbaijan, Kurdistan, North, South and Razavi Khorasan, in addition to known areas including Sepehr-1 and Sepehr-2 in Marvast and the Bafq mining belt. Identified mineralisation includes lanthanum, cerium, neodymium and praseodymium , used in permanent magnets, electric vehicles, advanced electronics, wind turbines and defence systems. Iran is already among the world’s most mineral-rich countries , with approximately 57 billion tonnes of proven reserves across 68 mineral types and more than 6,000 active mines. The country’s significant resource’s value is based at an estimated 27.3 trillion US dollars. Its critical-minerals profile extends beyond rare earths : Iran ranks highly in strontium, barite, iron ore, molybdenum, fluorite and lead, while also possessing substantial copper, zinc and titanium resources. In March 2025 , Tehran announced the discovery of 7,000 tons of antimony (chemically known as Stibium), a key element for sectors such as renewable energy and defence technology, as it continues its exploration programs. In November 2025 , the MP Materials Corp., the US Department of War, and Saudi Arabia’s Ma’aden signed a binding agreement to build the region’s first rare earth refining facility, anchored by a deposit the Saudi government ranks as the fourth most valuable rare earth reserve on earth. In addition, US recent efforts to secure mineral resources in Ukraine (with a deal that provided nearly exclusive access, signed on 30 April 2025 ) illustrate the US objective of reducing dependence on Chinese-controlled critical-mineral networks. China retains the world’s largest rare-earth reserves and a dominant position in mining, separation and processing . Beijing has also developed extensive infrastructure and economic networks across resource-rich countries, supporting access to strategic minerals and their associated supply chains. In light of ongoing competition, which has shifted to the Middle East, China is targeting Iran’s untapped assets to maintain its monopoly. Why Does It Matter? Iran’s emerging rare-earth potential should therefore be assessed within the wider US-China competition over critical-mineral supply chains rather than solely as a domestic mining development. Tehran’s prioritisation of critical minerals reflects the need to diversify beyond hydrocarbons , reduce exposure to sanctions and external supply disruptions, and secure domestic inputs for advanced industrial and defence capabilities. The discovery of new deposits could eventually support non-oil exports and industrial development, but the immediate strategic value lies in their potential integration into global supply chains. The Islamic Republic currently faces a substantial gap between geological potential and strategic capability : commercial exploitation requires further assessment, while large-scale rare-earth production depends on specialised separation technology, capital, technical expertise and reliable energy infrastructure. This is where China’s position becomes decisive. Beijing possesses capabilities that Iran lacks and has already established scientific cooperation with Tehran on rare-earth exploration and processing, including a joint research programme announced in August 2026 . Tehran has undertaken pilot extraction and separation activities, but there is no evidence that China is transferring technologies subject to its export restrictions. Chinese early engagement nevertheless provides Beijing with a low-cost strategic position from which to assess Iran’s resources and potentially shape future investment, processing and supply-chain arrangements if deposits prove commercially viable. For the Middle Eastern Republic, cooperation offers access to capital, expertise and technology otherwise constrained by Western sanctions; however, it risks replacing dependence on Western suppliers with technological and financial dependence on China . This is particularly significant because strategic leverage in rare earths derives primarily from processing and downstream industrial capacity rather than from possession of ore alone. Iran’s energy shortages further constrain its ability to establish large-scale processing facilities. China can mitigate some of these bottlenecks but cannot eliminate them, making the development of indigenous processing and industrial capacity the key determinant of Tehran’s strategic autonomy. Western sanctions may reinforce the process: by restricting access to Western finance, technology and industrial partnerships, they increase the relative value of Chinese cooperation and may accelerate Iran’s integration into a China-oriented resource and technology network. The Islamic Republic’s parallel engagement with Russia and South-South partners, including Bolivia over rare-earth deposits, further indicates an effort to diversify external economic relationships, although these partnerships remain less developed than Beijing’s technological and industrial position. The principal intelligence significance is therefore not the discovery of additional deposits itself, but whether Chinese involvement progresses from scientific cooperation towards financing, technology provision, joint ventures, infrastructure development or preferential access to future production. Such developments would indicate that Iran’s geological potential is being incorporated into a broader China-centred critical-minerals architecture . Conversely, successful development of indigenous processing capacity would increase Tehran’s ability to use its mineral endowment as an instrument of economic resilience and strategic autonomy. The central question is consequently not whether Iran possesses valuable rare-earth resources, but who will control the capital, technology, processing capacity and infrastructure required to convert them into strategic power. Outlook Iran’s rare-earth potential is unlikely to generate significant geopolitical leverage in the short term. Its significance lies in the possibility that an emerging resource base will become integrated into the broader contest between Washington and Beijing over critical-mineral reserves and supply chains. Monitoring Chinese financing, technology cooperation, joint ventures, infrastructure projects and access arrangements will provide the clearest indicators of whether Iran is developing an autonomous critical-minerals sector or becoming another node in China’s wider resource and processing ecosystem. body: Russia-Iran Military Cooperation and Project C430L Russia-Iran Military Cooperation and Project C430L Image generated with the support of artificial intelligence technology. Executive Intelligence Snapshot Project C430L indicates a deepening of Russian-Iranian military-technical cooperation, with evidence of Moscow’s expertise transfer in ramjet propulsion and increasing complementarity between the two countries’ defence-industrial capabilities. For Moscow, such cooperation could contribute to raising the operational costs of the US military presence in the Middle East, while for Tehran it may support the acquisition of high-end capabilities and progressive technological autonomy. Available evidence nevertheless places C430L at the early stages of technology transfer and development, with insufficient evidence to assess an Iranian supersonic ramjet capability as operational. Context An investigation published by the Financial Times on 1 September 2026 revealed a covert, multi-year military assistance programme between Russia and Iran , codenamed Project C430L . According to documentation reviewed, the programme is intended to assist Tehran in developing ramjet propulsion systems for a new generation of supersonic cruise missiles. The programme concerns the transfer and refinement of ramjet technology, which enables a cruise missile to sustain supersonic speeds during atmospheric flight. According to the investigation, the technology could be applied to long-range anti-ship and land-attack systems . Initial activity dates back to 2023 . Travel records and documentation indicate repeated visits to Iran by officials from Rosoboronexport and specialists from NPO Mashinostroyenia prior to the signing, in November 2023, of a contract with Iran’s Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics. In 2025, NPO Mashinostroyenia reportedly received technical material relating to Iranian ramjet tests . Russian engineers analysed telemetry from a flight test, focusing on combustion stability, air intake performance, fuel delivery and engine-nozzle performance. The documentation also indicates that the programme remained active in 2026, with the two sides discussing a subsequent development phase. The programme therefore represents a more advanced form of cooperation than the earlier relationship, in which Iran primarily provided UAVs and associated expertise to Russia. In the C430L case, the available evidence indicates a transfer of Russian technological and engineering expertise to Iran’s defence industry. On 1 September 2026 , Dmitry Shugaev, Director of Russia’s Federal Service for Military-Technical Cooperation , stated that air-defence systems were currently the principal area of military-technical cooperation with Iran, adding that cooperation also covered aviation and small arms. The statement confirms the breadth of bilateral military-technical cooperation but does not, in itself, publicly confirm the C430L programme. Analysis Russia-Iran cooperation is evolving towards a strategic partnership based on military complementarity, know-how exchange and political coordination , while falling short of a symmetrical military alliance. On 27 April 2026 , Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg. The Russian delegation included Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Presidential Aide Yuri Ushakov and Igor Kostyukov, head of the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Armed Forces , commonly referred to as the GRU. In Russian practice, the attendance of the head of military intelligence at an exclusively diplomatic meeting is unusual. The presence of Kostyukov was already an indicator of the significance attached to the security and intelligence dimensions of the bilateral relationship between the two actors. The relationship can be characterised as a strategic compensation partnership : each actor provides capabilities, expertise or technological access that the other cannot readily obtain or develop independently. The relationship therefore remains predominantly transactional while preserving significant freedom of manoeuvre for both sides. Iran possesses several capabilities of particular relevance to Russia: extensive experience in asymmetric warfare; extensive employment of relatively low-cost missile systems; UAV development under prolonged sanctions; saturation capabilities; relatively low-cost production; experience operating against technologically superior adversaries; knowledge of the Middle Eastern operational environment; logistics infrastructure and networks designed to function under conditions of interdiction. The Ukraine conflict has transformed some of these capabilities from predominantly regional instruments into assets of value to a conventional power engaged in a high-intensity industrial conflict. Russian production of Shahed systems represents the clearest example. The relationship is therefore no longer limited to the sale of Iranian systems to Russia. Available evidence indicates a process of know-how transfer, industrial adaptation and reciprocal learning. Iran has developed substantial autonomy in the missile sector, but missile autonomy does not equate to complete technological autonomy. Tehran has longstanding expertise in ballistic and cruise missiles, anti-ship systems, propulsion, UAVs, seekers, guidance and electronic warfare. Moving from experimentation with ramjet technology to a reliable, reproducible and militarily integrable system nevertheless represents a distinct technological challenge. The principal value of the Project C430L therefore lies in the potential transfer of tacit expertise. Design procedures, troubleshooting, tolerances, materials, test methodologies and the ability to interpret experimental data can be more difficult to acquire independently than hardware or technical documentation alone. For Moscow, one potential objective is to increase distributed pressure on the United States without directly deploying Russian forces into the Middle Eastern theatre . A credible Iranian supersonic anti-ship capability could increase missile-defence requirements, force dispersion and protection requirements, as well as the complexity of US naval planning in the Persian Gulf. The strategic effect would therefore derive from increasing the costs of the US regional presence rather than necessarily from direct Russian force deployment. A second potential interest is the combination of Russian experience in conventional warfare, missile technology and integrated systems with Iranian experience in denying an adversary’s technological superiority. Iran has not structured its military posture primarily around achieving conventional parity with the United States. Its deterrence architecture is instead oriented towards preventing an adversary’s technological superiority from translating into operational freedom. This approach integrates missiles, UAVs, anti-ship systems, mines, electronic warfare, dispersion, mobility, geographical depth and partner capabilities. The potential acquisition of a supersonic ramjet capability would therefore represent a qualitative evolution of this architecture. Integrating a higher-end strike capability with systems designed around mass and saturation could increase the complexity of the adversary’s defensive problem. For Iran, the strategic value of such technology would not necessarily depend on the ability to destroy an aircraft carrier. A sufficiently credible anti-ship capability could already be relevant if it imposed greater stand-off distances, increased defensive asset requirements or altered US naval operational planning. The Ukraine conflict has been the principal accelerator of Russian-Iranian military complementarity. Before 2022, the relationship was primarily characterised by systems supply, military-technical cooperation and regional interaction. After 2022, Russia’s employment of Iranian UAVs created a cycle of reciprocal adaptation . Russia gained ex

body: US Operation Economic Outcast and Chinese Countermeasures Operation Economic Outcast: The US-Iran Economic War and Chinese Countermeasures Executive Intelligence Snapshot Operation Economic Outcast represents an evolution in the US strategy of coercion towards Iran: through secondary sanctions, pressure on oil and financial flows, and the targeting of intermediary networks, Washington aims to constrain Tehran’s economic capacity and, indirectly, limit Sino-Iranian integration. The growing exposure of Chinese interests, however, introduces a second theatre of strategic competition, in which Beijing is called upon to balance the protection of its energy supplies and alternative financial infrastructure against the risk of US sanctions, increasing the likelihood of a gradual economic and regulatory escalation between the two powers. Information Context On 19 August 2026 , Donald Trump announced on Truth what he described as the most extensive economic pressure operation ever undertaken against a country, Operation Economic Outcast , directed against Iran. The US Treasury Department will no longer target solely the Islamic Republic, but also any entity supporting its economy , through a system of secondary sanctions. The financial coercion strategy stems from the inability to achieve a decisive military victory, six months after the beginning of the offensive. The objective is to disrupt Iranian financial and oil flows, with direct repercussions for Chinese strategic interests as well. Beijing has responded through Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian, describing US secondary sanctions as illegal and unilateral, as they are not authorised by the UN Security Council. Jian reiterated that Sino-Iranian energy and trade cooperation complies with international law and that China will take all necessary measures to safeguard its national interests and its companies. Chinese involvement is not accidental: Beijing absorbs approximately 80–90% of Iranian oil exports. For this reason, the Trump administration has placed on the blacklist several private Chinese and Hong Kong-based companies active in shipping and refining, while for the time being avoiding China’s major state-owned banks, in order to limit the risk of destabilising the global financial system. Pressure on Beijing is also part of a broader intensification of the US-China economic confrontation. During the same weeks as Operation Economic Outcast , the White House advanced a new tariff package targeting China. Following the conclusion of investigations under Section 301 of the US Trade Act , concerning Chinese overcapacity and the export of goods at below-market prices, Washington formally put forward the possibility of an additional 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods. The measure would be added to targeted tariffs already ranging between 10% and 12.5%, introduced to counter alleged violations in supply chains involving forced labour, as well as to the punitive sanctions of 50% envisaged for goods originating from countries providing Iran with assistance or commercial and military components. Potential Chinese countermeasures, ranging from restrictions on critical mineral exports to commercial retaliation, are particularly significant because they come only weeks before the official meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping , reportedly under consideration at the White House for 24 September 2026 . Analysis Operation Economic Outcast is not merely a sanctions package targeting Iran, but a global secondary financial coercion operation . For Beijing, it represents a direct challenge to its security and development architecture. The first vulnerability concerns supply security. China is the world’s largest crude oil importer and absorbs approximately 80–90% of Iranian oil exports , primarily destined for independent Chinese refineries, the so-called teapots in Shandong. These refineries purchase crude at heavily discounted prices using yuan or barter arrangements, thereby reducing their exposure to the US dollar. On the financial front, Iran and China have developed a parallel circuit to circumvent Tehran’s exclusion from SWIFT and from dollar- and euro-denominated payments. Iran uses CIPS ( Cross-Border Interbank Payment System ) to settle transactions in yuan, but Iran’s major state-owned banks predominantly access the system indirectly, through intermediaries, shell companies in Hong Kong, smaller Chinese financial institutions and dedicated banks such as Kunlun Bank . These are precisely the channels now being targeted by the “economic D-Day”. Iran’s entry into BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) has also accelerated negotiations to directly connect Iran’s SEPAM banking network to China’s alternative CIPS system and Russia’s SPFS. Integration nevertheless remains partial for two reasons. The first is Beijing’s caution: direct access by Iran’s most heavily sanctioned banks is restricted in order to shield Chinese intermediaries with significant international exposure from the risk of US secondary sanctions. Any institution providing Tehran with a financial lifeline risks exclusion from the dollar payment system, the US interbank market and SWIFT. So far, Washington has primarily targeted intermediary companies, but the threat of sanctioning major Chinese state-owned banks involved in payments has increased pressure on Beijing. Approximately 80% of the interbank messaging used globally by CIPS still relies on the ISO/SWIFT standard; consequently, when handling sensitive flows to Tehran, China resorts to dedicated data transmission routes. The financial dimension therefore intersects with the geopolitical one. The Trump strategy seeks to weaken the alternative international order that Beijing is building with its Middle Eastern partners and BRICS, while simultaneously using pressure on Iran as a negotiating lever vis-à-vis China ahead of the forthcoming bilateral summit. A central element of this multipolar order is de-dollarisation. The Sino-Iranian circuit does not rely solely on CIPS (and therefore the yuan), but also on gold and digital assets. By targeting the cryptocurrency, gold and alternative clearing channels used by Iran to trade with China, Washington demonstrates that it can also intercept China’s informal commercial networks. In 2021, China and Iran signed a twenty-five-year strategic cooperation agreement theoretically valued at $400 billion . A complete erosion of Iran’s economic capacity would render Tehran financially inactive, reducing the value of Chinese infrastructure investments and strategic presence linked to the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in the western Middle East. From this perspective, several analysts argued following the attack on Iran in February 2026 that, while Israel’s objective was the destabilisation of the revolutionary leadership, the United States’ objective could have been Beijing, by then deeply embedded in the Persian Gulf. The use of Iranian sanctions as a tool of pressure against China is not, however, new. In 2021, in order to counter US long-arm jurisdiction , Beijing developed a legal response based on two pillars. The first is the Blocking Rules issued by the Ministry of Commerce, which allow the Chinese government to order companies operating in China not to comply with foreign restrictions deemed unjustified, such as those preventing trade with Iran. The second is the Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law (AFSL) , adopted by the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress. Article 12 prohibits individuals and organisations operating in China from implementing foreign “discriminatory restrictive measures”. If a company applies US sanctions and causes harm to a Chinese partner, the latter may therefore bring proceedings before Chinese courts to seek compensation. The law remained for a long time primarily a deterrent and political instrument, but acquired an enforcement framework in March 2025 , when the State Council issued the Provi
title: Operation Economic Outcast: The US-Iran Economic War and Chinese Countermeasures

body: Economic D-Day: The New US War of Attrition Against Iran Economic D-Day: The New War of Attrition Against Iran Image generated using artificial intelligence technology Executive Intelligence Snapshot The Trump Administration has launched an unprecedented financial offensive against Iran, dubbed “Economic D-Day”, in an attempt to pressure Tehran into submission following six months of war that have failed to achieve the anticipated objective of government change. The measure comes at a point of mounting domestic pressure in both Washington, which is confronting an unpopular conflict ahead of the mid-term elections, and Iran, where a political faction is increasingly advocating an end to the war while the military leadership remains committed to continuing the conflict. Background The conflict between the United States and Iran has entered its sixth month. US military operations, conducted with the stated objective of facilitating government change in Tehran, have severely degraded Iran’s deterrence infrastructure, including the country’s senior leadership. However, they have failed both to bring down the Iranian government and to eliminate Iran’s uranium-enrichment capabilities. Against the backdrop of diminishing weapons stocks and increasingly fragile domestic support, the United States has shifted towards a strategy of comprehensive economic strangulation . On 19 August 2026 , Trump announced the measure, describing it as the most crushing economic operation ever undertaken against a country, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent characterised it as the largest coordinated economic isolation campaign in history. The stated objective is to systematically target and eliminate Tehran’s remaining channels of financial support . In a post on Truth Social, Trump stated that any country permitting its financial institutions, commercial enterprises, airports or government entities to provide Tehran with any form of economic lifeline would face severe economic consequences. Specifically, the US President called for the immediate cessation of activities involving the smuggling of oil, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries and front companies that provide support to Iran. On 21 August 2026 , US authorities also updated the reported casualty figure for the overseas mission, placing the number of personnel killed or wounded at more than 750 . Why Does It Matter? Washington’s decision to reinforce economic coercion rather than pursue another round of military escalation indicates a change in posture rather than a change in strategic objective . Bessent has explicitly presented financial pressure as an alternative to renewed large-scale kinetic operations. This suggests that the Trump Administration regards its lower-cost military options as largely exhausted, at least in the short term, while the political cost of the conflict is becoming increasingly significant ahead of the mid-term elections. From this perspective, “Economic D-Day” also serves a domestic political and strategic-communications function . It allows the administration to demonstrate a decisive escalation without explicitly acknowledging military stalemate. The release of the US casualty figures can likewise be interpreted within this framework of strategic communication. The announcement that US casualties have exceeded 750 comes at a moment of tactical transition. The disclosure of a significant aggregate figure may indicate that the active or high-intensity phase of the operation has reached a turning point;in this case, a shift in operational doctrine. The publication of a high aggregate casualty figure may also serve a specific communications purpose: to concentrate the political shock within a single news cycle . If casualties were disclosed incrementally, their cumulative impact on public opinion and the media would remain persistent, generating sustained and potentially damaging coverage. Releasing the aggregate figure at once effectively saturates the news cycle, allowing institutional communications in subsequent days to redirect attention from casualties towards the new phase of economic warfare. More broadly, the release of an isolated aggregate figure without immediate rigorous categorisation creates a degree of narrative ambiguity . Providing a headline number without simultaneously specifying the severity and distribution of individual cases creates scope for differentiated messaging. For the domestic audience, the political impact can be moderated by distinguishing minor injuries from permanent disabilities and fatalities. For allied partners, the figure demonstrates the scale of the US commitment and the seriousness of the threat encountered. For the adversary, it communicates that, despite the human cost incurred, US operational capacity remains intact and that the response is not being dictated by panic. The most consequential vulnerability in the newly announced economic campaign is the sustainability of the ultimatum directed at US allies and Tehran’s commercial partners. A de facto “with us or against us” approach risks affecting regional partners of the United States, including Pakistan . China is likely to be particularly affected, given that it absorbs the majority of Iranian crude exports through independent refineries and smaller financial institutions with limited exposure to the US financial system. Historically, secondary sanctions against Chinese purchasers have had only partial effectiveness because Beijing possesses alternative payment channels and sufficient negotiating leverage to absorb sanctions-related risk, particularly where the political cost of yielding to Washington is perceived to exceed the economic cost of sanctions. The inclusion of regional financial and commercial hubs might also affect Turkey and the Gulf states and, therefore, would also introduce a significant risk of friction with partners that remain strategically important to the United States in the region. On the Iranian side, the most significant development is not the US measure itself (Tehran has been subject to sanctions for more than four decades) but rather the emergence of public convergence between President Pezeshkian, Parliamentary Speaker Ghalibaf and even Central Bank Governor Hemmati regarding the assessment that Iranian oil exports have already been reduced to a minimum and that the country cannot sustain the conflict indefinitely . Pezeshkian’s statements , arguing that it would be preferable to end the war “from a position of strength and dignity” before conditions deteriorate further, together with Ghalibaf’s position that national security cannot rest solely on military capability in the absence of economic growth and functioning financial circulation, suggest that the so-called “realist” faction within the revolutionary political system is increasingly using economic constraints as an instrument of domestic political pressure in support of a negotiated exit strategy. This position, however, is encountering overt resistance from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp s and hard-line political currents, which interpret any form of accommodation as capitulation. Mohsen Rezaei , a prominent hard-line figure, close ally of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei and Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has, in fact, threatened to target the economic and energy infrastructure of neighbouring states should they cooperate with the US economic campaign. Moreover, Rezaei stressed that while so far only military bases were targeted, if the plan to impose economic sanctions on Iran proceeds, Tehran will strike the US oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere. The fracture between the two principal components of the Iranian establishment , the economic and political actors exposed to domestic discontent, and the military-security establishment, which is comparatively less sensitive to economic costs, therefore remains the key variabl

body: Iran-Tajikistan and the Persian-Speaking Union Proposal Persian-Speaking Union Proposal: Iran-Tajikistan Bilateral Outlook Image generated using artificial intelligence technology Executive Intelligence Snapshot Iran and Tajikistan are actively expanding a bilateral partnership based on common Persian heritage, broadening their focus from foundational cultural exchange toward joint technical, energy, and economic initiatives. Despite ongoing conflict in the Persian Gulf, the Proposal of a “union of Persian-speaking countries and regions” illustrates that Tehran remains committed to a pragmatic, non-ideological Central Asian policy aimed at building regional cooperation. Simultaneously, Central Asian states continue to view Iran as an indispensable security partner and a vital gateway for maritime trade and transport infrastructure. Background On 16 August 2026 , during a meeting with Tajik Minister of Energy and Water Resources Dalir Jum’a , Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref proposed establishing a “Union of Persian-Speaking Countries and Regions” to strengthen cultural and civilisational cooperation among Persian-speaking communities. The Iranian diplomat stressed that that Iran and Tajikistan’s shared cultural, civilisational and linguistic heritage provides a strong foundation for expanding bilateral relations. Relations between Tehran and Dushanbe experienced a deep freeze from 2015 to 2019, triggered largely by Iran hosting Muhiddin Kabiri, the leader of the Islamic Renaissance Party of Tajikistan (IRPT) at a conference. In response, Tajikistan restricted the activities of various Iranian organizations within its borders. Tensions escalated further in 2017 when Tajik state television aired a documentary accusing Iran of subversion during Tajikistan’s 1990s civil war. Iranian authorities have consistently denied these allegations. To this day, contemporary sources remain divided on whether Tehran funded insurgent groups, as conclusive evidence has never emerged. Since 2021, a total strategic reset occurred , yielding visa-free travel , defence cooperation (the opening of an Ababil-2 drone factories in Tajikistan), and dozens of Memorandums of Understanding signed across trade, energy, infrastructure, cultural exchange, and security sectors. Bilateral trade turnover grew substantially over recent years, jumping from $377.7 million in 2024 to approximately $483.9 million in 2025, a roughly 28% year-on-year increase. Continued upward trajectory persisted into 2026, with first-half trade reaching $254.3 million (up 14.8% compared to the same period in 2025). In 2025, Iran entered the top five of Tajikistan’s largest trading partners, ranking fifth by total trade turnover. Iran’s primary exports include petrochemical products (oil bitumen, polyethylene, polypropylene), construction materials (cement, clinker), and agricultural/food products (sugar, pasta, citrus fruits). High-level bilateral commission meetings between officials (such as Tajikistan’s Ministry of Energy and Water Resources and Iran’s Oil Ministry) have established ongoing supply agreements for diesel, crude oil, and aviation fuel. Furthermore, to sustain trade momentum, both nations have advanced transport initiatives, including planned direct railway connectivity via Turkmenistan to optimise cargo and supply chain movements across Central Asia. Why Does It Matter? The proposal by Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref to establish a union of Persian-speaking countries and regions is a pan-Persianist soft-power posturing , which has long characterised the two countries ties. Relations with Central Asia underwent a complete step-change under the Raisi presidency. It is no coincidence that these shifts materialised after 2021, the year of his election. Acting in alignment with the directives set out by Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei, Raisi vigorously pursued Iran’s “Look East” policy following years of inconclusive diplomacy aimed at rekindling ties with European markets. Although relations with individual Central Asian republics had experienced friction in preceding years, the thirteenth Iranian administration reversed the trend, ushering in an unprecedented wave of state visits. The success of these policies stems from mutual necessity: for Tehran, the northern frontier serves as an economic relief valve away from the south-western borders, where Iran finds itself militarily encircled. Conversely, for landlocked republics, Iran offers vital access to international waters and direct connectivity to Gulf and Indian markets. Now Tehran wants to lock in this momentum. Facing sustained Western isolation, Iran leverages Pan-Persian cultural rhetoric as a low-cost vehicle to anchor itself in Eurasia. It frames trade, transit infrastructure, and scientific transfers under a shared civilizational umbrella. The Organization of Turkic States (OTS) , driven by Turkey, Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan, has gained massive momentum in Central Asia. Iran feels culturally and geopolitically squeezed by Turkic block-building . Promoting a Persian-speaking alliance serves as Tehran’s counterweight to Ankara’s expanding influence in the region. This strategy has gained even more urgency as the US war on the Islamic Republic is favouring the Western-led Middle Corridor, which regional actors currently view as safer. While with “union of Persian-speaking countries” Aref clearly referred to Tajikistan, with “regions” he implicitly references the non-Pashtun, Dari-speaking populations of Afghanistan (Tajiks, Hazaras). Since the Taliban takeover, both Tehran and Dushanbe share deep security anxieties regarding Sunni extremism , ethnic Pashtun dominance, and cross-border terrorism, even as both navigate complex, pragmatic realities with Kabul. Iran has been a major player in countering regional Sunni terrorism and has a relevant role in the security architecture established by the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) . Being Tajikistan one of Central Asian most affected countries, the security issue might lay a common ground for cooperation. President Emomali Rahmon will not sign up for an anti-Western or anti-Russian bloc. Tajikistan depends on Moscow for security, Beijing for financial support, and Western/Gulf investments for development and humanitarian aids. Dushanbe will take Iranian energy, transit (Chabahar port), and trade, but will reject risky institutional alignment that might trigger secondary sanctions. Iran, in fact, is an Islamic Republic with Shia-centric power structures. Tajikistan is a hyper-secular state that aggressively suppresses political Islam . Rahmon would view religious influence from Tehran as a threat to his regime’s survival. Nevertheless, unlike in the Middle East where the deterrence posture of Iran also required spreading religious influence to build the so-called Axis of Resistance, Tehran’s approach to Central Asia has been characterised by a pragmatic strategy with bilateral relations based on trade, security and common infrastructure. While Aref rightly pointed to cultural and civilisational cooperation , this also marks a revival. Decades of Soviet engineering severed direct cultural ties between the populations. For instance, Tajiks use the Cyrillic alphabet, while Iranians use the Perso-Arabic script. Moreover, while Afghanistan officially recognised the name “Dari” for its dialect of Persian in its 1964 Constitution to promote a national identity distinct from Iran, the Soviet Union did artificially codify “Tajik” as a separate language in the 1920s to weaken regional Persian cultural continuity following 19 th century imperial conflicts between the Russian and Qajar empires over shared borderlands. This broader Soviet strategy of national delimitation also led to the inclusion of historic Persian cultural centres like Samarkand and Bukhara within Uzbekistan rather than Tajikistan. body: UAE–Iran Shadow Diplomacy and Regional Security UAE–Iran Shadow Diplomacy and Regional Security Image generated using artificial intelligence technology Executive Intelligence Snapshot This report evaluates if the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Iran might develop shadow diplomacy channels during the Middle East crisis to negotiate informal security guarantees and economic exchanges. The operational use of these covert avenues underscores how Tehran successfully leverages its asymmetric deterrence strategy to compel regional neighbours into transactional risk-mitigation agreements. Consequently, these quiet interactions might signal a broader strategic shift where states prioritize pragmatic off-the-record negotiations to safeguard critical infrastructure over traditional, open diplomatic alignments. Context Recent findings indicate that a Royal Jet Boeing 737-7KK, registered A6-RJA, allegedly carried out two short-duration missions to Iran . The first occurred on 11 August 2026 , from Abu Dhabi to the Iranian airport of Mehrabad (Tehran). The second took place on 12 August 2026, to the Iranian airport of Payam (Karaj). Time spent on the ground was reportedly under one hour in both instances. The flight paths align with available tracking data. According to unconfirmed Iranian sources, the flights transported between 1.5 and 2 metric tons of gold, with an estimated value of up to approximately $283 million. On 12 June 2026 , open sources reported that the Emirates had agreed to unfreeze billions of dollars benefiting Iran. According to the same accounts, A6-RJA had conducted a flight from Abu Dhabi to Mehrabad on 8 June 2026, transporting $3 billion in cash as the first tranche of an agreement reportedly involving a total supply between $10 billion and $20 billion. In light of these elements, one possible interpretation is that the Emirati government, despite publicly denying these operations, is transferring funds to Tehran or proceeding with the unfreezing of previously blocked Iranian assets. This mechanism could be linked to an informal understanding aimed at securing from Iran a suspension or reduction of attacks against UAE territory. Contrasting this hypothesis is a second possibility: shadow diplomacy taking place between the two countries, centered on Sheikh Tahnoun bin Zayed Al Nahyan , National Security Advisor of the UAE and a pivotal figure in Abu Dhabi’s financial apparatus. Tahnoun serves as Chairman of the UAE’s largest conglomerate, International Holding Company (IHC); Chairman of one of Abu Dhabi’s strategic sovereign wealth funds, First Abu Dhabi Bank (FAB); and Chairman of one of the world’s largest sovereign wealth funds, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA). He also chairs the artificial intelligence holding company G42, the technology investment fund MGX, and the private firm Royal Group. Why Does It Matter? The United Arab Emirates represents one of Israel’s key Arab partners in the Gulf. Since 2020 , Abu Dhabi has maintained formal diplomatic relations with Tel Aviv under the Abraham Accords. Bilateral cooperation has since expanded to encompass security and defense sectors. In 2026, an Iron Dome battery, along with the Israeli personnel responsible for its operation, was reportedly provided to Abu Dhabi to assist in safeguarding Emirati territory from Iranian attacks. Regarding relations with Washington, the United States designated the UAE as a “Major Security Partner” in 2021 , a status previously granted only to Bahrain. Bilateral cooperation includes activities related to military bases, training, intelligence, weapons systems, and armed forces interoperability. Recent developments, however, suggest a potential pragmatic shift in this posture. The effectiveness of the Israeli-American security architecture in protecting Emirati interests has demonstrated significant limitations. Infrastructure across several Gulf Cooperation Council states has suffered severe damage and, in some cases, was reportedly destroyed. These factors may have incentivised Abu Dhabi to reactivate dialogue channels with Tehran through discreet means. According to several news accounts, starting in June 2026, the UAE began funding a bilateral ceasefire mechanism with Iran. Under this framework, Abu Dhabi is reportedly transferring resources to Tehran as part of an understanding aimed at reducing the likelihood of Emirati territory being targeted in Iran’s asymmetric response to US strikes. This account remains unconfirmed. While certain unofficial Iranian sources support it, the Emirati government has denied the existence of such agreements and has offered no conclusive public explanation regarding the flights mentioned above. A potential component of the rapprochement between Iran and the UAE may involve the activities of Sheikh Tahnoun bin Zayed Al Nahyan, UAE National Security Advisor and a central figure in Abu Dhabi’s financial apparatus. Tahnoun controls or exerts significant influence over sovereign wealth funds and financial conglomerates managing assets in the hundreds of billions of dollars. The concentration of political, financial, and security power in his hands makes him one of the most influential figures within the Emirati state apparatus. Tahnoun has been identified as a key interlocutor in de-escalation efforts between Abu Dhabi and Tehran. He has led diplomatic missions to Iran aimed at reopening lines of communication and easing tensions across the Persian Gulf. The underlying rationale for these activities appears primarily driven by the protection of Emirati economic interests : safeguarding investments, securing trade routes, and protecting the financial and technological hubs of Abu Dhabi and Dubai. The primary objective is to mitigate the risk of a prolonged escalation among Iran, the United States, and Israel causing systemic fallout on the UAE economy. Available accounts point to a line of action driven by a business-first approach. As the key figure oversight manager for major financial and investment platforms in the emirate, Tahnoun has a vested interest in preserving sufficiently stable regional conditions to protect Emirati assets , maintain attractiveness to international capital, and sustain the growth of Abu Dhabi and Dubai as technology and finance hubs. In December 2021 , Tahnoun led a high-level mission to Tehran, meeting with the S ecretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Ali Shamkhani, and President Ebrahim Raisi . The visit contributed to reopening a direct channel of communication between the two nations, laying the groundwork for the subsequent restoration of diplomatic relations and the return of the Emirati ambassador to Iran. During subsequent phases of military escalation and heightened tension among Iran, the United States, and Gulf states, Tahnoun reportedly operated through informal channels alongside Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani. Together, they participated in mediation efforts aimed at de-escalation and shaping informal understandings between Washington and Tehran. His position also serves as a potential indirect communication link with Western partners . The network of relationships he has cultivated across financial, diplomatic, and security spheres enables the UAE to act as a discreet interlocutor with Iranian leadership, facilitating confidential message exchanges without relying on formal diplomatic channels. Outlook The premise that Abu Dhabi is transferring funds, unfreezing Iranian assets, or simply conducting behind-the-scenes bilateral diplomacy highlights a pragmatic lack of confidence in the ability of the Israeli-American defense umbrella to fully protect critical Emirati infrastructure from asymmetric attacks. This points toward a broader transition toward a doctrine of appeasement and risk mitigation. The UAE reinforces its intent to avoid binding alignments with any regional bloc. body: Armenia, Putin e la Presenza Militare Russa A Gyumri Armenia: Putin Mette in Discussione la Presenza Militare Russa A Gyumri Executive Intelligence Snapshot Le recenti dichiarazioni del Presidente russo Vladimir Putin mettono formalmente l’Armenia di fronte alla scelta se confermare o richiedere lo smantellamento della presenza militare russa presso la 102a Base militare di Gyumri. Tale posizione apre per il governo di Yerevan un’opportunità di affrancamento politico, ma introduce contemporaneamente un grave vincolo di sicurezza strutturale. L’eventuale vuoto strategico generato dal disimpegno russo difficilmente potrà essere colmato nell’immediato da garanzie difensive vincolanti da parte dell’Unione Europea o degli Stati Uniti, esponendo in modo diretto l’integrità territoriale armena alle possibili pressioni militari del blocco azerbaigiano-turco. Contesto Informativo Durante il 26° summit dell’Organizzazione della Cooperazione di Shanghai (SCO) , il presidente russo Vladimir Putin ha incontrato il Premier armeno Nikol Pashinyan e fornito una revisione tattica del posizionamento di Mosca nel Caucaso meridionale, in special modo mettendo in discussione la presenza militare russa presso la base di Gyumri . Durante la conferenza stampa tenutasi a Bishkek, il Presidente Vladimir Putin ha dichiarato in modo esplicito che la Russia è pronta a ritirare il proprio contingente militare da Gyumri anche nell’immediato, qualora il popolo e le autorità armene considerino non più necessaria tale infrastruttura. Putin ha sottolineato che Mosca non intende imporre alcuna presenza armata in territorio estero, trasferendo la responsabilità di una simile scelta alla sovranità delle istituzioni di Yerevan. La 102a Base militare russa, con dislocazioni a Gyumri, è stata istituita mediante un accordo bilaterale esteso nel 2010 con validità formale fino al 2044 con lo scopo di deterrenza e contrasto contro ogni minaccia esterna diretta all’integrità armena. Nonostante le dichiarazioni interlocutorie del vertice del Cremlino, esponenti dell’apparato di sicurezza russo, come il Segretario del Consiglio di Sicurezza Sergei Shoigu , hanno ribadito nei mesi precedenti che non sussistono presupposti operativi per lo smantellamento della struttura, avvertendo contemporaneamente che la ricerca di protezione esterna presso attori occidentali espone Yerevan a gravi rischi di instabilità. La leadership armena guidata dal Primo Ministro Nikol Pashinyan e i vertici parlamentari hanno finora evitato di formalizzare una richiesta di chiusura della base o ritiro del personale militare russo, pur avendo congelato la partecipazione e i finanziamenti nell’Organizzazione del Trattato di Sicurezza Collettiva (CSTO) ed espresso l’intenzione di accelerare il percorso d’integrazione verso l’Unione Europea. Analisi Le parole del presidente russo Vladimir Putin hanno un peso fondamentale sia a livello politico che di comunicazione strategica considerando anche lo stato attuale delle relazioni bilaterali fra le parti. Infatti, i rapporti tra Mosca e Yerevan negli ultimi anni sono stati altalenanti con diversi scambi di parole e opinioni che nel tempo hanno provocato una situazione di raffreddamento. In passato, ad esempio, lo stesso Primo Ministro armeno Nikol Pashinyan aveva sottolineato come la decisione delle precedenti amministrazioni armene di affidarsi soltanto a un solo partner per la propria difesa, ossia la Federazione Russa, era stata un errore che si era poi rivelato fatale negli anni successivi. La decisione di Yerevan, poi, di aumentare la cooperazione con l’Occidente , fattore che ha favorito l’accordo di pace con l’Azerbaigian siglato nell’agosto del 2025 a Washington alla presenza del Presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump , ma ha anche dato vita al progetto del Corridoio TRIPP , sono alcune delle direttive dell’Armenia in politica estera che hanno scontentato Mosca e favorito, così, una pressione politica, economica e mediatica da parte del Cremlino per indurre il governo armeno a ripensare la propria strategia. Quindi, le parole di Putin e l’apparente flessibilità manifestata dalla Russia possono, in realtà, nascondere un’operazione d’influenza psicologica e politica volta a esporre le vulnerabilità del governo Pashinyan . La mossa retorica del Cremlino mira a fare leva sulla frammentazione politica interna dell’Armenia e sul fatto che, nonostante solamente nel giugno 2026 Pashinyan ha ottenuto nuovamente la guida del Paese grazie alla vittoria nelle elezioni parlamentari, esiste all’interno dell’Armenia un consistente bacino di elettorato e di opposizione politca che vedono nella presenza militare russa l’unico deterrente reale contro il riattivarsi delle ostilità con Baku e Ankara. Sfidare la leadership armena a richiedere il ritiro significa forzare una decisione in grado di polarizzare l’opinione pubblica , alimentando tensioni sociali che potrebbero destabilizzare l’esecutivo. Inoltre, il distacco da Mosca espone Yerevan a ritorsioni macroeconomiche asimmetriche . La Russia mantiene una posizione dominante su asset infrastrutturali critici in Armenia, inclusi la rete ferroviaria, il monopolio sulle forniture di gas naturale e la gestione delle principali reti di distribuzione energetica. A ciò si aggiungono la dipendenza dai flussi commerciali bilaterali e l’afflusso continuo di rimesse da parte della comunità armena residente in Russia. L’adozione di sanzioni informali o l’interruzione di queste forniture produrrebbe uno shock inflazionistico immediato, compromettendo la stabilità finanziaria e il rating di credito del Paese. Sotto il profilo della difesa pura, la potenziale smilitarizzazione russa crea un vuoto strategico difficilmente colmabile dagli attori occidentali nel breve periodo considerando che, ad oggi, gli Stati Uniti sono impegnati attivamente nel conflitto in Medio Oriente contro la Repubblica Islamica dell’Iran e, al contempo, supportano insieme all’Unione Europea l’Ucraina nel conflitto contro la Russia . La presenza occidentale rimane confinata a missioni civili di monitoraggio dei confini (EUMA) o alla vendita di sistemi d’arma difensivi, strumenti del tutto insufficienti a fungere da deterrente contro un’azione militare convenzionale. A questo quadro si sovrappone la complessa reazione degli attori regionali confinanti. La Repubblica Islamica dell’Iran definisce l’integrità territoriale dell’Armenia e in particolare la continuità del confine nella provincia di Syunik una priorità nazionale per impedire il completamento del corridoio azerbaigiano di Zangezur. Tuttavia, Teheran mantiene una linea di assoluto rigetto verso l’insediamento di infrastrutture o forze militari statunitensi o collegate alla NATO lungo i propri confini settentrionali. Di conseguenza, un tentativo armeno di sostituire il contingente russo con truppe occidentali provocherebbe l’ostilità simultanea di Mosca e Teheran, lasciando Yerevan isolata. Per contro, l’asse formato da Azerbaigian e Turchia vedrebbe la partenza della Russia come il definitivo azzeramento della deterrenza, aumentando la pressione diplomatica e militare per imporre concessioni territoriali e infrastrutturali all’Armenia. Scenari Futuri L’attuale situazione politica e di sicurezza armena, unita ai rapporti bilaterali con la Russia e alla presenza militare russa presso la Base di Gyumri, permette di delineare i seguenti possibili scenari: Scenario 1: Sostituzione occidentale e instabilità istituzionale interna. Yerevan decide di formalizzare la richiesta di ritiro del contingente russo da Gyumri e allo stesso tempo avvia accordi di cooperazione di sicurezza e presenza militare con partner occidentali quali Stati Uniti e Paesi europei. Questa decisione può comportare la reazione di Mosca che si traduce in ritorsioni economiche e blocchi commerciali, mentre l’Iran manifesta una netta opposizione diplomatica e la Turchia e l’Azerbaigian incrementano la pressione lungo le linee di confine.
