body: From tech hub to rising performing arts destination - Chinadaily.com.cn WS6aa4bfb3e4b06d4aa055db38 China Edition | Global Edition | ASIA | 中文 China Latest Society Innovation Education Cross-Strait HK/Macao Health Environment Military Video World Asia-Pacific Americas Europe Middle East Africa Business Policies Companies Industries Technology China Up-close China Data Motoring Video Culture Art Music and Theater Film and TV Books Heritage Events and Festivals People Cultural Exchange Video Photo Gallery Fashion Health Travel News City Tours Guides and Tips My Footprints Around the World Features Photo Video Food Sports Soccer Basketball Volleyball Tennis Golf Track and field Swimming Motor China Stars Opinion Cartoons Editorials Global Lens We Comment Columnists Global Views Chinese Perspectives Opinion Line Regional Newspaper China Daily PDF China Daily E-Paper China Daily Global PDF China Daily Global E-Paper Mobile CULTURE News Heritage Art Film Theater Fashion Cultural Exchange Books Photo Video HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE 中文 CULTURE News Heritage Art Film Theater Fashion Cultural Exchange Books Photo Video Home / Culture / Cultural Exchange From tech hub to rising performing arts destination By XING WEN | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-12 10:57 Share - WeChat Polish dancer-actress Natalia Gabrielczyk in a scene from The Deal. [Photo provided to China Daily] Polish dancer-actress Natalia Gabrielczyk originally planned to spend just one year in Shenzhen, Guangdong province. She came to the city to perform in The Deal, an immersive physical theater production in Shekou district. Now, she has signed on for a second year. "I feel like the stories of my characters aren't complete yet," she says. "There's so much more detail and life experience I can find, which is exciting enough to keep me going for a little longer." It is the first time she has stayed in one place for this long after spending eight years moving between cities across Europe. "Life here is very comfortable and sweet," she says. Offstage, she fills her days with yoga, martial arts, salsa dancing, and rock climbing. In a city where traditions and cultures from different continents intersect, she finds that every new experience feeds back into her art. "I find the city open and friendly," she observes. "It's incredible how many varieties of things there are — food, experiences and shows. There's so much to choose from. It feels very approachable." Most importantly, she finds herself in a supportive environment through The Deal. "We already have opportunities to be creative and submit ideas. We have studios we can use any time of day, even in our free time. We have amazing performers to collaborate with." Her decision to stay reflects a broader transformation underway in Shenzhen. A city once best known for advanced manufacturing and high-tech industries is now placing increasing emphasis on the performing arts. The Deal, inspired by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's epic Faust and Nikolai Gogol's The Overcoat, is Shenzhen's first resident immersive physical theater production. Staged across seven decks and 4,600 square meters of immersive space aboard the historic Minghua cruise ship, the production brings together performing artists from 12 countries. Since its premiere in October 2025, it has sustained strong ticket sales, drawing audiences not only from the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area but also from elsewhere in China and overseas, according to Zhang Ruolin, marketing director of the cruise ship project. "We can feel that the city's cultural and artistic scene is growing stronger. With Shenzhen's support for building itself into an international performing arts hub, we have received guidance from project planning to thematic development," says Zhang. "Our vision is to follow the model of London's West End and New York's Broadway, using performing arts as a driving force to boost the city's cultural development and cultural tourism economy." That systematic support is also taking shape through concrete policy measures. A three-year support plan issued by the Shenzhen municipal bureau of culture, radio, television, tourism, and sports, which took effect on April 28, sets out subsidy standards for accredited performance spaces in three categories: language-based theater, immersive theater and live music. Xu Yu, general manager of Shenzhen Performance Company, says the policy encourages event organizers to plan more high-quality concerts and further promotes the performing arts sector. "The policy offers substantial funding support for top-tier artists, 1,000-seat theaters, and high-grossing productions," Xu says. "This will help Shenzhen attract more high-quality theatrical works." The city is already demonstrating its ambitions. The pioneering immersive production Sleep No More, which ended its decade-long Shanghai run in August, is set to debut at Shenzhen Bay next year. Wang Yi, president of Shenzhen Jucheng Theater, is optimistic about the city's performing arts market. He says the city benefits from a large young audience, strong consumption demand and extensive reach across the Greater Bay Area. Wen Liangfu, lead organizer of the annual World Cup Universal Open Dance Festival in Shekou, points to another advantage: the city's geographic location and convenient transportation have helped make the festival increasingly international. "This year, dancers from 36 countries and regions came to compete in August," Wen says, adding that the competition has become a major performing arts event with growing social impact. It draws international participants while allowing domestic dancers to experience top-tier dance without leaving China.

By Jimena Esteban | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-12 10:51 Share - WeChat The Chilean final of the Chinese Bridge Chinese Proficiency Competition, held in Santiago early this year, reflects the enduring cultural and people-to-people ties between Chile and China that figures such as Pablo Neruda helped foster decades before formal diplomatic relations were established. [Photo/Xinhua] Inside one of the University of Chile's main buildings, visitors will see a seashell that carries a story far larger than its size. It is displayed among marine specimens linked to Pablo Neruda (1904-73), the Nobel Prizewinning Chilean poet known for his love of seashells, which he described as "small countries of mother-of-pearl". In 1954, he donated his private collection of thousands of shells to the university. The shell displayed in the university's main building stands out for what it reveals about a time when culture often outpaced diplomacy. In his memoir, Neruda describes receiving a rare shell during a visit to China: "I remember that in the Peking Museum, the most sacred box of mollusks from the China Sea was opened to give me ... the Thatcheria mirabilis." He said it was one of only two known specimens of that particular mollusk. Long before Chile and China established formal diplomatic relations in 1970, Chilean writers and artists were already taking journeys across the Pacific. They traveled, wrote, and helped build institutions that turned curiosity into exchange. Their encounters helped shape a relationship that now runs through trade, education and tourism. 1 2 3 4 Next >>| 1/4 Next Related Stories Chinese literature reaches global youth through library cultural exchanges Great Wall restoration teams uncover trove of secrets Museum shows its true colors Jade craftsmanship helps carve out more opportunities China's literary world captures Russia's young readers Photo Gallery A rally of friendship A photographer's lifetime dedication to Huangshan Mountain College artists shine at National Fine Arts Exhibition in Beijing Tales and Trails Qingdao 'city drink': Brewing coastal charm China Vibes Bund lights beckon thousands daily in Shanghai 24 Solar Terms End of Heat Editor's Pick Serving up emotions: A chat with director Wen Muye A toast to tradition and innovation Video Mid-Autumn Festival brings nostalgia back to mooncakes Hotel robots surprise visitors, streamline operations Most Viewed in 24 Hours Chinaculture.org Five great Chinese love legends: Romance across millennia The Silk Road: a facilitator of cultural convergence Copyright 1994 - . body: A conversation across 1,000 years - Chinadaily.com.cn WS6aa4befde4b06d4aa055db20_1 China Edition | Global Edition | ASIA | 中文 China Latest Society Innovation Education Cross-Strait HK/Macao Health Environment Military Video World Asia-Pacific Americas Europe Middle East Africa Business Policies Companies Industries Technology China Up-close China Data Motoring Video Culture Art Music and Theater Film and TV Books Heritage Events and Festivals People Cultural Exchange Video Photo Gallery Fashion Health Travel News City Tours Guides and Tips My Footprints Around the World Features Photo Video Food Sports Soccer Basketball Volleyball Tennis Golf Track and field Swimming Motor China Stars Opinion Cartoons Editorials Global Lens We Comment Columnists Global Views Chinese Perspectives Opinion Line Regional Newspaper China Daily PDF China Daily E-Paper China Daily Global PDF China Daily Global E-Paper Mobile CULTURE News Heritage Art Film Theater Fashion Cultural Exchange Books Photo Video HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE 中文 CULTURE News Heritage Art Film Theater Fashion Cultural Exchange Books Photo Video Home / Culture / Music and Theater A conversation across 1,000 years Young musicians aim to make Nanyin accessible to a broader audience, reports Chen Nan. By Chen Nan | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-12 10:54 Share - WeChat Headed by Chen Huanxi (second from right), Nanyin New Force is helping young audiences connect with Nanyin, an ancient musical tradition from Quanzhou in Fujian province. [Photo provided to China Daily] For more than 1,000 years, the music of Nanyin — one of the oldest existing musical genres in China — has carried the sounds of southern China through generations. Now, a group of young musicians in Quanzhou, Fujian province, is giving the ancient tradition a contemporary voice by pairing its distinctive melodies and vocal style with folk, pop, blues, electronic music and modern instrumentation. Called Nanyin Xin Shili, or Nanyin New Force, the ensemble is less a fixed band than a creative collective. Its members come from different musical and artistic backgrounds, using Nanyin as a starting point rather than a boundary. At its center is Chen Huanxi, a Nanyin inheritor who has been immersed in the tradition since childhood. Yet her relationship with Nanyin was far from straightforward. As a child, Chen was energetic and easily bored. She began learning pipa (four-stringed Chinese lute) largely because her friends were doing it. The slow pace of Nanyin initially frustrated her, and she once argued with her parents because she wanted to study painting instead. Known for its restrained melodies, distinctive singing style and traditional instruments such as the pipa, dongxiao (Chinese vertical bamboo flute), sanxian (three-stringed lute) and erxian (a two-stringed instrument), Nanyin is often described as a "living fossil" of Chinese music and was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009. "I always thought I didn't like Nanyin," says Chen, born in 1995. "It was only much later that I suddenly realized I had never been able to separate myself from it." That realization came after years of working with the tradition in increasingly unconventional ways. Chen graduated from Quanzhou Normal University in 2017, where she studied Nanyin. She went on to teach the music, perform in local teahouses and eventually became a freelance musician, taking Nanyin to the streets, bars and cafes. She began explaining the centuries-old art form to curious passersby and asking audiences what they wanted to hear. "What surprised me was that some people in Quanzhou didn't even know what I was singing," she says. "I thought, this isn't right. This is such beautiful music. People should be able to understand it." For Chen, the challenge was not simply preserving Nanyin, but closing the distance that had grown between the tradition and the people whose lives it once accompanied. 1 2 Next >>| 1/2 Next Related Stories Charity concert supports arts education for children The first emperor's dancing birds A focus on the formative Casting a lasting shadow Retrieving history from the past Photo Gallery A rally of friendship A photographer's lifetime dedication to Huangshan Mountain College artists shine at National Fine Arts Exhibition in Beijing Tales and Trails Qingdao 'city drink': Brewing coastal charm China Vibes Bund lights beckon thousands daily in Shanghai 24 Solar Terms End of Heat Editor's Pick Serving up emotions: A chat with director Wen Muye A toast to tradition and innovation Video Mid-Autumn Festival brings nostalgia back to mooncakes Hotel robots surprise visitors, streamline operations Most Viewed in 24 Hours Chinaculture.org Five great Chinese love legends: Romance across millennia The Silk Road: a facilitator of cultural convergence Copyright 1994 - . body: US marks 25 years since 9/11 - World - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE World Asia-Pacific Americas Europe Middle East Africa China-US China-Europe China-Japan China-Africa Home World / Americas Home / World / Americas US marks 25 years since 9/11 Country unites in remembrance as New Yorkers vow to 'never forget' By BELINDA ROBINSON in New York | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-12 10:14 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE A woman holds a candle as she looks at victims' names on the reflecting pools during a vigil to commemorate the 25th anniversary of Sept 11 in New York on Thursday. RYAN MURPHY/AFP New York vowed to "never forget" the people who died in the horrific terrorist attacks of Sept 11, 2001, as the city united with the nation on Friday in solemn remembrance of the lives lost, 25 years after the day that changed the United States. The hallowed ground where the twin towers at the World Trade Center in New York once stood is a permanent memorial to the nearly 3,000 victims. Two expansive, beautiful, calm, reflecting pools with streaming water allow visitors time to reflect. In a coordinated attack, four commercial airliners were hijacked by 19 al-Qaida operatives. Two planes were flown into the twin towers, a third crashed into the Pentagon, and a fourth went down into a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back against the hijackers, stopping it from reaching its intended target, thought to be in Washington. All of the passengers and hijackers died. Many New Yorkers saw it firsthand or watched it on TV. Some felt the ground shake as the north and south towers collapsed, causing dust and debris to engulf the city. One admits that the moment is still etched into his mind. Stanley O' Connor, 71, a local tour guide for the city who lives in New York, still remembers that fateful day vividly. "I had just walked my girlfriend out to the subway, and I walked back, and my housemate was taking a shower, and he opened the bathroom door and said, 'Stan, the radio says that the World Trade Center is on fire.' That hasn't happened since 1993 ... So I started calling her, saying 'please come home'," O' Connor told China Daily. She worked in a building near the twin towers, and he said that he watched it all on TV. "I literally tore my hair out when the north tower fell." He continued frantically trying to reach her — and eventually she returned home safely, unlike many others who lost their lives. He recalled that throughout New York and the entire US, the fear was palpable as they "didn't know what was going on". Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, accused by the US of being the mastermind of the attacks, will stand trial in June 2028, along with three co-defendants at the US naval base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. O'Connor said he is extremely thankful that he also narrowly escaped being in the twin towers that day. "I was supposed to take people on a tour to the south tower that night," he said. "I was still at home at 9 am because this was a 2 pm to 8 or 9 pm gig." In the wake of 9/11, he worked around the Ground Zero site as a pedicab driver. He later developed post-traumatic stress disorder, a mental health condition that affects someone after they witness or experience a terrifying event. He got bronchitis and contracted melanoma — a type of cancer — but he had it removed. He is just one of the people eligible for the September 11 Victim Compensation Fund, or VCF, which provides financial compensation to people who qualify because of illnesses related to the attacks. Health challenges He says his health challenges still shape his life. He sustained some issues from the poor air quality in Lower Manhattan in the years after 9/11. He showed off an inhaler that he carries around daily. In the weeks after 9/11, New Yorkers were assured that air quality near the felled towers was safe. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration announced on Tuesday that it will release the post-9/11 air quality records to coincide with the 25th anniversary. The records, which were reviewed early by The New York Times, showed that asbestos was found nearly a kilometer away from the towers over 10 months after 9/11. The 170,000 pages of records covering air quality, contamination records and correspondence among city officials were stored in 68 boxes in a city office and were only rediscovered last year, according to The Times. On the day of the attacks, 412 emergency personnel died, including 343 firefighters, 37 Port Authority Police Department officers, 23 New York police officers, eight emergency medical technicians and one New York Fire Patrol member. The first responders who toiled in the collapsed World Trade Center rubble in 2001 inhaled dust, noxious gases, particulates, chemicals and fibers from the debris. Reuters reported that the government-funded World Trade Center Health Program has provided healthcare for 9/11-related illnesses to more than 150,000 responders involved in rescue and recovery efforts and survivors who lived, worked or studied in the disaster area, according to data collected through June 30 by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. As of June 30, people in the program had received roughly 85,000 certifications for World Trade Center-related health conditions. About half were linked to inhaling or swallowing toxic dust, and about 30 percent were for cancer. John Feal worked as a construction supervisor and was exposed to the toxic dust at the 9/11 site, nicknamed "the pile" by workers. He developed gangrene, then sepsis, and lost his foot after a steel beam fell on it at Ground Zero shortly after he arrived. Feal told China Daily: "(At Ground Zero) we had health problems right away. Everybody was complaining about their sore throats, runny eyes. We knew that what we were inhaling wasn't any good, and that was right away. I was only there for five and a half days before I got hurt. But I had a sore throat, burning eyes and a burning nose." He became an activist lobbying Congress for benefits for other survivors alongside comedian and The Daily Show co-host Jon Stewart. Both Feal and Stewart worked together to extend federally funded programs such as the VCF. Feal, who established his Feal-Good Foundation, was also instrumental in getting the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act passed in 2010 and renewed over the years. More than 9,000 people tracked by the World Trade Center Health Program have died since the attacks, though officials say it's difficult to determine the role that 9/11 played in their deaths, Reuters reported. At the two 9/11 reflecting pools, the names of victims are etched, and single roses have been placed in remembrance a few days before the 25th anniversary. The National September 11 Memorial & Museum had a long line of people waiting patiently to get inside. At stalls located in the area, small keepsakes such as keyrings, T-shirts and tote bags are for sale. Many bear the mantra: "New York City, Never Forget." A "flag of honor" with the names of every person who died in the Sept 11 attacks and the February 1993 attack on the World Trade Center is displayed at Ground Zero. A crowd gathered quietly near the 9/11 Survivor tree — a Callery pear tree that was discovered severely burned in the rubble at Ground Zero in October 2001. It was rejuvenated and replanted near the museum to be a symbol of resilience, rebirth and hope, according to the museum. In the days before the anniversary, a trio of bagpipers played a solemn song in remembrance of the lives lost, drawing a crowd of onlookers who applauded them. body: Chinese robots step into UK spotlight - World - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE World Asia-Pacific Americas Europe Middle East Africa China-US China-Europe China-Japan China-Africa Home World / Europe Home / World / Europe Chinese robots step into UK spotlight By XING YI in London | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-12 09:57 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE A member of staff with LEC Robotics gives a presentation for visitors in a session on logistic robotics during the Robot Week in London. [Xing Yi / China Daily] Robot Week, a 10-day showcase of Chinese robotics technologies across five industry scenarios, is underway in London, attracting interest from both the general public and experts in the United Kingdom. From Monday until Sept 18, visitors can watch live demonstrations of robots working in logistics, hospitality, facility management, healthcare and retail sectors. Startup LEC Robotics, the host of the event, said more than 200 people attended in its first two days. Jack Perry, founder and CEO of LEC Robotics, said that although the demand for robots in real-life applications is still limited, it will change dramatically. He predicted robots will be widely deployed in construction, agriculture, and other sectors in the next five to ten years. "There will be an 80 percent share of the export market in robotics," he said, adding that China is well ahead in terms of gathering working environment data for training robots, while the UK is lagging behind and needs to work with Chinese partners. "There's no other country in the world that can scale, except China, in robotics," said Perry, who is also the chairman of the 48 Group, a British organization dedicated to promoting Sino-UK trade cooperation since the 1950s. Jack Perry, founder and CEO of LEC Robotics, at the company's first robotics showroom in London. [Xing Yi / China Daily] However, Perry noted the complexity involved in selling tech products like robots and tailoring them to carry out specific tasks across industries. He said he has made frequent visits to robot companies in China to bridge the communication gaps and help them better understand local needs in the UK. Currently, Perry's team is in talks with more than 30 robotics companies in China, and many of his partners have supplied their latest robot models, such as the XBOT coffee robot and KEENON delivery robot, to be displayed in the company's House of Robotics, which is located at 3 Imperial Road in Chelsea, west London. Perry said the showroom is the first of its kind in the UK for robots made by Chinese companies. Live demonstrations Some companies also sent local staff and experts to take part in live demonstrations. Among them is BOTINKIT, which showcased its robotic kitchen solution to address the shortage of experienced chefs in the catering industry. Kevin Hartley, the EU corporate chef with BOTINKIT, operated a cooking robot to serve beef chili with bitter chocolate and nachos with sour cream in only six minutes for a dozen visitors. A chef demonstrates the use of a cooking robot at the House of Robotics in west London on Tuesday. [Xing Yi / China Daily] "It's like me standing with a pan making it, but it's automatically adding the right ingredients at the right time," said Hartley. "It does a consistent product at a standard that I'm happy with. It reflects me." The Shenzhen-based company has been selling its cooking robots in quantity in the Asian market and has started expanding into Europe, with clients in the UK, Ireland and Sweden. Kaif Kohari, a visitor who worked for an AI startup in England, said he came to look into how these robots can be put into use to reduce manual labor. "I think the speed at which robotics develops is improving day by day, and we are very close to the future," said Kohari, who saw robots being used in hotels and shopping malls during his visit to Beijing earlier this year. "In China, it's already being done," he said. xingyi@chinadaily.com.cn Photos US marks 25 years since 9/11 Chinese robots step into UK spotlight Houthis seize strategic port in Red Sea Immigrant story Dear You touches hearts ECB hikes rates again but remains cautious on future path Merz cancels phone call with Trump World in Focus Cultural ambassador Asia Focus + Toxic haze chokes lungs Indonesia's man-made arboreal bridges offer orangutans a lifeline Special Coverage + 2025 A Date with China GMD SCO Summit Cities Tianjin Friends Afar + Livestreamer brings life in Shanxi to Latin America Ties That Bind + Vital pass to boost China-Pakistan trade Top BACK TO THE TOP English 中文 HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper

body: US market sours on $6b Treasury buyback - World - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE World Asia-Pacific Americas Europe Middle East Africa China-US China-Europe China-Japan China-Africa Home World / Americas Home / World / Americas US market sours on $6b Treasury buyback Investors push back on offer as 10-year yield reaches its highest in three years By MAY ZHOU in Houston | China Daily Global | Updated: 2026-09-11 09:56 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE The United States Treasury Department said on Wednesday that it will buy up to $6 billion of 10-year to 20-year Treasurys when it executes its buyback operation on Thursday afternoon, but the bond market didn't respond as expected. Earlier on Wednesday, the Treasury's scheduled release put the number at $4 billion. According to the announcement, there will be six more buyback operations targeting longer-term debt through early November. The Treasury said future buybacks will be a minimum of $4 billion each. After that, the Treasury Department will reveal its plans for the next three months. Last month, the buyback was $2 billion. The purchases are intended to increase bond prices — which would reduce their yields, as they are inversely related to price — with the aim of lowering interest rates. However, the bond market rebuked the US administration's move by pushing the 10-year yield to its highest in three years to an intraday high of 4.857 percent on Wednesday. The intraday high for the 20-year yield climbed to 5.322 percent, also the highest in three years. Investors had expected a larger buyback — between $7 billion and $8 billion — to help lower costs associated with borrowing. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday before the announcement that part of his job is to ensure that the markets are not misreading the fundamentals of the US economy. "Now I try to slow things down, to get people to get out of their fever dream and look at the facts," Bessent said. The higher Treasury yield means increased interest rates for companies to borrow money to invest, and for consumers to buy houses, cars and other things bought on credit. "Make no mistake, investors are worried about the US economy," said Anthony Moretti, associate professor at the Communication and Organizational Leadership Department at Robert Morris University in Pennsylvania. "So, too is the average American. Inflation, gas prices and mortgage rates. All three are eating into Americans' purchasing power," Moretti told China Daily. Multiple factors The rising yields are driven by multiple factors, according to experts. There is no foreseeable end to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which is pushing oil prices higher. On Wednesday, Brent crude futures rose above $100 a barrel for the first time since late July, and West Texas Intermediate futures increased more than 3 percent to above $96 a barrel. Also, rising government debt, which hit $40 trillion in August, is driving up bond yields through increased government borrowing to fund the deficit. "This decision might help temper some of the worst economic news, but yet again the big question has to be asked: What is the strategy? Good luck getting a firm answer," Moretti said. Brett House, an economist at the Columbia Business School, told CBS News that the buyback doesn't solve the deficit problem. "Unless Bessent forces the Fed to print money to buy these bonds, it is still coming out of Treasury revenues, and doesn't cure the fact that this government is building up a deficit and as a result is going to have to issue more debt," he said. In addition, investors are borrowing heavily to fund massive AI data center buildouts. While investors were disappointed in not getting a larger buyback, some experts are against such moves. Stanley Druckenmiller, chairman and CEO of Duquesne Family Office, and ex-mentor of Bessent — both of whom worked under the famous financier and hedge fund manager George Soros — wrote in an op-ed piece in the Wall Street Journal that "every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination". "Suppressed long rates sugarcoat the interest-cost projections, shrink the apparent urgency, and let incumbents assure voters the debt is someone else's problem," he wrote. He said the government's move to manipulate the bond prices would damage the credibility of the Treasury market. "That asset doesn't regain its value so easily," Druckenmiller said. "Governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose." mayzhou@chinadailyusa.com Photos IMF says uncertainty for global economy remains high after 6 months of US-Iran war Fiji tourism rebounds amid record visitor arrivals Chinese overseas firms focus on building brand trust UN chief warns against stoking Gulf tensions China's mission in Geneva, UN human rights body co-host event on economic, social, cultural rights Toxic haze chokes lungs World in Focus Cultural ambassador Asia Focus + Toxic haze chokes lungs Indonesia's man-made arboreal bridges offer orangutans a lifeline Special Coverage + 2025 A Date with China GMD SCO Summit Cities Tianjin Friends Afar + Livestreamer brings life in Shanxi to Latin America Ties That Bind + Vital pass to boost China-Pakistan trade Top BACK TO THE TOP English 中文 HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper

body: Fiji tourism rebounds amid record visitor arrivals - World - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE World Asia-Pacific Americas Europe Middle East Africa China-US China-Europe China-Japan China-Africa Home World / Asia-Pacific Home / World / Asia-Pacific Fiji tourism rebounds amid record visitor arrivals By ALEXIS HOOI in Sydney | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-11 09:14 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE Fiji's tourism sector recorded its highest monthly visitor arrivals in July, surpassing 100,000 for the first time, with steady growth in the major Chinese market contributing to the boom. The South Pacific archipelago welcomed 105,791 visitors in July, up 6.5 percent from a year earlier, according to data released by the nation's statistics bureau. The figure was the highest monthly total on record and the first to exceed 100,000, as Fiji continues its post-pandemic recovery. Most visitors came from Australia, New Zealand, the United States and China. The Chinese market accounted for 3,117 arrivals in July, up from 2,497 in June, according to the latest industry figures. Fiji received 986,367 visitors last year, compared with 982,938 in 2024 and 929,740 in 2023. Paresh Pant, CEO of Tourism Fiji, the government's tourism marketing agency, described the record as "a significant milestone for Fiji and a strong vote of confidence in our destination". "Surpassing 100,000 international visitor arrivals in a single month for the first time demonstrates the strength of Fiji's tourism recovery and the continued demand for Fiji across our international markets," Pant said. China "remains a strategically important market for Fiji, both for its current contribution and its long-term growth potential", he added. In the first seven months of the year, Fiji welcomed 17,274 visitors from China, up 6.19 percent year-on-year, he said. Chinese travelers are "increasingly diverse in how they travel and what they look for from a destination", Pant said. "Fiji's resorts and beaches remain important attractions, but we are seeing strong interest in diving, island hopping, honeymoons and family holidays, alongside a broader desire for more personalized and experience-led travel," he said. Beyond its physical attractions, one of Fiji's greatest strengths is its people, Pant said, adding that the "human connection" is an essential part of the visitor experience. 'Digital journey' As Chinese travelers increasingly use digital platforms to discover and plan their vacations, Fiji also needs to become "more accessible throughout that digital journey", Pant said. Initiatives such as the use of AI for travel planning, bookings and itineraries are helping create "a more connected digital journey for Chinese travelers", he said. Fantasha Lockington, CEO of the Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association, said the arrivals milestone confirmed that the post-pandemic recovery "has moved past rebuilding into sustained growth". But she said the sector's fundamentals — staffing levels, service standards and infrastructure — need to keep pace with demand. "It's a positive signal for continued investment in the sector," Lockington said. Steady growth from China is encouraging, particularly as the market diversifies its visitor base, she said. Chinese travelers "tend to value curated experiences, quality dining and, increasingly, sustainability and authentic cultural engagement", she added. Yuan Li, a 39-year-old software engineer in Shanghai, said he plans to visit Fiji later this year with several friends, marking their first trip to the island attractions. "We will do some scuba diving and just relax around the beaches," Yuan said. "Many of us are also into photography, so there'll be good opportunities to take some picturesque shots," he added. body: Chinese overseas firms focus on building brand trust - World - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE World Asia-Pacific Americas Europe Middle East Africa China-US China-Europe China-Japan China-Africa Home World / Americas Home / World / Americas Chinese overseas firms focus on building brand trust By RENA LI in Los Angeles | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-11 09:12 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE Chinese companies expanding overseas increasingly face a new challenge: moving beyond simply entering the North American market to building brands, local partnerships and long-term trust, business leaders and experts said at a recent forum in California. Michael Jordan, a global communications adviser and media relations strategist, said that the shift requires Chinese companies to rethink how they communicate with overseas audiences. He made the comment at the Going Global Conference, held as part of the North America Investment Forum from Sept 4 to 7 in Orange County. The event brought together entrepreneurs, investors and professionals in branding, retail, e-commerce, AI, legal services and cross-border business to discuss strategies for Chinese and other Asian companies expanding in North America. Jordan said international perceptions of China range from strongly supportive to firmly skeptical, with the greatest opportunity lying among audiences in between who remain open to persuasion. "The only way to persuade that middle audience of skeptics is with evidence-driven content," he said. More people in the United States and other Western countries are recognizing China's advances in areas such as electric vehicles, robotics and AI, Jordan said. But technological achievements alone do not automatically translate into trust in a company. "Only credible evidence can touch the mind of a skeptic," he said. "You present concrete, credible, even verifiable evidence, and they start to believe you." At the same time, companies need to make their stories more relatable by highlighting the experiences of founders, employees, business partners and customers, Jordan said. "Humanizing content can touch the hearts of a skeptic," he said. Uri Ferruccio, cofounder of KOVA, an e-commerce platform, said building a business in a new market is ultimately about creating a community of investors, partners, creators and customers who share the same values. Companies should look for partners aligned not only with what they do, but also with how they operate and the value they seek to create, he said. "What we care about most is people who are excited about bringing their products, their brands, and building trust across an international partnership," he said. Participants said the next phase of globalization requires companies to move beyond simply taking products overseas toward deeper localization involving brands, capital, local teams, supply chains and ties with communities. Long-term process Jing Zhao Cesarone, founder and president of the Global Corporate Social Responsibility Foundation, said the challenge is no longer simply selling products in the US. "Going global is not a short-term sales campaign," she said. "It is a long-term process of building a brand, connecting with capital, earning trust and creating local value." Wang Mingming, general manager of Thunder International Group, said manufacturers entering the US often need to respond quickly to local requirements by adjusting packaging, licensing, trademarks and branding. Local elected officials at the forum highlighted Orange County as a potential base for international businesses and investment, citing its diversity, redevelopment opportunities and public-private partnerships. Orange County, in Southern California, had an estimated population of 3.15 million last year. About 25 percent of residents identified as Asian and 30 percent were foreign-born, according to the US Census Bureau. The county's supervisor, Donald Wagner, said the region's diversity is accompanied by shared aspirations for family life, safety and economic opportunity. He cited Irvine as an example of a highly diverse community with a sizable Chinese population, saying Orange County seeks to provide an environment where residents and businesses from different backgrounds can prosper. [CHEN YUYU / FOR CHINA DAILY] For Canadian Millen Sandhu, 21, the dilemma was whether to look east or look west. Waiting along with scores of others, Sandhu and his three friends held up their phones to capture the spectacular moment tens of thousands of lights illuminated the buildings on the Bund in Shanghai. Every evening at 7 pm, people gather on either side of the Huangpu River to witness the magical moment the skyscrapers on the Lujiazui stretch on the east bank of the river and the historical buildings lining the west bank are illuminated in tandem, creating an awe-inspiring spectacle for those watching. "You can't see something that is so traditional yet so technologically advanced anywhere else. It is a mix of everything in one. This seems like living in the future," said Sandhu, a fourth-year undergraduate student from the University of British Columbia. Visiting China on a 10-day vacation, the student, who majors in opera performance, learned about the light show on social media. The dazzling night lights along both sides of the Huangpu River have long been one of Shanghai's most iconic sights. Shen Qiang, head of Huangpu district's Bund scenic area management office, told the Shanghai Observer that more than 40,000 visitors were recorded on the Bund waterfront at 7 pm on Aug 15. Janet Beemer from the United States, who is visiting her daughter Katie Welch Hu in Shanghai, couldn't stop gushing about her experience. "I love it. It's amazing. There's so much history on this side, and all the new modern buildings and architecture across the river," she exclaimed. Terming the show unique, Beemer said that though she had seen some light shows in other countries before, none matched Shanghai's scale. The history Beemer refers to are the buildings on the west bank of the river that were mostly built in the early 20th century. At 7 pm sharp daily, the chime of the Customs House clock signals the start of the spectacle of golden lights spreading from one building to another — with all 38 landmarks lighting up within 10 seconds. The lighting adds a dynamic, layered and almost painting-like dimension to the skyline. And it's a show that has been enthralling crowds for 36 years. According to Li Wei, deputy director of Huangpu district's lighting office, the lights are not controlled individually by each building. Instead, they're connected and controlled in real time via a network, using dedicated channels and high-speed wireless communication to achieve the rolling effect of the buildings lighting up one after another. As signal transmission speed varies and voltage load considerations have to be taken into account, it takes between five and 10 seconds to light up all of the more than 30,000 lights that create the final effect. Across the Huangpu River, Shanghai's iconic high-rises in Lujiazui come alive with their own distinctive light patterns. Take the Oriental Pearl Tower for example. Once the city's tallest building at 468 meters, it lights up in specific colors or displays scrolling messages on important occasions. For some visitors, once is not enough to savor the experience in full. Visiting Shanghai for the first time, French tourist Ophelia Diaz swore she would be back the next day to witness the light show again. Learning about the light show from a Chinese online travel agency, Diaz said she saw a light show in Hong Kong a couple of years ago and made it a must-do for her visit to Shanghai. "It's really nice. It's really iconic. Everyone should go and see it," said Diaz after waiting for 45 minutes to catch the magical sight. Welch Hu, Beemer's daughter who lives in China, said: "I went to Times Square in New York City, which is kind of similar, also very international, also very bright, but not the same. "The feeling is different; the culture is different; it's definitely something special about Shanghai. I think we will come back sometime in the future for sure. It was fun."
title: Bund lights beckon thousands daily in Shanghai

From beloved global classics like Swan Lake , The Nutcracker , and Giselle to original productions by China's leading ballet companies, China offers a rich variety of ballet performances throughout the year, staged at some of the country's finest venues. Whether you're a devoted ballet fan or simply looking to add an unforgettable cultural experience to your trip, these 10 venues stand out for their artistic excellence, strong ties to leading ballet companies, and outstanding lineups of international and domestic productions. If ballet is part of your travel wish list, these are 10 stages worth adding to your itinerary. Beijing | Tianqiao Theatre Opened in 1953, Tianqiao Theatre is one of China's most celebrated ballet venues. [Photo/VCG] Why visit? If you want to experience Chinese ballet at its finest, Tianqiao Theatre is the place to start. As the principal home stage of the National Ballet of China, it presents everything from beloved classics such as Swan Lake and Giselle to iconic Chinese productions like The Red Detachment of Women, Raise the Red Lantern and A Dream of Red Mansions. About the theater Opened in 1953, Tianqiao Theatre is one of China's most celebrated ballet venues. It regularly hosts performances by the National Ballet of China and has welcomed many of the world's leading ballet companies. The theater also served as the venue for multiple editions of the China International Ballet Season, cementing its reputation as a major center for ballet in China. The National Ballet of China's original ballet production A Dream of Red Mansions premieres at Tianqiao Theatre in 2023. Destinations − Suzhou Dunhuang Yunnan Shanxi Scenic Spots World Heritage Sites Museums Plan Your Visit + Entering China How to Pay Helpful Tools Calls & Internet To Pack Getting Around Where to Stay Health & Safety Attractions Ticketing Etiquette & Culture Frequently Asked Questions Shopping Best Bites www.chinaservicesinfo.com www.chinadaily.com.cn Home > Snapshots of China Yaoli Ancient Town, Jingdezhen, Jiangxi Updated: 2026-08-29 | China Bound Yaoli, meaning “kiln village”, reflects its role as the birthplace of Jingdezhen’s porcelain industry. By the early Song Dynasty (960-1279), porcelain production here had reached its peak. The town is known as the “source of porcelain, hometown of tea and sea of forests”. Surrounded by mountains, it is crossed by the Yaohe River, while well-preserved Huizhou-style buildings dating from the Ming and Qing dynasties (1368-1911) are scattered along the river and nestled against the hills. Yaoli was also an important stop along the Huirao Ancient Trail, which connected the historic regions of Huizhou (present-day Shexian county in Anhui province) and Raozhou (present-day Poyang county in Jiangxi province) and witnessed centuries of trade and travel between the two areas.
title: Yaoli Ancient Town, Jingdezhen, Jiangxi province

body: Home I Want To Travel in Shanghai 2026 Shanghai Tourism Festival Shanghai Tourism Festival floats set to tour city english.shanghai.gov.cn The Shanghai Tourism Festival is bringing one of its signature attractions back to the streets this September, with 21 newly designed floats set to traverse the city. The floats will make their debut at the 37th Shanghai Tourism Festival Grand Parade on the Bund on Sept 12, joining 21 performance groups from China and abroad. From Sept 13 to Oct 6, the floats will travel to 10 locations — Jing'an, Chongming, Hongkou, Jiading, Qingpu, Xuhui, the Lin-gang Special Area, Minhang, Putuo, and Songjiang — for parades and displays. What to look for This year's floats draw inspiration from Shanghai's cultural attractions, traditional crafts, technology, and international connections. A wildlife-themed float jointly created by Shanghai Zoo, Shanghai Wild Animal Park, and Shanghai Haichang Ocean Park. [Photo/Shanghai Municipal Administration of Culture and Tourism] A wildlife-themed float, developed collaboratively by Shanghai Zoo, Shanghai Wild Animal Park, and Shanghai Haichang Ocean Park, will bring together some of the city's best-known animal attractions. Nanxiang Ancient Town's float combines local cultural landmarks with its famous xiaolongbao and collectible figures. [Photo/Shanghai Municipal Administration of Culture and Tourism] Shanghai's historic towns will also take center stage. Nanxiang Ancient Town's float pairs trendy collectible figures with its famous xiaolongbao , or steamed soup dumplings, while floats inspired by Zhujiajiao and Xinchang showcase the charm of Jiangnan water towns. Songjiang's float brings together its four landmarks, including Guangfulin Cultural Relics Park. A technology-themed float highlights Shanghai's innovation and the growing use of artificial intelligence in cultural and tourism experiences. [Photo/Shanghai Municipal Administration of Culture and Tourism] Technology also features prominently. One float will feature robots serving as tour guides and servers, offering a glimpse of how artificial intelligence is finding its way into travel and everyday life. Etihad Airways will join the float parade for the first time with a design inspired by a Boeing 787, while a collaboration between Shanghai Arts and Crafts Factory and the Xiling Seal Engraver's Society uses light and shadow to give traditional Chinese seal engraving a contemporary twist. Floats from cities including Suzhou, Ningbo, and Nanjing will showcase the culture of the Yangtze River Delta, while another from Dehua in Fujian province will highlight the area's renowned white porcelain. Where to see the floats Following their Bund debut, the 21 floats will travel around Shanghai on the following schedule: Jing'an district Sept 13, 8–8:30 pm Life Hub @ Daning (大宁国际) Chongming district Sept 15, 6:55–8:55 pm Chongming Avenue and Wanda Plaza Hongkou district Sept 17, 7:30–8 pm The Inlet (今潮8弄) and Life Hub @ Bund Central (滨港商业中心) Jiading district Sept 19, 6:30–8:30 pm Wuwei Road, between South Guyiyuan Road and Chaxi Road Qingpu district Sept 24, 6:30–9 pm Qingpu Wuyue Plaza (青浦吾悦广场) Xuhui district Sept 25, 7:30–8:30 pm Xiaomuqiao Road, between Middle Longhua Road and Ruining Road Lin-gang Special Area Sept 26, 6:30–9 pm Ring of Glory (荣耀之环), Dishui Lake Celebration Square (庆典广场), and Turing Square (图灵广场) Minhang district Sept 27, 7–7:30 pm The route runs west along Zhujian Road from Longpanqiao Road, then south along Lianyou Road to Minbei Road. Putuo district Sept 28, 6–8 pm Global Harbor (环球港) and the nearby section of North Kaixuan Road Songjiang district Sept 29–Oct 6, 6:30–8:30 pm Guangfulin Cultural Relics Park (广富林文化遗址), Xuanwu Gate entrance All 21 floats will assemble at Guangfulin Cultural Relics Park from Sept 29 to Oct 6. A series of events marking the close of the Shanghai Tourism Festival will also be held in Songjiang on Oct 6. *The schedule is subject to change. Visitors are advised to check official updates before setting out. [Photo/Dazhong News] The hull of the P-84, an over 100,000-metric-ton floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) unit with an all-electric design, has been completed in Yantai, East China's Shandong province. Built by China International Marine Containers Group for Brazil's Petrobras, the vessel is the largest FPSO hull project ever undertaken by a Chinese shipyard. The P-84 FPSO has a daily crude oil production capacity of 225,000 barrels and can process 10 million cubic meters of natural gas per day. Its all-electric architecture, paired with zero routine flaring, waste heat recovery, and deep-sea water cooling, is expected to cut greenhouse gas emissions per barrel by about 30 percent, making it one of the most energy-efficient platforms in the world. The project is one of Shandong's development highlights in high-end marine engineering. The province's Qingdao–Yantai–Weihai cluster has developed a complementary industry value chain, with Yantai specializing in offshore engineering assembly and support. One in every 10 ship orders in China now originates from Shandong, putting the province third nationwide. body: The "Link-Up Argentina Youth Entrepreneurship Support" project launches in Yiwu on Sept 8. [Photo/Tide News] The "Link-Up Argentina Youth Entrepreneurship Support" project was launched on Sept 8 in Yiwu, a county-level city in Jinhua, Zhejiang province, involving 130 offline and online participants and marking the city's first regular cross-border e-commerce training initiative for overseas youth. The Zhejiang Provincial People's Association for Friendship With Foreign Countries leads the program, organized by the Yiwu Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, Tongyue Social Work Service Center, the General Business Confederation of the Argentine Republic, and the National University of Tucuman. Spanning one and a half months, the training includes online courses, practical exercises, and field visits in Yiwu, with more than 10 professionals, scholars, and legal experts serving as international volunteer mentors. Wu Qiang, an Argentine cross-border e-commerce entrepreneur rooted in Yiwu, said that he hopes to help young people from his homeland master e-commerce skills and bring Yiwu's quality products to South America. Yiwu's evolution from a small trading town to a global supermarket continues to attract international attention, with the city's exports to Argentina exceeding 5 billion yuan ($745.36 million) in 2025, up more than 120 percent year-on-year. Project leader Chen Feng highlighted that the Link-Up project will continue to use Yiwu's supply chain and e-commerce expertise to enhance cultural exchange and global trade.
title: Argentine entrepreneurs take training program in Jinhua

Over the past five years, Wuhan has produced 7,049 PCT (Patent Cooperation Treaty) applications and 122,556 scientific papers, and completed 730 venture capital transactions. Notably, 7 percent of its PCT patent applications were co-submitted with inventors from outside the city, with Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou, Shanghai-Suzhou, and Beijing being the top three collaborative regions. WIPO assesses innovation clusters in its annual index based on three key indicators: the location of inventors on PCT patent applications, the affiliation of authors of published scientific papers, and the location of companies that received venture capital funding, then compiles and ranks these indicators to identify the most active regions globally for innovation activities. China has maintained its position as the country with the most clusters on the list for four consecutive years. Among the top 10 clusters by size, China's "Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou" cluster has topped the list for two years running, with the Beijing cluster in 5th place and the "Shanghai-Suzhou" cluster in 6th place. [Photo/Agencies] Storming through the qualifiers into the quarterfinals in New York, Zheng Qinwen has swung her way back into the elite ranks of women's tennis with a scintillating US Open run, reviving her game just in time for a string of upcoming home tournaments in China. Despite a narrow defeat to second seed Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan in a thrilling quarterfinal clash, China's currently 121st-ranked Zheng has every reason to leave New York as proud as a winner, after capping off her most successful campaign at any tournament this year since coming back from a long injury layoff in February. Her seven straight victories over the past fortnight, including three in qualifying rounds and two upset wins against major-champion opponents, have proved Zheng has recovered her pace and strength on court, confirming that the former world No 4, who underwent arthroscopic surgery on her right elbow last summer, is fit and healthy again and set to pick up where she left off on the WTA Tour. "The wins I had so far for sure are great," Zheng said after losing to Rybakina 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 in two hours and 14 minutes at Arthur Ashe Stadium in what was their sixth career meeting since 2022. "Obviously today in the match I had a lot of chances in the third set, but I didn't take them. That was a big pity for me." As showed during the match, particularly when Zheng had a break point leading 4-3 in the third set, which was later saved by Rybakina, the gap between the resurgent Chinese ace and the very best in the game has significantly narrowed, giving Zheng encouragement — if any was needed — that she is getting back to her best. "I think the good thing is I know how to compete better than the beginning of the year," said Zheng, who fell to No 160 in June and hadn't won over two matches in a row at any tournaments before arriving in New York. "In the beginning of the year, I had totally lost the tournament rhythm, and obviously this tournament has helped me find it little by little. "In general (reflecting on the whole US Open journey), I can take some positive things from it, and then I can go back and look at what I can do better in future tournaments," said the 23-year-old who won China's first tennis singles Olympic gold medal in Paris in 2024, the best year of her career till her elbow injury put any further progress on hold. Zheng's run to the last eight in Flushing Meadows included a remarkable rally against 2025 Australian Open champion Madison Keys, who held a 5-0 lead in the third set only for Zheng to win the last seven games and pull off a huge 1-6, 7-6 (3), 7-5 upset over the home favorite in the third round. She repeated the epic comeback in the next round, overcoming another 0-5 deficit in the first set against Iga Swiatek before sending the six-time major champion packing in tears after a 7-5, 6-3 round-of-16 win. Zheng Qinwen's storming run through qualifying to the US Open quarterfinals has the 2024 Olympic gold medalist finally feeling like a force on the court again. [Photo/Agencies] With a quarterfinal run this week matching her previous best at the US Open (2023, 2024), Zheng is guaranteed to break into the top 60 on Monday, just in time for the WTA Tour's "China Swing", where the home star is expected to fire up her fans at the 2026 Billie Jean King Cup Finals in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, before returning to Beijing for the WTA1000 China Open. Scheduled to face Italy in a quarterfinal tie on Sept 24 at the Cup, the world women's national team tournament, host China will need its leading ace Zheng to stay red-hot in its challenge against the two-time defending champion squad at the Shenzhen Bay Sports Center. Zheng will then fight for her own sake in Beijing having already secured a main-draw entry at the China Open as a wildcard, before a possible appearance at another 1000 tournament in Wuhan, capital of her home province Hubei. "I'm always so excited to play in China," said Zheng, who made a brief return at last year's China Open, before having to retire from her second-round encounter with reigning Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova due to a recurrence of her elbow injury. "Playing at home I'm always more motivated, but at the same time I also carry some pressure, because I really want to do well here," said Zheng, who won her career-first hard-court WTA title on home soil in Zhengzhou in 2023. "I just want to keep calm and train day by day, focus on the present and take it match by match." Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan celebrates winning her quarterfinal match against Zheng at the Arthur Ashe Stadium in New York on Wednesday. [Photo/Agencies]
title: Back in the swing of things

body: Arteta lauds in-form Odegaard as 'remarkable' Arsenal edges Napoli - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE Sports Soccer Basketball Volleyball Tennis Golf Track & field Swimming Home / Sports Home / Sports Arteta lauds in-form Odegaard as 'remarkable' Arsenal edges Napoli Agencies | Updated: 2026-09-11 08:56 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE Arsenal's Martin Odegaard celebrates scoring the winning goal against Napoli on Wednesday. [Photo/Agencies] NAPLES, Italy — Mikel Arteta hailed Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard for another match-winning moment as his goal sealed a 1-0 victory over Napoli on Wednesday that the Gunners boss said did not reflect a "remarkable" performance from his side. Last season's runner-up began its Champions League campaign with a win at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona that was settled by Odegaard's 75th-minute bullet strike on a night it racked up 26 shots, a club record away from home in the competition. Odegaard has started the 2026-27 season in sensational form, scoring four goals in five games, including back-to-back winners against Chelsea and Napoli. It marks a notable change in output from the Arsenal skipper, who scored one goal in 36 appearances in all competitions last season, and Arteta was asked about the attacking midfielder's increased productivity in front of goal. "First of all, he needs to be available, and last year he missed so many games through injuries," Arteta said. "He's got that edge and he's got different relationships around him as well. That helps. "Now he can start to occupy some different heights in the team, especially in the attacking phase. When we get him into those positions, he's a really dangerous player. "What we need is players with that mindset to decide a game," he added. "To play with that personality, that if an action might not happen, the next one, the next one, keep taking chances and risks. "He's getting into those positions much more in recent games and you feel he has this emotional state that he knows the ball can go in, and he scored an incredible goal tonight." Napoli rues absentees Arsenal has started the season strongly, winning all three of its Premier League games after brushing Manchester City aside in the Community Shield last month. "(I'm) very happy," said Arteta, who felt the result undersold the quality of his team's display in Naples. "The way we attacked the game from the very first minute, the way we competed, the clarity we had with how we had to attack them to disorganize them, the purpose, the quality. The amount of chances we generated. "For sure the scoreline has to reflect a very different result. We'll get there, because if we were a bit more precise it would have been much bigger. "But to do what we've done today in this stadium against this opponent is remarkable from the team." For Napoli, the defeat marked another setback for new coach Massimiliano Allegri, whose side suffered a third consecutive loss in all competitions following Serie A reverses to Como and Inter. Injuries to key players Scott McTominay and Frank Anguissa complicated matters for Allegri, who targeted three points in its next league game on Sunday. "To get back on track, we need a solid win against Bologna, which won't be easy," Allegri said. "There is definitely some bitterness and disappointment; we are coming off three defeats. "I liked the performance technically, but in the second half we lacked the legs; (Billy) Gilmour and (Kevin) De Bruyne were playing their first games. "We need to stay calm and collected. If we defended at certain points in the games like we did in the second half tonight, we might not have lost against Como and Inter." Mac Allister lifts Liverpool A day after revealing his disappointment over the lack of a new contract offer by Liverpool, Alexis Mac Allister delivered the perfect response with the winning goal in a 2-1 victory against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on Wednesday. Mac Allister unleashed a ferocious strike from outside of the box as Liverpool came back from a goal down at Anfield. The Argentina international, who joined Liverpool in 2023, raced away to celebrate in front of the home fans. It was in stark contrast to his sombre tone ahead of the game when discussing the uncertainty over his position at the club. "I received the news that the club was not in a position to offer me a new contract," he said during a prematch news conference on Tuesday. Mac Allister's contract runs until 2028, so there is no urgency for Liverpool to renew yet. But his goal five minutes after halftime was a reminder of his qualities, firing powerfully into the corner and beyond the reach of Atletico goalkeeper Jan Oblak. "Normally when I'm in those positions I like to shoot," Mac Allister said. "It doesn't happen very often but I'm happy because I love to score goals. Today, it was a nice goal and was important for the team as well, which is what I want." body: Former superstar hurdler Liu donates entire salary to charity - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE Sports Soccer Basketball Volleyball Tennis Golf Track & field Swimming Home / Sports / Track and field Home / Sports / Track and field Former superstar hurdler Liu donates entire salary to charity By Li Yingxue | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-09-10 13:30 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE Liu Xiang Olympic champion Liu Xiang said on Thursday that he completed a buyout with Shanghai sports authorities on Sept 1, receiving 494,000 yuan, and would have no further association with the sports bureau. “On Sept 1, I had already completed the buyout and received 494,000 yuan in buyout compensation,” Liu said in a post on his personal social media account. “From now on, I will have no further association with the sports bureau.” The 43-year-old former hurdler also said that he had received a total of 982,935 yuan in salary and subsidies from April 7, 2015, when he retired, until the completion of the buyout. Liu said he donated the entire amount to the China Charity Federation on Sept 2 for disaster relief following mudslides in the Xizang autonomous region. Liu's latest post came after a public dispute over his post-retirement career arrangement triggered widespread discussion on Chinese social media. On Aug 26, Liu posted a photo commemorating his victory at the 2004 Athens Olympics and said the sports authorities had asked him to choose between becoming a coach and accepting a buyout. The Shanghai Sports Bureau said afterward that Liu was an outstanding athlete who had made significant contributions to Shanghai's sports development. It said the Shanghai Competitive Sports Training Management Center had communicated with Liu and would handle his post-retirement arrangement in accordance with relevant national and municipal regulations, mainly through organizational placement or self-employment. In his latest post, Liu also addressed what he described as the issue of being “on the payroll but not at his post”, saying he had not received any formal position or post since his retirement. “I have not received any official post or position since I retired,” Liu said. “I respect the rules and accept that there may have been oversights, but rules should never be an excuse.” He questioned why the issue had taken 11 years to address, saying that the choice between becoming a coach and accepting a buyout had come too late to be regarded as a genuine career choice. Liu said he hoped his case would encourage greater attention to the career transition of retired athletes and called for more flexible and diverse arrangements. “Putting the issue of resettlement in the public eye is not about using public opinion to seek a third option,” he said. “I hope organizations will seriously consider the future of every retired athlete and treat them well.” Liu won the men's 110-meter hurdles at the 2004 Athens Olympics with a time of 12.91 seconds, becoming the first Asian athlete to win an Olympic gold medal in a men's track event. He went on to win the world title in 2007 and set a world record of 12.88 seconds in 2006. [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] Hubei province's 11th Traditional Sports Games of Ethnic Minorities concluded on Sept 8 in Xuan'en county after five days of fierce competition. Held in the Enshi Tujia and Miao autonomous prefecture, the event drew 29 delegations, with nearly 3,000 athletes, coaches, and referees registered. Organizers described it as the largest edition since the provincial games began in 1986. Hubei's 11th Traditional Sports Games of Ethnic Minorities concluded on Sept 8 in Xuan'en county after five days of fierce competition. [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] The program featured 12 competitive sports and one demonstration category. Dragon boat racing and pearl ball made their debut, alongside established events such as stilt racing and spinning tops. For local Qin Yao, stilt racing brought back childhood memories. "I played on stilts as a child, but I never imagined it would become an event at a sports meet," Qin said. "Watching the athletes move so quickly on stilts was incredible." Hubei's 11th Traditional Sports Games of Ethnic Minorities concluded on Sept 8 in Xuan'en county after five days of fierce competition. [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] The celebrations extended beyond competition venues. The opening ceremony was staged along the Gongshui River, incorporating bridges and waterfront landmarks. Cultural groups from eight provincial-level regions, including Xinjiang, Guangxi and Inner Mongolia, joined local performers for street parades and public activities. Luo Qijing, a staff member of the games' executive committee, said the event had strengthened exchanges among athletes from different ethnic groups, introduced traditional sports to a wider audience, and helped more visitors discover Xuan'en. Hubei's 11th Traditional Sports Games of Ethnic Minorities concluded on Sept 8 in Xuan'en county after five days of fierce competition. [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] The county also sought to ensure benefits beyond the five-day gathering. No new competition venues were built. Instead, existing facilities were upgraded, with plans to make them available free of charge for public fitness activities after the games, according to provincial authorities. At the closing ceremony beside the Gongshui River, hundreds of performers joined hands in a circle to sing and dance. The games flag was handed to Yunxi county in Shiyan, which will host the next edition. Hubei's 11th Traditional Sports Games of Ethnic Minorities concluded on Sept 8 in Xuan'en county after five days of fierce competition. body: SSC drives sustainable development - Opinion - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE Opinion Cartoons Editorials Global Lens We Comment Columnists Global Views Chinese Perspectives Opinion Line Home Opinion / Global Lens Home / Opinion / Global Lens SSC drives sustainable development By Stefan Liller | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-11 09:47 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE MA XUEJING/CHINA DAILY Each year, the United Nations Day for South-South Cooperation offers an opportunity to recognize a simple but powerful idea: countries facing similar development challenges have much to learn from one another. Knowledge, experience, and solutions developed in one part of the globe can often be applied elsewhere and adapted to different contexts through strong partnerships that take advantage of countries' respective strengths. Today, this matters more than ever. Amid growing geopolitical fragmentation and compounding crises from climate change and biodiversity loss to widening inequalities, debt pressures, and rapid technological change, the world faces an annual $4 trillion financing gap for sustainable development, with official development assistance falling by 23 percent in 2025 compared to the previous year. The Sustainable Development Goals — the UN's global blueprint to safeguard humanity and the planet by 2030 — are hanging on by a thread. Yet, despite this difficult landscape, the world does not lack promising ideas. Across countries, governments, communities, researchers and entrepreneurs are already devising practical responses to shared challenges. Too often, however, many of these solutions remain localized, isolated, or underfunded, limiting the potential scale of their impact. South-South and Triangular cooperation can help bridge this gap. By bringing together practical experience, technical expertise, innovation and financing, it can help impactful solutions reach more people around the world, addressing challenges from poverty alleviation to disaster recovery. In the case of China, its remarkable development journey over the last several decades has made it an increasingly critical international development partner. Today, given its scale, what China does has the potential to affect livelihoods and economies around the world, as well as our planet. By actively sharing experience and expertise in areas such as poverty reduction, renewable energy, digital innovation, and infrastructure, accompanied by affordable, long-term financing, China can offer valuable lessons and relevant resources that countries across the globe can benefit from, helping to advance collective progress toward the SDGs. Indeed, China has already demonstrated a strong commitment to this goal. The Global Development Project Pool — a mechanism established by China to bring together development projects at different stages and help to connect promising initiatives with partners, expertise, and financing — now encompasses more than 1,800 projects with priority areas from poverty reduction and food security to climate and the digital economy. And the Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund, originally established by China in 2015, is backed by total funding of $4 billion, and has supported projects across more than 60 countries, benefiting over 30 million people. UNDP's partnership with China has looked to leverage its experience and combine it with our global network across 170 countries and territories. Together with the government of China, UNDP has implemented close to 40 projects across 26 countries in Asia, Africa, Eastern Europe and Latin America, benefiting over 18 million people. This cooperation has ranged from pandemic response and recovery to climate information and early-warning systems, helping climate-vulnerable communities better anticipate disaster risks. Having previously served as UNDP resident representative in Bangladesh, I have seen first-hand the tangible effect of these projects on local communities in partner countries. Beneficiaries there received vocational training and productive assets including sewing machines, IT equipment, and business carts, to help establish or expand small businesses. As of June, the project had reached 387,000 people across six cities. Such results demonstrate what South-South and Triangular cooperation can achieve when financing, expertise and country-level knowledge are brought together around locally identified priorities. Moving forward, the challenge will be to build on successful projects and create stronger pathways for effective solutions to be adapted at speed and scale across different contexts through a broader cooperation ecosystem. Doing this will require actions across three main areas: First, further strengthen bilateral engagements with multilateral support through triangular cooperation. Greater integration between China's bilateral development programs and the UN system's technical expertise, safeguards, and extensive on-the-ground presence can ensure alignment with international best practices and make cooperation more responsive and inclusive — particularly for communities at risk of being left behind. Second, expand the range of partners involved. Engaging more institutions from across the globe, including from academia, financial institutions, technology providers and foundations, can unlock additional resources, ideas and capabilities while creating new opportunities for mutual learning. Third, make innovation accessible and locally relevant. Projects that leverage digital, AI and green technologies must be accompanied by investments in capacities, institutions and enabling policies. This will allow developing countries not only to adopt new technologies, but also to apply them responsibly and according to their priorities. South-South and Triangular interventions are most effective when they are demand-driven and shaped through engagement with the communities they serve. This allows solutions to fit the local ecosystem and makes for more sustainable impact in the long-term. Ultimately, the challenges the world faces today are far too complex and widespread for any single country to address alone. The only path forward is one that countries walk together — where international cooperation enables us to exchange knowledge, mobilize greater investment, and accelerate collective progress. When China's experience and resources are combined with the leadership of partner countries and the expertise and global reach of organizations such as UNDP, proven solutions can travel further and deliver results at greater scale. Realizing this potential will require sustained commitment from all partners to exchange knowledge, mobilize investment and translate successful approaches into lasting development gains. Ultimately, the measure of South-South and Triangular cooperation will always be its ability to improve people's lives and help countries advance together toward a more inclusive, resilient and sustainable future. The author is the resident representative of the United Nations Development Programme in China. The views don't necessarily reflect those of China Daily.
