body: Western politicians need to stop fearmongering about Chinese goods - Opinion - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE Opinion Cartoons Editorials Global Lens We Comment Columnists Global Views Chinese Perspectives Opinion Line Home Opinion / Chen Weihua Home / Opinion / Chen Weihua Western politicians need to stop fearmongering about Chinese goods By Chen Weihua | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-11 09:48 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE A drone photo taken on June 12, 2025 shows harvesters working in wheat fields in Zhanghuzhuang village of Gaomi city, East China's Shandong province. [Photo/Xinhua] Some politicians in the United Kingdom made the bizarre claim in British media last week that China could use tractors and other internet-linked agricultural machinery to spy on farmers there. The Coalition on Secure Technology, headed by Labour MP Graeme Downie, claimed that UK's agricultural sector is dangerously exposed to a hidden security risk embedded in widely used farming tools, saying that chips in GPS-guided machines, drones and irrigation systems open the back door to data on UK food security. If this were true, it would mean machinery and equipment made in the UK and other Western countries have already compromised people around the world for a long time now. The CST claimed that Beijing could use these tractors to gather data on crop yields, production forecasts and livestock populations. But why would China want to gather such data so painstakingly via tractors when they are all readily available public data published by the UK government authorities? The CST went on to claim that the tractors could do more harm than just gathering intelligence; they can potentially be remotely shut down through a so-called "kill switch". Such paranoia is nothing new. Senior US officials from the previous Joe Biden administration in the United States, such as then commerce secretary Gina Raimondo, made similar claims years ago in a bid to ban Chinese electric vehicles in the US and shield US automakers, which are lagging far behind in the field. I wonder if Raimondo and Downie would say the same about Tesla cars. Or even Boeing and Airbus planes, which could just fall from the sky because of a similar sudden "kill switch". Also, are these planes gathering data while flying over China and other countries? How about the tens of millions of cars made and sold in China by General Motors, Ford, Volkswagen and Toyota, or Apple's iPhones and watches? To be sure, I am just mimicking the hysterical paranoia of some Western politicians. In contrast, China has been far more accepting of Western technology. Since the late 1970s when China was still relatively uncompetitive, China pursued reform and opening-up, actively welcoming Western products and investment despite the enormous pressure this placed on certain domestic industries. Yet China chose to use this pressure as a driving force to push through economic reform and industrial upgrading, rather than shutting its doors or smearing foreign products as security threats. Some Western politicians have also fearmongered about toys and various electric appliances made in China, such as rice cookers, TV sets, microwave ovens and air conditioners. After all, they all contain smart chips that, in the eyes of some Western politicians, could be used as leverage. The latest reckless fearmongering about Chinese technology reflects the desperation that has set in as Chinese technological advancement has left many Western countries behind. For these Western politicians, countries such as China should be condemned to making only cheap low-end and labor-intensive goods, and never be allowed to become a peer competitor, let alone surpass them. Instead of trying to catch up with China in those areas, their underhanded strategy is to pull China down by smearing Chinese products and adopting protectionist measures. That only helps distract those countries from fixing their own problems. However, such a strategy won't succeed and won't stop China from further climbing the tech ladder and global supply chains. The advancement of Chinese EVs, solar panels, wind turbines and lithium batteries should be celebrated by all because these clean technology goods contribute to the vital global fight against climate change. The fact that China made 10 of the top 15 bestselling EV brands in the world in 2026 shows that customers like these cars despite the fearmongering by Western politicians who are trying to deprive them of such great products. It's time those politicians stopped fearmongering about Chinese goods. body: Up to 200 km/h: what Kazakhstan’s first air taxi will be like News » Articles in English Up to 200 km/h: what Kazakhstan’s first air taxi will be like 20 July, 18:24 1017962 Elena Kovalchuk Editor Photo by: DKNews.kz/AI-generated Kazakhstan prepares for first public eVTOL flight in Astana. Astana will host Kazakhstan's first demonstration flight of an electric air taxi on July 24, 2026 , marking another milestone in the country's efforts to develop Urban Air Mobility (UAM). The event will take place at the Kazanat Hippodrome , where visitors will witness a demonstration of next-generation electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) technology, DKNews.kz reports. AutoFlight Prosperity to take to the skies The demonstration will feature the AutoFlight Prosperity passenger eVTOL aircraft. The aircraft is designed to carry: One pilot Five passengers Its key performance characteristics include: Maximum speed of up to 200 km/h Flight range of up to 200 km The demonstration is being organized by Kazakhstan's private company Alatau Advance Air Group Ltd. (AAAG) in partnership with China's AutoFlight . Kazakhstan moves from testing to implementation The upcoming flight follows Kazakhstan's first successful eVTOL demonstrations held in Alatau City in May 2026. Since then, the country has introduced a comprehensive legal framework to support the deployment of urban air mobility technologies. Key legislative milestones include: The adoption of the Constitutional Law "On the Special Legal Regime of Alatau City" on May 8, 2026 , establishing the city as a pilot zone for innovative transport technologies, including Urban Air Mobility Amendments signed by the President of Kazakhstan on June 24, 2026 , introducing the country's first legal definitions for eVTOL aircraft, vertiports and unmanned traffic management (UTM) systems Kazakhstan joins global leaders in Urban Air Mobility The new legislation places Kazakhstan among countries actively developing Urban Air Mobility technologies. These include: United States China Republic of Korea United Arab Emirates Member states of the European Union The legal framework provides the foundation for testing, regulating and eventually integrating electric air taxis into the country's transport system. A step toward the future of transportation The Astana demonstration represents the next practical phase in Kazakhstan's Urban Air Mobility programme. By combining new legislation with real-world flight demonstrations, the country is moving beyond regulatory development toward the practical introduction of advanced aviation technologies that could reshape urban transportation in the years ahead. Why it matters Urban Air Mobility is emerging as one of the fastest-growing sectors in global aviation. Kazakhstan's decision to establish a legal framework and begin public demonstrations signals its ambition to become an early adopter of eVTOL technology, opening new opportunities for innovation, investment and future transport solutions. eVTOL Air Taxi Astana Urban Air Mobility Kazakhstan Share news Reading now Trump congratulates Kazakhstan and calls Tokayev a strong leader 12 September, 23:45 30646 Kazakhstan Invites Hong Kong to Invest in New Manufacturing Projects 11 September, 08:40 23419 Tokayev’s BRICS Visit a Diplomatic Success, Says Former Indian Envoy 13 September, 22:29 21307 Xinhua Headlines: Xi to attend New Delhi summit to boost greater BRICS cooperation 11 September, 11:10 21032 Full text of Chinese President Xi Jinping's speech at Session I of the 18th BRICS Summit Today, 08:51 18612 DKNews International News Agency is registered with the Ministry of Culture and Information of the Republic of Kazakhstan. body: FlyArystan launches direct flights from Almaty to Chongqing News » Articles in English FlyArystan launches direct flights from Almaty to Chongqing 20 July, 17:28 1199385 Elena Kovalchuk Editor Photo by: FlyArystan FlyArystan has announced a new international route connecting Almaty and Chongqing , further expanding its presence in the Chinese market, DKNews.kz reports. The inaugural flight is scheduled for September 23, 2026 , making Chongqing the airline's fifth destination in China alongside Urumqi, Yining (Ghulja) and Xi'an. Flights to operate twice a week The new route will be served twice weekly. The flight schedule includes: Departures from Almaty on Wednesdays and Saturdays Return flights from Chongqing on Thursdays and Sundays The journey will take approximately five hours . FlyArystan expands its China network FlyArystan President and CEO Johan Eidhagen said the new destination reflects the airline's strategy of expanding international connections in line with growing passenger demand. «The launch of flights to Chongqing reflects our commitment to steadily expanding FlyArystan's international network in response to the growing demand for travel between Kazakhstan and China. We take a careful approach to selecting new destinations: they must meet passenger demand, align with the capabilities of our fleet, and demonstrate strong long-term potential. Chongqing meets all of these criteria. As one of China's largest metropolitan areas, Chongqing has not previously had direct air connectivity with Kazakhstan. Thanks to the recent agreements reached between the aviation authorities of our two countries, launching this route has become possible. We are proud that FlyArystan will be the first Kazakh airline to introduce direct flights on this route». A gateway to southwestern China Chongqing is one of China's largest metropolitan areas and a major tourist destination known for its dramatic urban landscape and modern engineering. Among the city's best-known attractions are: Liziba Monorail Station, where trains pass through a residential building Multi-level city architecture built into mountainous terrain Easy access to Zhangjiajie National Forest Park, famous for its towering quartz sandstone pillars that are widely associated with the landscapes featured in the Avatar films The new route is expected to improve travel opportunities for both tourists and business travellers while strengthening air connectivity between Kazakhstan and China. Tickets already on sale One-way fares under the Standard fare begin at KZT 96,000 . Passengers can book tickets through: The official FlyArystan website The FlyArystan mobile application Other authorized sales channels Ticket prices may vary depending on exchange rate fluctuations. Why it matters China remains one of Kazakhstan's key economic and tourism partners. The launch of direct flights to Chongqing expands travel options for passengers, supports business exchanges and tourism, and strengthens transport links between the two countries. It also marks the first direct air connection between Kazakhstan and one of China's largest metropolitan areas. body: Kazakh Students Win Gold at European AI Olympiad News » Articles in English Kazakh Students Win Gold at European AI Olympiad 20 July, 16:48 1213817 Arman Korzhumbayev Editor-in-Chief Kazakhstan has struck gold. All four members of the national team won medals at the first Central European Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence. Kazakhstan secured one gold, two silver and one bronze medal, DKNews.kz reports. EUROAI 2026 was held from July 14 to 19 in Cluj-Napoca, Romania. The Kazakh students competed online alongside some of Europe’s strongest teams. Who Won Gold for Kazakhstan? Abu Kanabek claimed the gold medal, achieving the best result among the members of the Kazakh team. Islamnur Khusainov and Dauzhan Beketov won silver medals. Sultanbi Isatay received bronze. As a result, every student representing Kazakhstan finished the competition with a medal. What Challenges Did EUROAI Participants Face? EUROAI is an annual regional Olympiad dedicated to artificial intelligence. Contestants compete individually rather than in teams. The tasks cover machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing and computer vision. These technologies power modern chatbots, translation services, voice assistants and image-recognition systems. Programming skills alone are not enough. Participants must analyse data, select the right algorithms and improve their models’ accuracy within a limited time. Students Built AI Models from Scratch The main competition lasted two days. During that time, the students developed artificial intelligence models from scratch and solved practical problems. The format tested more than technical knowledge. Contestants had to analyse complex tasks, find effective solutions and correct errors under intense time pressure. Kazakhstan’s results demonstrate how the country’s Olympiad movement is expanding into new areas. Students are now competing not only in mathematics and computer science but also in building functional AI models. Bagdat Mussin Praises the Team’s Success Bagdat Mussin, head of the Kazakhstan Federation of Sport Programming, said the achievement was the result of systematic support for young talent. “By performing successfully at EUROAI 2026, our young talents have once again demonstrated that Kazakhstan’s artificial intelligence and competitive programming school can compete at the global level. Such an outstanding result is no coincidence — it reflects systematic efforts to support young talent. I am proud of our students!” ©️ Tengrinews.kz / Turar Kazangapov The EUROAI results served as an important test for Kazakhstan ahead of the team’s biggest international competition of the season. The Next AI Olympiad Will Take Place in Astana The national team’s next competition will be the International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence, or IOAI. The global event will take place in Astana from August 2 to 8, 2026. Around 500 students from 110 countries are expected to attend. Kazakhstan’s team will compete on home soil against some of the world’s strongest young AI specialists. Kazakhstan will face a double challenge. The national team will compete for medals, while Astana will host one of the world’s largest international events dedicated to artificial intelligence. body: Plant seeds of peace today for a harmonious tomorrow - Opinion - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE Opinion Cartoons Editorials Global Lens We Comment Columnists Global Views Chinese Perspectives Opinion Line Home Opinion / Global Lens Home / Opinion / Global Lens Plant seeds of peace today for a harmonious tomorrow By Ronald Sakolsky | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-11 09:45 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE Ronald Sakolsky (R) sniffs a sapling after planting it with Yin Yuzhen in the Maowusu Sandy Land in North China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region, Aug 24, 2026. [Photo/Xinhua] Returning to China after 26 years was nothing short of miraculous. My 10-day journey was an odyssey of rediscovery and reflection, allowing me to witness the profound transformations that have taken place in the country I once called my second home. When I was leaving for the United States in 2000, I was very fearful that China would continue to move forward but in the process forget its past. As I traveled through the Inner Mongolia autonomous region, Luoyang and Beijing, I was struck by how much has been achieved without losing sight of the country's rich heritage. There is no doubt in my mind that, although China has moved into the 21st century, it still holds on to its beautiful past. This seamless blend of modernity and tradition is a testament to the central government's determination to foster pride among Chinese people of all ethnicities. One of the most poignant moments of my visit was returning to the Sakolsky Forest, a place that holds deep personal significance. Over two decades ago, I had the privilege of planting trees there alongside the indomitable Yin Yuzhen, a model worker who has spent four decades fighting desertification in the Mu Us Sandy Land. Her vision and perseverance have helped transform a barren desert into a lush forest, a living testament to determination and hope. As I walked across the sand, Yin said, "Your children are waving to you." Her words were deeply moving, and brought tears to my eyes because I literally felt like a parent who had been reunited with a child after a long separation. The transformation of this once desolate landscape into a thriving ecosystem is a beacon of hope for environmentalists. It is a powerful reminder of our shared responsibility to care for our planet. As President Xi Jinping said, lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets. When Mother Earth is taken care of, she gives back through fruits, vegetables, shade and much more. My fervent plea to anyone who is reading this: Please plant a tree. Planting trees indicates that the future is bright. The highlight of my visit was not only meeting Yin but also reconnecting with students and colleagues from more than 27 years ago. For a teacher, it is very rewarding to see that your students have grown into accomplished adults and that you played a small role in their development. Their success stories and warm embraces filled my heart with pride and gratitude. Their achievements are a testament to the enduring power of education and the bonds we form through it. I am deeply thankful to each and every one of them for remembering me and for the joy they brought into my life during this visit. I was on cloud nine, though I was crying tears of joy. This journey also reinforced my belief in the power of people-to-people connections to bridge divides between nations. The relationship between China and the United States, like any relationship, can be strengthened by focusing on our shared values rather than our differences. Encouraging our leaders to pursue Xi's vision of a community with a shared future for humanity is essential for fostering mutual understanding and cooperation. By building bridges, one brick at a time, we can create a more harmonious world. China's growth and development have captured the attention of the world. As the nation continues to open its arms to the global community, it is my hope that the world will reciprocate. The lessons I learned during my journey are universal. They speak to the resilience of the human spirit, the importance of nurturing our planet, and the power of education to transform lives. As I reflect on my journey, I am filled with a sense of hope and optimism. The transformation I witnessed in China is a microcosm of the potential for positive change in the world. It is a reminder that with vision, determination, and cooperation, we can overcome the challenges we face and create a brighter future for all. Yuan fen (a Chinese saying for the fated bond that brings people together)! The author is a retired educator from the United States. The views don't necessarily reflect those of China Daily. body: Two ancient civilizations, two modern journeys - Opinion - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE Opinion Cartoons Editorials Global Lens We Comment Columnists Global Views Chinese Perspectives Opinion Line Home Opinion / Global Lens Home / Opinion / Global Lens Two ancient civilizations, two modern journeys By Vikram Doraiswami | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-11 09:41 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE [Photo/Xinhua] On Aug 15, India marked 79 years as an independent modern nation. A moment not only for national reflection, but also for revisiting the extraordinary and parallel journeys of two of the world's oldest continuous civilizations. India and China both began their modern nation-building endeavors within years of one another in the mid-20th century. As we mark this milestone, it is worth pausing to consider what our two ancient societies have built, what we have learned from one another, and what possibilities lie ahead as both nations continue to rise. Long before the modern age, India and China were already connected, through the movement of ideas, trade and scholarship. With contact over the ages came understanding and the mutuality of benefit: philosophy, medicine, astronomy. Even everyday goods such as sugar, spices, paper and ink traveled across these ancient networks, creating new bridges of contact between our peoples. That tradition of learning from each other's civilizations continued through the 19th and early 20th centuries, as we made our respective journeys toward national liberation and freedom. When India gained independence in 1947, it inherited a society scarred by the trauma of Partition and colonial exploitation. Some 90 percent of India's 340 million people at the time lived below the poverty line, literacy stood under 16 percent, and life expectancy was around 31 years. Even in that adversity, India's founders chose a path grounded in constitutional democracy and pluralism for all citizens, regardless of race, religion or gender, and thereby becoming among the first post-colonial nations to adopt universal adult suffrage. In many ways, this was a continuation of our civilizational democratic ethos. And unlike most other countries that chose such a path after becoming prosperous societies, we did so in the most challenging conditions. China, too, has undertaken a remarkable transformation over a comparable period, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty. While our developmental paths have differed, both our nations have shared a common conviction that the well-being of our people must remain at the heart of nation-building, and that it is for the people of each nation to decide on the system that best suits their circumstances. Today, like China, India is a country of rapid transformation. India is among the fastest-growing major economies in the world, sustaining growth of around 7 percent. This transformation has also been underpinned by political stability and a growing degree of policy continuity, providing greater predictability for businesses and investors. Under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in a decade, among the more remarkable achievements of India are the facts that electricity has reached 100 percent of rural and urban India, and that the proportion of Indians with bank accounts has risen from around 40 to over 80 percent. Today, India records the world's largest number of fintech transactions, over 130 billion a year, across interoperable payment platforms that, much as in China, have all but obviated the need for cash. India is also a space-capable nation with end-to-end launch capability, the world's second-largest smartphone market, and among the fastest-growing populations of internet users, at some of the lowest data costs anywhere. This dynamism is carried forward by the world's largest youthful workforce, with several hundred million Indians under the age of 30, and by a vibrant startup and innovation ecosystem. As two of the world's most populous emerging economies, a stable, predictable and amicable relationship between India and China is not only in the interest of our 2.8 billion people, but is also a significant factor for peace, stability and prosperity in Asia and the wider world. As Asia and the wider international landscape become increasingly multipolar, India and China both have a stake in ensuring that global governance structures evolve to reflect the aspirations and interests of the developing world. This shared interest finds concrete expression in platforms such as BRICS, which is an important voice for emerging economies on issues ranging from sustainable development and financial architecture to technology cooperation and people-centric growth. As we look toward the upcoming BRICS Summit hosted by India, there is a valuable opportunity to deepen India-China cooperation on issues of mutual concern, from trade and investment to climate action, public health and the digital economy, while contributing constructively to a more balanced, inclusive and equitable global order. Last year, President Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed that India and China are cooperation partners who are each other's development opportunities. This perspective is in keeping with the long history of mutually beneficial contact between our two civilizations. Maintaining peace and tranquility in the India-China border areas is vital to building this partnership. We must build on that foundation, guided by mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest, while ensuring that differences, which are natural between nations, do not become disputes. In doing so, our partnership can contribute to the well-being of our two peoples and to a more stable, peaceful and prosperous world. The author is India's ambassador to the People's Republic of China. The views expressed are personal and don't necessarily represent those of China Daily. [Zhang Zhengyou/Asia News Photo] On Sept 10, when China celebrates its 42nd Teachers' Day, a new generation of young teachers is stepping into classrooms across the country's vast interior. From Guizhou's mountains and Yunnan's valleys to Inner Mongolia's grasslands, these graduates are not passing through, but returning home to make a lasting impact. For decades, talent flowed almost always from the rural regions in the west to wealthy cities in the east. Remote rural schools struggled to recruit or retain qualified teachers and ensure consistent quality. The urban-rural education gap is essentially a teacher gap, especially in subjects like English, science and music. Many rural schools had to rely on minimally trained substitutes, and those who did arrive often left after a few years. In 2006, China launched the special post-teacher program, sending over a million educators to rural schools. This was followed by tuition-waived normal programs that offered free higher education in exchange for a commitment to teaching in one's home region. While these initiatives provided some relief, the deeper question remained: How could rural teaching become a sustainable career? Policymakers realized that the solution lay in recruiting from the communities they would serve. Locally-rooted teachers share dialects, cultural references, and personal stakes in their communities' futures. Research shows that they have a stronger and more lasting impact and are more likely to continue in their positions. Thus began a project to recruit top students from central and western provinces and prepare them as quality teachers for China's 832 counties that had been lifted out of poverty. In 2021, Beijing Normal University launched the "Project to Strengthen Teaching Force", offering full scholarships for a six-year commitment to teaching in underdeveloped counties from their home provinces. The mantra was simple: Recruit from the neediest areas and train them for their future classrooms. Yet, recruitment alone is not enough. This initiative evolved into a comprehensive system built upon six flagship components: pre-service cultivation, targeted placement, in-service support, honorary incentives, diagnostic monitoring and collaborative quality enhancement. Together, these form a closed-loop system exemplifying UNESCO's "holistic teacher policy". Xiong Guojin, one of the first graduates of the "Project to Strengthen Teaching Force", grew up as a "left-behind child" in rural Guizhou. He was just three months old when his parents left him with relatives and moved to work in eastern cities. What kept him going were his teachers. "Education changed my destiny," he says. "It took me out of the mountains. But I always knew I wanted to come back — not as a visitor, but as a teacher." Today, Xiong teaches geography at Cengong No. 1 High School, integrating local landscapes into lessons. "I want my students to see their origins as a foundation to build upon," he says. Through the Qihang Plan, he received mentorship and professional development, while the Teacher Capacity Enhancement Plan provided training in practical strategies tailored for resource-limited classrooms. "Passion alone is not enough," he says. "The system gives me the tools to turn passion into lasting impact." In Kashgar, Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, Dou Zhuojun has committed to teach middle school English in his home county of Yecheng. Before graduating from Beijing Normal University, he interned at a top Beijing middle school, then spent two weeks in a rural school to understand his future students' conditions. Leading a research team, he compared impoverished Kashgar counties with urban schools. "The disparities were eye-opening," Dou says, "but they gave me a sense of purpose." Through the framework, he benefits from ongoing mentorship. "There is a whole system behind me." Despite the strong recruitment efforts, one challenge persists: ensuring remote teachers continue to grow professionally. Without sustained support, even the most committed teachers can burn out. Technology is playing a transformative role in addressing this issue. For Wang Yiying, a geography teacher in Inner Mongolia autonomous region's Siziwang Banner, Ulaanqab, the hardest part was staying effective without the professional community urban teachers take for granted. She needed mentorship and fresh ideas. In 2022, a digital platform was launched to address this need. The "Strengthening Teaching Force" online platform now serves over 630,000 teachers nationwide, offering free courses developed by more than 40 institutions. It blends online learning with in-person workshops. Wang now accesses mentors who review lesson plans, recorded lectures, and a supportive community of remote teachers. "It means I'm no longer fighting alone." What once felt isolated now feels connected. Behind teachers like Xiong, Dou, and Wang is the larger institutional support. In 2022, the Ministry of Education established 10 regional university clusters led by top normal universities to build lasting capacity in western teacher-training colleges. The goal was to strengthen local institutions to train and support their own teachers. The partnership between Beijing Normal University and Qinghai Normal University illustrates this: over five years since 2022, they have exchanged faculty, trained students, and developed regionally tailored programs. The strategy is simple: teach local institutions how to fish rather than simply giving them fish. The urban-rural education gap has not been bridged, and disparities remain. But the trend has changed. From emergency recruitment in 2006 to a comprehensive career-spanning support system now, the evolution of policy reflects a growing recognition that sustainable change requires building systems that recruit, train, support, and retain teachers over the long term. On this Teachers' Day, the shift is visible across western China — in the confidence of young teachers returning out of conviction, and in students who see a future that includes their hometowns. Behind every rural teacher stands a robust national framework designed to reach every corner. The teacher gap that once seemed insurmountable is slowly and steadily being bridged. Liu Tianyi is program coordinator; and Zhao Yuchi is executive director at the UNESCO International Research and Training Center for Rural Education and associate research fellow at the China Institute of Education and Social Development, Beijing Normal University. body: CIFTIS 2026 - Chinadaily.com.cn The China Story at your Fingertips OPEN a1 a1 Introduction This year's CIFTIS will showcase the latest progress in financial technology, digital and smart healthcare, and energy conservation and environmental protection. Around 90 countries, regions and international organizations will stage exhibitions or events, while more than 1,800 companies will participate off-line. All 16 News Updates Highlights abound at China's trade in services fair By Song Yi Visitors explore the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) at Shougang Park in Beijing, on Sept 13, 2026. The 2026 CIFTIS concluded in Beijing on Sunday. [Photo/Xinhua] The 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) concluded in Beijing on Sept 13, reaching more than 1,200 deals, according to Xinhua News Agency last Sunday. The five-day event featured about 200 forums, meetings and business matchmaking and promotional activities, with more than 1,830 companies participating on site, and over 5,300 companies tuned in online. "Ninety countries, regions and international organizations set up exhibitions or held events at this year's CIFTIS, and a number of innovative technologies, products and services made their debut at the fair," Zhu Guangyao, an official from the Ministry of Commerce, told Xinhua News Agency. The event also featured the release of several reports, presentations on cutting-edge research and discussions on the latest trends in the services trade, helping promote international exchanges and cooperation, Zhu said. The fair produced fruitful outcomes across multiple sectors, with 103 companies and institutions unveiling 233 new products, technologies and other achievements, according to Lu Huiling, deputy head and spokesperson of the Beijing municipal commerce bureau. "Norwegian exhibitors, representing this year's guest country of honor, signed six cooperation agreements with Chinese companies and institutions," Lu said. The 2026 CIFTIS was held at Shougang Park in Beijing from Sept 9 to 13. CIFTIS boosts consensus on services cooperation People visit the booth of Peru at the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS), in Beijing, Sept 9, 2026. [Photo/Xinhua] BEIJING - The 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS), held in the Chinese capital of Beijing from Sept 9 to 13, has deepened consensus on strengthening cooperation in the services sector and injected strong momentum into the world economy. Fruitful outcomes were achieved during the five-day fair, which saw the holding of nearly 100 conferences and forums as well as over 100 matchmaking and promotion events, said Zhu Guangyao, an official with China's commerce ministry, at a news conference on the conclusion of the fair. Zhu said the successful event sent a clear signal to the world that China will unswervingly expand high-standard opening up and promote high-quality development. According to Lu Huiling, deputy head and spokesperson of the Beijing municipal commerce bureau, the 2026 CIFTIS has achieved more than 1,200 outcomes in seven categories, effectively promoting resource matching, exchanges and cooperation. As the guest country of honor, Norway signed six cooperation agreements with Chinese enterprises and institutions, she said. This year's fair gained rising popularity, drawing an increasing number of visitors to Shougang Park, the event's venue. As of Sunday noon, the core areas of CIFTIS had received nearly 420,000 visits, up 36.6 percent year on year, Lu said. Themed "Global Services, Shared Prosperity," the event saw more than 1,800 enterprises exhibit on site, including over 470 Fortune Global 500 companies and industry-leading enterprises. Exhibitions showcased new technologies, solutions, and achievements in services trade, including information and communication, fintech, digital and intelligent healthcare, smart education, energy conservation and environmental protection. According to Zhu, China will continue to deepen international cooperation in services trade, innovate cooperation models, expand cooperation areas, tap cooperation potential, align with the development strategies and cooperation initiatives of various countries, and use major exhibition platforms such as CIFTIS as a bridge to promote mutually beneficial cooperation among countries. "We welcome service enterprises from around the world to explore the Chinese market and share in the opportunities of China's super-large market," Zhu said. Trade in services, a key component of international trade, is playing an increasingly important role in driving global economic growth and industrial upgrading. According to guest speakers at the fair, services are becoming an increasingly integral part of global supply chains, supporting not only production but also design, management, logistics, and distribution. The CIFTIS, as one of the world's largest platforms for trade in services, embodies a vision of openness, cooperation and shared development, according to Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, who also serves as the current chairperson of the African Union. By bringing together governments, international organizations and investors, this fair provides a unique opportunity for exchange, sharing of experiences, and the creation of opportunities, he said. China's innovations at CIFTIS could be your 'best cure' By Xu Jiayi and Sun Chi How will AI, robots and innovative medicines, China's "new new three" innovations, reshape daily life? How does a helmet safeguard riders? How can tech make fuse beads art more fun? What hope can a new drug bring to patients? Let's see which of China's innovations is the best cure for you! CIFTIS showcases digital, green and cultural service innovations By Li Jiaying [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] Digital upgrades, low-carbon services and new approaches to cultural exports featured prominently among 67 service demonstration cases unveiled at the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services in Beijing on Friday. The release event at Shougang Park drew nearly 300 participants from 31 countries and international organizations. This year's cases cover six areas, ranging from service trade standardization and technology applications to green innovation, services consumption, cultural creativity and support for businesses expanding overseas. A major focus was the use of technology to solve operational problems. Selected projects apply artificial intelligence, automation and digital twins to logistics and shipping, while others support transport upgrades overseas and help Chinese railway suppliers reach international markets. An intelligent airport baggage transfer solution, presented at a related exchange event, offered one example of how technology is being applied to everyday service tasks. Other presentations covered data labeling standards and AI tools for small and medium-sized enterprises. Green and low-carbon services received a dedicated category for the first time, with nine cases selected. These included digitally supported recycling services and a platform that records and supports participation in carbon reduction. Cultural and creative services also gained their own category, with five cases selected. The projects also illustrate efforts to connect cultural outreach with commercial services, alongside closer integration of culture, tourism, sports and exhibitions. Among them was the overseas performance program of the Colorful Guizhou art troupe, which brings the southwestern province's music, dance and acrobatics to international audiences. An international matchmaking event that afternoon gave participants a closer look at how the services work. Representatives from six selected cases shared practices, including standardized labeling of spatiotemporal data, intelligent airport baggage transfer and AI services for small and medium-sized enterprises. body: China to enhance gig workers' welfare - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE China News Society Innovation HK/Macao Cross-Strait Cover Story Photo Environment Health Military Video Home / China / Society Home China Society China to enhance gig workers' welfare Push aims to expand facilities, protect rights and spur social governance role By WANG XIAOYU | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-10 09:38 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE China has intensified efforts to protect the rights and interests of couriers, ride-hailing drivers and other gig workers, while encouraging them to participate in social governance as part of broader efforts to advance socialist democracy, a senior official said on Wednesday. Official estimates show that China has about 200 million people in flexible employment, including 84 million engaged in new forms of employment, such as food delivery workers, couriers and ride-hailing drivers. The latter group accounts for 21 percent of the total workforce. "The size of these groups has been expanding rapidly in recent years, and they serve as vital links that sustain urban operations and meet the needs of the public," said Zhao Shitang, vice-minister of the Society Work Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, at a news conference held by the State Council Information Office. To safeguard their rights and interests, the country has guided and urged platform-based enterprises to implement standardized employment procedures in accordance with the law and protect new workers' rights to fair pay, time off, safe working conditions and social security, Zhao said. "In response to prominent issues that undermine their interests, for example, we have worked with other departments to carry out comprehensive governance of platform algorithms. We started with eight key platform-based enterprises last year and expanded the scope to a total of 25 companies this year," he said. As a result, problems such as unreasonable order assignment and opaque pricing rules have been effectively addressed, Zhao said. "Recently, some localities have introduced measures such as pausing the timing system when delivery riders are waiting at red lights, allowing them to work more calmly and safely," he added. Local authorities have also built facilities in communities and business districts to meet the working and personal needs of gig workers, including parking spaces, battery-charging facilities, meals and rest areas, Zhao said. "Some regions have set up designated service areas for truck drivers at highway rest stops or gas stations. Others have introduced rider apartments or provided skills training, giving new employment groups a sense of security in their living arrangements and a promising path for personal development," he said. Meanwhile, gig workers can play a role in social governance by collecting public opinions, identifying risks and hidden dangers, and assisting with emergency rescue efforts, thanks to their familiarity with grassroots communities, Zhao said. He cited a recent case in which a delivery rider jumped into the water alongside an auxiliary police officer to rescue four people trapped inside a car that had stalled in floodwaters in Huzhou, Zhejiang province. The rescue was captured in a short video that attracted widespread attention online. body: COSCO Shipping charts greener path for sustainable development - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE Business Macro Companies Industries Technology Motoring China Data Finance Top 10 Home / Business / Companies Home Business Companies COSCO Shipping charts greener path for sustainable development By Ren Qi | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-10 09:13 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE A drone photo taken on July 1, 2026 shows CSB Glory, a bulk carrier under COSCO Shipping, about to dock an ore terminal of the Tianjin Port in North China's Tianjin. [Photo/Xinhua] Integrating sustainable development and social responsibility deeply into top-level corporate strategies and the entire operational chain is essential for navigating the future of the global maritime industry, experts said. Over the past decade, COSCO Shipping has actively embraced its role as a key player in the global logistics network. Lin Ji, president of the company, highlighted its commitment to maintaining the security and stability of global supply chains. By advancing an integrated operational model encompassing shipping, ports and logistics, the group has served as a crucial stabilizer for international trade. Lin noted that the company has consistently supported the high-quality development of the Belt and Road Initiative while fostering technological and industrial innovation within the maritime sector. Lin made the remarks at the group's social responsibility results news conference in Beijing, where it officially launched its new corporate social responsibility brand: "Sailing Together". In the push for a low-carbon transition, the company has significantly expanded its green footprint. According to Lin, new energy-powered vessels accounted for 33 percent of the group's newly added capacity and vessel orders in 2025. Beyond fleet upgrades, the group has driven the electrification of major hub ports and spearheaded the development of a zero-carbon demonstration zone on Dongyu Island in Boao, Hainan province, providing a practical model for green development in tropical regions. Furthermore, the company has actively participated in the formulation of the International Maritime Organization's emission reduction rules, proposing Chinese solutions for key global maritime issues. On the social front, the group has prioritized employee welfare and cross-cultural exchanges. The company has established a comprehensive system for better protecting the rights, occupational health and career advancement of its global workforce, ensuring that employees share in the fruits of its high-quality development. Detailing the new reporting framework, Luo Bing, vice-president of the group, noted that the newly introduced "Sailing Together" brand reflects the company's commitment to collaborating with global partners and driving a sustainable future, aligning with the vision of building a community with a shared future for mankind. COSCO Shipping has also launched a comprehensive"1+N+M" sustainable development reporting system. Luo explained that the framework is designed to provide a transparent and systematic overview of the company's multi-dimensional practices. The "1" stands for the annual main sustainability report, which recently earned a five-star excellence rating from a national evaluation committee. The "N" represents specialized reports on targeted areas such as low-carbon initiatives, overseas social responsibilities, supply chain synergy and crew rights protection. Meanwhile, the "M" includes 33 independent sustainability reports published by 24 domestic and overseas tier-two subsidiaries in 2025, ensuring that responsible practices reach the grassroots level of operations. Expanding its philanthropic footprint, the COSCO Shipping Charity Foundation teamed up with the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda to launch the "Panda Captain, Guarding the Homeland" public welfare project. Hai Xia, chairman of the foundation, explained that the initiative will fund rewilding programs to help captive giant pandas learn survival skills and successfully integrate into wild populations. Additionally, the project will explore the psychological "healing power" of the animals, aiming to apply these therapeutic benefits in practical scenarios such as schools, workplaces and hospitals. Since its inception in 2005, the charity foundation has been recognized as a 4A-level social organization by the Ministry of Civil Affairs. Over the past two decades, it has donated more than 1.5 billion yuan ($223.65 million) and supported over 1,100 charitable projects, ranging from education and disaster relief to rural vitalization. Following the introduction, the panda research center presented a donation certificate to the foundation, marking the official rollout of the conservation plan. The health bureau said it acted on a public tip about an illegal operating theater in the city's Tianding Street area. Health and police officers arrived at the scene immediately, sealed off the premises and took six people into custody. The investigation is ongoing, the bureau said. In a separate case, health authorities in Wuhan, the capital of neighboring Hubei province, said on Tuesday that eight people had been detained in connection with an illegal assisted reproduction laboratory discovered in the city's Wuhu Street area following online reports. China maintains strict oversight of institutions that provide fertility treatments, including in vitro fertilization and egg-freezing technologies. Only certified medical institutions are permitted to perform such procedures, while all forms of commercial surrogacy are prohibited. According to data from the National Health Commission, China currently has 645 medical facilities licensed to provide fertility treatment services, with clinical success rates reaching internationally advanced levels. body: CORPORATE WINDOW : Rethinking Pakistan’s food plate Manan Aslam Published December 15, 2025 Email Your Name * Recipient Email * Cancel 0 Listen to article 1x 1.2x 1.5x comments Join our Whatsapp Channel Add Dawn as a trusted source Food in Pakistan is usually discussed in cultural or emotional terms. What people eat is linked to habit, tradition, and affordability, while the deeper economic forces shaping these choices remain largely unseen. Yet, food is also an outcome of markets, policies, and corporate decisions. Viewed through a corporate window, Pakistan’s food plate reflects decades of incentive structures, subsidy regimes, and investment patterns that have quietly shaped both production and consumption. Understanding this perspective is essential if food awareness is to be raised without moralising, preaching, or medicalising everyday choices. At the centre of Pakistan’s food economy lies wheat. Its dominance is often justified through tradition and necessity, but its true strength comes from policy design. Government procurement, minimum support prices, and subsidised flour distribution have institutionalised wheat as the most reliable and affordable staple. These interventions were critical in addressing food insecurity during periods of shortage. Over time, however, they have also created a narrow consumption base. When one crop is consistently protected, markets respond predictably: farmers allocate land to wheat, processors invest in wheat-based products, and retailers prioritise wheat-derived foods. Dietary uniformity, in this sense, is not a cultural inevitability but an economic outcome. From a corporate window, this concentration represents both risk and inefficiency. Climate variability, groundwater depletion, declining soil fertility, and rising input costs increasingly threaten wheat productivity. Yet, the policy response has largely been to preserve existing arrangements rather than diversify the food base. Gradual adjustments such as reducing procurement bias, supporting pulse cultivation, and investing in vegetable logistics can crowd in private capital and encourage innovation An economy that relies too heavily on a single staple exposes itself to supply shocks and fiscal pressure. Diversification, therefore, is not a lifestyle argument; it is a risk-management strategy for both the state and the private sector. Balanced diets that include boiled rice, lentils, vegetables, and simpler, non-spicy food preparations are often framed as matters of personal discipline. This framing misses the economic reality. Consumers behave rationally. They choose foods that are affordable, accessible, and convenient. Wheat dominates because it satisfies all three conditions. Shifting consumption patterns requires changing price signals, availability, and product formats, not assigning responsibility to households. Rice offers a clear illustration of missed opportunity. Pakistan is one of the world’s leading rice exporters, yet, domestic consumption remains underdeveloped in value-added forms. Most rice innovation is directed outward rather than inward; this represents untapped potential. Parboiled, packaged, and ready-to-cook rice products can serve urban households seeking convenience while strengthening domestic agro-processing. Encouraging rice-based diversification does not threaten wheat security; it broadens consumer choice and deepens value chains. Lentils and pulses reveal an even sharper structural gap. Despite suitable agro-ecological conditions, Pakistan imports a substantial portion of its pulse consumption. This dependence reflects weak seed systems, limited extension support, and insufficient processing infrastructure rather than consumer resistance. From an entrepreneurial perspective, pulses offer a relatively low-risk entry point. Investments in cleaning, grading, packaging, and branding can transform pulses from bulk commodities into competitive retail products, reducing import dependence while expanding dietary options. Vegetables further expose inefficiencies in Pakistan’s food economy. High post-harvest losses, inadequate cold-chain infrastructure, and fragmented wholesale markets raise costs and suppress supply. These inefficiencies eventually appear on the consumer’s plate as volatile prices and inconsistent quality. Public conversations around food habits often drift toward prescription. People are told what they should eat and how they should cook. This approach overlooks how deeply consumption patterns are embedded in economic architecture. Subsidies, procurement priorities, and regulatory frameworks quietly shape everyday decisions. When these structures reward uniformity, diversity becomes economically irrational for producers and consumers alike. Large food companies influence sourcing decisions, product formulation, marketing narratives, and shelf space. That said, expanding portfolios to include lentil-based products, vegetable mixes, and low-spice meal options is not merely a social gesture. It is a strategic response to changing urban demographics, rising female workforce participation, and time-constrained households. Firms that adapt early are likely to capture emerging demand rather than chase it later. Entrepreneurship amplifies this shift. At present, youth-led startups are experimenting with cloud kitchens, food delivery platforms, and agri-tech services. Integrating balanced food options into these models strengthens commercial viability while broadening consumer choice. Simplified cooking formats, regional ingredients, and plant-based options allow innovation without disrupting cultural preferences. These ventures represent early signals of a diversifying food economy. The role of the state remains central, but reform need not be abrupt. Diversification does not imply abandoning wheat or undermining food security. It requires recalibrating incentives to avoid over-concentration. Gradual adjustments such as reducing procurement bias, supporting pulse cultivation, and investing in vegetable logistics can crowd in private capital and encourage innovation. When policy signals reward diversity, markets respond with investment and experimentation. Importantly, food awareness can be raised without moral judgment. Linking wheat-heavy diets to subsidies, price controls, and market failures re-frames the discussion away from individual choice and toward systemic design. Advocating balanced diets through economic logic respects consumer autonomy while highlighting inefficiencies that constrain choice. This approach aligns with the tone of informed public debate rather than prescriptive guidance. Pakistan’s food plate is less a reflection of taste and more a product of incentives. What people eat is shaped by what markets make available, affordable, and convenient. Aligning these factors with diversification goals can gradually reshape consumption without coercion. A diversified food system also carries macroeconomic benefits. Reduced import dependence for pulses, expanded domestic value addition in rice, and lower post-harvest losses in vegetables strengthen trade balances and rural incomes. For agribusinesses, diversification opens new revenue streams and reduces exposure to single-crop volatility. For consumers, it expands choice without increasing cost. Ultimately, rethinking Pakistan’s food plate requires rethinking the markets behind it. From a corporate window, food is not simply nourishment; it is an ecosystem of policies, businesses, and consumers interacting daily. Raising awareness without preaching, advocating balance without prejudice, and encouraging entrepreneurship without disruption offers a pragmatic path forward. A more diversified, resilient food system is not an abstract ideal. It is an economic necessity, built one incentive, one investment, and one choice at a time. The writer is affiliated with the School of Management, Jiangsu University, P.R. China, and the Department of Agribusiness and E
title: Rethinking Pakistan’s food plate

body: Local You can’t have an authentic Arabic meal without these two dips on your table Humus and Mutabal are the perfect additions to make appetisers, breakfast and snacks healthier and tastier! Fawzia Nisar 09 Mar, 2026 Mezze or appetisers are part of the way of life of the Arab world. They are served as snacks, at the beginning of a meal, or as a meal in itself. Probably the best known mezze in the world are the bread dips, Humus bi Tahina and Baba Ghanooj , and the Egyptian bean dish of Ful Medames . These traditional dips are a must on any mezze table and are now well known in Europe, America and other parts of the world. This is mainly due to the fact that its marvellous aroma blends well with most meat dishes especially kebabs. It is in fact the pride of Arabic cuisine. Humus bi Tahina Ingredients: 2 cups chickpeas 1 cup Tahina sauce (A nutty flavoured paste made of toasted crushed sesame seeds.) 1 clove of garlic, crushed juice of 2 to 3 lemons salt chilli powder olive oil 2 tablespoons chopped parsley (for garnishing) Method: Bring the chickpeas to boil until they are tender. Leaving a few grains for the garnish, liquidise the rest until a thick paste is formed. Empty this paste into a large bowl and add the crushed garlic and Tahina sauce and mix it together. If the paste thickens, add some water and keep mixing. After adding the salt and lemon juice, place the paste on a dish. Sprinkle some chilli powder on the paste, and garnish it with chopped parsley, wholes chickpeas and olive oil. Serve it with pita bread ( Khubuz ), naan , or bread. Mutabal or Baba Ghanooj This Syrian-Lebanese speciality is another must for the Mezze table, it is a dip similar in principle to Humus bi Tahina , but eggplant is used in this dish instead of chickpeas. It is also eaten with bread. Ingredients: 2 large eggplants ( baingan ) 2 cloves of garlic, crushed juice of 2-3 lemons 2-3 tablespoons Tahina sauce 2 tablespoons yogurt salt olive oil 2 tablespoons chopped parsley (for garnishing) Method: Make two slits in each eggplant and cook them over charcoal, or in a hot oven, until the skin is black and the flesh feels soft when poked with a finger. Peel off the skin and mash the flesh with a fork. Put it in a large bowl, add garlic, Tahina sauce, yogurt, lemon and salt, and mix well. Spoon the mixture onto a plate and garnish with chopped parsley and olive oil. This recipe was originally published in Dawn’s Tuesday Review on December 1, 1992.
title: You can’t have an authentic Arabic meal without these two dips on your table

body: Fewer beggars, better lives: A story of China's progress - Opinion - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE Opinion Cartoons Editorials Global Lens We Comment Columnists Global Views Chinese Perspectives Opinion Line Home Opinion / Kang Bing Home / Opinion / Kang Bing Fewer beggars, better lives: A story of China's progress By Kang Bing | China Daily | Updated: 2026-09-08 09:41 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE A farmer harvests at a wheat field at Yantang village of Kaiyang county in Guiyang, Southwest China's Guizhou province, May 31, 2023. [Photo/Xinhua] More than 82 million foreign-entry trips were recorded in China last year. While sharing their travel experience, many of them said they were impressed by the country's good public security situation, modern infrastructure, low costs and the many free public toilets. Some said they were surprised at not having seen a single beggar during their stay in China. Happy as I am at hearing these words about my country, I have to point out that begging still exists in China — I do see a few beggars now and then while traveling. A more accurate description would be to say that begging has reduced drastically in China. I still recall a dozen or so beggars, broken bowls in hand, knocking on our door during my childhood, begging for a piece of steamed bun. Frequent natural disasters such as droughts and floods in the area left millions of farmers and their families hungry. Begging became their last means of survival. But the number of beggars has dramatically gone down, thanks to agricultural reforms China undertook nearly five decades ago. Encouraging farmers to toil on their own plots, instead of working collectively for the people's communes, helped improve productivity, enabling farmers to harvest more and store for a rainy day. Tens of thousands of beggars could be seen on the streets even at the turn of the century. Some were people who had run into difficulties while many others, as was revealed in investigative reports, were lazybones who found begging an easier way to make money than toiling. There were also many organized gangs forcing children, women and people with disabilities to beg for them. Some gangsters reportedly turned millionaires by just running such organized begging gangs. Following decades of government efforts to contain organized crime and tackle the begging problem, such activities have largely disappeared. Sociologists here attribute the disappearance to the following reasons: better living conditions in rural areas, wider social welfare coverage, a more effective social assistance system and the disappearance of cash in society. At the end of 2020, China had successfully eliminated absolute poverty in its rural areas. Last year, the per capita disposable income in the rural areas stood at 24,456 yuan ($3,644.4). Though the number remains low, it is enough to ensure rural residents have houses to live in and food to eat. When such basic living conditions are met, one has no excuse to go and beg. The introduction of social welfare measures such as insurance came as a big plus to improving the quality of life in rural areas. Those aged above 60 can now expect to receive a few hundred yuan in pension every month. When ill, more than half of the medical bills can be covered under the New Cooperative Medical Scheme, a voluntary insurance program introduced in 2003 for rural residents. Kids can be sent to schools for nine years of free compulsory education and, quite often, provided free lunch. Those who can no longer work because they have disabilities or some mental health issues, and have no relatives to care for them, are sent to the local nursing homes to spend the rest of their lives. Statistics show there are 16,000 such homes with 1.68 million beds in rural China. If the vulnerable people prefer to stay near their villages, there are more than 140,000 mutual-aid elderly care service facilities serving them. The few who still want to try their luck will soon find they can hardly get any alms because citizens nowadays no longer carry cash. However, there are some smart beggars who have already printed their QR code, which they carry along with them, but not all compassionate donors would want to scan it in this era of telecom fraud. The dip in the number of beggars is the result of China's strong governance as well as a natural consequence of work done by the country for disadvantaged groups. In images circulating on social media, a fluffy cat rests on top of a giant green wax gourd, draping its paws over the smooth surface as if embracing a "natural air conditioner". The contrast between the drowsy furball and the colossal vegetable has captivated internet users. "Even cats have found their perfect summer companion," one online fan joked. The trend has renewed interest in the wax gourd, an everyday vegetable familiar to Chinese households. In Foshan, Guangdong province, however, it is anything but an internet novelty. For generations, it has anchored the local summer diet and embodied the Lingnan tradition of eating with the seasons. Known for its high water content, mild flavor and refreshing texture, the wax gourd is a popular summer staple across southern China. In Guangdong's sweltering climate, families turn to it for light soups that offer respite from the heat. Farmers harvest wax gourds in a field in Shijiazhuang, Hebei province, on July 7. [Photo provided to China Daily] For 65-year-old farmer Ou Yingqiu in Foshan's Sanshui district, growing wax gourds is more than a livelihood; it's a lifelong bond with the soil. "My family has been growing wax gourds for decades," Ou said. This year, Ou and his wife planted about 65 percent of a hectare. Sown around Spring Festival, the crop is shielded by plastic sheeting during cold snaps. Ready for harvest in roughly 90 days, Sanshui's main season stretches from mid-May to early August. Harvesting the crop is backbreaking work. Mature gourds must be cut and lugged from the fields, prompting Ou to hire extra hands. Sanshui black-skinned wax gourd, a national geographical indication product, is prized for its jet-black, glossy rind, firm flesh and exceptional shelf life. While a typical gourd weighs 15 to 20 kilograms, Ou's heaviest tipped the scales at around 35 kg. Ou credits Sanshui's sandy, fertile soil for the gourds' dense texture. While rainfall and temperature dictate growth and sales, excessive downpours can curb harvests, even as soaring temperatures boost demand. The gourd's hardiness has long made it a pantry essential. An intact specimen can be stored for months in a dry, ventilated place — potentially until year-end. Once cut, however, leftovers must be chilled and eaten promptly. Today, Sanshui wax gourds command shelves in Foshan, Guangzhou and other cities. Some are exported via cold chain to overseas markets, including the United States and Singapore. For local residents, the typical way to enjoy the gourd remains a simple bowl of soup. "We usually make wax gourd soup," Ou said. At home, he combines gourd and pork to create a light, naturally sweet broth. The method is simple: Simmer the gourd first, add the pork once the water boils, and cook for about 10 minutes. "Every meal is prepared fresh. If left overnight, the flavor changes," he said. The dish has accompanied Ou since childhood. His family once grew wax gourds primarily for household consumption, only venturing into commercial sales after China's reform and opening-up. Across Guangdong, it is also braised with pork ribs or dried scallops. Another classic summer dish combines it with duck and coix seeds. These recipes epitomize the Cantonese preference for fresh ingredients and delicate, balanced flavors. They also illustrate the Lingnan practice of eating with the seasons. Wax gourds arrive on market stalls as temperatures peak, making them a natural staple — not for rarity or luxury, but because they suit the local climate and lifestyle. But growing the crop remains challenging. Ou said that fewer young people are taking up farming, while many current growers are well into their 50s or beyond. Perhaps this online trend will inspire a new generation to rediscover the value of these humble giants. In this special joint episode of the World Economic Forum and CGTN, hosts Robin Pomeroy from the World Economic Forum and CGTN anchor Guan Xin sit down with Professor Arun Sundararajan of New York University's Stern School of Business, a member of the WEF AI Governance Alliance and author of The Sharing Economy. They dive into the most pressing questions surrounding artificial intelligence. From the future of employment to the deepening divide over AI governance and technological sovereignty, this conversation brings together perspectives from the US, China, and the global stage on how AI is reshaping economies, societies and geopolitics. We invite Dr. Chang Zhigang, director of Critical Care Medicine at Beijing Hospital; Roberta Lipson, founder of United Family Healthcare; Dr. David Furman, professor and director of the AI and Bioinformatics Platform at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging; and Dr. Sean Xiao Leng, professor of Medicine, Molecular Microbiology and Immunology, and Health Policy and Management at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. body: Who runs China? Portraits of the deputies to the 13th NPC. Public security Conflict Corruption and bribery Smuggling Supervision Crime The people Work-related crime Legitimate rights and interests Impartial law enforcement Public security Conflict Maritime affairs Legitimate rights and interests Criminal Legal person Judicial justice Reform Supervision Intellectual property rights Number of NPC Deputies 2,975 Each of the 2,975 deputies is tasked with voicing the interests and concerns of millions of people in one's region. Hover over each dot to learn more about a deputy. China's Two Sessions is one of the country's most important political events. Each year in March, thousands of representatives gather in Beijing to propose and announce policies that will shape the country's development. During the event, the National People's Congress (NPC) convened its deputies representing the interests of their communities throughout the country. As China's top legislature and highest organ of state power, the NPC gathers about 3,000 deputies to discuss national affairs. But who are they? What are their educational backgrounds? What ethnic groups do they belong to? This year, exactly 2,975 deputies attended the second session of the 13th NPC. Generally, each congress is elected for a term of five years, and a session is held each year. Each dot represents one deputy. Number of NPC Deputies 2,975 Proportion of female deputies increased Male 2,233 Female 742 Among the 2,975 deputies to the 13th NPC, there are 2,233 males and 742 females . We see more women are being represented. At this session, female deputies account for 24.94 percent of the total, up from 20.2 percent during the 10th NPC (2003-2008). The female deputy's proportion since 2003 Post-60s: Backbone of NPC Post-90s: More women than men In terms of age, over half of the deputies were born in the 1960s, bringing the congress's average age to 53.77 years. Among others, 1,672 deputies were born in the 1960s , taking up over a half of the total. They are the backbone of China's top legislature. Meanwhile, the younger the deputies, the more balanced the gender ratio. The most well-represented ethnic group: Tatar The gathering also draws deputies from all of China's 56 ethnicities . The largest group of deputies comes from the Han nationality, making up 85 percent of the attendees. This is close to the roughly 92 percent of Han Chinese in the general population. The second largest group in raw numbers comes from the Hui nationality with 62 deputies. The ethnicities of the deputies can also be grouped based on how well represented they are compared with the general population. As such, the Tatar people are the most represented, with one deputy for every 3,600 members from the ethnic group within China. The Lahu is the least represented with one for every 500,000, and the Han comes second with one for every 480,000. Nine in 10 deputies hold a bachelor's degree or above The educational backgrounds of the deputies reflect the country's standards for its government. Out of the 2,198 deputies that we have educational data for, 88.5 percent of them have a bachelor's degree or higher. Those with a master's degree made up the largest group (836) , while PhDs come second (584). For those with degrees higher than a bachelor, about 64 percent (911) were born in the 1960s . For those born in the 1980s , only one in 10 had a master's degree or PhD. Liberal arts grads outnumber science grads Most popular major is management science Liberal arts grads outnumber science grads, most popular major is management science What did university grads study? When looking at the highest degrees attained for the 1,777 deputies that we have data for, about 66 percent (1,165) majored in the liberal arts , almost twice the number of science majors (612). Specifically, one fifth of them studied management science , followed by engineering, economics, law and science. Moreover, 122 deputies received overseas education . Out of the total 2,975 deputies from 35 delegations, 2,172 are members of the Communist Party of China (CPC), 423 have no party affiliation, and 380 are from non-CPC parties. Reports are often dry, but official Chinese reports can provide a glimpse into what policies and direction the country places importance on. Premier Li Keqiang delivered the 2019 government work report to deputies at the opening of this year's NPC. We took a look at the keywords that stood out and how they fit into the country's past and future. Since 1954, the 51 released government reports had a total of 977,643 words, with the 1955 report being the longest at 51,623. "Development" continues to top the word count in those reports with 5,410 mentions, while "construction," "economy" and "reform" trail right behind. Since 1954, we see that the country's priorities for development have changed. Also, attention to the quality of economic growth has increased since 2014, with greater mentions of "development models and problems." The word count for a report tends to spike whenever there is a change in NPC deputies or a five-year plan begins. Since 2005, the government work report has used quantitative indicators such as GDP, CPI, urban job creation and others to highlight the country's development. We can also look at development trends in China's legal and judicial apparatuses by analyzing work reports of the Supreme People's Court (SPC) and the Supreme People's Procuratorate (SPP). They are the country's highest court and highest prosecutorial organ, respectively. The reports, delivered to NPC deputies during the Two Sessions, show the growing emphasis on the rule of law since they were first released in 1980. "Rule of law" first became a key phrase in both work reports in 2001. It has remained a central focus of the reports ever since. People's Courts The latest SPC work report shows that in 2018, the country's highest court handled nearly 34,794 cases, among which 31,883 were concluded, up 22.1 percent and 23.5 percent year on year, respectively. Local courts handled 28 million cases and concluded 25.168 million cases, up by 8.8 percent and 10.6 percent from the year before, respectively. It also notes that Chinese courts concluded 28,000 graft cases involving embezzlement, bribery and dereliction of duty last year. Among the 33,000 people involved were 18 former officials at the provincial level or above. People's Procuratorates The 2019 SPP report states that in 2018, procuratorial organs in the country approved the arrest of 1,056,616 criminal suspects and prosecuted 1,692,846 criminal suspects, down 2.3 percent and 0.8 percent year on year, respectively. The report notes that violations against environmental preservation, property rights, minors and martyrs protection were severely punished in 2018. Over the past 40 years, both reports have seen an increase in terms related to civil society, and a drop in phrases like "cracking down on criminal activities." Meanwhile, terms related to economic development, judicial justice and safeguarding people's rights and interests have appeared more often. From this, we see that China's legal and judicial systems are becoming more preoccupied with the well-being of ordinary citizens. Reference Information on the NPC deputies comes from npc.gov.cn. Information concerning the highest academic credentials, majors, and overseas education experience is gathered from open sources on the Internet. Classification of academic disciplines is based on the Discipline Catalogue of Degree Awarding and Talent Training approved by the Chinese Ministry of Education. Other statistics are translated from reports by the Xinhua News Agency and other media outlets. Note The NPC deputies are grouped according to Chinese surname.
