body: Xinhua Headlines: Southern Europe shows renewed economic resilience amid eurozone slowdown-Xinhua Xinhua Headlines: Southern Europe shows renewed economic resilience amid eurozone slowdown Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-14 18:00:16 A Geely E2 electric vehicle is displayed along Madrid's Gran Via during a launch event in Madrid, Spain, on Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo by Zhang Yuheng/Xinhua) * Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece, all deeply affected by Europe's sovereign debt crisis over a decade ago, have shown renewed vitality and resilience in recent years. * Southern Europe's service-heavy economies and growing use of renewable energy had made them less vulnerable to some of the energy and trade shocks weighing on Europe's industrial core. * The IMF's 2025 Regional Economic Outlook urged Europe to accelerate structural reforms while keeping trade open. Southern European countries have sought to combine the two, building on post-crisis reforms and existing industrial strengths while pursuing trade and investment ties with emerging economies. * China has played a constructive role in this process through trade, investment and industrial partnerships. MADRID, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- As the eurozone faces a subdued growth outlook, a different economic picture has emerged along its southern flank: Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece, all deeply affected by Europe's sovereign debt crisis over a decade ago, have shown renewed vitality and resilience in recent years. In the second quarter of 2026, seasonally adjusted GDP in the euro area increased by 1.0 percent year-on-year. In contrast, Spain, Portugal and Greece recorded growth of 2.7 percent, 2.5 percent and 1.9 percent, respectively, while Italy matched the eurozone rate. A report published in June by Allianz, an insurance company, described Southern Europe's post-2021 performance as "a clear shift in the geography of Eurozone growth, with Southern economies moving from chronic underperformance to cyclical leadership." Analysts and market observers attribute this resilience to three overlapping shifts: a broader mix of growth drivers, financial and institutional repair reinforced by EU investment, and a pragmatic openness to external markets, capital and technology, including expanding industrial partnerships with China. Together, these factors have helped Southern Europe withstand some of the pressures weighing on the eurozone's traditional industrial core. SHOCKS SHIFTED SIDES Recent shocks -- from supply-chain disruptions to energy-price spikes and trade tensions -- have not fallen evenly across the eurozone. "In the current cycle, the asymmetry of external shocks has, so to speak, shifted sides," Pablo Sanz, a professor at Spain's National University of Distance Education, said in an interview with Xinhua. Sanz said Southern Europe's service-heavy economies and growing use of renewable energy had made them less vulnerable to some of the energy and trade shocks weighing on Europe's industrial core. The difference is also visible in the drivers of growth. In the second quarter of 2026, Spain's economy ministry said growth was supported by domestic demand, investment and industry, while Portugal's rebound was driven mainly by net external demand. Investment, construction and services have supported Italy in recent years, while investment, consumption and net exports all contributed to Greece's growth in 2025. Tourism also remains an important source of activity, employment and services exports, particularly in Spain, Portugal and Greece. A changing energy mix has provided another buffer. Eurostat data showed that over 60 percent of gross electricity consumption in Portugal, Greece and Spain came from renewable sources in 2025. The European Commission said growing renewable generation had lowered wholesale electricity prices, with gas influencing prices in only a minority of market hours in the Iberian Peninsula. Labor supply has provided further support, particularly in Spain. According to Sanz, labor-market reforms that reduced excessive reliance on temporary contracts helped stabilize household incomes, while immigration expanded the workforce and supported employment and domestic demand. Public investment has added another leg to the recovery. Allianz estimates that Italy, Spain, Portugal and Greece together account for almost 60 percent of funding under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the centerpiece of NextGenerationEU. "Public capital injected through NextGenerationEU funds has therefore served as a countercyclical firewall, financing green-transition infrastructure, digitalization and key industrial projects without placing excessive strain on national finances," Sanz said. An employee works by the batteries of the energy storage system on the island of Tilos, Greece, May 9, 2022. (Photo by Marios Lolos/Xinhua) REFORM DIVIDENDS The recent divergence also reflects differences in the timing of adjustment. The sovereign debt crisis forced Southern Europe to confront long-standing financial and structural imbalances. The process varied across countries. Greece and Portugal entered broad assistance programs covering fiscal consolidation, bank repair, pension reform, and changes to labor and product markets. Spain received assistance focused on its banking sector, while Italy remained outside a bailout program and followed a more gradual course. The adjustment carried a high economic and social cost, as domestic demand contracted and unemployment surged. Over time, however, banks reduced non-performing loans, households and businesses cut debt, and labor- and product-market rules were revised. Spain and Portugal also broke with a pattern of running external deficits during periods of expansion and began regularly recording current-account surpluses. A 2026 study by the National Bank of Belgium found that Spain, Portugal and Greece grew at an average annual rate of 1.7 percent between 2019 and 2025, compared with 0.6 percent for Germany, France, the Netherlands and Belgium. It linked their stronger performance partly to post-crisis reforms and fiscal consolidation. Greece shows how the repair extended to the functioning of public institutions. According to the IMF, measures targeting tax evasion and informality helped narrow its value-added tax compliance gap from 24 percent in 2019 to about 9 percent in 2024. Reforms have also covered the judiciary, business regulation and tax administration, although weak productivity and judicial delays remain constraints. After the pandemic, EU conditionality took a different form. Rather than focusing primarily on correcting imbalances, RRF funding was tied to national recovery and resilience plans combining investment projects with reform commitments, with at least 37 percent of the budget allocated to climate and biodiversity and a further minimum of 20 percent to digital measures. The plans have directed funding toward renewable energy, power grids, sustainable transport, industrial decarbonization and digitalization. According to Sanz, Spain and Portugal have used EU funding for electric-vehicle value chains, industrial decarbonization and the digitalization of public administrations and small businesses, while Italy has coupled investment with reforms of public administration, the justice system and public procurement. However, these gains should not be overstated. Sanz cautioned that, except in some technological and renewable-energy niches, Southern Europe's productivity gap with Northern Europe remained substantial. An analysis published by the Jacques Delors Institute noted that the four countries entered the pandemic on different growth trajectories and have deployed RRF funds at different speeds. Although the facility has supported demand and investment, the analysis said, its lasting impact will depend on whether the projects and reforms raise productivity and potential growth. body: In Yan'an, visitors see how CPC turns history into progress-Xinhua In Yan'an, visitors see how CPC turns history into progress Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-14 16:06:15 Actors perform a revolutionary-themed immersive drama in Yan'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, on July 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Yibo) YAN'AN, Shaanxi, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- When Ivan Racan was still a boy, not yet 10 years old, his father returned to Croatia from China in 1981, carrying with him a sanxian -- a traditional three-stringed Chinese instrument. The instrument hung on the wall of his childhood room, bringing a piece of distant China into his everyday life. More than 40 years later, Racan came across a similar instrument at a museum in Shanghai. He was struck by the realization that while the sanxian had remained much the same, China itself had transformed dramatically. For Racan, a member of the Croatian Parliament and son of former Croatian Prime Minister Ivica Racan, the instrument connects two periods of China's modern history. His father had visited China as an official of the former Yugoslavia. When he returned, he brought back stories that captured the early days of a transformation, one that would go on to reshape the country over the decades to come, Racan said. Decades later, Racan visited China himself and made a point to travel to Yan'an, which was once a center of the Chinese revolution. During his journey through the city in northwest China's Shaanxi Province, he encountered a modern country that would have been difficult to imagine in 1981. On Sept. 10, more than 200 representatives from over 50 countries attended a thematic briefing in Yan'an. Through stories of rural development, ecological conservation, industrial upgrading and cultural heritage protection, the event demonstrated how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has translated long-term goals into changes that reach communities and ordinary families. "This is something that has to be commended, appreciated, studied," Racan told Xinhua. Actors perform a revolutionary-themed play at a scenic spot in Yan'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, on July 28, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Yibo) For Petre Danci, a parliamentary advisor at the Office of the Secretary of the Romanian Senate and secretary of the Romania-China Friendship Group within the Alliance for the Union of Romanians, China's transformation is not an inherited memory. It is part of his own life. Danci, who speaks fluent Mandarin, arrived in Beijing in 2011. He studied Chinese at the Capital University of Economics and Business before completing bachelor's and master's degrees. During seven years of study and life in Beijing, he experienced China through lectures, friendships and the everyday norms of student life. "Every single time I come to China, I see a lot of development," he said. "Even if I go to a very familiar city, like Beijing, or Shanghai, or some other big cities, I still see the improvement." His latest journey to Yan'an brought him face to face with an earlier chapter of China's history. Danci learned about the period when Yan'an served as a center of the Chinese revolution and said he could still feel the Yan'an spirit in China today. That connection became clearer when he heard about the development of Liangjiahe Village, the technological upgrading of traditional industries and the restoration of environmentally fragile land through years of afforestation. "It takes function, leadership and organization," Danci told Xinhua. He believed China's experience in agriculture, ecological restoration and industrial modernization could offer useful references for Romania. Such experience should not be copied mechanically, he said, but adapted to local conditions through exchanges among people, businesses and governments. Having studied the Chinese language and experienced the country as a student, Danci said he hoped to help strengthen communication between Romania and China. A fruit farmer bags apples in Nangou Village of the city of Yan'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, June 13, 2024. (Xinhua/Liang Aiping) The connection between Yan'an's revolutionary history and China's present-day development was expressed most directly by Leevameng Leebouapao, deputy director general of the Land Department at the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment of Laos. During a visit to Nangou Village in Yan'an, he saw how poverty alleviation, public infrastructure and improvements to the rural environment had changed people's lives. "Socialism creates conditions for equality," he said. "People have equal access to education, healthcare, transport and other public services. China has demonstrated this in practice." What impressed him was that development had not been limited to major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai. Roads, communications networks and public services had also reached rural communities. In Nangou Village, he said, the practical work of the CPC and the government had made life more convenient for villagers and significantly improved their living environment. He added that China's experience in poverty alleviation and improving people's livelihoods deserved to be studied by other developing countries, including Laos. Beneath Pagoda Hill in Yan'an, visitors did not simply listen to stories about the CPC's past, but also to how the spirit formed in Yan'an continues to shape China's development today. ■ You may like World's first museum devoted to prehistoric flying reptiles opens in NW China's Xinjiang Two teachers devote their lives to a remote mountain village Chinese dance drama "A Dream of Red Mansions" makes U.S. debut in New York A glimpse of Yinxu Museum in Anyang, China's Henan EcoChina | A scenic drive into Hainan's rainforest InPics | Shougang Park reinvents itself as vibrant urban destination More from GLOBALink BRICS cooperation: Shared prosperity for half of world's population What BRICS family saw at CIFIT: markets, investment and new partnerships How AI is reshaping everyday services at CIFTIS

body: Rooftop terraces lift Beijing urban renewal to new heights-Xinhua Rooftop terraces lift Beijing urban renewal to new heights Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-14 16:03:15 People look out of the windows of a coffee shop near Shichahai Lake in central Beijing, capital of China, June 10, 2023. (Xinhua/Chen Zhonghao) BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- "If you think you've seen Beijing, you haven't been here yet," Elizaveta, a Russian woman who has lived in China for seven years, wrote on her social media account. The "here" she refers to is a rooftop terrace atop a commercial building on the site of the original Longfu Temple, a 15th-century Buddhist landmark. Now part of a vibrant cultural hub, the terrace offers one of Beijing's most compelling vantage points, where history and modernity meet beneath the skyline. To the east, Beijing's glass-and-steel skyline rises against the horizon. To the west lies the older city, with the glazed roofs of the Palace Museum glistening, the forested slopes of Jingshan Hill stretching and the white pagoda of Beihai Park standing gracefully in the distance. "For a moment," Elizaveta wrote, "I really feel like I'm standing at the edge of two eras." The terrace reflects a broader citywide shift. Earlier this year, Beijing issued a plan for high-quality urban development, vowing to make better use of historic streets and industrial heritage, upgrade key commercial districts, and create new consumption scenarios. The initiative is part of a national drive to turn 1,500 old neighborhoods and industrial districts into new engines of consumption and culture by 2030. Subject to building height limits, Beijing's central areas preserve a low skyline defined by iconic imperial red walls, yellow-tiled roofs and traditional alleys, where residents still live amid dense greenery. These open vistas offer visitors ample opportunities to appreciate the city's distinctive architectural heritage. Amid urban renewal efforts, Beijing's Dongcheng district, home to many of the capital's most treasured historic sites and blocks of siheyuan, or quadrangle courtyards, launched in 2025 a "Breeze Terrace" initiative to turn idle rooftops into public gathering spaces. Government, residents and merchants have worked together to bring in viewing decks, reading corners, dining spaces and craft workshops. According to planners, the idea is to let people see the city from a different angle without major demolition or construction. Since its launch, the initiative has drawn more than 1 million visits. This summer, it added about 300 terraces across the district, linked by four themed routes covering Central Axis vistas, hutong discoveries, literary corners and night tours. Chen Shiqi, an influencer who scouts shops and restaurants for his followers, called terraces "one of the surest ways to go viral" on Chinese social media. Comparing his own posts on Xiaohongshu, a popular Chinese lifestyle-sharing app, he found that using terrace photos as cover images consistently draws more readers. Over the past year, about 30 to 40 percent of the spots Chen has reviewed have been rooftop venues. Sometimes when he doesn't name the location, followers message him privately to ask where it is. Chen's observation points to a broader trend of the social media era. Visitors no longer simply experience a view. They photograph and share it, and rooftop terraces, with their sweeping backdrops and curated aesthetics, serve that purpose perfectly. Yet all of this would be unthinkable without the blue skies above. Beijing's anti-pollution campaign, launched in 2013, has cut the annual average of PM2.5, the fine particles linked to respiratory disease, from 89.5 micrograms per cubic meter to 27 last year, a sharp drop of nearly 70 percent. "Beijing blue," once a novelty worth a social media post, has become the background of daily life. In addition, Beijing's temperate climate and relatively low rainfall provide more clear-sky days for rooftop outings than many other major Chinese cities -- Shanghai included -- giving the city a natural edge for its growing terrace economy. On a rooftop garden of the Jinbao Place shopping mall, visitors can join sunset yoga, pick herbs, attend moonlit cocktail parties, try on Hanfu, or even hold a wedding. The once-forgotten space has become a vibrant consumer destination. "Rooftop terraces, as a key setting for urban renewal, hold great potential to nurture new consumption, improve public spaces and revitalize the old city's cultural heritage," said Xing Yan, deputy chief planner at the Beijing Tsinghua Tongheng urban planning and design institute. The next step, Xing added, is to extend Beijing's urban renewal efforts across the ground level, building facades, and rooftops, unlocking greater value from the city's existing space. The growing appeal of these rooftop spaces makes them a must-visit for Chen and his photography-obsessed friends. "The only problem," Chen said with a laugh, "is that my friends are so obsessed with getting the perfect shot that they can easily spend an hour taking photos." "Sometimes the food gets cold, and we have to ask the waiter to reheat it!" ■ You may like World's first museum devoted to prehistoric flying reptiles opens in NW China's Xinjiang Two teachers devote their lives to a remote mountain village Chinese dance drama "A Dream of Red Mansions" makes U.S. debut in New York A glimpse of Yinxu Museum in Anyang, China's Henan EcoChina | A scenic drive into Hainan's rainforest InPics | Shougang Park reinvents itself as vibrant urban destination More from GLOBALink BRICS cooperation: Shared prosperity for half of world's population What BRICS family saw at CIFIT: markets, investment and new partnerships How AI is reshaping everyday services at CIFTIS

body: Chinese naval escort task group to visit Bangladesh, Myanmar, Malaysia-Xinhua Chinese naval escort task group to visit Bangladesh, Myanmar, Malaysia Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-14 20:08:15 BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- The 48th escort task group of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy will visit Bangladesh, Myanmar and Malaysia on its return voyage from the Gulf of Aden, according to a Chinese military spokesperson. The task group recently completed its missions in the Gulf of Aden and set off on its return to China, said Jiang Bin, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, at a press briefing on Monday. During the upcoming visits, professional exchanges and ship open days will be held to further enhance long-standing friendship and strategic mutual trust between the Chinese side and its counterparts, contributing to the building of a community with a shared future with neighboring countries, Jiang noted. Composed of the guided-missile destroyer Tangshan, the guided-missile frigate Daqing and the comprehensive supply ship Taihu, the task group set sail for escort missions in the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia on Oct. 11, 2025. The PLA Navy began conducting escort missions in the Gulf of Aden and the waters off Somalia in December 2008. ■ Chinese naval escort task group to visit Bangladesh, Myanmar, Malaysia

body: Economic Watch: Smart technologies power high-quality development of China's mining industry-Xinhua Economic Watch: Smart technologies power high-quality development of China's mining industry Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-14 19:38:30 TIANJIN, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- At the exhibition booth of Unissky (Nanjing) Technology Co., Ltd., a four-legged inspection robot moved steadily, autonomously adjusting its movements when encountering obstacles and following predefined routes. Designed for inspection in confined and hazardous spaces such as underground mines, the robot drew the attention of many visitors to the 2026 China Mining Conference and Exhibition. "This product is primarily designed for confined and hazardous environments such as underground mines, and it has broad application potential in the mining sector," said Xu Tao, a solution manager at Unissky. The global mining industry is undergoing a profound digital transformation. In recent years, China has embraced smart technologies to modernize its mining industry, with digital twins, autonomous mining, and AI-powered exploration gaining ground across operations. China's push for smart mining is helping drive the industry into a new stage of development. The coal industry offers a glimpse of this transformation. By the end of 2025, China had 1,066 intelligent coal mines, with intelligent production capacity accounting for more than 65 percent of total coal production capacity, according to data from the China National Coal Association. Artificial intelligence is being rapidly adopted across the coal industry, with applications spanning production and operations, safety management, and equipment maintenance. Autonomous driving technology is also gaining ground in open-pit mines. In China, more than 4,000 autonomous mining trucks were in operation by the end of 2025, according to industry statistics. In 2024, seven Chinese government departments jointly issued the guiding opinions on advancing the construction of intelligent mines and promoting the safe development of mines. The document calls for establishing a comprehensive system covering technology, equipment and management for smart mining by 2030, with greater integration and broader sharing of mining data. Ren Shoumai, an official at the China Geological Survey, said geological mapping is like drawing a "geological navigation map" for the subsurface mineral world. On Friday, the Ministry of Natural Resources unveiled an AI-powered mineral exploration system, AI-OreSeeking, and an AI-powered geological mapping system, AI-GeoMapping, aiming to reshape geological survey workflows and provide a new technological paradigm for global mineral exploration. AI-GeoMapping has been widely trialed on nearly 100 1:50,000-scale geological map sheets in Qinghai, Xizang, Xinjiang, Fujian, and other provincial-level regions of China, and has also been promoted in Morocco, Saudi Arabia, Laos and other countries. It identifies geological bodies with overall accuracy exceeding 90 percent and improves the efficiency of data processing, integrated analysis and geological map compilation by more than 50 percent compared with traditional methods. Experts attending the event said cutting-edge technologies such as artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things and 5G have become increasingly integrated into the entire mining lifecycle, driving breakthroughs in areas such as smart mine development and mining machinery manufacturing. At Huangling Mining Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of Shaanxi Coal and Chemical Industry Group, production data at the No. 1 Coal Mine are updated in milliseconds on screens at the surface dispatch and command center. Folds in rock layers and variations in coal seam thickness that were previously difficult to observe are now converted into 3D visual data through smart technologies, enabling more precise prediction and dynamic control of underground operations. At Yidong Group's Lijiata Coal Mine, a high-precision personnel positioning system and a 5G-based communication and dispatch system have created an underground high-speed information network, significantly improving mine safety management and emergency response. At Qinglong Coal Mine, operated by Guizhou Qianxi Energy Development Co., Ltd., intelligent shearers equipped with memory cutting and automatic following, as well as intelligent roadheaders featuring inertial navigation, laser positioning and infrared remote control, are being used in mining operations. These technologies have significantly reduced the physical workload of workers while boosting production efficiency. "Mining robots are helping enable unmanned operation at fixed workstations and robotic operations at hazardous posts," said Wang Lin, a marketing manager at CITIC HIC Kaicheng Intelligence Equipment Co., Ltd. The company's coal-gangue sorting robot on display at the conference uses big-data-based intelligent recognition technology to automatically identify and separate coal from gangue, helping mining companies improve sorting efficiency and operating returns, Wang said. Smart mining practices are also being extended to other fields. During the construction of a reservoir bridge in Macheng, central China's Hubei Province, the project team of China Railway 18th Bureau Group Co., Ltd. applied smart technologies to key construction processes and independently developed a range of tools, including a precision positioning device for embedded sleeves in track slabs. These innovations have helped address long-standing challenges such as significant positioning deviations in traditional manual operations, significantly improving construction quality and precision. Wang Sufeng, deputy director and secretary-general of the Smart Mine Professional Committee of the China Association of Work Safety, said smart mining is key to developing new quality productive forces and enhancing workplace safety, and is an essential path to the industry's high-quality development. Looking ahead, experts said the industry needs to improve intelligent decision-making and inter-system coordination, build centralized data platforms to enable data sharing, and accelerate the development of technologies for transparent geological information and safer, more energy-efficient power systems. Industry insiders called for closer cooperation among government agencies, mining companies, equipment manufacturers, universities and research institutes to advance smart mining and inject new momentum into the industry's high-quality development. ■ Economic Watch: Smart technologies power high-quality development of China's mining industry

title: Economic Watch: Smart technologies power high-quality development of China's mining industry

body: Economic Watch: China's services trade fair emerges as institutional platform for open, innovative cooperation-Xinhua Economic Watch: China's services trade fair emerges as institutional platform for open, innovative cooperation Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-14 19:23:30 BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- The China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) is turning China's market momentum into shared global opportunities, mirroring a broader trend of Chinese trade fairs becoming dynamic platforms for global innovation and open trade. Held annually in Beijing, this year's CIFTIS concluded on Sunday with more than 1,200 outcomes achieved, facilitating resource matching, exchanges and cooperation, according to Lu Huiling, deputy head and spokesperson of the Beijing municipal commerce bureau. "China's opening-up in the services sector provides vital certainty to global trade in services," said Yang Zhengwei, vice president of the Development Research Center of the State Council, who attended the fair. CATALYST FOR CROSS-BORDER SYNERGY As one of the world's largest platforms for trade in services, CIFTIS serves as a key institutional platform for China's opening-up and a crucial window for the world to see opportunities in China's increasingly open services sector. This year's CIFTIS, its 13th edition, attracted participants from 90 countries, regions and international organizations, with more than 1,800 enterprises displaying their industry solutions. "For Norwegian companies, the Chinese market holds many opportunities," said Henning Kristoffersen, commercial counsellor at the Norwegian Embassy in China. Norway, the guest country of honor for 2026 CIFTIS, utilized its 260-square-meter pavilion to move beyond traditional exports, exploring deep cooperation with China in emerging fields such as green maritime transition, marine nutrition and digital technologies. Kristoffersen said the fair provides an essential platform for Norwegian firms to assess market demand, match with Chinese partners and establish long-term strategic collaborations in these specialized sectors. While Norway's land-based aquaculture, recirculating aquaculture systems and other technologies in its fisheries are attracting increasing attention from China, China's emerging technologies and services in AI and robotics are drawing in Norwegian businesses. At the fair, Klaus Hoseth, CEO of a Norwegian aquaculture tech company, showcased a highly-automated salmon processing line. Noting that manual feeding remains labor-intensive during peak volumes, Hoseth saw a solution in China. "Chinese robotics might come in handy," he said, having visited a Beijing-based start-up specializing in both hardware and software for embodied AI robots ahead of the fair. Beyond technology, CIFTIS is catalyzing a broader form of cross-border synergy -- one driven by China's expanding market access in telecom, allowing global network resources and AI services to better meet local enterprise demands. As one of the first batch of Hong Kong-invested enterprises in China's pilot program for expanding the opening-up of value-added telecommunications services, Hong Kong Telecommunications (HKT) positioned itself as an "international connector" at the exhibition, with a focus on showcasing its AI product operations and global network resource services. Mak Chi-fai, general manager of the China Business of the Commercial Customer Business of HKT, said the company is bringing its seasoned international telecommunications operations and AI service experience into the Chinese mainland to empower enterprises to achieve intelligent and efficient operations. BRIDGE FOR GLOBAL INNOVATION Beyond showcasing China's open market, CIFTIS serves as a powerful catalyst for collaborative global innovation. This role is reflected by initiatives like the China-Europe Innovation Industrial Park, launched at this year's fair to directly translate conceptual agreements into long-term cross-border projects between European and Chinese enterprises. Huzur Devletsah, U.S. pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly's vice president and China general manager, highlighted the country's pivotal role in the company's global strategy. Leveraging China's policy incentives and research strengths, Lilly is accelerating the rollout of an integrated chain covering R&D, manufacturing and commercialization, deeply integrating into China's pharmaceutical innovation ecosystem. "Looking ahead, Lilly will continue to use CIFTIS as a bridge to unite industry, academia, and research partners, accelerate the commercialization of cutting-edge global innovations in China, and support the Healthy China 2030 initiative," Devletsah said. The collaborative innovation is supported by an increasingly enabling regulatory environment. Wu Xuchu, vice chairman of KPMG China, noted that institutional opening-up in areas like cross-border data flows has turned China into a vital "innovation testing ground" for global services firms. "This provides an opportunity both for Chinese professional firms to grow alongside businesses and for global counterparts to participate in China's development," Wu said. Reinforcing this commitment to high-standard innovation frameworks, the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) served as a co-host of the Global Trade in Services Summit at the 2026 CIFTIS for the first time, addressing IP protection -- a core compliance priority for multinationals establishing local R&D centers. Trade data tells the same story about cross-border innovation. The Ministry of Commerce said that in 2025, China's total trade in knowledge-intensive services grew by 6.6 percent. In the first seven months of 2026, knowledge-intensive services accounted for 53.5 percent of China's total services exports, up 3 percentage points compared to last year. PLATFORM FOR SHARING CHINESE SOLUTIONS CIFTIS also acts as a platform promoting China's global service practices, which are transferable, replicable and open to cooperation. Even after the physical exhibition halls of CIFTIS close, its global impact continues. A dedicated exhibition area for Chinese service cases was set up for the first time at the core of the thematic exhibition, offering a window into the development of China's services. One example is PowerChina's work on the Kananga-Kalamba Mbuji road project in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where the company integrated infrastructure delivery with human capital development, training nearly 700 local workers and facilitating technology transfer to foster enduring local capabilities. Fintech cooperation is another area highlighted at CIFTIS. China's strengths in digital services are playing a key role in helping developing nations bridge the digital divide. By sharing digital capabilities and infrastructure, China is helping to make financial services more accessible and inclusive across emerging economies. "Trade in services is increasingly becoming trade in knowledge," said Benjamin Hung, President of International at Standard Chartered. He added that China's sharing of expertise in fintech, AI, payment systems and digital platforms can significantly empower innovation across the Global South and throughout the broader global economy. Alongside CIFTIS, other Chinese trade fairs serve as institutional mechanisms to promote trade and advance multilateralism, amid mounting global trade uncertainties. The recently concluded China International Fair for Investment and Trade in Xiamen facilitated two-way investment. The Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou next week is poised to set new benchmarks for digital commerce, while the China International Import Expo in November, the world's first national-level import-themed expo, is expected to further turn China's vast market into a shared market for the world. body: China's yuan loans increase by 10.44 trln yuan in Jan.-Aug. period-Xinhua China's yuan loans increase by 10.44 trln yuan in Jan.-Aug. period Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-14 19:19:45 BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 10.44 trillion yuan (about 1.54 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first eight months of 2026, central bank data showed on Monday. At the end of August, outstanding yuan loans stood at 282.35 trillion yuan, up 4.9 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China. M2, a broad measure of money supply that covers cash in circulation and all deposits, had increased by 7.5 percent year on year to 356.81 trillion yuan by the end of last month. M1, which covers currency in circulation, corporate demand deposits, personal demand deposits and provisions received by non-bank payment institutions, reached 115.77 trillion yuan at the end of August, a rise of 4.1 percent from a year earlier. China's outstanding aggregate financing to the real economy stood at 464.8 trillion yuan at the end of August, up 7.2 percent year on year, the central bank noted. "At present, China's aggregate financial volume is growing at a reasonable pace, and social financing conditions have remained relatively loose," said Tian Xuan, dean of Peking University's Guanghua School of Management. The central bank said in its latest monetary policy report that it will continue to implement a moderately loose monetary policy in the second half of 2026, strengthen counter-cyclical adjustment, and take solid steps to promote sustained and improved economic development. It will also maintain ample liquidity, guide financial institutions to enhance the balance of credit supply, and align the growth of social financing and money supply with expected targets for economic growth and overall price levels. Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating, said that looking ahead, the country's monetary policy will strengthen coordination with fiscal and industrial policies and step up counter-cyclical adjustment. Structural monetary policy tools are expected to see further price cuts, increased quotas and expanded coverage, to boost financing support for tech companies and private enterprises, facilitate the shift to new growth drivers, and stabilize overall employment, Wang said. ■ China's yuan loans increase by 10.44 trln yuan in Jan.-Aug. period

body: Do robots dream of human forms, or just practical tasks?-Xinhua Do robots dream of human forms, or just practical tasks? Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-14 16:36:16 Visitors watch a robot performance during the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) at Shougang Park in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 13, 2026. (Photo by Liu Zhihan/Xinhua) by Xinhua writer Chen Wangqi BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Watching humanoid robots do backflips is surely impressive. But after the sense of novelty wears off, I always find myself wondering: Is it ever going to help me fold my laundry? Henning Kristoffersen, commercial counselor at the Norwegian Embassy in China, asked me a similar question on the sidelines of the just-concluded 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS). Calling China's humanoid robots "hugely exciting" and "super impressive," Kristoffersen said a part of him thinks, "Oh my gosh, this is changing the world. And another part of me is saying: Oops, in what way is this changing?" So I put that to the exhibitors on the showroom floor. WHY HUMANOID? A robot vacuum cleaner can effortlessly slide under a sofa that requires a human to drop to their hands and knees, making it hard to see what a humanoid robot would add. "Specialized robots may outperform at one specific job, but humanoids are designed to tackle all sorts of tasks, offering general-purpose capabilities," said Hu Zheqi, vice president of Yue Quan Bionics Ltd., a developer of bionic humanoid robots. "A robot vacuum can only vacuum. You need another machine to cook, and yet another to do the laundry. A humanoid rolls them all into one, so it's the best choice," Hu said. "Our world is designed entirely for people, from our size to the way we use tools. Building a robot that fits into those existing spaces keeps costs and challenges down, rather than having to redesign the environments from scratch for task-specific machines." However, Mo Yilin, a tenured associate professor at Tsinghua University's Department of Automation and chief scientist at LingYu Robotics, offered a different perspective. As the global robotics industry is still in its infancy, it is difficult to envision what form a truly general-purpose machine should take, Mo told Xinhua. "Thus, many people's default reaction is: Well, humans can do a bit of everything, so let's just make it look like a person -- at least we're locked in general versatility." "But a robot can't be tightening bolts in a factory today and rescuing hikers on Mount Tai tomorrow," he said. "Once a product's actual use case is clear, its physical design will naturally diverge ... After all, the more specialized the roles, the higher the efficiency." Mo noted that currently, it is nearly impossible to balance the ideal "triangle" of generalizability, performance and autonomy. "Things evolve in stages. You can't expect a robot to morph into the Terminator overnight." Though the sector is still nascent, China has already secured a massive edge in robotics, Mo said. Driven by its robust supply chains, vast data and rich real-world scenarios, China has what it takes to pull off hardware, data, models and applications all at once, he noted. Visitors tour the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) at Shougang Park in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Xin) BRAIN, BODY AND BUSINESS USE In a corner of the CIFTIS exhibition hall, visitors were crowding around, playing rock-paper-scissors with a robotic hand. The hand can also catch haphazardly tossed objects of any size, shape or material, picking them up and stowing them away in a box without a scratch, said Sun Jia, co-founder and CTO of CasiaHand Robotics, which has won several international awards for innovation. What controls hand movements is the CasiaHand Brain Si 0.5 -- an algorithm that merges the strengths of the vision-language-action model and the world model, both key model types in embodied AI. While the "big brain" handles comprehension, task planning and analysis, the "little brain" oversees low-level control, Sun told Xinhua. "When a user says, 'Hand me that bottle,' the big brain translates natural language into robotic commands, maps out which hand to extend, how far to move forward, and the exact grip pressure needed to lift the bottle. Meanwhile, the little brain orchestrates the five digits to pick up the bottle smoothly, ensuring it does not spill," she said. From tightening screws to brewing coffee, these robotic hands have already found applications in nuclear power inspections and emergency explosive disposal, she noted. Building a smarter brain requires massive amounts of data. Leju Robotics gathers data through VR teleoperation, with human operators wearing headsets and controllers to map their physical data directly onto the robots. Fed with real-world data capturing variables like friction and lighting, the robot handles unseen scenarios with ease, adapting seamlessly to changes in object angles and the position of light, said Sun Dong, general manager for the northern China region at Leju. What makes all this possible is the robot's body. Yue Quan Bionics has developed highly biomimetic humanoid robots featuring what Vice President Hu Zheqi described as the world's smallest chassis. Moving beyond basic tasks like hauling workshop cartons, its compact size allows it to navigate and work in narrow spaces that other robots find hard to enter. And these humanoid robots are already walking out of the factory into our daily lives. Mo Yilin said LingYu Robotics' humanoids are now employed in JD Supermarket, navigating dense crowds and unpredictable traffic, reliably handing out food samples, restocking shelves, and guiding customers through the racks. Visitors look at a humanoid robot at the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) at Shougang Park in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Ju Huanzong) INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION Building on partnerships with European manufacturing giants like Schaeffler and Hutchinson, Leju sealed deals at the recent World Robot Conference to establish strategic hubs in Britain and the Netherlands for research and manufacturing, Sun Dong told Xinhua. "This is a deep strategic partnership, not just a hardware sale," said Sun Dong. "Leju will provide algorithms and services, while our partners bring their industry expertise, leveraging each other's strengths to drive the development of this technology." As the guest country of honor of this year's CIFTIS, Norway saw a record number of companies visiting China to build and expand partnerships, said Vebjorn Dysvik, the Norwegian ambassador to China. Ole J. Rugset, CEO of Kristiansund and Nordmore Business Association, told Xinhua that the Norwegian delegation visited several humanoid robot companies ahead of CIFTIS. "We are here to learn, especially about artificial intelligence," he said, adding that he hopes to bring those connections back to Norway and looks forward to future collaboration. Ambassador Dysvik told Xinhua he believes humanoid robotics will be a key growth area, saying there remains immense potential for collaboration. "China is far ahead on a lot of this, but we are also quite advanced, especially when it comes to autonomous vehicles in the sea that can withstand harsh conditions," he said. "I think a lot of Norwegian companies that are advanced in this sector will be looking to China to see where they can cooperate, where that is possible." Impressed by China's robots after experiencing hotel-delivery bots firsthand, Nanno Mulder, chief of the International Trade Unit at the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, expressed optimism for the industry's future, stressing that robots should only take over mundane tasks to free humans for more productivity-enhancing roles. body: Yemen's Houthis claim major missile, drone attack on Saudi air base-Xinhua Yemen's Houthis claim major missile, drone attack on Saudi air base Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-14 19:39:30 SANAA, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Monday that it had launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at a major military air base in southwestern Saudi Arabia, marking a significant escalation in the widening cross-border confrontation. In a statement carried by Houthi-run al-Masirah TV, military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, a southwestern Saudi city near the Yemeni border. Sarea said the operation targeted fighter-jet hangars, radar systems, runways, ammunition depots and other military facilities at the base, claiming that the strikes were "precise and direct" and caused significant damage. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on Monday's Houthi claims or information on possible casualties and damage. Sarea said the operation was carried out in retaliation for what the group described as an intensifying Saudi air campaign across Yemen, claiming that Saudi F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets had conducted more than 300 airstrikes on several Yemeni provinces in recent days. He warned that the Houthis would continue launching attacks deep inside Saudi territory as long as airstrikes on Yemen continue, saying any further escalation would be met with broader military operations. The claim came amid a sweeping Houthi offensive launched on Sept. 3 that has rapidly redrawn front lines along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with the group capturing several government-held areas in the Red Sea Hodeidah province and neighboring southwestern Taiz province. The Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mocha on Thursday before pushing south into the Bab al-Mandab Strait area and seizing Mayun Island at the heart of the strait, tightening their grip on the vital shipping chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Following the advance on Friday, the Houthis said international navigation through the strait remained "free, safe and smooth," while stressing that Saudi vessels remained excluded under a maritime ban the group imposed on July 20. Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. ■ Yemen's Houthis claim major missile, drone attack on Saudi air base

body: Singapore PSI forecast to remain moderate to unhealthy-Xinhua Singapore PSI forecast to remain moderate to unhealthy Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-14 19:38:15 SINGAPORE, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) is forecast to remain in the high-moderate to mid-unhealthy range, the National Environment Agency (NEA) said on Monday. In its latest advisory, the NEA said brief showers fell over parts of Singapore on Monday. As at 6 p.m. local time, one-hour PM2.5 concentration readings ranged from 56 to 115 micrograms per cubic meter, placing them in Band 2, the "Elevated" band. The 24-hour PSI stood at 88 to 117, ranging from the moderate to unhealthy range. Due to a shift in the prevailing winds to blow from east-southeast, moderate to dense smoke plumes from fires in Kalimantan drifted towards Singapore. Some smoke haze was also observed to drift from southern Sumatra, the agency said. It said dry conditions are expected to persist over Singapore and the surrounding region in the coming days. ■ Singapore PSI forecast to remain moderate to unhealthy

[Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] A seminar for the revolutionary film Light Chaser was held at the China Film Archive in Beijing earlier this week, marking the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's victory in the Long March. Set against the Battle of Xiangjiang, one of the bloodiest engagements of the Long March (1934-36), the film follows Red Army soldiers separated from their main forces in the mountains of northern Guilin, Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. The story centers on two brothers, Jinsheng and Shuisheng, who are tasked with protecting a precious medical kit. Along the way, they forge ties with the local Yao ethnic community while holding on to their revolutionary ideals. After enduring a series of hardships, Shuisheng undergoes a profound transformation and ultimately sacrifices himself to protect his comrades. Jinsheng then leads the surviving soldiers in their search for the main force. Liao Changyou, general manager of Guangxi Cultural Industry Group, said the film steers away from grand narratives and large-scale battle scenes, instead focusing on ordinary soldiers separated from their comrades after the Battle of Xiangjiang. "It is an artistic exploration of a small entry point with a grand theme — using individual fates to reflect the power of faith and interpreting the Long March spirit through ordinary people's perseverance," he said. A seminar for Light Chaser in Beijing held earlier this month. [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] Director and chief screenwriter Qiu Huaiyang said the project was inspired by oral histories of Red Army soldiers who became separated from their units in Guanyang, Guangxi. "What moved me most was their pursuit of ideals and their unwavering commitment to their faith," he said. He also explained the metaphorical meaning behind the film's title, Light Chaser . "Only those who find themselves in darkness, yet still hold on to a faint hope and a glimmer of possibility, are true light chasers," Qiu said. Song Zhiqin, director of the Movie Art Center under the China Federation of Literary and Art Circles, said the film's focus on ordinary soldiers expands the creative possibilities of revolutionary historical films. "By focusing on ordinary people's struggles in isolation and adversity, it allows audiences to deeply feel the weight of their faith and empathize with their choices," he said. [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] At the opening of his exhibition in Beijing's 798 Art Zone, Phenix Varbanov engaged the audience with an immersive performance. He folded a large round sheet of xuan paper on the ground, sprayed it with ink, and then flattened it out, revealing the unique textures and effects that resembled a bird's-eye view of snowcapped mountains. His distinctive approach challenges conventional perceptions of Chinese ink art and expands the boundaries of a tradition that has endured for centuries. The work he created during the opening will remain on the gallery floor through the exhibition, allowing visitors to take a close look at its details. Phenix Varbanov's exhibition in Beijing's 798 Art Zone reflects his diverse cultural influence. [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] Varbanov comes from a diverse cultural background. He has a Chinese mother, a Bulgarian father, and he grew up and lives in Paris, although he also spends time in Beijing, his mother's hometown. These rich cultural experiences and perspectives have given his paintings on xuan paper a sensibility that is both ancient and modern, Eastern and Western. Varbanov is reserved with his use of color. His works are largely rendered in monochromatic ink, reminding one of a philosophical concept of Chinese painting that "ink has five shades" with which one can still depict the world. He is especially drawn to the darker shades, whose depth conveys an infinite expanse. body: Wuxi–Vientiane direct flights to be resumed in October L M S en.wuxi.gov.cn | Updated: September 11, 2026 Wuxi Shuofang Airport. [Photo provided to en.nantong.gov.cn] Guangzhou-based 9Air, a low-budget airline, is set to resume its direct passenger service between Wuxi Shuofang Airport and Vientiane, the capital of Laos, on Oct 9. The route, operating under flight numbers AQ1233 and AQ1234, is scheduled to run three times weekly on Wednesdays, Fridays, and Sundays. Flight AQ1233 departs Wuxi at 11:20 am and arrives in Vientiane at 2 pm. The return flight, AQ1234, leaves Vientiane at 3 pm and lands in Wuxi at 7:25 pm. A spokesperson from 9Air's marketing department said the airline initially launched the route last year but suspended operations due to rising fuel costs. The decision to resume the service was driven by a combination of factors: oil prices have since declined, the winter-spring period is the peak tourist season for Laos, and there has been growing trade activity between cities in the Yangtze River Delta region and Laos. Laos welcomes travelers during the cool, dry season from November through February, when temperatures are moderate and road conditions are favorable. The Wuxi–Vientiane link is one of the international and regional passenger routes currently operating from Wuxi Shuofang Airport, which also connects to destinations including Osaka, Seoul, Jeju, Nha Trang, and Sihanoukville.
title: Wuxi–Vientiane direct flights to be resumed in October

body: Mandarin taught me about the Chinese philosophy of social life - Opinion - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE Opinion Cartoons Editorials Global Lens We Comment Columnists Global Views Chinese Perspectives Opinion Line Home Opinion / From the Readers Home / Opinion / From the Readers Mandarin taught me about the Chinese philosophy of social life By Sadiq Salihoddin | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-09-14 16:31 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE The author and his students in Nanning, Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. [Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn] "Language shapes our worldview." This is the hypothesis put forward by two of the most influential linguists of the 20th century, Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf. But if we look more closely, what examples might actually demonstrate this hypothesis? When I first arrived in China as a Malay language teacher, I took the initiative to learn Mandarin so that I could become accustomed to living among local people. I needed it for ordinary things: ordering food, reporting a problem with my room, calling a taxi, and simply making conversation with people around me. All of these everyday interactions required at least a basic command of Mandarin. So I bought HSK textbooks and began studying the language autodidactically. What fascinated me was that, as I went deeper into Mandarin, I discovered that a language spoken by more than a billion people contains expressions that are difficult to translate not only into Malay, but even into English. I remember thinking: perhaps this is precisely what Sapir and Whorf meant when they argued that language shapes our worldview. Take the word guanxi , for example. In English, it can be translated as "relationship, connection, network, contact or acquaintance". Yet none of these words, nor even a combination of them, fully captures the meaning of guanxi . Guanxi is more than simply being friends or being connected. It begins with a personal relationship that can subsequently develop into a network of trust, mutual assistance, and even business partnership. In a world that increasingly emphasises individualism, one might ask: "What can this relationship do for me?" The philosophy underlying guanxi , however, encourages a different question: "How can this relationship strengthen our bond, and what responsibilities do I have in maintaining our mutual well-being?" This helps explain why business relationships among Chinese communities around the world — including the Chinese community in Malaysia — have often been remarkably strong. People do not simply pursue prosperity individually; they build networks through which opportunities, assistance, and success can be shared. They struggle together, and they prosper together. Another fascinating concept I encountered was lian , which is closely related to mianzi . In Malay society, we have the concept of air muka — literally "the face" — which refers to a person's dignity and reputation, something that may be guarded almost as carefully as one's own life. I was delighted to discover the concepts of lian and mianzi , because they reminded me of a similar concern for courtesy and dignity in Malay society. This philosophy helps explain why openly criticizing someone can be considered undesirable in Chinese social interaction: doing so may cause the other person to "lose face". I see this tendency in a positive light. Excessive bluntness can sometimes damage the harmony of a relationship — precisely the kind of relationship that guanxi seeks to cultivate. Criticism does not necessarily become less honest simply because it is delivered with consideration for another person's dignity. On the contrary, I believe criticism expressed in a way that preserves the other person's "face" can be more harmonious and, ultimately, more effective, because the effort to preserve the relationship is itself appreciated by the person receiving the criticism. Then I encountered another beautiful concept: yuanfen . English has the words "fate" and "coincidence", but neither quite captures what yuanfen conveys. It describes a meaningful encounter between people — the feeling that two people were meant to cross paths. A meeting may appear accidental, yet it can subsequently be understood as something that carries a deeper significance. This reminds me of how I met my partner. Sometimes, as the saying goes, when you know, you know. My encounters with my students at Guangxi Minzu University feel much the same. I do not regard these meetings merely as accidents of geography or circumstance. They have meaning. We were meant to meet, to learn from one another, and, in some way, to grow together. A part of who I am is now shaped by Chinese culture, and perhaps that, too, is a form of yuanfen . In the Confucian tradition, wisdom is often associated with balance: neither excess nor deficiency, neither one extreme nor the other, but the appropriate measure. Much of this can be captured by the concept zhongyong . The principle extends beyond philosophical discussion into everyday life. We should not overindulge in eating and drinking; nor should we carry any tendency to excess into our relationships, emotions, or conduct. Zhongyong is closely related to another useful concept , fencun : knowing one's limits, knowing how far to go and understanding what is appropriate in a particular situation. I find fencun especially valuable because it suggests that social wisdom is not always a matter of deciding between right and wrong. Sometimes the more difficult question is: how much is appropriate here? When should I speak? When should I remain silent? How directly should I express myself? How much should I ask of another person? How close should I become? These questions require an ability to read the situation — a form of social intelligence that cannot always be reduced to a set of explicit rules. As a final thought, I would like to end with one Chinese word that I believe could serve as a useful principle for people of all ages and backgrounds: dongshi . The word is commonly used when talking about children. Parents may praise a child for being dongshi when the child behaves appropriately, understands the situation, and does not need to be told what to do. But the concept carries a much broader philosophy than simply being a well-behaved child. At its heart is the ability to read a situation and understand what others may need without everything having to be explicitly stated. In a world increasingly influenced by individualistic values, this quality can sometimes appear to be fading. Knowing when to put others first, when to remain silent, when to speak, when to step forward and when to step back — these are not merely manners. They are social skills that must be learned and cultivated. Perhaps there is something we can all learn from the Chinese philosophy contained in dongshi : understand the situation before insisting on yourself. In this sense, learning Mandarin has convinced me that language does indeed offer its own distinctive way of seeing the world. Learning a foreign language is not merely about knowing how to order food when traveling abroad. It can also teach us how another society understands relationships, dignity, obligation, emotion, and appropriate conduct. This, for me, is the real intellectual pleasure of learning Mandarin. I came to China as a teacher of Malay, but in learning the language of the people around me, I have also begun to understand something about the way they see the world. And I am still enjoying that discovery here in Nanning, Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, in the far southern region of China. The author is a Malay language lecturer at the Faculty of Southeast Asian Languages and Cultures, Guangxi Mi
title: Mandarin taught me about the Chinese philosophy of social life
