body: Ukraine A Quiet Ukrainian Counteroffensive, A 'Rout' For Russian Forces By Mike Eckel September 15, 2026 17:30 CET A Quiet Ukrainian Counteroffensive, A 'Rout' For Russian Forces Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Ukrainian forces have built a line of defenses, anchored by the two cities of Kramatorsk and Slovyansk, that Russian troops are hellbent on capturing. Sometime around late May, as Russia's all-out invasion neared the 4 1/2-year mark and the summer fighting season shifted into higher gear, Ukrainian commanders quietly ordered some of the country's most battle-hardened units into positions about 50 kilometers north of the Donetsk region city of Slovyansk. Mainly taken from Ukraine's Third Army Corps, the units confronted a bulge in the 1,100-kilometer front line where Russia's 20th Combined Arms Army had been grinding westward, pushing out from a bridgehead on the west bank of the Zherebets River amid villages, farmland, and rolling fields. The goal for Russia: cut off supply lines for Ukrainian forces in Slovyansk, one of two main Ukrainian-held cities in the Donetsk region. Ukrainian soldiers unload supplies from a military vehicle as they arrive for a combat mission in the Donetsk region on September 9. Over the summer months, Ukrainian forces battled northward out of the town of Lyman while also pushing to the south toward the villages of Ridkodub, Katerynivka, and Nove. That effort, according to open-source researchers, experts who have traveled to the battlefield, and Ukrainian and Russian war bloggers, is nearing a remarkable success for Ukrainian forces: Much of the Russian force in the area has been pushed back to the Zherebets River, with small pockets of soldiers encircled and likely to be captured or killed in the coming days. Map: A Quiet Ukrainian Counteroffensive Pushes Russia Back (September 15, 2026) By most accounts, it is shaping up to be one of the largest shifts on the battlefield in months, possibly in a year. For the moment, the success relieves some pressure on the Ukrainian defenses trying to hold the line of cities, towns, and roads running north to south and encompassing Slovyansk and the city of Kramatorsk, a swath known as an "agglomeration." Moreover, the nearly four-month offensive also took place in an unusual information vacuum, with virtually no information leaking out among war bloggers on Telegram in Ukraine or Russia until recent days. "Ukrainians took back some of the territory. Russia lost more territory," Konrad Muzyka, a Polish-based military expert who has spent substantial time on Ukraine's front lines, told RFE/RL. "It's significant, not because of what's happening around Lyman, but because I think it thwarted a big Russian plan that was seeking to envelop the Slovyansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration from the north and from the south." "The Russians keep trying this envelopment" of the entire Donetsk region, said Dara Massicot, an expert on the Russian military with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, a Washington-based think tank. "For now, it looks like the northern attempt is blunted." SEE ALSO: On Ukraine's Battlefield, Russia Has Lost Ground, Experts Say. But Don't Expect A Major Reversal For Kyiv. A chorus on Russian war channels on Telegram, meanwhile, has also pointed to significant Ukrainian gains. "A rout on the Lyman front," said one prominent Telegram blogger named Anatoly Shariy, a former Ukrainian politician who has been convicted in absentia of high treason in Ukraine and sentenced to 15 years in prison. "The situation at Lyman is alarming," said Rybar , a Telegram blogger previously affiliated with the Russian Defense Ministry. "We suffered an unpleasant tactical defeat," said another channel, called Dnevnik Desantnika . "However, encirclement did not occur; most of our personnel were withdrawn, and now everything depends on whether [Ukrainian] forces can exploit this success east of the Zherebets River." At least one pro-Russian blogger, Yury Kotenok , complained specifically about the lack of information that has leaked out from Ukrainian sources. "Ukraine is conducting an offensive near Lyman under information silence," he wrote. "Silence on our part is already customary, but on the enemy's side it seems somewhat unusual, which is alarming. Here we have a deliberate, targeted regime of silence." SEE ALSO: Here's Why Russia's Vladimir Putin Is Fixated On Ukraine's Donbas Ukraine's military press office declined to comment, citing ongoing operations. But in a statement released on September 15, the commander for the Third Army Corps, Brigadier General Andriy Biletskiy, broadly confirmed the counteroffensive. "We confirm reports of a Ukrainian Army offensive in the north of Donetsk Oblast. Maintaining information silence, the units eliminated pockets of enemy infiltration," he was quoted as saying. "There is currently a lot of information in open sources suggesting that the ultimate goal of our offensive operations is to reach the banks of the Zherebets River.... There will be good news." The Russian Defense Ministry did not respond to a query seeking comment. The battlefield success is unlikely to translate into any broader strategic shift for Ukraine, military experts said. Overall, Kyiv remains at a disadvantage, outnumbered and in many places outgunned by Russia. SEE ALSO: On Ukraine's Battlefield, Spring Weather, New Fighting Season, A Big Russian Assault Despite suffering astronomical casualties and losing ground in some places, Russia continues to grind forward along parts of the front line. Military commanders have prioritized trying to capture Slovyansk and Kramatorsk, which would give them control over the entirety of the Donetsk region -- and the entire Donbas. That is a major priority for Putin and the Kremlin. Russia has vowed to capture all of the Donbas by force if Ukraine refuses to cede the territory it still holds, a step Kyiv has firmly ruled out. The issue of territorial control in the Donbas is a key sticking point in the on-again, off-again US-led peace efforts. Still, 2026 has been a relatively stable year for Ukraine's frontline troops; in some places, Kyiv has taken back more territory than Russia has gained. The success of the Lyman counteroffensive also highlights the fighting prowess of some of Ukraine's best units -- including the Third Army Corps -- and some of the continuing problems Russia has had on the battlefield, particularly as it sends new volunteers to the front with minimal training. Ukrainian troops patrol a road near Kramatorsk, Donetsk region, on September 11. "I think it shows that the Russians can concentrate [only] in one main sector at a time, which right now is in southern Donetsk. That occasionally opens a few weaker spots elsewhere that can be exploited," Massicot said. "I get the sense that the 20th Combined Arms Army wasn't the strongest and so it might have been a good spot [for Ukraine] to push on," she said. "Ukraine has now effectively removed the encirclement threat to [Lyman] and are threatening the Russian salient north of the city," said Black Bird Group, a Finnish-based research organization. "The Russian summer campaign of 2026 can be considered a failure," said Emil Kastehelmi, the group's co-founder. body: News Ukrainian Olympian Urges US To Bar Russian Athletes From 2028 Games By Alex Raufoglu September 15, 2026 14:20 CET Ukrainian Olympian Urges US To Bar Russian Athletes From 2028 Games Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google During training at the 2026 Winter Olympics, Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych wears a helmet in tribute to Ukrainian athletes who have died amid Russia's invasion of Ukraine. WASHINGTON -- Ukrainian skeleton racer and Olympian Vladyslav Heraskevych is urging US lawmakers and the State Department to deny visas to Russian athletes who seek to compete under the Russian flag at the 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles, arguing that Moscow has turned sport into an instrument of war propaganda. Heraskevych, who is visiting Washington to meet with members of Congress and other US decisionmakers, said the United States has a role to play in preventing the Los Angeles Olympics from becoming a platform for Kremlin messaging. His appeal comes after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) moved to restore the Russian Olympic Committee's status and lifted recommendations that had restricted Russian participation in international competitions. "We are living in a real world," Heraskevych told RFE/RL in an interview on September 14. "Competitions are taking place in real countries, in real places." He said that while international sports bodies can make recommendations, governments control access to their territory -- giving the United States a potential means of preventing Russian athletes from taking part. Heraskevych is calling on Washington to maintain restrictions that allow eligible Russian athletes to compete only as neutrals, without Russian flags, symbols, or official delegations. "Our main goal is to show these particular cases, these particular names, and to present that sport is not out of politics," he said. Russian Sport 'Used In Propaganda' Heraskevych said policymakers need to abandon what he called the mistaken assumption that sport can be separated from politics. Many people "believe that sport is out of politics," he said. "But Russian sport is being used in propaganda." He pointed to Russian athletes' participation in political events, support for President Vladimir Putin's ruling political establishment, and activities connected to Russia's war effort against Ukraine. Heraskevych also cited what he described as Russian athletes' involvement in events linked to Ukrainian children who were forcibly taken to Russia and their participation in military-related activities. Embed share With 20,000 Teddy Bears In Washington, Ukrainian Activists Say 'Bring Kids Back' From Russia by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:00 0:00 He said the use of sport for political purposes predates Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, pointing to the massive doping scandal surrounding Russian sport and the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. "We all remember how Russian security services were involved in this scandal," he said. Heraskevych said Russia has since expanded its use of sport to promote militarization and normalize the occupation of Ukrainian territory. He cited Russia's so-called Youth Army movement, which he said is aimed at preparing a new generation for military service, as well as sporting competitions in which Russian organizers present occupied Ukrainian territories as part of Russia. "These are just a few examples of how Russia uses sport, uses this platform to spread their propaganda, to empower and to make their war machine powerful," he said. Kateryna Lisunova, a media adviser at the US-based nonprofit Razom for Ukraine, which is supporting Heraskevych's Washington campaign, said the effort is also aimed at warning Americans about how Moscow uses seemingly apolitical institutions. "It is important to inform American representatives and American people as well as for them to not become a tool in Russian hands in war propaganda," Lisunova told RFE/RL. She said Russia has used "many good things such as art and sport" to promote and normalize the war and make audiences feel "as if nothing is happening." Visa Bans Heraskevych said visa restrictions could provide a practical way for the US to enforce its own policy regardless of decisions by international sports organizations. He pointed to recent cases in Europe and Canada in which Russian athletes were denied visas after evidence was presented to authorities of their support for Russia's war or use of pro-Kremlin symbols. He cited a 2026 European Taekwondo Championship in Germany, where Russian athlete Vladislav Larin was denied a visa after evidence was submitted showing that he had publicly collected money for the Russian military. Ukrainian Olympic Athlete: Russia Uses Sports As Part Of 'War Machine" by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:07 0:00 He also cited a 2026 junior world curling championship where Russian athletes were denied visas after evidence was presented showing them posing with symbols associated with Russia's invasion. Latvia has similarly denied visas to Russian athletes seeking to participate in international competitions, Heraskevych said. "We have cases, successful cases," he said. "I believe it's a great experience, and we should share it with the US." He acknowledged that visa bans alone would not change Russia's policy but argued they could prevent international sports events from being exploited as propaganda platforms. "I believe it's one of the possibilities what we can do, and it's also what lawmakers can do," he said. Heraskevych's Own Olympic Protest The Ukrainian athlete's campaign is also rooted in his own experience at the 2026 Winter Olympics, where he was penalized after displaying a message on his helmet honoring Ukrainian athletes killed during Russia's war against Ukraine. Heraskevych said he still does not understand why he was disqualified , arguing the message was simply an act of remembrance. "I believe it's connected, and it's not a coincidence," he said. For Heraskevych, the dispute is ultimately about what the Olympic movement is supposed to represent. "The Olympic Games and Olympic movement -- it's everything about peace, about peaceful mission, about building bridges," he said. "But when you're allowed to compete and giving this platform to terrorists, then it has nothing to do with peace and peaceful mission." He said the goal of his Washington visit is not to prevent the Olympics from serving as a venue for international competition but to ensure Russia cannot use the event to legitimize its war. "We should protect this platform and we should try to make it a better place, but not a place where Russia will spread their propaganda," Heraskevych said. body: News 'Putin Is Watching': US House Panel Advances Russia-Iran Sanctions Bill By Alex Raufoglu September 15, 2026 10:52 CET 'Putin Is Watching': US House Panel Advances Russia-Iran Sanctions Bill Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google The US House Rules Committee has advanced legislation named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham (pictured). The bill targets Russian banks, energy revenues, and oligarchs. WASHINGTON -- The US House Rules Committee has advanced legislation imposing tougher sanctions on Russia and Iran, clearing a key procedural hurdle for a possible House vote later this week but exposing deep Democratic concerns over the measure's expansion of presidential tariff authority. The committee voted 7-3 late on September 14 to advance a rule setting up debate on the legislation. Debate on the rule is expected to begin around noon local time on September 15. If the rule is approved, the House is expected to consider final passage of the sanctions package on September 16. The legislation, known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, is named for the late Republican senator who championed the measure before his death. The Senate approved the legislation by an overwhelming 86-11 vote in August, giving the House a measure with substantial bipartisan backing in the upper chamber. US Representative Wilson: Russia Sanctions Will Impact China, India by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:53 0:00 The House version was introduced by Republican Representative Michael McCaul of Texas with Democratic Representative Steny Hoyer of Maryland and other bipartisan cosponsors. But the legislation has faced a more difficult path in the House, where Democrats have objected primarily to provisions that would give President Donald Trump broad new authority to impose tariffs on countries buying Russian energy or helping Moscow evade sanctions. McCaul: 'Putin Is Watching' McCaul, a senior Republican voice on foreign policy, urged lawmakers to move quickly. "Putin is watching," McCaul told the committee, warning that Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea were working together to challenge the United States and its allies. He argued that the legislation would target the financial networks supporting Russia's war effort, including Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and the so-called shadow fleet used to transport Russian oil. The bill also extends sanctions on Iran that are due to expire at the end of the year, targeting funding for Iran's energy and weapons sectors. McCaul argued that Russia and Iran could not be treated as separate challenges because of their military cooperation. Embed share Russia Expert Melia Points To 'Evidence That Sanctions Are Working' by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:01 0:00 The legislation would give Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas and countries accused of helping Moscow evade energy sanctions. Democrats say that authority is too broad and could raise prices for American consumers or be used beyond the bill's stated Russia-related purpose. Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he strongly supports additional pressure on Russia but opposed the bill in its current form. Meeks said the president already has extensive authority to impose sanctions on Russia and argued that the legislation would do less to force new sanctions than it would to expand presidential control over tariffs. "American families will pay the cost of this bill. Vladimir Putin will not," he argued. SEE ALSO: Russia-Iran Sanctions Bill Could Reach Trump’s Desk Within Days, Says Congressman Meeks and other Democrats proposed amendments that would have removed the secondary tariff provisions, tightened the president's ability to waive sanctions, clarified that the European Union could not be treated as a single "country" for tariff purposes, and provided additional military financing for Ukraine. Another Democratic proposal would have identified 10 countries as initially eligible for tariffs of up to 100 percent because of their purchases of Russian oil and gas or their alleged role in sanctions evasion. The list included China, India, Azerbaijan, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Hungary, Slovakia, Singapore, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan. Meeks also sought to require that sanctions be waived only when doing so was "vital to the national security of the US." The committee rejected the Democratic amendments. SEE ALSO: Trump Says Russia, Ukraine Agree To Halt Strikes On Energy Targets Hoyer, a Democratic cosponsor of the bill, also sought a change that would specifically identify countries potentially subject to the tariffs. He nevertheless opposed removing the tariff mechanism altogether. "If we do not pass this bill, there will be great joy in the Kremlin and great devastation in Kyiv," Hoyer said. The dispute reflects a broader dilemma for House Democrats: many support stronger measures against Russia and continued assistance for Ukraine, but they have also opposed what they regard as unchecked presidential use of tariff powers. The White House supports the sanctions legislation, and Trump has indicated he wants Congress to provide the administration with additional tools to pressure Russia and countries that continue buying Russian energy. The timing is also significant. The House is scheduled to leave Washington later this week for an extended recess ahead of the midterm elections, potentially making this one of the last opportunities for lawmakers to act on the legislation this year. 'Leverage On Mr. Putin' After the Rules Committee vote, McCaul told RFE/RL in an interview that the legislation was needed to give Washington leverage over Russian President Vladimir Putin and push him toward negotiations. "Without leverage on Mr. Putin, he'll never come to the negotiating table," McCaul argued. He pointed to his meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and argued that Ukraine needs both military and economic support while the United States seeks to pressure Moscow toward a settlement. "We believe that it will put enough economic pressure on Mr. Putin to finally come to the table and negotiate a peaceful settlement," McCaul said. SEE ALSO: Russia's Jet-Powered Drones: A Major New Threat To Ukraine Amid Speeding Arms Race Asked about concerns that the bill could be used against European allies, McCaul rejected the argument that it would give Trump unrestricted authority to expand tariffs. "The bill very narrowly defines the tariffs," he said, arguing that the provisions focus on the largest importers of Russian energy and cannot simply be expanded to other countries. McCaul also pointed to support for the legislation from European officials and Zelenskyy, saying the measure could represent an important moment in efforts to pressure Moscow. "I think this is a moment in time we have a chance to vote on something that can really change the course of history," he said. McCaul said he was confident the bill would be approved if it reached the House floor. "I'm optimistic this will be passed on the floor and will be signed by the president," he said. He also dismissed arguments that the debate should be viewed primarily through the lens of domestic politics. "Putin wants nothing more than for this bill to fail, and it plays right into his hands," McCaul said. "This is not about domestic politics. This is about saving Ukraine from this aggression from Putin. A vote against this bill is a vote for Putin." summary: The US House Rules Committee has advanced legislation imposing tougher sanctions on Russia and Iran, clearing a key procedural hurdle for a possible House vote later this week but exposing deep Democratic concerns over the measure’s expansion of presidential tariff authority.

body: Listen (6 mins) Save Share South Korea embraces Central Asian leaders, looking to boost regional clout on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev shakes hands with South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung at the Blue House in Seoul, South Korea, on September 15, 2026, ahead of the first South Korea-Central Asia summit [Jung Yeon-je/Pool via Reuters] By Agnieszka Pikulicka-Wilczewska Published On 15 Sep 2026 15 Sep 2026 South Korea is set to welcome the heads of the five Central Asian states for the first-ever presidential summit between Seoul and the region, a meeting local media have dubbed “historic”. Wednesday’s summit, preceded by bilateral meetings between South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and leaders of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, aims to deepen economic engagement between Central Asia and the host, and put them on a more permanent footing. “The first expectation is political. The summit will raise a dialogue that has existed since 2007 to the level of heads of state. But the real test is whether it produces a workable agenda in critical minerals, energy, digital technologies and transport,” Sanat Kushkumbayev, from the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera. “For Central Asia, the value of the meeting is also in showing that the region can engage external partners collectively without giving up national priorities. I would expect a framework for regular high-level cooperation, followed by more detailed bilateral deals.” Central Asian states, which are increasingly positioning themselves as a bloc known as C5+, are looking for investments, access to technology and to diversify their international partnerships beyond Moscow and Beijing, analysts said, while South Korea needs to diversify its economic and supply-chain dependencies. “Currently, South Korea has a limited domestic resource base and a significant supply-chain exposure to China, particularly in critical materials, components and other industrial inputs. Central Asia can offer South Korea critical minerals, energy, alternative production opportunities and greater supply chain diversification. Korea, in return, can provide technology, capital and industrial expertise,” said Sabina Insebayeva, a political scientist at Nazarbayev University. Advertisement She explained that the K-Silk Road initiative, South Korea’s strategy for Central Asia launched in 2024, aims to go beyond securing raw materials to develop processing, manufacturing and technology capacity in partnership with local companies. Central Asia no longer wants to position itself as an exporter of raw materials. Instead, it is seeking the skills and technology needed for domestic industrial hubs. South Korea can act as a long-term partner to achieve this goal, particularly in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. “Kazakhstan already accounts for much of South Korea’s trade and investment presence in the region, so it can reasonably push for larger industrial projects, research facilities and local supplier networks. The difficult part will be moving from assembly and memorandums to genuine localisation and commercial production,” Kushkumbayev explained. By the end of 2025, the lump-sum volume of South Korea’s direct investment in Central Asia reached about $6.4bn. But its appeal in Central Asia goes beyond its potential as an investor and technology provider, as a social connection has long been in place. South Korea’s historical ties to the region In 1937, at the order of Joseph Stalin, more than 170,000 Soviet Koreans were forcibly relocated from the USSR’s Far East to Soviet Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, under the pretext of preventing Japanese sabotage. “When my grandparents arrived in southern Kazakhstan, it was autumn, and it was already cold, but they had no houses to live in. That winter they lived with local Kazakh people who supported them and deportees from other countries,” said Roman Zakharov, a half-Korean artist from Kazakhstan. His grandparents waited for a year to receive housing from the authorities, but as deportees, they had no permission to leave the collective farms they worked on until Stalin’s death. The deportees and their descendants, collectively called Koryo-saram, have sought to stay connected to their roots, but this has not been easy. “Koryo-saram tried to adapt local products like carrots to make Korean pickled food. But local Korean culture changed through time ... My grandmother tried to listen to South Korean programmes on TV, but she couldn’t understand anything. It was a different language than my grandparents spoke,” said Zakharov, whose art pieces were shown at an exhibition in South Korea in 2023. When the Soviet Union collapsed, South Korea began founding cultural centres across Central Asia, where local people, including Koryo-saram, could learn the language and engage with Korean culture. Zakharov’s sister attended traditional Korean dance classes. Advertisement But the breakthrough for Korean soft power in Central Asia came in the 2010s when soap operas and K-pop became the talk of the town. “The South Korean government has been popularising Korean culture in Central Asia and using it as a soft power which is already very strong,” said Aiganym Toleuliyeva, a 28-year-old Kazakh researcher, who moved to South Korea to study in 2019. “In Astana, there is a Korean kimchi festival, and a Korean music festival funded by the Korean embassy. It’s through this kind of soft power and encouraging young people from Central Asia to study in South Korea that Korea is expanding in the region.” When she first visited Korea in 2015, few locals were familiar with her homeland. But as time went by, the relations grew too. Today, Central Asia is a tourist destination for South Koreans and for some in the region, Seoul’s appeal extends beyond music, the beauty industry and soap operas. “Central Asian workers in Korea are also treated better than immigrants in Russia, where the situation is becoming increasingly dangerous,” said Toleuliyeva. “Today Korea offers more opportunities for immigrants from Central Asia; they feel supported. People from Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan – and soon Kazakhstan, too – can join special programmes for labour workers, study the language for free and move to Korea to work on construction sites.” In a region trying to diversify its partnerships beyond China and Russia, South Korea could be seen as a less politically loaded partner. “There is a geopolitical element too. Seoul wants a stronger and more visible position in a region where China, Russia, the European Union, Turkiye and the Gulf states are already active,” Kushkumbayev said. “But the Korean approach is likely to remain commercially driven and relatively low-key, rather than openly geopolitical.”

body: Home Southern Africa Eswatini Related stories Human Rights News 4 December 2024 “Independence day”: Diego Garcia asylum seekers celebrate arrival in UK Human Rights News 15 January 2024 Asylum seekers sent by UK to Rwanda report sexual abuse and harassment Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email Warning: This story contains descriptions of self-harm and suicide. BANGKOK A Sri Lankan Tamil asylum seeker detained by the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT) administration for nearly five years died by apparent suicide on 13 September in Mbabane, Eswatini’s largest city, according to local news reports and relatives of the deceased. His death comes two years after the BIOT administration granted him international protection, preventing his forcible return to Sri Lanka, during which time he lived in a legal limbo in multiple countries. Kishanth Peramaiya, 36, was one of 89 Tamil asylum seekers who had fled Sri Lanka and India before being rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when their fishing vessel faltered near the British-held island of Diego Garcia, which lies within BIOT. Hundreds of additional arrivals followed on later vessels, most of whom agreed to return to Sri Lanka or left by boat to Mauritius or the French island of Réunion. Around 60 remained in BIOT custody, living in a fenced tent camp in Diego Garcia’s tightly controlled UK-US military facility. They faced rat infestations, deteriorating psychological and medical conditions, and the threat of being prosecuted or shot if they violated strict movement restrictions. Most were approved to enter the UK in November 2024. The following month, the BIOT Supreme Court ruled their detention on the island had been unlawful. But Kishanth was one of three members of the group denied entry to the UK because they had been convicted of crimes or were under criminal investigation during their detention. Another is serving the remainder of a three-year prison sentence in Montserrat for sexual offences against a child; and the third appeared to be serving a sentence on Diego Garcia for an undisclosed crime as of April 2026. Kishanth’s case, according to analysis by the London-based GSC Solicitors, “underscores the complexities of balancing humanitarian considerations with public safety concerns”. His transfer to Eswatini and subsequent death raise further questions about how the UK government decided to address these complexities, particularly since his suicidality was known to UK authorities for years. Local media in Eswatini have reported that his transfer to the country was permanent. If confirmed, it would appear to be the first publicly documented instance of an asylum seeker being granted international protection by a British authority before being permanently resettled in a different country. The closest precedent was a 2022 plan to send asylum seekers from the UK to Rwanda for processing and potential resettlement. This faced legal challenges and was scrapped in 2024 before transfers began. Three asylum seekers sent from Diego Garcia to Rwanda in 2023 for medical treatment said they were harassed or threatened there, including by a hospital worker. The New Humanitarian spoke by phone on 15 September to Kishanth’s relatives in India, which hosts a large, effectively stateless Sri Lankan Tamil population. His mother said he was transferred from Diego Garcia to the Maldives six months ago because of the US-Iran war. A month later, she said, he was brought to Eswatini, where he received two successive three-month visas, the second of which was due to expire on 20 September. Swaziland News reported in July that an agreement between the UK and Eswatini governments allowed Kishanth to stay in the country permanently. “At the end of the period of up to three years, the UK will no longer cover any costs of the continued presence of the Relocated Migrant in Eswatini. The Relocated Migrant is expected to be self-sustaining as a member of Eswatini society,” reads an excerpt of the agreement, according to the local outlet. An Eswatini lawmaker criticised the country’s prime minister for turning the country into a “dumping ground” by admitting a “delinquent” from Sri Lanka. On 15 September, the Times of Eswatini reported that a Sri Lankan national “was found hanging from the rafters at a guest house” the previous weekend, prompting a police investigation. The New Humanitarian has approached the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and the BIOT administration for clarification on Kishanth’s status in Eswatini and the circumstances surrounding his death. Toufique Hossain of Duncan Lewis Solicitors, which represented Kishanth in legal challenges to the UK and BIOT governments, said he was not authorised to comment. Kishanth had been “ tortured, sexually assaulted and abused ” by Sri Lankan military personnel before fleeing to India in 2007. He was one of eight members of the Diego Garcia group to be granted international protection on the basis of individual assessments, some on similar grounds. But he was barred from entering the UK with the rest of the group because of a series of criminal convictions: sexually assaulting another asylum seeker four times, assaulting and harming a security officer who tried to intervene in his suicide attempt, and arson “ in connection with an attempted suicide by self-immolation ”. “Whilst we understand the need to separate him from the community, his right to privacy and to be accommodated in a humane and dignified manner must be upheld.” In response to his behaviour and unravelling mental state, BIOT authorities kept him separate from the rest of the asylum seeker group. He was confined for around eight months in a laundry room with only supervised access to other areas of the compound and two weeks alone in a police cell with no natural light. Following a late 2023 monitoring visit, UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency, said it was “ deeply concerned ” by the conditions of his detention, citing his sleeping area’s exposure to noise, shower leaks, and toilet smells. “Whilst we understand the need to separate him from the community, his right to privacy and to be accommodated in a humane and dignified manner must be upheld,” the monitoring team said in a 2024 report. Throughout his detention, he attempted suicide numerous times, sometimes in quick succession, prompting medical evacuation to Bahrain in 2024, according to court records. The New Humanitarian spoke briefly with Kishanth following his return to Diego Garcia from medical treatment in Rwanda in 2023. In broken English, he described receiving “not correct treatment”, “no sleeping”, and being confined to a “military area”. Another asylum seeker recalled witnessing him “walking alone”, “seeing dreams”, “screaming at night”, and threatening to harm himself with a shard of a broken mirror. A psychiatrist quoted in 2024 court proceedings said “it is very difficult for him to be so isolated for an indefinite period”, and ending his isolation “would hugely improve his mental health”. In 2025, a UK court dismissed Kishanth’s legal challenge to being barred from the country, allowing the government to base its decision on public safety concerns. With return to Sri Lanka ruled out and the UK refusing him admission, his only remaining solution was relocation to a third country. His mother told The New Humanitarian he sounded depressed when they spoke on 13 September, the same day his body was found. She had asked him to come back to India. Seemingly unaware or disbelieving his stay in Eswatini was permanent, he told his mother he was planning on waiting there for a few days before being sent to a third country. If you are in crisis, click here to find a helpline near you (via the International Association for Suicide Prevention). Edited by Andrew Gully. body: Home Middle East and North Africa Yemen Related stories Conflict Analysis 14 September 2026 How Rwanda-backed M23 rebels finance their war in DR Congo Conflict Opinion 11 September 2026 Visible crises, invisible people Conflict Analysis 9 September 2026 Finding a path to peace: Nigeria’s long, faltering history of dialogue with Boko Haram Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email TAIZ, Yemen Some 125,000 people have been forced from their homes across Yemen in the past two weeks as a major new escalation linked to both the US-Iran conflict and Yemen’s own nearly 12-year war deepens hardship for millions already struggling to survive. Hafedhaa Murshed had spent more than five years in a displacement site in western Taiz province before clashes broke out on 3 September near the site where she, her husband, and their seven children were staying. As the fighting drew nearer, the family grabbed their most valuable and lightest possessions. “We walked nearly three kilometres on foot,” Murshed told The New Humanitarian, speaking from the makeshift camp elsewhere in Taiz where they are now staying. “There were no vehicles to transport our belongings, so we arrived here with only a few kitchen utensils and a blanket.” Taiz has long been a flashpoint of Yemen’s war. Fighting, sieges, and restrictions on aid and trade access have been hallmarks of life in the southwestern province for years . Houthi rebels and a coalition of fighters allied with the internationally recognised government have been fighting since early 2015, and Taiz lies between territory currently controlled by the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government. A 2022 truce had ushered in a period of relative calm, but the Houthis (officially called Ansar Allah) launched an offensive on multiple fronts in early September, part of their bid to control the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait. Saudi Arabia has hit back with airstrikes and the United States has reportedly sent advisers to aid the kingdom’s military efforts, raising fears of a return to all-out war. Controlling the strait allows the Houthis – who have ties to Iran – to further block Saudi Arabia from exporting oil via the Red Sea (the kingdom has been using the strait to export oil since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz). It is also part of the longstanding stated goal of the Houthis to take the Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed fighters. While the reasons behind the new offensive are murky and complex, the impact on Yemen’s most vulnerable civilians – among them more than 5.2 million who were already displaced before this uptick in fighting – have been clear and direct. Like many others, Murshed was already dealing with extreme poverty before her latest displacement. But she had been staying with another displaced relative, who at least shared their mattresses and blankets. The UN reports that 125,000 people have been newly displaced in just two weeks and the numbers are rising quickly – including tens of thousands in Taiz alone . Entire communities are being forced from their homes, and some are now fleeing the country altogether, with the UN’s migration agency reporting that 2,000 people have reached Djibouti's northern shores . With the response to Yemen’s humanitarian crisis already chronically underfunded, and now compounded by the economic impacts of the US-Iran war, people like Murshed are finding themselves trapped in an endless cycle of displacement, with little to no assistance. “Our life wasn’t perfect, but at least we had a safe camp,” Murshed said of life at the previous site, which was already her family’s second displacement. “The fighting has forced us to flee again, and to begin the suffering of displacement and starting from scratch again.” Khalid Al-Banna/TNH When Hafedhaa Murshed fled the camp where she lived with her family for the past five years, she was only able to take a few cooking supplies and a blanket. Fuel prices and day wages Long before Murshed and her family were forced to leave their camp, Yemen’s economic crisis was already battering people like her far from the front lines. “Even before we fled last week, we lacked many of the basics because work opportunities were scarcer than before. Men would leave in the morning looking for work and return by midday empty-handed,” Murshed explained. The growing regional fallout from the Iran-US conflict triggered a sharp surge in fuel prices across government-controlled areas in Yemen. A 20-litre container of diesel has jumped from 25,000 YER ($17) in May – several months after the war began – to 45,000 YER ($30) today. A source at the Yemeni Petroleum Company in Aden told Reuters in May that the rise in fuel prices – even back then – was the result of a supply crisis and rising global fuel prices driven by the regional conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. That surge has had a cascading effect since, driving up the cost of goods and services that are dependent on fuel and transportation – including construction materials – hitting day labourers first. The only jobs that many displaced men like Murshed’s husband can get now are day-by-day jobs on construction sites or loading and unloading building supplies at local shops. “I don’t remember a time in my life when we ate only bread and tea for breakfast and dinner like we do now. We buy just enough food to stay alive because our income doesn't allow for more, and we can't afford the food we actually want.” Murad Thabet, a construction worker in his 50s who has worked in the industry across various parts of Yemen, described the current crisis as “the worst in his life”. “I have been working for around 40 years, but these days are the worst,” he told The New Humanitarian. “The price of building materials is rising dramatically, so many contractors and property owners have halted work until things stabilise.” Thabet, who is displaced from his village in the southwest of the province and rents a home in Taiz city for his wife and three children, said many day labourers are struggling to provide their families with basic necessities. “I don’t remember a time in my life when we ate only bread and tea for breakfast and dinner like we do now,” he added. “We buy just enough food to stay alive because our income doesn't allow for more, and we can't afford the food we actually want.” Thabet stressed that his main problem is the lack of job opportunities rather than the cost of food itself. This has long been the case in Yemen, where economic collapse as a result of their own 12-year war has been a major driver of hunger. US-funded food insecurity monitor FEWS NET has consistently said that displaced people and those without income are of greatest concern across a country where 15-16 million people are expected to need food aid through September – not taking into account this month’s developments. “If we have an income, we can buy food even if prices rise a bit,” said Thabet. “But when we have no work, as is the case now, we cannot afford food even if it is cheap.” Nasser al-Sakkaf/TNH In Taiz, construction remains one of the few jobs open to displaced people, 4 July 2026. Competition and sacrifice Thabet said he is among many men who wait at the same spot in Taiz every morning looking for work. Most leave disappointed. “When someone arrives looking for one labourer, around 10 people run after him and accept any wage because they desperately need work,” he said. Abdullah Mohammed, a displaced father of three in his late 30s, recently lost his job as a construction worker and guard at a building site in Taiz. Before the building’s owner suspended construction in May and dismissed all the workers, it was enough for Mohammed to rent a home and take care of his family. “The building owner told us he would resume construction when things calm down and prices drop, but it seems he won’t anytime soon because things are

body: Home Global Related stories Aid and Policy Cheat Sheet 11 September 2026 UK condemns “settler terrorists”, Sudan’s chemical weapons exposed, and Yemen’s war escalates Aid and Policy Interview 10 September 2026 “When do you put your foot down?” Why this de-mining group is rejecting US funding Aid and Policy Podcasts 10 September 2026 Rethinking Humanitarianism | Will aid-for-hire become the new normal? Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email GENEVA The Trump administration dismantled aid and attacked the global system as wasteful. Now a Trump pick looks set to lead one of the world’s biggest humanitarian agencies. US agriculture official Luke Lindberg will be named the new head of the World Food Programme, two aid officials familiar with the selection process told The New Humanitarian. Officially, the UN secretary-general and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s director-general choose the WFP leader, in consultation with WFP’s executive board. A special session of WFP’s board is scheduled for 18 September. A letter shared within humanitarian circles also confirms Lindberg as the pick. News of Lindberg’s pending appointment was first reported by Devex over the weekend. Is the World Food Programme getting Luke Lindberg, “America First” Trump appointee, or Luke Lindberg, rookie international civil servant and impartial humanitarian leader? It follows months-long delays in choosing a new executive director at WFP – and for some, worry over what putting a Trump-aligned pick at the heart of the emergency aid system will mean. WFP has been without an official executive director since Cindy McCain announced her departure earlier this year, citing health concerns. Lindberg’s selection would continue a long history of opaque UN appointments and American dominance at the helm of WFP. The executive director role has been held by an American since 1992, under the UN’s practice of backroom horse-trading key roles. It’s also another example of top leadership jobs going to the politically connected, whether at UN agencies or big NGOs . Lindberg is the son-in-law of US Senate majority leader John Thune , and currently undersecretary for trade and foreign agricultural affairs in the US Department of Agriculture. Lindberg appears to have no experience in emergency response, but he will join a UN agency that is often seen as the lynchpin of the international humanitarian system. His public record so far contrasts sharply with the neutrality and impartiality principles that the humanitarian sector often foregrounds. Lindberg has voiced support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (who has an active arrest warrant for war crimes accusations), and touted weapons exports amid the Israeli military’s onslaught on Gaza. Critics say the US is increasingly co-opting the humanitarian system along ideological lines – using funding and policy to align aid with geopolitical interests , and to sideline reproductive health and equity, for example. Lindberg will lead a key agency at a time of deep budget cuts, severe hunger, and spiralling emergencies – in some cases in crises provoked by US military actions and US government policies. Some 151.6 million people face crisis levels of hunger or worse, according to famine analysts . Crises are spiralling, deepened by conflict, climate change, and the flouting of international laws. At the same time, donor funding cuts have left the global emergency response system at a breaking point , triaging budgets to target only a fraction of the more than 239 million people said to need emergency aid. WFP’s projected funding this year sits at around $6.4 billion – less than half of what it was in 2022 , and its lowest in about a decade. The US funds about 30% of the agency’s budget. Here are four key questions: Who does Lindberg answer to? Is the World Food Programme getting Luke Lindberg, “America First” Trump appointee, or Luke Lindberg, rookie international civil servant and impartial humanitarian leader? The Trump administration has used foreign aid funding as a hammer: It steers its humanitarian and health money to align with geopolitical interests instead of needs; and sharpened its discriminatory global gag rule to sideline reproductive health and equity programmes funded by other donors. This has put an extra spotlight on the delayed search for a new WFP chief. Will they be beholden to Washington, or to the organisation’s humanitarian mandate? “We never really had to ask this question before for a UN appointee quite so explicitly,” said Sam Vigersky, a former US humanitarian adviser and now a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a New York-based think tank. “That to me in itself is a concerning development in our field.” Before the Trump administration backed Lindberg for the UN role, other rumoured candidates had pushed to make US support to WFP conditional on aligning with foreign policy interests, Vigersky said. Lindberg hasn’t outlined such plans, and should be judged based on what he does when he starts at WFP, he said. “Is Lindberg able to unlock sums of money from the Congress and the Trump administration that otherwise would be sidelined because there wasn’t an insider at the helm... or does this end up being an appointment to a multilateral agency that ends up running a political operation for the Trump administration to potentially be punitive towards NGOs they think are critical of the administration,” Vigersky said. “A lot of the aid coming out of [the] State Department has directly framed how they are making decisions. So I’m going to be looking for the firewall between the two.” Many of the issues at the heart of WFP’s work may contradict the current US administration’s interests – from climate change as a cause of crises, to famine declarations that are politically inconvenient for allies like Israel, to pushing back on aid cuts. Still a US government official for now, Lindberg’s recent public comments have defended the cuts as a sort of “level-setting”. ”This idea that we’re retreating is an unfair characterisation of the pause that was taken to re-evaluate and re-design some of the structures and the way in which we do business,” Lindberg said during a CFR briefing this month. A study in The Lancet estimated that donor cuts could lead to 9.4 million deaths by 2030. In his short time in the agriculture department, Lindberg has been open about using US aid for US interests. The USDA-managed Food for Peace programme, which sends US commodities as food assistance, now targets only a handful of countries , after a restructuring overseen by Lindberg. It notably leaves out several countries facing severe levels of hunger – such as Mali, Somalia, Sudan, or Yemen – while including some that are not. These choices balanced hunger needs, the availability of distribution partners, and “the geopolitical interests of the United States”, Lindberg said . How do other humanitarian agencies see Lindberg? Lindberg is mostly unknown in humanitarian circles, but his social media feed has done most of the talking so far. His personal accounts have been peppered with pro-Israel posts, pics of Lindberg grinning and gripping a rifle to be exported to the Israeli military, and plenty of cowboy hats. A newer Twitter account created for his WFP bid presents a milder image, tinted with shades of UN blue, frequent retweets of WFP posts, and inoffensive statements about resilience and ending hunger. Lindberg is “obviously MAGA” and the gun pics are concerning, but he appears to be less risky than other names floated for key positions, one aid official told The New Humanitarian. “Basically, I think he’s someone we can work with,” said the official, who compared Lindberg’s potential to that of David Beasley, the former South Carolina governor appointed as WFP executive director during Trump’s first term. title: Aid and Policy Analysis 15 September 2026 What will Luke Lindberg mean for WFP and humanitarians?

body: Home Americas This article is also available in French Arabic Share & more Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email NAIROBI NAIROBI, 2 November 2011 (IRIN) - More than 18 months since the earthquake struck Haiti in January 2010, women and girls living in makeshift camps remain vulnerable to sexual violence. IRIN's latest film follows a survivor of rape, Shirley Christoff, as she attempts to rebuild her life in a rundown informal settlement in Port-au-Prince. Christoff, together with thousands of other women, lives in constant fear for her safety. According to human rights organizations, continued lack of security is one of the main factors contributing to high levels of rape in and around the internal displacement camps. More than 250 cases of rape were reported in several camps in the first 150 days after the earthquake, according to Amnesty International. Sexual violence and other forms of gender-based violence were widespread in Haiti even before the earthquake. In the 1990s, Human Rights Watch (HRW) documented the use of rape as a form of oppression during the regime of Raoul Cédras. From 2004 to 2006, the UN Security Council estimated that 35,000 women and girls were subjected to rape and sexual violence. "After you have been raped, you have nowhere to go, you have to return to the camp and face the person who raped you," says Christoff. As police stations and courts were reduced to rubble during the earthquake, the few protection mechanisms that did exist were destroyed. According to Amnesty and HRW, the post-earthquake humanitarian and government response to gender-based violence has been wholly inadequate. While effort was being invested to ensure basic needs were met, little to no attention has been paid to the rights of women and girls to be protected from sexual violence. Survivors of sexual violence have taken matters into their own hands, with two grassroots organizations providing support to thousands of women. The first emergency response system dedicated to sexual violence was set up in October and a call centre has already recorded 400 cases of rape. This film is the 10th in a series of films about displacement, Forced to Flee. Others in the series include Bolivia’s Changing Climate , Israel’s African Migrants and Haiti’s Homeless Hotel . This article was produced by IRIN News while it was part of the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. Please send queries on copyright or liability to the UN.
