body: Iran As Trump Courts Xi, Pressure Mounts To Confront China Over Support For Iran By Alex Raufoglu September 25, 2026 07:25 CET As Trump Courts Xi, Pressure Mounts To Confront China Over Support For Iran Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US President Donald Trump hosts a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in Washington, D.C., on September 24. WASHINGTON -- US lawmakers and national-security experts are pressing President Donald Trump to take tougher action against Chinese entities accused of helping Iran with satellite intelligence, weapons components, and oil revenue. The calls intensified as Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the White House on September 24 for a high-stakes meeting with Trump, followed by a lavish state dinner that underscored the delicate balancing act between the world's two largest economies. Trump made no explicit mention of Iran during his public remarks with Xi despite growing pressure from lawmakers who warned that Washington risks encouraging deeper cooperation between Beijing and Tehran if it fails to impose costs. SEE ALSO: Why China Is Unlikely To Pressure Iran Ahead Of Trump-Xi Summit "This summer, it was all over the press that China gave Iran satellite imagery intelligence and that intelligence led to the death of American troops," Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the Republican chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said on the Senate floor the day Xi arrived. "So, I would certainly suggest that the president try to get an answer to that." Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and 18 other Democratic senators accused Trump of failing to hold Xi accountable for Chinese companies' alleged support for Iran. The White House has not publicly detailed whether Trump confronted Xi over the allegations in their private talks. Trump said the two had a "great meeting" on September 24, adding he and Xi "have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries." He gave few details, however. China's official Xinhua news agency said that during the meeting Xi called on Iran and the United States to resolve their problems through dialogue as soon as possible. The two leaders will meet again on September 25 before Xi heads back to China. Shaheen had earlier called on Trump to crack down on three areas of alleged Chinese support: satellite imagery and targeting assistance, components for Iranian missiles and drones, and purchases of sanctioned Iranian oil. Beijing is Tehran's most important oil customer and has significant economic leverage over Iran. But Iran represents only a small fraction of China's overall trade, giving Beijing considerably more room to maneuver than Tehran. For some US experts, however, the issue goes beyond China's relationship with Iran and raises broader questions about how Washington responds to Beijing when Chinese entities are accused of supporting countries hostile to the United States. Embed share US Senator Shaheen: China Will Feel Impact Of Russia Sanctions by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:05 0:00 Direct link 240p | 1.4MB 360p | 1.8MB 480p | 2.6MB 720p | 3.9MB 1080p | 6.4MB Mary Kissel, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute and CEO of the Kissel Group, said Washington should hold Chinese entities involved in supporting Iran accountable. "One of the great mistakes of the past several decades was the willingness of US administrations -- of both parties -- to excuse China's malign activity across the economic, military, and diplomatic spheres," Kissel told RFE/RL. "If we want China to curb its support for the Islamic republic of Iran -- which is a worthy goal -- then we need to hold Chinese state-backed banks, companies, and individuals accountable for their actions." Otherwise, she said, Washington would send a message that China "is allowed to play by a different set of rules," with implications extending to Beijing's partners in Moscow, Tehran, and Pyongyang. That concern is particularly acute over allegations that Chinese entities provided Iran with satellite imagery that could have been used in attacks on US forces. SEE ALSO: What If China Doesn't Play Ball? US Sanctions Campaign Faces Its Biggest Test Christopher Walker, vice president of the Center for European Policy Analysis, said such reports should be viewed as part of a wider strategic challenge. "Given that US intelligence have tied Chinese satellite imagery to attacks against American service members in the Middle East region, it's crucial that the US takes tougher action against Beijing, which will seek every opportunity to exploit US vulnerabilities," Walker told RFE/RL. He described Chinese support for Iran as part of Beijing's broader effort to assist like-minded governments forming what he called a loose but dangerous "axis of autocracies." The satellite-imagery allegation, however, remains contested. The Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported that Chinese entities provided Iran with high-resolution imagery of a US base in Jordan before an Iranian strike killed three US soldiers and wounded four others. Beijing has denied providing Iran with military or intelligence support. SEE ALSO: Christopher Walker: The West Must Stop Treating Russia, China, And Iran As Isolated Challenges Gawdat Bahgat, a professor of national-security affairs at the National Defense University's Near East South Asia Center for Strategic Studies, urged caution about treating the allegations as established fact. "Both China and Iran have not confirmed sharing satellite imagery [or] weapons components," Bahgat told RFE/RL. At the same time, Bahgat said, Beijing has a clear economic interest in maintaining its relationship with Tehran, particularly through the purchase of discounted Iranian oil. "I doubt that China will stop buying Iranian oil," he said. Citing the US Treasury Department, Shaheen said 90 percent of Iran's oil exports go to China, generating billions of dollars for Tehran despite US sanctions. She said much of the trade moves through shadow fleets, front companies, and Chinese refineries. In an interview with RFE/RL last week, Shaheen also said Iran was receiving targeting information from both China and Russia to help strike American assets. Republican Senator John Kennedy made a similar argument on September 24, telling reporters that Xi could use Beijing's influence to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Xi "could open up that strait with a phone call," Kennedy said, while accusing China of assisting Iran with military equipment and intelligence. The pressure from lawmakers comes amid deep partisan divisions over the broader US war with Iran. At the White House on September 24, the emphasis was on dialogue and strategic stability. Xi said he and Trump held "sincere and in-depth exchanges" and reached a "common understanding on many issues" but did not specify whether Iran was among them. According to China's state-run Xinhua news agency, Xi told Trump that Beijing supported a return by Washington and Tehran to an earlier agreement aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Trump, meanwhile, had already signaled reluctance to publicly confront Xi over allegations of Chinese intelligence support to Iran. body: News US Pushes To Turn Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Deal Into Investment Opportunity By Alex Raufoglu September 24, 2026 13:26 CET US Pushes To Turn Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Deal Into Investment Opportunity Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov whispers in the ear of his Armenian counterpart, Ararat Mirzoyan, during a meeting about the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) in New York on September 23. NEW YORK -- The Trump administration is trying to turn a US-brokered opening between Armenia and Azerbaijan into something more tangible: a transport corridor linking Central Asia and the South Caucasus with Western markets and an investment opportunity for American companies. Senior regional officials and executives from more than 40 companies gathered in New York on September 23 to discuss the next steps for the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a centerpiece of Washington's efforts to turn the Armenia-Azerbaijan opening into greater regional trade and investment. The event, held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, featured US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Republican Senator Steve Daines of Montana, as well as officials from Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and the five Central Asian states. The challenge now is turning a political agreement into steel, asphalt, and investment. No construction has begun, feasibility studies are still under way, and companies are not expected to begin competing for major contracts until late 2026 or early 2027. Washington envisions TRIPP as a multimodal corridor through southern Armenia linking Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave while creating a wider east-west connection between the South Caucasus, Central Asia, and Western markets. Map: Proposed Trump Route For International Peace And Prosperity (TRIPP) The proposed Armenian section is only about 43 kilometers long, but it seeks to resolve one of the most contentious issues to emerge from decades of conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan: how to connect mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. Armenia and Azerbaijan fought two major wars over Nagorno-Karabakh, an internationally recognized part of Azerbaijan that for decades had a predominantly ethnic-Armenian population. Azerbaijan regained full control of the territory in 2023, prompting almost all of its ethnic-Armenian population to flee. The two countries agreed on the text of a peace treaty in March 2025 but have yet to complete a final agreement. At a White House summit five months later, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a US-brokered joint declaration aimed at ending decades of conflict and opening regional transport links. TRIPP emerged from that agreement. TRIPP is intended to provide unimpeded transit between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan through Armenian territory while preserving Armenia's sovereignty, territorial integrity and jurisdiction -- a politically important provision given long-running disputes over control of the route. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev (left) and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian at a meeting in Bishkek last month. The project would be developed by a US-Armenian company in which the United States would have a controlling stake, giving Washington a significant role in a strategically important region where Russia has traditionally wielded considerable influence. Under the plan, the Armenian section would eventually carry rail and road links as well as energy and digital infrastructure. From Peace Deal To Trade Route Witkoff credited Pashinian and Aliyev with recognizing that a peace agreement offered a better alternative to decades of conflict. "Unlike many other conflicts that we see in the world, we had all the ingredients of a deal here," Witkoff said, describing the two leaders as "incredibly pragmatic and mature." He also credited Trump with pushing the process forward after US officials found communication between Yerevan and Baku had stalled. The focus in New York, however, was on whether the diplomatic opening can now produce economic benefits. Witkoff said the economic implications of TRIPP had become increasingly apparent as officials and companies examined its potential role in international supply chains. "Everybody's focused now on transmission and speed to market," he said, citing estimates that the route could cut some trade journeys by up to three weeks. TRIPP could feed into the wider Trans-Caspian, or Middle Corridor, an east-west network carrying goods between China and Central Asia through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus, and onward to Europe. The route has attracted increased attention as governments and businesses seek alternatives to traditional transit routes through Russia. Witkoff said he expected the project to generate "huge investment," particularly in Armenia. Speaking separately in New York on September 23, Pashinian said implementation of TRIPP would "fully unlock" regional connectivity and "open a new era" for Armenia and its economy. For now, however, the corridor remains largely on paper. The State Department says engineering and feasibility studies are examining the proposed railway route, including technical, environmental, and social considerations. A separate pre-feasibility study is looking at placing energy and digital infrastructure alongside transportation links. Officials expect the railway feasibility work to be completed by late 2026 or early 2027, after which companies could bid for contracts. Construction of the railway would take at least another 18 months, while electricity connections could potentially begin operating in 2027. Bringing In US Capital Washington is also building financial and corporate structures intended to turn those plans into investable projects. The United States and Armenia are establishing a TRIPP Development Company, a joint venture in which Washington is expected to hold a majority stake and which would oversee infrastructure development and competitive tenders. A separate Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund is intended to mobilize private capital for connectivity projects across the wider region. SEE ALSO: Armenia Courts Central Asia As TRIPP Corridor Takes Shape Andrew D'Anieri, associate director of the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center, said the two initiatives signaled deeper US economic engagement. "Advancing TRIPP and announcing the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund in the presence of senior regional officials and major US companies sends a strong signal that America means business," D'Anieri told RFE/RL. "TRIPP will advance more slowly given the degree of technical project difficulty and geopolitical sensitivities," he said. A New Route Through A Crowded Region Those sensitivities extend well beyond Armenia and Azerbaijan. The South Caucasus connects Europe with Central Asia in a region where Russia, China, Iran, and Turkey all have significant interests. Angela Howard, a research analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies' Center on Economic and Financial Power, said US-backed infrastructure could create new trade links while reducing dependence on Russian-controlled or influenced routes. "US investment in the Caucasus places an American foot in the gateway to Central Asia," she told RFE/RL. SEE ALSO: US Congressman Abraham Hamadeh: Armenia-Azerbaijan Peace Deal Could Come Before Trump's Term Ends She cautioned, however, that US-backed projects would require safeguards against corruption and foreign influence. "Strong guardrails and extensive oversight will be critical moving forward," Howard said. Daines said Washington needed to sustain its engagement and argued that the region should be viewed not only through the lens of past conflicts but also as a potential hub for trade and investment. summary: The Trump administration is trying to turn a US-brokered opening between Armenia and Azerbaijan into something more tangible: a transport corridor linking Central Asia and the South Caucasus with Western markets -- and an investment opportunity for American companies.
title: US Pushes To Turn Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Deal Into Investment Opportunity

body: Features Amid Russian Provocations And Warnings Over Possible Attack, Europe Mulls Contingency Plans By Alex Raufoglu and Rikard Jozwiak September 23, 2026 15:14 CET Amid Russian Provocations And Warnings Over Possible Attack, Europe Mulls Contingency Plans Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google NATO troops at a training exercise near Poland's border with Lithuania. (file photo) NEW YORK/BRUSSELS -- Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics disagrees with the mounting calls and reports that Russia may attack NATO or the European Union in the coming months in an attempt to weaken their support for Ukraine. He says they've already started. "We are not talking about a conventional war. We are talking about all kinds of provocations, all kinds of acts of sabotage, all kinds of tests, and definitely this is something that is already happening as we speak," the Latvian leader told RFE/RL in an interview at United Nations headquarters on September 21. European intelligence officials, the CIA, and even French President Emmanuel Macron and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk have all warned in recent days of assessments that Moscow may go as far as to launch an air attack in some form on NATO territory in the coming months to show the military alliance's Article 5 common defense pledge is little more than a few words on a piece of paper. Latvian President: Putin Still Believes He Can Win In Ukraine by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:15 0:00 Instances of attacks in recent months attributed to Russia -- what the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) calls a "coordinated series of kinetic campaigns" -- include arson, assassination plans, and the sabotage of infrastructure, such as railway vandalism and electronic interference. Moscow consistently denies any involvement in the sabotage operations attributed to it by European governments, but officials from NATO and EU capitals have ramped up efforts to draw up contingency plans and measures to counteract. The Narva Scenario One such scenario is the so-called Narva scenario, which describes a hypothetical military scenario in which Russia would attack a NATO country using hybrid warfare tactics similar to the initial phase of the actual 2014 Russian invasion of Ukraine's Crimea. Narva is a small city with a sizeable Russian population on the Estonian side of the border with Russia. Analysts have said that such a move from Russia could be taken as a means to test NATO's willingness to risk a direct confrontation over strategically insignificant territory. SEE ALSO: Ratcliffe's Moscow Warning: What We Know A Week Later, According To Ex-CIA Officers Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna warned of growing Russian hybrid attacks across Europe in an interview with RFE/RL this week, saying there are lots of rumors that Putin is going to wage a full-scale military operation against the Baltic states or Poland. But, he added, "our intelligence doesn’t see any serious military movements on the other side of our borders because Russia is stuck in Ukraine." Analysts at the ISW, however, said on September 21 that while Estonia and Latvia have both said that they have yet to observe any evidence of a buildup of Russian forces near their borders that would be necessary for a full-scale invasion of their countries, "scenarios for Russian action have not received the detailed analysis they deserve and require." SEE ALSO: US, Poland Making Progress On Permanent American Army Base, Trump Says RFE/RL contacted several diplomats with knowledge of EU and NATO preparedness planning, but none would give concrete examples of what is in the works saying the information was classified. One Central European official acknowledged that there are informal discussions on a working level on what to do logistically in case the Baltics and Poland are attacked, but added there are no official guidelines and real preparations in place. A NATO official said the alliance has the national defense plans of members, "which are top secret but essentially spell out what we do in all types of war scenarios." Rinkevics said calling the current wave of Russian attacks "hybrid" may also be stifling the urgency needed among European officials to address the situation. "I think that when we use the word "hybrid," then it somehow sounds less, let's say, dangerous, kind of more innocent terminology than actually those acts per se," he said. "I think that the most dangerous scenario would be if Russia gets reckless, if we do not respond in an efficient manner and there are real casualties happening...Our part of Europe is trying to be as ready as possible. But look, if Russia launches a missile attack, then it is absolutely clear this is Article 5, and then it's absolutely clear that there is going to be a response." A Permanent US Base In Poland? The increased tensions have caught the attention of Washington, which has been looking at its European troop deployments, basing arrangements, status-of-forces agreements, and general host-nation negotiations. Last week, US President Donald Trump says Washington and Warsaw are making "major progress" toward establishing a permanent US Army base in Poland, potentially expanding the American military presence on NATO's eastern flank. The move came a day after Polish authorities temporarily closed airports in Lublin and Rzeszow as Russian strikes targeted parts of Ukraine near the Polish border, according to Polish officials. He too said such incidents could be intended to test NATO's response and undermine allied unity. The assessment was based on intelligence from NATO, Ukraine, and the United States, according to Tusk. Similarly, the Baltics were rattled last year when three Russian jet fighters violated Estonia’s airspace for 12 minutes. According to Estonian officials, the Russian pilots acknowledged but disregarded communication from two Italian pilots in F-35 fighter jets, which had been scrambled from NATO’s Baltic Air Policing Mission in Amari Air Base in Estonia, before ultimately being escorted into international skies. The strike came on the same day that another attack drone struck a Warsaw-bound passenger train at a Ukrainian station nearby. summary: In the wake of intelligence reports that Russia may be planning an attack on NATO, questions have arisen over whether European officials have contingency plans ready to deal with such an event.
title: Amid Russian Provocations And Warnings Over Possible Attack, Europe Mulls Contingency Plans

body: Afghanistan An Afghan Mother And Her Daughters Left Their Homeland In Search Of A Better Life. They Died Of Thirst By RFE/RL's Radio Azadi September 23, 2026 14:30 CET An Afghan Mother And Her Daughters Left Their Homeland In Search Of A Better Life. They Died Of Thirst Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Afghan refugees deported from Iran return to their homeland. (file photo) When Nizam Hematkhil heard the news, he rushed to a remote corner of Iran near the border with Pakistan. A group of illegal migrants from Afghanistan had died in Iran’s southeastern province of Sistan-Baluchistan. When Hematkhil arrived in the village of Mak Sukhteh, he found the bodies of his stepmother and her four daughters. “The cause of their deaths was thirst,” Hematkhil told RFE/RL’s Radio Azadi. “I personally recovered their bodies.” They were among the 17 Afghans who died of extreme dehydration in mid-September after crossing Iran through Pakistan, according to foreign-based Iranian human rights group Haalvsh . The deaths have highlighted the dangers faced by Afghan migrants and refugees who risk crossing illegally into Iran to escape extreme poverty and the Taliban’s repressive rule. Locator map: Sistan-Baluchistan, Iran and Balochistan, Pakistan Escaping Extreme Poverty Hematkhil’s stepmother and her daughters, who were aged between six and 15, had been on their way to join him in Iran. The family had all moved to Iran in search of a better life, but most of them returned to Afghanistan last year. “Instead of finding a way to start over, we exhausted all our savings and resources," said Hematkhil, whose family are from the northern Afghan province of Baghlan. “There was little work and no realistic way for the family to support themselves.” “Consequently, they were compelled to return to Iran to survive, as there was practically no other option left," he added. The Taliban’s seizure of power in 2021 worsened one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises. Without international development assistance, the Afghan economy has further shrunk as joblessness and poverty rise. Meanwhile, the hard-line Islamist group has committed gross human rights violations, including extrajudicial killings and torture, leading to an exodus to neighboring countries. Embed share Five Afghan Family Members Die Of Thirst While Trying To Reach Iran by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:20 0:00 Critical Condition Hematkhil’s stepmother and her young girls had crossed into Iran without taking water with them, said a relative who accompanied them on the journey. Hematkhil’s stepmother's son, who was also with them, survived. "The son was in critical condition. He had left the women behind," the relative said. "Locals transported him to [the Iranian town of] Saravan, and fortunately, he is doing well." A Taliban diplomatic source confirmed to Radio Azadi that a mother and her four daughters died on September 11 due to severe thirst while crossing Iran. But the source disputed Haalvash’s claim that 17 Afghans had died. Haalvsh released a video appearing to show locals digging graves. Another video purportedly shows people listening to a sermon in Pashto, one of Afghanistan’s two main languages. SEE ALSO: The Iranian Border Is Increasingly Deadly For Afghans Deadly Routes For decades, millions of Afghans fleeing war, persecution, and poverty have sought refuge in Iran. Hundreds of thousands more have moved to the Islamic republic since 2021. The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, estimates that around 4.5 million Afghans live in Iran, including more than 2 million undocumented migrants. Many undocumented Afghans pay traffickers to smuggle them into Iran. The journey is arduous, and migrants often have to cross remote stretches of desert and mountains where food and water are scarce. In July, the bodies of 14 Afghan migrants were found in a desert in southeastern Afghanistan near the border with Iran. The group was believed to have been attempting to cross illegally into Iran. Similar cases have been reported in the past, with migrants dying after running out of water or food. Embed share Iranian Film Casts Real Refugees To Show Plight Of Displaced Afghans by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:04:13 0:00 Crossing the 921-kilometer-long border has become increasingly dangerous for many Afghans as Iran violently cracks down on illegal migrants. At least 10 Afghans were shot dead by Iranian border guards in December, according to Taliban officials, after they entered Iran illegally from western Afghanistan's Farah Province. Seven others were shot dead by border guards in November. The incidents underscore the risks Afghans are willing to take to escape poverty and the dire economic situation in their country. "They think about their futures, believing that if they reach Iran, they can at least find work and earn an income to provide a better life for their families,” Sefatullah Zahedi, a Germany-based migrant rights activist, told Radio Azadi. body: News US Set To Unveil Next Steps for Trump-Backed Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Corridor By Alex Raufoglu September 23, 2026 13:58 CET US Set To Unveil Next Steps for Trump-Backed Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Corridor Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (left) and Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan after signing an agreement related to the TRIPP project in Yerevan in May. NEW YORK, United States -- The United States is set to unveil the next stage of its effort to develop the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP, a planned transport and infrastructure corridor through southern Armenia that Washington says could open new trade routes between the South Caucasus, Central Asia, and Western markets. Senior State Department officials told reporters that the New York event on September 23 will focus on the institutional and financial mechanisms needed to move TRIPP from last year's Armenia-Azerbaijan peace initiative toward implementation. The event is expected to bring together the foreign ministers of Armenia and Azerbaijan, representatives of the five Central Asian states -- with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan showing particular interest -- US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Republican Senator Steve Daines, and executives from more than 40 companies, many of them American. Officials said the event will highlight how TRIPP aims to "pop the cork" on the Middle Corridor, unlocking a westward trade route that connects Europe to Central Asia while reducing reliance on transit through Russia, China, and Iran. Map: Proposed Trump Route For International Peace And Prosperity (TRIPP) The gathering will also feature the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund, which officials said will invest in opportunities arising from TRIPP and the wider Trans-Caspian trade route. The fund operates at arm's length from the US government under a White House-appointed board and receives grant funding from the State Department. It is distinct from the TRIPP Development Company, the joint US-Armenian corporate entity being established to develop and oversee the corridor. 'A Major Security Issue' TRIPP is intended to provide unimpeded access between Azerbaijan proper and its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory while respecting Armenia's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security. "This becomes a major security issue for us," the official said, describing the removal of existing trade "choke points" as a central objective. The transit route will be developed and managed by a US-controlled company, giving Washington exclusive rights while effectively excluding Russia from a strategically important project in one of its traditional spheres of influence. SEE ALSO: Armenia Courts Central Asia As TRIPP Corridor Takes Shape The project emerged from an August 2025 White House summit at which Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a US-brokered joint declaration aimed at ending decades of conflict between the two South Caucasus neighbors. Armenia and Azerbaijan fought two major wars over Nagorno-Karabakh, an internationally recognized part of Azerbaijan that for decades had a predominantly ethnic-Armenian population. Azerbaijan regained full control of the territory in 2023, prompting almost all of its ethnic Armenia population to flee. The two sides agreed on the text of a peace treaty in March 2025, but a final agreement has yet to be completed. Officials said there have been no cease-fire violations since the August summit and pointed to limited trade in fuel and agricultural products as evidence of growing economic integration. According to them, Azerbaijani fuel supplies have contributed to an estimated 20 to 30 percent decline in Armenian fuel costs. They noted there had been more interaction between Washington and Baku during the previous 13 to 14 months than during the preceding 13 to 14 years. A senior State Department official said Yerevan and Baku were acting as though peace were "inevitable," although additional steps remain before a final agreement can be completed. Washington intends to develop TRIPP in parallel with that process, arguing that greater economic integration could help remove remaining obstacles. Physical Construction Still Some Way Off Despite plans to move TRIPP toward implementation, construction of the roughly 43-kilometer section through Armenia is not yet ready to begin. The section is expected to include a railway, road, pipelines, electricity infrastructure, and digital data links. The senior State Department official said Azerbaijan has already been building infrastructure toward the Armenian border at its own expense, while Turkey is similarly developing infrastructure up to the border. The remaining section through Armenia is still to be developed. “We're not there yet,” the official said when asked how soon physical construction of the Armenian section could begin. The administration hopes to begin looking for business and investment opportunities by the end of 2026 or the first quarter of 2027. SEE ALSO: US Congressman Abraham Hamadeh: Armenia-Azerbaijan Peace Deal Could Come Before Trump's Term Ends The railway will take longer. A feasibility study is expected by the end of 2026 or early 2027, after which companies will be able to bid. The official said completing the railway would likely take at least 18 months, complicated by difficult topography. Electricity connections could come sooner. Discussions are already underway, with officials expecting electricity operations to begin in 2027, potentially linking the Armenian and Azerbaijani grids with wider Central Asia, Turkish, and European regional networks. Passenger rail is also planned. TRIPP Leadership The briefers provided more detail about the planned structure of the TRIPP Development Company (TDC) but no names for its future leadership. The TDC is being established as a corporate joint venture between the US government and Armenia. The senior State Department official described it as a first-of-its-kind arrangement in which the US will hold a majority stake, with its own board, voting procedures, and management. Several legal matters still need to be finalized before the company can formally be announced. Projects involving rail, roads, electricity, oil, gas, and data will go through regular tender processes for construction or concessions. The US Development Finance Corporation (DFC) has been involved in the legal and institutional setup, but the TDC itself will operate as a separate US-Armenian corporate entity. The United States is prepared to invest once feasibility studies establish that individual projects are commercially viable. The State Department is financing part of the feasibility work, with engineering firm AECOM set to present investors with projects unlocked by TRIPP during the event on September 23. 'A Difficult Neighborhood' Officials described TRIPP as an alternative to existing east-west routes, with the proposed corridor offering Central Asian trade another route to Western markets that bypasses Russia and Iran. SEE ALSO: Russia Uses Economic Chokehold To Counter Armenia's Westward Tilt The senior State Department official said Washington had held discussions with regional competitors but declined to characterize their private views. "There have been numerous conversations with all of the competitors in the region," the official said, adding that Washington was aware of the potential for "hard conversations" in what officials called a difficult neighborhood. The event is intended to mark a shift from the 2025 peace initiative toward implementation, with more than 40 companies attending. The project still requires completing feasibility studies, legal arrangements, financing, tendering, and ultimately construction. While Washington says Armenia and Azerbaijan are on an
summary: The United States is set to unveil the next stage of TRIPP, a planned transport corridor through southern Armenia that Washington says could open new trade routes linking the South Caucasus and Central Asia with Western markets.
title: US Set To Unveil Next Steps for Trump-Backed Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Corridor

body: Russia Investigation: Amid Setbacks In The Sahel, Russia Quietly Builds Ties In Madagascar By Mark Krutov and Sergei Dobrynin September 23, 2026 10:51 CET Investigation: Amid Setbacks In The Sahel, Russia Quietly Builds Ties In Madagascar Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Madagascar President Michael Randrianirina (left) greets Major General Andrei Averyanov, a top officer in Russia's military intelligence agency, in Madagascar on February 18. Last January, Madagascar politicians joined military officers at Ivato International Airport for the ceremonial start of new training exercises for the country’s 1st Airborne Battalion. The ceremony marked the first phrase of a program overseen by Russian instructors. The effort also included a sizable cache of unspecified Russian weaponry being transferred to the Indian Ocean island nation. Among the guests watching from a shaded pavilion was a Russian man wearing a white shirt and a blue tie: Anton Papshev, a naval officer with the Russian military intelligence agency known as GRU. Anton Papshev, a naval officer with Russia's military intelligence agency, watching a ceremony launching Russian-Madagascar military training exercises in January 2026. It wasn’t exactly clear when Papshev arrived in the country, which had been roiled in October by a coup that propelled a commander of an elite Madagascar military unit to power. But a notorious Russian general who oversees GRU operations in Africa flew into Madagascar the month prior, along with 40 members of a Russian Defense Ministry mercenary group called Africa Corps, according to a flight manifest obtained by the research organization AEOW/INPACT in partnership with Systema, RFE/RL’s Russian investigative unit. Taken together, the events are the latest sign of Russia’s quiet inroads on the strategically located island – and the latest push by Moscow to cultivate influence across Africa. Map: Russian Activities In Africa In February, the month after the ceremony, Michael Randrianirina, the colonel who became interim president following the coup, traveled to Moscow, where he was met at the airport by Major General Andrei Averyanov -- the officer who had flown to Madagascar with the Africa Corps contingent. Meeting with President Vladimir Putin, Randrianirina heartily welcomed the Russian presence in Madagascar: “In the social sphere, health care, education, as well as energy, hydrocarbons, infrastructure development, and, of course, the military sphere.” From Mali To Madagascar The effort in Madagascar comes as Russia’s wider push to cultivate economic and military ties across Africa produces mixed results. The effort dates back at least a decade, when a brash Kremlin-connected restaurateur named Yevgeny Prigozhin arrived in the Central African Republic and set up a sprawling and wildly lucrative business empire. SEE ALSO: Wagner's Successors Wage Campaign Of Terror In Central African Republic It centered on Prigozhin’s notorious mercenary company, Wagner Group, which was hired to provide security to CAR’s government and train its armed forces. In return, Prigozhin got access to gold, diamonds, timber, and other lucrative natural resources. After Prigozhin staged an abortive mutiny and was killed in a suspicious August 2023 plane crash, his businesses were broken up and taken over by private businessmen. Wagner was also broken up, with different contingents taken over by different military operations. Russia’s Defense Ministry took over one contingent, and rebranded it Africa Corps. In the Central African Republic, parts of Prigozhin’s business ventures are still operating, and Russian military personnel occupy top posts in the government’s security agencies. SEE ALSO: Wagner Fanta: Russia's Defunct Mercenary Group Hopes To Make A Killing On Bottled Water In strife-torn Libya, Russia has backed a powerful warlord, Khalifa Haftar, and built a quiet presence . However, in parts of the Sahel -- a region stretching across Africa south of the Sahara -- Africa Corps has had mixed success. In Mali, an Africa Corps contingent has filled a vacuum left when French troops were pushed out following a military coup. But the Russian troops have suffered numerous losses after attacks from rebel groups. In Niger, Africa Corps units played a role in putting down a mutiny in August. Russian personnel are also involved in guarding some 1,000 tons of Nigerien uranium yellowcake which Nigerien authorities seized from a French-owned mine and have been trying to sell and export. The yellowcake has been at the international airport in Niamey, Niger’s capital, for months. 'Special Services To The Congolese Nation' A graduate of the Ushakov Naval Institute in Russia’s Baltic Sea exclave of Kaliningrad, Papshev’s training appears to largely focus on electronic communications. In 2009, he served as an assistant to the department head at a GRU unit called the 1237th Center for Strategic Radio-Electronic Intelligence, or military unit 25137. Leaked databases show that Papshev’s family lives near a building in Moscow where GRU employees and relatives are known to reside. A few years later, in 2013, Papshev was serving as a counselor at the Russian Embassy in South Africa, a post he held for five years. SEE ALSO: Russia Hoped Africa Corps Would Replicate Wagner's Success. It's Not Going Well. He then shifted to Ethiopia, where he served as assistant military attache at the embassy in Addis Ababa, until at least 2022. Another GRU officer, Yury Mikheyev, served alongside him. As of last year, Papshev served with military unit 45807, also linked to the GRU. Among other things, that unit was involved in efforts to recruit Russian prison inmates to fight in the war against Ukraine, according to findings by RFE/RL’s Russian Service and Systema . He’s also spent time in the Republic of the Congo. Since January 2025, the Africa Corps has provided security for President Denis Sassou-Nguesso, who has ruled the country since 1979 with only a brief interruption. Russia’s activity in the Republic of the Congo intensified ahead of the March presidential election, which Sassou-Nguesso won again. On October 30, 2025, the official government newspaper of the Central African nation announced that four Russian citizens had been awarded the Order of Merit, a special commendation. A press release from the official government newspaper of the Republic of The Congo on October 30, 2025, announcing the award of four medals to Russian GRU officers. Averyanov was one of those named, along with another officer, Aleksei Orekhov, who has accompanied GRU delegations on trips around Africa since 2023. Last year, Orekhov became head of the Russian general staff’s main department for international military cooperation. Two other Russians were also listed as receiving awards: Mikheyev and Papshev. Papshev, meanwhile, traveled to Madagascar as recently as July, flying from the Indian archipelago of the Seychelles. According to documents obtained by AEOW, Papshev arrived on a privately rented jet accompanied by two Belarusian businessmen; one, Alyaksandr Zingman, has extensive interests in African mining and agriculture sectors. Zingman had been negotiating with Madagascar officials in 2025 for agriculture-related contracts. A letter sent in February 2025 by Zingman to Belarusian Foreign Minister Maksim Ryzhankou -- obtained by AEOW researchers — indicates that Zingman’s company Aftrade was slated to supply Madagascar with 360 Belarusian tractors and other equipment. SEE ALSO: Coup Plots, Poison, Hacking, Sabotage: What Is The GRU’s Unit 29155? Aftrade signed a contract worth 30.8 million euros ($35.2 millon) with the Madagascar government for "services to implement the transformation of Madagascar’s agricultural system." For citation and references to the material, please indicate: Zhanna Sagyndykova, Access to education for children of migrants in the Aktobe region of Kazakhstan: recommendations for the evidence-based decision making (policy brief) 2026, CABAR.asia. The primary objective of the study is to foster greater social integration and equal opportunities for all migrant children and, ultimately, to resolve the issue of school enrollment for all children of foreign nationals—regardless of their parents’ migration status—in accordance with the International Convention on the Rights of the Child, ratified by Kazakhstan in 1994. The publication notes that migrant children frequently face social isolation and discrimination within educational institutions. A lack of adequate social support and inclusive programs exacerbates challenges related to adaptation and academic success. The publication highlights that, following a project workshop titled “Planning an Advocacy Campaign Based on Existing Policy Briefs/White Papers,” a decision was made to adopt targeted engagement with government agencies as the primary advocacy method; this entails submitting direct inquiries to the relevant state bodies. The author proposes a series of specific recommendations for relevant agencies. In particular, Sagyndykova suggests amending the regulations governing education for the children of foreign nationals to eliminate legal conflicts and gaps, and proposes considering measures for their temporary registration and the granting of residence permits alongside their parents. It is also proposed that parents of foreign children be granted the right to choose their children’s school—a right they currently lack. Sagyndykova further argues that the term “labor migrants” needs to be clearly defined in legislation. Regional and district education departments are advised to ensure their specialists are promptly informed of any changes to bylaws concerning migrant children. Additionally, they are encouraged to develop measures to support migrant children during the adaptation process, as well as methods to monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of these measures.

body: © CABAR - Central Asian Bureau for Analytical Reporting Please make active links to the source, when using materials from this website На русском The publication “ Access to education for children of migrants in the Aktobe region of Kazakhstan: recommendations for the evidence-based decision making (white paper) ” was prepared by Zhanna Sagyndykova with the support of the IWPR Representative Office in Central Asia and the regional analytical platform CABAR.asia. For citation and references to the material, please indicate: Zhanna Sagyndykova, Access to education for children of migrants in the Aktobe region of Kazakhstan: recommendations for the evidence-based decision making (white paper) 2026, CABAR.asia. This study evaluates current policies regarding the education of migrant children in the Aktobe region of Kazakhstan and offers evidence-based recommendations to improve the situation in this area. Experts estimate that over 2 million migrants from neighboring Central Asian countries enter Kazakhstan annually. In December 2022, the Minister of Education of the Republic of Kazakhstan approved new regulations governing access to education for foreign nationals and stateless persons permanently residing in the country. The order specifies the categories of foreign nationals whose children are eligible to attend schools in Kazakhstan; however, these categories represent only a small fraction of the foreign nationals actually present in the country. Furthermore, the order contains contradictions, gaps, and inconsistencies that hinder its implementation. As a result, a large number of children of foreign nationals have been deprived of the right to school education. These include the children of irregular migrants temporarily present in the country without the right to legal employment, as well as the children of undocumented migrants, those with undetermined citizenship status, and others. The report notes that it is impossible to determine the exact number of foreign children who are ineligible to attend schools in Kazakhstan. Between December 2024 and October 2025, the “Daris-2016” Public Foundation conducted a comprehensive and detailed analysis of the situation, comprising two sequential stages: Desk research: December 2024 – March 2025; II. Data collection: February – October 2025. The analysis identified key barriers hindering access to education and educational integration for migrant children. These include gaps and contradictions in the legislative framework, a lack of awareness among migrants regarding their children’s right to education, a shortage of statistical data on key indicators, language barriers, and insufficient coordination among relevant agencies. The issues identified also result in the inadequate implementation of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration—agreements to which Kazakhstan is a party. As a result of this work, recommendations have been developed for government agencies, local self-government bodies, educational institutions, and migrant families; these recommendations aim to eliminate barriers preventing the educational integration of migrant children in the Aktobe region. Implementing these recommendations will, in particular, facilitate the development of more effective support strategies and programs, thereby creating conditions for the better adaptation of migrant children.

body: Condos in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, often use scarce potable water to support non-native plants such as roses. Credit: Walt Ohnesorge Subscribe for ads-free reading Can gardens act as a network of miniature sponge cities to have a positive impact on climate change in Central Asia? A preponderance of aesthetic decisions and other barriers hold back the adaptation of Central Asia’s cities, but individuals and local authorities can make a difference. Kyrgyzstan, and Central Asia more broadly, are experiencing stress on available groundwater reserves. As Dr. Eric Rudenshiold noted in an article for the Caspian Policy Center last year, “Driven by regional temperature increases, the region’s glaciers are melting at a rate four times faster than the global average and far faster than anticipated.” Central Asia’s glaciers feed rivers and streams throughout the year. One can easily imagine a future in which rivers run dry and entire cities are required to use only water gathered from rain that falls in just a few short months of the year. In a future like this, having the ability to retain water in place could mean the difference between thriving and ceasing to exist. Stronger storms, floods, droughts, deadly heatwaves, and mass migration are putting pressure on policymakers to follow through with plans to update infrastructure. An empty canal in Bishkek. Water from rain and glacial melt is directed through and away from the city to evaporate downstream. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge) What Can Central Asia Learn from Sponge Cities? During a public lecture in 2003, architect Kongjian Yu coined the term “sponge cities” while outlining a set of urban planning principles developed to manage water in flood-prone regions of China. Sponge cities have since been enshrined in Chinese public policy by the Chinese Communist Party as a regulatory framework for development in the country. Kyrgyzstan has been interested in China’s governance model as a way to alleviate poverty, but its development and domestic urban planning initiatives offer other lessons. Time is running out for risk-prone areas of the world to make lasting, meaningful changes in the face of climate change, and some adaptation ideas may have been overlooked in parts of Central Asia. This oversight is evidenced by the colossal loss of green space in Bishkek since the Soviet era. While Kyrgyzstan’s cities have lost greenery, China has mandated the construction of climate-resilient urban spaces. Adopting a strong approach to state funding and regulation of green spaces is likely to create jobs in the industry and holds potential, where green spaces are fruit-bearing, to reduce food insecurity. Both of these outcomes could reduce poverty in Kyrgyzstan, and Bishkek’s own Green Cities Action Plan acknowledges the need for climate resilience and adequate green spaces. However, in lieu of decisive regulatory action and funding, much of the work of adapting to new climate realities falls on individual gardeners and cooperatives. Climate change has a disproportionate impact, both geographically on specific regions of Kyrgyzstan, and particularly on marginalized communities. As members of the El-Too foundation point out, “at the municipality and political level, women are not included in the decision-making processes; all issues related to land are discussed with the participation of men mainly... The situation is especially difficult for women that are employed as invisible forces in agriculture and have no other source of income.” Miniaturizing Sponge Cities While researching this topic, we were struck by a lack of sources for community-lead gardening initiatives in Kyrgyzstan. We discovered that Bishkek has no immediately identifiable grass roots collectives piloting alternative or sustainable agriculture inside the city. Even a cursory glance at New York City yields several sources and projects, and the same is true for other global cities. It is far easier to identify the challenges, like existing attention to inefficient practices, than attempts at solutions. The scale of new development in Bishkek is profound, dwarfing initiatives to create a greener city, preserve green spaces, and retrofit existing spaces for greater efficiency. With that in mind, we considered what it might look like if individuals in Bishkek took it upon themselves to implement better water preservation systems. Homemade drip irrigation feeds an area near a condo in Bishkek, where residents improvise to utilize water efficiently during summer months. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge) One dacha owner, Asel, shared that she has never thought of climate change when managing her garden. She planted species that her landscape designer recommended, who was guided by beauty rather than water management or other climate change concerns. The same could be said about the managed gardens of some condominium buildings. Bakyt, a groundskeeper at one such building, said, “We plant roses here and use drinking water to water them.” Another dacha owner, Zarina, said she’d never seen a list of plants recommended for the local climate, but expressed interest in such a list. This interest leads us to believe that, given a coordinated campaign to make information and tools available, individuals might be easily motivated to shift their habits toward more sustainable gardening practices. A small container garden near a condo in Bishkek reflects a local desire for more green spaces. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge) As Walt Ohnesorge, an artist and designer (and one of the authors of this piece) observed of many condos in Bishkek, “they could attach a catchment system to the gutter and plant perennial, food bearing plants to save drinking water, supplement tenants’ groceries, and utilize rain water for a more efficient system.” Nuraiym Syrgak, Kyrgyzstani social researcher and ecologist, and former executive director of the El-Too Public Foundation and a board member of the Association of Legal Entities “Green Alliance of Kyrgyzstan,” shared her ideas and experience implementing ecological projects. There are things people can do, at all levels, to help the land adapt to a changing climate. She noted that specific patterns of water allocation in villages have consequences. “Water for irrigation is mainly given to large plots. Gardens and zones within the village receive little water,” Syrgak said. “Therefore, we wanted precisely these small areas to become the center of attention.” Syrgak added that women, in particular, are good agents of change. “Men tend to be skeptical of anything new, especially at first, whereas women try to apply every new thing. In this sense, women are fantastic change agents. That is why we started working with them and later brought the men on board. As a result, we ended up with a family-based approach to agriculture.” Beyond villages and gardens, parks can also be transformed into miniature sponges within urban landscapes. “We often see these trees in our parks, which are not adapted to our climate,” Syrgak noted “Of course, they are beautiful. But at the same time they do not give more function. They do not give shade. They require a lot of work. And permaculture is such a philosophy, so that a person works less. And cooperates with nature to minimize work.” Syrgak stressed that there was no clear list of priority species for cultivation to fight climate change, but the centering of local species is a good place to start. “If you look at our deserts or abandoned zones, there are always these elms, which is a local type of tree and does not require watering,” Syrgak pointed out. “Then there are a lot of species like local shrubs, which could be useful for changes. body: Credit: UN Photo Subscribe for ads-free reading Amid his 20-minute remarks before the United Nations General Assembly this week, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov took time to complain about sanctions and thank U.S. President Donald Trump for ceasing support to NGOs. “...[T]oday sanctions are, in some cases, used by individual countries as an instrument of interference in the internal affairs of sovereign states,” Japarov said. “The negative consequences of unjustified unilateral sanctions also affect small countries such as ours, which are at the stage of formation and development, and this raises concern among other small states as well.” Japarov went on to claim that “some major states, in pursuit of their own interests, put pressure on smaller countries such as Kyrgyzstan, attempting to force them to bargain over certain matters and issuing ultimatums.” At no point did Japarov lay out specifically what countries he believes are pressuring Kyrgyzstan, and to what end. Then, in the middle of his commentary about sanctions, Japarov pivoted to lauding the U.S. president – although the Trump administration has maintained the prior administration’s sanctions on various Kyrgyz entities. “In this context, I would like to take this opportunity to note the decision made by the President of the United States His Excellency Mr. Donald Trump after taking office to halt funding of non-governmental organizations around the world,” Japarov said. “As a result, interference by NGOs in the internal affairs and policies of developing states has practically ceased.” For Japarov, the two issues are inextricably linked. Last year at UNGA , he stated that “sanctions imposed on Kyrgyzstan are based on false information spread by certain non-governmental organizations and malicious citizens.” Japarov has not specified which NGOs or “malicious citizens” have provided this “false information” that supposedly landed Kyrgyz business and banks on sanctions lists. In April, Kyrgyzstan’s Bakai Bank won a case in a Belgian commercial court against the Open Dialogue Foundation (ODF) for its publication of reports alleging that the bank was involved in the circumvention of sanctions against Russia. Note that the bank had not been sanctioned. The court classified the NGO as a “commercial enterprise,” opening it to liability as if it were a market competitor. As the World Liberty Congress , a global alliance of pro-democracy leaders, said in a statement: “The court required published information to meet a commercial verification standard designed for disputes between market operators, a test that is structurally impossible for any organization working in an authoritarian jurisdiction where access to primary banking records is unavailable.” Meanwhile, also in April 2026 , the EU aimed its “anti-circumvention tool” at Kyrgyzstan, the first country so targeted. In the subsequent months, Kyrgyz authorities pantomimed taking action. In June 2026, two state-owned banks claimed to have ended partnerships with more than 130 clients due to sanctions risks. In August , another round of cut connections was announced. However, Kyrgyz authorities have never specified which companies were affected, making it all but impossible to confirm whether companies that present actual sanctions risks have been cut loose. According to RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service, Azattyk , as of June 2026, 31 companies from Kyrgyzstan were under Western sanctions, including five banks. While three Tajik banks were removed from the EU sanctions list in May, the Kyrgyz banks – such as Keremet Bank , Kapital Bank, Eurasian Savings Bank , and EcoIslamicBank – remain designated by the EU, the U.K., and/or the U.S. After thanking Trump “for ending the funding of NGOs,” Japarov continued discussing sanctions, arguing that the decision to impose sanctions should “be taken in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and exclusively within the mandate of the Security Council.” Kyrgyzstan this year won a non-permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council . Japarov went on to speak of the U.N. in terms that seem divorced from the body’s current hamstrung reality. “Every decision of the United Nations should be implemented without delay. If a state fails to implement such decision and other countries cease cooperation with it, the effectiveness of sanctions will increase,” he argued. The permanent members of the UNSC – China, Russia, France, the U.K., and the U.S. – stand on diametrically opposed ends of the global order and this has effectively neutered its possible decisiveness – whether on sanctions or anything else. For example, in September 2022, Russia vetoed a Security Council resolution condemning Moscow’s attempted annexation of parts of Ukraine. The U.S. has repeatedly blocked resolutions targeting Israel . China joined Russia earlier this month to veto an effort to extend the mandate of independent experts monitoring sanctions on Iran. Suggesting that the UNSC become the central clearinghouse for all sanctions is effectively a call for there to be no sanctions, ever. Already have an account? Log in . body: Listen (1 min) Save Share Twelve Kazakh soldiers die in Caspian Sea training incident on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Kazakhstan's coastal region of Magystau, where the incident took place [Al Jazeera] By Reuters Published On 24 Sep 2026 24 Sep 2026 Twelve Kazakh military personnel have died after being swept out to sea during naval training exercises on the Caspian coast, authorities have said. The accident happened on Thursday in Kazakhstan’s western Mangystau region, which adjoins the Caspian Sea, during a combat drill mission. Seventeen personnel were swept out in total, according to preliminary information, and 12 deaths have been confirmed so far, the regional government said ⁠on Telegram. Earlier, the Ministry of Defence said nine soldiers had died. It said the servicemen died while carrying out a combat training mission, with the incident occurring following a “sudden deterioration in weather conditions and intensifying winds”. A commission led by Defence Minister Dauren Kosanov was urgently deployed to the site to establish the circumstances behind the incident and coordinate search and rescue efforts, it added. Three people have been rescued. A search and rescue operation for the remaining two personnel was still under way. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev declared a nationwide day of mourning for Friday following the incident. The Caspian is bordered by Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Turkmenistan.
title: Twelve Kazakh soldiers die in Caspian Sea training incident

body: Listen (4 mins) Save Share 20 countries propose global oversight body to manage AI dangers on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google People walk past the United Nations headquarters as the world body prepares to host world leaders for the 81st UN General Assembly in New York City, US, on September 21, 2026 [David 'Dee' Delgado/Reuters] By John Power Published On 22 Sep 2026 22 Sep 2026 Twenty countries and the European Union have issued a call for international cooperation to ensure AI remains under human control, including the potential creation of a global oversight body to set and enforce standards. The countries, including Germany, South Africa, Canada, Australia, the United Arab Emirates and Singapore, issued the joint statement on Monday as global leaders prepare to discuss the risks posed by rapidly advancing AI at the annual gathering of the United Nations General Assembly. The declaration, released by the office of Finnish President Alexander Stubb, calls on governments and industry to act immediately to ensure that AI is developed in line with international law and remains under “human direction, oversight and control”. “To realise AI’s potential, industry, governments and society must act now,” the statement says. “We must address these risks and strengthen oversight – without widening the gap between countries in access to the benefits of AI.” The declaration urges countries to develop and coordinate “common standards”, share reports of serious safety incidents, and explore the establishment of an international institution to “set standards, enable verification, and convene states when capability thresholds are crossed”. Signatories include German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Kenyan President William Ruto, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan. Advertisement The United States and China, the world’s two leading AI powers, did not join the statement, which remains “open for endorsement” by other countries. US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to discuss AI when they meet at the White House on Thursday for their third face-to-face summit in less than a year. Washington and Beijing, which are in a race to dominate cutting-edge technologies, have both rebuffed calls to slow down AI development to ensure greater safety. Other AI players not among the signatories include India, South Korea, Japan, the UK and France. The declaration comes as the AI sector is engaged in a heated debate about safety following calls for a slowdown in development by top industry leaders. In an essay earlier this month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on firms to “slow the pace” of development to mitigate risks, a proposal that was swiftly endorsed by rivals including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Amodei’s call followed a series of cases of AI models engaging in unsanctioned malign activity, including an incident in July in which AI agents being tested by OpenAI hacked the AI start-up Hugging Face. In the latest intervention by industry on Monday, OpenAI said the US should lead an international effort to develop technical standards for advanced AI. “The United States is well positioned to lead because its AI industry is at the technical frontier, and it still stands in a privileged global network position in critical areas such as finance, trade, defense, technology, and information systems,” the San Francisco-based AI giant said in a blog post. “Leading now will determine whether the United States shapes the global AI framework or watches a fragmented, uneven, and conflict-ridden system take hold around it.” The UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, which examined the Hugging Face incident, on Monday also added its voice to calls for new guardrails, saying the cyberattack had exposed the “unravelling” of existing safeguards.
title: 20 countries propose global oversight body to manage AI dangers

body: Listen (7 mins) Save Share Inside Kazakhstan’s push to become a regional AI centre on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Valeria Tio, Astana Hub’s managing director, says AI is becoming a 'real social elevator' in Kazakhstan [Courtesy of Valeria Tio] By Agnieszka Pikulicka-Wilczewska Published On 21 Sep 2026 21 Sep 2026 A young woman in a sleek bun and a jacket with Kazakh patterns smiles from the screen at a directors’ meeting of Samruk-Kazyna, Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund. In late 2025, she became the company’s newest board member. But SKAI (or Samruk-Kazyna Artificial Intelligence) is not the first woman to join the all-male board: She is the first artificial intelligence programme with voting rights to support the company’s push for greater transparency and better governance. In Kazakhstan, AI is the new talk of the town, and part of its new branding and modernisation agenda to improve public services, attract investment and diversify the economy beyond reliance on raw materials. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev declared 2026 the “Year of Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence” to introduce advanced technologies in all sectors of the economy, develop skills, startups and Kazakh-language technologies. In 2025, the government created a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, and last month, it approved an action plan through 2029 that includes promoting AI literacy in schools and universities, digitalising healthcare, public services, tax collection and the energy sector. In 2025, Kazakhstan became the second jurisdiction, after the European Union, to pass a law governing AI. In the futuristic ball-shaped EXPO building in the capital Astana, a new AI museum invites visitors to wander through digital installations and robots, try AI models and immerse themselves in an otherworldly experience. Advertisement At the nearby Astana Hub, the largest innovation cluster in Central Asia, which runs the museum, hundreds of schoolchildren are taught programming, generative artificial intelligence, 3D animation, and motion design – for free. For adults, the “Tomorrow School” seeks to develop Kazakhstan’s brightest tech talents. “We have students from 18 to over 50, coming from various backgrounds who at some point decided to change their profession and become IT workers,” Valeria Tio, Astana Hub’s managing director, told Al Jazeera. “The candidate selection is strict. Of the 25,000 applications that we have received, we took less than 2 percent of the most talented people.” The candidates first play a logic and memory game to select those with the best potential. Then, during an intensive four-week course called the “Pool”, organisers select a student cohort to participate in training for two years. While Kazakhstan’s AI push has made it a pioneer, it “is still far away from becoming a Silicon Valley, but it is becoming a regional AI centre”, said Yuri Misnik, chief technology officer at InDrive, a unicorn company actively training a new generation of IT specialists in Kazakhstan. “Thanks to proximity to China, Kazakhstan can have the best of two worlds: The western innovation and insights from the east ... Similar to what happened 15 years ago with digital transformation, the winners change the business, the processes, and the business models.” ‘A real social elevator’ Eighteen months into the Tomorrow School programme, the hub has trained 500 people. Some have secured jobs. This month, pools open in 12 Kazakh regions. “A girl who worked as a barista in our cafeteria found work as a developer after one year of study. This is a real social elevator,” Tio said. Astana Hub also has a startup incubator, which helps to create new teams, develop IT products, and sell them to other markets. They partner with hubs in Dubai, Shanghai, Malaysia and the United Kingdom and closely cooperate with the government. Thanks to that, their residents pay zero tax. One percent of their income goes towards the hub’s development. Over eight years of operation, Astana Hub has helped to incubate Kazakhstan’s first unicorn company – a privately held startup valued at more than $1bn – named Higgsfield, a video-generating programme. By 2030, Tio said, the hub hopes to have five unicorns. At the nearby Nazarbayev University, another company tries to break new ground. The Institute of Smart Systems and Artificial Intelligence was the first academic entity in Central Asia to operate a supercomputer . Advertisement In 2019, scientists realised that neither of the popular AI voice assistants at the time, such as Siri or Alexa, recognised the Kazakh language. The team decided to build its own national product. When the coronavirus hit in 2020, researchers encouraged local Kazakh speakers and traditional toastmasters who were at home without work to record themselves reading texts using different emotions to train the new Kazakh model. It worked: In December 2024, the company launched its local answer to ChatGPT. The MagniSoz model works with text and audio in 11 different languages. Oylan, an updated version, which translates from Kazakh into “Think!”, works with images, too, in English, Russian and Kazakh. “It has deep-thinking, reasoning and web search functions,” said Yerbol Absalyamov, the institute’s executive director. “To ensure protection of data, we decided to deploy it locally on our servers. It is available open source to all Kazakhstani people, including the government. Our work has two principles: First, AI for good, and second, AI for Kazakhstan.” While ChatGPT today works in the Kazakh language, too, Absalyamov says a local large language model is still key. First, because the data it collects stays within the country and second, because it represents local culture, history and traditions. “Our mindset might be different from the European or North American one, so while creating these models, we collect data that represents Kazakhstan, our people, culture, history and identity,” he said. Concerns over human rights, power supply But AI development is not without issues. The decision to create large data centres in Kazakhstan, which require stable water and electricity supply, has raised concerns. “Kazakhstan still imports power at peak times, and a large share of plants and grids are old. When it comes to the environment, the ministry said cooling will use immersion systems rather than water, but no assessment has yet been made public,” said Tlegen Kuandykov, programme coordinator at CAPS Unlock, a local think tank. “Whatever the engineering answer turns out to be, that transparency gap is a real policy failure.” Another potential problem is the use – and potential misuse – of data. “Human rights are a big issue. The new AI law contains protective language, but enforcement is not clear yet and it might not include serious public oversight. Biometric identification and facial recognition are being rolled out rapidly,” Kuandykov said.
title: Inside Kazakhstan’s push to become a regional AI centre

body: Listen (3 mins) Save Share UAE bars Iranian airlines as US sanctions squeeze Iran’s aviation sector on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google A flight information board at Imam Khomeini international airport in Tehran, Iran, on September 23, 2026 [Vahid Salemi/AP Photo] By Al Jazeera Staff , AFP and Reuters Published On 25 Sep 2026 25 Sep 2026 The United Arab Emirates has halted flights operated by Iranian airlines, joining several other countries in adopting United States sanctions aimed at pressuring Tehran’s aviation sector. On Thursday, a statement carried by the Emirati WAM news agency said, “The General Civil Aviation Authority announced the suspension of all flights operated by Iranian airlines to and from the UAE.” It said the decision was “based on the US sanctions imposed on Iranian airlines preventing them from using airports around the world ”. The UAE has joined Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkmenistan in restricting or suspending access for Iranian airlines amid the new US sanctions threat. Dubai, the UAE’s commercial hub, is a major destination for Iranian carriers, with multiple daily flights, a large Iranian community and close business links. An Iran Airtour flight from Tehran to Dubai was cancelled shortly before its scheduled departure on Thursday morning, after tickets had already been issued, according to the AFP news agency. The UAE, which was repeatedly hit by Iranian missiles and drones throughout the US-Israel war on Iran, suspended trade and financial exchanges with Iran last month. On Wednesday, the UAE’s central bank blocked transactions involving Iran’s Bank Melli, claiming the financial institution had violated rules on money laundering, terrorism and arms proliferation. The US Treasury announced sweeping sanctions on Iran’s aviation sector earlier this month, targeting 27 airlines and dozens of companies that support them. The measures aim to cut off Iran’s air links entirely, warning that any airport or company still servicing Iranian carriers risks being cut off from the US dollar system. Advertisement Iran’s Civil Aviation Organization spokesman Majid Akhavan said: “Diplomatic and aviation talks are under way to remove the restrictions and restore flights” to the UAE. Akhavan added that Turkmenistan also turned back a flight from Tehran to Dushanbe on Thursday. “Turkmenistan’s refusal to allow the Iranian aircraft to pass through its airspace meant the flight could not continue on its route and had to return,” Akhavan told the Iranian IRNA news agency. Several smaller Iranian airlines continue flying to China and Armenia, both of which have resisted US pressure, while routes to Turkiye remain open for some carriers.
title: UAE bars Iranian airlines as US sanctions squeeze Iran’s aviation sector
