body: “La liberté d'expression contre la liberté de la presse ?” : lancement d’un livre plaidoyer pour le journalisme au profit de RSF Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Ce 25 septembre 2026, Thibaut Bruttin, directeur de Reporters sans frontières (RSF), publie, dans la collection Libelle des éditions du Seuil, l’essai La liberté d’expression contre la liberté de la presse , plaidoyer pour le journalisme face au culte du free speech , dont 100 % des droits d’auteur seront reversés à l’ONG RSF. Dans l’essai La Liberté d'expression contre la liberté de la presse ? , Thibaut Bruttin, à la tête de RSF depuis juillet 2024, alerte sur le risque de disparition du journalisme comme force centrale dans le débat public et met en évidence une lame de fond géopolitique : le dévoiement et l ’instrumentalisation de la liberté d’expression par l’administration du président américain Donald Trump , invoquée à tout bout de champ, pour promouvoir ses intérêts. L’ouvrage revient, en une centaine de pages, sur les fondements juridiques et les définitions de la liberté de la presse et de la liberté d’expression, mettant en évidence la réécriture américaine de l’histoire constitutionnelle et politique du premier amendement, principal texte à opérer la distinction entre les deux notions. Il montre également l’usage fort peu diplomatique du free speech de l’administration Trump, employé comme prétexte pour déréguler les plateformes technologiques et faire pression aussi bien sur le Brésil que sur l’Union européenne. Pire encore : la méthode Trump fonctionne et fait des émules à travers le monde, tentés d’avoir recours à la violence verbale contre la presse et à la délégitimation répétée des journalistes, aux “faits alternatifs” et aux fariboles érigées en récit politique, encourageant la polarisation à outrance, et de parler aux influenceurs au détriment des professionnels des médias. Dénonçant une offensive mondiale contre l’intégrité de l’information par un dévoiement du free speech ,Thibaut Bruttin appelle à un New Deal pour le journalisme , au respect d’un vrai pluralisme et à la mobilisation autour du droit à l’information, vecteur d’engagement citoyen. Les États-Unis pourraient-ils aspirer à un modèle de société inédit où les faits ne sont plus qu’une opinion parmi d’autres ? Liberté d’expression ou liberté de la presse ? Les deux, répond ce livre ! L’ouvrage est dédié à Christophe Deloire, directeur général de RSF de 2012 à 2024, que le Journal du dimanche , sur sa une du 18 février 2024, osa désigner comme un fossoyeur de la liberté d’expression. 100 % des droits d’auteur seront reversés à RSF. Thibaut Bruttin est directeur général de RSF. Depuis 2014, il contribue au développement d’initiatives clés comme la Journalism Trust Initiative, les évacuations de journalistes afghans et les centres de la liberté de la presse en Ukraine. Par ailleurs historien du cinéma, il a publié plusieurs ouvrages, dont le plus récent est Michel Audiard-Jean Herman/Vautrin (Actes Sud/Institut Lumière, 2023). body: Moussa Kaka, disparu au Niger : quatre décennies de journalisme et de combat pour la liberté de la presse Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Moussa Kaka est une figure du journalisme au Sahel. Celui qui a disparu depuis le 31 août raconte le Niger depuis près de 40 ans, notamment au sein de la radio qu’il a lancée, Radio Saraounia. C’est un témoin privilégié de la vie de son pays et du Sahel. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) retrace le parcours de ce journaliste chevronné et réaffirme son appel aux autorités du Niger à ouvrir une enquête. Quand on le retrouve sur le terrain, à Niamey, la capitale du Niger, ou dans les autres localités du pays, Moussa Kaka échange volontiers, donne des conseils et encourage les plus jeunes qui ont choisi le métier qu’ils aiment : le journalisme. Ainsi va la vie de ce journaliste de renom, disparu depuis le 31 août dernier après avoir quitté son bureau en fin de journée pour regagner son domicile, mais n’y est jamais arrivé. Raconter en profondeur le Niger, vaste pays de près de 1,27 million de kilomètres carrés, frontalier de sept autres pays dont le Mali et le Burkina Faso, a toujours été le sacerdoce de ce “baroudeur de l’information”, sillonnant souvent les vastes étendues désertiques du Sahara, traversant les hameaux les plus reculés, ou même fréquentant les salles de réunion des hôtels de la capitale, pour collecter des informations. “Là où beaucoup de journalistes hésitaient souvent pour leur sécurité, Moussa a toujours été sur le terrain dans les centres urbains comme dans le désert au moment des conflits armés,” témoigne un doyen de la presse nigérienne. À plus de 66 ans, fort de 40 années de pratique journalistique, Moussa Kaka est celui qui était toujours sur “l'actualité chaude”, raconte un journaliste de sa génération. Il a couvert évènements, conflits, dialogue et plusieurs aspects de ce territoire au nom du droit des populations sahéliennes à l’information. “Par son métier, Moussa Kaka a toujours eu des contacts avec toutes les couches de la société ; avec les différents hommes politiques, la société civile, et les mouvements armés et l'armée, au point que beaucoup s'interrogent sur pourquoi lui et pas les autres”, explique un journaliste. Il a commencé sa carrière à la radio nationale du Niger, puis a créé en 1999 Radio Saraounia , qui sera suivie en 2011 de la chaîne de télévision du même nom. Moussa Kaka se retrouve à la tête d’un groupe de presse de 70 personnes dont 35 à Niamey. Le groupe a des antennes entre autres, dans les régions de Tahoua, Maradi et Madaoua. Moussa Kaka a aussi raconté le Niger à l’international. Il a été correspondant pour Radio France Internationale ( RFI ) jusqu’en 2023 – année à laquelle ce média a été suspendu par les autorités militaires.Il a également fait partie des correspondants de RSF, documentant les violations de la liberté de la presse et se mobilisant pour la protection de ses confrères. Porté disparu après un putsch avorté... Depuis le 31 août 2026, après qu’il s’est mis en route, vers 19 heures, pour rentrer chez lui, Moussa Kaka n'a plus donné signe de vie. Les autorités du Niger n’ont, à ce jour, ni déclaré publiquement avoir ouvert une enquête ni communiqué sur sa disparition, intervenue dans un contexte particulièrement tendu, quelques jours après la tentative avortée de coup d’État du 29 août à Niamey. “Cette disparition, depuis près d’un mois, envoie des signaux inquiétants aux acteurs de la presse du pays qui s'efforcent d’exercer un journalisme indépendant, loin de la propagande, avec courage et résilience. La mobilisation de tous, en premier lieu des autorités, est nécessaire pour retrouver Moussa Kaka et lui permettre de retrouver sa famille, ses collègues et reprendre son travail. Sadibou Marong Directeur du bureau Afrique subsaharienne de RSF Certains de ses confrères décrivent Moussa Kaka comme faisant partie d’un groupe de journalistes parmi les plus persécutés ces dernières années. Entre septembre 2007 et octobre 2008, il a d’ailleurs passé 384 jours derrière les barreaux, pour une accusation contestée d’“acte de nature à nuire à la défense nationale”. Les pressions n’avaient jamais cessé pour celui qui est décrit par Harouna Ibrahim, ancien président de la Maison de la presse de Niamey, comme “un journaliste ayant connu beaucoup de difficultés dans [leur] pays”. En octobre 2025, Moussa Kaka avait été interpellé , ainsi que cinq autres journalistes, après avoir annoncé sur les réseaux sociaux une conférence de presse au sujet d’un fonds de solidarité créé par le gouvernement pour lever des fonds pour soutenir les opérations des forces de sécurité de l’État. Les autorités les avaient inculpés de “complicité de diffusion de document de nature à troubler l'ordre public” en vertu de la loi sur la cybercriminalité. La constance professionnelle de Moussa Kaka, malgré les persécutions, fait consensus. “ C’est un professionnel rigoureux qui travaille dans le respect de l'éthique et la déontologie du métier", conclut Harouna Ibrahim. body: Demande de liberté provisoire de Ravi Nair rejetée : le journaliste d’investigation ciblé par un harcèlement judiciaire après ses enquêtes sur le groupe Adani Le journaliste d’investigation Ravi Nair, détenu depuis le 17 sept au Gujarat dans une affaire de diffamation liée au groupe Adani, s’est vu refuser sa libération sous caution. Image:RSF Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Ce 23 septembre, le journaliste d’investigation Ravi Nair s’est vu refuser sa libération, alors qu’il est détenu depuis le 17 septembre dans la prison centrale de Sabarmati, dans l’État du Gujarat pour une affaire de diffamation au pénal déposée par l’entreprise Adani Enterprises Limited. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) alerte sur un acharnement judiciaire contre le journaliste d’investigation, visé par plusieurs procédures judiciaires liées à son travail d’investigation sur le vaste conglomérat indien dirigé par le milliardaire Gautam Adani. Mise à jour du 25/09/26 : Un tribunal de Gandhinagar a accordé une libération sous caution au journaliste le 24 septembre dans l’affaire de diffamation pénale engagée par Adani Enterprises Limited, ouvrant la voie à sa remise en liberté. En Inde, enquêter sur le groupe Adani peut conduire un journaliste en prison. Pour le journaliste d’investigation indépendant Ravi Nair, c’est l'aboutissement d’une affaire qui remonte à septembre 2021, lorsque Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL) a engagé une procédure pénale en diffamation contre lui à propos d’ une série de 17 posts diffusées sur X entre octobre 2020 et juillet 2021. Ces messages relayaient notamment des articles de presse tels ceux du média indépendant NewsClick , du Guardian ou du site indépendant sri-lankais Newsfirst , dont quatre de ses propres enquêtes, et des informations déjà publiques. Le 10 février 2026, un tribunal de Mansa l’a condamné au pénal pour diffamation à un an de prison. Ravi Nair a fait appel devant la haute cour du Gujarat et obtenu, le 9 mars, la suspension de sa peine et sa remise en liberté sous caution. À une audience du 3 septembre, pour laquelle il avait demandé une dispense de comparution pour raisons médicales, le juge a refusé la dispense et émis un mandat d’arrêt sans possibilité de libération sous caution. Le 17 septembre, Ravi Nair s’est présenté en personne devant le tribunal, qui a rejeté sa demande de retrait du mandat d’arrêt et ordonné son incarcération. Le journaliste a saisi la haute cour du Gujarat le 19 septembre pour contester son arrestation et sa détention. Ce mercredi 23 septembre, la haute cour du Gujarat a mis son jugement en délibéré et a rejeté sa demande de libération provisoire. Une nouvelle audience est prévue le 30 septembre 2026 pour examiner sa demande d’annulation du mandat d'arrêt. ““L’arrestation de Ravi Nair alors qu’un appel est en cours contre sa condamnation dans une affaire pénale de diffamation montre de façon choquante comment les lois sont utilisées comme une arme par de puissants intérêts privés pour faire taire le journalisme indépendant. Emprisonner un journaliste d’investigation pour avoir mis sous les projecteurs un conglomérat comme le groupe Adani sur des questions d’intérêt public crée un précédent inquiétant pour la liberté de la presse en Inde. RSF demande aux autorités judiciaires de libérer immédiatement le journaliste victime d’une procédure-bâillon. Le gouvernement indien doit adopter une loi contre les poursuites-bâillons présentant des garanties de nature à empêcher que la diffamation ne puisse être invoquée abusivement devant les tribunaux et conduise à des peines particulièrement sévères. Les journalistes qui enquêtent sur des sujets d'intérêt public doivent être protégés, pas criminalisés. Célia Mercier Responsable du bureau Asie du Sud de RSF Journaliste d'investigation indépendant de 52 ans, Ravi Nair a réalisé de nombreuses enquêtes sur les pratiques commerciales et les liens politiques du groupe Adani. Une grande partie de son travail d’investigation sur le groupe a été publiée sur la plateforme d’investigation Adani Watch . Ses articles ont également été publiés dans des médias tels que le Huffpost , le Leaflet , Frontline et Caravan . Affilié à l’Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), Ravi Nair a participé à une enquête d’août 2023 publiée par le Financial Times et le Guardian , qui révélait que deux investisseurs secrets du groupe Adani avaient des liens étroits avec la famille Adani, soulevant des questions sur d’éventuelles violations de la loi indienne. Plus récemment, en octobre 2025, Ravi Nair a co-réalisé une enquête du Washington Post selon laquelle des responsables indiens auraient rédigé une proposition visant à orienter environ 3,9 milliards de dollars d’investissements de la Life Insurance Corporation of India, une entreprise publique, vers les entreprises du groupe Adani. Ravi Nair est actuellement visé au total par trois procédures en diffamation liées à ses reportages et à ses publications sur les réseaux sociaux concernant le groupe Adani. Ces affaires s’inscrivent dans une offensive judiciaire plus vaste du groupe Adani , documentée par RSF, visant des médias et des journalistes qui enquêtent sur le conglomérat. body: Cuba : face aux coupures prolongées, RSF déploie une aide d’urgence pour assurer l’alimentation électrique et la connectivité de la presse indépendante Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel L’aggravation de la crise énergétique à Cuba constitue un obstacle supplémentaire pour les journalistes, dans un pays où l’exercice indépendant de la profession reste soumis à de sévères restrictions. Alors que les pannes du réseau électrique perturbent les communications à travers le pays, Reporters sans frontières (RSF) apporte son soutien aux professionnels indépendants affectés, afin de leur permettre de maintenir un accès minimal à l’énergie et à la connectivité et de poursuivre leur travail d’information. Le 18 septembre, le réseau électrique cubain a été frappé par une nouvelle panne généralisée, privant des millions de personnes d’électricité. Ces dernières semaines, certaines zones de La Havane ont connu des coupures de plus de 30 heures, tandis que la situation s’est avérée plus critique dans plusieurs provinces. “Tout devient très difficile lorsqu’on n’a pas d’électricité. La vie change complètement, car les habitudes et les horaires de travail sont bouleversés” , témoigne auprès de RSF un journaliste indépendant cubain, dont l’identité est tenue secrète pour des raisons de sécurité. L’absence d’électricité complique le rechargement des téléphones, ordinateurs, appareils photo et autres équipements indispensables. Elle perturbe également l’accès à Internet, les échanges avec les sources et la transmission des informations. Pour en limiter les conséquences, RSF fournit aux journalistes présents sur l’île des solutions d’alimentation électrique et de connectivité alternatives. “Ce soutien me permet de garantir que je puisse terminer mon travail”, t émoigne l’un des bénéficiaires . “Pour les journalistes indépendants à Cuba, la crise énergétique ne se résume pas à la seule question de l’accès à l’électricité. Les coupures entravent directement leur capacité à communiquer, à accéder à l’information et à documenter la situation sur l’île. Dans un contexte où ils sont déjà confrontés à de sévères restrictions, à la surveillance et aux intimidations, leur garantir un accès minimal à l’énergie et à la connectivité est essentiel pour permettre le maintien d’un journalisme indépendant. Artur Romeu Directeur du bureau Amérique latine de RSF La crise énergétique vient encore fragiliser un environnement médiatique déjà très contraint à Cuba. L’État y conserve un contrôle étroit du paysage médiatique, tandis que les journalistes indépendants font face à de nombreuses restrictions. La combinaison des coupures d’électricité, d’un accès limité à Internet et des pressions exercées sur la presse risque de compliquer davantage leur travail, notamment pour documenter les conséquences de la crise et permettre au public d’accéder à une information indépendante. Dans son Classement mondial de la liberté de la presse 2026, RSF place Cuba au 160e rang sur 180 pays. body: Turquie : Tuğba Tekerek placée en détention, la liberté de la presse mise à mal dans le cadre d’une répression contre la communauté LGBTQ+ Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Reporters sans frontières (RSF) demande la libération immédiate de la journaliste indépendante Tuğba Tekerek. Elle a été arrêtée dans le cadre de la campagne nationale de perquisitions “Ailem Güvende” (“Ma famille est en sécurité”) visant les organisations LGBTQ+ et est placée en détention provisoire depuis le 15 septembre. Elle fait l’objet d’une enquête pour un article journalistique datant de 2024, publié sur le site d’information Kaos GL, consacré à la communauté LGBTQ+ en Géorgie. Deux reporters qui couvraient les manifestations contre ces perquisitions ont également été placés en garde à vue. RSF considère ces événements comme une nouvelle escalade de la répression contre le journalisme indépendant en Turquie. Le procureur d’Ankara a accusé Tuğba Tekerek de gérer le compte Instagram de l’organisation LGBTQ+ Kaos GL . Cependant, la journaliste a déclaré aux procureurs lors d’un interrogatoire le 15 septembre qu’elle n’avait rédigé qu’un seul article pour le site d’information de cette organisation, également intitulé Kaos GL , en octobre 2024, sur la situation des personnes queer en Géorgie à l’approche des élections législatives dans ce pays, et qu’elle ne s’était même jamais rendue dans les locaux de l’organisation. Le 15 septembre, un tribunal a placé Tuğba Tekerek et sept membres du conseil d’administration de Kaos GL en détention provisoire. Parmi les motifs invoqués pour justifier leur détention figurent des violations présumées de la loi sur les associations et des accusations relatives à des publications “obscènes”. Le site web principal de Kaos GL et son portail d’information ont depuis été bloqués sur décision judiciaire. “Lorsque les droits des minorités sont mis sous pression, la liberté de la presse l’est souvent également. Les récentes attaques contre la communauté LGBTQ+ ont ouvert la voie à une répression étatique plus large, puisque sont pris pour cible ceux qui traitent de sujets jugés par les autorités comme contraires à la conception étatique de la moralité et de la protection de la famille. Lorsque le travail journalistique sur les minorités sociales est criminalisé, c’est en fin de compte toute la population de la Turquie qui est privée de son droit à une information indépendante. Christian Mihr Directeur exécutif de RSF Allemagne Plusieurs journalistes interpellés en l’espace de quelques jours Dans le cadre du plan plus large du gouvernement turc visant à “protéger la famille”, les organisations LGBTQ+, les personnalités publiques et les comptes sur les réseaux sociaux ont été qualifiés de menace pour les structures familiales et ont fait l’objet de mesures répressives sévères. Selon le ministre turc de la Justice, Akın Gürlek, les autorités ont engagé des poursuites judiciaires contre 162 personnes, neuf associations et 13 entreprises dans 15 provinces depuis le 13 septembre. Ces perquisitions et arrestations ont déclenché des manifestations. Le 15 septembre, la police est intervenue lors d’une manifestation devant le tribunal de Çağlayan, à Istanbul, et a placé 109 personnes en garde à vue, dont des journalistes venus couvrir les manifestations. Sarya Toprak , journaliste au quotidien BirGün , et Şener Azak , caméraman au bureau d’Istanbul de la chaîne publique allemande ARD , ont notamment été placés en garde à vue. Tous deux ont été remis en liberté dans les 48 heures suivant leur interpellation. RSF recense depuis des années le recours à la détention préventive et aux poursuites pénales contre les professionnels des médias critiques à l’égard des autorités turques. En mai 2026, RSF avait appelé à la libération des journalistes Alican Uludağ , Merdan Yanardağ et İsmail Arı , qui avaient été placés en détention en raison de leur travail journalistique. Merdan Yanardağ est toujours en détention. RSF a également demandé la relaxe des journalistes poursuivis pour leur couverture des manifestations de masse de mars 2025 . La Turquie occupe la 163e place sur 180 pays dans le Classement mondial de la liberté de la presse 2026 . body: Media advisory OSCE Chairpersonship conference in Zug to focus on de-escalation in cyberspace Date: 22 September 2026 Place: VIENNA/BERN Source: OSCE Chairpersonship VIENNA/BERN, 22 September 2026 – The Swiss OSCE Chairpersonship will convene its conference on “De-escalation in Cyberspace: Mediation and Preventive Diplomacy” in Zug on 29-30 September 2026. It will bring together participating States, experts, academics and private sector representatives to discuss ways to reduce tensions and prevent the escalation of cyber incidents. The conference is the last of four thematic conferences organized by the Swiss OSCE Chairpersonship this year and will focus on the role of preventive diplomacy and mediation in addressing risks of escalation in cyberspace. Participants will discuss the development and implementation of the OSCE’s cybersecurity confidence-building measures (CBMs), including their role in strengthening transparency, communication and trust among participating States. The participants will also discuss the potential of cyber mediation as an emerging tool for managing tensions and preventing escalation. They will explore practical approaches, challenges and the role of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, in supporting mediation efforts. The discussions will further address the contribution of the private sector, technical communities, academia and civil society to preventing and managing cyber crises. Drawing on Switzerland’s long-standing experience in conflict prevention and mediation, as well as its expertise in cybersecurity and new technologies, the conference underscores the role of cyber diplomacy as an instrument of international peace and security and Switzerland’s commitment to an open, safe and peaceful cyberspace and responsible State behavior. Media representatives are invited to the opening of the conference, which will feature addresses by Swiss Federal Councillor Martin Pfister, Head of the Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport and Director of the Swiss National Cyber Security Centre Florian Schütz. OSCE Chairman-in-Office, Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis, will deliver concluding remarks at the end of the event. Media representatives are required to obtain accreditation in advance. Interested journalists are invited to register no later than Friday, 25 September 2026, at 14:00 (CEST) via the following link . The Media Corner provides practical information on the venue, programme, accreditation, photos and useful links. body: News News Item OSCE supported CYBER NOMAD FEST 2026 to strengthen Kyrgyzstan’s cyber resilience Issued on: 25 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Bishkek Bishkek, 22 September 2026 - The OSCE Programme Office in Bishkek joined national partners in supporting CYBER NOMAD FEST 2026, a national cybersecurity festival that brought together more than 700 representatives of government institutions, critical information infrastructure entities, the financial and banking sector, telecommunications and IT companies, academia, international organisations, cybersecurity experts and the professional community. The festival was organised by the State Committee for National Security of the Kyrgyz Republic and the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic, together with SkySOC Beeline and the OSCE Programme Office in Bishkek. The event provided a platform for strengthening co-operation among government institutions, the private sector, the technology and expert communities, and international partners in addressing current and emerging cybersecurity challenges. One of the key events of the festival was the first meeting of the Interagency Commission on Information and Cybersecurity, which focused on effective co-operation between state bodies and local self-government authorities, assessment of current cyber threats, and further development of national co-ordination mechanisms in the field of information and cybersecurity. The programme featured the Cyber Conference, a forum with panel discussions on the protection of government information systems and critical information infrastructure, emerging cyber threats, cybersecurity in the financial and telecommunications sectors, capacity-building and the development of national cybersecurity. The festival also included Cyber EXPO, a technology exhibition showcasing cybersecurity solutions and technologies, as well as the Cyber Nomad CTF, practical cybersecurity exercises and competitions designed to strengthen participants’ technical skills and incident-response capabilities. The final stage of the Cyber Nomad CTF was held in an Attack/Defense format, simulating real-world cyber confrontation scenarios. Teams were required to protect their own infrastructure while identifying vulnerabilities in opponents’ systems, detecting attacks, analysing incidents, responding rapidly and defending their systems against further attacks. The Kyrgyz Republic and the OSCE have been co-operating in the field of cybersecurity for several years. In 2021 and 2025, the OSCE supported the organisation of national cyber exercises, which contributed to strengthening preparedness and developing the capacity of relevant stakeholders to respond to cyber incidents. The OSCE Programme Office in Bishkek’s engagement in CYBER NOMAD FEST 2026 reflected the importance of continued co-operation among national institutions, the private sector, technical and expert communities, and international partners in strengthening Kyrgyzstan’s cyber resilience. body: News News Item ODIHR supports Kyrgyzstan’s parliament in strengthening inclusion of people with disabilities Issued on: 25 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights Fields of work: Democratization , Tolerance and non-discrimination Identifying and addressing barriers to the participation of people with disabilities in parliamentary life was the focus of an assessment in Bishkek from 22 to 24 September 2026, supported by the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR). Organized together with the Jogorku Kenesh, Kyrgyzstan’s parliament, and its Working Group on Accessibility, and with the OSCE Programme Office in Bishkek, the activities brought together parliamentarians, parliamentary staff and organizations of people with disabilities and other representatives of civil society. “Our task is not to conduct a formal inspection or compile a list of shortcomings. We need to obtain an objective picture of the current situation, identify existing barriers, and jointly determine realistic ways to systematically eliminate them,” said Mederbek Aliev, First Deputy Speaker of the Jogorku Kenesh and Chair of the Working Group. The assessment combined a workshop, interviews and focus groups with a check of accessibility on the parliament’s premises and in its communications. It examined how people with disabilities are represented and involved in parliamentary work, including in representation, lawmaking, oversight and consultation, as well as the accessibility of parliamentary infrastructure, services and processes. This comprehensive disability inclusion assessment of the Kyrgyz parliament demonstrates not only the identified needs, but also the will to advance inclusion exists alongside the need,” said Tea Jaliashvili, First Deputy Director of ODIHR. “It is particularly encouraging to see the partnerships being developed between the state institution – the parliament – and civil society and international organizations in achieving the objective for the benefit of the society as a whole. Such an effective partnership is already half-way to success.” The involvement of organizations for people with disabilities brought first-hand experience and expertise into the assessment, helping identify obstacles to participation and changes needed to make parliament more inclusive. “In Kyrgyzstan, there is still insufficient understanding of disability as a matter of equal rights and opportunities. The medical and charity-based approach continues to prevail, with persons with disabilities often seen as recipients of assistance rather than as full and equal members of society, with the right to live independently, work and participate in decision-making,” said Askar Turdugulov, Chair of the New Age Public Foundation, Adviser to the Mayor of Bishkek, and Ombudsperson on Disability Issues]. The findings will inform practical recommendations to help the Jogorku Kenesh improve its infrastructure, services and working practices, supporting the equal participation of people with disabilities in parliamentary life. The assessment forms part of ODIHR’s work to advance disability-inclusive parliaments . Through its assessment methodology, ODIHR helps parliaments examine barriers across their work and identify concrete steps towards institutions that better represent and serve everyone. body: News News Item OSCE strengthens capacities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Serbia through regional forged document training-of-trainers Issued on: 25 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Montenegro Fields of work: Policing From 21 to 25 September, the OSCE Transnational Threats Department, in close co-operation with the OSCE Missions to Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), Montenegro and, Serbia, held a regional training-of-trainers (ToT) course on detecting forged documents and impostors at border crossing points. Hosted at the Police Cooperation Centre in Trebinje, BiH, the course brought together 18 experienced border police officers and forensic document experts from BiH, Montenegro and Serbia to strengthen their technical expertise and build their capacity as trainers, ensuring the long-term transfer of skills within their national border police services. Delivered by experts from BiH and Serbia, the programme combined theory, hands-on exercises with genuine and forged specimens, peer learning, and participants’ presentations to build their confidence in training their colleagues. Sessions covered practical detection skills, including substrate analysis, security printing techniques, recognition of printing methods and document evaluation under realistic conditions. The regional focus reflects the ongoing threat of document forgery and identity fraud in South-Eastern Europe, where counterfeit and fraudulently obtained travel documents continue to facilitate migrant smuggling, trafficking in human beings and other forms of organized crime. Strengthening frontline officers' ability to detect such fraud is key to disrupting criminal networks and enhancing security and stability across South-Eastern Europe and the wider OSCE area. With 18 participants trained as trainers, the course is designed to multiply its impact, equipping national border police services to extend detection skills to a much wider group of frontline officers. Since 2015, the OSCE Transnational Threats Department has delivered a series of similar ToT courses across the region, helping to standardise detection procedures at border crossings. “I am confident that participants will leave this training with practical, hands-on skills for verifying document authenticity and detecting forgeries and impostors, which they can apply immediately and pass on to colleagues through future courses they deliver themselves,” said Slobodan Krstić, a trainer and retired member of the BiH Border Police. “Bringing together border police from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, and Montenegro also creates a valuable opportunity to exchange experiences and build a regional network of trainers in this field.” The course concluded with the handover of certificates, marking participants' readiness to serve as national trainers and roll out training to frontline officers across the region in 2026-2027, supported by follow-up mentoring for sustained impact. This event is part of a series of activities on the detection of forged travel documents and impostors organized by the OSCE Border Security and Management Unit across the OSCE region since 2015. body: News News Item Sharper skills, stronger stories: Kosovo journalists learn through the OSCE Media Fellowship Issued on: 25 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission in Kosovo Between April and September 2026, eight journalists working for Albanian- and Serbian-language media in Kosovo stepped beyond their familiar media environments as part of the OSCE Mission’s Media Fellowship Programme. Through meetings in Prishtinë/Priština and a study visit to Belgrade, Podgorica and Tirana, they exchanged experiences with media professionals and organizations. The fellows met with journalists, media outlets and journalists’ organizations to discuss issues at the heart of journalism today, from media sustainability, working conditions and media independence to regulation, AI and new technologies. Topics also included journalists’ safety, disinformation, professional standards and support mechanisms available to media professionals facing threats and other challenges. The eighth edition also highlighted the value of sustained exchange between journalists from different communities. Comparing newsroom realities helped the fellows recognise shared professional challenges and consider how colleagues working in another language could offer additional perspectives on a story. The contacts made during the programme provide a basis for seeking advice, exchanging information and exploring future co-operation beyond the study visit. “Through the Media Fellowship Programme, we want to create opportunities for young journalists from different communities to learn from one another, broaden their professional perspectives and build connections beyond their immediate media environment,” said Arlinda Osmanaj, Programme Officer at the OSCE Mission in Kosovo. The seven participating journalists were: Arianita Hoti (KOHA), Anastasija Đorđević (Kontakt Plus Radio), Milena Jevtić (Radio Mitrovica Sever), Shqipron Xhema (Kallxo), Sanja Kostić (former Kossev), Diellza Berisha (Klan Kosova), Festim Gërguri (IKD / Betimi për Drejtësi) and Behar Mustafa (BIRN). Established in 2017, the Media Fellowship Programme has brought together 64 young and aspiring journalists as part of the OSCE Mission in Kosovo’s efforts to strengthen professional standards and encourage exchange across communities. For the eighth cohort, the programme combined learning relevant to their daily reporting with direct access to peers across Kosovo and the region, and a shared platform to keep that exchange active. For more visit the @omikmediafellowship page on Instagram. body: News News Item EU and OSCE donated technical equipment to support awareness raising on radiation safety in Tajikistan On 18 September 2026, the European Union (EU) and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) donated technical equipment to the Sughd branch of the Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Safety and Security Agency of the National Academy of Sciences of Tajikistan. Issued on: 25 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe Fields of work: Environmental activities On 18 September 2026, the European Union (EU) and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) donated technical equipment to the Sughd branch of the Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Safety and Security Agency of the National Academy of Sciences of Tajikistan. The equipment was handed over during an official ceremony in Dushanbe with the aim of strengthening the Agency’s institutional and technical capacity and contributing to its long-term work in radiation safety. The donated equipment will enhance the technical capacity of the Agency’s Training and Press Centre in Buston, Sughd Branch. The Centre already plays an important role in organizing radiation safety training and information campaigns for local populations in areas affected by the uranium legacy. The equipment will strengthen these ongoing activities by providing modern technical means for regular training and educational activities, as well as for raising awareness among local communities about the risks associated with uranium legacy sites and measures to mitigate them. The equipment is particularly important for Sughd region, which is affected by the legacy of former uranium mining and processing activities. Uranium legacy sites may include former mining areas, waste dumps and tailings, which can present environmental and radiation-safety concerns and require continued monitoring, awareness and risk mitigation. Strengthening the Training and Press Centre’s technical capacity will support regular radiation safety training and help local stakeholders and communities better understand the potential risks associated with uranium legacy sites and measures to reduce them. The donation was provided within the framework of the EU-funded project on “Stakeholder Engagement for Uranium Legacy Remediation in Central Asia - Phase III”, implemented by the OSCE and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. By supporting stakeholders and communities to strengthen knowledge, collaborate and take action on environmental challenges, the project reflects the shared EU-OSCE-UNDP commitment to environmental protection and meaningful engagement and aimed to reduce environmental and health risks associated with uranium legacy sites in Central Asia, which remain a source of potential contamination and hazard for communities. body: 22/09/2026 Press release France en fa fr Syria National courts RICCARDO MILANI / HANS LUCAS / HANS LUCAS VIA AFP Following the conviction of Sabri Essid for genocide and crimes against humanity, the Paris Criminal Court has issued an important ruling on the civil claims, formally recognising the harm suffered by the civil parties and awarding them damages. This financial reparation will unfortunately remain very symbolic. Paris, 22 September 2026. Six months after the historic conviction of French Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) fighter Sabri Essid (alias Abou Dojanah al-Faransi), the Paris Criminal Court has issued its decision on the civil claims, providing judicial recognition of the lifelong and multifaceted harm suffered by the survivors of the Yazidi genocide. On 20 March 2026, Sabri Essid was sentenced in absentia to life imprisonment for genocide, crimes against humanity and complicity in these crimes, committed in Syria between August 2014 and throughout 2016 against Yazidi women and children. This marked the first conviction of a French national for genocide, as well as the first time that a French court addressed the atrocities committed by ISIS against the Yazidi community. In its decision on the civil claims, the Court formally recognised the extent of the harm inflicted by Sabri Essid on the three Yazidi women and their eight children, including the damage arising from the fear of impending death (prejudice d’angoisse de mort imminente), the loss of affection (prejudice d’affection) and the moral damage (préjudice moral), and granted them financial awards. The Court also acknowledged the moral damage suffered by the Yazidi associations that joined the proceedings as civil parties – Kinyat, the Free Yezidi Foundation (FYF) and Yazda – as well as by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the Ligue des droits de l’Homme/droits humains (LDH) and awarded them one symbolic euro. In practice, these financial awards will unfortunately remain largely symbolic. As Sabri Essid has never been located, the victims cannot claim compensation from him. Additionally, under the current French legal framework, foreign victims of international crimes committed abroad are not eligible for compensation from the Commission d’indemnisation des victimes d’infractions (CIVI). " There can be no meaningful justice without effective reparation. Although this is an important decision, it will remain symbolic as French law does not allow foreign victims to have equal access to compensation mechanisms and to effectively benefit from reparations awarded by the courts, in cases where the accused is not present or solvent, " declared the five civil party associations . body: 18/09/2026 Press release Turkey LGBTQI+ rights KEMAL ASLAN / AFP In Turkey, LGBTI+ associations and venues frequented by the community were hit by a wave of police raids and arrests. These operations are part of an ongoing campaign from the authorities, with explicitly discriminatory aims and justifications, in contradiction with international law. 18 September, 2026. In Turkey since this past weekend, the authorities have launched waves of police raids targeting the LGBTI+ community, amid a vast campaign dubbed " Ailem Güvende " (in english " my family is safe "). At least 116 people have been detained as part of these operations, 44 of them LGBTI+ rights defenders and at least 82 have since been remanded in pre-trial detention. The majority of those arrested are trans women, charged with a combination of prostitution, drug and obscenity offences as well as violations of the Law on Associations. At least 125 additional people were detained across Ankara, Istanbul and Izmir following protests in support of the initial victims of the crackdown. Solidarity with LGBTI+ communities has also been censored through restrictions on the social media accounts of journalists and activists. The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), and its member organisation in Turkey, İnsan Hakları Derneği (IHD), denounce in the strongest terms these arrests and demand the immediate dropping of all prosecutions based on discriminatory accusations. They urge international actors to react strongly to Turkey’s broader anti LGBTI+ turn and its infringement of international human rights law, including freedom of expression, freedom of association, freedom of peaceful assembly (United Nations, Council of Europe), as well as its political commitments (European Union-EU accession) and economic commitments (Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development-OECD standards and policies). " Faced with these unacceptable violations, and with no prospect of any backing down nor reparations from the authorities, the EU must firmly acknowledge Turkey’s incompatibility with the values of the Union and therefore place an indefinite hold on its accession process by immediately stopping the pre-accession funding, " commented Alexis Deswaef, FIDH President . Turkey has seen a sustained erosion of freedoms of expression, association, and peaceful assembly in recent years , with LGBTI+ people and organisations among the primary targets . " Obscenity " and " child protection " laws have been weaponized to effectively criminalise LGBTI+ people’s existence. Pressures on civil society are rampant, with surveillance, police and judicial harassment, political banning and dissolutions enacted on any opposition, real or perceived. The LGBTI+ community has become a regular fixation for Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who recently pronounced the next ten years as the " Decade of Family and Population ". No concept of " family values " should be used as a tool to justify an ever increasingly authoritarian and conservative power in Turkey. FIDH and IHD urge Turkish authorities to immediately release all individuals detained in the framework of this operation and to put an end to the criminalisation of LGBTI+ civil society. They call on international actors, in particular the European Union, the Council of Europe and United Nations mechanisms, to firmly condemn the raids and detentions carried out by Turkish authorities. body: Facebook Twitter Вконтакте On October 14, 2026, Anti-Discrimination Centre Memorial Brussels organises a side event during the annual Warsaw Human Dimension Conference of the OSCE (Warsaw, Sofitel Victoria Hotel, Saski room, 16:00–17:00 CET). Anti-Discrimination Centre Memorial (Brussels) proposes to integrate the human rights approach into the ongoing discussion among many indigenous activists on the idea of overcoming Russian colonial oppression, guaranteeing the cultural, economic, environmental and political rights of each group. While there are sound voices of the peoples of the Caucasus, the Urals and Siberia insisting on the future as independent national republics based on the cultural and political heritage of the local peoples, there are also concerns about the rights of other groups living on the same territories – such as small-numbered Indigenous peoples and other minorities. Most anti-colonial activists agree that the future political models should be democratic and inclusive. However, the question is how to ensure non-discrimination and equity, how to protect the rights of those who can’t form an independent state, but need their rights to be realised within those future new political subjects? Another burning question would be – how to solve the existing problem of Russian domination (language, political and economic resources, ideas of the past and historical heritage)? What examples of the European historical past should be considered or could serve as a warning against too radical (even violent in some cases) approach? The 20th century showed many waves of politically dominated relocation of ethnic groups: Soviet repressions against peoples and later their efforts to get back to their native territories; German attempts to replace the population of the occupied lands, that ended with the exile in 1945 of millions of Germans from some parts of Central Europe; among other examples one can think of Polish and Ukrainian (Soviet) treaty of 1944 and the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey. Maybe thinking of the relevant cases of the past century, trying to avoid the mistakes and prevent the crimes could help to plan a non-discriminating and inclusive future, and bring the idea of human rights protection as the most necessary element to these actual discussions. These issues will be discussed by representatives of the Indigenous rights movement with human rights experts at the side event of ADC Memorial Brussels. Speakers: Ruslan Valiev , Aspects of Bashkortostan Maria Ochir-Goryaeva , historian, decolonial activist from the Republic of Kalmykia Tavlan Salpagarov , Indigenous Peoples Global Unity (via Zoom) Viacheslav Shadrin , expert on the Indigenous peoples’ rights, representative of Yukaghir Indigenous people (via Zoom) Natalia Sineaeva-Pankowska , “Never Again” Association Co-moderators: Stephania Kulaeva (ADC Memorial Brussels) and Ruslan Valiev (Aspects of Bashkortostan) Date: 14 October 2026, 16:00-17:00 CET Location: Warsaw, hotel Sofitel Victoria, room Saski Languages: The event will be held in Russian and English, with simultaneous interpretation. Refreshments and beverages will be provided. The side event will be organized as part of the project “Indigenous Peoples’ Rights for a Democratic Future”, which is being implemented by INFOE (Institut für Ökologie und Aktions-Ethnologie e.V.), ICIPR (International Committee of Indigenous Peoples of Russia), the Never Again Association and the ADC Memorial, with the support of the German Federal Foreign Office. body: India Continues to Weaponize Terrorism Laws to Detain Religious Minorities | USCIRF Skip to main content Search Sort by Relevance Order Asc Desc Search India Continues to Weaponize Terrorism Laws to Detain Religious Minorities Sep 24, 2026 India Continues to Weaponize Terrorism Laws to Detain Religious Minorities Washington, DC – In light of the Indian government’s decision to grant bail to British-born Sikh activist, Jagtar Singh Johal, the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom ( USCIRF ) urges the U.S. Department of State to work with Indian authorities to facilitate the release of other freedom of religion or belief (FoRB) prisoners, many of whom, including Jagtar Singh Johal, are included as a FoRB Victim in USCIRF’s Frank R. Wolf Freedom of Religion or Belief Victims List. “ We welcome the New Delhi High Court’s decision to grant bail to Jagtar Singh Johal, after nearly nine years of unlawful suffering in arbitrary detention. However, uncertainty remains regarding his return to the United Kingdom and reunification with his family ,” said Chair Asif Mahmood . “ Under the terms of his bail, Johal was required to surrender his passport, is banned from communicating with the press, and still faces the death penalty in eight charges against him .” In 2017, authorities unjustly arrested Johal on false charges of murder and terrorism under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA), a law that several United Nations special rapporteurs have characterized as noncompliant with international standards and India’s international obligations. Prior to his arrest, Johal had blogged about human rights abuses against India’s Sikh community, action that is protected under international law regarding freedom of expression. Johal’s trial faced continuous delays throughout his detention, and authorities failed to produce credible evidence against him. In 2022 the United Nations recognized his imprisonment as arbitrary detention and more recently described it as amounting to psychological torture. Furthermore, Johal reports that he has been physically tortured by authorities with electric shocks, sleep deprivation, stress positions, and threats to his life, ultimately leading to a forced confession. USCIRF urges the United States government to press Indian officials to conduct a full investigation into Johal’s detention and treatment and the U.S. government should hold perpetrators of such particularly severe violations accountable in accordance with the International Religious Freedom Act. “ Johal’s case is demonstrative of a larger pattern by the Indian government to silence or imprison religious minorities ,” said Vice Chair CeCe Heil . “ Several other FoRB prisoners, including Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam , continue to languish in pre-trial detention for perceived UAPA violations, for simply engaging in peaceful protest. In recent years, the Indian government has even gone so far as to orchestrate assassinations and assassination attempts against members of the Sikh community in North America in clear acts of transnational repression meant to intimidate, coerce, and harass the diaspora .” USCIRF recommended in its 2026 Annual Report that the State Department designate India as a Country of Particular Concern (CPC) for engaging in systematic, ongoing, and egregious religious freedom violations. USCIRF raised these poor religious freedom conditions during its May hearing , “Deteriorating Religious Freedom Conditions in India,” and in its “India Country Brief” publication in August. ### The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) is an independent, bipartisan legislative branch agency established by the U.S. Congress to monitor, analyze, and report on religious freedom abroad. USCIRF makes foreign policy recommendations to the President, the Secretary of State, and Congress, intended to deter religious persecution and promote freedom of religion and belief. To interview a commissioner, please contact USCIRF at [email protected] .
title: India Continues to Weaponize Terrorism Laws to Detain Religious Minorities

body: U.S.-China Summit Must Address China’s Religious Freedom Repression | USCIRF Skip to main content Search Sort by Relevance Order Asc Desc Search U.S.-China Summit Must Address China’s Religious Freedom Repression Sep 18, 2026 U.S.-China Summit Must Address China’s Religious Freedom Repression Washington, DC – The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom ( USCIRF ) has reported for years that China’s violations of freedom of religion or belief (FoRB) have been too numerous to count and too heinous to ignore. USCIRF asks President Donald J. Trump to directly raise with President Xi Jinping China’s systematic, ongoing, and egregious violations of FoRB during the U.S.-China summit in Washington, D.C. on September 24, 2026. “ The Chinese Communist Party (CCP), under the leadership of President Xi, has undertaken a genocidal campaign against Uyghurs and other Turkic minorities. It has attempted to eliminate or take complete control of Tibetan Buddhism, and it threatens the free succession of the Dalai Lama ,” said Commissioner David A. Anderson . “ It has arrested independent Protestant church leaders and breached China’s protocols with the Catholic Church. It has attempted to separate ethnic Mongolians from their religious and cultural traditions. It has harassed and imprisoned Falun Gong practitioners, Church of Almighty God members, and followers of other religious and belief communities. And it has carried out a campaign of transnational repression far beyond its borders, including within the United States of America .” In July, a wide-ranging Ethnic Unity and Progress Law, which represents the forced imposition of CCP ideology and ethnonationalist supremacy over all of China’s diverse ethnic and religious groups, took effect across China. It codifies into Chinese law an even more comprehensive and totalitarian system of repression of religious freedom while declaring that the CCP has the authority to pursue organizations and individuals outside of China for undermining the new law. “ The Ethnic Unity and Progress Law has raised alarms across the international community, requests for clarification from UN special rapporteurs, and concerns from U.S. lawmakers ,” said Commissioner Gene Mills . “ USCIRF asks President Trump to use this crucial opportunity of direct talks with his Chinese counterpart, President Xi, to bolster U.S. interests and priorities by advancing religious freedom for all of China’s people .” USCIRF recommended in its 2026 Annual Report that the U.S. Department of State keep China on the Country of Particular Concern (CPC) list for engaging in systematic, ongoing, and egregious violations of religious freedom. USCIRF raised China’s abysmal religious freedom conditions during its “FoRB Violations Against Christians Abroad” hearing in January and in its “China’s Codification and Escalation of the ‘Sinicization of Religion’” publication in May. ### The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) is an independent, bipartisan legislative branch agency established by the U.S. Congress to monitor, analyze, and report on religious freedom abroad. USCIRF makes foreign policy recommendations to the President, the Secretary of State, and Congress, intended to deter religious persecution and promote freedom of religion and belief. body: @HRF View post Today marks 12 years since the Chinese regime sentenced Ilham Tohti, a respected Uyghur economist and academic, to life in prison for “separatism.” Ilham peacefully advocated for Uyghur rights through data, research, education, and open dialogue. Before his arrest in January 2014, Ilham taught economics at Minzu University in Beijing and ran a website discussing social and economic issues affecting Uyghurs. He advocated for policies to address poverty, unemployment, and ethnic tensions and promoted greater understanding between Uyghurs and Han Chinese. After a two-day, closed-door trial in September 2014, a Chinese court convicted Ilham of “separatism” and sentenced him to life in prison. His appeal was rejected in a hearing held inside the detention center and without his lawyer present. @JewherIlham has reportedly been held in solitary confinement, and his family has been denied visits since 2017. UN experts have raised concerns about his health and access to medical care. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found his detention arbitrary and linked it to violations of his rights to freedom of expression and due process. Ilham’s continued imprisonment reflects Beijing’s broader repression of Uyghur intellectuals, writers, and academics. HRF condemns the Chinese regime’s continued imprisonment of Ilham, demands his immediate and unconditional release, and calls for his unrestricted access to his family and independent counsel. body: @HRF View post HRF condemns Delcy Rodríguez’s regime for continuing to weaponize state censorship and political repression in Venezuela. The regime continues to block more than 200 digital domains, including 65 independent news outlets. As local NGO @vesinfiltro noted, ending this blackout requires no legal reforms — only the political will to order internet service providers to lift the blocks immediately. Digital censorship is just one layer of a continued, systematic pattern of repression and control. @CNPcaracas registered 134 attacks against journalists and media outlets between January and July, including 23 arbitrary detentions, 15 deportations of foreign correspondents, and 4 station shutdowns. Furthermore, state security forces under minister Diosdado Cabello have routinely harassed and intimidated reporters to prevent them from documenting critical events, including the aftermath of the earthquakes. Despite promises of reform, the regime’s repressive apparatus remains fully intact and operational. UN High Commissioner Volker Türk ( @UNHumanRights ) expressed concern that human rights violations and reports of torture in detention centers persist. Meanwhile, @ForoPenal confirmed that at least 328 political prisoners remain arbitrarily detained in Venezuela, enduring severe conditions even as official channels routinely inflate release numbers. While HRF welcomes the release of political prisoners, true freedom cannot be conditional. Releasing individuals under heavy judicial restrictions, travel bans, and ongoing court presentations — only to re-arrest others through a continuous “revolving door” mechanism — is a tactic to silence dissent. Democracies, and the United States in particular, must not be deceived by partial releases: They must demand an immediate end to censorship, the dismantling of the repressive state apparatus, and the unconditional release of all political prisoners. body: 17 September 2026 Mathieu Lemoine Tags Bruce Pannier Central Asia Independent Media Kazakhstan Kyrgyzstan RFE/RL Tajikistan Turkmenistan Uzbekistan Interviewing Abdullah Abdullah at RFE/RL in spring 2001. Photo: Courtesy of Bruce Pannier. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Bruce Pannier has watched Central Asia change for more than three decades – from the final years of the Soviet Union to a generation that no longer remembers it. In an interview with Novastan English Editor-in-Chief Mathieu Lemoine, the veteran journalist reflects on independent media, Russia’s changing role, generational shifts, overlooked communities and what outsiders still misunderstand about Central Asia. In the summer of 1990, Bruce Pannier arrived at Tashkent State University. The Soviet Union still existed. Central Asia’s five future independent states did not. Friends in Jizzakh viloyat, June 12, 1982. Photo: Courtesy of Bruce Pannier. More than three decades later, Pannier has become one of the most familiar English-language voices on Central Asia. At Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), he co-created and co-hosted Majlis , a podcast that brought together journalists, scholars and analysts to discuss developments across the region and, increasingly, to amplify perspectives from Central Asians themselves. Today, he is part of the team behind Turan, a project covering Central Asia and the wider Turkic world. In this interview with Novastan, Pannier looks back at more than three decades of reporting and reflects on the changing media landscape, the impact of the war in Ukraine, generational change, overlooked communities and a region that, in his view, is increasingly defining its future on its own terms. Novastan: You have been covering Central Asia for several decades. How did your interest in the region first begin? Bruce Pannier: I was learning Russian and doing Soviet Studies in college. But I suppose everything started with two books: Eastern Approaches by Sir Fitzroy MacLean and Setting the East Ablaze by Peter Hopkirk. That was in the early and mid-1980s. The leading American authority on Central Asia was Edward Allworth, who taught at Columbia University. I was fortunate to go and study under him. He loved Central Asia and, best of all, he knew thousands of years of the region’s history. He treated the Soviet period as just another chapter in that history, so we never looked at Central Asia through a Russian or Soviet lens. Then I went to summer school at Tashkent State University in 1990, and I was completely hooked after that. Were there particular places in Central Asia – a city, a region, a border area, a mountain landscape, a desert, a bazaar or an everyday encounter – that changed the way you understood the countries and societies you were covering? Many. I worked in villages in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan in 1992 and 1993. They all had similar lives, working on farms growing crops or herding animals, but there were different ways to do this work in every village and different attitudes about living and working in rural areas. I was amazed to find out how religious people remained there. I arrived in spring 1992 and, in one of the first villages I worked in, someone died. We all went to the very Muslim funeral, and almost everyone knew the prayers. I was doing sociological research and one of the questions I asked was: “What building or facility would you like to see in your village?” The answer every time – and I mean every time – was a mosque. I certainly gained a new respect for herders. I was instructed to do what the people in the villages did. I especially disliked picking cotton, but taking a herd out to pasture was my type of work. You have a few dogs, a stick to keep stragglers moving and a couple of rocks to throw in front of animals, usually sheep, that are moving too far ahead. You find a good grazing area and sit under a tree watching the animals eat. When it’s time to go back, you round up the herd and head back to the village. Batken, summer 1999, covering the insurgency of the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan. Photo: Courtesy of Bruce Pannier. If the job paid better, I would be doing it now. Of course, the inter-ethnic violence in Osh in June 2010 was a shock. I had thought, or at least hoped, that was all behind everyone. Remember, I was at Tashkent State in summer 1990 when it happened before, though we couldn’t get much information about what was going on. When I was in Osh and other parts of the Fergana Valley in 1992, the events of 1990 seemed very far away. People didn’t talk about it much. I would be remiss if I didn’t mention the mountains. I love mountains and enjoyed the many times I was in the Central Asian mountains. I liked doing the trip between Bishkek and Osh in a marshrutka just because of the views. The road was in terrible shape until the end of the 1990s, but it didn’t matter to me when I was staring out of the window, or when we stopped along the road. One time I was with a Kazakh friend in Shymbulak – then called Chimbulak. It’s a good ski area now, and even in 1992 there was a ski lift there. There were no skiers, but I convinced one of the park rangers, for five dollars, to turn on the ski lift long enough to take my friend and me to the top. I remember him saying, in Russian, “For God’s sake, don’t break anything.” We walked back down, and the view was magnificent. And obviously, the Silk Road cities were amazing. Samarkand looks so different now compared with the early 1990s, but even back then it had a charm. It was not well tended, and the old buildings looked old and in need of repair, but it really made me appreciate how old they were. And since I worked in villages, I could imagine what it was like for a farmer or herder to visit one of the big and bustling cities. When you first started following Central Asia, what did outside observers most often misunderstand about the region? Has that changed today? Well, when I first started following Central Asia, there were not many outside observers. Some Western media outlets were having difficulties even spelling the names of the Central Asian countries. Probably the biggest misconception was that the people in Central Asia had accepted that they were part of the Soviet Union. When I was at TashGU that summer, there were people from all over Central Asia studying there, and it was clear they regarded Russia as a colonizer that was pilfering the region’s resources and trying to force them to become a “Soviet man or woman.” That has clearly changed since the USSR collapsed. Since the Kremlin launched its full-scale war against Ukraine in February 2022, we have seen some lively discussions in Central Asia about colonization and exploitation under Tsarist and then Soviet rule. Even the leaderships of some Central Asian countries are calling it a dark period in the region’s history. Read more on Novastan : “I only needed a passport” : In Ukraine, Central Asian prisoners of wars caught between loyalty and regret Majlis became one of the most recognizable English-language formats for discussing Central Asia. What was the original idea behind the podcast? Muhammad Tahir and I started Majlis in 2014 in response to the increase in fighting in northern Afghanistan. Our first programme was about Turkmenistan being the Achilles heel of Central Asian security. We weren’t sure then that we would ever do any more podcasts, but RFE/RL management liked it, and I agreed there was a wide variety of topics beyond deteriorating security in northern Afghanistan that we could cover, starting with the great reporting RFE/RL’s Central Asian services were doing in local languages and Russian. Muhammad was something of a showman. He really embraced being th
