body: Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE “Cautious optimism” justified: Uzbekistan’s performance halfway through Chess Olympiad Uzbekistan’s men’s national team has won all six matches at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand and leads the standings outright. In the sixth round, the hosts defeated defending champions India. China awaits next. Gazeta reviews the performances of the country’s three men’s and three women’s teams. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 23 September 2026, 19:11 Sport Halfway through the international Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, both Uzbekistan’s men’s and women’s teams are living up to their supporters' expectations and challenging for the top places. Gazeta columnist Georgy Shvanov takes a closer look at their performances. After the sixth round, Uzbekistan’s men’s national team moved into sole possession of first place in the tournament. The team consists of Nodirbek Abdusattorov (2762), Javokhir Sindarov (2778), Nodirbek Yakubboev (2685), Shamsiddin Vokhidov (2654) and Mukhiddin Madaminov (2611), all five of whom are grandmasters. Particular attention at this Olympiad is focused on Sindarov, who is set to play a match for the world chess title later this year. After six rounds, having missed one, he has scored 4 points out of a possible 5, with three wins and two draws. Sindarov’s preparation and participation in international tournaments, including the Chess Olympiad, as well as his work with coaches, are supported by the National Bank of Uzbekistan . Javokhir Sindarov. Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE Advertising on Gazeta Before the competition began, coach of Uzbekistan’s first men’s team Rustam Kasimdzhanov said he had “cautious optimism”. Serious tests for his players began in the third round, when Uzbekistan faced Austria, led by experienced grandmaster Kirill Alekseenko, who competed in the 2020−2021 Candidates Tournament. The classic team strategy worked in that match: players with the black pieces aimed to hold their opponents, while those playing White sought to win. The result was two wins and two draws, giving Uzbekistan a 3−1 victory. They were followed by Türkiye, which many experts considered a highly underrated team. In the fourth round, 15-year-old Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, playing on the first board, scored 4.5 points out of 5 and had already entered the online top 20. He had the initiative against Abdusattorov as well, but in a better position opted to repeat the position. Sindarov and Vokhidov drew their games with the black pieces, while Yakubboev, playing on the third board, found a refutation to Vahap Sanal’s adventurous idea. His opponent had played inaccurately in the opening, which resulted in the loss of a pawn. Yakubboev went on to win comfortably, securing a 2.5−1.5 victory for Uzbekistan. In the fifth round, Uzbekistan faced Hungary. On the first board, the Europeans fielded Richard Rapport, a top grandmaster known for his unconventional style, while on the second board was his complete chess opposite, the extremely resilient Peter Leko, who once played Vladimir Kramnik in a World Championship match. But neither their status nor their experience helped the Hungarian players. When Abdusattorov and Yakubboev confidently and quickly reached winning positions, Sindarov and Vokhidov could have offered draws to secure the team victory. Instead, they continued playing and eventually overcame their opponents, finishing the match with a clean 4−0 score. Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Gukesh Dommaraju. Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE India, another Olympiad favorite, was also moving at a strong pace. In the first round, Arjun Erigaisi unexpectedly lost to young international master Prin Laohawirapap from Thailand, but after that India went on a long winning run, taking victory in all five of its remaining matches. The sixth-round match between Uzbekistan and India carried additional symbolism: it brought together the winners of the previous two Olympiads. Uzbekistan won the tournament in Chennai in 2022, while India won in Budapest in 2024. The opening stages confirmed that the match would be difficult. Abdusattorov failed to gain an advantage against Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa, while Sindarov was holding a strategically questionable position against Erigaisi. Vokhidov equalized against reigning world champion Gukesh Dommaraju. All three games ended in draws, leaving Yakubboev’s game against Nihal Sarin as the decider. Nodirbek Yakubboev. Photo: Michal Walusza Yakubboev’s position was no better, but in a sense it was safer. Apparently, this prompted him to reject a simple continuation that would have been sufficient for a draw and instead choose a line that was objectively losing but allowed him to create attacking chances. By move 31, the situation looked particularly unpleasant: Yakubboev had less than 10 minutes remaining, while Sarin, known for his fast play, had 38 minutes. However, Sarin was the first to lose his composure. Sarin played overly optimistically, exposing his king to attacks. He first missed a winning opportunity and then allowed a tactical blow following a knight fork, which led to Yakubboev’s victory. Yakubboev later admitted that this moment of the game was very emotional for him. https://twitter.com/ChessbaseIndia/status/2102055391454757319 Thus, Uzbekistan won all six of its matches without losing a single individual game. The main rivals, defending champions India, have already been defeated, but there is no room for complacency. In the seventh round, Uzbekistan will face China — another dangerous opponent and a two-time Olympic champion. Over the first six rounds, China has missed out on a team victory only once, drawing with Armenia. Former world champion Ding Liren appears to be returning his form and defeated German grandmaster Vincent Keymer, who is in the world top 10. China won the match 3−1. Ding Liren. Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta Wei Yi, who competed in the latest Candidates Tournament, is also performing excellently. He began with three wins over grandmasters before holding two games with the black pieces against strong opponents. Although Sindarov is unlikely to fear a meeting with the Chinese grandmaster, whom he has defeated both at the World Cup and in the Candidates Tournament — Sindarov won the Candidates Tournament in April this year and is now awaiting his World Championship match against Dommaraju — the balance of power in this matchup is far from clear. Javokhir Sindarov and Wei Yi at the Candidates Tournament. Photo: Michal Walusza Besides China, Armenia could also pose a challenge for Uzbekistan. Their team spirit has repeatedly compensated for differences in ratings. The United States could also become a threat if they manage to find their rhythm and reach the pace expected of a team of their status. Uzbekistan’s second team is also producing excellent results. Its lineup consists of Jakhongir Vakhidov (2527), Abdimalik Abdisalimov (2548), Mukhammadzokhid Suyarov (2540), Khumoyun Begmuratov (2514) and Ortik Nigmatov (2484). Pavel Eljanov is the captain. Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta After six rounds, the team is in 13th place. Having lost only to the strong German team, Uzbekistan’s second team has defeated all its other opponents, including a strong Spanish side. On the first board, Vakhidov has held his own against some of the strongest players from other countries, while Abdisalimov and Suyarov, playing on the second and third boards, can be described as the team’s “hitters”. The third team currently occupies 65th place, ten places below its starting position. Saidakbar Saydaliev (2475), Almas Rakhmatullaev (2418), Bakhrom Bakhrillaev (2412), Mukhammadali Abdurakhmonov (2390) and Asrorjon Omonov (2347) have lost only to higher-rated teams, Germany and Australia. Their draw against Austria should be considered an achievement. Omonov is showing excellent form, having won all five of his games. Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta Uzbekistan’s main women’s team also made an ex
title: “Cautious optimism” justified: Uzbekistan’s performance halfway through Chess Olympiad

body: Photo: Saida Mirziyoyeva / Telegram Head of Presidential Administration discusses YouTube monetization launch in Uzbekistan with Google Head of the Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva met with Google vice president of government affairs and public policy Karan Bhatia in New York. They discussed launching YouTube monetization in Uzbekistan, which is currently unavailable for local audiences. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 23 September 2026, 19:10 Economy Head of the Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva met with Google vice president of government affairs and public policy Karan Bhatia during her visit to New York. “We discussed the possibility of launching YouTube monetization in Uzbekistan,” Mirziyoyeva wrote on her Telegram channel. “In recent years, we have improved legislation on personal data processing and digital payments, making international payment systems available in Uzbekistan,” she noted. Advertising on Gazeta “There are many opportunities for partnership with the company. There is a lot of work ahead,” Mirziyoyeva added. Uzbekistan is among the countries where the YouTube Partner Program (YPP) is unavailable, preventing local video creators from earning advertising revenue through the platform. YouTube users in Uzbekistan also do not see ads when watching videos. Some Uzbek creators can still earn from foreign audiences. For example, bloggers may run channels in foreign languages. The earnings accumulate in an account, from which the money can be transferred to a bank card. Some creators also work through media agencies. One of the main sources of income for video bloggers is special projects, native advertising and product placements in their content. In 2024, Uzbekistan’s digital technologies minister Sherzod Shermatov noted that Uzbek YouTube creators could earn more by producing videos in languages with high demand, such as English. A study by the Center for Economic Research and Reforms said that Uzbekistan loses up to $50 million a year because YouTube monetization is unavailable. body: Photo: Interior Ministry of Uzbekistan France’s Interior Ministry representative for Central Asia starts work in Tashkent France’s Interior Ministry representative Cyril Gou has started work in Uzbekistan. He is the country’s only internal security attaché in Central Asia and is authorized to address all matters of common interest, including combating organized crime, cybercrime, terrorism and illegal immigration. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 22 September 2026, 11:09 Politics France’s Interior Ministry representative in Uzbekistan Cyril Gou has started work in Tashkent. Uzbekistan’s Interior Ministry said last week, following a meeting between Gou and head of the ministry’s Department of International Cooperation Nodirbek Makhmudov . The sides discussed expanding cooperation between the interior ministries of the two countries, including the exchange of experience and training for personnel. Gazeta asked the French Embassy about the representative’s responsibilities in Uzbekistan. Advertising on Gazeta It said that the decision to create the position of internal security attaché in Uzbekistan was made in 2025 following meetings between the presidents of France and Uzbekistan, with the aim of strengthening technical cooperation. “The police officer appointed to this position has regional responsibility for all of Central Asia (Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan) [and] is based in Tashkent. He is the only French internal security attaché in the region and is authorized to address all matters of common interest in the field of internal security,” the embassy said. The areas of cooperation include training for internal security personnel, combating organized crime, cybercrime, drug trafficking, protecting high-ranking officials, counterterrorism, border security, combating illegal immigration networks, civil protection and security. “Technical cooperation with Uzbekistan already exists and will be further strengthened through the exchange of experience between police academies, in the areas of civil protection, protection of high-ranking officials, combating cybercrime, road safety and combating drug trafficking,” the embassy added. body: Photo: Saida Mirziyoyeva / Telegram Head of Presidential Administration to address UN General Assembly debate this year Head of Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva will represent Uzbekistan at the general debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. She met with UN secretary-general António Guterres. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 22 September 2026, 11:07 Politics Head of the Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva will represent Uzbekistan at the general debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York this year, sources confirmed to Gazeta . On 21 September, Mirziyoyeva met with UN secretary-general António Guterres on the sidelines of the session. The High-Level Week begins here on 22 September. “We discussed all the key areas that Uzbekistan and the UN are developing together,” she wrote on her Telegram channel. Advertising on Gazeta “In this challenging time for the international system, I thank Mr Guterres for his strong global leadership and support for our country across all key areas of security,” she added. Saida Mirziyoyeva with Presidential Administration representative in the US Komil Allamjonov (left) and Uzbekistan’s permanent representative to the UN Ulugbek Lapasov (right). Nearly 130 heads of state and government are expected to participate in the High-Level Week this year to deliver their messages to the world. The general debate will take place from Tuesday, 22 September, to Saturday, 26 September, and on Monday, 28 September. This year’s theme is “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all”. Last year, president Shavkat Mirziyoyev addressed the general debate of the 80th session of the UN General Assembly. In March 2023, Mirziyoyeva, who was then head of the Communications and Information Policy Sector of the Presidential Administration’s Executive Office, spoke at a UN conference on water resources. She presented the “Aral Culture Summit” project and spoke about Uzbekistan’s challenges and achievements in water resource management. body: Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Vladimir Putin. Photo: Press service of president of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev congratulates Vladimir Putin on successful State Duma elections President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev congratulated president of Russia Vladimir Putin on the successful State Duma elections. Mirziyoyev described the results as evidence of citizens' trust in Russia’s strategic development course under Putin’s leadership. Uzbekistan puts businessman Muminjon Yuldashev on Interpol’s wanted list Businessman Muminjon Yuldashev has been placed on Interpol’s international wanted list at Uzbekistan’s request on charges of embezzlement. In 2019, the World Bank sanctioned Yuldashev and companies linked to him following an investigation into a water supply project in Syrdarya region. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 20 September 2026, 18:12 Society Businessman from Fergana region Muminjon Yuldashev has been placed on an international wanted list at Uzbekistan’s request. Interpol has published his Red Notice on its website. An Interpol Red Notice is an international request to locate and provisionally arrest a person. It asks law enforcement agencies in other countries to find and temporarily detain the individual pending a decision on extradition. Advertising on Gazeta According to Interpol, Yuldashev was born on 18 February 1976 in Fergana region. He is 175 cm tall, weighs 95 kg and speaks Uzbek and Russian. The Red Notice cites article 167, part 3 of Uzbekistan’s Criminal Code, which Interpol lists as “Larceny by Embezzlement”. Under the article, the offense is punishable by a fine of 300−360 basic calculation units ($11,000−13,000), corrective labor for up to 3 years or imprisonment for five to 10 years. In April, Gomel (Belarus) Regional Executive Committee chairman Ivan Krupko held talks with Yuldashev, who was described as a businessman from Uzbekistan. In July, chairwoman of the Belarus' Bellegprom concern Nadezhda Lazarevich met with a delegation from Fergana region. Yuldashev was introduced as a co-investor in INKAS company. Yuldashev was a shareholder in the private Madad Invest Bank in 2023 but is no longer listed among its shareholders. In 2019, the World Bank sanctioned Yuldashev and companies linked to him following an investigation into a water supply project in Syrdarya region. The bank said he had threatened a representative of a competing bidder and colluded with government officials. Yuldashev, his company Quvasoy Tamir Qurilish, later renamed Stroy Montaj Invest, and affiliated entities were barred from participating in World Bank-financed projects for several years. The decision also led to similar bans by several international financial institutions. A 2022 UzInvestigations report identified Yuldashev as a major shareholder and chairman of the supervisory board of Madad Invest Bank, although he is no longer listed among its shareholders. The report also linked him to companies in the construction, textile and footwear industries, including Baxodir Log’on Tekstil, Vodiy Shoes and Royal Dizayn Loyiha. body: A video still from social media Bright object seen in Tashkent sky may be part of Chinese rocket A bright object with a long trail over Tashkent was unlikely to be a meteor or bolide, the Institute of Astronomy of Uzbekistan said. The most likely explanation is a spent stage of China’s Long March-2D rocket. Scientists are continuing to investigate. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 20 September 2026, 12:02 Society A bright object with a long trail was observed in the sky over Tashkent on the evening of 19 September. Videos of the object were shared on social media . The press service of the Academy of Sciences of Uzbekistan commented on the phenomenon. Following a preliminary analysis of photos and videos, experts from the Institute of Astronomy of the Academy of Sciences said the object’s appearance, movement and trail showed no signs of a meteor or bolide. They said it was more likely to have been part of a rocket. According to senior researcher at the institute Kamoliddin Ergashev, the most likely explanation is the spent first stage of a Long March-2D (Chang Zheng-2D) launch vehicle. The rocket was launched from China’s Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center and successfully placed four PIESAT-2 series satellites into orbit. “Initial orbital calculations show a very close match between the launch time, the rocket’s orbit, the time and direction of the phenomenon observed in the sky over Tashkent. Therefore, the most likely explanation at this stage... may be related to the rocket stage of this space launch or one of the subsequent orbital processes,” he said. However, it is still too early to definitively identify the object as part of this rocket, Ergashev added. International orbital catalogs do not yet contain the necessary elements and data for the newly launched objects to independently identify the object. body: Photo: Tashkent hokimiyat School attendance in Tashkent to be monitored by cameras A Face ID-based student attendance system, SI Davomat (“AI Attendance”), is being introduced in Tashkent. It is currently being tested at 26 schools in Sergeli district. Following the pilot, the system is planned to be gradually introduced in other public schools. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 17 September 2026, 22:23 Society A Face ID-based system for monitoring student attendance, called SI Davomat (“AI Attendance”), is being tested at 26 schools in Tashkent’s Sergeli district . The system uses smart cameras and Face ID technology to record attendance during lessons . A total of 446 smart cameras have been installed at the 26 schools involved in the pilot. Based on its results, the system is expected to be gradually introduced in other public schools across the capital. Advertising on Gazeta The rolling out of the system was discussed on Thursday at the Tashkent hokimiyat (administration) Situation Center at a meeting attended by the city hokim (mayor) Shavkat Umurzakov, the hokimiyat said . If a student misses classes without a valid reason, their parents would receive an SMS notification. The information would also be automatically sent to the school principal, prevention inspector, National Guard officer and mahalla (neighborhood) representatives, the statement noted. SI Davomat is integrated with the ERP Maktab (Preschool and School Education Ministry’s school education management) and the Ministry of Health’s DMED (unified digital healthcare) systems. This would allow the system to distinguish students who miss classes due to illness from those who are absent without a valid reason. Based on attendance data, schools will be categorized as “green,” “yellow” and “red” based on their attendance rates, the hokimiyat said. In August last year, the Tashkent hokim signed a decision providing for the introduction of an artificial intelligence-based monitoring system in the capital’s schools to monitor the quality of education, student attendance and students' psychological well-being. Plans to introduce a system using Face ID to track how long students remain on school premises were announced in spring 2021. body: Timothy Smart Photo: Embassy of the UK in Uzbekistan “Uzbekistan's independence matters to the UK.” Ambassador Timothy Smart on reforms, cooperation, and regional security The British Ambassador to Uzbekistan, Timothy Smart spoke about the results of his mission and the development of relations between the two countries. In an interview with Gazeta.uz, he explained why Uzbekistan’s independence matters to London and set out how he sees the prospects for cooperation. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 17 September 2026, 14:09 Politics The British Ambassador to Uzbekistan, Timothy Smart, is completing his mission in Tashkent. He served as His Majesty’s Ambassador from 2023 to 2026. In his final interview before departing, he told Gazeta.uz what has changed over the three years in trade, investment, education and security, why Uzbekistan’s independence and territorial integrity matter to Britain, and what lies ahead for cooperation with the Central Asian region. — You served in Uzbekistan for three years, from 2023 to 2026. Looking back, what objectives did the British government set for you before the start of your mission in Uzbekistan? — When I came to Uzbekistan, my focus was on strengthening the relationship between this country and mine: what we can do for growth in trade and investment, and what we can do on security and on people-to-people links. All of that was building on the foundation laid by the ambassadors before me — Tim Torlot, Chris Allan, and everyone who worked here before them. Without forgetting your great history and culture, we recognised that the real transformation in our relationship and in the region came after 2016. By 2023, when I arrived, we had only just come out of COVID, the fall of the government in Kabul had already happened, and so had Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. So by then, the geopolitics had become even more difficult. Just a month before I came out to Tashkent, I joined a meeting in the UK between Uzbekistan’s Foreign Minister, Bakhtiyor Saidov, and the then Foreign Secretary, James Cleverly. There was a really nice moment when they met for the first time — they gave each other a great big hug. And I saw right away that genuine warmth and welcome. Photo: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Uzbekistan Your reform agenda is genuinely impressive, and we are ready to be your partner in those areas where our support can bring real benefit . We understand that your country sits in a difficult region, including because of the situation south of your border, in Afghanistan. We also recognise that you understand your country’s geopolitical position better than we do. Yes, we will urge you to do whatever you can to help bring the war in Ukraine to an end, but we know how difficult that question is for you. So, first of all, we want to hear from you: how can we help? How can we support your reform agenda, your territorial integrity, and your independence? And I have heard every British minister, every foreign secretary and everyone else who has met their Uzbek counterparts open a meeting with exactly that message: “We are here as a partner and a friend — where can we help?” It is in our mutual interest to help you. That has been the guiding light of my whole posting. — How would you characterize this period of your career? — Diplomacy is sometimes hard to measure in KPIs, in indices. What we deal in is often the wars not fought and the lives not lost. But in Uzbekistan, you can measure it. Advertising on Gazeta When I arrived, bilateral trade stood at 275 million pounds. The latest figure, to the end of July 2026 , is 1.3 billion pounds, and for 2025, the total was 2.1 billion pounds. Much of that is the UK buying gold. But even so, trade has grown several times over. In conversations with opinion formers, with ministers, and with people from the Presidential Administration, I hear the same key message time and time again: around a million people are born in Uzbekistan every year, and a landlocked country needs, above all, to expand trade and attract investment. Today, Uzbekistan is moving towards a modern, reformed market economy. A transformation like that takes time. And the country wants to build trade links in every direction: north, south, east, and west. To do that, it needs reliable partners. Investment is flowing into Uzbekistan from China, from the Gulf, and from more traditional partners too. The questions I ask are these: What is needed to support the reforms? What brings stability? What will attract investment? What can Britain offer so that it works to our mutual benefit? Clearly, it is access to capital in London — the London Stock Exchange, debt and equity capital, private finance, Islamic finance — these are the areas where I am told time and again that we can help. And we are helping with the listing of the assets of the Uzbekistan National Investment Fund (UzNIF) in May this year, for example. The government is planning to list other state assets over the next few years. We want to be part of that story with you. — As you mentioned, a significant part of your work was connected with supporting reforms in the country. In our previous conversation, you said that people need time to prove themselves and reforms need time to deliver results. In which areas do you already see results, and which have moved more slowly than expected? — When David Cameron came here, when he was foreign secretary, he put it very precisely and very fairly: your democracy is essentially eight years old — today it is ten. It took Britain more than 300 years to give women the vote. And look how far you have already come. One area I supported wherever I could: shortly before I arrived, or around the same time, the President announced that he wanted an international commercial court, adapted specifically to Uzbekistan but modelled on what already exists in Dubai and Astana, because that would help attract foreign direct investment. The creation of such a court was announced recently and, from what I can see, it will be genuinely independent. That means arbitration does not have to go to London, New York, the Gulf or Astana — that business will come here. And it will help my successors deliver one of the key asks: bringing investment into Uzbekistan. When I arrived, too few British companies knew about Uzbekistan; today far more do. When they hear that you are about to join the WTO, when they hear about the reform agenda or see GDP growth above 7 per cent, they will also ask: What guarantees do I have in a market I do not know? An independent commercial court will be the answer to that question and will draw investors in; in a market that is new to them, they will feel far more confident. There are, of course, areas where progress is slower — but for entirely understandable reasons, and I am not sure many countries in the world could speed it up. You have made impressive progress on gender-based violence legislation. But beyond everything the state does, an enormous cultural shift has to happen. Understanding what it is like to be a woman in any of our cultures is something too few men in the world spend time thinking about. The women in our lives and in our society need greater support and understanding from men. Until women in our countries can be active participants in economic growth — entrepreneurs, ambassadors — we are losing 50 per cent of our workforce. For sustainable economic growth, all of us need to make sure women are fully included. Culturally, what impresses me most is the way Uzbekistan combines Islamic tradition with openness, modernity, and respect for its many-layered historical heritage. A wonderful example of that can be seen in the new Centre of Islamic Civilisation in Tashkent, which sets out every layer of the country’s history, including Zoroastrianism, Buddhism and the Bactrian kingdom, while at the same time emphasising the values that unite us: the pursuit of knowledge, the love of science and our share
title: “Uzbekistan's independence matters to the UK.” Ambassador Timothy Smart on reforms, cooperation, and regional security

body: Model consumers will be allowed to make a 15% advance payment for electricity and gas. Photo: Yevgeniy Sorochin / Spot As Spot previously reported , on September 22, Shavkat Mirziyoyev signed a decree introducing new measures to develop the fuel and energy sector. The document amends the Rules for the Use of Electricity and Natural Gas, approved by the Cabinet of Ministers in May 2024. The changes mainly concern the procedure and conditions for businesses to pay for energy resources. In particular, Group I electricity consumers — large industrial and budget organizations — will pay the standard tariff at night, from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. During semi-peak periods, a reducing coefficient of 1.5 will apply. Previously, the opposite system was in place: the standard tariff applied during semi-peak periods, while the night-time tariff was 1.5 times lower. Since June 1, Group I consumers have been charged the standard tariff of 1,100 soums per kWh. During semi-peak periods, the rate will be approximately 733 soums per kWh. The decree also introduces the concept of a “model consumer” of electricity and gas. This status will be granted to businesses that meet the following conditions: connection to automated electricity and gas monitoring and metering systems; installation of a meter with remote-control capabilities; timely payments over the previous two months; no violations related to the use of energy resources. “Model consumers” will be able to make a monthly advance payment of 15% of the contracted electricity and gas volume instead of 100%. The remaining amount will be paid as the resources are consumed. If a “model consumer” has no funds left in its ASKUÉ billing account, electricity supply will be automatically suspended. Once payment is made, the supply will also be automatically restored. In addition, the fee for reconnecting consumers to gas networks after disconnection due to outstanding debt will be abolished. The fee was 2 BCV (880,000 soums) for household consumers and 5 BCV (2.2 million soums) for industrial and utility organizations. Advertising on Spot Blogger and financier Otabek Bakirov linked the lower tariffs during semi-peak periods and higher night-time tariffs to changes in the power generation structure. Currently, most electricity generated during the day comes from solar and wind power plants, while at night it is produced mainly by more expensive gas-fired power plants. body: The head of the Presidential Administration discussed plans to launch the TIFC with the company’s executives. Photo: Saida Mirziyoyeva / Telegram Saida Mirziyoyeva, head of the Presidential Administration of Uzbekistan, held talks with executives of investment firm BlackRock in New York. She announced this on her official Telegram channel. The meeting was attended by BlackRock President Robert Kapito, Vice Chairman Thomas Donilon, Global Infrastructure Partners CEO Adebayo Ogunlesi, Global Head of Financial and Strategic Investors Charles Hatami, and BlackRock’s Head of the Middle East Charles Hatami. The parties discussed the launch of the Tashkent International Financial Centre, which is scheduled for 2027. According to Mirziyoyeva, “BlackRock is helping develop the concept and structure of the Centre”. “Uzbekistan is opening up to major, high-quality investments”, the head of the Presidential Administration said. A joint roundtable was also held with representatives of US business circles. The discussion focused on Uzbekistan’s and Central Asia’s development prospects over the coming decades. Advertising on Spot BlackRock in Uzbekistan In June 2025, Mirziyoyev met with Hamad bin Jassim Al Thani, Chairman of Al Mirqab Capital, and Adebayo Ogunlesi, Senior Managing Director of investment firm BlackRock. Following the talks, the parties agreed to adopt a roadmap for the systematic advancement of promising projects. Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade Laziz Kudratov said Uzbekistan had presented Al Mirqab Capital and BlackRock with a portfolio of eight major investment projects covering transport, energy, infrastructure and tourism. A joint working group was established following the meeting to prepare feasibility studies and implementation terms. The president met Ogunlesi again during his visit to the United States last September. The parties discussed expanding the strategic partnership with BlackRock, particularly in the development of energy, transport and water infrastructure. The parties backed plans to establish a joint fund. The concept of the platform is expected to be agreed soon, followed by the practical implementation of joint projects. Cooperation between Uzbekistan and BlackRock intensified at the beginning of the year after Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP), part of the BlackRock group, began talks with the Uzbek government on attracting long-term capital for industrial, energy and infrastructure projects. In January, Investment, Industry and Trade Minister Laziz Kudratov held talks with GIP executives, while Uzbekneftegaz signed an information-sharing agreement with the company to assess potential investment projects in the oil and gas sector. At the same time, Shavkat Mirziyoyev met with Ogunlesi on the sidelines of events in Davos. The president backed BlackRock’s initiatives to acquire stakes in several Uzbek companies, establish co-investment mechanisms and attract international expertise to improve the country’s investment climate. body: Uzenergoinspection will shift its focus to preventing violations and identifying them at an early stage in the sector. Photo: Yevgeniy Sorochin / Spot Shavkat Mirziyoyev approved new measures to develop the fuel and energy sector by a decree dated September 22 ( DP-202 ). The functions of government agencies in the energy sector are being revised. The Ministry of Energy will no longer issue individual permits for contractual, service and other business relations involving sector enterprises and consumers. Energy-sector enterprises will independently conduct commercial activities in the fuel and energy sector. These include the extraction and production of energy resources, as well as their processing, transportation, storage, distribution and sale. The Agency for the Development and Regulation of the Energy Market will receive additional responsibilities related to the phased introduction of market mechanisms in the supply of natural and liquefied gas. The Inspectorate for Control over the Use of Electricity, Petroleum Products and Gas (Uzenergoinspection) will be given preventive control functions. It will focus on early identification of risks, as well as preventing and mitigating violations. Advertising on Spot From July 1, 2027, a unified digital platform for the Interagency Tariff Commission in the fuel and energy sector is to be launched. The platform is intended to make the commission’s work more transparent, efficient and prompt. The platform will be used to receive and process tariff applications, as well as financial, technical and other information needed to calculate tariffs. Calculations will be carried out automatically in accordance with procedures approved by the Cabinet of Ministers. body: A toll road to Khanabad and a new border crossing with Kyrgyzstan are also planned. The president outlined several major projects aimed at expanding the region’s transport and logistics potential. In particular, the launch of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway will increase cargo transportation tenfold to 15 million tonnes per year. Construction of a 300-hectare logistics complex in Qo‘rg‘ontepa and Khanabad is expected to begin by the end of the year to serve the future railway. The project is estimated to cost $600 million. Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan have agreed to build a new border crossing, “Keskanyor”, the president said. Its capacity will be twice that of the largest existing crossing, “Do‘stlik” (“Dostuk” on the Kyrgyz side). Practical work on the construction of the Tashkent-Andijan toll road will begin in 2027, Mirziyoyev said. The design of a new 78-km road between Andijan and Khanabad will also begin. The president also noted the launch of a high-speed train between Tashkent and Andijan earlier in September. As a result, travel time between the two cities has been cut from six to four hours. body: The new industrial zone will accommodate more than 50 enterprises and produce over $200 million worth of goods annually. During his visit to Andijan region, Shavkat Mirziyoyev toured a technopark in the Khojaabad district and reviewed the production of “smart” water meters, the presidential press service reported. The plant was built in a new industrial zone with a $25 million investment from Chinese company Sanchuan. Together with Huawei, the company has launched production of smart water meters using 5G connectivity. The devices allow users to monitor water consumption, water quality, equipment condition and the remaining balance online. The meters are designed to prevent water accumulation and feature a frost-resistant casing. The plant will produce up to 1 million smart water meters of 15 types annually. Around 80% of production processes are automated. Advertising on Spot A dual education system has also been introduced at the enterprise. By 2030, companies producing components and spare parts for the meters are planned to be established, raising the localization rate to 70%. The Andijan Technopark, covering 100 hectares, has a total construction cost of around $300 million. Once fully operational, the complex is expected to host 51 industrial enterprises and create up to 3,000 jobs. body: Alternatives include sovereign bonds, securities issued by supranational organizations and other fixed-income instruments. Photo: Yevgeniy Sorochin / Spot The Central Bank of Uzbekistan plans to gradually expand the investment portfolio of the country’s international reserves beyond US Treasury securities. Central Bank Deputy Chairman Abror Mirzo Olimov said this on September 18 at the first International Forum on State Asset Management in Tashkent, Spot correspondent reports. According to him, gold will remain a strategic reserve asset for the country. However, as the portfolio grows, the regulator plans to expand its range of investment instruments and strengthen diversification. “We intend to move beyond US Treasury securities and shift to other highly liquid assets. These could include sovereign bonds, securities issued by supranational organizations and other fixed-income instruments”, Olimov said. At the same time, the Central Bank deputy chairman stressed that diversification is not limited to adding new asset classes. Before taking on additional risks, the regulator needs to strengthen its institutional capacity to understand, assess and manage them. Advertising on Spot This year and next year, the Central Bank, together with international financial institutions, is working on strategic asset allocation, investment policy and strategy, independent risk management and other areas, Olimov noted. “Our experience, as well as that of other countries and reserve managers, shows that there is no one-size-fits-all reserve portfolio. The structure of reserves should take into account each country’s liabilities, intervention needs, market structure, acceptable level of risk and institutional capacity”, Olimov said. According to the Central Bank deputy chairman’s presentation, the next stage, described as “diversification with institutional capacity,” is planned for 2027 and beyond. It envisages expanding the investment space while simultaneously strengthening the reserve management framework. The presentation lists government bonds issued by G7 countries and other sovereign issuers, high-quality fixed-income instruments and other eligible high-quality assets among the areas for expanding the investment portfolio. The expansion will be carried out within the approved risk parameters. A separate section focuses on strengthening the institutional framework. It includes strategic asset allocation, investment policy and strategy, independent risk management, as well as the development of systems, analytics and corporate governance. The Central Bank also plans to expand cooperation with external asset managers and the World Bank under the RAMP program, strengthen knowledge sharing, adopt technologies and risk analysis tools, and develop internal expertise. body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan to revise official exchange rate calculation method from September 15 Uzbekistan will change how its official exchange rate is formed from September 15, incorporating interbank over-the-counter transactions alongside exchange deals to more accurately reflect conditions in the domestic currency market. 10 September, 19:00 1 min read 1 884 views 0 comments 0 Uzbekistan will begin using both exchange and interbank over-the-counter currency transactions to determine its official exchange rate from September 15, replacing the current approach based solely on deals concluded on the currency exchange. The Central Bank said the official exchange rate will be calculated based on the weighted average exchange rate of transactions conducted on the exchange and in the over-the-counter interbank market. According to the regulator, the change will allow a broader range of transactions in the domestic currency market to be considered when calculating the official exchange rate and will enable the rate to more accurately reflect market conditions. The Central Bank will also apply the official exchange rate announced for the last working day to weekends, including Saturdays and Sundays. On September 10, the U.S. dollar fell by UZS 15.29 to UZS 11,797.92 per $1, according to previously published data. The changes come amid a broader decline in dollarization in Uzbekistan’s banking system. The share of foreign-currency deposits has fallen from nearly 50% to around 20%, while the share of foreign-currency loans has decreased from 54% to 37%, indicating a reduced reliance on foreign currencies in the banking sector. # currency # dollarization # economy # finance # uzbekistan ZG Author Zaynabbegim Gʻaybullayeva All stories Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? body: Kazakhstan Kazakhstan conducts first passenger drone taxi flight in Astana Kazakhstan has conducted its first passenger-carrying drone taxi demonstration flight in Astana, as the government explores using eVTOL aircraft for tourism, emergency services, logistics and future urban transport. 9 August, 20:19 2 min read 494 views 0 comments 0 Kazakhstan has conducted its first passenger-carrying drone taxi flight in Astana, testing an EH216-S electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft as the country explores new applications for urban air mobility and tourism. The demonstration flight took place over a designated area of the capital as part of the Future Games 2026 international tournament, Kazakhstan's Ministry of Transport reported. The flight marked the country's first test of an autonomous passenger-carrying eVTOL aircraft under real-world conditions. The EH216-S is designed to carry up to two passengers and can reach speeds of up to 130 km/h. The aircraft has an autonomous flight range of up to 35 kilometers. As a first step, the government is considering launching demonstration and tourist routes over Kazakhstan's natural, cultural and historical attractions. These flights could last between five and 30 minutes. In the longer term, autonomous air taxis could become part of Kazakhstan's urban transport system, complementing existing modes of transportation. Beyond passenger transport, the aircraft could also be used for emergency medical services, medicine delivery, search-and-rescue operations, firefighting and logistics. Source: Kazakhstan's Transport Ministry The Transport Ministry said another area under consideration is the localization of passenger drone taxi production in Kazakhstan through international cooperation. The project could create new high-tech manufacturing capacity and jobs while expanding industrial cooperation, according to the ministry. Kazakhstan has also established a regulatory framework for urban air mobility. Legislative amendments have been introduced to regulate the use of eVTOL air taxis, vertiports and unmanned air traffic management systems, providing a legal basis for integrating the technology into the country's transport infrastructure. In May, Kazakhstan conducted its first eVTOL air taxi test in the Almaty Region, described as the first such trial in Central Asia. The electric aircraft was presented as a potential tool for reducing congestion, connecting tourist destinations and shortening travel times. Iran also launched its first official air taxi service in May 2025, with the initial route connecting Karaj and Qazvin. # airtaxi # aviation # kazakhstan # technology # tourism ZG Author Zaynabbegim Gʻaybullayeva All stories What do you think? body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan beats China 3–1 at Chess Olympiad in Samarkand Uzbekistan remained the sole leader of the Open section after recording two consecutive wins over India and China, with Nodirbek Yakubboev securing victories in both matches. 24 September, 15:00 468 views 0 comments 0 Uzbekistan’s men’s national chess team defeated China 3–1 at the ongoing Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, allowing the host team to maintain its position as the sole leader in the tournament standings. Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Nodirbek Yakubboev secured victories in their respective games, while Javokhir Sindorov and Muhiddin Madaminov drew their matches. The two wins and two draws gave Uzbekistan an overall 3–1 result against the Chinese team. Abdusattorov defeated Ding Liren, while Yakubboev won against Yu Yangyi. Sindorov drew with Wei Yi, and Madaminov shared the point with Xu Xiangyu. The result added another team victory to Uzbekistan’s campaign at the Olympiad and allowed the national team to remain alone at the top of the standings following the round. Uzbekistan is hosting the 2026 Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, with national teams competing in the open and women’s sections. The tournament continues with Uzbekistan entering the remaining rounds as the sole leader in the men’s competition. Nodirbek Yakubboev secured the only win of the match, defeating Nihal Sarin on board three after a tactical sequence that allowed him to win a queen and convert the advantage. body: Uzbekistan Uzbek journalists explore Pakistan’s media, culture and history The visit, organized at the invitation of the Government of Pakistan, brings together Uzbek journalists, broadcasters, digital media representatives and content creators for meetings with Pakistani officials, media organizations and cultural institutions. 17 September, 13:05 473 views 0 comments 0 An Uzbek media delegation, including a correspondent from Daryo, is visiting Pakistan as part of a multi-day program focused on media cooperation, bilateral relations, cultural exchange and people-to-people contacts between Uzbekistan and Pakistan. The delegation includes representatives of Uzbek print, television and digital media, as well as content creators and social media representatives. During the visit, participants are scheduled to meet representatives of Pakistani public and private institutions and visit media organizations and cultural and historical sites. In Islamabad, the delegation visited the Pakistan Monument at Shakarparian and Faisal Mosque. The program provided participants with an introduction to cultural and architectural sites in the Pakistani capital. The Uzbek journalists subsequently visited Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, where they met Hassan Ali Zaigham, Director General for Central Asia, along with other officials and experts working on Central Asian affairs. During the meeting, Pakistani officials briefed the delegation on regional developments and relations between Pakistan and Uzbekistan. Discussions covered political contacts as well as prospects for expanding economic and trade cooperation. The Pakistani side highlighted historical, religious and cultural links between the two countries and discussed opportunities to develop bilateral partnerships in different sectors. The participants also discussed Pakistan’s regional partnerships and broader developments in the region. Zaigham highlighted the role of media organizations and journalists in providing information about bilateral relations, cultural links and opportunities for cooperation. The meeting also addressed the potential for media exchanges to contribute to contacts between the two countries. Following its visit to the Foreign Ministry, the Uzbek delegation toured Pakistan Television (PTV), the country's national broadcaster. Participants visited different departments and were briefed on PTV's broadcasting operations and media production processes. The program provided an opportunity to observe the broadcaster's organizational structure and production activities. The delegation also visited private television channels SAMAA News and Hum News. During these visits, participants toured newsrooms and broadcasting facilities and reviewed different aspects of the channels' operations. The media component of the visit is intended to facilitate exchanges of professional experience, expertise and content between media representatives from Uzbekistan and Pakistan. Participants are also examining the development of television, digital platforms and social media in Pakistan. The delegation's itinerary includes visits to cultural, historical and tourist destinations in Islamabad and other parts of Pakistan. In addition to the Pakistan Monument and Faisal Mosque, the program includes visits to sites in Murree, Taxila and Lahore. Taxila will provide the delegation with an opportunity to examine sites associated with the region's ancient history, while the Lahore portion of the program will focus on the city's cultural, architectural and historical heritage. The delegation is expected to continue its tour with visits to Lahore and other locations included in the itinerary. The visit is taking place at the invitation of the Government of Pakistan and is intended to expand contacts between Pakistani and Uzbek media organizations. The program also aims to provide Uzbek media representatives with information about Pakistan's political, diplomatic, media, cultural and tourism sectors. Participants are expected to share information and observations from the visit with audiences in Uzbekistan through television, digital media and social platforms. Earlier Daryo reported that as part of his state visit to Pakistan, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev joined Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif at a business forum in Islamabad, which brought together representatives of more than 300 major industrial companies, trading firms and business associations from the two countries. The Pakistani side was represented by a range of major companies, including PEL, Waves Singer, Sadaqat, Fauji, Platinum, Fast Cables, National Fruit, Amson Group, Shaigan, Hans International, Secure Logistics Group, NLC, Fairmont, Go Dairy, Engro, Herbion, AGP, Arco, Habib Rafiq, Pakistan Steel Mills, Siddiq Sons, Uniworth, Diners, Fatima Group, Fateh Group, Hub Leather, Siddiq Leather, Royal Leather and Ahsan Dyeing. Addressing the forum, Mirziyoyev said the high-level negotiations had opened a new stage in relations between Uzbekistan and Pakistan, with particular emphasis on expanding trade, economic and investment cooperation. The two countries also signed a protocol establishing a new framework for economic engagement and setting a target of increasing bilateral trade to $2bn. Relevant officials were instructed to prepare a comprehensive roadmap and introduce a mechanism for promptly addressing issues that may arise during its implementation. Uzbekistan ranked as Pakistan’s second-largest trading partner among Central Asian countries in 2025, with bilateral trade totaling $445.9mn. Pakistan’s exports to Uzbekistan amounted to $120.9mn, led by food products at $56.2mn and chemicals at $45.3mn, followed by manufactured goods worth $6.4mn and finished products at $5.2mn. Meanwhile, Pakistan imported $325mn in goods and services from Uzbekistan, including $260.2mn in food products, $30.1mn in services, $21.2mn in manufactured goods and $13.2mn in non-food raw materials. # itinerary # media # observations # organizations # platforms # program What do you think? body: Uzbekistan Trump’s foreign policy in Central Asia: balancing acts amid rising influence from China and Russia Traditionally, this region has not been a top priority for American presidents. However, shifting geopolitical dynamics, particularly involving China and Russia, are reshaping the U.S. approach to Central Asia. The adoption of the "U.S. Strategy for Central Asia 2019-2025: Advancing Sovereignty and Economic Prosperity" during the Trump administration marked a strategic shift. How do external forces determine U.S. foreign policy in Central Asia? 8 November 2024, 18:50 11 min read 21,170 views 0 comments 0 With Donald Trump being elected as the next President of the United States, the country's foreign policy in Central Asia is anticipated to be heavily influenced by external factors. Traditionally, this region has not been a top priority for American presidents. However, shifting geopolitical dynamics, particularly involving China and Russia, are reshaping the U.S. approach to Central Asia. The adoption of the "U.S. Strategy for Central Asia 2019-2025: Advancing Sovereignty and Economic Prosperity" during the Trump administration marked a strategic shift. How do external forces determine U.S. foreign policy in Central Asia? Let's explore the transactional nature of past engagements, the objectives of the new strategy, and the challenges and opportunities emerging in the region. USA 2024 Election Results Google Central Asia's Peripheral Status in U.S. Foreign Policy A key indicator of Central Asia's marginal position in U.S. foreign policy is that, historically, no sitting American president had ever visited the region or held a summit with all Central Asian leaders. Central Asia often remained overshadowed by other global priorities. There have been instances where Central Asian leaders visited the United States but did not secure meetings with the American president, underscoring the limited priority given to the region. However, in September 2023, President Biden hosted the first-ever U.S.-Central Asia Summit with the leaders of the five Central Asian countries, signaling a potential shift in engagement. Despite this unprecedented summit, high-level interactions remain infrequent. In 2024, there was only a foreign ministers' meeting , and it is not known whether there will be meetings at the level of heads of state in the future. This indicates that while there may be increasing attention, Central Asia is still not a primary focus in U.S. foreign policy. The Transactional Nature of U.S. Engagement U.S. foreign policy in Central Asia has historically been transactional, often influenced by global events rather than regional priorities. The U.S. engaged in the region not for its intrinsic importance but due to external factors such as the situation in Afghanistan, concerns over China's control of rare earth elements, and attempts to counterbalance Russia's historical influence. Military involvement in Afghanistan heightened Central Asia's strategic importance as a logistical hub and for regional security cooperation. Additionally, the U.S. explored alternative sources of rare earth metals in Central Asia to reduce dependence on China and initiated diplomatic and economic efforts to weaken Russia's ties in the region. The "U.S. Strategy for Central Asia 2019-2025" Adopted during the Trump administration, the "U.S. Strategy for Central Asia 2019-2025: Advancing Sovereignty and Economic Prosperity" signaled a renewed commitment to the region. The strategy aimed to build a more stable and prosperous Central Asia that is free to pursue political, economic, and security interests with a variety of partners on its own terms. The United States emphasized support for the sovereignty and independence of the Central Asian states, aiming to strengthen their resilience against short and long-term threats to their stability. The strategy outlined six overarching objectives : Support Sovereignty and Independence : Enhancing diplomatic engagement and providing assistance to strengthen democratic institutions and economic prosperity, helping Central Asian states function as cooperative partners. Reduce Terrorist Threats : Working with Central Asian nations to develop resilience to extremist ideologies and prevent the region from becoming a haven for terrorist organizations. Support Stability in Afghanistan : Encouraging Central Asian countries to develop economic and trade links with Afghanistan, contributing to regional stability. Encourage Regional Connectivity : Promoting closer ties between Central Asia and Afghanistan across energy, economic, cultural, trade, and security lines. Promote Rule of Law and Human Rights : Assisting in developing and implementing justice sector reforms, strengthening civil society, and enhancing government responsiveness. Promote U.S. Investment : Working with Central Asian countries to undertake reforms needed to attract more foreign investment, including from American businesses. The Future of the C5+1 Format Under Trump The strategy also emphasized the importance of the C5+1 diplomatic platform, which brings together representatives from the five Central Asian states and the United States to address common concerns and promote regional dialogue and cooperation. Under President Trump, the future of the C5+1 format at the presidential level remained uncertain. While the strategy outlined continued support for the platform, the actual engagement depended on the administration's priorities and responses to initiatives by Russia or China in the region. A lack of U.S. response to significant projects launched by these powers could be perceived as a sign of weakness, potentially diminishing American influence. Delegating Institutionalization to External Powers A unique phenomenon in Central Asia is the delegation of institutionalization processes to external actors. Central Asian nations increasingly allow countries like the U.S. and China to guide their institutional frameworks. This raises concerns about the region's autonomy and the long-term implications for regional integration. The reasons behind this delegation include the slow pace of intraregional integration, where countries often unite only in response to crises and prefer bilateral relations during stable periods. This sporadic cooperation opens the door for external powers to introduce their own formats of cooperation. The strong involvement of external powers is evident, with Central Asia showing openness to allowing these players to shape the regional agenda. Structures like the B5+1 Business Forums and the China-Central Asia Secretariat exemplify this trend. Moreover, the lack of a central coordinating body, unlike the European Union or ASEAN, makes Central Asia more dependent on external structures to coordinate policies, further enabling external actors to influence the region's institutional processes. Impact on Regional Integration Delegating institutionalization to external actors has both drawbacks and benefits for Central Asian integration. On the downside, relying on external powers may increase their influence over regional affairs, potentially sidelining the interests of Central Asian countries. Engaging with powerful external actors complicates balancing regional priorities with the interests of these powers. The sustainability of commitments also becomes uncertain, as changes in the political dynamics of external actors can affect the continuity and effectiveness of cooperation mechanisms. On the positive side, external actors facilitate regular summits and dialogues, providing platforms for discussing regional issues. Mechanisms like the C5+1 support long-term goals and projects beneficial to the region. Initiatives aimed at promoting cultural and educational exchanges foster mutual understanding among Central Asian populations. body: Uzbekistan The implication of Israel-Iran War for Central Asia The escalating conflict between Iran and Israel, highlighted by Iran’s missile strike on Israel on October 1, 2024, is reshaping the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East. This intensifying rivalry, particularly through Iran’s “Sadiq-2” operation, carries significant implications not only for the immediate region but also for Central Asia. Central Asian countries, which maintain complex ties with both Iran and Israel, now face new security threats, potential disruptions to trade, and shifting alliances. As tensions rise, these nations must carefully navigate the conflict to preserve their neutrality while addressing the growing risks to regional stability and economic interests. 6 October 2024, 21:03 14 min read 24,784 views 1 comments 0 The Middle East has long been a center of geopolitical rivalry and armed conflict between Israel and Iran . Currently, the region is experiencing a significant phase of growing divergence , with tensions escalating in Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, and Yemen , largely manifesting increase in hostility between Iran and Israel. Major General Hossein Salami, Commander-in-Chief of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Reuters It was demonstrated by Iran's missile attack on Israel on October 1, 2024, the country launched missile strikes against Israel , and the operation, named “Sadiq-2,” was ordered by Major General Hossein Salami, Commander-in-Chief of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), from the Combat Room. This event marks a pivotal shift in the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East, with significant implications not only for the Middle East and South Asia but also for Central Asia. As tensions rise, Central Asian countries must navigate a complex setting of security threats, shifting alliances, and economic challenges. Hence, the ballistic missile strike is part of a broader conflict shaped by historical disputes, strategic rivalries, and intricate alliances. As the situation develops, the consequences of these events extend beyond the immediate regional players, influencing Central Asia in terms of geopolitics, security , and economics. Understanding these impacts is crucial for policymakers, scholars, and security analysts as they navigate the complexities of international relations in an increasingly multipolar world. Central Asian countries have varying levels of engagement with both Iran and Israel in areas such as diplomacy, security, and trade . Their involvement in the Middle East, which is fundamentally focused on combating extremism, advancing defense technologies, and enhancing cybersecurity capabilities, enables them to remain neutral during the Iran-Israel conflict. Furthermore, these countries have an opportunity to contribute to long-term stability and peace efforts in the Middle East. Any departure from neutrality or taking sides in the conflict could diminish their influence and role in the region. Before delving into the impact of the missile attack carried out by Iran on Israel on October 1, 2024, and its implications for Central Asian countries, we will first explore a brief overview of the historical context of relations between Iran and Israel. Historical Context of Iran-Israel Relations The long-standing enmity between Iran and Israel is deeply rooted in ideological (religious extremism and opposition to democracy), political, and geopolitical conflicts. After the 1979 Iranian Revolution , which led to the overthrow of the Pahlavi monarchy, Iran emerged as a staunch opponent and regional adversary of Israel, positioning itself as a leader in resistance to Western imperialism. Iran's support for various jihadist groups, particularly militias backed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) , further solidified its role as a key actor opposing Israeli influence. Some of these groups include Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza, Liwa Fatemiyoun in Syria, and the Ansarullah Houthi rebels in Yemen. Thus, several major events over the years have escalated tensions between Iran and Israel. 1: 1982 Lebanon War: Known as Israel's invasion of Lebanon, the conflict aimed to dismantle the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) , but instead led to the emergence of Hezbollah, a militia strongly supported by Iran. This marked the beginning of a protracted proxy conflict between the two nations. 2: Iran's Nuclear Program: Iran's nuclear ambitions, initially launched in the 1950s with U.S. support under the "Atoms for Peace" program, have been a major source of global tension, particularly between Iran and the West. After the 1979 revolution, cooperation on nuclear development ceased, and Iran pursued its program covertly. Israel views the prospect of a nuclear-armed Iran as a grave existential threat, pushing for international action to prevent Iran from acquiring such weapons. The ongoing enrichment of uranium and Iran’s secretive activities have prompted consistent surveillance by the U.S. and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) , seeking to prevent Iran from reaching nuclear capabilities and thus counter a growing threat to Israel in the region. 3: Regional Proxy Wars: Iran’s involvement in conflicts across the Middle East, particularly in Syria’s civil war and its support for Shia militias in Iraq, has further complicated its relations with Israel. These conflicts have led to direct confrontations, such as Iran’s missile strikes on Israel, most recently on October 1, 2024. Iran’s strategy, using loyal militias to counter Israeli influence, has resulted in prolonged proxy wars, adding a sectarian dimension (Shia versus Sunni, and Muslim versus Jewish) to the broader regional power struggle. This proxy war also has far-reaching diplomatic, security, and economic consequences for Central Asia and beyond, contributing to the region’s destabilization and fueling migration flows toward Europe. The ideological, strategic, and military rivalry between Iran and Israel continues to shape the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East, with consequences that extend well beyond the immediate conflict zone. This protracted enmity not only affects regional security but also has economic implications, influencing international relations and migration patterns, particularly as instability drives people to seek refuge in Europe. Iran’s recent missile strikes on Israel and the related rhetoric signify a potential shift towards more direct military confrontation, which could have negative diplomatic, security, and economic impacts on Central Asian countries. The repercussions for Central Asia’s geopolitical landscape may manifest in respective modes. a: Realignment of Alliances - The ongoing conflict between Iran and Israel might force Central Asian countries, such as Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan, to reconsider their traditionally neutral stance. As Iran emerges as a regional power and supports various jihadist groups and militias backed by the IRGC. These nations may feel pressured to side with Western powers, particularly the U.S., to safeguard their interests against potential Iranian expansionism. - The U.S. might increase diplomatic and military engagement with Central Asian nations to counterbalance Iranian influence in the region. This could lead to stronger military cooperation and intelligence-sharing agreements. - On the other hand, Russia, which plays a significant role in maintaining stability in Central Asia, might deepen its military and economic ties with these countries to ensure, they remain within its sphere of influence. However, Iran's growing influence may complicate Russia's relationships with Central Asian states, especially those wary of Iran's intentions. b: Emerging Security Frameworks - With rising tensions in the Middle East, Central Asian countries may seek to establish new security frameworks. Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov held talks with JICA President Akihiko Tanaka in Tokyo, where the sides discussed accelerating projects under the Cooperation Program through 2030. Lines, Sojitz, All Nippon Airways, Shimizu, JETRO, Sumitomo, JBIC, Toyo Engineering, Toyota Tsusho, Marubeni, Mitsui, Mitsubishi and other major Japanese companies attended the meeting. body: Uzbekistan From childhood dream to entrepreneurial success: Elyor Bozorov's journey from Uzbekistan to the United States "Becoming an economist was a childhood dream. Why? Because economists know how to make a lot of money." This is how Elyor Bozorov begins his story. Bozorov was the founder of successful enterprises like Elmakon and olcha.uz in Uzbekistan, and now an IT entrepreneur in the United States. 19 April 2024, 20:04 11 min read 4,160 views 0 comments 2 "Becoming an economist was a childhood dream. Why? Because economists know how to make a lot of money." This is how Elyor Bozorov begins his story. Bozorov was the founder of successful enterprises like Elmakon and olcha.uz in Uzbekistan, and now an IT entrepreneur in the United States. Elyor Bozorov It all started with the farm My childhood coincided with the period of the collapse of the Soviet Union when finding normal consumer goods was also a thousand troubles. Our family moved from my hometown of Navoi to the capital, Tashkent, in search of a better life. I grew up under the supervision of my grandparents until I entered the fourth grade. My grandfather, the owner of a large farm, taught me the secrets of agriculture and livestock. Although at that time I did not understand the essence, watching my grandfather's reasonable management in the supply chain, and how he led the workers, I increasingly formed entrepreneurial, leadership skills. It was then that I realized what I wanted to achieve in this life. My parents wanted me to become a doctor, but my dream was to become an economist. The reason being: economists know how to earn money! Childhood adversities, the desire to help the family encouraged me to work on myself in all respects, be progressive in my studies and public affairs. Being an active student, I was repeatedly elected as “Minister of Education" and “President" at the school. When I was in the fifth grade, my mother opened a children's clothing store. Helping her to run the store after school taught me practical knowledge about supply chains, margins, accounting, money circulation. In the ninth grade, I was lucky enough to study for a year in the United States on an exchange program. With a grade point average of 3.7, I became a member of the American Club of Future Business Leaders and presented my business projects at national competitions. I was also awarded a special medal by the President Obama’s Administration for completing 200 hours of volunteer work. That year in America has installed in me the independence and interpersonal skills that are essential for an entrepreneur. Bozorov at his University graduation. A ticket to a happy life Studying at a prestigious university in Uzbekistan was considered as a luxury at that time. I couldn't pass the cost of education on to my parents, because living in the United States taught not only decision-making, but also financial independence. I was lucky to take part in the competition of the Ministry of Transportation in 2011 with my business project for the production of electric cars in Uzbekistan, and won a full four-year grant for any university. At a time when higher education was a dream if you didn’t have the money, this achievement was my ticket to a happy life. This ticket allowed me to become a student at the Faculty of Economics and Finance at the University of Westminster, one of the country’s leading international higher education institutions. The socks business. Next destination is Dubai While studying at university, I started my business. After a three-month market analysis, I came to the conclusion that selling socks is profitable. By showing my business project to my uncle, who is one of the largest distributors of mobile phones in Uzbekistan, I was able to get 100 thousand dollars to get started. During my trip to China, I ordered 30 thousand dollars worth of socks and started a wholesale business. Within three years I opened eight stores, which brought the company an annual revenue of almost $2.5mn. Right after graduating from university, I was invited to work for BM Electronics, a mobile phone and consumer electronics distribution company based in Dubai. It was a big step towards my goal of becoming a top-manager. I was tasked with solving a supply chain problem that was considered a problem point during the first six months of my career at the company. By implementing a new ERP-system in warehouse operations, I managed to expedite the delivery service by 20% - from 15 days to a week. Like Steve Jobs: “E verything was started from a small garage” During my time in Dubai, I founded a new online trading business in Central Asian countries – BMBOX.com. This was my first online project that offered a delivery service for electronics and perfumes from Dubai within a week. The project quickly became popular in Uzbekistan due to the fact that in just three steps it was possible to purchase products from different countries. Almost all new mobile phones were first sold on BMBOX.com and then on the open market. By 2016, the platform had sold almost 4,500 phones and perfumes worth $1.5mn. At the end of 2015, I returned to Uzbekistan and headed the BM Electronics business development team. In those years, young people were inspired by Steve Jobs, and stories in the genre “everything was started from a small garage” were very popular. And I also came up with an idea to assemble a team in my own garage. With this team, we established cooperation with HTC and were able to increase sales of phones of this brand by 60 %. Halal installments – in Elmakon In 2017, Uzbekistan’s economy was reformed and began to open up. To take distribution activities to a new level, I founded the retail chain Elmakon . Elmakon allowed us to directly communicate with customers and gave us a more realistic picture of the market. In two years, I launched 11 stores in different regions of Uzbekistan reaching $2mn monthly sales. In essence, Elmakon was a great opportunity to understand every single aspect of the business, because it involved marketing through all channels, supplying on time, retailing, warehousing, recruiting on a big scale, managing big teams, teamwork, negotiating with partners, and vendors, accounting, forecasting and planning, and everything else. The “cherry” of the Uzbek online business In December 2017, I launched another online sales platform - olcha.uz (olcha – cherry). The goal was to become the cherry on the cake of an online business. Thanks to the comprehensive website and CRM system developed by our team, at a time when the delivery of goods throughout Uzbekistan usually took a week, we set up delivery within 3 days. In 2020, due to the pandemic, online services have reached a new level, in particular, olcha.uz sold 20 thousand units of products worth $2.4mn through it. We have also been able to ensure timely and high-quality delivery of orders even under strict lockdown restrictions. We have brought Huawei to second place in popularity When Huawei started entering the Uzbek market, I received an offer from the company. My main task was to systematize the brand's online and retail sales. However after we started work, because of sanctions implemented by the US on Huawei, it could no longer use the Android system owned by Google. As a result, the company introduced its alternative operating system, HMS. Although the new operating system brought inconveniences to customers, we managed to increase sales of Huawei phones even more than expected (by 20%). body: Auto Uzbekistan imports 83,800 cars from China in 11M 2023 The average prices for the imported vehicles remained steady at $18,000. 27 December 2023, 00:47 1 min read 4,800 views 0 comments 0 Uzbekistan has witnessed a remarkable surge in the import of passenger cars from China over the course of 11M 2023, marking a sixfold increase, as per the data reported by Tazabek, citing information from the General Administration of Customs of China. BYD car at the Uzbekistan-China Cooperation Expo. Source: Daryo / Madina Nurman In 11M 2023, the volume of exported passenger cars from China to Uzbekistan skyrocketed to 83,800 units , reaching $1.5bn , a figure six times higher than previous records. The average prices for the exported vehicles remained steady at $18,000 . Earlier in 9M 2023 Uzbekistan has substantially augmented its imports from China, recording a 5.8 times increase, totaling 65,300 vehicles. The supply of cars in monetary terms surged 5.9 times to $1.2bn , and the average car price saw a 2.4% rise to $18,600 . Moreover, in 8M 2023, Uzbekistan has significantly bolstered its imports of electric vehicles (EVs), reporting an influx of almost 1,500 EVs at a cost of $46.4mn . This marks an increase of 1,000 units compared to the same period last year. Notably, nearly 90% of these electric cars were imported from China, with the UAE, Germany, and Hong Kong following in the rankings. Additionally, in July, there was a resurgence in the demand for cars, with a 40% increase in sales of electric vehicles. The continuous growth in the car trade underscores the evolving dynamics of the automotive market between China and Uzbekistan.
