body: Schemes: Investigating Ukraine Exclusive: 'Key Targets': A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine By Olya Ivleva , Kyrylo Ovsyaniy , Kira Tolstyakova , Valeriya Yegoshyna and Schemes October 08, 2026 17:21 CET Exclusive: 'Key Targets': A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Kyiv's Darnytsia Thermal Power Station after a Russian attack in February. KYIV -- Early on September 30, Russia hammered Kyiv and the surrounding region with what Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskiy said was the most massive attack on energy infrastructure in the area since 2025. A child was found dead under the rubble of a home outside the capital – one of five people killed that day, officials said, and one of tens of thousands of civilian casualties in Russian attacks since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Among the facilities targeted that day were two combined heating and power plants in Kyiv and a thermal power plant outside the city. Those three plants, and dozens of other vital pieces of infrastructure across Ukraine, are featured in a detailed document that sets out a potential blueprint for a campaign by Moscow to inflict enormous suffering on civilians with attacks aimed at sharply cutting supplies of power, heat, and water. Schemes, the investigative unit of RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service, obtained a copy of the Russian-language document from sources in Ukraine’s defense forces. Emergency workers at a Kyiv aprtment building following a Russian missile strike in August 2025. The content suggested it is the same document that The New York Times , in a report last week that cited unnamed sources, said Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal showed European officials at a September 17 meeting in Paris. “I briefed our partners on Russia's plans to strike energy infrastructure, based on information provided by Ukrainian intelligence,” Shmyhal said in a Telegram post that day. The document obtained by Schemes identifies four “priority goals” -- power generation and supply, water supply, sewage systems, and heating. It contains an analysis of Ukraine's energy infrastructure and detailed calculations of the number of missiles, drones, and bombs Russia would need to cut power in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa by as much as 90 percent and drastically curtailing supplies of heat and water in those cities, which are Ukraine’s largest. Other "priority cities" include Dnipro, Zaporizhzhya, Mykolayiv, Kherson, Poltava, Chernihiv, Kryviy Rih, Cherkasy, Kropyvnytskiy, Lviv, Vinnytsia, and Ivano-Frankivsk. The Rivne Nuclear Power Plant in western Ukraine (file photo) A list of 60 “key targets” includes the three operating nuclear power plants that are controlled by Ukraine -- the Zaporizhzhya plant is occupied by Russia -- as well as 10 major hydroelectric power plants and dozens of other facilities. In addition to power plants and other infrastructure, the document indicates that one aim would be to disable substations, transmission lines, and interconnectors near the western border through which electricity is imported from Europe and distributed deeper in Ukraine. 'Cold, Precise' Shmyhal gave no details about the intelligence in his September 17 post, but in subsequent comments on national television, he indicated he had shown “two large [Russian] documents” to the Europeans at the meeting. "It shocked our partners, just as it did us, with its cynicism -- that cold, terrorist calculation of how to destroy our energy infrastructure.... The documents are drafted in a very cold, precise manner,” he said, according to RBC-Ukraine. “They include tables and specify the quantity of weaponry needed to destroy each target. The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones.” This description corresponds to the document obtained by Schemes. For example, it states that two Iskander missiles would be needed to take out one high-voltage installation that transmits electricity from a nuclear power plant. The document assesses power plants solely in terms of electricity consumption, making no mention of any potential threat from radiation, for example, but includes a fine-print warning that attacks with certain types of weapons on heating plants close to populated areas could cause civilian casualties. The document is titled Analytical Brief: Analysis Of Ukraine’s Power Generation And Utilities Sector, and is dated August 2026. The authors are not named in the copy obtained by Schemes, which is missing some pages, and the metadata has been altered. It does not indicate whom it was presented to in Russia. However, the brief itself cites sources of its data, including publicly accessible services such as OpenStreetMap and Worldometers as well as the official websites of Ukrainian power companies and the Energy Ministry. It also refers to "technical specifications of generating capacities" and the master plans of Kyiv and other cities. Most references cite assessments by unnamed experts or representatives of the Russian Armed Forces and an analysis by a "working group" whose members and affiliations are not identified. Russian officials have not commented on the document or on Shmyhal’s meeting with European energy officials in Paris last month. However, in early October, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov suggested that Russia would step up strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure, casting Russian attacks as “retribution” for Kyiv’s hits on Russian energy and logistics facilities. A Kyiv resident warms up by a fire in front of a veteran-run food truck during a power blackout following Russian strikes on civil infrastructure in January. Russia has been seeking to turn cold and darkness into weapons since the first year of the full-scale invasion: Attacks on power and energy infrastructure began in the initial weeks. By the autumn of 2022, it became a concerted campaign, and Ukraine’s first big blackout occurred that November. Each autumn has brought an upsurge in attacks. The Ukrainian Prosecutor-General’s Office told Schemes it is investigating 3,374 Russian strikes on 1,177 energy facilities in Ukraine. Ukrainian energy industry experts say that every month this summer and in September, Russia launched about 160 strikes against critical infrastructure outside the frontline zone -- meaning in and around cities far from the fighting on the ground. But analysts and military insiders said that they were familiar with similar documents from previous years and that it fell short of being an actual attack plan. 'Maximum Hardship' Similar documents “have been appearing -- at least to my knowledge -- since 2023,’” Oleksandr Kharchenko, director of the Kyiv-based Energy Industry Research Center, told Schemes. Some of the names of the weapons have changed and there have been “certain distinctions and differences” year to year, Kharchenko said. He added that "the briefing document underwent significant changes in 2024, but since then, I haven't really seen any major alterations." An Iskander missile at an arms show outside Moscow (file photo) Kharchenko also pointed to something that seems evident in the format and wording of the document. "This is not a combat order,” he said. “It is a document designed to demonstrate a concept to high-ranking Russian officials, intended to elicit a reaction like: 'Oh yes, we’ll destroy everything; the plan is excellent.'” Russia, he said, is “attempting to destroy critical infrastructure, cut off heat and electricity to key population centers, and cause us maximum hardship.” A Ukrainian defense industry representative whom Schemes asked to verify the document said he was already familiar with it. Speaking on condition of anonymity for security reasons, he also said it was not an operational combat plan, but a set of calculations. "It is a document used
summary: As Ukraine prepares for its fifth winter since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, a document obtained by RFE/RL sets out a potential blueprint for a campaign by Moscow to inflict enormous suffering on civilians with attacks aimed at sharply cutting supplies of power, heat, and water.
title: Exclusive: 'Key Targets': A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine

body: Moldova More Drones, More Missiles, No Air Defenses: Moldova In The Cross Fire Of Russia's War On Ukraine By Ionut Benea and Cristina Popusoi October 08, 2026 13:35 CET More Drones, More Missiles, No Air Defenses: Moldova In The Cross Fire Of Russia's War On Ukraine Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian drones targeting Ukraine are increasingly crashing onto Moldovan territory, rattling the government, which has limited ability to defend against them. This Gerbera-type drone crashed in northern Moldova last November. CROCMAZ, Moldova -- The watchman was napping in a small hut overlooking a vineyard along Moldova's southeastern border when the afternoon exploded, the earth erupted, and the windows of the outbuilding blew out. The man, who declined to be interviewed, and others in the district flooded local emergency numbers, asking police what was going on. Ion Tabac, an officer with the district border patrol, was one of the responders to the incident on the afternoon of August 9. "We found the trees scorched and destroyed. Smoke was still rising," Tabac told RFE/RL's Moldovan Service. "When the war started in 2022, they weren't flying overhead like this, but lately it happens all the time," he said. Russian drones and missiles zipping through Moldovan airspace is not a new phenomenon for Chisinau. It is, however, something occurring with alarming frequency over the past several months. Moreover, Moldovan authorities say they're tracking a growing number of aerial weapons that are crashing and exploding on Moldovan territory itself. Earlier this week , a border guard was injured when a Russia projectile -- authorities did not say what the object was -- hit the ground near the Palanca crossing along the border with Ukraine and ricocheted. It was the first time a Moldovan law enforcement officer had been injured by a Russian weapon. Russian drones and missiles like this one have flown through Moldovan airspace since the first year of the Russian war on Ukraine. In Crocmaz, what made the crash there even more alarming, officials said, was that the projectile was a new hybrid cruise missile drone called an S-8000 Banderol Despite the uptick in incidents, most Moldovans remain largely apathetic, said Andrei Curararu, a Moldovan political expert. "You can really see splashes of public reaction and fury when something bigger happens. But up to this point, it has been mostly drones exploding in open spaces or with lesser damage. So many people have grown to live with it," said Curararu, who co-founded the Chisinau think tank WatchDog.MD. "It's apathy linked to the fact that it happens. We do not have the capacity to react to it quite concretely," he said. Caught In The Cross Fire Wedged between Romania -- its linguistic and cultural cousin and NATO member -- to the west and war-ravaged Ukraine to the east, Moldova has struggled since the onset of the all-out Russian invasion to minimize the fallout. Since 2022, Russian drones and missile have routinely crossed Moldova airspace en route to Ukrainian targets, usually launched from Black Sea naval ships and installation on the occupied Crimea peninsula. But the increased frequency of both overflights and impacts within Moldova itself has rattled authorities who worry about the possibility of injuries or deaths from Russian weapons. The Defense Ministry says it has recorded nearly 90 "unauthorized incursions" into Moldova airspace, including both drones and missiles. Another Russian Drone Crashed In Northern Moldova by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:04 0:00 More than half, 48 in total, crashed onto Moldovan soil. The tally included decoys, various loitering strike drones, and missile fragments brought down by Ukrainian air defenses operating close to the border. In August alone, officials recorded 17 incidents where Russian drones crashed or exploded in Moldovan territory, eclipsing the total recorded number for all of 2025. On September 9, a Russian drone hit a crossing along the Moldovan-Ukraine border near Odesa, damaging the border post, sparking a fire, and forcing the evacuation of 16 people. President Maia Sandu wrote in a social media post afterward that Russia's front line is moving further west. A day earlier, a Russian drone over Moldovan airspace prompted authorities to halt flights, including that of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was flying from Moldova to Norway. "Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped," she wrote in a post on October 3 after another incident in which she said Banderol missiles and drones "violated our airspace and exploded on our soil." SEE ALSO: Russian Drone Attack Kills 2 Near Moldova As Norway Says Zelenskyy's Plane Nearly Struck While most of the crashes have taken place in rural or unpopulated regions like Crocmaz, several drones have detonated on the outskirts of the capital, Chisinau, rattling sleeping residents. Moldovan authorities are largely helpless against the Russian weapons. The country has two relatively new radar systems, one bought from France and the other donated by the EU, that can detect drones or missiles. Moldova also has some short-range air defenses: mainly so-called MANPADS, shoulder-launched missiles. But it does not have medium- or long-range interception systems capable of shooting down a Russian drone over Ukrainian air space or the Black Sea. "The core problem here is that Moldova doesn't have an effective air defense," Curararu said. "We are in a long line for buying some medium-range defense equipment, but now everything is booked for years and years, and most of it goes to Ukraine." A scorched tree partially damaged by the Russian drone that crashed and exploded near Crocmaz in early August In July, the European Union, of which Moldova is a candidate country, committed 120 million euros toward a medium-range air-defense system for Moldova. But experts say that will take time to acquire and deploy, likely meaning it won't help during the current Russia-Ukraine conflict. Speaking to reporters on September 21, Sandu said the limited air defenses the Moldovan military has at its disposal are deployed to protect critical infrastructure such as the electricity and power grid. "Moldova itself will never do anything as suicidal as going to war with Russia or anything else," Curararu said. "We understand that Moldova is too small to be a factor in this war, anyway. So it could be a collateral victim more than an actor." RFE/RL senior international correspondent Mike Eckel contributed to this report from Prague. summary: Moldova saw more Russian drones crash on its territory in August than it did over all of 2025. Moldovan authorities are increasingly rattled—but there’s little a cash-strapped government can do beyond complaining diplomatically.
title: More Drones, More Missiles, No Air Defenses: Moldova In The Cross Fire Of Russia's War On Ukraine

body: News Dozens Killed In Russian Strike On Passenger Buses In Kramatorsk By Serhiy Horbatenko and RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service October 08, 2026 13:04 CET Updated October 08, 2026 21:04 CET Dozens Killed In Russian Strike On Passenger Buses In Kramatorsk Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google KRAMATORSK, Ukraine -- Dozens of people were killed in a Russian strike on the Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk on October 8, according to local authorities, a day after another deadly barrage killed at least 25 people across Ukraine. The death toll from the Kramatorsk attack has risen to 33, with 18 others wounded, according to the latest reports from regional authorities and the prosecutor's office. Footage taken by RFE/RL correspondent Serhiy Horbatenko, who visited the site shortly after the attack, showed two buses burned out by the strike, with bodies strewn around the scene. "The bodies are lying right in the middle of the road," the RFE/RL correspondent said while describing the aftermath of the deadly attack. Embed share Russian Strike On Ukrainian Buses Kills More Than 30 Passengers In Kramatorsk by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:28 0:00 The Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office said the Russian strike hit two buses that were carrying passengers at the time of the attack. It added that Russian forces likely used guided bombs to strike the vehicles. The strike came a day after at least 25 people nationwide, including two in the capital, Kyiv, were reported killed in the October 7 barrage. In Pryluky, about 150 kilometers east of Kyiv, rescuers searched through the rubble of a destroyed apartment building in northern Ukraine for survivors following a Russian missile attack that killed 22 people, including five children. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it one of the "most vile" attacks in recent memory, and he noted they occurred on the birthday of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Russian forces "destroyed" a residential building "as a birthday 'gift' to Putin," Zelenskyy said in a post to X. At least 10 other such buildings were damaged elsewhere, along with Ukrainian energy infrastructure, one of Moscow's other "key targets," he said. Embed share Massive Russian Attack Kills At Least 22, Devastates Pryluky Apartment Block by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:53 0:00 "The fire was right in front of my eyes. There were explosions. I was screaming in my apartment. Extremely scary. I can't describe it," one woman, who gave her name as Lidia, told Current Time at the scene in Pryluky. "So many people have died. I knew everyone here," she added, holding back tears. With a fifth wartime winter approaching, the bombardment was part of near-daily attacks that have steadily increased in frequency and ferocity as the Kremlin struggles on the battlefield front line. Moscow has previously sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by attacking the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures. Recently, it has also stepped up attacks on Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure, causing Internet outages in some of the country's regions. Since this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia and middle-range strikes targeting its key logistics in Ukraine's occupied eastern and southern regions. Embed share Oil Tanker Hit By Naval Drones Near Sochi, Sparking Massive Fire On Black Sea by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:53 0:00 Direct link 240p | 1.4MB 360p | 1.9MB 480p | 2.8MB 720p | 4.6MB 1080p | 8.0MB On October 8, Russia's leading AI and technology company, Yandex, said one of its five largest data centers in the Ryazan region had been attacked, adding that the company was trying to restore affected services. The Yandex site hosts tens of thousands of servers. Zelenskyy confirmed Kyiv had struck the facility, saying it was "mirroring" previous Russian attacks on similar sites in Ukraine. Separately, Ukrainian forces also struck the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery and petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan, sparking a fire, according to Ukraine's military . Russia's Defense Ministry reported on October 8 that the country's air defenses had intercepted and destroyed 399 Ukrainian drones overnight. SEE ALSO: Exclusive: 'Key Targets': A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine The developments came amid renewed US interest in negotiating a diplomatic settlement to the long-running war. While US President Donald Trump has long said resolving the conflict is one of the key goals of his presidency, Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions. Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the Kremlin has shown no willingness to compromise on its key demands, including full control over Ukraine's key eastern Donetsk region, which Russian forces have not yet been able to capture. Zelenskyy said Ukraine expected fresh talks with the United States in the coming days, adding that Kyiv hoped its European partners would join the discussions. body: Iran No Safe Haven: How Iran And Russia Target Exile Enemies By Ray Furlong October 08, 2026 07:10 CET No Safe Haven: How Iran And Russia Target Exile Enemies Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google (illustration) On a Thursday lunchtime in early March, Milad Pourtalebian came home to find his apartment had been broken into and trashed. He then noticed a chilling detail suggesting that this was not a burglary: His "Make Iran Great Again" baseball cap had been skewered to the wall with a large kitchen knife. Pourtalebian is an Iranian citizen who, since arriving in Canada in 2024, has been organizing exile opposition rallies in his adopted hometown of Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. The break-in, days after US and Israeli air strikes launched a war with Iran, followed a series of online threats to the 32-year-old relating to his activities. He immediately reported the incident to local police, telling them he had been targeted for political reasons. Pourtalebian poses with a portrait of Iran's exiled former crown prince, Reza Pahlavi. He says his support of Pahlavi has made him a target. "The incident was initially extremely frightening for me," he told RFE/RL, adding that he has since overcome this feeling. "I decided not to allow fear to stop me from expressing my political views. I think about the thousands of Iranians who have lost their lives seeking freedom." Photos, police documents, and social media screenshots shared by Pourtalebian with RFE/RL give a sense that, despite being thousands of kilometers from Iran, he is not beyond the reach of the country's security services. One Telegram post denounces him for "propaganda activities against the political establishment" and supporting "the attack by America and the Zionist regime against Iran." It concludes by saying, "This person lives in Saskatoon. A few months ago, we tracked him down and conveyed our message to him at his home." This, Pourtalebian said, was "particularly disturbing." Nothing was taken from his apartment, and nobody has been arrested. Transnational Repression Pourtalebian's experience is specific but appears to be part of a wider phenomenon in which authoritarian states pursue their opponents even after they find shelter in apparently safe Western countries. Iran has practiced assassinations and attacks for decades, but its global pressure goes far beyond physical threats. Factnameh, a Persian-language fact-checking service based in Canada, recently noted an increase in "crowdsourced surveillance, doxxing, and cyber-enabled intimidation targeting critics outside Iran." The toolbox includes Alaj, a website where people can make denunciations, that reportedly holds files on some 1,600 people. Iranian state TV threatened those named with "seizure of assets, complete suspension of consular services, and Interpol Red Notices," Factnameh said. Another tool, Goorkan (Persian for "Grave Digger"), publishes personal details of what it calls "traitors." SEE ALSO: Anthropic Disrupts Iran's Use Of Claude To Spread Propaganda, Spy On Dissidents US, British, and Dutch intelligence reported last month that Iran was mounting a global cybercampaign. The FBI said malware named Heavygram was used "to conduct malicious cyber activity to target Iranian dissidents, journalists opposed to Iran, and other opposition groups around the world." Iran is not an outlier in its pursuit of overseas critics. Yana Gorkhovskaia, head of research and analysis at Washington-based Freedom House, has spent years studying the phenomenon. "China, Iran, Russia are among the top 10 perpetrators of transnational repression according to our data. China by far outstrips all other governments," she told RFE/RL. "Of those three, Russia is by far the most violent in terms of assassinations and assaults." Prominent examples include the poisonings of defectors Aleksandr Litvinenko and Sergei Skripal in Britain and a hammer attack on opposition activist Leonid Volkov , an associate of deceased Russian dissident Aleksei Navalny, in Lithuania. 'A Kind Of Paranoia' It is something that's extremely worrying for Mikhail Klimaryov, a Russian cybersecurity expert and Kremlin critic who fled Russia after it launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Embed share 'Psychological War': Exiled Russian Activist Describes How Kremlin Targets Critics Abroad by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:21 0:00 Now living in Berlin, where he collaborates with Volkov, the 53-year-old told RFE/RL he detected "a kind of paranoia" in his behavior owing to the threat. "I'm overly concerned about security. At least from the perspective of a normal, healthy person. When I'm out and about, I check whether I'm being followed. Before I touch the door handle to my apartment, I examine it first because there was that case where they smeared a door handle with Novichok," he said. But Klimaryov said his day-to-day life was also affected by a multitude of smaller pressures, ranging from phishing attacks to administrative difficulties, that amount to "a psychological war" waged by Moscow on people like him. He cannot, for example, renew his Russian passport, which expires in 2029. This will impact his residency status in Germany. "It will be an administrative problem, and not as simple as it may seem. I'll need to hire a lawyer," he said. Klimaryov explained he does not have asylum in Germany and does not want to apply for it because this would mean he'd be unable to continue running a business that employs 20 people. Klimaryov insists that despite the Kremlin pressure, he is not a victim. "I'm not in prison. I can earn a living." Travel is another issue. Russia has put him on a terrorist list that can cause a problem at any border. He recalled that while returning from a recent trip to the United States, he was hauled from the boarding line by an officer "with a machine gun and a dog" and questioned for 30 minutes. The danger of extradition means he needs to be careful about which countries he visits. Klimaryov is also listed as a foreign agent in Russia and has debts of some $1 million in fines levied on him by the authorities for, he says, political reasons. In many cases, he was unable to deal with administrative issues mounting against him at home because his Russian phone number was canceled, preventing him from interacting with authorities online or accessing his Russian banking. SEE ALSO: 'Civil Death': The Kremlin Is Building A Legal Purgatory For Exiled Russians Klimaryov says he doesn't use a phone unless required to by German authorities and doesn't give the number to anyone else due to hacking fears. He helps other Russians who come under phishing attacks and says he once almost succumbed to one himself. "I managed to stop myself right at the last moment. It was such a high-level scam," he said, describing a sophisticated back-and-forth exchange of messages with someone posing as a potential client for his company. After weeks of communication, he nearly entered a code delivered by Telegram that could have compromised his account. "Does all this affect me psychologically? Of course it does," Klimaryov said. "I've sought medical advice.... I get hit by panic. Panic attacks -- do you know what those are?" Despite this, Klimaryov insisted he doesn't regard himself as a victim. "I'm better off than many people. I'm not in prison. I can earn a living." But Klimaryov added he is considering medical advice to pause his political activities as a result of the pressure. Gorkhovskaia underlined that this was exactly the point of it. "Surveillance, intimidation, threats to family, digital threats -- they do work, to make people at least second guess whether attending a protest or doing something public is worthwhile," she said. Accor
summary: Authoritarian states such as Russia and Iran are increasingly pursuing their opponents even after they find shelter in apparently safe Western countries. RFE/RL talks to some of those affected.
title: No Safe Haven: How Iran And Russia Target Exile Enemies

body: Belarus Sanctioned Belarus Trucks And A Mystery Logo: 'HAL' Vehicles Spotted In Minsk October 07, 2026 17:14 CET By RFE/RL's Belarus Service Photo: threads.com (Courtesy Image) Belarus Sanctioned Belarus Trucks And A Mystery Logo: 'HAL' Vehicles Spotted In Minsk October 07, 2026 17:14 CET By RFE/RL's Belarus Service Sanctioned Belarus Trucks And A Mystery Logo: 'HAL' Vehicles Spotted In Minsk Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Fleets of unusual vehicles have been spotted in Minsk in recent days that may be linked to a murky trade deal with Indonesia. Trucks with a military color scheme and nearly identical to the Belarus-made MAZ-5316 have been seen sporting the logo "HAL" in place of the usual MAZ badge. The MAZ-5316 is a heavy-duty 4WD truck produced since the early 2000s by the Minsk Automobile Plant. The vehicles are used for civilian and military purposes, including as troop carriers . A 2016 file image of an MAZ-5316 in service with the Ukrainian military Sightings of HAL-branded vehicles first emerged this summer, when dozens of trucks covered with concealing material were spotted in Indonesia. Reports from the Asian country claimed the partially concealed vehicles were part of an order of some 1,500 Belarusian trucks for Indonesia's Defense Ministry. A screengrab of a video shows concealed trucks with the HAL brand. In May, an Indonesian delegation toured Belarus's MAZ plant as part of a trip to "explore the company's export potential." In July, Belarusian leader Aleksandr Lukashenko visited Indonesia to meet with the country's president, Prabowo Subianto. Belarus declared the primary purpose of the July trip to be "issues of bilateral military-technical cooperation" and "the deepening of industrial cooperation between Minsk and Jakarta." Indonesian Economics Affairs Minister Airlangga Hartarto inspects a MAZ truck during a trip to Belarus in May. So what is HAL, and why would Belarusian trucks sport the unfamiliar logo? Belarusian truck manufacturer MAZ is under EU and US sanctions, a status that blocks many countries from dealing with the company. Indonesia has not imposed sanctions against Belarus but faces the risk of secondary penalties for dealing with entities on Western blacklists. An Indonesian company called PT HAL Teknologi functions as a distributor for supplies of specialized equipment for defense agencies and other entities in the country, but it is unclear if the company has been involved in vehicle imports from Belarus. Uladzimer Zhyhar from BelPol, an organization of former Belarusian security officials, told RFE/RL's Belarus Service there is a history of sanctioned Belarusian businesses creating new branding to minimize the risk that purchasing countries will be stung for dealing with sanctioned entities. "Previously, they tried to organize something similar with [Belarusian heavy transport equipment company] BelAZ deliveries to Poland. They sold entire dump truck assemblies without labels, without the country of origin. And then it was all pieced together [in Poland], but the dump trucks were branded as something else," Zhyhar said. He added that for some militaries, the kinds of hardware produced in Belarus is desirable enough that risky, complex import schemes are deemed worthwhile. Factories such as MAZ, Zhyhar said, "generally produce a product that, I would say, belongs to previous generations. But this is exactly what some countries need, because the types of weapons that they have require exactly the older, 'quasi-Soviet' models," he said. An image shared on social media purporting shows a HAL-branded truck near the MAZ factory in Minsk. In some cases, Zhyhar said, products from sanctioned Belarusian companies have been paid for through bartering to avoid financial services that are closely watched by regulators. Belarusian state-linked brands order commodities up to the value of the products being exported, resulting in "goods, not money going to Belarus," Zhyhar said. The National Statistics Committee of Belarus has not published detailed data on foreign trade since 2021, but in 2020 Indonesia purchased 8 unidentified trucks from Belarus at a cost of $56,138 per vehicle. Recent reports from the Indonesian Statistics Service do not include information on truck deliveries from Belarus, though there is data on small deliveries of parts including brake systems and clutches. The Minsk Automobile Plant did not response to a query from RFE/RL's Belarus Service on whether MAZ was involved the production of trucks with the HAL logo. Amos Chapple contributed to this report. summary: Belarus’s Minsk Automobile Plant is under Western sanctions, limiting who can buy the vehicles produced there. That may be the reason trucks branded with the previously unknown “HAL” badge have been spotted amid strengthening trade relations between Belarus and Indonesia.
title: Sanctioned Belarus Trucks And A Mystery Logo: 'HAL' Vehicles Spotted In Minsk

body: News EU Says Kosovo's Changes To War Crimes Court Law Violate International Obligations By RFE/RL's Kosovo Service and Gjeraqina Tuhina October 07, 2026 15:34 CET EU Says Kosovo's Changes To War Crimes Court Law Violate International Obligations Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google People celebrate in Pristina after parliament passed legislation limiting the decisions of a Hague-based war crimes court on October 6. The EU has expressed "deep concern" over the amendment. The European Union has expressed "deep concern" over Kosovo's adoption of legislation that seeks to narrow the jurisdiction of a Hague-based war crimes court, saying the changes violate the country's international obligations toward the bloc. The amendments, approved by parliament on October 6, target the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which last month convicted former President Hashim Thaci and three other former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders of war crimes. In a response to RFE/RL on October 7, an EU spokesperson said the legislation "goes against Kosovo's international obligations toward the EU." "Their current mandate and independence must be fully respected," the spokesperson said. "The Kosovo Specialist Chambers are rendering justice, based on the principle of individual criminal responsibility." Perparim Gruda, a lawmaker from the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK), which initiated the amendments, rejected the EU's assessment. "I can assure the EU that we are not violating any international obligation with this law," he told a news conference. SEE ALSO: Kosovo Elects President After Opposition Agrees To Last-Minute Deal Gruda said he had not personally seen the EU statement. He cited European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent remarks in Pristina, which he characterized as affirming Kosovo's right to amend the law. RFE/RL contacted Kosovo's government about the EU's criticism but had received no response by publication. During the bill's first reading on October 5, Prime Minister Albin Kurti said his Vetevendosje party considered the changes rushed and had little time to analyze them but would support them nonetheless. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers declined to comment directly on the legislation. "The Specialist Chambers is fully focused on implementing its mandate to ensure fair, impartial, and secure judicial proceedings, and to ensure the protection of witnesses and victims," it told RFE/RL on October 7. The amendments' adoption was part of a last-minute agreement between the PDK and Vetevendosje that also paved the way for Justina Shiroka Pula's election as president on October 7. The legislation would restrict the court's jurisdiction to offenses directly linked to organ-trafficking allegations outlined in a 2011 Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly report. Embed share Police, Protesters Clash In Pristina As Lawmakers Debate Bill On War Crimes Court by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:40 0:00 It would also limit jurisdiction to crimes allegedly committed in Kosovo between July 1, 1999, and December 31, 2000, excluding the earlier period beginning in January 1998. Cases outside that remit would be transferred to Kosovo's regular courts. The amendments also envisage serving sentences in Kosovo and eligibility for presidential pardons. The PDK introduced the initiative five days after the September 16 verdict. Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi each received 25-year sentences, Kadri Veseli 18 years, and Rexhep Selimi 13 years. All four were convicted of war crimes and acquitted of crimes against humanity. Organ-trafficking allegations were not part of their indictment. The verdict is not final, and defense teams have announced appeals. Parliament's approval does not itself overturn those judgments or mean those convicted will be released. SEE ALSO: What Comes Next After The Conviction Of Kosovo's Former President? Gruda also said the final amendment sought to reserve constitutional review of the legislation for Kosovo's Constitutional Court in Pristina, excluding the Specialist Chambers' constitutional chamber in The Hague. Legal experts have warned that changes to the court's mandate could raise constitutional issues and conflict with international obligations. The EU stressed that the court operates within Kosovo's legal system and is enshrined in its constitution. It urged Kosovo to ensure accountability and justice for victims from all communities. In an exchange of letters in April 2014 between Kosovo’s then-president, Atifete Jahjaga, and then-EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton, Kosovo made a series of commitments concerning the Specialist Chambers. The exchange formed the basis of the agreement that paved the way for the institution widely known in Kosovo as the Special Court. Among those commitments was an obligation to consult the EU on any proposed legislative changes affecting the court’s mandate or judicial proceedings arising from investigations by the Special Investigative Task Force (SITF). Kosovo also committed to allowing the Specialist Chambers and the Specialist Prosecutor’s Office to continue their work until the relevant investigations and proceedings were completed. Still, the bloc also welcomed Shiroka Pula's election, expressing hope for renewed institutional stability. "While the EU is available to continue supporting Kosovo, our partnership implies not only shared interests but also shared responsibility," the spokesperson said. After the war in Kosovo, she moved to Brussels and since then has covered EU and NATO-related activities in the Western Balkans. This item is part of News Kosovo Europe
summary: The European Union has expressed “deep concern” over Kosovo’s adoption of legislation that seeks to narrow the jurisdiction of a Hague-based war crimes court, saying the changes violate the country’s international obligations toward the bloc.
title: EU Says Kosovo's Changes To War Crimes Court Law Violate International Obligations

body: News Analysis Testing Times For Mecca Alliance Partners As Iran-Aligned Houthis Mount Attacks By Daud Khattak October 07, 2026 15:25 CET Testing Times For Mecca Alliance Partners As Iran-Aligned Houthis Mount Attacks Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Fighters loyal to Iran-aligned Houthi rebels march during a rally last month to recruit more fighters in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabian allies Pakistan and Turkey are facing a major test just two months after signing a joint defense agreement as the rise of Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen test the deal, which says "any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all." As fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces rages in Yemen, experts believe that any active military interference by Pakistan or Turkey -- the other two partners in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement -- in support of Saudi Arabia, may heighten regional tensions amid the US-Iran conflict. "(The Islamic republic) can still support the Houthis but if Turkey and Pakistan enter (the war), the situation would become complicated," Frankfurt-based Middle East analyst Ali Sadrzadeh told RFE/RL's Radio Farda. SEE ALSO: Yemen Conflict Intensifies, Reverberating Beyond The Region The three sides held an emergency meeting in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, on October 5, the day Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces announced that they had secured effective control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a claim denied by the Houthis. Last month, the Houthi rebels captured the Red Sea port city of Mocha and other areas around the strait, a key route for Saudi oil exports to Asia that has gained in importance with the disruption of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz because of the Iran war. The Houthis have also warned that Saudi airspace "will be the theatre of operations of our armed forces." The renewed fighting has displaced some 184,000 people and threatened shipping through the vital chokepoint linking the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. In an apparent reference to recent Houthi strikes on the Saudi cities of Mecca and Medina, two of Islam's most sacred locations, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Sultan said in a social media post that the alliance meeting "reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom and the holy sites." He added that the three sides agreed to activate collective deterrence measures within the framework of the alliance in response to the attacks and "all those responsible for them." A Festering Conflict The conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has festered for years. Saudi Arabia launched a military intervention in Yemen in March 2015, after Houthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government to flee the country. The conflict is widely viewed as part of the broader Saudi-Iranian rivalry, with the two countries backing opposing sides. Major fighting subsided after a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but the conflict was never fully resolved and has escalated again this year. Alarm bells rang when the Houthis last month stepped up attacks against Saudi targets, including a key oil pipeline, and advanced toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. A joint statement released after the emergency October 5 meeting stated that it was meant to address the "security developments and threats facing the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia." SEE ALSO: What Houthi Gains In Yemen Mean For The Iran War Experts believe the joint statement of the Mecca alliance, affirming the provision of "agreed military forces and capabilities" and their "rapid deployment in the Kingdom" is a clear declaration of support for Saudi Arabia in the face of increasing attacks from the Houthis. But they say such support also risks triggering another confrontation in the region. Sadrzadeh said that, although there are an estimated 30,000-40,000 Pakistani troops based in Saudi Arabia, he does not think the nuclear-armed country would agree to send forces to Yemen because Pakistan "wants to maintain its relationship with the Islamic republic." Just a day ahead of the emergency meeting, Iran Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei warned that any "new intervention" in (Yemen) would further complicate the situation. In a reference to Pakistan's reported deployment of troops in Saudi Arabia to fight the Houthis in Yemen, Baqaei said that "we hope that it is not true and really is just a rumor," adding that "any new intervention in developments related to Yemen would only make the situation more complicated." Rabia Akhtar, a professor of international relations at the University of Lahore, believes that Pakistani forces taking part in strikes against the Houthis could lead to a confrontation with Iran. "Tehran could see that as Pakistan joining a campaign against its regional interests, even if Islamabad insists that its involvement is limited to supporting Saudi Arabia," she told RFE/RL. Walking A Tightrope Nuclear-armed Pakistan shares a roughly 900-kilometer-long border with Iran along its southwestern frontier. Unlike its often-fraught relations with India and Afghanistan, its other two neighbors to the east and west, ties between Islamabad and Tehran are mostly stable. Akhtar said that Saudi Arabia is an important partner for Pakistan, but Iran is a neighbor and Islamabad "will have to live with the consequences of its decisions long after this particular episode ends." SEE ALSO: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey Sign Joint Defense Pact Amid US-Iran Tensions Pakistan has been walking a tightrope by not taking sides since the United States and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on February 28. Despite maintaining traditionally close relations with Saudi Arabia and several other oil-rich Gulf countries, Pakistan has restricted itself mostly to statements of condemnation in the face of Iran's drone and missile attacks on its Arab neighbors over the past few months. Islamabad has also presented itself as a mediator and hosted the first-ever face-to-face talks between Iranian and US officials since 1980 in April. While experts see the October 5 emergency meeting of the Mecca alliance as a fresh escalation amid the regional hostilities, Khalid Sultan of the National University of Modern Languages believes that it should not automatically be interpreted as a precursor to a broader ground war in Yemen. "The (Mecca) agreement's significance lies not simply in military cooperation, but in the emergence of a collective regional deterrence mechanism," he told RFE/RL, adding that the success of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement will ultimately be measured not by how quickly it enters a war, but by how effectively it prevents one. "For Pakistan, in particular, the policy challenge will be to honor its defense commitment to Saudi Arabia while avoiding an open-ended military entanglement in Yemen." Akhtar said any Pakistani participation in attacks on Houthis could undermine its role as a mediator with Tehran. "A clearly limited role in defending Saudi territory could remain compatible with mediation," she said. "Joining an offensive campaign in Yemen would make that position much harder to sustain." body: Iran Rubio In Athens Warns Iran It Will Never Have A Nuclear Weapon By Alex Raufoglu October 07, 2026 13:21 CET Rubio In Athens Warns Iran It Will Never Have A Nuclear Weapon Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (left) speaks during a joint press conference with Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis in Athens on October 7. ATHENS -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran will never be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon, declaring that preventing Tehran from doing so is a red line for President Donald Trump. “Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Simple, period, end of story,” Rubio said on October 7 in Athens, where he held talks with Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis during the sixth US-Greece Strategic Dialogue. Asked whether Washington was prepared to accept some Iranian uranium enrichment, Rubio declined to specify what level of enrichment might be acceptable. Instead, he said any agreement would have to ensure that Iran “will never have a nuclear weapon.” “That is what our position is. That is the reason why this began,” Rubio said. Rubio also accused Tehran of trying to build such a large conventional military arsenal that it would eventually become difficult for the United States or its allies to act against its nuclear program. “What Iran was trying to do was build up a conventional capability so massive that they would become untouchable,” Rubio said. SEE ALSO: US Sanctions 17 Vessels Linked To Iran's Shadow Fleet He said US military action had severely weakened Iran, including by destroying or degrading much of its drone and missile capabilities and its navy and air force. “They are far less powerful militarily today than they were,” Rubio said. Iran's military capabilities have been significantly degraded during the conflict, although Tehran retains missile and drone capabilities. The current state of its nuclear program remains difficult to assess. with the International Atomic Energy Agency citing limited access for international monitors. Iran Faces 'Freefall' Rubio also portrayed Iran as facing a deepening economic crisis, saying its economy was heading toward “complete freefall.” He pointed to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the continued flow of oil through the strategic waterway, saying Tehran had lost control of the crucial waterway. SEE ALSO: Iran's Hormuz Leverage Is Fading, But It Isn't Gone While oil shipments have resumed, traffic through the strait remains disrupted and Iran has continued to insist that its full reopening depends on Washington meeting conditions set by Tehran. Rubio blamed Iran's leadership for the country's economic problems, accusing the government of spending its resources on Hezbollah, Hamas, Iraqi militias, and the Houthis rather than improving living conditions at home. “They should have spent their money on their people, and instead they spend the money on terrorism, on weapons,” he said. SEE ALSO: Iran's Medicine Shortages Fuel Black Market For Essential Drugs Rubio said Tehran had previously had multiple opportunities to reach agreements over its nuclear program but had failed to do so. Greece A Key Ally Rubio described Greece as a critical US ally at a time of growing instability in Europe and the Middle East, citing conflicts involving Iran, Russia and Ukraine, and the Red Sea. He called Greece “a source of stability in an unstable world” and praised Athens for increasing defense spending. Greece is on track to meet a commitment to spend 5 percent of its gross domestic product on defense this year, Rubio said, with more than 3.5 percent going toward core defense spending. SEE ALSO: Rubio In Iceland Signals Deeper NATO Push As Russia, China Challenge Arctic Security He also announced that Greece will join the US National Guard's State Partnership Program and be paired with the Florida National Guard, further expanding military cooperation. The two countries also agreed to strengthen cooperation on counterterrorism and information-sharing between law-enforcement agencies. Rubio cited Greece's position on major migration and trafficking routes as making it particularly exposed to terrorism, human trafficking, and transnational crime. Washington and Athens also plan to expand cooperation on US liquefied-natural-gas exports, electricity and gas interconnections, emerging technologies, and regional energy security. The countries are also working together to combat the trafficking of Greek and other Mediterranean antiquities into the United States. Rubio To Make Case For The West Rubio is due to deliver a speech later on October 7 at Athens' Pnyx, overlooking the Acropolis, where he is expected to make a broader argument about democracy, national identity, and the future of the West. According to excerpts of his prepared remarks released by the State Department ahead of the speech, Rubio will call for what he describes as a “great renewal of the Western spirit.” He is expected to argue that ancient Athens embodied qualities that came to define the West, including individual ambition, exploration, invention, competition, and a drive to overcome limits. “Here in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West,” Rubio will say, according to the excerpts. He will contrast the ancient Greek pursuit of excellence with what he portrays as a modern emphasis on safety and comfort at the expense of ambition and achievement. “The men who made the Parthenon built upwards,” Rubio is expected to say. 'The Next Decade' Rubio is also expected to portray the West as standing at a historic crossroads. “The next decade will write the story of the next century,” he will say, according to the prepared remarks. He is expected to argue that the United States under Trump has chosen “the unapologetic pursuit of national power,” including rebuilding US manufacturing, strengthening defense, securing critical supply chains, and competing for leadership in emerging technologies. Rubio is also expected to emphasize advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, drones, weapons, semiconductors, critical minerals, cybersecurity, energy, and space exploration. His remarks will also challenge the idea that foreign policy should put the interests of a “global community” ahead of a country's own citizens. Rubio is expected to argue that loyalty to one's nation and defending its interests are not selfish, invoking ancient Greek examples of duty, sacrifice, and honor. He will also draw a sharp contrast with Iran's clerical leadership, according to the excerpts, accusing its “radical mullahs” of glorifying death and martyrdom. “Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause; but they do not worship death,” Rubio will say. The speech is expected to cast the confrontation with Iran as part of a wider struggle over the values and future direction of the West, taking Rubio's message in Athens beyond security and diplomacy to a broader defense of national power, Western identity, and democratic traditions. body: Russia Two Decades On, Politkovskaya's Daughter Says Little Has Changed In Russia Since Her Mother's Murder By RFE/RL October 07, 2026 12:45 CET Two Decades On, Politkovskaya's Daughter Says Little Has Changed In Russia Since Her Mother's Murder Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Activists attend a rally in honor of slain journalist Anna Politkovskaya in Moscow. (file photo) Two decades after the murder of Anna Politkovskaya, a tenacious investigative reporter who exposed the brutality of Russia's war in Chechnya and documented how President Vladimir Putin curtailed democracy in Russia, her daughter, Vera, says little has changed in the country's political climate. People told her, “You’re exaggerating. You see everything through a dark lens,” she told RFE/RL's Russian Service in an interview ahead of the 20th anniversary of Politkovskaya's brutal killing on October 7, 2006. "And now it’s the same thing, except that the divide has deepened so much. Everything has become so stark, even compared with what she predicted more than 20 years ago". Politkovskaya, who worked for the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, was gunned down in her Moscow apartment. The shooting occurred on President Vladimir Putin's birthday, prompting speculation that it was meant as a "gift" to the president. Embed share 20 Years Since The Death Of Russian Journalist Anna Politkovskaya by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:29 0:00 Direct link 240p | 4.6MB 360p | 6.2MB 480p | 8.9MB 720p | 14.7MB 1080p | 25.1MB Former Russian police officer Sergei Khadzhikurbanov -- who denied the charges -- was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his role in organizing the assassination but received a pardon from Putin in 2023 after taking part in Moscow's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Two natives of Russia's North Caucasus region of Chechnya, Rustam Makhmudov and Lom-Ali Gaitukayev, were subsequently handed life sentences after a jury found Makhmudov guilty of shooting Politkovskaya, while Gaitukayev was convicted of organizing the assassination. Gaitukayev later died in prison. Another defendant in the case, former Moscow police officer Denis Pavlyuchenkov, was sentenced to 11 years in prison after he confessed to organizing the surveillance of Politkovskaya before she was murdered. Six Novaya Gazeta journalists and contributors -- Igor Domnikov (2000), Yury Shchekochikhin (2003), Politkovskaya (2006), Anastasia Baburova (2009), Stanislav Markelov (2009), and Natalya Estimirova (2009) -- have been killed in attacks that the newspaper and human rights activists say were retribution for their work. SEE ALSO: Daughter Blames 'System' Built By Putin, Kadyrov For Rights Activist Estemirova’s Death Since Politkovskaya's death, Russian authorities have gradually expanded the legal toolbox used to punish dissent, censor independent media, shutter civil society groups, and silence opposition lawmakers. This includes measures such as the "foreign agent" law, which punishes individuals and groups that receive foreign funding, and the "undesirables" law, which bans foreign organizations deemed a threat to national security and criminalizes people who work for, associate with, or donate money to such organizations. Such moves are exactly what her mother's reporting was aimed at exposing, said Vera Politkovskaya, who now lives abroad at an undisclosed location. "Essentially, the main theme of my mother's work was telling the stories of ordinary people," she said. "And how that everyday person was run over by the political and military system...That's what my mom witnessed and talked about back then. She saw, so to speak, further ahead than many other people did. And people didn't believe her." SEE ALSO: The List Is Long: Russians Who Have Died After Running Afoul Of The Kremlin Anna Politkovskaya was born in New York in 1958, the daughter of a Soviet diplomat from Ukraine. She was won numerous Russian and international awards, including an Amnesty International Global Award for Human Rights Journalism in 2001, a PEN Freedom to Write award in 2002, and an Olaf Palme Prize in 2004. In 2007, she became the first person ever to receive a posthumous UNESCO/Guillermo Cano World Press Freedom Prize. body: News Russia Missile Blasts Ukraine Apartment Block, Killing At Least 22 By Serhiy Nuzhnenko and Andriy Kuzakov October 07, 2026 12:09 CET Updated October 07, 2026 16:41 CET Russia Missile Blasts Ukraine Apartment Block, Killing At Least 22 Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google People carry a casualty as emergency services work to rescue residents from under the debris at the site of an apartment building hit by a Russian missile strike in the town of Pryluky, in Ukraine's Chernihiv region on October 7. PRYLUKY, Ukraine -- Rescuers frantically picked through rubble and debris of a destroyed apartment building in northern Ukraine as they search for survivors of a Russian missile attack that killed at least 22 people . At least 25 people nationwide, including two in the capital Kyiv, were reported killed in the October 7 barrage. The bombardment was part of near-daily attacks that have steadily increased in frequency and ferocity, as the Kremlin struggles on the battlefield front line. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it one of the "most vile" attacks in recent memory, and he noted they occurred on the birthday of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Russian forces "destroyed" a residential building "as a birthday 'gift' to Putin," Zelenskyy said in a post to X. At least 10 other such buildings were damaged elsewhere, along with Ukraine's energy infrastructure, one of Moscow's other "key targets," he said. The five-story building was mostly torn apart by the Russian strike with its roof destroyed, windows blown out. "The fire was right in front of my eyes. There were explosions. I was screaming in my apartment. Extremely scary. I can't describe it," one woman, who gave her name as Lidiya, told Current Time. "So many people have died. I knew everyone here," she added, holding back tears. SEE ALSO: 'We'll Die This Autumn': Ruined And Flooded, Russian-Occupied Oleshky In Ukraine Starves Under A 'Total Blockade' With a fifth wartime winter approaching, Russian strikes on Ukraine have become a daily occurrence. Moscow has previously sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by attacking the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures. Since this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia and middle-range strikes targeting its key logistics in Ukraine's occupied eastern and southern regions. Tanker Hit In Black Sea Following the latest Russian attacks, Zelenskyy later reported on what he called Kyiv's "just responses." He said Ukrainian forces had targeted two of Russia's oil facilities and a military training ground overnight on October 7, adding, "There was also a response in the Black Sea." Hours earlier, Russia's Transport Ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked by "naval drones" near the Black Sea resort city of Sochi. It later added that the crew of 23, all Indian citizens, had been rescued and the fire had been extinguished. According to the Ukrainian monitoring site BlackSeaNews, the vessel was used by Russia as part of its so-called shadow fleet, a network of vessels used to transport Russian fuel and evade sanctions. Sochi's local authorities said access to the city's coast and beaches was being restricted. Previous Ukrainian strikes on energy targets in southern Russia have caused oil slicks, prompted beach closures, and led to toxic black rainfall. The developments came amid renewed US interest in negotiating a diplomatic settlement to the long-running war. While US President Donald Trump has long said it is one of the key goals of his presidency, Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions. Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the Kremlin has shown no willingness to compromise on its key demands, including full control over Ukraine's key eastern Donetsk region, a stronghold Russian forces have not yet been able to capture. body: News Rubio In Iceland Signals Deeper NATO Push As Russia, China Challenge Arctic Security By Alex Raufoglu October 07, 2026 10:55 CET Rubio In Iceland Signals Deeper NATO Push As Russia, China Challenge Arctic Security Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Iceland's foreign minister, Thorgerour Katrin Gunnarsdottir (right), welcomes US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at Keflavik Airport on October 6. REYKJAVIK -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has signaled a renewed American push to strengthen security in the Arctic, warning that US adversaries and competitors are already acting in a region of growing strategic importance. Rubio, standing alongside Iceland's foreign minister, Thorgerour Katrin Gunnarsdottir, on the first stop of a three-nation tour of NATO allies, cast the strategically located NATO member as a critical link in the defense of North America and Europe. The trip comes as Russia's military and covert capabilities and China's expanding Arctic ambitions drive greater attention to the north. SEE ALSO: NATO Launches 'Arctic Sentry' Mission "Iceland sits at the center of many of the questions surrounding the security and defense of our shared region," Rubio said. "Those threats are growing, which is why this focus on the Arctic in general and Iceland, in particular, is so critical." His visit included a stop at Hofdi House, the site of the 1986 summit between US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. Forty years later, Rubio and Gunnarsdottir recreated the leaders' famous handshake, highlighting Iceland's enduring role in the strategic relationship between North America, Europe, and the Arctic. Rubio did not announce plans for a new permanent US military base in Iceland, but he signaled Washington is open to expanding its security presence. Asked whether the United States could increase its military footprint or surveillance capabilities following a new US-Danish-Greenland defense agreement, Rubio said Washington would work with Icelandic authorities to determine what more could be done. "I think there's a willingness to do more together," he said, pointing to Iceland's infrastructure, technology, and ability to provide surveillance and domain awareness. SEE ALSO: Russia's Big Arctic Oil Bet: Who Benefits? The United States ended its permanent military presence at Keflavik in 2006, but allied activity has continued through exercises, maritime patrols, and rotational deployments. Rubio said the strategic environment has since changed. "The world has changed over the last 20 years. There's a lot of focus on the Arctic," he said, arguing Iceland's location is important not only to NATO's defense of Europe but also to the defense of the US homeland. More than 1,200 Americans participated with allied forces in the Northern Viking 2026 exercise last month, part of annual military cooperation in and around Iceland. Rubio stressed that Iceland's lack of a conventional military does not prevent it from making an important contribution to NATO. Instead, the country provides territory, infrastructure, surveillance capabilities, and access for allied forces. "We want to continue to build upon that as a way to prevent conflict," Rubio said. "History teaches us that deterrence is the best prevention of violence and the best preventer of war." Rubio said the security risks facing Iceland and its allies extend beyond conventional military threats. Asked whether Iceland faces a direct threat from Russia, he cited covert activity, threats to undersea cables, and vulnerabilities around shipping lanes. "There are direct threats," Rubio said. "And those threats in the 21st century aren't just military threats; they're also economic, commercial threats that have implications on the national security of our respective countries." The comments reflect a broader NATO concern that the Arctic and North Atlantic are becoming increasingly important strategic spaces for submarine activity, maritime routes, communications infrastructure and access to North America. Map: Arctic Crossroads (Greenland ai2html) Erlingur Erlingsson, a senior visiting fellow at the Institute of International Affairs at the University of Iceland, told RFE/RL that Iceland has welcomed improved allied security awareness in the High North, including NATO's Arctic Sentry initiative and growing European capabilities. But he cautioned against losing sight of the larger European security picture. "Russian capabilities, particularly gray-zone warfare, long-range strike, and submarine, remain a significant threat," Erlingsson said. He said NATO's eastern flank remains the alliance's primary security concern and continued support for Ukraine is critical to European security. Kristinn Arni Lar Hrobjartsson, co-founder of the Icelandic security think tank Varda, said Reykjavik is also seeing heightened Russian interest in the region. Arctic Focus "Iceland certainly feels the increased focus on the Arctic, driven by Russian activities and continued war of aggression," he told RFE/RL, pointing to the presence of a Russian spy ship around Iceland during the summer. Hrobjartsson also cautioned against overstating China's role in Iceland, saying Chinese activities are "largely exaggerated" compared with the more immediate military dangers facing NATO on its eastern flank. Iceland's importance is likely to grow as the United States strengthens its position in Greenland and the wider Arctic. Rubio welcomed a recent agreement involving the United States, Greenland, and Denmark on Greenland's defense, saying it was important for regional security. Hrobjartsson said Iceland's strategic location and support for allied forces make it an important part of the emerging Arctic defense network. "The new Greenland agreement and potential build out of more bases there will undoubtedly call for even more contribution from Iceland," he said. SEE ALSO: NATO Ministers Seek Unity As Arctic Security And Spending Targets Come Into Focus Rubio also sought to broaden the relationship beyond defense, highlighting opportunities in geothermal energy, biotechnology, marine industries, and other areas. But he stressed that security remains the foundation for economic cooperation. "Security underpins everything else," Rubio said. "If you're not secure, you can't be prosperous." He suggested that while a traditional US-Iceland free-trade agreement may be difficult in the current environment, the two countries could pursue closer bilateral trade and investment ties. For Iceland, the challenge will be balancing its growing strategic importance with the need to maintain a strong and predictable transatlantic alliance. Erlingsson said Rubio's visit could help repair some of the damage caused by recent tensions over Greenland, but warned that wider questions about US commitments to NATO remain. For Washington, Iceland's strategic value is tied to its location between North America, Europe and the Arctic, as NATO increases its focus on the High North and the North Atlantic. Rubio said the goal was not to provoke conflict but to strengthen deterrence. "We want to continue to build upon that as a way to prevent conflict, not as a way to encourage conflict or provoke conflict, but prevent it," he said. "History teaches us that deterrence is the best prevention of violence and the best preventer of war." body: Iran Iran's Medicine Shortages Fuel Black Market For Essential Drugs By Behnaz Jalalipour October 06, 2026 16:20 CET Iran's Medicine Shortages Fuel Black Market For Essential Drugs Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Iranians buy medicines at a pharmacy in Tehran in April. The Iranian Pharmacists Association says around 800 medicines are currently on the country's shortage list. Iran's worsening medicine shortages are pushing patients toward a growing black market, where essential drugs can be found at several times their official prices. The Iranian Pharmacists Association says around 800 medicines are currently on the country's shortage list. The shortages have been compounded by financial constraints, difficulties importing medicines and raw materials, and flight restrictions following the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025 and the ongoing conflict with the United States. Mehdi Pirsalehi, head of Iran's Food and Drug Administration, has cited financial difficulties such as a shortage of the foreign currency needed for imports as a major cause of the crisis. SEE ALSO: 'Just To Survive': Soaring Inflation Puts Iranians' Lives On Hold For patients, the consequences can be severe. A 45-year-old woman being treated for breast cancer told RFE/RL's Radio Farda that pharmacies repeatedly said they were out of stock of the Iranian-version of Aromasin, a drug she must take daily. A 30-tablet pack officially costs 4 million rials (about $1.50). She paid 50 million rials (about $19) on the black market, 12.5 times the official price. She also said she paid at least 30 million rials (about $11) per injection of Zometa, and that two of them turned out to be counterfeit and caused her complications. Like other people who spoke to RFE/RL's Radio Farda, she asked that her name be withheld for security reasons. A 39-year-old man being treated for lung cancer said he now spends 750 million rials (about $279) a month on Sandostatin LAR, which he obtains from pharmacies run by the Iranian Red Crescent Society. Last year, he spent 220 million rials (about $82), marking an increase of 241 percent. According to the Iranian Statistics Center, the average monthly salary in Iran is around $400–500, with wages in cities such as Tehran seen at about double that level. Radio Farda is barred from operating in Iran, and the accounts in this report could not be independently verified. Sold Through Telegram While pharmacies in Iran run short on supplies, Radio Farda found sellers advertising medicines through Telegram groups and other online channels. They were offering drugs for Parkinson's disease, asthma, depression, diabetes and heart conditions. One seller offered RhoGAM, an injection given to Rh-negative women during pregnancy or after miscarriage to prevent complications. The same seller also carried Symbicort, which is prescribed for asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and nortriptyline, which used for depression and migraines. SEE ALSO: Iran Lurching Toward 'Severe Economic Collapse' As War Takes Its Toll Some sellers said flight restrictions imposed because of the war had made it harder to import medicines but that alternative routes remained open. One importer urged buyers to confirm availability first, then offered a long list of medicines for delivery by post. Another seller, a woman, said she worked with her brother, who sources medicines "from wherever he can," while she handles marketing and sales. "You just place the order," she said. "Selling medicine is not profitable at all. We only sell medicine so that we can survive." No Fixed Price Prices on the black market vary widely and often far exceed pharmacy prices. A seller in Isfahan offered Madopar, a Parkinson's drug, for 20 million rials (about $7). At roughly the same time, a seller in Yazd quoted 72 million rials (about $27), more than three times as much. Estradiol valerate, an estrogen medicine, was offered for 40 million rials (about $15), compared with 6 million rials (about $2) at pharmacies. Official prices are climbing, too. A spokesman for the Iranian Pharmacists Association told Iranian media recently that medicine prices had risen by an average of 30 to 70 percent this year. Some foreign-branded drugs had risen by as much as 300 percent. For patients who can find their medicines, the question is increasingly whether they can afford them. For the sellers, as the woman who works with her brother put it, the trade is about getting by. summary: Iran’s worsening medicine shortages are driving patients to a booming black market, where essential drugs can cost several times official prices. Cancer and chronic disease patients face soaring costs, while authorities struggle with imports, currency shortages, and supply disruptions.
title: Iran's Medicine Shortages Fuel Black Market For Essential Drugs

body: Russia Death At Russian Plague Lab: How Much Should We Worry? By Farangis Najibullah October 06, 2026 13:51 CET Death At Russian Plague Lab: How Much Should We Worry? Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A view of the entrance to the grounds of the research institute in the city of Irkutsk where a laboratory technician died of a suspected case of pneumonic plague. A suspected case of pneumonic plague killing a laboratory technician in Russia has sparked global alarm about the possibility of wider transmission. But how easily does pneumonic plague spread, how dangerous is it today, and why are laboratories working with the bacteria that causes it? RFE/RL spoke to Brendan Wren , a professor of microbial pathogenesis at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, whose research includes studying Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague, about the situation and Russia's moves to deal with it. RFE/RL: If this was pneumonic plague, how does it spread between people, and how easily can it spread? Brendan Wren: Pneumonic plague is transmitted by the respiratory route but is not particularly transmissible and certainly not as transmissible as the respiratory SARS virus. The unfortunate incident in Russia is clearly an isolated occupational infection and to date has not been transmitted to another person, so is not an outbreak. Other persons may have been in contact with the infected person, so isolation and observation of those potentially affected is a sensible measure. SEE ALSO: Siberian Anti-Plague Institute Staff Isolated After Worker's Death RFE/RL: How rare and how dangerous is pneumonic plague? Can it be treated effectively? Wren: It is such a rapid and fatal infection that can kill within 24 hours, so although antibiotics may be available, it may be too late if administered when the infection has taken hold. There are also increasing reports of antibiotic-resistant Yersinia pestis strains, the causative bacterial agent of plague. So some antibiotics may not work. There are approximately 1,000 cases of plague worldwide each year. It is endemic in parts of Russia, China, and the United States. RFE/RL: Why would a laboratory be working with plague bacteria in the first place? What are such laboratories studying or trying to achieve? Wren: Generally, to make improved vaccines that could be used in regions of the world where plague is endemic. If Yersinia pestis was weaponized, a vaccine for military personnel may be desirable. RFE/RL: Based on what is publicly known so far, how concerning is this case? Does it pose any meaningful risk to the wider public? Wren: In my view this is an isolated case. We no longer live in medieval times, and plague is not particularly transmissible in modern times. It would seem that the authorities are taking sensible procedures to contain this single laboratory-acquired case. Death At Russian Plague Lab: How Much Should We Worry?
