body: Wider Europe Wider Europe Briefing: The New EU Enlargement Strategy By Rikard Jozwiak October 06, 2026 12:01 CET Wider Europe Briefing: The New EU Enlargement Strategy Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Welcome to Wider Europe, RFE/RL's newsletter focusing on the key issues concerning the European Union, NATO, and other institutions and their relationships with the Western Balkans and Europe's Eastern neighborhoods. I'm RFE/RL Europe Editor Rikard Jozwiak, and this week I'm drilling down on two issues: the EU's new enlargement strategy and the EU's game plan to keep Russia (and Belarus) out of sports. Embed share Wider Europe Briefing: Wider Europe Briefing: The New EU Enlargement Strategy by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:12:48 0:00 Direct link 128 kbps | MP3 64 kbps | MP3 Pop-out player Briefing #1: The EU’s New Enlargement Strategy What You Need To Know: The European Commission is on October 6 presenting its long-awaited pre-enlargement strategy, outlining how a potentially bigger European Union in the future could function. The draft document, seen by RFE/RL, will be debated for the first time when EU leaders meet in Brussels for a summit on October 15-16 and will be a jump-off point for the potential changes that need to be made as candidate countries are approaching membership. Perhaps the most controversial ideas in the document concern the diluted EU membership that newcomers would experience in the event that some of these proposals indeed become rules. In many ways, it reflects the fears in some EU capitals of taking in poorer, unprepared countries with diplomats privately talking about the need to “avoid another Hungary” -- a reference to the many rule of law issues that faced Budapest under Viktor Orban. Deep Background : Though not explicitly spelled out, the strategy is written with the four current front-runners -- Albania, Moldova, Montenegro, and Ukraine -- in mind. With Montenegro still aiming to be EU member 28 by 2028 and the other three hoping to join shortly thereafter, the document argues that enlargement is “not only about preparing candidate countries to join the Union. It is equally about preparing the Union to welcome new Member States while strengthening its capacity to deliver.” Most of the 16-page paper is dedicated to classic Brussels discussion points that either are already happening or will never see the light of day as EU member states struggle to enact them. In the latter category, the European Commission is repeating its long-held belief that more decision-making in the club, notably in foreign policy, should move from unanimity to qualified majority voting (55 percent of member states representing at least 65 percent of the total EU population). But the document concedes that this very move requires unanimity and hence would stumble on the same obstacle as all previous efforts to make changes. In the former category, the idea of candidate countries gradual integration into the EU in various areas is already under way. Key examples are Moldova and Ukraine, which are already in the EU’s “Roam Like at Home” cell data program, and the non-EU Western Balkan countries, which are on track to join the same scheme. Or take the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA), which several EU hopefuls recently became part of or soon will be. Drilling Down: What is new in the paper -- and would make any new EU addition something of a second-tier member -- are the proposed safeguard measures. Essentially, there are three new ideas spelled out here. Firstly, the text notes that “new Member States would undertake, for a limited period, not to oppose Council decisions requiring unanimity.” This would mean that a newcomer cannot exercise a veto on, for example, most foreign-policy issues, such as sanctioning Russia. This limited period could stretch up to 15 years. The text further explains that “new member states could also undertake not to prevent an otherwise existing consensus in the European Council. Such commitments would apply not only to sectoral policies but also to cross-cutting institutional matters, including decisions relating to future enlargements.” Though not explicitly stated, there is a fear in Brussels that new member states would block EU membership for neighboring candidate countries, often in order to extract some bilateral concessions, which is not exactly an uncommon practice to date. This is what Slovenia did over land and maritime border disputes when Croatia was negotiating its EU entry, delaying Zagreb’s membership by nearly a year. Unsurprisingly, Croatia is currently putting on the brakes when it comes to Montenegro’s accession talks, blocking the closing of several key accession chapters to put maximum pressure on Podgorica in numerous areas of policy. The second proposal in the paper is even more contentious. (We know that because, for a long time, it was the only part in the text that was in parentheses, meaning that it wasn’t settled internally within the European Commission until the very last moment.) The passage concerns the length of legal safeguards, which act as a sort of "phased-in probationary system" for new members in order to protect existing EU economies. Most of these are safeguards in the fields of economics, the internal market, and home affairs and essentially mean that a new member either isn’t fully participating yet or that it easily can be suspended from aspects of cooperation if the country is backsliding politically. These safeguards are normally there for three years, but the European Commission is pushing for them to remain up to 10 years. That is not the only thing. The European Commission wants additional safeguards. The third, new proposal is “a temporary institutional safeguard clause.” This would kick in if there is “a particularly serious breach” of common EU values and would include “the temporary suspension of specified rights deriving from membership, such as voting rights in the Council.” This is essentially the EU’s famous nuclear option, known as Article. 7. Both Hungary and Poland were previously under the Article 7 procedure even though their voting rights were never stripped. The two countries were protecting each other, as the move to take away their voting rights required consensus. What the European Commission now is proposing is that voting rights for fresh members could be removed for a while by a simple qualified majority, which is substantially easier to achieve than unanimity. The rule, however, would not apply to current members, meaning that democratic backsliding in an older member would be more difficult to punish. Briefing #2: Europe’s Game Plan To Keep Russia (And Belarus) Out Of Sports What You Need To Know: When European Union foreign ministers meet in Luxembourg on October 12 , they will have an initial discussion on how to address the slow but steady return of Russian and Belarusian athletes in various international sport competitions. The reason is essentially two-fold. Firstly, to find a common position after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) earlier in the summer decided to provisionally lift the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC) -- a move that essentially can lead to athletes representing Russia at the 2028 Los Angeles Summer Olympics instead of participating as neutrals. (The same decision on Belarusian athletes came earlier in the spring). The move is also seen as a way to avoid any “nasty surprises” in this field, as one EU diplomat recently put it, referring to a similar dilemma in the cultural sphere where the European Commission was caught off guard when the Venice Biennale allowed Russia to reopen its national pavilion at the prestigious art exhibition. summary: In this week's Wider Europe, Rikard Jozwiak drills down on two issues: the EU's new enlargement strategy and the EU's game plan to keep Russia (and Belarus) out of sports.

body: Credit: olympic.uz Subscribe for ads-free reading In April 2023, when he was serving as deputy head of the Presidential Security Service, Otabek Umarov – Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s son-in-law – reportedly acquired citizenship in the United Arab Emirates. He’s also alleged to be the owner of around $7 million worth of Dubai real estate. Those are the central allegations of a new investigation published by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) and RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service, Ozodlik . Under Uzbek military law, which governs the position Umarov held at the time, holding a second citizenship is prohibited. Since acquiring citizenship typically includes swearing an oath of allegiance, many countries bar security (and other) officials from doing so – a second passport represents possible divided loyalties and a counterintelligence risk. As OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and [the process] requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.” Umarov was shifted out of his security service role in November 2024, in the extended wake of the assassination attempt on Komil Allamjanov. Allamjanov, at the time of the October 2024 attempt, had recently stepped down from his role as deputy head of the presidential administration. He has since returned to government service, as an adviser to the powerful head of the presidential administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva (the president’s eldest daughter). As of January 2026 he was also appointed to a seemingly bespoke role: advisor-ambassador and representative of the presidential administration in the United States. Umarov, meanwhile, was named first deputy chairman of Uzbekistan’s National Olympic Committee – his father-in-law, the president, is the chairman. According to OCCRP and Ozodlik, at some point in 2025, Umarov became the owner of 13 properties in Dubai, worth around $7 million. The properties previously belonged to his younger brother, Oybek Umarov, who purchased them in 2021 and 2022, according to leaked Dubai real estate data obtained by OCCRP. It is not clear precisely how or when they came to be listed with Umarov’s name on the deeds, whether the properties were gifted or purchased. While Umarov has notably expensive tastes – for example, he’s been pictured wearing a limited edition Richard Mille watch valued at up to $1.9 million – his government position doesn’t quite explain his apparent wealth. Uzbek officials do not have to disclose their income declarations publicly. OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Public commercial registries show no record of [Otabek Umarov] owning private companies during his time as deputy presidential security chief.” His brother, however, does have extensive business holdings, including in banking, cement, and metalwork. A high-ranking government source told The Diplomat in late 2024 that Umarov’s assets and businesses were held in the names of others, including Ulugbek Shadmanov who was implicated in an apparent attempt to manipulate the U.S. sanctions system to target Allamjonov and another Uzbek official in the months before the assassination attempt. Shadmanov was earlier named in the Pandora Papers as connected to an offshore company, though there are few details available. In December 2024 he was detained in Dubai and extradited rapidly – apparently without the proper legal process – to Uzbekistan, regardless of the fact that he held what’s known as a “ Golden Visa ” in the UAE. Despite high-powered legal representation and a campaign on his behalf, very little has been reported since about his case. Ultimately, the OCCRP and Ozodlik investigation raises far more questions than it answers; that’s the nature of investigations into the opaque underbelly of Uzbek politics (and those of the UAE, to boot). As I told Ozodlik , we don’t know exactly how Umarov acquired UAE citizenship, who was involved, and who knew about it. As noted above, the process to acquired UAE citizenship necessitates a nomination by a royal court or senior official. It’s nearly impossible to believe that Umarov’s role and connections were unknown at the time to the UAE’s authorities. Then there are questions of what comes next. Uzbekistan does not officially recognize dual citizenship. Holding a second citizenship isn’t illegal per se – though it does violate laws related to Umarov’s specific position at the time. Nevertheless, “voluntarily acquiring a passport of a foreign state” is listed as possible grounds for revocation of Uzbek citizenship. Already have an account? Log in . body: A Wildberries pickup point in Bashkortostan, Russia. Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Artyom Vasilyev Subscribe for ads-free reading During World War II, Soviet authorities moved industry and people – often forcibly – away from the frontier in Europe into the heartland of Eurasia. The strategic relocation of factories and critical production to the Urals, Siberia, and Central Asia fundamentally changed economies across the union. Now, amid a different war on the European front, Russian industry is looking again to Central Asia for relative safety to continue conducting business. Wildberries & Russ, the parent company of Russia’s largest e-commerce retailer, Wildberries, reportedly signed an investment agreement this week with the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry, and Trade to expand its logistics capacity in Uzbekistan. The deal comes in the wake of an early August announcement from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Trade and Integration that Wildberries would expand its warehouse capacity in that country. Starting in July 2026, Ukraine began targeting major Wildberries warehousing facilities in Russia. Through mid-August, Ukrainian drones had struck at least 20 Wildberries hubs, many of them near Moscow. According to the Moscow-based e-commerce consultancy Data Insight, as reported by DW in mid-August, Wildberries had lost 480 billion rubles worth of goods ($5.7 billion) and a third of its warehouse space. As The Diplomat’s Albert Otkjær pointed out in August , WIldberries’ effort to build out its warehousing capacity in Kazakhstan predates the current crisis – though not the February 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. Wildberries’ expansion into Kazakhstan began in 2023 , when the company opened its first logistics center in Astana, followed by a warehouse complex in Almaty. In September 2023 , Wildberries opened a sorting center in Uralsk, the company’s fifth logistics center in the country. Similarly, in May 2023 Wildberries opened its first logistics center in Uzbekistan, in the Tashkent region, followed by plans for a second in Fergana. In October 2023 Wildeberries announced that it would build another logistics center in the Tashkent region. The recently announced deal pertains to a planned logistics hub in the Zangiata district of the Tashkent region, to be built on a a 67.3-hectare site. According to the company, the facility will generate at least 7,500 jobs. As such, the wave of attacks this summer targeting Wildberries is not the sole motivation for its efforts to expand capacity in Central Asia. Those efforts began earlier. The region is, even absent the ongoing conflict, a large market for Russian companies and a bridge deeper into Asia. Factoring in the war in Ukraine only deepens the commercial logic for expansion into Central Asia. It also deepens the risks. Ukrainian authorities have justified the strikes on an ostensibly civilian enterprise by arguing that Wildberries warehouse are “involved in supplying the Russian military with drone components, navigation equipment, and other gear,” as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in late July . Similarly, Ukraine justified attacks on Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) infrastructure near Novorossiysk – in November 2025 and July 2026 – given the critical importance of oil revenues to the Russian war machine. But collateral damage to Kazakhstan’s export of oil through the CPC led to pushback from both Astana and Washington. In February 2026 , Ukraine’s ambassador to the United States said that Kyiv had received a formal demarche from Washington. The complaint, Ambassador Olga Stefanishyna said, cited the risks posed to “American investments which are being performed through Kazakhstan.” In early August, Bloomberg reported, citing a U.S. official, that Ukraine had agreed to not strike CPC infrastructure critical to Kazakhstan’s oil exports in the Black Sea, as well as avoid striking non-Russian vessels – provided they’re not separately sanctioned or carrying Russian cargo. Could Ukrainian drone strikes target Wildberries facilities in Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan? It’s highly unlikely, though not impossible as the war drags on. Such a strike would mark a significant expansion of the conflict and be ruinous to Kyiv’s relations with the Central Asian states, and likely the United States, too, given Washington’s intercession on Kazakhstan’s behalf in regard to the CPC. body: The Karlag Museum in Dolinka. Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Yakov Fedorov Subscribe for ads-free reading In “ Farewell to Russia: A Journey Through the Former USSR ” journalist Joe Luc Barnes travels across the 15 states that once comprised the Soviet Union. In the excerpt below, Barnes stops off in Karaganda, the heart of Kazakh coal country and once the site of a notorious gulag. *** The steppe stretches in all directions under the massive sky. There are no trees, no hills, no natural points of interest of any sort, save for a herd of horses grazing by the roadside. The openness of Central Asia makes itself felt immediately. Kazakhstan alone spans an area larger than Western Europe. But these northern plains are not featureless. Factories dot the landscape, their chimneys raised like middle fingers in defiance of the mighty heavens. Thin trails of smoke seep from them and a vast network of pylons and railway tracks sprawl from their feet. Karaganda and its environs are home to some of the largest-scale coal-mining on the planet. At the time of my visit, much of this industrial landscape belonged to steel giant ArcelorMittal. “We don’t like them here. They don’t care about employees; they pay us nothing, and don’t give a shit about our safety,” my taxi driver tells me. “Do you work down the mines?” “Used to. I’m an invalid now; was forced to retire. My lungs can’t take it any more.” “Would you like to be back down there?” “Of course!” he says, displaying that gritty courage you often get in mining communities, where a hard day’s graft is the highest form of honor. As it happens, this former miner is taking me to one of the predecessors of ArcelorMittal – another institution that has a rather patchy record when it comes to worker rights. Around a century ago, Karaganda didn’t really exist. Coal had been discovered here in the late 19th century, but the nascent mines were soon abandoned – for some reason it proved difficult to persuade people to leave their families behind and toil down the pit in the middle of the frigid steppe. Besides, there were too few houses and nowhere near enough food to supply a large-scale mining settlement. But all that changed in February 1927, when Article 58 of the Russian penal code was brought into force. Article 58 justified the arrest of those suspected of counter-revolutionary activity. The law cast a wide net as the precise meaning of “counter-revolutionary activity” was left deliberately vague, leaving Alexander Solzhenitsyn to ask: “Who among us has not experienced its all-encompassing embrace? In all truth, there is no step, thought, action, or lack of action under the heavens which could not be punished by the heavy hand of Article 58.” People may not have fancied moving to the steppe, but fortunately for economic planners the Soviet justice system had suddenly created a large pool of laborers who had little choice in the matter. Between 1921 and 1953, an estimated 18 million people passed through the Soviet forced-labor camp system known as the Gulag. The number of those who died is disputed, but is thought to be around 1.5 to 1.6 million. These numbers suggest that while the Gulag experience was unimaginably brutal, it was not necessarily the death sentence it is often portrayed as. The Karaganda Camp (or Karlag) was created in 1930 to solve the problem of supplying the coal mines. It grew so rapidly that, by 1940, the area of the camp covered 6,500 square miles and was home to 65,000 prisoners. The Kazakh SSR became a repository for all manner of “undesirables,” from the political dissidents convicted under Article 58 to the so-called rich peasants, or kulaks, who were seen to be standing in the way of the equal distribution of land. They were joined by whole groups of “disloyal” ethnicities such as Poles and Chechens, Koreans and Crimean Tatars. In the early 1940s, half a million ethnic Germans, who had been living along the banks of Russia’s Volga River for almost two centuries, were also forced to relocate here. Between them they played a large part in the building of Karaganda, which went from a small settlement in the late 1920s to a city of over 200,000 twenty years later. The camp headquarters, and now the site of the Karlag Museum, was in a small town called Dolinka, about 30 miles from Karaganda proper. There are few other visitors, so the young woman at the ticket office is happy to give me a free tour. She takes me to the dormitories first. It’s draughty even at the height of summer. Rough woolen sheets filled with straw are draped over bunk beds whose supporting planks are so thin I doubt they would have supported any but the scrawniest of inmates – though I suppose the diets here were unlikely to have left anyone particularly rotund. “Local people used to ride here on horseback and throw kurt over the walls of the camp for the prisoners to eat,” my guide tells me. Kurt is a hard, extremely salty ball of dried cheese. It’s not particularly appetizing but lasts a long time and has been used for centuries as a protein-rich snack for those spending days in the saddle. The traditional Kazakh diet is heavy on these milky staples. Another is kumis – fermented horse’s milk – which I was made to sample on my first evening here. It wasn’t the tastiest of concoctions, but I imagine that both kurt and kumis would hit the spot if you’ve been forced to build a coal mine on Oliver Twist’s rations. I also imagine that this story isn’t true – the idea of noble, empathetic Kazakh horsemen coming to the aid of the desperate, oppressed prisoner is, well, a stretch. However, there is well-documented evidence of large-scale black-market trade in food and rations in the Karlag, whose walls were more porous than other camps due to its size and proximity to Karaganda. We come to the commandant’s study, set up as it would have been in the early 1950s: portrait of Stalin on the wall behind the desk and some heavy bookshelves, well stocked with the works of Lenin, Marx, and Engels. The only touch of personality is betrayed by an old gramophone. “Concerts were organized on Sundays and Mondays,” she tells me. “Those were the days when the prisoners were tortured; the music drowned out the screams.” The other rooms are dedicated to the fate of the Kazakhs – that is, the people who had lived here for centuries before these lands became an integral part of the Gulag. In 1897, under the tsars, the land we now call Kazakhstan was 82 percent Kazakh. The early years of the 20th century saw the authorities encourage Slavic people to settle in the areas that had traditionally been inhabited by Kazakh nomads. “Kazakhs lived at one with the steppe,” Klara, an IT worker who lived in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, had told me before my trip. As soon as she found out about my post-Soviet odyssey, she made it her mission to make her country my next destination. “They traveled to where food and water was before moving on. This way, the land was allowed to recover in the meantime. The European arrivals began to change that, and the Soviets put it on fast-forward. They were obsessed with collectivizing people. The idea of being a nomad didn’t fit into their concept of a worker-led revolution. Maybe Marx skipped our role in his grand theory of history,” she said, giving me a wan smile. The result of this crash-collectivization was famine. The room has exhibits on the famines of 1919–22 and 1932–3. Kazakhs suffered disproportionately as they lived on fertile land that could produce a lot of wheat. They were forced to abandon their nomadic lifestyle and produce food first for the Red Army, and then for Stalin’s five-year plans. Those who resisted were shot. Many fled to China or Mongolia. Many more starved. In the Soviet census of 1926 the Kazakh population was 3.6 million; by 1939 this had dropped by a third to 2.3 million. By 1959 Kazakhs numbered a mere 30 percent of the population of the Kazakh SSR. Along with the demographic assault came the

body: Credit: Pixabay Subscribe for ads-free reading Tajikistan has started importing oil and petroleum products from Iran. Deliveries began in late August, the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources told Asia-Plus on September 24, without disclosing the volumes, prices, suppliers, or transit route. The shipments followed August 15 talks in Tehran, where Energy Minister Daler Juma and Transport Minister Azim Ibrohim met Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad and agreed to set up a working group to prepare a long-term supply agreement . Dushanbe asked for up to 2.55 million tons a year (2 million tons of crude, 300,000 tons of diesel, 150,000 tons of gasoline, and 100,000 tons of jet fuel) along with discounted prices, dedicated tank-car trains, and a “green corridor” across Iran’s rail network. The scramble is a product of Russia’s fuel crisis. Russia supplied 91.1 percent of the 599,500 tons of petroleum products Tajikistan imported in the first half of 2026, free of export duty. Tajikistan is not a member of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), and Carnegie Politika’s Galiya Ibragimova described the cheap Russian fuel as “payment” for Dushanbe’s “political loyalty” to Moscow. But loyalty bought less fuel once Ukrainian drones began disabling Russian refineries, including the Omsk plant, which was knocked offline in early July. Moscow has extended its diesel export ban month by month, most recently through October 31. Deliveries under intergovernmental agreements are exempt , but the carve-out has not kept Tajikistan supplied : diesel shortages began in June. By July, some stations were capping sales at 20 liters per vehicle and diesel had climbed to $1.40-$1.66 per liter. In Tajikistan, domestic refining covers about 0.5 percent of gasoline consumption. Alternatives are scarce and expensive. U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28, and Iran’s subsequent restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz kept oil prices above $100 a barrel in September. Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan are competing with Tajikistan for the same limited supplies from Belarus, China, Kazakhstan, and Turkmenistan. Iran is an unlikely lifeline. Relations collapsed after Tehran hosted exiled Islamic Renaissance Party leader Muhiddin Kabiri in December 2015, months after Dushanbe banned his party as an extremist organization. In 2017, Dushanbe accused Iran of involvement in political killings during the 1990s civil war. The thaw came with the 2022 opening of an Iranian drone factory in Dushanbe and accelerated with President Masoud Pezeshkian’s January 2025 state visit, when the two sides signed 23 agreements. Bilateral trade reached $438 million in 2025, up 28 percent from the year prior. However, Tajikistan and Iran don’t share a border. Moving 2.55 million tons of petroleum products by rail through third countries would take about 51,000 tank cars a year, according to Tajikistan’s Transport Ministry – roughly 140 a day. Iran may have little to offer beyond crude oil and jet fuel: Hamid Hosseini of Iran’s Union of Oil, Gas and Petrochemical Products Exporters said gasoline and diesel exports were not under discussion because of shortages in Iran itself, and put likely shipments at around 5,000 tons a month. The requested crude also exceeds Tajikistan’s refining capacity. The TK-Oil plant in Danghara has a design capacity of 1.2 million tons a year but has long run below it for lack of feedstock; another Asia-Plus report put the country’s two refineries at about 500,000 tons combined. Then there is Washington. On August 24, the U.S. Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast, widening the range of Iran-related conduct exposed to secondary sanctions and promising every country a “defined timeline” to shut down Iran-related activity. A Treasury official told RFE/RL that anyone in Iran’s petroleum sector “incurs that risk themselves.” Edward Lemon of the Oxus Society noted that the modest scale of Tajik-Iranian trade may keep Dushanbe below Washington’s threshold of attention. The practical exposure likely lies with whichever Tajik banks settle payments for Iranian cargoes, particularly if they clear dollars or deal with designated Iranian entities. Russia still supplies nine of every ten tons of Tajikistan’s fuel, and on available evidence the Iranian route is unlikely to change that this winter. But it gives Dushanbe a second supplier at a moment when Moscow cannot guarantee much, albeit at the cost of sanctions exposure that grows with every ton delivered. Already have an account? Log in . body: Subscribe for ads-free reading On the night of February 21, 2026 Pakistan launched air and missile strikes on three border provinces in Afghanistan . What was Pakistan bombing? Suspected camps of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan – the TTP for short – and the Islamic State of Khorasan Province. The Taliban regime in Afghanistan retaliated by hitting Pakistani border posts. Pakistan then upped the ante. Its military launched Operation Ghazab Lil-Haq — which means Righteous Fury — against Afghanistan. “Our patience has now run out. Now it is open war between us,” Pakistan’s defense minister said on February 27. Pakistan and Afghanistan have engaged in numerous strikes and counter-strikes in the months since. While these have declined in frequency and magnitude, thanks to mediation efforts by China, the military strikes were still happening into September 2026. TTP attacks in Pakistan have also continued. Few would have expected Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban to turn on each other. They had been close allies for over 30 years – through the Taliban’s entire existence. When the Taliban captured power in Kabul in August 2021, Pakistan celebrated. So why did Pakistan declare “an open war” against its one-time protégé? Is there more to Pakistan’s military strikes on Afghanistan than taking out TTP camps? And can the Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship be salvaged? Already have an account? Log in . body: Credit: Shutterstock Subscribe for ads-free reading Tajikistan’s Humo Bank has warned its Russian clients that their cards will be blocked on October 1 unless they visit one of its offices in Tajikistan by September 30 to undergo biometric identification. “If you can’t come to Tajikistan in person and complete the identification, unfortunately, your card will be closed,” the bank told Russian news site Lenta.ru, advising clients to move their remaining balances to ruble cards before the deadline. The bank cited the need to protect clients from fraud. A Russian client, however, told the Telegram channel Ostorozhno Novosti that the bank’s support staff explained it had decided to restrict services for “certain categories of non-resident individuals” whose cards were opened online. She said a transfer of about 300 euros had been stuck for a week and that the bank had stopped responding to her complaints. Humo offered her a new card if she traveled to Tajikistan, valid only for the duration of her legal stay and for no longer than a year. With Visa and Mastercard gone from Russia since 2022, Russians have relied on cards issued in “friendly” countries to make payments abroad. When Kazakhstan limited non-resident cards to 12 months and required in-person issuance in January 2025, intermediaries moved their business to Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. Humo and the International Bank of Tajikistan began offering remotely issued five-year cards in U.S. dollars and euros, sold through intermediaries for roughly 15,000 to 70,000 rubles. Humo is a newcomer to banking. Owned by the Japanese investment holding Gojo & Company , the former microcredit deposit organization received a full banking license from the National Bank of Tajikistan in July 2025. It was also among the few Tajik financial institutions with access to Visa Direct, a real-time payment service that became a conduit for Russian money headed to Europe. An investigation by The Bell found last year that Sberbank clients could send money to Revolut and N26 accounts through Central Asian intermediaries, with the funds appearing to originate from Dushanbe or Tashkent. The Humo ultimatum follows a year of Western pressure on Tajik banks. In October 2025, the European Union included Dushanbe City Bank, Spitamen, and Commercebank of Tajikistan in its 19th sanctions package, targeting banks closely linked to Russia’s financial system or processing cross-border payments that support the Russian economy. The three banks held roughly a fifth of all deposits in Tajikistan, and other Tajik banks responded by restricting transfers to Russia. In December, Revolut stopped accepting top-ups from cards issued in Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan for EU residents, citing payment systems’ classification of those countries as high-risk. The EU removed the three Tajik banks from its sanctions list in April 2026, with the National Bank crediting improved compliance and anti-money laundering standards. For Dushanbe, the stakes go well beyond fees collected from Russian cardholders. Remittances, mostly from Tajik migrants in Russia, reached $5.8 billion in 2024, or the equivalent of 45.3 percent of Tajikistan’s GDP, the highest share in the world. By the end of 2024, over 90 percent of payments in Tajik-Russian trade were settled in rubles, and the head of the National Bank said Tajik banks work only with Russian banks not under sanctions. Tajikistan needs its financial channels to Russia open and its banks connected to SWIFT and Visa at the same time. Neither Humo nor the National Bank has said whether the decision came from regulators, payment systems, or the bank’s own risk assessment. But a young bank that watched three of its peers cut off from European counterparties has every reason to shed remotely onboarded Russian clients before Brussels or Visa forces its hand. Russians will likely take their business to Kyrgyz and Uzbek banks, as they did when Kazakhstan closed its doors, until those banks face the same pressure. Already have an account? Log in . body: Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis Credit: Uzbekistan Presidency Subscribe for ads-free reading For the second time in the span of a year a brutal child abuse case has sparked heated public discussion in Uzbekistan. Reportedly, a five-year-old girl was repeatedly raped in a public kindergarten by a facilities manager who worked at the school in the Uchkurgan district of Namangan. According to the mother of the survivor, the alleged perpetrator is their neighbor and she became suspicious after she saw him smiling at her five-year-old daughter. She gently asked the girl questions only to find out that the facilities manager would buy sweets for the girl, tell her he loved her, and promised to buy more presents and sweets if she didn’t expose him. The mother suspects the man had threatened her daughter. Last year a similar case, which also occurred in Namangan, where a previously imprisoned convict raped a seven-year-old girl, caused a wave of demands by the public to restore the death penalty for serious crimes such as the sexual assault of minors. Public discussions over the death penalty typically emerge in Uzbekistan after news of an especially brutal crime against children breaks. An earlier wave of loud discussions took place in 2024 after a three-year-old was stabbed 12 times. What’s new this time is that high-ranking political figures are getting involved. Saida Mirziyoyeva, the head of the presidential administration and a deputy chair of the Security Council (and also the president’s daughter) chimed in. “In my opinion, the death penalty should be used for such heinous crimes. Unfortunately, the current legislation does not provide for the death penalty,” she wrote on her Telegram channel on September 27. “We are preparing a proposal to amend the legislation to maximize liability for this type of crime,” she added. Echoing Mirziyoyeva’s words, Alisher Qodirov, leader of the Milliy Tiklanish (National Revival) Democratic Party and deputy speaker of the Uzbek parliament, called death penalty a “necessity.” Qodirov is famous for making nationalist, sometimes controversial statements. “The continued existence of those who intentionally kill innocent people, especially child murderers and pedophiles, is a motivation for further crimes of this kind!” Qodirov wrote on his Telegram, reposting Mirziyoyeva’s earlier statement. This is not the first time Qodirov has voiced his position on the death penalty. Previously, in 2024, after news reports about a three-year-old girl being murdered, Qodirov suggested “cleansing” society. “It’s illogical to use our taxes to support a criminal who’s become an animal, keep him healthy, feed him, and then wait for someone else to die! Society needs to be cleansed of such people!” he wrote . Both Mirziyoyeva and Qodirov know that Uzbekistan abolished capital punishment in 2008 and acceded to the Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR aimed at abolition. Uzbekistan has no mechanism to reinstate the death penalty without a much larger legal overhaul, and no such overhaul is presently underway. In a rather unusual course of developments for Uzbekistan, the discussion over the death penalty divided the country’s political parties. As a new bill to increase liability for violence against children was introduced to the Legislative Chamber on September 29, Qodirov announced a neutral position on the proposed bill and doubled down on his stance regarding the need to resurrect the death penalty. Qodirov referred to Norwegian neo-Nazi and mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik , stating that he had complained “about the lack of facilities for writing a book, and those conditions were subsequently provided for him.” Qodirov’s interpretation isn’t quite accurate. While Breivik did complain about the “stab-resistant” pen he was made to write with and was reportedly provided with an electronic typewriter, Breivik’s communications continue to be censored by prison authorities and he has not published a book. Nevertheless, using Breivik as a point of reference, Qodirov questioned the compatibility of Uzbek values and international law. “Whose footsteps are we following!?” he asked. “We will also be forced to create conditions for our pedophile if he asks, because the international law we follow sees him as a human being, not as a dead person.” Bobur Bekmurodov, a member of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis and leader of the Yuksalish movement, opposed Qodirov’s statements openly. His arguments are clear: the constitution prohibits the death penalty, bringing the death penalty back could put child victims in greater danger, break Uzbekistan’s international obligations and raise the possibility of errors in judicial practices. “If child rape is punishable by death, there is nothing to stop the perpetrator from destroying the only witness, the child himself,” wrote Bekmurodov. While the grief over the case is genuine, the debate over the death penalty is a populist, opportunistic response. In a country where no other important questions are debated by high (or low) profile politicians, children and women’s abuse is a risk-free topic. Not only does it attract empathy from millions of citizens, but it also gains praise from international organizations. Siding with an innocent child is always a winning move. As outrage grows, officials do their best to appease the public. The investigation over the case is now under the prosecutor general’s control . Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva, another daughter of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and the first deputy director of the National Agency for Social Protection, reported that her agency is also involved in the case and the survivor’s family will be moved to another city and provided with housing. The agency also suggested changing the girl’s surname to ensure her privacy as she rehabilitates. The Ministry of Preschool and School Education formed a working group to address the situation. Right now, all attention is being given to maximizing punishment for one perpetrator and not letting another incident happen. What is left out of these debates is the failure of the systems that should have protected this girl. The mother of the survivor told local media that the cameras in the kindergarten did not record anything that day. And more absurdly, she had been told that the perpetrator was responsible for the cameras. The perpetrator’s wife allegedly offered her a bribe to close the case, too. The staff of the kindergarten who are supposed to protect the children in their care, are hiding behind paperwork instead of showing compassion. The director of the kindergarten said she was on a holiday when the alleged incident occurred and she had already provided explanatory letters to the police. She also added that children are never left unsupervised. The girl’s teacher also swore the girl was never left alone – “Not an hour, not a minute, would [she] be left unattended.” Local media outlets and the authorities have not disclosed the perpetrator’s name or released a mugshot. Netizens, however, have found his photos and full name and doxed his identity on social media pages. Yesterday, Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva noted that her agency, together with other relevant bodies, had been working on a draft law that would introduce life imprisonment for crimes involving child sexual abuse. “We also propose to strengthen the responsibility of parents for neglecting children and of educators for allowing violence and discrimination, and to provide legal assistance and protection to child victims at every stage of the investigation and trial,” the agency’s Telegram post stated . From 2022 to 2026 445 cases of rape involving minors under 14 years old were formally registered in Uzbekistan. Not all cases make headlines. Journalist and economist Bakhodir Abdullayev noted that the legislation on lifetime imprisonment for sexual abuse of minors was supposed to be passed by April 2026. But it wasn’t until the current furor, when
title: Uzbekistan’s Death Penalty Debate Returns After Child Abuse Case

body: Credit: Depositphotos Subscribe for ads-free reading Last week, Kyrgyzstan’s parliament, the Zhogorku Kenesh, officially set a date for the next presidential election: January 27, 2027. The country’s Central Election Commission (CEC) then opened the door for formal nominations . So far, incumbent President Sadyr Japarov and Omurbek Suvanaliev – a politician and former minister of internal affairs – have announced their intentions to run. In August, Japarov announced that he would seek a second term , something his political surrogates have been floating for some time . Japarov was elected, formally, in January 2021 after rising from literal prison to power amid the October 2020 unrest. At the time, Kyrgyzstan’s constitution mandated a single six-year presidential term. A referendum that took place at the same time as the presidential election in 2021 ushered in what critics called the “ Khanstitution , ” which provides for two five-year terms for the presidency. In February 2026 , Kyrgyzstan’s Constitutional Court clarified that Japarov’s current term does count as his first. Japarov confirmed his ambition to seek a second term in an interview in which he also revealed that he’d initially planned for his former ally and former head of Kyrgyzstan’s State Committee for National Security, Kamchybek Tashiev, to ascend to the presidency. Japarov claimed he’d told Tashiev, “Be prepared, cleanse your circle, educate your people... Then I see: he’s not ready.” Tashiev was convicted of a coup attempt in July , but spared a prison sentence. Prosecutors sought a harsher punishment on appeal only to have the charges reclassified and the sentence lessened further in September. He long denied any ambition to run for president. A month before his abrupt February dismissal , Tashiev responded to mounting rumors that he would seek the presidency by saying, “Many have tried and continue to try to sow discord between us, claiming that I aspire to the presidency. But this is not true... I do not intend to overthrow Sadyr Nurgoyevich [Japarov]... In this life, only death can separate us.” Under the Kyrgyz Constitution, any citizen who is at least 35 years old, speaks the state language (Kyrgyz), and has lived in the country for at least 15 years is eligible to run for president. Potential candidates must gather at least 30,000 signatures and pay a nonrefundable fee of 1 million som (around $11,400). Individuals can nominate themselves or be nominated by a party. Under 2025 legislation , individuals with criminal records are barred from running for president. Suvanaliev announced his presidential ambition in a September 24 interview with RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service, Azattyk . Suvanaliev served as minister of internal affairs from 2006-2007 under the Kurmanbek Bakiyev administration, then as governor of Naryn from 2008-2009, among other positions over the years, many of which appear to have been related to security and law enforcement. More recently, in 2019 then-President Sooronbay Jeenbekov appointed Suvanaliev a deputy secretary in the Security Council, a position he was dismissed from in October 2020 as the Jeenbekov administration collapsed in the face of protests. Until May 2021 , he was serving as a representative of the government in Batken region . In 2011, Suvanaliev contested for the presidency as an independent candidate. He recorded just over 16,000 votes, or 0.89 percent, in an election that Almazbek Atambayev won with 63.83 percent. According to Azattyk , Suvanaliev positioned himself as opposition. He said he believes that a candidate who can challenge the incumbent president should run in the elections. Japarov said in his August interview that the door was open for anyone to run against him: “Anyone who wants to run for office can do so. As they say, go ahead. We won’t restrict anyone. The elections will be transparent, and there will be no obstacles for competitors.” In the country’s most recent election, a snap parliamentary poll held in November 2025, Japarov’s allies did particularly well amid a political atmosphere that observers referred to as “stifled” or dead . As the presidential election approaches – and candidates step forward – the proof will be on the ballot and in the aftermath. Already have an account? Log in . Log in . Last week, Kyrgyzstan’s parliament, the Zhogorku Kenesh, officially set a date for the next presidential election: January 27, 2027. The country’s Central Election Commission (CEC) then opened the door for formal nominations . So far, incumbent President Sadyr Japarov and Omurbek Suvanaliev – a politician and former minister of internal affairs – have announced their intentions to run. In August, Japarov announced that he would seek a second term , something his political surrogates have been floating for some time . Japarov was elected, formally, in January 2021 after rising from literal prison to power amid the October 2020 unrest. At the time, Kyrgyzstan’s constitution mandated a single six-year presidential term. A referendum that took place at the same time as the presidential election in 2021 ushered in what critics called the “ Khanstitution , ” which provides for two five-year terms for the presidency. In February 2026 , Kyrgyzstan’s Constitutional Court clarified that Japarov’s current term does count as his first. Japarov confirmed his ambition to seek a second term in an interview in which he also revealed that he’d initially planned for his former ally and former head of Kyrgyzstan’s State Committee for National Security, Kamchybek Tashiev, to ascend to the presidency. Japarov claimed he’d told Tashiev, “Be prepared, cleanse your circle, educate your people... Then I see: he’s not ready.” Tashiev was convicted of a coup attempt in July , but spared a prison sentence. Prosecutors sought a harsher punishment on appeal only to have the charges reclassified and the sentence lessened further in September. He long denied any ambition to run for president. A month before his abrupt February dismissal , Tashiev responded to mounting rumors that he would seek the presidency by saying, “Many have tried and continue to try to sow discord between us, claiming that I aspire to the presidency. But this is not true... I do not intend to overthrow Sadyr Nurgoyevich [Japarov]... In this life, only death can separate us.” Under the Kyrgyz Constitution, any citizen who is at least 35 years old, speaks the state language (Kyrgyz), and has lived in the country for at least 15 years is eligible to run for president. Potential candidates must gather at least 30,000 signatures and pay a nonrefundable fee of 1 million som (around $11,400). Individuals can nominate themselves or be nominated by a party. Under 2025 legislation , individuals with criminal records are barred from running for president. Suvanaliev announced his presidential ambition in a September 24 interview with RFE/RL’s Kyrgyz Service, Azattyk . Suvanaliev served as minister of internal affairs from 2006-2007 under the Kurmanbek Bakiyev administration, then as governor of Naryn from 2008-2009, among other positions over the years, many of which appear to have been related to security and law enforcement. More recently, in 2019 then-President Sooronbay Jeenbekov appointed Suvanaliev a deputy secretary in the

body: Credit: Shutterstock Subscribe for ads-free reading In the U.S. state of Hawai‘i, Iris lives far from the pressures of urban China. Growing up in Zhejiang, she spent much of her childhood on what her mother called “self-improvement”: Olympiad math, piano lessons, and daily swimming. After graduating from New York University (NYU), Iris chose a simple, quiet life in Hawai‘i, using geographic distance to protect her personal autonomy from the pressure facing Chinese women in their 20s to settle down, marry, and have children. Halfway across the world, Jessica is confronting the same expectations from within China. After studying in Shanghai and Europe and working at an international organization in New York, where a mentor once urged her to stop working late and “enjoy the New York night,” Jessica returned to China to finish her master’s thesis and enter the domestic job market. There, she met a second, more intimate pressure: the expectation that she should marry and have children. Rather than quietly accepting it, she confronted the idea directly, over dinner with her mother, asking: “Are you actually happy in your own marriage? What has it genuinely brought you?” Iris and Jessica belong to a highly educated cohort of young Chinese women whose lives are unfolding alongside a demographic problem the state is eager to solve. Facing an aging population, a shrinking workforce, and historically low fertility rates, Beijing introduced the Three-Child Policy in 2021 , allowing Chinese couples to have up to three children. China’s government has since increasingly emphasized marriage and childbearing as social priorities . Yet China’s demographic crisis gained steam during the same decades of modernization that gave women access to more education, higher incomes, and greater mobility. That means women like Iris and Jessica have more reasons, and more means, to delay or reconsider marriage and motherhood. Research on China’s education expansion by Jiwei Chen and Jiangying Guo of Nanjing Agricultural University found that increased female education can delay entry into marriage and childbirth and reduce fertility, in part by raising the opportunity costs of childrearing. The modernization that expanded women’s choices has made the traditional sequence of adulthood – marry, have children, settle near family – less inevitable. Jessica confronts this tension directly, pressing her own mother on whether marriage delivered what it promised and treating parenthood as a choice to question rather than a milestone to check off. Iris resists more obliquely: rather than arguing with the assumption that a good daughter eventually settles down close to home, she puts enough distance (first New York, then Hawai‘i) between herself and the people who would enforce the traditional path, letting their expectations fade into background noise instead of demands she has to answer. Neither is rejecting family, marriage, or children outright. Both are refusing to treat any of these options as the default for a Chinese woman. Jessica: Deconstructing the Script Upon returning to China to finish her thesis, Jessica found the job hunt less a search for a career than a reckoning with what kind of life she was willing to accept. In Europe and New York, she’d grown used to a workplace culture defined by what she calls “松弛感”: ease, dignity, being treated first as a person. One night, working late in New York, her mentor stopped her: “You are in New York. You should go enjoy the night.” The line stuck with her. The anecdote formed a sharp contrast with Jessica’s internship at a major Chinese internet company, where a hyper-competitive, results-only culture left people passing their anxiety down the hierarchy. She posted a comparison of the two experiences on Xiaohongshu and it sparked a fight in the comments: some dismissed it as a naive “student mindset”; others agreed with a Chinese woman writing from Europe, who argued that Western employers need their workers enough to treat them decently, while Chinese managers can simply replace anyone who underperforms. For Jessica, the real question was how much room there was for personal choice to override social norms. That questioning carried over from professional pressures straight into marriage. Years abroad had sharpened her sense of independence, but her father still pictured a conventional future for her, and relatives kept the pressure alive by mentioning which of her peers had already married. Jessica pushed back on the premise itself, arguing that a mother-daughter bond can matter as much as a marital one. She half-jokingly tells relatives that if marriage is unavoidable, it’s better to get in and out of it quickly than drag out something broken. The same skepticism shapes how she thinks about children. She’s fond of them but treats parenthood as a serious undertaking that shouldn’t simply follow marriage on a fixed timeline. She has watched enough families to conclude that unhappy marriages, and kids who are under-supported despite material comfort, are more common than the success stories that get celebrated. Teenagers hit adolescence with mental health struggles, some withdrawing from school, often because parents were too consumed by work to be present. Jessica has also watched women of her mother’s generation absorb the burden of family life, reshaping careers around husbands and children. She has no intention of doing the same by default. That came to a head at a family dinner, when marriage came up again and Jessica turned the question back on her mother: was she actually happy in her marriage? What had it given her? It was an invitation to examine whether women’s sacrifices for family are as inevitable as they’re made to seem. “If my pain can never be carried by anyone else,” Jessica told The Diplomat, “then my happiness has to be mine to build, too.” She’s stopped ruling out partners by age, and increasingly by nationality; a good match is rare enough without narrowing the field further. Her mother has softened too, no longer pressing on timelines. None of this makes her anti-marriage or anti-motherhood. But Jessica insists on the right to decide what place they hold in her life, rather than letting either define her adulthood before she’s had the chance to define it herself. Iris: Exiting the Room Growing up in Zhejiang, Iris Liu’s school breaks were a rotation of enrichment classes: Olympiad math, swimming, roller skating, dance, painting, piano. As an only child, she absorbed her mother’s conviction that giving her every possible advantage was simply what good parenting looked like. Before Iris had even reached middle school, her mother was already telling her she needed to learn to swim: American Ivy League universities, she’d heard, liked students who could swim. The plan was always aimed outward, toward a future far from home. Years later, Iris would indeed leave China. She just wouldn’t use that mobility the way her mother had imagined. The first crack came early, almost by accident. A two-week middle-school trip to Los Angeles was supposed to preview the life her mother was preparing her for. Instead, Iris came home unimpressed: a suburban campus, cafeteria pizza, none of the excitement she’d expected. Her disappointment rippled into her mother’s plans: the pressure around swimming eased, and the push toward an international high-school track quietly faded. Still, the broader trajectory held. Iris went on to NYU, and after graduation had the kind of options her education was supposed to produce: interviews for corporate jobs with six-figure salaries. She did not end up in any of these. She chose instead a job in Hawai‘i. Her parents had a particular idea of success. When Iris told them about interviews with major firms with salaries over $100,000 a year, they barely reacted. Her father countered instead with a story about a colleague’s child who’d quit an investment-banking job after three years, burned out. It was mea
title: China’s Young Women Are Rewriting the Rules of Adulthood

body: A Taliban checkpoint in Balkh province, Afghanistan. Credit: Agnieszka Pikulicka Subscribe for ads-free reading In the female section of an upscale restaurant in Kabul’s Shar-e Naw, a waiter brings me a menu and a form. Only two lines are filled in: one bears an Italian name, the other a local one. The waiter explains that guests are required to fill it in at the request of the Ministry of Interior. It is for the guests’ own safety, he emphasizes, slightly uneasy. It is hard to tell if he believes it. I look at the form. It asks for the guest’s name, date of birth, passport number, address in Kabul, as well as when they visited the restaurant. “It is for your security,” the waiter repeats. I give him the blank form back. “I feel secure without it,” I say. He doesn’t insist. He takes my order and disappears. Five years after the withdrawal of NATO troops from Afghanistan, and into the rule of the Taliban, the group’s control over the country is stable. While the Taliban might not have access to the newest surveillance technologies, their infiltration of local communities is high. They had learned their lesson from their first period of rule, the emirate that ended in 2001 with the U.S. invasion, a United Nations official tells me. “You can say that fundamentally, ideologically, they haven’t really changed. But in terms of control, consolidation, management, messaging, they are far more sophisticated now,” he says. “The first emirate was a brand new experiment. The second emirate is still an experiment, but they have learned a lot of lessons. They are smart.” Kabul still reminds me of its former self, as if time had stopped. The streets are bustling with life; street vendors cover the pavements, selling products ranging from food and cigarettes to clothes and electronics. The new regime is seen in the details: fewer women walk the streets, less rubbish lies scattered across the city center – a lasting feature of the corrupt rule back in the Republic days – and the streets seem less chaotic. But at first glance, the changes are small, sometimes imperceptible. A Taliban checkpoint in Balkh province, Afghanistan. Photo by Agnieszka Pikulicka. Everyone I speak with says that the country has become safer. Twenty years of war and decades of fighting have taken their toll on people. The Taliban, while brutal and devoted to anti-modern ideas, has nevertheless brought peace. The paradox is that the Taliban were the main perpetrators of violence during the Republic days. It was due to their attacks on cars that traveling between provinces used to be dangerous and caution was advised. Since they took power, traveling between different regions of Afghanistan has suddenly become possible. Now, Taliban checkpoints cover the whole country. Some of them are stricter, with soldiers standing under the white flag bearing the Shahada, the Islamic declaration of faith, and the Taliban symbol, checking travel permits meticulously. Other checkpoints are more relaxed, and it is enough to slow down and let the Taliban gaze into the car. There are few roads that the group does not control. To leave their place of residence, drivers need special permits, and so do tourists. A letter from “Afghan Tour,” a unit responsible for travelers, is required to travel and stay in another province. It is unclear what its purpose is, other than surveillance. In Kabul, the “Afghan Tour” official says that getting a travel letter requires paying for an expensive tour. But it is possible to get it in Bamyan, another province, for a small fee. Most other regions also issue such letters in exchange for booking an inexpensive “tour” with an official guide. It is unclear if its price is official or simply a bribe paid for obtaining the letter. It is also hard to call it a tour. As part of the “tour” I book to stay in Mazar-i-Sharif, the local guide shows me into the Blue Mosque, the shrine of Imam Ali, first built in the 12th century before Genghis Khan leveled the original building to the ground. But the tour included little in terms of a history lesson. The guide complained about his low earnings, suggesting I pay extra for his time. Then he demanded that I share my local contacts with him. For my own safety, of course. Today the new Taliban administration is stable. Ministries work, and courts solve disputes without the need to pay bribes, I am told. 96 percent of the poppy fields have been eradicated and hundreds of addicts who formerly squatted on Kabul’s streets and under bridges have been forced into rehabs. This is the kind of “stability” I know all too well from Central Asia’s autocracies, Afghanistan’s neighbors: they are brutal and relentless, but the pavements are clean. According to a recent report from Human Rights Watch , censorship of local media outlets and restrictions on freedom of expression have intensified, while journalists, activists, academics and other regime critics have faced repression, torture, and arbitrary arrests. “The Taliban always accuse us of being spies, it’s hard to work these days,” one local photojournalist told me. The Blue Mosque, the shrine of Imam Ali, in Mazar-i-Sharif. Photo by Agnieszka Pikulicka. Women have been denied basic rights, such as the right to education beyond sixth grade. A woman visiting her parental home who does not return to her husband can be deemed a criminal. That includes survivors of domestic violence. A woman accused of touching, shaking hands with, or hugging a man who is not her mahram, a close male relative with whom marriage is prohibited, can spend a year in prison. Two months if a girl or a boy is seen dancing. A new “Preachers’ law” defines Muslims as followers of the Hanafi school of Islam. Local Hazaras, or Ismaili minority groups, are now officially deemed heretics. “Many Ismailis now hide their faith,” one man from the community tells me. He lost his job in a school in Badakhshan due to his faith. All that in the name of the “peaceful and clear sky above us,” as Uzbekistan’s late President Islam Karimov used to say in justifying his own repressive rule. Except that this is not the reality for most Afghans. While the war might be over – except for skirmishes in Badakhshan province and regular attacks from Pakistan – Afghanistan is hardly facing a post-war recovery. The withdrawal of U.S. and NATO troops and the coming to power of the Taliban, a government recognized only by Russia, meant that the United Nations mandate became much more restricted in scope. Cooperation with the de facto Taliban authorities has focused mostly on securing people’s very basic needs. Most international non-governmental and governmental organizations, and media, have left, and with them hundreds of local jobs disappeared. The biggest difference is noticeable in large cities: Kabul, Herat, or Mazar-i-Sharif, where previously educated, English-speaking men and women could find employment and develop careers. As another local journalist told me, during the Republic days he could support his family working as a photographer and videographer. Now, work is scarce. He has not had any projects for several months. “The situation seems to get worse every day and every year. Unemployment has reached a very high level, especially for people like me who work in the arts and creative fields,” he says. “People of Afghanistan are facing many other serious problems, including unemployment, untreated illnesses, hunger, poverty, and lack of adequate shelter. I do not see a clear government plan to address unemployment at its roots.” According to the United Nations , more than 17 million people, or 40 per cent of Afghanistan’s population, are projected to face acute food insecurity. And the situation is worsening. While following the U.S. withdrawal, thousands of Afghans left the country in search of a better life, this trend is now reversing – though not voluntarily. Over the last few years, Iran and Pakistan have forced millions of Afghans to return home. Ev

body: By Ali Abu Issam Independent researcher specialising in Russian and Central Asian affairs. Published On 29 Sep 2026 29 Sep 2026 Listen (8 mins) Save Share Can Tajikistan’s economic boom survive its debt gamble? on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google The World Bank approved a further $300m grant for the Rogun hydropower plant, the government’s flagship project, on June 30 [File: Al Jazeera] Tajikistan’s gross domestic product grew by 8.2 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, while fixed-capital investment rose by 18.4 percent. On June 30, the World Bank approved a further $300m grant for the Rogun hydropower plant, the government’s flagship project. Rapid growth and fresh multilateral support appear to validate years of state-led investment. They also sharpen the central question: is the boom generating enough export income to meet future obligations, or does it still depend on migrant earnings and public spending? The warning is that Tajikistan’s strong growth masks significant external and fiscal vulnerabilities. The glittering investment and growth figures mask a fragile construct: an economy dependent on remittances, a narrow export base and politicised state corporations is piling up debt that is becoming ever harder to service. The World Bank still classifies Tajikistan at high risk of debt distress . That does not mean default is imminent, but it leaves little room for a financing mistake or external shock. Growth with a narrow base The headline investment figure needs careful reading. Fixed-capital investment measures spending on buildings, machinery and infrastructure; it does not show foreign investors moving into Tajikistan in search of high returns. The World Bank says foreign direct investment weakened in 2025 even as growth reached 8.4 percent. The main source of foreign currency is clear. Remittances amounted to about 46 percent of GDP in 2025 , according to the World Bank, which says they were the principal driver of growth. Aluminium and other exports matter, but TALCO’s strategic weight does not make it the country’s main source of hard currency. The economy’s principal external income still comes from workers abroad. Advertisement The share of the population living below the World Bank’s $4.20-a-day poverty line fell from 55 percent in 2010 to about 14.8 percent in 2025 . Foreign-exchange reserves reached $5.6bn, more than eight months of imports. These gains make the economy more resilient than a simple crisis narrative suggests. Yet the same data reveal weaknesses. The trade deficit widened to 35 percent of GDP in 2025, domestic production remains limited, and household consumption relies heavily on income earned abroad. A slowdown in Russia or tighter migration rules could therefore weaken domestic demand and the balance of payments simultaneously. The case for Rogun Rogun’s long delays do not erase the economic case for completing it. The World Bank expects the plant to generate 14,400 gigawatt-hours a year , roughly 60 percent of Tajikistan’s present electricity generation. A substantial share of its low-cost output is intended for domestic demand, which could reduce chronic winter shortages, while the remainder could be exported to countries including Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The bank also estimates that the project could create more than 30,000 direct and indirect jobs. The financing structure has improved. The latest $300m International Development Association grant brings total World Bank financing for Rogun to $650m . Other multilateral and bilateral partners are involved, and the government has pledged part of future revenue to social programmes. Grant and concessional financing reduce pressure on the budget. But international backing is not a blank cheque. The World Bank itself says Rogun’s scale exceeds what Tajikistan can finance alone and that partner support is necessary to prevent the project from absorbing too much of the budget. Its expected export earnings depend on completion, transmission links, reliable regional purchase agreements and transparent operation. Until those pieces are in place, projected revenue cannot be treated as cash already available for debt service. The risk lies beyond sovereign debt Tajikistan is not carrying an unusually high sovereign debt ratio. Public debt continued to fall through 2025 and into 2026, while foreign-exchange reserves continued to provide a substantial buffer. The IMF assessed the debt as sustainable . The high-risk classification arises mainly from heavy external repayments relative to export earnings in 2025-27. The immediate vulnerability is therefore the repayment schedule and the narrow export base, rather than the headline debt stock alone. Advertisement But the headline ratio omits a material part of the public-sector exposure. The IMF’s baseline does not include non-guaranteed debt of state-owned companies because information on those liabilities is incomplete. In a tailored stress test, it adds potential liabilities equal to 11.7 percent of GDP. These include arrears at Barqi Tojik estimated at 8.2 percent of GDP and TALCO’s external debt at 2 percent. TALCO is also facing continuing attempts to enforce an arbitral award now worth more than $300m. The company has sought substantial new investment, yet its unresolved liabilities complicate efforts to attract fresh financing. Arbitration suits against TALCO inevitably heighten compliance risks and due-diligence requirements for any prospective financiers. When payments flow through intersecting banks and jurisdictions, legal risks in one segment of assets do not remain contained. The dispute has also moved into cross-border enforcement proceedings, with creditors seeking information about assets and transactions in several jurisdictions. Moreover, TALCO deserves particular attention because its financial problems feed directly into another state company. The IMF says most of the aluminium producer’s arrears are owed to Barqi Tojik. Weak payment discipline at TALCO therefore adds to the power utility’s losses, while a guarantee, recapitalisation or assumption of either company’s debts could shift the burden to the budget. The stress test is not a forecast that the state will assume every obligation, but it shows why a low sovereign-debt ratio understates the broader fiscal risk. A new financing agreement illustrates both sides of the argument. In August, the Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development signed a $200m budget-support loan with a 20-year term, a 10-year grace period and a 1 percent interest rate. Those are highly concessional terms and show that substantial official financing remains available to support the government’s reform programme. The fund also said the loan was needed in part because Eurobond repayments were putting pressure on the budget. A test of reform The policy choice is not between abandoning Rogun and borrowing without restraint. Tajikistan can use grants and long-maturity concessional finance for the dam while limiting non-concessional debt, publishing audited accounts for major state firms, and disclosing guarantees and arrears. Independent reporting on Rogun’s costs, procurement, safety, resettlement and power-sale agreements would allow creditors and citizens to judge whether future revenue assumptions remain credible. The government also needs growth that generates domestic jobs and exports outside the state sector. That requires stronger competition, more reliable rules for private investors and a financial system that can channel part of the country’s remittance income into productive businesses rather than consumption and imports. The data support a sober conclusion. Growth is real, and sovereign collapse is not imminent. Lower poverty, sizeable reserves and concessional support have bought the country time. The boom will last only if Dushanbe broadens the economy and makes the debts of TALCO and other state companies visible. Rogun can support that t
title: Can Tajikistan’s economic boom survive its debt gamble?
