body: Press release Genuine competition in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s elections in fragmented political environment and with difficulties in electoral administration, international observers say Date: 5 October 2026 Place: SARAJEVO Source: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights SARAJEVO, 5 October 2026 – There was genuine competition in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 4 October general elections and contestants were largely able to reach voters. The political landscape is deeply fragmented, characterised by conflicting narratives still rooted in wartime divisions, the international election observers said in a statement of preliminary findings and conclusions today. The first-time countrywide use of information and communication technologies (ICT) was introduced to address longstanding electoral integrity concerns, although delays and shortfalls limited transparency in the implementation stage, the statement says. The election administration made considerable efforts, but persistent institutional and operational constraints, combined with its increased responsibilities, affected the efficiency and timeliness of its work, the observers said. Suffrage rights continue to be subject to discriminatory restrictions based on ethnicity and residence. Some broad legal provisions unduly restricted political discourse in the pre-election period. “Yesterday marked an important milestone for elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with new voting technologies used country-wide for the first time. This achievement was made possible in part thanks to the sustained efforts of the Central Election Commission, and to all those who participated in and contributed to this process,” said Luis Graça, Special Co-ordinator and Leader of the OSCE short-term observer mission. “We encourage the newly elected leadership and legislators to build on this progress, advance further electoral reforms, and continue strengthening democratic institutions and processes in Bosnia and Herzegovina.” “More than three decades after the Dayton Peace Agreement, the stability of Bosnia and Herzegovina remains important for the security of the entire Western Balkans and the wider Euro-Atlantic area," said Sverre Myrli, Head of the NATO PA observer delegation. “The NATO Parliamentary Assembly is pleased to contribute to international efforts to support election monitoring and strengthen democratic governance. Strong democratic institutions, respect for the rule of law, and political dialogue are fundamental elements of that stability, which we will continue to support jointly with the rest of the international community.” The election-related laws and regulations overall provide an adequate basis for holding democratic elections and recent amendments strengthened safeguards. Still, important ODIHR and Venice Commission recommendations remain unaddressed, including on ethnicity- and residency-based restrictions on suffrage rights, misuse of public resources, election dispute resolution, campaign finance oversight and dissuasive sanctions. The technical preparations were marked by significant challenges, including notable delays in the receipt of the ICT devices, difficulties in forming polling station committees and recruiting technical operators, as well as late and insufficient training of election commissioners and voter education on the new voting methods and the new ballot. The 2024 legal amendments provide for countrywide use of electoral ICT. The introduction of ICT was made in response to previous concerns of voter impersonation and fraudulent counting. The law lacks sufficient provisions for effective implementation, and the deployment of ICT devices was carried out hastily, with limited time for testing, voter education, and training of election officials. “Election day unfolded in a generally calm and peaceful atmosphere, both inside polling stations and in their surroundings. Our observers were able to follow the process without impediment and were welcomed by election officials across the country,” said Allessia Claes, Head of the OSCE PA observer delegation. “This is encouraging, but our observation also identified shortcomings that should be addressed. We encourage the authorities and all relevant stakeholders to draw on these findings and continue working to strengthen the electoral process ahead of future elections.” Election day proceeded in an orderly manner, but a number of technical difficulties and issues with the complex voting process were observed. Polling officials generally managed the use of the devices adequately, but the process was assessed negatively in a significant number of polling stations observed. Negative observations were mainly attributed to serious shortcomings in ensuring secrecy of the vote and technical issues with the new devices. In one-fifth of the polling stations observed for the count, there were significant procedural omissions, indicating polling officials had a limited understanding of the complex procedures and made attempts to find practical shortcuts. There were only minor discrepancies between the manual and electronic counts in polling stations observed. Fundamental freedoms were respected, although the broad application of the ban on early campaigning resulted in numerous political actors being sanctioned, affecting political discourse. In the absence of sufficient regulation against the misuse of public resources, entity, cantonal and municipal authorities increased salaries and pensions, and provided social benefits and one-time payments to entice voters, undermining the equality of opportunity for contestants. “The introduction of new technologies strengthened the integrity of the vote,” said Davor Ivo Stier, Head of the EP observer delegation. “On the country’s EU path, further reform of electoral legislation is needed to address the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights and the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.” “Democracy begins with a simple principle: Every citizen matters and every vote counts,” said Jone Blikra, Head of the PACE observer delegation. “Free and fair elections must guarantee that people can make their choice freely, that all votes are treated equally, and that the will of the voters is respected. These are fundamental values of the Council of Europe.” In an overall inclusive process, the CEC registered 7,028 candidates, including 2,977 women. Despite uniform compliance with the 40 per cent gender quota for candidate lists, women headed only about 14 per cent of lists for state and entity legislatures and concerns about their nomination as mere placeholders persisted. Recent amendments requiring parties to promote gender equality during campaigning did not result in a tangible increase in the visibility of women candidates in these elections. Campaign regulations are also applicable online, but institutional frameworks for addressing issues in the online environment are insufficient. ODIHR’s social media monitoring identified a polarized online environment, shaped by anonymous media websites and social network accounts, clickbait networks and AI-generated content, which often included misleading information, divisive and inflammatory rhetoric. The absence of safeguards to protect the online information environment, coupled with the lack of obligations on big tech companies to mitigate risks, leaves voters more vulnerable to manipulative information. “ODIHR has been present in Bosnia and Herzegovina for six weeks, and in this time, we have seen how the divisions in the country are reflected in campaign rhetoric, in the information available to voters both online and in traditional media, and in the election administration. This has continued to impact the level of trust in the election process,” said Tana de Zulueta, Head of the ODIHR election observation mission. “The introduction of new technologies could contribute to building this trust, but the process needs to be more transparent, and vo
title: Genuine competition in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s elections in fragmented political environment and with difficulties in electoral administration, international observers say

body: Press release Warsaw Human Dimension Conference opens with call to turn human rights commitments into action Date: 5 October 2026 Place: WARSAW Source: OSCE Chairpersonship , OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights WARSAW, 5 October 2026 – More than 1,800 participants from across the OSCE region are taking part in the 2026 Warsaw Human Dimension Conference (WHDC), the largest annual human rights conference in Europe, which opened today. Organized by the Swiss OSCE Chairpersonship with the support of the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), the conference provides a platform for participating States, OSCE institutions and structures, national human rights institutions and civil society to take stock of the implementation of OSCE human dimension commitments and discuss developments affecting democracy, human rights and the rule of law across the OSCE region. “This conference is about two things: holding ourselves to the commitments that we have made and keeping alive a space for dialogue among all participating States, especially when dialogue has become difficult”, recalled OSCE Chairman-in-Office, Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis. “As OSCE Chair this year, we want to turn existing commitments into concrete actions”. At a time when civic space is under growing pressure, participants will discuss how to strengthen implementation of OSCE human dimension commitments across a broad range of issues, including judicial independence, media freedom, democratic elections, national minorities, gender equality, freedom of assembly and association, torture prevention, and tolerance and non-discrimination. “In today’s volatile security environment, the foundation we built together over decades on human rights and democratic principles matters more than ever. It is at the heart of the OSCE's comprehensive approach to security. Advancing peace and security in our region depends on us preserving it - and doing so is our shared responsibility,” said OSCE Secretary General Feridun H. Sinirlioğlu in his opening remarks. “The Warsaw Human Dimension Conference provides a unique space for participating States, civil society and international partners to come together and discuss openly the implementation of our Human Dimension commitments. The value of these discussions goes beyond these two weeks: the dialogue and exchange taking place here are essential to keeping our shared commitments alive and turning them into action throughout the year,” said ODIHR Director, Maria Telalian. Among the high-level speakers at the conference's opening session was also the Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Radoslaw Sikorski. At the margins of the conference, the Swiss Chairpersonship will present its Roadmap on the Prevention and Eradication of Torture, a practical tool to strengthen the implementation of existing commitments. In his opening remarks, State Secretary of the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs Alexandre Fasel said: “Torture prevention has long been a priority of Switzerland and was already a focus of our 2014 Chairpersonship. This year, we want to build on that foundation. The Roadmap on the Prevention and Eradication of Torture helps participating States translate existing international obligations and OSCE commitments into practice”. The Swiss Chairpersonship has also introduced new elements to the conference format, including dedicated roundtables with OSCE institutions and field operations. Around 90 side events will complement the ten plenary sessions, allowing for more in-depth exchanges on thematic and country-specific contexts. With more than half of registered participants representing civil society, the conference also provides a vital space for human rights defenders, journalists and civil society organizations to bring their concerns and experience directly into dialogue with participating States. The conference will continue until 15 October, providing opportunities for participants to exchange views and experiences on the implementation of human rights and fundamental freedoms across the OSCE region. body: Media advisory OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media to pay an official visit to Kyrgyzstan and convene the Central Asia Media Conference in Bishkek Date: 5 October 2026 Place: VIENNA Source: OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media VIENNA, 5 October 2026- On 9 and10 October, the Office of the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media, in collaboration with OSCE field operations from the region, will hold the Central Asia Media Conference, "Building Shared Reality: Information Integrity, Media Ethics and Trust in the Digital Age", at Novotel Bishkek City Center, starting at 9:30. Key themes of the conference include: Fostering trusted information landscapes Implementing the RFoM Policy Manual on Media Freedom in the Age of Big Tech Platforms and AI in Central Asia Information integrity in Central Asia Digital security for journalists Strengthening journalist protections through a gender-sensitive approach Journalism education and professional standards Newsroom policies on the use of artificial intelligence Journalists are invited to cover the conference. More information is available at: https://rfom.osce.org/event/667392 In addition, on 9 and10 October, the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media, Ambassador Jan Braathu, will pay his first official visit to Kyrgyzstan. During his visit, he will meet with high-level officials, as well as representatives of civil society and various media stakeholders in the country. body: News News Item OSCE Mission to BiH: Supporting continued progress in electoral reform Issued on: 6 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina SARAJEVO, 06 October 2026 – The OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina (Mission) welcomes the preliminary findings and conclusions of the International Election Observation Mission , which provide a comprehensive assessment of the 4 October General Elections and highlight areas for further attention and improvement. For the first time, voters across Bosnia and Herzegovina cast their ballots with new election technologies in place countrywide. Their introduction represented a significant undertaking and an important new element of the electoral process. The OSCE Mission to BiH has been a committed partner throughout this process. Working closely with the BiH Central Election Commission (CEC) and other partners, the Mission supported the CEC in preparations for the introduction of the new technologies and helped inform voters about what to expect on Election Day. Introducing these technologies across the country required considerable preparation and effort. The Mission recognizes the work undertaken by the CEC in this regard. We also recognize the important contribution of the “Pod lupom” coalition and its citizen observers, whose work across the country helped provide independent oversight of the electoral process and contributed to greater transparency and public confidence. The electoral process is ongoing, and the ODIHR Election Observation Mission continues its work. Its final assessment and recommendations will provide an important basis for considering further improvements to the electoral process. The Mission will remain a strong partner in advancing electoral reform and supporting a process that puts integrity at its core – one in which every vote is protected and every voice counts. And in doing so it will continue working with the authorities, civil society and other partners to address identified challenges and strengthen the electoral process. Ultimately, elections belong to citizens. We commend everyone who went to the polls, made their choice and exercised their democratic right to help shape their own future and that of their country. Their participation is what gives democracy its strength. We also congratulate all those entrusted by citizens to represent them over the next four years. We wish them every success in fulfilling that responsibility and look forward to the timely formation and effective functioning of institutions at all levels, working effectively in the interests of all citizens.
title: OSCE Mission to BiH: Supporting continued progress in electoral reform

body: Enhancing youth crime and drug use prevention through education on legality and awareness campaigns addressing threats of organized crime and corruption Project Update OSCE side event highlights whole-of-society approaches to preventing youth recruitment into organized crime Issued on: 29 September 2026 Issued by: Transnational Threats Department , Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities Fields of work: Policing , Youth On 29 September 2026, the OSCE Transnational Threats Department (TNTD) and the Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities (OCEEA) hosted a side event on the margins of the UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, bringing together 40 participants to discuss emerging trends in the recruitment of children and young people into organized crime and effective approaches to prevention. The event was organized in co-operation with the Permanent Missions of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the OSCE, UN and other international organizations in Vienna, Germany, Kyrgyzstan and Switzerland. Across the OSCE area, organized crime groups are increasingly targeting young people for recruitment. They are exploited to transport and sell drugs, and even to commit violent offences. Policymakers, practitioners and young people participating in the side event discussed recruitment trends and risk factors, including the growing role of social media. Preliminary findings of the new OSCE study The use of social media for youth recruitment into organized crime show that online recruitment is increasingly strategic and targeted, with criminal networks using youth-tailored language, gamification and peer-to-peer approaches to identify and engage vulnerable young people. “It takes joint action by law enforcement, social and educational services, and civil society, identifying at-risk youth early and offering credible alternatives before criminal networks reach them,” said Bernardo Stadelmann, Vice-Director of the Federal Office of Justice and Head of the Criminal Law Division at the Federal Department of Justice and Police of Switzerland. Participants exchanged views on how to address these emerging challenges and shared good practices for prevention. They highlighted the importance of fostering trust and co-operation among law enforcement, education and social services, civil society, and young people themselves to address root causes of recruitment. Discussions further explored how technology and social media can be used to support prevention and awareness-raising efforts. “When it comes to prevention, children and young people should not only be seen as beneficiaries of prevention efforts; their experiences and perspectives can help us design measures that actually reach those at risk,” stated Rüdiger Bohn, Permanent Representative of Germany to the United Nations in Vienna, Chair of the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in his opening remarks. “The OSCE is proud to support participating States in strengthening early identification of youth at risk of recruitment and enhancing interagency co-operation. As social media becomes an increasingly important recruitment channel, we look forward to publishing new research to help policymakers better understand evolving threats and design effective prevention responses,” said Alena Kupchyna, Co-ordinator of Activities to Address Transnational Threats in her closing remarks. The event drew on lessons learnt from the OSCE extrabudgetary project “Enhancing youth crime and drug use prevention through education on legality and awareness campaigns addressing threats of organized crime and corruption” , jointly implemented by the OSCE TNTD and OCEEA. Contacts Transnational Threats Department, OSCE Secretariat OSCE Secretariat, Transnational Threats Department Wallnerstrasse 6 1010 Vienna Austria Email: tntd@osce.org
title: OSCE side event highlights whole-of-society approaches to preventing youth recruitment into organized crime

body: News News Item OSCE calls for respect for freedom of peaceful assembly and expression Issued on: 29 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina Fields of work: Human rights , Rule of law SARAJEVO, 28 September 2026 - The OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina (Mission) is concerned by recent reports of local police measures taken against members of Serbia's "Student List – Students Win" during campaign-related activities in several cities in Bosnia and Herzegovina in recent days that appear to have limited the Student List participants freedom of speech and freedom of peaceful assembly. Freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of expression are fundamental human rights. As recognized in the OSCE commitments and international human rights standards, authorities should facilitate and protect peaceful assemblies, wherever possible, and address any safety or public order concerns through measures that are proportionate to the identified risks, represent the least restrictive means available, and that are necessary in a democratic society. The enjoyment of the rights to freedom of assembly and expression extend to all persons under the jurisdiction of the State, irrespective of nationality or citizenship status. The Mission calls on all authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to respect and apply the aforementioned commitments and standards when it comes to peaceful assemblies. Any and all actions taken in this regard must remain proportionate in a democratic society. Any possible reported attacks against those who organize or participate in peaceful assemblies must be swiftly investigated and those found responsible brought to account through appropriate legal proceedings. The Mission will continue to closely monitor developments.
title: OSCE calls for respect for freedom of peaceful assembly and expression

body: News News Item OSCE and Council of Europe convene the Annual Meeting of National Anti-Trafficking Co-ordinators and Rapporteurs Issued on: 28 September 2026 Issued by: Office of the Special Representative and Co-ordinator for Combating Trafficking in Human Beings National Anti-Trafficking Co-ordinators and Rapporteurs from across the OSCE and Council of Europe regions gather in Vienna today and tomorrow for their 10th annual meeting, with representatives from 60 countries. This is the 9 th such meeting jointly organized by the Council of Europe and the OSCE. Building on the OSCE political commitments and the Council of Europe's Convention on Action against Trafficking in Human Beings, this joint meeting creates a unique platform to identify synergies and mutually reinforce efforts in combating human trafficking, translating shared standards into concrete action, and ensuring that victims and survivors receive consistent protection and support across all participating and member States. At a time when traffickers are adapting and using technology at increasing speed, the need for co-ordinated action has never been greater: "Ten years of this annual meeting represent ten years of collective resolve. Human trafficking remains a persistent crime that thrives on silence and impunity. This meeting is a testament to our shared determination to ensure that every victim is seen, every survivor supported, and every trafficker held to account," said Kari Johnstone, OSCE Special Representative and Co-ordinator for Combating Trafficking in Human Beings. “Multi-stakeholder collaboration is essential for the success of our efforts to combat human trafficking. This year’s meeting brings around the table two groups of actors that can play an important role in the fight against human trafficking: local and regional authorities, and penitentiary services,” noted Petya Nestorova, Executive Secretary of the Council of Europe Anti-Trafficking Convention. The two-day meeting features three thematic sessions: Integrating anti-trafficking responses into broader organized crime strategies; Enhancing the role of municipalities and regions in prevention and victim referral; Improving victim identification in detention settings and applying the non-punishment principle. A dedicated working group is exploring how local and regional authorities can improve victim identification and referral, strengthen multi-agency partnerships, and ensure equitable access to protection and assistance across regions.
title: OSCE and Council of Europe convene the Annual Meeting of National Anti-Trafficking Co-ordinators and Rapporteurs

body: Enhancing youth crime and drug use prevention through education on legality and awareness campaigns addressing threats of organized crime and corruption Project Update OSCE side event explores gender-sensitive approaches to preventing women’s involvement in organized crime Issued on: 26 September 2026 Issued by: Transnational Threats Department , Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities Fields of work: Policing , Youth On 26 September 2026, the OSCE Transnational Threats Department hosted a side event on the margins of the United Nations Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, bringing together 30 participants to discuss women’s involvement in organized crime and inclusive approaches to prevention, exit and witness protection. The event was organized in co-operation with the Permanent Missions of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the OSCE, UN and other international organizations in Vienna, France and Sweden. Traditionally, organized crime has been viewed as a predominantly male phenomenon, with women often recognized primarily as victims. However, OSCE research highlights a more complex reality. The OSCE assessment Understanding the role of women in organized crime draws on data from 14 participating States across North America, Europe and Asia and shows that women and girls are active participants in organized crime groups, involved across criminal markets and at different levels of the criminal hierarchy. Participants of the side event discussed how women and girls are recruited into organized crime, including through social media, and the roles they play within criminal networks. The discussion also highlighted how persistent gender stereotypes can leave women’s involvement less visible to criminal justice practitioners and result in women falling beneath the radar of prevention, exit and witness protection initiatives. The event also provided an opportunity for participants to exchange experiences and good practices from across the OSCE area and discuss ways to strengthen regional dialogue and co-operation on preventing the recruitment and exploitation of women and girls by organized crime groups. “If we want to be effective in our response to organized crime, we can’t afford to have blind spots. By increasing our knowledge on women’s participation, both our work to prevent and investigate will be sharper”, said Anders Fällgren, Director of the Division for Internal Security at the Ministry of Justice in Sweden. “Today’s side event is crucial to raise awareness on an often-overlooked dimension of organized crime: the active involvement and role of women. It provides a powerful platform to address this knowledge gap and to exchange lessons learned and good practices for women’s inclusion in organized crime prevention and exit initiatives”, stated Danka Savic, Permanent Representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United Nations during her opening remarks. “It is key to recognize women’s agency in organized crime groups. Only by acknowledging their involvement, can we identify, support and include them in prevention, exit and witness protection initiatives”, said Alena Kupchyna, OSCE Co-ordinator of Activities to Address Transnational Threats in her closing remarks. body: News News Item OSCE fosters collaboration among Central Asian specialists through a Regional Explosive Ordnance Disposal course in Tajikistan On 2 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe, in partnership with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Tajikistan, organized a three-week Regional Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) Level 1 course at the Regional Explosive Hazard Training Centre (REHTC) of Tajikistan’s Ministry of Defence in Chorgulteppa, Rudaki District. Issued on: 8 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe Fields of work: Arms control On 2 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe, in partnership with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Tajikistan, organized a three-week Regional Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) Level 1 course at the Regional Explosive Hazard Training Centre (REHTC) of Tajikistan’s Ministry of Defence in Chorgulteppa, Rudaki District. The course, conducted in compliance with the International Mine Action Standards, enhanced the professional skills and knowledge of specialists from the armed forces, law enforcement agencies, security services and humanitarian mine action organizations across Central Asia involved in EOD and humanitarian mine action, A total of 18 specialists from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan improved knowledge on explosive ordnance, safety measures, EOD equipment and protective gear. Participants also learned about reconnaissance, initiation methods and the safe transportation, storage and disposal of explosive ordnance. A participant demonstrates techniques for the controlled destruction of explosive ordnance, Chorgulteppa, Rudaki District, 1 October 2026. In addition to technical EOD training, participants exchanged experience and good practices, discussed practical approaches to EOD operations and established new professional contacts. Colonel Tohir Holmakhmadzoda, Head of the REHTC of Tajikistan’s Ministry of Defence, emphasized: “By clearing explosive ordnance, you are not simply making the land safer; you are paving the way for life, security and a peaceful future.” Speaking at the graduation ceremony, Major General Asozoda Abdulmumin, Director of the State Institution “National Mine Action Centre of Tajikistan”, noted: “The knowledge and skills you have acquired today will strengthen your professional capabilities. They will also contribute to humanitarian mine action and, most importantly, to saving human lives.” Abdugani Vahobov, National Training Officer at the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe, said in his concluding remarks: “Today, we are completing this course, but we are not completing our shared mission. The knowledge you have gained will strengthen your professionalism, our co-operation will build trust, and our joint efforts will contribute to enhancing security in Central Asia.” Participants from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan receive certificates upon completion of the Regional EOD Level 1 course in Chorgulteppa, Rudaki District, 2 October 2026. The OSCE remains committed to strengthening regional co-operation and supporting national capacities to address the risks posed by explosive ordnance across Central Asia. body: News News Item OSCE Youth School equips young people with tools for good governance in Tajikistan From 28 September to 2 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe organized a five-day Youth School on Good Economic and Environmental Governance in Hisor, on the outskirts of Dushanbe, bringing together 20 young people aged 18 to 25 from across Tajikistan. Issued on: 8 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe Fields of work: Good governance From 28 September to 2 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe organized a five-day Youth School on Good Economic and Environmental Governance in Hisor, on the outskirts of Dushanbe, bringing together 20 young people aged 18 to 25 from across Tajikistan. The Youth School was the first joint initiative of five units of the Programme Office’s Economic and Environmental Department, covering good governance and anti-corruption, economic challenges to security, environmental threats to security, water management and energy security, and disaster risk reduction. It explored how good governance principles can be applied to economic, environmental, water, energy, climate and disaster-related challenges. Through interactive sessions, case studies, role-plays and group exercises, participants strengthened their understanding of six principles of good governance: transparency, accountability, participation, the rule of law, integrity and co-ordination. They also discussed civic participation and access to environmental information under the Aarhus Convention, as well as disaster risk reduction. “For me, the Youth School was not only about learning. We exchanged ideas, worked together and made friends with other young people. The opportunity to build a network was one of the most valuable parts of the School,” said Surush Alisherzoda, a participant. Robiya Muhamadieva, another participant, said the format made the learning more engaging: “What I liked most was the way the sessions were conducted. We had different trainers and topics, but instead of just listening to lectures, we spent much of our time debating, working through real-life cases and developing our own projects. This made the information much clearer and easier to remember.” International OSCE expert Raimundas Kalesnykas from Vilnius, Lithuania, highlighted the participants’ enthusiasm: “The School showed how interested young people are in good governance and economic and environmental issues. They were actively involved in the interactive sessions and contributed their ideas. I believe they will be able to put the knowledge and skills they gained here into practice in the future.” On the final day, participants developed youth-led initiatives addressing regional challenges related to the green economy, water and energy, climate change and disaster risk reduction. The School also helped participants build connections and skills for more transparent and sustainable decision-making. Participants celebrate the completion of the Youth School on Good Economic and Environmental Governance with their certificates, Hisor, 2 October 2026. The OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe continues to promote youth engagement and practical learning opportunities that contribute to good governance, sustainable development and environmental security in Tajikistan. body: News News Item OSCE Mission to Montenegro supports capacity-building of Parliamentary Education Centre trainers Issued on: 7 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Montenegro Fields of work: Democratization , Youth From 28 to 30 September, the OSCE Mission to Montenegro supported the professional development of trainers at the Parliament’s Education Centre through a three-day capacity-building training on non-formal education and youth work. The Centre is responsible for developing and delivering educational programmes that bring the Parliament of Montenegro closer to the public, with a particular focus on young people. The training brought together educators who deliver workshops for children and young people, focusing on practical approaches they can use in their everyday work. It was tailored to their needs, identified through interviews assessing their existing competencies and areas for further professional development. Participants explored key concepts and approaches in youth work, including its historical development, different models, ethical principles, and code of conduct. They also examined the methodological specificities of non-formal education, the learning process, the role of trainers as learning facilitators, and group dynamics. Finally, programme also covered quality standards and educator competencies, as well as the role of reflection and evaluation in improving educational activities. Throughout the training session, participants explored practical methods and tools through simulations, experiential learning, and real-life examples, strengthening skills they can directly apply when working with young people. By investing in the professional development of the Centre’s trainers, the training programme contributes to strengthening the quality and effectiveness of its educational programmes. In turn, this will help ensure that children and young people participating in the Centre’s workshops enjoy engaging, meaningful, and high-quality learning experiences. body: Mitigating Climate Change Threats to Critical Energy Infrastructure Story The summer our energy systems hit their limit. What comes next? Date: 1 October 2026 Source: Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities Fields of work: Economic activities , Environmental activities Focus area: Energy security Copied Summer 2026 was the hottest many of us have ever lived through — a season of record temperatures, shrinking rivers, and energy systems pushed to the brink. Across Europe and beyond, extreme heat and drought exposed just how vulnerable critical energy infrastructure has become in a rapidly warming world. In July, water levels on the Danube fell so sharply that long‐submerged WWII wrecks resurfaced near Prahovo, Serbia, preventing regular commercial ship travel. The same low water levels forced Hungary’s Paks nuclear power plant, normally responsible for nearly half of the country’s electricity, to scale back operations because the river could no longer provide sufficient cooling water. Hydropower output across the Alps dropped significantly, with Austria producing only 51% of its usual generation and Switzerland 48%. Serbia’s Djerdap 1 hydropower plant fell to just 20% of capacity. Similar patterns unfolded globally: heatwaves strained grids from California to Jordan, drought reduced reservoir levels across North Africa, and wildfires disrupted transmission lines in multiple regions. These are not isolated incidents, but early signals of a systemic challenge to how billions of people access energy. This reality demands that those responsible for securing our energy future act now, using data, foresight and planning to future‐proof the systems we rely on every day. An unstable energy supply starts with affecting households, but continues with endangering economic stability, environmental safety and national security. When energy systems reach their limits Energy insecurity hits people unevenly. During heatwaves, lower income households struggle to afford cooling, older residents face higher health risks, and families worry about keeping fridges, medical devices, and childcare essentials running during outages. Vulnerable populations are left to endure extreme indoor heat as cooling costs surge. This summer, more than 14,000 people died as a consequence of the heat in Germany – smashing records from previous years. An unstable energy supply starts with affecting households, but continues with endangering economic stability, environmental safety and national security. In a world of interconnected energy systems, disruptions can quickly spill across borders, affecting various markets and grids. The 2026 heatwave is just one example among many of how extreme temperature changes can quickly set off a chain reaction; temperatures that soared above 40°C demanded increased air-conditioning across the board. Drops in river levels decreased hydropower output and limited cooling water for thermal and nuclear plants. Industry slowed down as electricity supply became less stable, and wholesale prices spiked under soaring demand. Emergency protocols needed to be activated across energy infrastructure, underscoring the strain on national security. And the fallout did not stop at borders: cooling‐water constraints in Hungary and Slovakia, for example, meant less available electricity to export and a higher need to import. Supply chains were disrupted across multiple countries, and electricity flow across borders was only possible thanks to regional balancing mechanisms. And while summer’s heat brings its own significant challenges, winters offers little relief. In January 2026, a historic cold snap triggered a gas‐supply crunch across Central Europe, creating a regional energy‐security shock. Households, schools and public facilities struggled with insufficient heating just as prices surged and fuel‐delivery logistics were disrupted by frozen infrastructure and transport delays. What began as a weather event quickly became a multi‐sector crisis, exposing how vulnerable communities and essential services are when our energy systems come under extreme stress. Functioning as an anticipatory risk system, it gives energy decision-makers the ability to look decades ahead and understand how climate trends could reshape the performance, reliability, and security of their energy systems. Preparing for what’s ahead Heatwaves, cold snaps, and severe weather will keep pushing our systems in ways we can’t fully control. But we can reduce how hard those shocks hit us by investing now in stronger grids, diversified energy sources, and smarter planning. Taking action early means our communities, economies, and public services are better protected when the next extreme season arrives. With this in mind, the OSCE built the Energy Security and Risks Platform – an interactive tool that shows where energy systems are most vulnerable to future climate conditions. Functioning as an anticipatory risk system, it gives energy decision-makers the ability to look decades ahead and understand how climate trends could reshape the performance, reliability, and security of their energy systems. The geospatial tool uses a curated sub-set of 60 climate indices to provide high resolution data on future climate risks to existing energy systems, including technologies such as hydropower, solar, wind, thermal, transmission networks and the energy demand side. The platform looks at factors like rising temperatures, changing rainfall, drought, wind patterns, and sunlight, and shows how these changes will affect different types of power plants by the 2050s. It highlights “hotspots” where several problems stack up at once, and where countries may need to have a closer look at their existing infrastructure or rethink long‐term plans. Through the dashboard, decision-makers might be able to answer questions such as “Where will our hydropower systems face drought?” or “Where should we build our next solar panels and wind turbines?” The platform also maps energy‐demand projections. It analyzes how demand is likely to shift under temperature extremes, from increased cooling needs during heatwaves to higher heating requirements during cold spells. A new foundation for energy security Our energy security depends on understanding how the climate will shape the physical limits of our energy systems in the future. To face the challenges that a warming planet is inevitably bringing, we need to be prepared. It will require better planning for grid stability, smarter investment in renewables, strong cross-border co-operation when neighbours face shared risks, and more resilient infrastructure built for the climate of the future. The OSCE’s new platform gives countries the foresight they need to stay ahead of these changes — and to keep the lights on in a warming world. body: 18/09/2026 Press release Iraq en es fr France Death Penalty IZZ ALDIEN ALQASEM / ANADOLU / ANADOLU VIA AFP France must urgently repatriate the 49 French nationals currently imprisoned in Iraq who are facing the death penalty. Their trial is due to begin this Sunday. The French State has the duty to ensure that all its nationals are guaranteed the rights to a defence and a fair trial, and protection from all forms of torture and the death penalty. 18 September 2026 . An estimated 50 French nationals were transferred to Iraq from north-eastern Syria where they had been detained without legal basis for many years. They have been accused of terrorism. Their trial is scheduled to start this Sunday in Baghdad. They all have been tortured and subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment in Syria and Iraq. Under Iraq’s Anti-Terrorism Law No. 13 of 2005, they are all facing the death penalty. Some of the French nationals are young adults who were forcibly taken to Syria by their parents when they were children. After being imprisoned for several years in north-eastern Syria they were transferred to Iraq. They are victims of their parents’ choices and of France’s refusal to repatriate them. France has the duty to protect its citizens, at all times and in all places, and to take reasonable measures to intervene in cases of torture, arbitrary death, and trials that are clearly unfair. The conditions under which 11 French nationals were tried by the Central Criminal Court of Baghdad and sentenced to death in 2019 leave no doubt as to the arbitrary nature of the current proceedings. Human rights institutions, United Nations experts, and human rights organisations have detailed and condemned every element of the flagrant denial of justice that these trials represent. On 13 April 2026, the Commission nationale consultative des droits de l’homme (CNCDH) called for the government to undertake : " the repatriation of all French citizens detained in Iraq who have been sentenced to death or are at risk of being sentenced to death; failing that, should France maintain its principled position, it recommends that authorities use all the means at their disposal to ensure that these individuals are not sentenced to death ". The government turned a deaf ear to the appeal. Beyond France, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) reiterated in its judgment of 2 March 2010, in Al-Saadoon and Mufdhi v. United Kingdom that " the absolute and fundamental nature of the right not to be subjected to the death penalty and the serious and irreversible harm that may be suffered " by those exposed to it. Through interim measures ordered in the cases of Saadoune, Pinner and Aslin v. Russia and Ukraine in June 2022, the ECHR indicated to the Government of Ukraine " to ensure, in so far as it was possible to do so, respect for the rights in the Convention " of the combatants sentenced to death in the " Donetsk People’s Republic ". France finds itself in a comparable situation and is consequently obliged to act to prevent its citizens from being sentenced to death. Firmly committed to the safeguards set out in Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights and to the prohibition of the death penalty as set out in its Protocols 6 and 13, the undersigned organisations solemnly call for French authorities to take all necessary measures to ensure that the fundamental rights of these French citizens are respected. For these victims of terrorism, urgent repatriation is the only means of preventing any irreparable breach of the rights enshrined in the international conventions ratified by France and of ensuring that the truth regarding the abuses committed by the Islamic State is brought to light. body: 14/09/2026 Press release Algeria en es fr APP / NURPHOTO / NURPHOTO VIA AFP After a summer of scorching heat marked by major forest fires in Algeria, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune announced his intention to amend the Criminal Code before 15 September 2026, to allow for the execution of individuals convicted of arson. His statement undermines the separation of powers and is an example of the political instrumentalisation of the death penalty, a form of punishment that is unjust, inhumane, and ineffective. Paris and Algiers, 14 September 2026. The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) stands in solidarity with the victims of the recent fires, their families, and everyone mobilised to help the persons affected. Notwithstanding, the legal response taking shape and advanced by President Abdelmadjid Tebboune is alarming. The gravity of the arson attacks and the resulting loss of life call for a serious, independent, and effective judicial response, but cannot justify the reinstatement of executions, especially when investigations have already led to the arrest of persons in connection with the fires. The Algerian Criminal Code already provides for the death penalty in cases where an act of arson results in the death of persons (article 399). The amendment sought by President Tebboune would expand and make effective immediately the application of the death penalty to arsonists who start forest fires in cases where there has been no loss of life. These changes would expand the use of the death penalty and represent a departure from the moratorium on executions in place since 1993. " The gravity of a crime can never justify the use of the death penalty. Be it for arson or any other offense, the justice system must prosecute, try, and punish the persons responsible, but it cannot respond to death with death. Reintroducing executions in Algeria would represent a step backward of historical proportions and would break with more than 30 years of a de facto moratorium. The Algerian authorities would show true stature not by bringing back the gallows, but by transforming the moratorium into a definitive abolition and an unequivocal affirmation that the right to life depends neither on the nature of the crime nor on political circumstances ", stated Aissa Rahmoune, Secretary General of FIDH and President of the Collectif de sauvegarde de la Ligue algérienne des droits de l’Homme (CS-LADDH) . No executions in Algeria since 1993 Death sentences are regularly handed down, but Algeria has not executed anyone for 33 years. Moreover, in recent years, Algeria has supported resolutions brought before the United Nations General Assembly calling on states to establish a moratorium on executions and ultimately abolish the death penalty. Raising the prospect of reinstating executions or expanding the use of the death penalty represents a major setback for human rights and sends a deeply concerning signal with respect to the country’s international commitments. Combating arson requires independent and rigorous investigations, the establishment of liability based on evidence, respect for the presumption of innocence, and full guarantees for the rights of the defence. Any person being prosecuted has the right to a fair trial before an independent court and must have access to effective legal remedies. As a founding member of the World Coalition Against the Death Penalty and a member of its Steering Committee, the FIDH and its member organization in Algeria, the CS-LADDH, reaffirm their opposition to the death penalty in all circumstances and regardless of the crime committed, its gravity, or the emotions it arouses. The justice system must punish crimes, but it must refrain from killing in the name of victims, society, or the State. body: 05/10/2026 Press release Ireland United Kingdom CHARLES MCQUILLAN / GETTY IMAGES EUROPE / GETTY IMAGES VIA AFP The authorities must balance the rights to peaceful assembly of both Protestant loyal order marchers and counter-protestors while safeguarding the rights of residents to freedom from sectarian harassment. Any restrictions on assemblies must be lawful, necessary and proportionate. With further court proceedings scheduled for Monday, a transparent and rights-based approach is essential to prevent further escalation. Paris–Belfast, 5 October 2026. The dispute over the Orange Order parade along Garvaghy Road in Portadown has re-emerged since the Parades Commission authorised a limited parade along the route for the first time in 28 years. Last week’s unexpected decision was only delivered 42 hours before the parade. A High Court injunction to delay the parade was successful, but was overturned by the Court of Appeal in the early hours of the morning. A few hours later the parade could not proceed as the police rightly decided it would be disproportionate to use force to remove a 1,000 or more counter protestors from the road. In the 1990s the summer Drumcree parading dispute repeatedly threatened to collapse the peace process with soldiers and police forcibly removing protestors to facilitate the parade in 1996 and 1997. Following the establishment of the Parades Commission, and the Drumcree-linked murder of three Catholic children by loyalist paramilitaries in 1998, the parade has been re-routed down a parallel road for 28 years. The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the Committee on the Administration of Justice (CAJ) stress that the authorities have a duty to balance competing rights under the European Convention on Human Rights, including freedom of assembly and the rights of others. In this context there have long been recommendations for the ‘right to freedom from sectarian harassment’ affirmed within the Good Friday Agreement to be expressly incorporated in the parading decisions framework. " Freedom of assembly is a fundamental right for both those who parade and counter protestors. Where necessary in a democratic society it can be proportionately restricted to protect the rights of others, " said Daniel Holder, Vice-President of FIDH and Director of CAJ . " The Parades Commission decision did not properly consider that the Drumcree parade was inevitably going to require balancing two competing rights of assembly, nor is there consideration of the risks of sectarian intimidation. Transparency and a human rights-based approach across all relevant issues are essential for future decisions. " FIDH and CAJ welcome that to date all assemblies have been peaceful and that there has been no use of force by the police. We also raise concerns at the continued discourse of "illegality" being applied to counter-protestors. A notification for 5,000 counter protestors was submitted before the parade and only stood down in light of the original High Court injunction. We also draw attention to ECHR-case law which has held that in certain circumstances rights to hold spontaneous peaceful protests in immediate response to events where the protest would be pointless if delayed may override notification requirements. As the courts consider the case on Monday, the organisations stress that the protection of human rights must remain at the centre of any resolution to the Drumcree dispute. body: 28/09/2026 Statement Singapore en es fr Human Rights Council FIDH On 28 September 2026, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) delivered a statement at the 63rd session of the United Nations (UN) Human Rights Council during the Interactive Dialogue for the adoption of Singapore’s Universal Periodic Review (UPR). The statement expressed criticism of the Singaporean government’s failure to accept key recommendations on the death penalty and freedom of peaceful assembly. Read the statement below. Mister President, We are once again disappointed that the Singaporean government missed an opportunity to address international concerns over the human rights situation in the country and to accept important UPR recommendations. The government has regurgitated its false claim that Singapore’s “outcomes” are largely consistent with the objectives of international human rights treaties. In fact, the government cherry picks only the parts of human rights treaties that fit its own political agenda, while leaving out the parts that are inconvenient. For example, when it comes to the death penalty, the government has repeated its false claim that in Singapore capital punishment is reserved only for the most serious crimes. However, the inclusion of drug trafficking among such crimes is inconsistent with the authoritative interpretation of international human rights law, according to which, while drug trafficking may be a serious crime, it is not one of “the most serious crimes.” The government has stated that it imposes the death penalty “with a heavy heart.” It’s hard to reconcile these words with the reality in Singapore. Since 2025, 36 individuals have been executed in the country – the highest documented number in Southeast Asia over this period. This year alone, 19 have been executed - the highest annual number in more than two decades. When it comes to the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, the government again referred to international human rights law. It said those who exercise such right should respect the rights of others, conveniently omitting the fact that permissible restrictions to this right under international human rights law must be necessary and proportional. This is certainly not the case in Singapore, where peaceful protesters, including human rights defenders, face unnecessary and disproportionate restrictions, including criminal penalties. Just over the past few weeks, 11 people have been charged under the repressive Public Order Act for participating in small, symbolic peaceful gatherings. We call on the government to immediately end the use of the death penalty, bring Singapore’s legal framework into line with international human rights standards, and ratify all core international human rights treaties. Thank you. body: 22/09/2026 Comunicado France en es fa fr Iraq International Justice RICCARDO MILANI / HANS LUCAS / HANS LUCAS VIA AFP Tras la condena de Sabri Essid por genocidio y crímenes de lesa humanidad, el Tribunal Penal de París ha dictado una importante resolución sobre las reclamaciones civiles, al reconocer formalmente el perjuicio que han sufrido las partes civiles y al concederles una indemnización por daños y perjuicios. Lamentablemente, esta reparación económica seguirá siendo muy simbólica. París, 22 de septiembre de 2026. Seis meses después la histórica condena del yihadista francés y antiguo alto cargo del Estado Islámico Sabri Essid (alias Abu Dojanah al-Faransi), el Tribunal Penal de París ha dictado su resolución sobre la responsabilidad civil, y ha otorgado así un reconocimiento judicial a los daños continuados y de múltiples tipos sufridos por las personas sobrevivientes del genocidio contra la población yazidí. El 20 de marzo de 2026, Sabri Essid fue condenado in abstentia a cadena perpetua por genocidio, crímenes de lesa humanidad y complicidad en dichos crímenes, cometidos en Siria entre agosto de 2014 y finales de 2016 contra mujeres, niños y niñas yazidíes. Hasta la fecha, ningún ciudadano francés había sido condenado por genocidio y se trata igualmente de la primera vez que un tribunal francés se pronunciaba sobre las atrocidades cometidas por el Estado Islámico contra la comunidad yazidí. En su resolución sobre la responsabilidad civil, el tribunal reconoció formalmente la magnitud del perjuicio causado por Sabri Essid a las tres mujeres yazidíes y a sus ocho hijos e hijas, en particular el daño por la angustia de muerte inminente, el daño afectivo y el daño moral, y les concedió una indemnización económica. El tribunal también reconoció el perjuicio moral sufrido por las asociaciones yazidíes que se constituyeron como partes civiles –Kinyat, la Fondation Yazidi Libre (FYF) y Yazda—, así como por la Federación Internacional por los Derechos Humanos (FIDH) y la Ligue des droits de l’Homme/droits humains (LDH), y les ha concedido un euro simbólico. Lamentablemente, en la práctica, esta indemnización será en gran medida simbólica. Debido al hecho de que no se ha logrado localizar a Sabri Essid, es imposible que realice el pago a las víctimas de las cantidades que otorgadas. Además, en el marco jurídico francés actual, las víctimas extranjeras de crímenes internacionales cometidos en el extranjero no pueden acogerse a las indemnizaciones que abona la Comisión de Indemnización de las Víctimas de Delitos (CIVI). " Es imposible que haya justicia verdadera sin una reparación efectiva. Aunque esta decisión es sin duda importante, será una resolución meramente simbólica, ya que el derecho francés no permite a las víctimas extranjeras acceder en igualdad de condiciones a los mecanismos de indemnización ni acogerse a las reparaciones económicas concedidas por los tribunales cuando el acusado no está presente o no sea solvente ", declararon las cinco asociaciones que se constituyeron en parte civil. body: Share KEN 001 / 0226 / OBS 012.1 Denial of entry / Obstacles to freedom of expression / Restrictions on freedom of movement /Right to fair trial K enya/Ethiopia 30 September 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), has received new information and requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Kenya . New information: The Observatory has been informed about the denial of entry and the continued arbitrary restriction of the freedom of movement of Mr Brian Kagoro, Zimbabwean human rights defender, constitutional lawyer, and Africa Director of the Open Society Foundations (OSF). On 15 September 2026, Mr Brian Kagoro travelled from South Africa via Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to return to Kenya and attend proceedings concerning his detention and deportation from Kenya in February 2026 . While on board of a Nairobi-bound flight in Addis Ababa, Mr Kagoro was removed from the aircraft by Ethiopian security personnel, questioned and prevented from reboarding. He subsequently returned to South Africa. The circumstances and legal basis for his removal from the aircraft have not been publicly clarified. Mr Kagoro's attempted return took place after the High Court of Kenya at Nairobi had issued a conservatory order on 8 June 2026 providing that he was free to enter Kenya for as long as he complied with the immigration laws and procedures applicable to other nationals of Zimbabwe. The Court further directed the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) to supervise and ensure compliance with the order and to designate an officer to facilitate oversight of Mr Kagoro's admission, entry and movement in Kenya. The order was issued in the context of a constitutional petition challenging Mr Kagoro's detention and deportation from Kenya. Following his removal from the flight, his legal team returned to the High Court to seek clarification and enforcement of the order. The Court subsequently directed Attorney General Dorcas Oduor to explain why Mr Kagoro continued to be denied entry into Kenya despite the existing court order, giving her 14 days to respond. The Observatory recalls that, on 22 February 2026 , Kenyan security authorities denied Mr Brian Kagoro entry into Kenya upon his arrival at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport in Nairobi. Officers from the National Intelligence Service (NIS) arbitrarily held him at the airport for more than 10 hours and questioned him over allegations that he had been involved in financing and coordinating protest activities in Kenya, while denying him access to a lawyer and preventing him from contacting his family or colleagues. Immigration officials subsequently issued a removal order authorising his return to Johannesburg, South Africa, citing Section 54 of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act of 2011, without providing any written explanation of the factual basis. Mr Kagoro rejected the allegations, and no formal charges were brought against him. This removal in Ethiopia by Ethiopian security personal takes place in a context of increased transnational repression in East Africa with cooperation between several governments to attack human rights defenders and civic space. The Observatory also recalls that this case takes place in a context of increased scrutiny by Kenyan authorities of civic actors and alleged foreign involvement in protest movements, particularly following the 2024 nationwide demonstrations against the Finance Bill. The Observatory had also previously raised concern about the deportation of Mr Martin Mavenjina , a senior legal advisor at the Kenya Human Rights Commission (KHRC), from Kenya in July 2025. These developments raise serious concerns regarding the protection of civic space in Kenya and the ability of human rights defenders and civil society actors to operate without interference. The Observatory further recalls that Kenya must comply with its obligations under international and regional human rights law, including the rights to liberty, freedom of movement, freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association, as enshrined in Articles 9, 12, 19, 21 and 22 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), as well as in Articles 9, 10 and 11 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR). Moreover, Article 47 of the Kenyan Constitution guarantees the right to fair administrative action, including the right to written reasons where rights are adversely affected. The Observatory is gravely concerned that Mr Kagoro was prevented from travelling to Kenya despite a High Court order expressly authorising his entry into the country, and that he was removed from a Nairobi-bound flight by Ethiopian security personnel. The Observatory is further concerned by the clear signs of cooperation between Kenyan and Ethiopian authorities to impede Mr Kagoro's freedom of movement and expression, and by the lack of transparency regarding the circumstances and legal basis of his removal from the flight. The Observatory calls on the Kenyan authorities to fully respect the High Court order of 8 June 2026 and to refrain from any further arbitrary measures, including through cooperation with Ethiopian authorities,restricting Mr Kagoro's freedom of movement or preventing him from participating in the judicial proceedings concerning his case. Actions requested: Please write to the authorities of Kenya asking them to: Immediately ensure full compliance with and implementation of the High Court order of 8 June 2026, including by guaranteeing Mr Brian Kagoro's right to enter and move within Kenya in accordance with the terms of the order; Provide an official, transparent and legally reasoned explanation of the circumstances and legal basis for removing Mr Kagoro from the Nairobi-bound flight in Addis Ababa and preventing him from continuing his journey to Kenya; Ensure that Mr Kagoro is able to participate freely and without obstruction in the judicial proceedings concerning his detention and deportation from Kenya; Ensure that all measures taken in relation to Mr Kagoro fully comply with Kenya's obligations under the Constitution, the ICCPR and the ACHPR, including the rights to liberty, freedom of movement, freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association, and the right to fair administrative action; Guarantee in all circumstances that human rights defenders, including foreign nationals engaging in legitimate civic activities, can carry out their work without arbitrary interference, harassment, intimidation, restrictions or reprisals; Please write to the authorities of Ethiopia asking them to: Clarify the circumstances and legal basis for Mr Kagoro's removal from the Nairobi-bound flight in Addis Ababa; Refrain from any measures aimed at harassing, intimidating or otherwise interfering with Mr Kagoro on account of his legitimate human rights activities; Ensure that no cooperation with foreign authorities results in reprisals or restrictions against Mr Kagoro in relation to his human rights activities; Addresses of Kenya: H.E. body: Share TUR 01 / 0926 / OBS 45 Arbitrary detention / Criminalisation Judicial harassment / Restriction to freedom of association 23 September 2026 Turkey The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Turkey . Description of the situation : The Observatory has been informed of a wave of raids and arbitrary detentions targeting LGBTQI+ human rights defenders and their organisations in Turkey, including Kaos GL, Muamma LGBTQI+ Association, Mersin 7 Renk LGBTQI+ Solidarity Association, SPoD, HEVİ LGBTQI+ Association, Lambdaistanbul, LİSTAG, as well as two organisations working with people living with HIV, Pozitif Yaşam and Pozitif-iz. Overall, the operation — launched at midnight on 12 September 2026 — extended across five provinces: Izmir, Aydın, Ankara, Mersin and Istanbul. In addition to LGBTQI+ rights defenders, tens of people, the majority of them LGBTQI+ persons -in particular trans women-, were detained in a mass operation dubbed “My Family is Safe” by the Minister of Justice. From 1 a.m. on 13 September 2026, simultaneous raids were carried out on the homes of 14 elected full and reserve members of the board of directors and supervisory board of Kaos GL, an association based in Ankara, who were taken into custody. Seven of them have since been formally arrested. Kaos GL's premises were also searched. In addition to Kaos GL’s board members, one journalist who once wrote an article for Kaos GL regarding LGBTI+ rights in Georgia was arrested. Association founders were arrested under charges of obscenity under Article 226 of the Turkish Penal Code, and violating Article 32/p of the Law on Associations by “establishing associations for the purpose of carrying out acts whose purpose or subject matter is explicitly prohibited by the Constitution and laws or constitutes a crime”, which carries a prison sentence of 1 to 3 years and a judicial fine. The arrest decisions reportedly cited the individuals' roles within the association, the association's social media posts, and the risk of flight or of tampering with evidence. In the night of 12 to 13 September 2026 in Istanbul, a first wave of operations targeted nightclubs and massage parlours in the Beyoğlu and Şişli districts (Taksim, Cihangir, İstiklal Avenue), followed in the morning by a second wave of raids on association premises. The premises of SPoD and the HEVİ LGBTQI+ Association were entered by police; those of the Pozitif Yaşam Association and the Pozitif-iz Association were entered with the assistance of a locksmith. The premises of Lambdaistanbul, LİSTAG and Kaos GL were also searched, with police reportedly forcing entry into the premises of Lambdaistanbul and LİSTAG. Founding members of SPoD, Lambdaistanbul, HEVİ, LİSTAG, Pozitif-iz and Pozitif Yaşam were also taken into custody. Electronic equipment and digital storage media (phones, computers, tablets, USB drives) were seized at the homes of those targeted, at association premises, and at some workplaces, across several cities. Fifteen of those detained are activists, 14 of whom are founders of these associations. On 16 September 2026, 20 of those brought before the court were arrested — including 10 LGBTQI+ rights defenders — while the rest were released under judicial control. According to the reasoning given for these arrests, the associations' "institutional structure was used as an instrument in carrying out acts/activities directed at children, weakening the essence of the Turkish family structure [and] acting in violation of the purposes outlined in the association's bylaws to encourage, promote, and popularize lesbian, gay, bisexual, transvestite, and transsexuality tendencies through fund-raising and organizing various events”. Association founders were arrested under charges of violating Article 32/p of the Law on Associations. On 13 September 2026 in Mersin, 34 people were detained; 26 were arrested and eight released under judicial control. Six of those arrested are office-holders of the Muamma LGBTQI+ Association and the Mersin 7 Renk LGBTQI+ Solidarity Association, among them one lawyer, who were arrested under charges of violating Article 32/p of the Law on Associations. On 13 September 2026 in İzmir, 20 people were detained; 18 were subsequently arrested on allegations including "obscenity" and "prostitution" under the Turkish Penal Code, while two were placed under judicial control. Two further people were arrested the following day. In Kuşadası (Aydın province), six people were detained and five arrested on similar allegations, including two LGBTQI+ activists . As of 17 September 2026, 11 a.m. local time, at least 116 people had been detained in connection with these operations, including 44 LGBTQI+ human rights defenders, and the relevant judicial proceedings regarding detentions in all provinces concerned had reportedly been completed. Of the total detained, 82 people were arrested and placed in pre-trial detention, including 25 LGBTQI+ rights defenders — 20 of them affiliated with LGBTQI+ organisations, two with HIV-related organisations, two independent activists, and one journalist — under charges of violating the Law on Associations and of obscenity under Article 226 of the Turkish Penal Code. Of the remaining 19 LGBTQI+ rights defenders detained, 17 were released under judicial supervision, one was released on age or health grounds, and one further release on the same grounds was expected at the time of writing. Previously, during the day and evening of 12 September 2026, anniversary of the 1980 military coup, the Istanbul 7th Criminal Judgeship of Peace had ordered in decision no. 2026/9559 the blocking of access to the websites and a large number of social media accounts belonging to LGBTQI+ associations, media outlets, student groups and human rights defenders. On 13 September 2026, the Bakırköy 4th Criminal Judgeship of Peace separately ordered, in decision no. 2026/9112 D.İş., the blocking of KaosGL1.org. Access restrictions have since extended beyond LGBTQI+ organisations, affecting the social media accounts of, among others, the newspaper Evrensel, Amnesty International Türkiye, Academics for Peace and the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA). Justice Minister Akın Gürlek stated on X that judicial proceedings had been launched against 162 people, 9 associations and 13 businesses as part of an operation entitled "My Family is Safe" ("Ailem Güvende"), coordinated by the Chief Public Prosecutors' Offices of Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydın and Mersin. According to remarks attributed to him in the press, the charges concern "facilitating prostitution or providing premises for prostitution" and "producing and disseminating obscene content" made accessible to children; some case files reportedly also include allegations relating to forming a criminal organisation and to drug-related offences. The Istanbul Governor's Office has reportedly notified the Public Prosecutor's Office of a request for the temporary suspension and dissolution of four associations : SPoD, Lambdaistanbul, LİSTAG and HEVİ LGBTI+. The Justice Minister further stated that reviews by the Financial Crimes Investigation Board (MASAK) had found that large sums had been transferred to certain associations from public institutions and foreign organisations abroad, and that the source of these funds and their connection to the activities under investigation were being examined. However, the MASAK report in the case file shows that these funds were legally received and duly declared to the Ministry of Interior in accordance with the Law on Associations. On 14 September 2026, the Ministry of Justice issued a circular to the 175 Chief Public Prosecutor's Offices across all 81 provinces of Turkey, instructing them to open investigations into content and ac
