body: Share SGP 001 / 0926 / OBS 044 Criminalisation / Judicial harassment / Obstacles to the right to freedom of peaceful assembly Singapore 22 September 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Singapore . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed about the criminalisation and judicial harassment of Mr. Jolovan Wham , a social worker and human rights defender, Elijah Tay , a human rights defender, who identifies as non-binary, affiliated with the Transformative Justice Collective (TJC), a civil society group advocating for human rights and the abolition of the death penalty in Singapore, as well as two other TJC activists, Mses Kirsten Han and Kokila Annamalai . On 3 September 2026, Mr. Jolovan Wham and Elijah Tay received notices to attend court on separate dates in relation to multiple charges brought under the repressive Public Order Act (POA) and the Penal Code arising from their peaceful activism. On 7 September 2026, Mr. Jolovan Wham appeared before the State Court of Singapore, where he was charged under the POA and the Penal Code. Three charges under the POA concerned his participation in candlelight vigils held without permit near Changi Prison on 22 November 2024, 29 November 2024, and 23 January 2025, ahead of the executions of death row prisoners. A fourth charge under the POA concerned his organisation, on 3 February 2025, of a public assembly without a permit in a prohibited area, in relation to an assembly near the State Courts to advocate for the abolition of the death penalty. The fifth charge, brought under Section 179 of the Penal Code, concerned his refusal to answer questions from police during questioning about the vigil conducted on 22 November 2024. These charges followed five additional charges brought against Mr. Jolovan Wham under the POA on 3 February 2025, in connection with his participation in peaceful candlelight vigils held outside Changi Prison ahead of the executions of prisoners sentenced to death for drug trafficking in 2022 and 2023. Two of these charges were dropped. On 13 May 2026, Mr. Jolovan Wham was convicted on the remaining three offences. He was fined SGD 3,500 (approximately 2,379 Euros) per offence, amounting to SGD 10,500 (approximately 7,135 Euros) in total. Mr. Jolovan Wham is currently appealing his conviction. On 9 September 2026, Elijah Tay appeared before the State Court, and was charged on nine counts under the POA and the Penal Code. In addition to Elijah Tay, five other women, including one foreign national, were charged under the POA in relation to their organisation and participation in various public assemblies, including those in relation to the situation in Gaza. Four charges against Elijah Tay under the POA concern their participation in public assemblies without a permit, including a gathering to submit letters opposing the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill to the Ministry of Home Affairs in June 2024 and vigils for prisoners sentenced to death on 22 and 29 November 2024 and on 23 January 2025. Another charge under the POA concerns their participation in an assembly in a prohibited area without a permit, in relation to gathering near the State Courts on 3 February 2025 to advocate for the abolition of the death penalty. A further charge under the POA concerns the organisation of a memorial event without a permit in January 2025 featuring over 100 pairs of shoes and a white burial shroud in solidarity with Palestinian students killed in Gaza. Elijah Tay also faces two charges under Section 179 of the Penal Code concerning their refusal to answer questions from police about the vigils, as well as a charge under Section 298A of the Penal Code in relation to their pro-Palestine chant during an indoor Palestine-focused event on 2 February 2024, which was deemed by the authorities to be prejudicial to the maintenance of racial harmony that could disturb "public tranquillity." On 17 September 2026, Mses Kirsten Han and Kokila Annamalai as well as two other individuals were charged under the POA for their participation in a public assembly in a prohibited area. Their charges stemmed from a peaceful gathering on 3 February 2025 outside the State Courts to show support for Mr. Jolovan Wham, who attended a court hearing in relation to the five above-referenced charges brought against him under the POA. The Observatory recalls that Mr. Jolovan Wham has repeatedly faced judicial proceedings in connection with his peaceful human rights activities. In November 2017 , he was charged with three counts of organising public assemblies without a permit, one count of vandalism and three counts of refusing to sign statements, in relation to peaceful gatherings held between November 2016 and July 2017. In January 2019 , Mr. Jolovan Wham was also convicted of organising an illegal assembly without permit in relation to a public discussion on civil disobedience and social movements held in November 2016. His conviction and sentence were upheld on appeal in October 2019, when he was fined SGD 3,200 (approximately 2,070 Euros). Moreover, in March 2020, the Court of Appeal upheld a separate conviction and sentence against Mr. Jolovan Wham of SGD 5,000 (approximately 3,290 Euros) for “scandalising the court” over a Facebook post concerning the Singaporean and Malaysian judiciaries. The Observatory also recalls that the charges against Mr. Jolovan Wham and Elijah Tay took place in a context of extremely limited civic space in Singapore, where human rights defenders and civil society organisations have repeatedly faced restrictions and harassment in relation to the exercise of their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. In January 2025 , restrictions were imposed on activists from TJC in relation to their online advocacy against the death penalty. In October 2025 , Ms. Kokila Annamalai and two other TJC activists, Mses Siti Amirah Binte Mohamed Asrori and Sobikun Nahar, faced judicial harassment in connection with the organisation of a peaceful pro-Palestinian protest. The Observatory further recalls that the POA remains the legislative cornerstone of Singapore’s repression of the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, particularly due to its highly restrictive authorisation regime. The POA requires all individuals who seek to organise a public assembly to give advance notice and apply for permission from the Commissioner of Police no less than 14 working days before the planned event. Under the POA, the Minister of Home Affairs can issue orders that prohibit public assemblies or processions in “any public place” (defined as a “prohibited area”), if it is “in the public interest to do so”. The Commissioner of Police may refuse to grant a permit if there are “reasonable ground[s]” to believe that the proposed assembly may result in “public disorder”, “a public nuisance”, “an obstruction in any public road”, or “feelings of enmity, hatred, ill-will or hostility between different groups in Singapore”. All these broadly defined grounds significantly restrict the exercise of freedom of assembly in Singapore and do not appear to be necessary or proportionate, as required by international standards. The Observatory is concerned that the multiple criminal proceedings against Mr. Jolovan Wham, Elijah Tay, Ms. Kirsten Han, and Ms. Kokila Annamalai unduly restrict their rights to freedom of expression and freedom of peaceful assembly and contribute to a chilling effect on other human rights defenders in Singapore. The Observatory calls on the Singaporean authorities to immediately put an end to all acts of judicial harassment against Mr. Jolovan Wham, Elijah Tay, Ms. Kirsten Han, Ms. Kokila Annamalai, and other human rights defenders, and to ensure that they are able to carry out the
title: Singapore: Criminal proceedings against human rights defenders Jolovan Wham, Elijah Tay, Kirsten Han, and Kokila Annamalai over peaceful activism Read more

body: Share BHR 001 / 0926 / OBS 043 Arbitrary arrest Arbitrary detention / Judicial harassment/ Bahrain 15 September 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Bahrain . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed of the arbitrary re-arrest of Mr Naji Fateel , a prominent Bahraini human rights defender and co-founder of the Bahrain Youth Society for Human Rights (BYSHR), more than two years after his release under a royal pardon. On 18 August 2026 at around 5:45am, plain-clothes police officers raided Mr Fateel's flat in Bani Jamra while he and his family were asleep and arrested him. According to the information received, the officers did not present a warrant or explain the reason for the arrest before taking him away, allowing him only enough time to dress before placing him in a police vehicle. His children and mother were reportedly left deeply frightened by the raid. It was only after Mr Fateel had been taken outside that officers informed him his arrest was related to an outstanding financial payment linked to one of the earlier cases against him. The Observatory notes that Mr Fateel had in fact engaged with the authorities on this very payment: he is reported to have spoken with officials on 16 August 2026 to document the amount owed with a view to reaching a settlement, and to have been told at the time not to attend the police station but instead to approach the Public Prosecution and the Sentence Enforcement Judge. Notwithstanding this, he was transferred on 20 August 2026 from East Riffa Police Station to Jau Prison, where he remains held. He is reportedly held together with at least three other former political prisoners detained over the same underlying issue, amid reports that further individuals have been arrested on the same grounds. Among the cases against him was the 2015 Jau Prison case, in which he was one of the 57 defendants convicted in 2016 over protests inside the prison. The defendants were collectively ordered to pay approximately USD 1.35 million (approximately 1,16 million Euros) in compensation for alleged damages, with Mr Fateel's individual share calculated at approximately USD 23,700 (approximately 20,355 Euros), payable in monthly instalments of approximately USD 996 (approximately 855 Euros). Individuals unable to meet these payments reportedly risk imprisonment. On 16 June 2026, Mr Fateel and a group of others facing the same fines wrote directly to the Crown Prince and Prime Minister, His Highness Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, copying the Ministers of Justice and Interior and the Sentence Enforcement Judge, asking the authorities to recognise the effect of the 2024 pardon on these outstanding penalties, to halt enforcement measures that could return them to prison, to clarify their legal position, and to ensure that no one released under the pardon would be imprisoned solely for being unable to pay. The Observatory further recalls that, in its Opinion No. 65/2022 of 14 November 2022, the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD) found Mr Fateel's earlier deprivation of liberty arbitrary on account of violations of international fair-trial standards, called on Bahrain to release him immediately and unconditionally, and to provide him with an enforceable right to compensation and other reparations, and called for a full and independent investigation into the circumstances of his arbitrary detention and his allegations of torture. The Observatory is seriously concerned that Mr Fateel's arbitrary re-arrest, less than two and a half years after a royal pardon and while he was actively engaging the authorities in good faith over the payment in question, amounts to judicial harassment against him for his previous human rights activities, and that the enforcement of financial penalties tied to convictions covered by the pardon may be used as a tool for returning pardoned defenders to prison by other means. Therefore, the Observatory calls on the Bahraini authorities to immediately and unconditionally release Mr Naji Fateel and put an end to the judicial harassment he is facing in connection with his legitimate human rights activities. Actions requested: Please write to the Bahraini authorities asking them to: Guarantee in all circumstances the physical and psychological integrity of Naji Fateel and of all human rights defenders in Bahrain; Release immediately and unconditionally Naji Fateel and any other former political prisoners held over the same financial liabilities; Clarify without delay the legal effect of the April 2024 royal pardon on financial penalties arising from the pardoned convictions, and ensure that no individual is imprisoned solely for an inability to pay such penalties; Comply with the WGAD's November 2022 opinion, including by providing Naji Fateel with an enforceable right to compensation and by conducting a full and independent investigation into his earlier arbitrary detention and his allegations of torture; More generally, ensure in all circumstances that human rights defenders in Bahrain are able to carry out their legitimate activities without harassment or fear of reprisal. Addresses: His Highness Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, Crown Prince and Prime Minister of Bahrain, X: @BahrainPMO Lieutenant-General Shaikh Rashid bin Abdullah Al Khalifa, Minister of Interior, Email: [email protected] , X: @moi_Bahrain Please also write to the diplomatic representations of Bahrain in your respective countries. *** Geneva-Paris, 15 September 2026 Kindly inform us of any action undertaken quoting the code of this appeal in your reply. The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders (the Observatory) was created in 1997 by FIDH and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT). The objective of this programme is to intervene to prevent or remedy situations of repression against human rights defenders. FIDH and OMCT are both members of ProtectDefenders.eu , the European Union Human Rights Defenders Mechanism implemented by international civil society. body: Share AZE 001 / 0926 / OBS 042 Conviction / Sentencing / Arbitrary detention Azerbaijan 9 September 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT) and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Azerbaijan . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed about the conviction and sentencing of Mr Anar Mammadli, a Václav Havel Human Rights Prize Laureate and founder of the Election Monitoring and Democracy Studies Center (EMDS), who has worked for almost three decades to promote democratic participation, independent election observation and human rights in Azerbaijan. On 7 September 2026, the Baku Court on Grave Crimes sentenced Mr Anar Mammadli to 13 years in prison and disqualified him from holding certain positions for three years on charges including currency smuggling, illegal entrepreneurship, tax evasion and money laundering. Mr Mammadli has been detained at the Baku Pre-Trial Detention pending transfer to a strict-regime correctional institution since April 2024. He has consistently denied the charges brought against him. The Observatory recalls that Mr Mammadli was arrested on 29 April 2024 , shortly after participating in international human rights advocacy activities at the UN Human Rights Council and the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, and following EMDS's work monitoring the conduct of Azerbaijan's presidential elections held on 7 February 2024. On 30 April 2024, the Khatai District Court of Baku ordered Mr Mammadli to be placed in pre-trial detention on charges of “smuggling by a group” under Article 206.3.2 of the Azerbaijani Criminal Code. The Observatory underlines that, prior to his arrest, state-controlled media had subjected Mr Mammadli and EMDS to a sustained smear campaign following their independent election-monitoring activities. Mr Anar Mammadli was also previously sentenced to five and a half years in prison in 2013 following his election-monitoring activities, before being released in 2016. In 2018, the European Court of Human Rights found his detention politically motivated. His second arrest in 2024 and recent sentencing, which occurred shortly after the presidential elections, appear to constitute a further attempt to punish and silence his legitimate human rights activities. The Observatory also recalls that the case of Mr Anar Mammadli is part of a broader crackdown on human rights defenders, journalists, media outlets and other independent civil society actors in Azerbaijan, particularly following the presidential and parliamentary elections in 2024. The Observatory strongly condemns the conviction and the 13-year prison sentence imposed on Mr Mammadli, which are solely linked to his legitimate election monitoring and human rights activities. The Observatory calls on the Azerbaijani authorities to immediately and unconditionally release him and all other human rights defenders and independent civil society actors detained for exercising their fundamental rights. Please write to the authorities of Azerbaijan , asking them to: Guarantee in all circumstances the physical integrity and psychological well-being of Mr Anar Mammadli and all human rights defenders in Azerbaijan; Immediately and unconditionally release Mr Anar Mammadli, and all human rights defenders in the country. Quash the conviction of Mr Anar Mammadli and all charges brought against him in connection with his legitimate human rights and election-monitoring activities; Adopt and implement all necessary measures to protect human rights defenders, ensuring they can carry out their peaceful and legitimate activities without fear of reprisals or undue restrictions. body: Share THA 001 / 0422 / OBS 027.1 Conviction / Sentencing / Judicial harassment / Thailand 4 September 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), has received new information and requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Thailand . New information: The Observatory has been informed of the conviction and sentencing of Ms. Tantawan "Tawan" Tuatulanon, a student activist associated with pro-democracy groups Draconis Revolution and Thalu Wang (Shattering the Palace), who has advocated for the abolition of Article 112 of the Thai Criminal Code ( lèse-majesté ) and the reform of the Thai monarchy. On 31 August 2026, the Bangkok Criminal Court convicted Ms. Tantawan on charges under Article 112 of Thailand’s Criminal Code and Article 14(2) and (3) of the 2007 Computer Crimes Act and sentenced her to three years in prison, reduced to two years, over a Facebook livestream she conducted on 5 March 2022 from a footpath on Ratchadamnoen Nok Road, opposite the UN ESCAP building in Bangkok, shortly before a royal motorcade was due to pass. The court held her remarks were intended to insult the monarchy rather than constituting an exercise of freedom of expression. Ms. Tantawan was also fined 600 baht (approximately 15.57 euros) for failing to comply with the police order to stop the livestream. The court reduced the three-year sentence to two years in consideration of her useful testimony in the case. She was granted temporary release on a 100,000 baht (approximately 2,606 euros) bail the same day pending appeal. FIDH President Alexis Deswaef attended the hearing as a show of solidarity with Ms. Tantawan and all human rights defenders unjustly prosecuted on lèse-majesté charges. In a separate case, on 6 July 2026, the Bangkok South Criminal Court acquitted Ms. Tantawan and six co-defendants of charges under Article 112 and Article 116 (sedition) of the Criminal Code, brought over a public opinion poll on royal motorcades that the group had conducted outside a Bangkok shopping mall on 8 February 2022. The court held that the campaign, which invited the public to give their opinion by placing stickers on a whiteboard, amounted to an exercise of the constitutionally protected right to freedom of expression, and found that it did not directly refer to the King, Queen, heir apparent or regent. Proceedings against co-defendant Ms. Netiporn "Bung" Sanesangkhom had been discontinued following her death in custody on 14 May 2024. Between November 2020 and August 2026, 293 individuals have been charged under article 112, including 20 children. Of these, 31 are currently detained (12 pending trial, and 19 serving their final sentences). The Observatory recalls that the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD), in its Opinion No. 49/2023, adopted on 30 August 2023, found Ms. Tantawan’s deprivation of liberty stemming from her Facebook livestream case, arbitrary. The Observatory strongly condemns the conviction and prison sentence against Ms Tantawan Tuatulanon as it appears to be solely aimed at punishing her for her legitimate human rights activities and the exercise of her rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. The Observatory calls on the Thai authorities to immediately and unconditionally quash the conviction and sentencing and end all forms of judicial harassment against her and all pro-democracy activists currently prosecuted. Actions requested: Please write to the Thai authorities asking them to: i. Guarantee in all circumstances the physical and psychological integrity of Tantawan Tuatulanon and of all human rights defenders in Thailand; ii. Quash the convictions against Ms Tantawan, cease all acts of harassment, including at the judicial level, against her and all other human rights defenders and pro-democracy activists in the country; iii. Guarantee in all circumstances the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly, as enshrined in Articles 19 and 21 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which Thailand is a state party; iv. Amend Article 112 of the Criminal Code to bring it into line with Thailand’s human rights obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. v. More generally, ensure in all circumstances that human rights defenders in Thailand are able to carry out their legitimate activities without hindrance or fear of reprisal. body: Share UGA 004 / 0826 / OBS 039 Arbitrary arrest / Arbitrary detention / Criminalisation / Restriction on freedom of peaceful assembly Uganda 24 August 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Uganda. Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed about the arbitrary arrest and detention of four young environmental human rights defenders, Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly , Mr Mugoya Hassan , Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick , members of the youth-led movement Rooted in Resistance , which advocates for greater accountability regarding Uganda's natural resources and for the protection of the environment. On 10 August 2026 at around 9:00 a.m., the four human rights defenders were peacefully marching along King George Way in central Kampala towards Parliament, where they intended to submit a petition calling for a new economic model centred on economic freedom and broad-based prosperity for Ugandans from the country's oil resources. They were reportedly wearing orange T-shirts bearing the words "Rooted in Resistance" and carrying placards stating, among others, "Prioritize other sectors of the economy", "Oil is Temporary, Nature is Permanent" and "Oil Today, Problems Tomorrow". Ugandan police intercepted and arrested the four activists during the peaceful march, after which they were taken to Central Police Station in Kampala. They were subsequently brought before the Buganda Road Chief Magistrate's Court in Kampala, before Grade One Magistrate Rophine Achayo, where they pleaded not guilty to charges of « public/common nuisance for allegedly disrupting traffic and creating road hazards » under the Road Act, Cap. 346 . On 10 August 2026, they were remanded to Luzira Maximum Security Prison, where they remain detained. Their next court hearing is scheduled for 28 August 2026. The arrests took place in the context of ongoing mobilisation by Rooted in Resistance concerning Uganda's oil sector and the environmental and social consequences of oil-related projects, including the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) . The movement, formerly known as Students Against EACOP Uganda, has repeatedly organised peaceful protests and petitions concerning the project and the use of Uganda's natural resources. The Observatory recalls that these incidents illustrate a persistent pattern of harassment targeting those opposing EACOP and defending environmental and human rights. Environmental rights defenders in Uganda have, in recent years, repeatedly faced arbitrary arrests, judicial harassment, and torture. For example, on 9 August 2024 , 47 students were arrested in Kampala during a peaceful protest against the EACOP project. Between May and June 2024 , environmental activists like Adriko Sostein , Julius Tumwiine , and Stephen Kwikiriza were arrested and arbitrarily detained, as well as Bob Barigye , Noah Katiiti , Newton Mwesigwa , Julius Byaruhanga , Desire Ndyamwesigwa , Raymond Binntukwanga , and Jealousy Mugisha Mulimbwa . In April 2025, 11 environmental defenders, known as #KCB11 were arbitrarily arrested and detained following a peaceful protest denouncing the Kenyan Commercial Bank’s decision to fund EACOP. In October 2024, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Human Rights Defenders sent a letter to the Ugandan government, raising concern about the increasing harassment of activists opposing the EACOP, particularly Students for Global Democracy. More recently, in April 2026 , eight young environmental defenders affiliated with Rooted in Resistance were convicted and sentenced to 11 months' imprisonment in connection with their participation in a peaceful protest against EACOP. These cases have occurred against a broader backdrop of increasing restrictions on civic space in Uganda, including in the context of the 2026 elections. Human rights defenders and other civic actors have increasingly faced arrests, judicial proceedings and other forms of intimidation in connection with their legitimate activities. In this context, the use of criminal proceedings and custodial sentences against environmental defenders opposing EACOP further raises concerns about the shrinking space for civic participation in Uganda. The Observatory also recalls that, as a State Party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), Uganda must respect and ensure the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly (Articles 19 and 21), as well as the right to a fair trial (Article 14). The Observatory expresses its utmost concern over the arrest and detention of Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly, Mr Mugoya Hassan, Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick in connection with their participation in a peaceful march to Parliament. The Observatory is also worried that their prosecution may have a chilling effect on civil society actors advocating for environmental protection and responsible management of Uganda's natural resources. The Observatory condemns the arbitrary arrest and detention and criminalisation of Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly, Mr Mugoya Hassan, Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick, which appear to be linked to their legitimate activities as environmental human rights defenders. The Observatory urges the Ugandan authorities to immediately and unconditionally release them, drop all charges brought against them and guarantee in all circumstances that environmental human rights defenders are able to peacefully express their opinion and participate in public debate without fear of reprisals or judicial harassment. Actions requested: Please write to the Ugandan authorities urging them to: i. Guarantee in all circumstances the physical integrity and psychological well-being of Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly, Mr Mugoya Hassan, Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick; as well as all human rights defenders in Uganda; ii. Immediately and unconditionally release Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly, Mr Mugoya Hassan, Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick and drop all charges against them as their prosecution is solely linked to their legitimate activities and peaceful exercise of their rights; iii. Guarantee that Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly, Mr Mugoya Hassan, Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick have immediate and unrestricted access to adequate food, healthcare, lawyers and family members, and ensure that their conditions of detention fully comply with international human rights standards; iv. Put an end to all acts of harassment, including judicial harassment against members of Rooted in Resistance and all environmental human rights defenders in Uganda, and guarantee that they are able to carry out their legitimate activities without fear of reprisals or intimidation; v. Ensure strict respect for fundamental freedoms, and in particular guarantee in all circumstances respect for the freedoms of peaceful assembly and expression, as guaranteed by international human rights law, in particular Articles 19 and 21 of the ICCPR, as well as the right to a fair trial, as guaranteed under Article 14 of the ICCPR; Addresses: • Mr Kaguta Yoweri Museveni, President of the Republic of Uganda, E-mail: [email protected] / [email protected] , X: @KagutaMuseveni • Ms Robinah Nabbanja, Prime Minister of the Republic of Uganda, Email: [email protected] , X: @RobinahNabbanja • Mr Adonia Ayebarer, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Uganda, Email: [email protected] ; X: @UgandaMFA • Hon. body: @HRF View post Dauletmurat Tazhimuratov, a prisoner of conscience in Uzbekistan, has shared a letter from prison detailing the abuse and severe mistreatment he is suffering while incarcerated. Tazhimuratov is a Karakalpak lawyer, journalist, and human rights defender who has been detained in Uzbekistan since July 2022, when the Uzbek government cracked down on protesters who opposed constitutional amendments that would have stripped Karakalpakstan of its status as a sovereign republic. Writing from detention, Tazhimuratov describes brutal beatings he has received at the hands of prison officials, who force him to recite the Uzbek national anthem or deny his Karakalpak identity by declaring that he is Uzbek. He is also denied access to bathing facilities, medical care, writing materials, and religious items. HRF calls on Uzbekistan to treat Dauletmurat Tazhimuratov with dignity and recognize his fundamental rights by providing him with access to basic necessities and investigating all incidents of violence against him. Most of all, the Uzbek government must enforce the opinion of the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention and release him from prison immediately. View post
source: Human Rights Foundation — Europe & Asie centrale

body: 2 octobre 2026 Rédigé par : Eléa Muresan Tags Armée Astana Bizutages Défense Jeunesse Service militaire Violences Un paramilitaire kazakh lors d'exercices militaire en 2000 (illustration). Crédit : Wikicommons Au Kazakhstan, l’automne marque le retour de la conscription. Si certains jeunes hommes considèrent le service militaire comme un devoir envers leur pays, d’autres cherchent par tous les moyens à y échapper. À Astana, les récits de recrutements forcés dans les lieux publics et de violences dans les casernes nourrissent une défiance persistante envers l’armée. Au Kazakhstan, le mois de septembre a marqué l’ouverture de la campagne automnale de recrutement de jeunes, dans le cadre de la conscription. Le gouvernement kazakh prévoit le recrutement de 23 000 hommes , âgés de 18 à 25 ans, d’ici fin décembre. Faites un don à Novastan Héritage de l’ère soviétique, le service militaire représente au Kazakhstan un fait de société important, car il concerne l’ensemble des jeunes hommes. En principe, tous sont soumis à l’obligation de servir l’armée pendant une année entière, à travers une formation physique et théorique permettant de se familiariser avec l’univers militaire et sa discipline. Mais dans la pratique, de nombreux jeunes cherchent à y échapper, mettant en place un volet de stratégies pour obtenir des dispenses. Associée à une réputation sulfureuse, l’armée peine à recruter, malgré le caractère obligatoire de la conscription. Des méthodes de recrutement plus offensives que la simple convocation se sont développées depuis quelques années, parmi lesquelles des formes d’enlèvement de jeunes orchestrés par la police dans des espaces publics. Violence et controverses dans l’armée Novastan est allé à la rencontre des habitants d’Astana, la capitale kazakhe, afin de comprendre leurs représentations et expériences relatives au service militaire. La majorité de ces échanges laissent entendre que le service militaire ne jouit pas d’une bonne réputation auprès des habitants de la capitale kazakhe. « Moi je n’irai pas. Chaque année il y a des centaines de garçons qui reviennent blessés . Certains meurent, d’autres qui se suicident, c’est hyper violent. Le Kazakhstan n’est même pas un pays en guerre, ça n’a aucun sens « , raconte Jordan, jeune informaticien âgé de 23 ans. Lire aussi sur Novastan : Dans les rangs de l’armée kazakhe, une violence inouïe : « Mes reins se sont déplacés à cause des coups » La conscription suscite effectivement de l’inquiétude auprès de nombreux kazakhs. Des drames survenant chaque année ont forgé une réputation de violence dans l’imaginaire collectif autour du service militaire : morts, blessures, harcèlement, suicides. Parmi les scandales les plus viraux des dernières années, le cas de Moukhtar Yerebatan, jeune homme de 18 ans, victime d’une commotion cérébrale dans le cadre de son service, avait également suscité l’indignation dans tout le pays. Après un coma de deux ans, la mort du jeune homme le 23 juin dernier avait relancé la polémique sur les violences au sein de l’armée. D’après les sources officielles, il se serait blessé à la tête en tombant dans les toilettes par accident, mais cette version est contestée par ses proches qui suspectent des violences intentionnelles. La semaine passée, la mort d’une dizaine de jeunes conscrits lors d’un accident dans la mer Caspienne a intensifié la colère et les inquiétudes des parents concernant le service militaire, ne croyant plus en la capacité de l’armée à assurer la sécurité de leurs enfants. Lire aussi sur Novastan : Dans les rangs de l’armée kazakhe, une violence inouïe : « Mes reins se sont déplacés à cause des coups » « Les nouvelles sont terrifiantes. Si j’avais un fils, en aucun cas je le laisserais rejoindre l’armée « , confie Samal, hôtesse de l’air et mère de famille à Astana. Nombreux sont les jeunes qui mettent en place des stratégies pour échapper à la conscription, souvent avec le soutien de leurs parents et de leur réseau. Ces méthodes peuvent se baser sur des dispositifs légaux, mais aussi sur des formes de corruption. Sont notamment exemptées les personnes déclarées inaptes lors de la visite médicale, et les inscrits à l’université. Timur, 22 ans, ancien étudiant en économie et commerce, raconte que beaucoup d’étudiants à l’université sont uniquement inscrits pour échapper à l’armée. Il explique les raisons pour lesquelles lui-même s’est soustrait au service militaire : « Je pense que c’est pas pour moi. J’ai pas envie de perdre un an de ma vie, c’est pas le bon moment, j’ai des projets personnels, je compte acheter un appart, voyager... « Rouslan, 26 ans, créateur de contenu, a suivi de longues études et obtenu un doctorat en anthropologie, un choix motivé à la fois par son intérêt pour la discipline et par la possibilité temporaire d’échapper au service obligatoire. « Après 25 ans, si on n’a pas encore servi, on peut être exempté en passant une formation militaire de 40 jours. C’est payant, mais les conditions sont beaucoup moins rudes, on est mieux traités que pour le service d’un an. « « Rapts » et « Kidnapping » Faute de parvenir à recruter un nombre de jeunes correspondant aux effectifs prévus annuellement, le ministère de la Défense met en place des mesures offensives. En particulier, ce que les locaux nomment des “rapts” ou “kidnappings” de jeunes, des formes de mobilisation forcées menées par la police et les militaires dans des lieux publics, sans être toujours justifiées légalement. Timour raconte que pendant les périodes de recrutement, à l’image de celle qui a débuté le 1er septembre, de nombreux jeunes évitent au maximum de fréquenter des lieux publics, par peur de se faire convoquer de force : « La police vient dans des endroits comme ça, par exemple dans le jardin botanique, où y’a beaucoup de jeunes, potentiellement ceux qui n’ont pas servi. Ça peut être un club, un billard, ou des salles de jeux vidéo, ce type d’endroits, où les mecs traînent souvent. » Lire aussi sur Novastan : Avec de nouveaux blindés, le Kazakhstan fait évoluer son armement pour une diversification prudente Un système de solidarité entre usagers s’est d’ailleurs développé sur l’application 2GIS, l’équivalent de Google Maps au Kazakhstan, pour s’entraider à éviter les lieux. Les utilisateurs peuvent se notifier entre eux et écrire des messages à propos de plusieurs lieux publics. Sur l’image, un utilisateur notifie « Police présente pour conscription, ils sont avec des camions « . Contrairement à ses amis qui réduisent leurs sorties pendant les périodes de recrutement, Timur a fait le choix de garder son mode de vie inchangé malgré le risque. « C ‘est impossible de surveiller partout où ils pourraient me trouver. Un ami est allé au magasin près de chez lui, et quand il est sorti, ils l’ont attrapé, embarqué dans une voiture et envoyé direct au bureau militaire. On peut se faire prendre n’importe où, mais je n’ai pas envie de rester enfermé chez moi constamment. J’ai peut-être de la chance « , sourit-il. Pourtant, au cours des deux dernières années, Timour a été embarqué par la police à plusieurs reprises, depuis qu’il a interrompu ses études. Pour s’en sortir, il compte surtout sur le soutien de son réseau. “ J’ai des amis, certains dans des organes d’État. Disons qu’ils ont des ressources administratives. Quand je les appelais, on me libérait directement ” explique Timour. Il relate le cas d’un ami qui a échappé de justesse à l’armée. Après avoir été embarqué par la police, il aurait été aidé par son père pour s’inscrire in extremis dans une université afin d’obtenir un sursis. D’autres, moins chanceux, ne disposent pas assez de ressources sociales et financières pour se tirer d’affaires. Si les bourses au mérite existent pour entrer dans l’enseignement supérieur, les places sont rares et la stratégie de l’inscription à l’université reste souvent coûteuse. « J’ai progressé dans tout » Malgré les controverses et les appréhensions de nombreux citoyens kazakhs, certains ayant
title: Au Kazakhstan, le service militaire continue d’inquiéter les jeunes hommes

body: 8 October 2026 Mathieu Lemoine Edited by: Maya Ivanova Tags Lkhagvadulam Purev-Ochir Mongolian cinema Ulaanbaatar Mongolian filmmaker Lkhagvadulam Purev-Ochir. Photo courtesy of Lkhagvadulam Purev-Ochir. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Mongolian filmmaker Lkhagvadulam Purev-Ochir speaks to Novastan about filming Ulaanbaatar, the country’s apartment obsession, masculinity and spirituality, and why contemporary Mongolia needs to be seen as more than folklore. International images of Mongolia are still dominated by the steppe: horses, yurts, nomadic herders and vast landscapes. The films of Lkhagvadulam Purev-Ochir look somewhere else. Her characters inhabit apartment blocks, bedrooms, cars, schools and the sprawling neighbourhoods of Ulaanbaatar. They worry about housing and money, negotiate sex and relationships, struggle with expectations placed on young men and women, and move between a rapidly changing urban Mongolia and older cultural and spiritual reference points. Read more on Novastan : “Mongolia cannot be understood through one lens”: Dr. Mendee Jargalsaikhan on democracy, China and Central Asia Purev-Ochir has emerged as one of the most distinctive voices in contemporary Mongolian cinema. After studying film direction and screenwriting, she attracted international attention with the shorts Mountain Cat , Snow in September and A South-Facing Window . Her first feature, City of Wind , continued her exploration of young Mongolians navigating the tensions between modern urban life, family, desire and spirituality. A still from Mountain Cat , Lkhagvadulam Purev-Ochir’s first short film. Courtesy of Lkhagvadulam Purev-Ochir. Yet her films are not simply portraits of Ulaanbaatar. Purev-Ochir describes the city itself as something difficult to capture: a place that, on screen, repeatedly becomes an “inner landscape”. Her interest lies in transitions – between adolescence and adulthood, intimacy and isolation, the physical and spiritual worlds, and different ways of imagining what it means to be Mongolian. These tensions are also playing out on a much larger scale. Mongolia has experienced extraordinarily rapid transformations across successive generations: communism, democratisation, globalisation and now the internet and artificial intelligence. Ulaanbaatar’s relentless expansion has made housing both an aspiration and a source of frustration, while the country’s international image remains closely associated with a nomadic culture from which many urban Mongolians have become physically removed. Read more on Novastan : “The idea of having choices was so new”: Oyungerel Tsedevdamba on Mongolia’s democracy 36 years later For Purev-Ochir, cinema offers a way to explore these contradictions without resolving them. Speaking to Novastan, she discusses why apartment ownership has become the Mongolian “dream and nightmare”, why she worries that Mongolians themselves are orientalising their culture, what shamanism means in contemporary urban life, and why she hopes a new generation might eventually imagine a different relationship between Mongolia’s cities and countryside. Novastan: Before we talk about the films themselves, could you tell us a little about your own path into filmmaking? What was your background, when did cinema become something you wanted to pursue seriously, and were there particular filmmakers, writers, artists or experiences that shaped you early on? Lkhagvadulam Purev-Ochir: Apart from the initial decision to study filmmaking, which was full of psychological drama because I was cutting ties with what my parents had envisioned for my future, I had a pretty straightforward and traditional path in filmmaking. I studied for my bachelor’s in film direction and master’s in screenwriting, and subsequently, upon graduating from my master’s, I made two short films which did very well at festivals. My first feature film, City of Wind , came out exactly five years after my graduation. I had written the script during my master’s in screenwriting. I made the decision to go into filmmaking and not pursue medicine like my mother because watching films and thinking about them was one of the only true pleasures in my life. I couldn’t imagine my early adulthood doing anything else and made the “bold” – or lazy – decision to go into filmmaking. When I made this decision, I was purely a film watcher. I had no knowledge about how films were made, no idea about montage, and no previous idea of what a film set was like. How would you describe yourself as a filmmaker today? What kinds of stories, characters or tensions do you find yourself returning to, and what do you think you are still trying to understand through cinema? I’ve noticed so far through my films that I wish to capture transitions and states of movement with cinema – specifically in the inner worlds and impressions of people. People who are more at war with themselves and their feelings than with external characters. Or people whose inner states are conflicting with exterior states, and the transition between these states. I like these transitory situations and feelings and contradictions. I prefer autumn and spring to summer and winter, for example. Autumn and spring are seasons that fight with themselves; there is tension and vast change from day to day and even between day and night. In Mongolia in autumn, it can feel like summer in the day and winter at night. There is conflict in temperatures, in expression and in affect. These seasons feel more reflective and reflexive. I think with cinema, I wish to capture something seasonal like this. Across the three shorts, Ulaanbaatar seems to change with the age and situation of your characters. In Mountain Cat it is a place of adolescence and possibility, in Snow in September it feels more enclosed and unsettling, and in A South-Facing Window adulthood seems almost physically trapped by apartments, traffic and financial pressure. Do you see these films as capturing different stages of growing up in the same city? I think it could be said like that. It’s true that the characters in my films are growing up – my next film is about a man in his mid-30s. On a different note, I find Ulaanbaatar strangely difficult to “capture” on camera. It’s a wide, steppe city spread out across a large valley. Even neighbourhoods which are more enclosed feel open and exposed. I feel that on the screen Ulaanbaatar is not very geometric and more landscape-like. And it gives a feeling of something more timeless and affective rather than something specific and geographic. I tried to depict Ulaanbaatar this way – to make it very characteristic and to connect its different spaces to different plot points and characters. But try as I might, the city always feels more like an inner landscape than an active location. In A South-Facing Window , the couple seem to be searching for a better life through real estate – visiting empty apartments and imagining another home. You have also described an apartment in central Ulaanbaatar as part of a kind of “Mongolian dream”. What interested you about housing as a symbol of aspiration, and do you think that dream still captures what younger Mongolians want today? Housing is the Mongolian Dream/Nightmare par excellence . Because of our nomadic background, the idea of real estate as individual wealth is relatively new. I think my grandparents’ generation was the first generation that slowly started to pursue living in apartments because it was more “civilised” and meant that you were part of the state – only state workers got apartments then. At the moment, all Mongolians are attempting to buy apartments because it’s an absolute “must” of modern life. And somehow it is thought of as the solution to all modern problems, as
title: Lkhagvadulam Purev-Ochir: “Housing is the Mongolian dream – and nightmare”

body: 5 October 2026 Mathieu Lemoine Tags Adygene Glacier Ala-Archa climate change Glaciers Gulbara Omorova Kyrgyzstan women in science Participants in the Ala-Archa expedition in front of the glacier. Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan A four-day expedition to Kyrgyzstan’s Adygene glacier brought seven women into the field with glaciologist Gulbara Omorova. For filmmaker Tynymgul Eshieva, the journey is part of a larger effort to document both the rapid transformation of Kyrgyzstan’s glaciers and the women working to understand them. In August, seven women set out into Kyrgyzstan’s Ala-Archa gorge for a four-day expedition. Some were experienced hikers; others had never undertaken a high-altitude trek of this kind. Their destination was the Adygene scientific station, around 11 kilometres into the mountains. They were not going simply to see a glacier. From 16 to 19 August, the participants worked alongside Kyrgyz glaciologist Gulbara Omorova, installing ablation stakes to measure melting, recording glacier movement with GPS and carrying out bathymetric measurements on lakes below the ice. Behind the expedition was documentary filmmaker and producer Tynymgul Eshieva. She is developing The Voice of the Glaciers ( Мөңгүлөрдүн үнү ), a feature-length documentary centred on Omorova and her work in Kyrgyzstan’s mountains. The film is still in development and is currently expected to be completed in 2028. But Eshieva has already been filming a landscape that is changing fast enough for those returning to it to see the difference with their own eyes. “We filmed the teaser in June last year, and then we went back for the expedition in August this year,” Eshieva told Novastan Editor-in-Chief Mathieu Lemoine. “The glacier looked completely different. You don’t need instruments to see it. You can see with your own eyes how rapidly it’s disappearing.” A glacier changing within a lifetime The measurements reinforce what the eye can see. During the expedition, around 1.4 metres of surface lowering was recorded near the glacier terminus over approximately one month. Over an entire ablation season, melting in the lower sections can amount to several metres. A field briefing during the expedition in Ala-Archa. Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Omorova’s longer-term research paints an even starker picture. The Adygene glacier system comprises three glaciers – Bolshoy Adygene, Panfilov and 30-let VLKSM. Bolshoy Adygene has decreased in area from approximately 3.5 square kilometres in 1962 to 2.8 square kilometres in 2025, a loss of around 20 percent. More strikingly, the annual rate of area loss has accelerated from 0.006 to 0.033 square kilometres per year. The smaller glaciers are retreating too. Between 1977 and 2024, Panfilov lost around 20 percent of its area and 30-let VLKSM around 29 percent. For Eshieva, however, seeing the process at close range changed the meaning of such figures. “It’s completely different to see it with your own eyes,” she said. “You can read the news, follow websites, see the numbers online. But when you go there, when you stand on the glacier and feel it, it’s something else.” What struck her just as strongly was the work required to produce those numbers. “She carries heavy equipment up the mountain. She takes the measurements again and again, with total commitment,” Eshieva said of Omorova. “It’s slow, repetitive work, sometimes even boring, but it’s absolutely necessary. Without people like her doing it year after year, we simply wouldn’t know what is happening.” The woman behind the measurements Eshieva has known Omorova since the mid-2000s. Long before either woman imagined making a documentary together, they talked, hiked and even climbed a peak near Bishkek. Expedition participants make their way towards the glacier. Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Eshieva only began documentary filmmaking in 2023. While editing her first feature documentary, also about a woman activist, she began searching for another project. She hopes to complete that film next year. The catalyst came through social media. The Adygene research station had been robbed and scientific equipment stolen. Omorova appealed publicly for help. People who had never visited a glacier responded, crowdfunding enough money to replace what had been lost. “That was the moment I thought: this could be a film,” Eshieva recalled. “Here is a woman who fights for her science, for the environment, for justice, and she doesn’t wait for anyone to do it for her. And ordinary people answered her call.” She began filming. Omorova’s route into glaciology itself began far from the ice. Trained in sociology, she travelled to villages to interview residents about social issues. During a visit to Batken, farmers told her about shortages of water. Already an experienced mountaineer with training in alpinism, she began asking why. That question eventually took her towards glaciology and the Adygene station. It also illustrates one of the central realities of glacier retreat: what happens high in Kyrgyzstan’s mountains does not remain there. Read more on Novastan : The recession of the Tian Shan glaciers and other recent studies From the glacier to the valley As glaciers retreat, they transform not only water availability but the landscape around them. Omorova’s monitoring has identified 16 new moraine-glacial lakes in the Adygene complex since observations began in 1977. Some glacial lakes can become unstable, making continuous observation essential. During the August expedition, the participants went out by boat to conduct bathymetric measurements using an echo sounder. By measuring water depth at different points, researchers can map the lake and track how it changes. Monitoring can also involve automatic loggers recording water levels and temperatures, water-column profiling and examination of the moraine dams holding back the lakes. Read more on Novastan : Life by the river: the Naryn in Kyrgyzstan The relationship between melting ice and downstream risk is complex. A lake that appears stable today may change as the glacier, surrounding terrain and permafrost evolve. The purpose of monitoring is therefore not to predict an outburst from a single measurement, but to observe the glacier-lake system continuously and identify changes that may eventually become warning signs. Expedition participants rest beside a mountain stream in Ala-Archa. Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Eshieva did not originally set out to make a film about the relationship between glaciers and water. “When I started, my idea wasn’t to connect what happens up on the glacier with what happens down below,” she said. “But the more I filmed, the more I saw that they are deeply connected.” Whether that relationship ultimately becomes central to the documentary remains open. “People often ask me at pitching forums: is this a film about water? For now, it isn’t,” she said. “Documentary is a long process. You follow a person’s life, sometimes for two or three years, sometimes ten. I don’t know yet where it will go.” Seven women on the ice The August expedition itself emerged partly from necessity. Eshieva had initially envisaged a camp for aspiring ecologists, selected through an open call and led by Omorova. But by August, funding for the film had not materialised and the summer field season was slipping away. “I felt I had to do something,” she said. She changed the plan, crowdfunded an expedition and invited women interested in learning about glaciers to join. There was no competitive selection process. Participants simply had to be willing and able to commit to four days in the mountains. Seven ultimately went. Their backgrounds and levels of mountain experience differed. Two already knew Omorova from pre
title: On a disappearing Kyrgyz glacier, seven women learn to read the ice

body: 4 October 2026 Mathieu Lemoine Tags Kazakhstan Russification Soviet Germans Lena Wolf, author of May the Universe Be Your Home! Growing up German in Kazakhstan. Photo courtesy of Lena Wolf. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Born in Latvia and raised in Kazakhstan, Lena Wolf grew up with fragments of a history that Soviet society rarely discussed openly. In her graphic memoir, she retraces the deportation of her German family to Kazakhstan, their struggle to preserve language and identity, and her own journey from Aktobe to Germany. For our readers in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan: Lena Wolf’s e-book is now available at reduced regional prices on Google Play Books in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. Available in English and Russian . For much of her childhood, Lena Wolf believed that all Germans came from Kazakhstan. Aktobe was home. Her grandmother cooked German dishes alongside baursaki and manti, organised clandestine religious gatherings and spoke German to her grandchildren, even when they answered her in Russian. Around them lived families whose own histories had been shaped by deportation, repression and displacement. Yet Wolf also learned early that being German could set her apart. “I don’t think I really understood what being German meant to other people until I was called a fascist for the first time,” she recalls. “I was probably about six.” Decades later, Wolf began piecing together the family history that had reached her in fragments behind closed doors. The result was a graphic memoir illustrated by Christoph Heuer, tracing almost two centuries of migration, persecution and repeated attempts to build a home. Migration of German communities to the Russian Empire from the eighteenth to the nineteenth century. Her grandmother Emilia was 25 when she was deported to Kazakhstan in 1941 with two young children. Like many Soviet Germans, the family initially believed the displacement might be temporary. “They left behind their houses, land, animals – everything – still hoping they would return,” Wolf says. They never did. Forced deportation routes of Soviet Germans in 1941, including destinations in Kazakhstan and Siberia. Even after Stalin-era special-settlement restrictions were lifted in 1955, Soviet Germans were not allowed to return to the areas from which they had been deported. Emilia eventually built a new life in Aktobe. “Kazakhstan did become home for her, partly because she knew she could never return to her village in Ukraine,” Wolf says. “She found her people there and had her family around her.” The contradiction would become central to Wolf’s understanding of her family history: Kazakhstan was both a place of forced exile and the country in which several generations of the family made their lives. “Somewhere along the way, she too became a German from Kazakhstan.” German communities in the Soviet Union and its successor states after 1945. Growing up German in Soviet Kazakhstan For Wolf herself, Kazakhstan carried no such ambiguity during childhood. “For me, Kazakhstan was simply home. I didn’t know anything else,” she says. “In fact, when I was very little, I thought all Germans came from Kazakhstan.” Read more on Novastan : Beyond any borders: a new multicultural generation in Kazakhstan Her family’s German identity nevertheless remained clearly marked in Soviet society. Official documents continued to identify Soviet Germans as nemets or nemka , even as German-language education, religious life and much of the community’s institutional culture had been suppressed. “You were expected to stop being German, but you were never allowed to forget that you were German,” Wolf says. In her family, survival meant avoiding attention. Her father’s advice was encapsulated in the Russian expression тише воды, ниже травы – “quieter than water, lower than grass.” “Don’t attract attention. Don’t stand out. That was how you survived.” Wolf remembers the word “German” being routinely associated with “fascist”, decades after the Second World War. Soviet Germans’ own experience of deportation and repression was largely absent from the history taught in schools. “When you don’t know the history, you fill the gaps with your own explanations,” she says. “So people assumed that because we had been deported, we must have been guilty. The deportation itself became proof of our guilt.” As a child, she even changed her surname when helping an elderly Soviet woman whose husband and son had died during the war. “I invented another name for myself: Volkova instead of Wolf.” The Russian name, she says, became a form of protection. When Russian became the common language Language is another thread running through Wolf’s memoir. Her grandmother spoke German to her; Wolf usually answered in Russian. She later recognised almost exactly the same pattern among Kazakh families: grandparents speaking Kazakh while younger generations responded in Russian. “When that happens, it isn’t only language that gets lost,” Wolf says. “Stories, traditions and knowledge can no longer be passed on in the same way.” She remembers receiving some Kazakh-language teaching at school but says it was far too limited for children to become proficient. Russian, meanwhile, dominated education, television and popular culture. “You didn’t necessarily have to force children to speak Russian,” she says. “Education, television, culture and opportunities were in Russian, while Kazakh was often seen as old-fashioned or backward. Of course children were going to choose Russian.” Read more on Novastan : The Lexicon of Kazakh Decolonisation Looking back, she says she is glad to see the Kazakh language gaining greater prominence today. A garden as survival – and as home One image reappears throughout Wolf’s family history: the garden. Her ancestors had originally migrated eastward to work the land. After deportation, a garden helped her grandmother and a neighbour survive wartime shortages. Decades later, during Wolf’s own childhood in Kazakhstan, home-grown food helped sustain the family when Soviet shops were empty. But the garden came to represent more than food. Wolf recounts the story of her father, whose mother was sentenced to the Gulag after attempting to leave the deportation zone and return to Ukraine. He was sent to an orphanage in Zaporizhzhia shortly after the war. One teacher once invited him to her home for dinner. While she cooked, he played in the garden with her son. “He remembers standing there among the flowers and plants and realising, for the first time, that the world was beautiful,” Wolf says. The memory remained with him throughout his life. Now 91, he can no longer maintain a large garden but still cares for flowers on his balcony in Offenbach, Germany. “Perhaps that is what a garden means in our family,” Wolf says. “It feeds you when there is nothing to eat, but it also gives you beauty when there isn’t much beauty around you. And wherever you end up, you can plant something and make that place your own.” A ‘return’ to a country they did not know In 1989, Wolf and her family left Kazakhstan for Germany. Officially, such migration was often presented as a return to an ancestral homeland. In practice, Wolf discovered that Germany was another unfamiliar country. “What surprised me most was that in Germany I wasn’t seen as German,” she says. “After everything our families had gone through in the Soviet Union because they were German – persecution, discrimination and sometimes literally fighting for survival – we arrived in Germany and suddenly we were foreigners.” At 17, Wolf initially tried to assimilate as completely as possible. She stopped speaking Russian, avoided food associated with her Soviet childhood and even began using the name Helene. I
title: ‘I am a German from Kazakhstan’: Lena Wolf on deportation, memory and finding home

Support Novastan Formed in Ulaanbaatar in 2023, Dotor Khuree blends Mongolian musical traditions with avant-pop, jazz, rock and other contemporary influences. In this interview with Novastan Editor-in-Chief Mathieu Lemoine, the band discusses its latest EP, the independent music scene in Ulaanbaatar and what it means to make distinctly Mongolian music today. Mongolian music has gained growing international visibility in recent years, but outside the country it is still often associated primarily with the morin khuur, throat singing and other immediately recognisable traditional forms. Ulaanbaatar-based band Dotor Khuree is exploring another path. Formed in April 2023 by musicians who met at the Mongolian State University of Arts and Culture, the group describes its sound as avant-pop, post-ethno and poly-genre. Its members draw on Mongolian long song, regional folk traditions and the musical vocabulary of instruments such as the morin khuur, while largely expressing those influences through contemporary instrumentation. The band released its debut LP, Zarimdaa Zuils , in September 2025, followed by the self-titled Dotor Khuree EP in May 2026. The latter pushed the musicians further towards what they describe as a distinctly Mongolian sound achieved without directly using traditional instruments. Novastan spoke with the members of Dotor Khuree about Mongolian musical identity, experimentation, Ulaanbaatar’s independent scene and their ambitions beyond Mongolia. Novastan: Could you introduce Dotor Khuree to readers who may be discovering you for the first time? How did the band come together, and what brought you to the kind of music you make today? Dotor Khuree : Mandaa : Dotor Khuree was formed on 12 April 2023 and consists of six musicians and two crew members – our band manager and sound engineer – making eight members in total. We are an avant-pop, post-ethno, poly-genre band. The band was first founded by our bassist Gombojav and me, Narmandakh, the keyboardist. We then started adding our other bandmates: vocalist Tsetsen, guitarist Orgil, sound engineer Enkhdalai, pianist Batzaya and drummer Chultemjamts. Our last addition was our band manager, Oyuntulkhuur, or Roxy. Dotor Khuree. Photo: Heradonlkham. The band members all met at the Mongolian State University of Arts and Culture and were already friends. The main calling to start making the music we aim to make today began with my childhood and my deep love for Mongolian long songs and the morin khuur while growing up in the countryside. The older I got, the more that love grew, and I aspired to incorporate traditional musical elements into my own music. After forming the band, I told the others about the kind of Mongolian music I wanted to make, and all our members received the idea with real enthusiasm. That was how the basis of Dotor Khuree’s present sound came to be. Another important factor was definitely our university mentors and teachers, who inspired and encouraged us to stay close to our Mongolian musical roots and stressed the importance of contributing to their development. That was something that really stayed with us. One of the things that immediately stood out to me was that your music can sound distinctly Mongolian even when you are using primarily contemporary instruments. How consciously do you think about creating a “Mongolian” sound? Mandaa : It is definitely a very conscious decision. Because we all love Mongolian music so much, we strongly believe that it is entirely possible to make our sound distinctly Mongolian without using traditional instruments. That is why we spend so much of our rehearsal time coming up with new ideas about how to achieve that. The song ideas usually come from me, and from there we collaborate as a team, discussing arrangements and musical timbres with the shared goal of creating a distinctly Mongolian sound using contemporary instruments. We feel that this goal is now gradually coming to life. We are really happy that you noticed it. What musical traditions, older songs or sounds from Mongolia have influenced Dotor Khuree most strongly? When you reinterpret traditional or older material, how do you decide what to preserve and what to transform? Gomboo : So many Mongolian musical traditions influence us. Long songs, or urtiin duu , and the morin khuur have so many different varieties. The techniques and sounds vary from region to region: the far western regions of Mongolia have very distinctive sounds, while the Gobi provinces have something different again. That is always very inspiring. Dotor Khuree by the river. Photo: Khulangoo. Several of our songs reflect those nuances of Mongolian folk music and long song. For example, when reinterpreting and rearranging the folk song Shiree Nuur , we made it sound nothing like the original. We shortened the lyrics, using only the first two lines and leaving more room for the listener’s interpretation. The song’s vocal accent in particular blended exceptionally well with our female vocalist’s tone. Rather than directly copying tradition, we wanted to express it through our own unique musical language. Could you tell us about your latest EP? What ideas connect the tracks, and how does it differ from your earlier work? Gomboo : It is always interesting for us to make music using traditional vocal styles and a Mongolian feel, while adding our own modern elements. While making this kind of music, it almost feels as though something awakens within us. In fact, the Dotor Khuree EP can be described as “our awakened spirit”. Through this EP, compared with our Zarimdaa Zuils LP, we express even more strongly our connection to our national culture and heritage – something that is always close to our hearts. Roxy : On our debut LP, Zarimdaa Zuils , the band explored a wider range of genres, even dipping into jazz fusion and bossa nova, so the record is more poly-genre. On the Dotor Khuree EP, the band continued exploring the original idea that began with songs such as Shiree Nuur and Ertnii Saikhan on the first LP. At its core, that has always been about creating a distinct Mongolian sound with a Dotor Khuree feel. Is there a particular song on the EP that you feel best represents what Dotor Khuree is trying to do musically? Could you take us through how that track developed? Manda a: Every song on the EP expresses the direction we want to take with our future sound, but especially Ergen Dervene , the album intro. The song includes many elements of Mongolian musical traditions, such as folk-song elements, ritual chants, biyelgee – traditional Mongolian dance rhythms – and circular dancing motifs. The lyrics were co-written by singer Tsetsen and keyboardist Narmandakh, who also finalised the composition, while the entire band collaborated on the production. The composition is vocal-oriented, with the voice playing the main role and the other musical instruments supporting the central melody. Roxy : We also recently finished a very creative and interesting project translating the song’s lyrics into English, with help from our friend Unurjargal, who is a book and film translator – a big shout-out to her. Her interpretation might give listeners even more insight into the song. She translated the title as Spreading Wings . Members of Dotor Khuree. Photo: Heradonlkham. Another of our favourites is Nariin Saihan Heer . The lyrics come from a Mongolian folk song of the same name, but the music is an entirely new Dotor Khuree composition. The title translates as The Fine Bay Horse , but the meaning of the song goes much deeper. There is often an expectation outside Mongolia that “Mongolian music” should involve
title: Dotor Khuree: “We want to make Mongolian music with contemporary instruments”

body: 2 October 2026 Daniyar Sadvakasov Edited by: Mathieu Lemoine Tags Artificial intelligence Electricity Infrastructure Kazakhstan A sign for the Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz, where Kazakhstan plans to develop a major cluster of AI and data centre infrastructure. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Kazakhstan has begun building a major data centre cluster in the industrial city of Ekibastuz. Its first phase will require around 50 MW of power, but the government’s longer-term ambition is to expand the site to as much as 1 GW. As the country seeks to position itself as a regional hub for artificial intelligence and computing, questions remain over whether its electricity and water infrastructure can keep pace In early 2026, Kazakhstan launched construction of its Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz, in the northern Pavlodar region, following instructions from President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. The first facility in the planned cluster is expected to have an energy capacity of around 50 MW. Depending on investor demand, however, the campus could eventually expand to as much as 1 GW and occupy up to 1,300 hectares. Ekibastuz was not chosen by accident. The city is one of Kazakhstan’s main energy centres and is home to the Ekibastuz GRES-1 and GRES-2 coal-fired power stations. Yet the scale of the project raises questions over whether Kazakhstan can generate enough electricity for such a large new consumer, how the data centres will be supplied with water, and what environmental pressures the development could create. What is Kazakhstan planning to build? According to the Pavlodar regional administration, the precise distribution of land between individual data centres, energy facilities and other infrastructure will be determined as project documentation is developed. The first stage includes data centre facilities, energy and engineering infrastructure, administrative buildings and AI computing infrastructure. Work is currently under way on site preparation, foundations, administrative facilities, checkpoints and the necessary engineering infrastructure. Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov inspects progress on the Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz. Photo: Prime Minister of Kazakhstan’s official website. The authorities say the initial stage will require around 50 MW, with capacity subsequently increasing in phases. Additional land has been reserved to allow the campus to expand if demand from investors and technology companies materialises. Kazakhtelecom, one of the operators involved in the Data Center Valley project, told Novastan that the project envisages a hybrid cooling system combining precision air conditioning with closed liquid-cooling circuits using non-freezing liquid solutions. Construction has already begun, but public hearings with local residents have not yet taken place. The Pavlodar regional administration said hearings would be held after the necessary project documentation had been completed and the procedures required for environmental assessment had been carried out. The biggest question: electricity Connecting a new consumer with an eventual capacity of 1 GW would be unrealistic under Kazakhstan’s current energy conditions if such capacity were required all at once, according to Yerkebulan Kozhmambet, a member of the Public Council on Fuel and Energy Issues under Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy. “If we are being honest, today this looks unrealistic, particularly given that the average age of our generating capacity is more than 65 years,” Kozhmambet said. A phased project would be possible, he added, provided new generation and grid infrastructure were developed at the same time. The first launch complex is expected to require 50 MW and is scheduled to enter operation in June 2027, while 1 GW represents a longer-term target rather than capacity the power system is expected to provide immediately. The scale is nevertheless considerable. According to Kozhmambet, a continuous 1 GW load would consume around 8.76 billion kWh of electricity annually. Kazakhstan’s total annual electricity consumption is approximately 110-115 billion kWh, meaning the completed Data Center Valley could theoretically account for around 7-8 percent of current national consumption. “No region today has a free reserve of this scale,” he said. The project also comes as Kazakhstan’s electricity system has faced shortages and imports, particularly from Russia during peak periods. Kozhmambet warned that if the full 1 GW capacity were introduced before Kazakhstan achieves a sustainable electricity surplus, the new data centres could absorb that additional generation and push the system back into deficit. Energy expert Asset Nauryzbayev takes a less pessimistic view. He argues that 1 GW would not necessarily pose a major problem for Ekibastuz if the development of the data centres is synchronised with new generating capacity. “If I understand the government’s intention correctly, it is based on the Soviet project to build four 4 GW power stations in Ekibastuz,” Nauryzbayev said. “In today’s conditions, the units would be 660 MW rather than 500 MW. An eight-unit station would therefore generate 5.8 GW. In those circumstances, 1 GW of consumption is absolutely not a large amount.” He also pointed to planned new gas generation in southern Kazakhstan, which he expects to reduce the country’s electricity deficit. But there is an environmental price. “This will undoubtedly create an enormous carbon footprint,” Nauryzbayev said, although he believes the price of carbon offsets is unlikely to fundamentally affect the economics of the project. Read more on Novastan : Carbon neutral by 2060? Kazakhstan’s green pledge faces a reality check There is another potential risk if data centres are completed before the generation intended to supply them. “Data centres will undoubtedly be able to pay more than ordinary consumers,” he said. “That could strongly affect the market if there is no direct link to newly built power stations. Data centres built quickly will take electricity away from ordinary consumers.” Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy says the government plans to add more than 26.3 GW of generating capacity by 2035 through modernisation, new conventional generation, renewable energy projects and nuclear power. Of this, 13.3 GW is planned through 2029. The ministry expects the country to be able to cover domestic electricity demand from 2027 onwards and subsequently develop a surplus sufficient to accommodate energy-intensive AI infrastructure and large data centres. Whether those projects are delivered on schedule will therefore be crucial to Data Center Valley’s longer-term expansion. Could water become the bigger constraint? Electricity may not be the only – or even the most difficult – resource question facing the project. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation told Novastan that it has not yet received an application to establish a water-use limit for Data Center Valley. No specific limit has therefore been set. The ministry said that the appropriate volume would be assessed once an application and supporting documents were submitted. Citing information from the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, it also said planned AI data centres in Kazakhstan would use immersion cooling with specialised liquids, which should not require large volumes of water or restrict supplies to existing users. This description differs from Kazakhtelecom’s statement that Data Center Valley will use a hybrid system combining precision air conditioning and closed liquid-cooling circuits.
