body: Photo: Presidential press service President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and President Serdar Berdimuhamedov held talks on October 8 in Avaza, Turkmenistan. The talks were held on the sidelines of the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, with the two sides focusing on further strengthening their strategic partnership. Photo: Presidential press service The leaders noted positive momentum in trade and economic ties. Bilateral trade has been growing steadily since the beginning of the year, supported in part by the Shavat–Dashoguz cross-border trade zone. The sides stressed the importance of adopting a plan of measures to substantially increase mutual trade. They also agreed to develop an industrial cooperation program covering energy, transport, agriculture and water management, including cooperation between regions. Photo: Presidential press service Following the talks, Mirziyoyev and Berdimuhamedov signed an agreement establishing the Supreme Council of Strategic Partnership. According to President Mirziyoyev’s press service, the agreement will provide an institutional framework for further political dialogue and expanded practical cooperation in priority areas.
title: Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan agree to establish Supreme Council of Strategic Partnership

body: Photo: Francesca Volpi/Bloomberg The figure was 7.7% lower than a month earlier, according to Central Bank data . The foreign currency component of the reserves fell by $702.8 million during the month, while the value of the gold holdings declined by $4.8 billion. At the same time, the physical volume of gold in the reserves increased from 14.1 million troy ounces to 14.3 million troy ounces. This means the decline in the value of the gold reserves was caused by lower prices on the global market rather than a reduction in the amount of gold held. Gold accounted for 90.2% of Uzbekistan’s total international reserves at the beginning of October, up from 90% a month earlier. The volume of international securities remained unchanged at $1.8 billion in September, accounting for around 2.5% of total international reserves. The National Statistics Committee said the Central Bank sold a total of $2.8 billion worth of precious metals from January through September. The figure was nearly three times lower than during the same period in 2025.
title: Uzbekistan’s international reserves drop 7.7% in September despite higher physical gold holdings

body: Photo: Kun.uz No temperature records were broken, but the month ranked among the warmest Septembers in the country’s meteorological records, according to a review published by Uzhydromet. Temperatures above average September brought typically warm early-autumn weather, without sharp temperature swings. Daytime temperatures across most of Uzbekistan generally ranged from 29°C to 34°C, rising to 35–37°C in some areas on the hottest days and reaching 38°C in the south and desert regions. These readings remained below the September temperature records, which stand at 38–40°C across most of the country and 41–42°C in the north, south and desert areas. Temperatures gradually declined during the final week of the month. Daytime highs generally stayed between 24°C and 27°C, reaching 28–30°C in the far south. The average monthly temperature was 1.2–2.5°C above normal across most of Uzbekistan. In the north and parts of the Fergana Valley, temperatures were close to the seasonal average. In Tashkent, September ranked fourth among the warmest months of its kind on record. Dry conditions across most of the country Rainfall was particularly scarce in September. Most of Uzbekistan, apart from the northern and eastern areas, received little or no rain, with only one to three episodes of brief, light showers in some locations. In most parts of Karakalpakstan and the Fergana Valley, however, rainfall exceeded the monthly norm by 1.5–3 times. In some areas, it was four to six times higher than average. Total precipitation in these areas reached 5–14 millimeters, compared with a typical September norm of 2–4 millimeters. Dust haze and strong winds Strong winds of 13–18 meters per second were recorded on some days in the north, south and desert areas, and less frequently in central Uzbekistan. Wind gusts reached 20–21 meters per second over the Ustyurt Plateau on September 2–3 and in the high-altitude areas of Tashkent region on September 20. In some locations, stronger winds stirred up dust close to the ground, while dust haze was frequently observed.
title: Uzbekistan records one of its warmest Septembers, with temperatures up to 2.5°C above normal

body: Ministry of Transport of the Republic of Uzbekistan The prospects for cooperation were discussed on October 7 when Uzbekistan’s Transport Minister Ilhom Mahkamov met with a JBIC delegation led by Hiroki Sekine, senior managing executive officer and board member of the Japanese bank. Sekine noted the growing interest of Japanese financial institutions in projects in Uzbekistan. JBIC plans to participate in financing 14 projects in the country over the next three years, two of them in the transport sector, the Transport Ministry said. The meeting focused on the status of two projects – construction of the new Tashkent airport and the supply of air traffic management systems for the Uzairnavigation Center. The sides discussed the possibility of attracting JBIC financing for both projects. The parties agreed to accelerate joint transport initiatives and continue cooperation on prospective projects. New Tashkent airport The new international airport is being built in Tashkent region under a public-private partnership. In October 2025, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev reviewed the project and formally launched construction. The private partners selected for the project are Saudi Arabia’s Vision Invest, Japan’s Sojitz and South Korea’s Incheon International Airport Corporation (IIAC). The consortium shares are divided among Vision Invest with 45%, Sojitz with 30%, IIAC with 15% and Uzbekistan Airports with 10%. The airport is expected to handle up to 20 million passengers and 129,000 tonnes of cargo annually once commissioned. It will be capable of handling up to 30 takeoffs and landings per hour and accommodating 62 aircraft simultaneously. The passenger terminal will be four times larger than the existing complex and could eventually handle up to 46 million passengers a year. More than 40 passenger boarding bridges and 160 aircraft parking stands are planned. The airport will be connected to the Tashkent–Samarkand, Tashkent–Andijan and Tashkent–Bostanlyk toll roads. A railway station for high-speed trains and shuttle services connecting Tashkent with New Tashkent are also planned. South Korea’s The Korea Herald
title: JBIC considers financing new Tashkent airport project

body: The man had travelled to Sergeli district to buy a car when the cash fell out of his bag while he was travelling on the metro from Olmazor station to Sergeli. Officers working in the Tashkent Metro found the money and carried out checks to establish its lawful owner. The $10,000 was subsequently returned to him in full, the Interior Ministry said . The man said he realized the money was missing only after reaching the car market. “I came from Olmazor metro station to Sergeli, and at some point the $10,000 fell out of my bag. I was in a hurry and had been running. I’m grateful to the metro staff. The Interior Ministry officers found the money and tracked me down using Face ID. I realized I had lost it at the car market,” he said in Uzbek. “I guess it came back to me because I had earned it through honest, hard work. Many thanks to the Interior Ministry.”
title: Tashkent Metro officers return $10,000 lost by Kazakh citizen

body: Photo: AP The bank also upgraded its 2027 growth forecast for Uzbekistan from 6.7% to 7.5%. The economy is expected to expand by 7.1% in 2028. The revised forecasts were published on October 6 in the World Bank’s latest Europe and Central Asia Economic Update, titled “Making AI Work: Jobs, Firms, and Productivity.” At 7.9%, Uzbekistan is expected to record the second-highest growth rate among developing economies in Europe and Central Asia in 2026, behind Kyrgyzstan at 9.6%. In 2027, Uzbekistan is projected to lead the group with 7.5% growth. The World Bank attributed Uzbekistan’s continued growth to resilient domestic demand, supported by higher real wages and employment, remittances and investment in infrastructure, energy and housing. It also pointed to ongoing structural reforms. Remittances to Uzbekistan rose 13% in the first half of 2026 to a record $9.2 billion for the period, with nearly 70% coming from Russia. Excluding gold, Uzbekistan’s exports increased by almost 30%, driven by stronger shipments to China and neighboring Central Asian countries. Overall exports declined, however, because of lower gold exports. The country also continues to attract substantial foreign direct investment, including into major energy, digital infrastructure and industrial projects. The World Bank said investments financed through foreign sources, including direct investment and loans, accounted for more than 70% of total investment in Uzbekistan. The bank expects Uzbekistan’s budget deficit to remain broadly unchanged in 2026 at 2.2% of GDP. Higher social and investment spending is expected to be offset by reduced energy subsidies and targeted lending to state-owned enterprises, along with stronger budget revenues. More than 60% of private-sector jobs in Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan remain informal, with little change in the share over the past five years. The World Bank said current economic growth was not generating enough productive formal jobs as the working-age population continues to expand. Central Asia remains the fastest-growing subregion Central Asia remains the fastest-growing subregion of Europe and Central Asia, with economic growth projected at 5.8% in 2026. Domestic demand and government investment in transport and energy are expected to continue supporting activity.
title: World Bank upgrades Uzbekistan’s 2026, 2027 growth forecasts

body: Photo: Getty images Speaking to the public, Ashropov said the risks associated with cross-border cybercrime were growing alongside the country’s digitalization. He said measures were being taken to combat cybercrime, introduce anti-fraud mechanisms in the banking and financial system, and strengthen information security. Mechanisms and measures to counter crimes committed using information technology have also been set out under the Uzbekistan–2030 strategy and a presidential decision dated April 30, 2025. Ashropov said law enforcement alone could not effectively tackle cybercrime, as fraudsters often exploit people’s carelessness and limited digital literacy. He urged parents, teachers, community activists and other citizens to help relatives and those around them understand basic cybersecurity rules. People were advised not to open or download suspicious or unknown files sent through social media, particularly APK files. The warning applies even when such files appear to have been sent by a friend or relative. Ashropov also warned against sharing personal information with callers from unfamiliar numbers who claim to represent government agencies or other organizations. He stressed that officials do not ask citizens for codes or passwords over the phone. People were also urged to avoid fake online platforms promising to multiply their money several times over in a short period. When shopping online, consumers should verify a seller’s reliability before making any advance payment. The deputy interior minister separately stressed that bank card PINs and SMS codes received on a phone should never be shared with anyone. According to official figures, cybercrime accounted for 49.6% of all crimes recorded in Uzbekistan in 2025. The number of such offenses has increased every year since 2021. The Central Bank, Interior Ministry and Prosecutor General’s Office are currently working together to combat cybercrime, the report said.

body: Thermal power plants have completely stopped using fuel oil, with its use being monitored by the National Committee for Ecology and Climate Change. Photo: Ministry of Energy Around 300 hectares of greenhouses in Tashkent have changed their business profile due to their impact on air pollution in the city, Tashkent Mayor Shavkat Umurzakov said in an interview with Gazeta.uz. body: The state-owned bank is considering exiting the market amid growing interest from private Korean lenders. Photo: kdb.uz Korea Development Bank (KDB) is considering selling its subsidiary KDB Bank Uzbekistan, Maeil Business reports . According to the publication, the South Korean state-owned bank plans to reorganize its overseas network to improve efficiency. It currently has 25 entities abroad, including 12 branches, seven subsidiaries and six representative offices. The optimization could primarily affect markets where KDB has operated for a long time but has not expanded its activities. Maeil Business cited its representative offices in Moscow and Abu Dhabi, which have been operating since 2013, as examples. KDB also plans to sell branches in countries where Korean commercial banks are beginning operations, including Uzbekistan. The state-owned bank entered the Uzbek market in 2006 after acquiring Daewoo Group’s stake in UzDaewoo Bank, which had been established nine years earlier. However, KDB Bank Uzbekistan has not shown “clear results” over the past two decades, the publication said. Advertising on Spot At the same time, private Korean banks have stepped up efforts in recent years to establish operations in Uzbekistan. Shinhan Bank is preparing to open a local subsidiary, while Hana Bank also plans to open an office in the country. Another South Korean state-owned lender, the Export-Import Bank of Korea, has a representative office in Tashkent. According to a Maeil source in the investment banking sector, KDB conducted a demand survey involving Shinhan Bank and Hana Bank. However, due to “negative sentiment toward the sale”, no decision has yet been made regarding KDB Bank Uzbekistan. The publication linked KDB’s overseas network restructuring to a policy aimed at improving the efficiency of government institutions launched by South Korean President Lee Jae-myung. In particular, the Ministry of Economy and Finance plans to consolidate overseas offices of South Korean state institutions in the US, Vietnam, Kenya and the UAE. Shinhan Bank has maintained a representative office in Tashkent since 2009. In February 2025, representatives of Shinhan Financial Group said they planned to strengthen their position in Uzbekistan’s banking market during talks with the Central Bank. South Korean media reported in April that Shinhan Bank planned to establish a subsidiary in Uzbekistan by 2027. The subsidiary’s establishment, along with digital banking and solutions for small and medium-sized businesses, was also among the key topics discussed by Shinhan Financial Group CEO Jin Ok-dong and President Shavkat Mirziyoyev during the latter’s visit to Seoul in September. body: Employers will be required to pay students a monthly salary of at least the minimum wage, currently 1.36 million soums. Photo: Yevgeniy Sorochin / Spot President Shavkat Mirziyoyev signed a decree on September 29 on developing the dual education system in higher education institutions. The document was published on Lex.uz. The decree introduces the “enterprise — university — targeted training” principle to prepare highly qualified specialists. The new approach is intended to strengthen the integration of employers with education and ensure graduates have guaranteed employment. Starting from the 2027−2028 academic year, universities will launch dual education programmes. Enterprises will be able to place orders for student training on the condition that graduates are subsequently hired. Each year, by September 1, universities, in coordination with the Ministry of Higher Education, will determine bachelor’s programmes where dual education will be offered. They will also be able to set admission quotas for these programmes. Advertising on Spot Students admitted under orders from organizations on a tuition-based contract will be enrolled by October 1. Depending on the employer’s order, applicants may be admitted to the relevant programme without exams or through competitive examination. The employer will be required to pay each student a monthly salary of at least one minimum wage, currently 1.36 million soums. In return, students will be required to work for the company for at least two years after graduation. The theoretical component of dual education must account for at least 30% of the programme. Practical training will take place at the employer’s facilities with the participation of a mentor. Each mentor may supervise up to 15 students and receive 30 hours of workload per student annually. State organizations will also be allowed to place training orders using funds from their extra-budgetary sources. Consortia involving several organizations and staff rotation between them will also be permitted. Graduates of technical schools enrolled in programmes integrated with the higher education system will be able to continue studying in their field through dual education from the second or third year. Students in dual education programmes in priority fields with high academic performance will be able to switch to state-funded places from their second year. These fields include engineering, manufacturing and processing, architecture and construction, and agriculture. Children from families listed in the Social Registry will study under dual education programmes on a state-funded basis throughout their entire period of study. Universities may also provide them with social scholarships. Employers will be allowed to establish practical training facilities at partner universities at their own expense. Universities, in turn, will be allowed to organize production or service activities related to their training programmes under direct contracts with employers. They will also be able to organize professional courses in fields that are in demand on the labour market. body: Satellite data will be used to monitor land, natural resources and environmental risks, as well as track pollution. Photo: Press Service of the President of the Kyrgyz Republic Kyrgyzstan’s first national satellite was launched into orbit on October 1 from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The launch was carried out using SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket, the Kyrgyz president’s press service reported . The satellite was placed into orbit as part of a group of spacecraft launched by a single carrier rocket. Its launch was the result of cooperation between Kyrgyzstan and the United Arab Emirates. The satellite will be controlled from a mission control center in Bishkek. The data collected will be used to monitor agricultural land, glaciers, water resources, forests and pastures, as well as changes in natural ecosystems. Satellite data will also help identify illegal use of mineral resources, unauthorized landfills and other sources of pollution, as well as optimize logistics routes. Another key area will be monitoring natural hazards. The data will help detect signs of droughts, floods, landslides, mudflows and forest fires, enabling a faster response and helping reduce potential damage. This will allow the data to be used in government decision-making, investment planning and monitoring the implementation of state programmes. “The use of satellite data combined with supercomputing capabilities will provide a foundation for more accurate and efficient management of Kyrgyzstan’s economic and natural resources”, the statement said. body: The current account deficit reached $6.2 billion in the first half of 2026, increasing by about $410 million in the second quarter. Photo: Ilya Semendeev / Spot Uzbekistan’s total external debt increased by $1.9 billion compared with the beginning of 2026, reaching $84.1 billion by the end of the first half of the year. This was reported by the Central Bank in its review of the country’s balance of payments, international investment position and external debt. Uzbekistan’s external sector continued to show positive trends recorded in previous periods. Key factors included higher exports of goods and services excluding gold, an increase in international remittances and continued strong inflows of foreign investment. In January-June, the current account deficit amounted to about $6.2 billion, compared with $5.79 billion in the first quarter . The deficit therefore increased by around $410 million in the second quarter. The main factor remained the negative trade balance, which reached $13.4 billion in the first half of the year, compared with $8.3 billion in January-March. Advertising on Spot Total exports amounted to $15.4 billion in the first half of the year, down 8.6% from the same period last year. In the second quarter, exports reached about $9.8 billion, compared with $5.6 billion in the first quarter. The decline in annual export figures was mainly driven by lower gold sales, while exports of goods excluding gold increased by 27% and exports of services rose by 45%. Imports increased by 24% year-on-year in January-June, reaching $28.8 billion. In the second quarter, imports amounted to about $14.9 billion, compared with $13.9 billion in the first quarter. The largest share of imports consisted of machinery and equipment, vehicles, chemical and mineral products, and food products. The negative trade balance was partly offset by positive balances in primary and secondary income, which amounted to $1.9 billion and $5.3 billion, respectively, in the first half of the year. In the first quarter, secondary income had a positive balance of $2.5 billion, while primary income recorded a deficit of $43 million. The current account deficit was financed through direct, portfolio and other investment operations, as well as other sources. Net foreign direct investment inflows amounted to $2.3 billion in the first half of the year, with about $1.6 billion recorded in the second quarter. Net portfolio investment inflows reached around $2 billion, compared with $4.1 million in the first quarter. Other investment recorded a net inflow of about $1.5 billion, around $400 million of which came in the second quarter. As a result, the financial account deficit increased from $5 billion in the first quarter to $7.5 billion in the first half of the year. Uzbekistan’s net international investment position declined by $8.3 billion in the second quarter, from $21.6 billion as of April 1 to $13.3 billion as of July 1. Overall, it decreased by 34% from the beginning of the year. The external assets of residents declined by $1.1 billion in the first half of the year, after increasing by $2.6 billion in the first quarter. This means assets fell by around $3.7 billion in the second quarter. International reserves decreased by $2.5 billion due to lower global gold prices, while assets related to direct and other investments increased by $1.4 billion. At the same time, external liabilities of residents increased by $5.8 billion in the first half of the year. By comparison, liabilities rose by $534 million in the first quarter, meaning they increased by around $5.3 billion in the second quarter. As of July 1, Uzbekistan’s total external debt stood at $84.1 billion, up from $82.2 billion as of April 1. Public external debt increased from $40.5 billion to $41.7 billion, while corporate external debt rose from $41.7 billion to $42.4 billion. The Central Bank clarified that corporate external debt includes private-sector borrowing without state guarantees. The government has no obligations related to this debt, and repayments are made from companies' and banks' own funds. The IMF has also noted Uzbekistan’s low debt burden, with a significant share of external debt raised on concessional terms. body: Entrepreneurs will receive tax incentives, preferential loans and discounts on advertising. Photo: Presidential Press Service The Uzbekistan Football Association has announced a tender to transfer 11 professional football clubs to entrepreneurs or groups of entrepreneurs under trust management. The UFA announced the tender on September 26 via its Telegram channel. The tender is being held in accordance with a presidential decree dated March 24, 2026, aimed at improving sports financing mechanisms and expanding private-sector involvement in the sector. The clubs included in the tender are Bunyodkor, Bukhara, Dinamo, Qizilqum, Navbahor, Nasaf, Neftchi, Lokomotiv, Mash’al, AGMK and Pakhtakor. Participants are required to provide sponsorship funding equivalent to at least 20% of the club’s total annual operating expenses. Advertising on Spot Entrepreneurs taking clubs under trust management will receive a number of tax and financial incentives. In particular, when calculating corporate income tax, taxable profit may be reduced by the amount of charitable donations allocated to financing the club’s activities, but by no more than 10% of taxable profit. Football players at the clubs will be exempt from personal income tax, while the social tax rate applicable to them will be set at 1%. Commercial banks will also provide five-year loans at an annual interest rate of 14%, with a one-year grace period, for acquiring clubs or constructing, reconstructing and renovating sports facilities. Borrowers will need to provide liquid collateral and a viable business plan. Buildings, structures and land plots held on the clubs' balance sheets cannot be used as collateral. In addition, entrepreneurs will receive a 50% discount on advertising their products and services on central and regional television channels of Uzbekistan’s National Television and Radio Company during broadcasts aimed at promoting sports. body: The military transport aircraft will primarily be used for humanitarian and search-and-rescue missions. Photo: Embraer Embraer has officially delivered the first C-390 Millennium aircraft to the Uzbekistan Air Force, the manufacturer reported . The handover ceremony was held on September 25 at Embraer’s facility in Gavião Peixoto, Brazil. It was attended by Major General Akhmad Burkhonov, Commander of the Uzbekistan Air Force, and Olimkhon Rustamov, Director of the state institution Uztechtrade. Uzbekistan will become the first operator of the C-390 in Central Asia, the company said. The contract for the supply of the aircraft and spare parts, as well as pilot training and technical support, was signed at the end of 2024. “The delivery of the first C-390 Millennium marks an important step in modernizing Uzbekistan’s air force. The aircraft’s exceptional performance, adaptability and multi-mission capabilities will enable us to carry out a wide range of tasks more efficiently”, Burkhonov said. Advertising on Spot Bosco da Costa Junior, CEO of Embraer Defense & Security, congratulated Uzbekistan on “joining the growing global community of C-390 operators”. According to him, the company is ready to support Tashkent in the aviation sector for decades to come. The C-390 Millennium military transport aircraft was designed in the early 21st century and has been produced by Embraer since 2014. It has a payload capacity of up to 26 tons and can reach a cruising speed of up to 470 knots (870 km/h). The aircraft can be used to transport cargo and passengers, conduct search-and-rescue and humanitarian operations, perform medical evacuations, and fight fires from the air. It is designed to operate from temporary and unpaved runways. The C-390 can also be equipped with a special aerial refueling system, allowing the aircraft to operate both as a tanker and as a receiver of fuel. In addition to Uzbekistan and Brazil, the C-390 Millennium is operated by the Czech Republic, Hungary and Portugal. The aircraft has also been selected by the air forces of the Netherlands, Austria, Slovakia, Sweden, Lithuania, Colombia, South Korea and the UAE. Embraer officially announced Uzbekistan’s purchase of C-390 Millennium military transport aircraft at the Singapore Airshow in February. According to the announcement, the aircraft will be used mainly for transport and humanitarian missions. In mid-September, the company announced that it had completed the first aircraft for Uzbekistan. At the time, it also published photos of the C-390 Millennium featuring Uzbekistan’s insignia and the aircraft registration number UK 39010. body: Foreign-currency bonds issued by Asia Alliance Bank and Universalbank are now trading on the exchange. Photo: Uzse Trading in foreign-currency bonds began on the Republican Stock Exchange “Toshkent” on September 28, the exchange’s press service reported . The exchange’s quotation list includes foreign-currency-denominated bonds issued by two issuers — Asia Alliance Bank and Universalbank. The total volume of the issues is $30 million. Asia Alliance Bank became the first issuer in Uzbekistan to register a foreign-currency corporate bond issue on September 10. The bank will place 200,000 securities with a nominal value of $100 each. The bonds will trade on the exchange under the ticker AAB1B3U for 1,095 days (three years). The coupon rate is 7% per year, with coupon payments made quarterly. Advertising on Spot Universalbank issued 100,000 foreign-currency bonds, each with a nominal value of $100. They are listed on the Tashkent Stock Exchange under the ticker UNVB1B2U. The bonds carry an annual coupon rate of 8.5%, with quarterly payments. The maturity period is 730 days (two years). In April, the National Agency of Perspective Projects approved regulations governing the circulation of foreign-currency bonds in Uzbekistan. The document regulates the issuance, placement, trading and redemption of foreign-currency bonds under the capital market “sandbox”. A company may have foreign-currency bonds worth no more than $50 million outstanding at any one time. Unsecured bonds may be issued only within the issuer’s equity capital. If this limit is exceeded, the company — except for certain banks with high credit ratings — must provide collateral for the amount exceeding the threshold. Collateral for the bonds may include real estate, cash, bank guarantees or insurance policies. Real estate must be appraised at market value and may be accepted as collateral for no more than 75% of the issue’s appraised value. At the same time, real estate may not account for more than 50% of the total collateral. The regulations also establish financial conditions, or covenants, for the issuance of foreign-currency bonds. In addition, they require individuals to purchase foreign-currency bonds only through the banking system. body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan sees 90% of cybercrimes committed from abroad Around 90% of cybercrimes affecting Uzbekistan originate abroad, while cybercrimes accounted for 49.6% of all crimes recorded in the country in 2025 as authorities expand anti-fraud and information security measures. Today, 17:30 2 min read 1 256 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Madina Nurman Around 90% of cybercrimes affecting Uzbekistan are committed from abroad on a cross-border basis, Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs Colonel Ramazon Ashropov said in an address to the public. According to Ashropov, cross-border cyber threats are increasing alongside the expansion of digital technologies. Nearly one in every two crimes committed in Uzbekistan currently involves the use of information technology. In 2025, cybercrimes accounted for 49.6% of all crimes recorded in the country. The number of such offenses has been increasing since 2021. Ashropov said measures are being implemented to counter cybercrime, introduce anti-fraud mechanisms in the banking and financial sectors and strengthen information security for citizens. The Uzbekistan-2030 strategy and a presidential decree dated April 30, 2025, set out mechanisms and measures aimed at combating crimes involving information technology. The Deputy Minister noted that law enforcement measures alone are insufficient to address cybercrime, as fraudsters can exploit a lack of digital literacy and insufficient caution among internet users. He called for parents, teachers, community activists and other citizens to explain cybersecurity rules to people around them. Among the recommendations, citizens were advised not to open or download suspicious or unknown files received through social media, particularly files in APK format. Ashropov said users should remain cautious even when such files appear to have been sent by acquaintances or people close to them. Citizens were also advised not to provide personal information to callers from unknown numbers who claim to represent government agencies or other organizations. Ashropov stressed that citizens are not asked to provide codes or passwords over the phone. The recommendations also covered online investment and shopping schemes. Citizens were advised not to trust online platforms promising to multiply their money several times within a short period. When purchasing goods online, users were advised against making advance payments before verifying the reliability of the seller. Ashropov separately warned against sharing bank card PINs or SMS verification codes received on mobile phones with other people. He identified adherence to basic cybersecurity rules and public vigilance as measures that can reduce exposure to cybercrime. body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan proposes new trade, transport and energy initiatives for Central Asia, Azerbaijan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has proposed new initiatives to expand trade and investment, strengthen transport corridors and deepen energy and technology cooperation between Central Asia and Azerbaijan at a regional summit in Turkmenistan. Today, 15:02 5 min read 667 views 0 comments 0 Foto: Prezident matbuot xizmati Uzbekistan has proposed new mechanisms to deepen trade, investment, transport, energy and technology cooperation between Central Asia and Azerbaijan, including a regional business forum and joint industrial and digital projects. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev made the proposals at the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, held in the Avaza National Tourist Zone in Turkmenistan on October 8. The meeting was chaired by Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedow and attended by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov and Tajik President Emomali Rahmon. Mirziyoyev noted that Central Asia had undergone significant changes in recent years and called for a flexible regional cooperation format based on mutual respect, trust and pragmatism. Source: Presidential Press Service “ “The world is changing rapidly, tensions are rising, trade and transport links are being reshaped and new risks are emerging,” the Uzbek president said. He proposed creating a broader space of cooperation with regions that have established historical, economic and transport links with Central Asia, with a focus on trade, transport, energy, industry and new technologies. The issues could be discussed at an international conference titled “Interregional Dialogue for Peace and Sustainable Interdependence: A Central Asian Approach”, which Uzbekistan plans to host in Tashkent next year. Source: Presidential Press Service Trade and investment Mirziyoyev called for economic cooperation to move beyond conventional trade toward joint production and investment. “ “We have already reached a point where standard mutual trade is no longer sufficient; we need to create finished products together.The formula "six economies – one product" perfectly captures the essence of what we should strive for,” he said. He proposed holding a Central Asian-Azerbaijani business forum in Khiva in 2027 and establishing a dedicated platform to provide financial and technical support for joint investment projects. The Uzbek president also proposed that the Council of Trade and Investment Ministers examine the initiative at its next meeting in Ashgabat. Source: Presidential Press Service Transport corridors Mirziyoyev also called for a more integrated approach to regional transport infrastructure, arguing that roads and railways should be developed alongside manufacturing, logistics and industrial facilities. “ “We can become one of the key land routes for global trade and, at the same time, a major hub of economic activity. But to achieve this, it is not enough simply to build roads and railways. We need a common approach to the development of transport infrastructure,” he said. Source: Presidential Press Service He proposed accelerating the establishment of an Infrastructure Development Council and holding its first meeting in Uzbekistan. According to Mirziyoyev, new transport corridors should be designed as interconnected economic systems, with manufacturing enterprises, logistics and service facilities and industrial zones located along them. Source: Presidential Press Service Energy and climate Energy was another key area of the proposed cooperation. Mirziyoyev highlighted the region’s diverse energy resources, including hydrocarbons, hydropower, solar and wind generation. He proposed developing a joint concept for the region’s low-carbon energy potential. The initiative would help coordinate the construction of new generation capacity, energy storage systems and new energy corridors. Source: Presidential Press Service The leaders also addressed water resources and climate change. Mirziyoyev called for wider use of digital monitoring, modernization of irrigation networks and expansion of water-saving technologies. He also called for the full implementation of the joint initiative to declare a decade of practical action on water management in Central Asia. Source: Presidential Press Service As Uzbekistan is set to chair the International Fund for Saving the Aral Sea next year, Mirziyoyev outlined priorities including improving the fund’s effectiveness, launching new environmental projects and attracting additional financing. He also called for a permanent and substantive dialogue with Afghanistan on water-resource use, taking into account the interests of all countries in the region. Source: Presidential Press Service Clean air and critical minerals The Uzbek president proposed launching the international consortium “Clean Air of Central Asia”, promoted by Uzbekistan, with a pilot programme aimed at the environmental modernization of industrial zones, agroclusters and transport hubs across the region. Critical minerals were also identified as a growing area of regional cooperation. Mirziyoyev called for intensified efforts to establish a regional alliance on critical minerals and proposed creating a unified digital map of critical mineral reserves in Central Asia as one of its first steps. Source: Presidential Press Service AI and regional data infrastructure Mirziyoyev also highlighted artificial intelligence and big data as key drivers of future economic competitiveness. “ “Artificial intelligence and big data are already transforming industry, transport, energy, agriculture, education, and public administration. The productivity of our economies and their ability to compete in the future will depend to a large extent on these technologies,” he said. Uzbekistan proposed combining the countries’ capabilities to develop common computing infrastructure based on a network of interconnected national data centers. The president also called for greater coordination in developing human capital. He proposed creating a regional atlas of professions and skills that will be in high demand, based on forecasts of future workforce needs. The initiative would allow universities and vocational institutions to train specialists for major regional projects in industry, transport, energy and digital technologies. Mirziyoyev concluded by calling for the achievements of recent years to be consolidated and regional cooperation to be developed as a long-term system. body: Economics Uzbekistan projects inflation to fall to 5% by 2027 Uzbekistan’s Central Bank expects inflation to decline from 6.5% in 2026 to 5% by 2027, while GDP growth is projected at 7.5–8% this year before moderating to 6–7% by 2028. 28 September, 15:27 3 min read 1 127 views 0 comments 0 “Daryo” / Madina Nurman Uzbekistan’s annual inflation rate is projected to decline to 5% by 2027, while economic growth could reach 7.5–8% in 2026, according to the Central Bank’s Monetary Policy Review. The regulator expects inflation to reach 6.5% in 2026 before declining further. For comparison, annual inflation stood at 9.8% in 2024 and 7.3% in 2025. The Central Bank’s forecasts also envisage stabilizing annual inflation at the 5% target by 2028. Economic activity is expected to remain relatively strong in the near term. The Central Bank projects Uzbekistan’s economy to expand by 7.5–8% this year, although growth is expected to moderate to 6–7% by 2028. The regulator expects economic conditions in Uzbekistan’s main trading partners to continue supporting external demand for Uzbek exports and remittance inflows. At the same time, it identified volatility in global energy prices and possible increases in logistics costs among the external risks to the inflation outlook. “The continued relative stability of economic activity in key trading partner countries is expected to support external demand for our exports and the inflow of remittances. At the same time, high volatility in energy prices and potential increases in logistics costs remain as external inflationary risks,” the Central Bank said. The review also refers to updated forecasts from the International Monetary Fund. According to the figures cited by the Central Bank, global economic growth is projected at 3% in 2026, 0.1 percentage points below the previous forecast. Growth is then expected to reach 3.4% in 2027, representing an upward revision of 0.2 percentage points. The outlook reflects continued constraints on global economic activity associated with geopolitical shocks and high energy costs in the short term, while a gradual recovery in energy supplies and logistics chains is expected in the following year. Uzbekistan’s current inflation target follows a presidential decree adopted in 2019, which set a permanent target of 5% and initially envisaged reaching that level by 2023. The target was not achieved within the original timeframe. The Central Bank has linked the delay to several factors, including the effects of monopolies and insufficient competition in some markets. Central Bank Chairman Timur Ishmetov said inflation forecasts depend on both domestic and external conditions and take into account the government’s structural reforms. “Our forecast is based on internal and external factors. However, if circumstances change, it is natural for the forecast to change as well. In our projections, we always factor in the government’s continued pursuit of structural reforms across various markets,” Ishmetov said. He noted that further market liberalization remains necessary for some commodity markets and that these conditions affect inflation. The Central Bank is working with the government to reduce the impact of non-monetary factors on price growth. “There are diverse commodity markets; in some, we still need to proceed with market liberalization. Naturally, this impacts inflation levels. Work is currently underway regarding those specific commodities,” Ishmetov said. According to the Central Bank chairman, work is also underway to strengthen competition and reduce the concentration of production and imports for five or six specific commodities. He said the effectiveness of these measures would influence the outcome of monetary policy. Recent data cited in the review show that annual price growth has remained below 7% since May. Annual inflation stood at 5.5% in May before reaching 6.4% in both June and July. It subsequently slowed to 6.2% in August. body: Kazakhstan Kazakhstan steps up efforts to restore Northern Aral Sea, preserve Caspian Sea Kazakhstan is expanding efforts to restore the Northern Aral Sea and preserve the Caspian Sea, with the Northern Aral Sea’s water volume reaching 23.4bn cubic meters as the government advances new restoration, water-efficiency and regional cooperation measures. Today, 14:20 4 min read 60 views 0 comments 0 Source: Official Information Source of the Prime minister of Kazakhstan Kazakhstan is stepping up efforts to restore the Northern Aral Sea and protect the Caspian Sea, with measures focused on increasing water inflows, restoring biodiversity, improving water efficiency and strengthening interstate cooperation. The initiatives are being implemented under directives issued by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in his State-of-the-Nation Address, “Kazakhstan in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Current Tasks and Solutions Through Digital Transformation.” The volume of water in the Northern Aral Sea has increased to 23.4bn cubic meters, up from 18.9bn cubic meters in 2022, 21bn cubic meters in 2023 and 22bn cubic meters in 2024. Around 1.5bn cubic meters of water has been directed into the sea since the beginning of 2026. Over the past two decades, the Northern Aral Sea’s surface area has expanded by 36%, while its water volume has nearly doubled and salinity has fallen by half, supporting the recovery of aquatic life and the surrounding ecosystem. The Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation maintains an annual flow of at least 2bn cubic meters of water through the Syr Darya riverbed to sustain these improvements. Kazakhstan, together with the World Bank, has also developed the next phase of the Northern Aral Sea restoration project. It includes reconstructing the Kokaral Dam and raising the sea’s water level to 44 meters above sea level under the Baltic elevation system. Over the next five to six years, the reservoir’s surface area is expected to reach 3,900 sq km, while its water volume is projected to increase to 34bn cubic meters. More than 160 projects to modernize and automate irrigation systems are also planned in the Aral-Syr Darya basin in the Turkestan and Kyzylorda regions. The projects are expected to improve water efficiency and allow conserved water to be redirected to the Northern Aral Sea. Kazakhstan is also continuing efforts to combat desertification on the dried seabed of the Aral Sea. The government plans to establish saksaul and other halophyte plantations across 1mn–1.5mn hectares of the former seabed. So far, 3,400 tonnes of seeds have been sown and 56.2mn saksaul saplings planted, covering 1.1mn hectares. A regional branch of the Kazakh Research Institute of Forestry and Agroforestry has been established to provide scientific support for the work. A 33-hectare forest nursery capable of producing 3mn saplings annually has also been completed. Another nursery is being established directly on the dried seabed to grow planting material under local arid conditions, improving the plants’ adaptation and survival rates. Kazakhstan prepares interstate program for Caspian Sea Kazakhstan is simultaneously strengthening efforts to address declining water levels in the Caspian Sea and protect its ecosystem. The Caspian Sea covers around 390,000 sq km and contains approximately 76,000 cubic km of water, with a coastline stretching 6,500 km. Around 130 rivers flow into the sea, supplying an average of 290 cubic km of water annually. The Volga accounts for about 80% of the inflow, while the Ural contributes around 3.5%. In the Zhaiyq-Caspian basin, 6 cubic km of water flowed from the Zhaiyq (Ural) River into the Caspian Sea in 2025, while the Qighash River contributed 4.9 cubic km. Combined inflows from the two rivers reached around 7.3 cubic km in 2026. Kazakhstan is preparing an interstate program for preserving the Caspian Sea with the participation of all five littoral states, alongside plans to establish a dedicated research institute. President Tokayev also proposed creating an SCO Water Research Center at an expanded meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in 2025. International cooperation on the Caspian Sea was discussed in Aktau during the High-Level Dialogue on the Caspian Sea, bringing together government officials, diplomats, UN representatives, international partners, scientists and industry experts. The discussions covered declining water levels, biodiversity protection, pollution and marine debris, monitoring and data exchange, and international financing. With Japanese government support, the project “Enhancing Resilience Amidst Caspian Sea Level Decline” is being implemented to assess and mitigate the effects of declining water levels using scientific data and digital tools. Kazakhstan is also working with the UN Development Programme and other international partners on projects covering marine and coastal resource management, circular economy development, waste management and plastic pollution reduction. A separate area of work focuses on protecting the Caspian Sea’s biodiversity, including the Caspian seal and its habitats. Kazakhstan has completed its legal framework for transboundary water management with neighboring countries and established bilateral commissions to coordinate the shared use of water resources. Following a decade of negotiations, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan signed an agreement last year on the joint management and rational use of transboundary water bodies. The government noted that water diplomacy and coordinated reservoir operation schedules along the Syr Darya have helped maintain stable water inflows into the Northern Aral Sea in recent years, including during periods of low water availability. # aral sea # caspian sea # environment # kazakhstan # restoring # water management Muharrir Moxinur Sultanova All stories Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? body: Sport Uzbekistan rises to 59th in FIFA live ranking after international friendlies Uzbekistan’s national football team has climbed to 59th in the FIFA live ranking after earning a net 6.88 points from three friendly matches, with wins over Iran and Syria and a defeat to South Korea moving the team into sixth place among Asian sides, ahead of Qatar. Today, 14:01 2 min read 5 098 views 0 comments 0 “Daryo” / Jamshidbek Mahmudov Uzbekistan’s national football team added a net 6.88 points to its FIFA ranking total after recording two wins and one defeat across three friendly matches during the FIFA international window. Uzbekistan began the series with victories over Iran and Syria. The national team defeated Iran 3–1, earning 6.83 ranking points, before recording a 4–1 victory over Syria, which added another 3.75 points. Following the two wins, Uzbekistan climbed to 58th place in the FIFA live ranking. The team then faced South Korea away on October 6. South Korea was ranked 32nd at the time of the match. Uzbekistan lost the third friendly 0–2, resulting in a deduction of 3.70 ranking points. The defeat moved the national team down one position to 59th place. Across the three matches, Uzbekistan gained a net 6.88 points and currently has 1,416.56 points in the live ranking. The results also moved Uzbekistan ahead of Qatar and into sixth place among Asian national teams. Japan remains the highest-ranked Asian team with 1,678.31 points and occupies 17th place globally. body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan receives 10.3mn tourists in January–September 2026 Uzbekistan welcomed 10.3mn international tourists in January–September 2026, up 20.4% y/y, while tourism service exports surged 51.2% to $5.3bn, reflecting continued expansion in the country’s tourism sector. Today, 13:34 2 min read 1 390 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Madina Nurman Uzbekistan welcomed 10.3mn tourists between January and September 2026, representing a 20.4% increase compared to the same period last year, according to data released by the Tourism Committee. The figures indicate continued growth in international tourist arrivals, with September alone accounting for 1.2mn visitors. The increase was recorded across several major source markets, including countries in Asia, Europe and North America. China recorded the highest growth rate in tourist arrivals to Uzbekistan during the reporting period. The number of Chinese visitors increased 2.1-fold compared to January–September 2025. Other Asian markets also registered increases. Tourist arrivals from Malaysia rose 1.9-fold, while the number of visitors from Indonesia increased 1.7-fold. Japan recorded a 1.5-fold increase in arrivals. Growth was also reported among visitors from Egypt and Romania, with tourist numbers from both countries increasing 1.8-fold. Arrivals from the United States rose 1.4-fold, while the number of Russian tourists increased 1.3-fold. European countries contributed to the overall increase in tourist arrivals. The number of visitors from Germany and the United Kingdom grew by 25% each compared to the corresponding period of 2025. Tourist arrivals from France increased by 21%, while Türkiye recorded a 15% rise. Alongside the increase in international arrivals, Uzbekistan recorded growth in the value of tourism service exports. According to the Tourism Committee, exports of tourism services reached $5.3bn during the first nine months of 2026. This represents a 51.2% increase compared to the same period in 2025. The growth rate in tourism service exports exceeded the 20.4% increase recorded in tourist arrivals during the reporting period In a separate development related to the country's tourism sector, Uzbekistan previously approved a list of 10 sites designated for the development of cave tourism. The initiative concerns the development of cave tourism as a specific segment of the country's tourism industry. Further details regarding the selected locations, implementation schedules and planned investments were not provided in the reported figures. Overall, the Tourism Committee's data show that Uzbekistan received 10.3mn international tourists and recorded $5.3bn in tourism service exports during the first nine months of 2026, with both indicators increasing compared to the corresponding period of the previous year. # Cave Tourism Development # International Tourist Arrivals # National Economic Development # Tourism Industry Growth # Tourism Service Exports Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan to rank among Europe and Central Asia’s fastest-growing economies in 2026 — World Bank Uzbekistan’s real GDP growth is projected to accelerate from 7.7% in 2025 to 7.9% in 2026, supported by resilient domestic demand, rising real wages and employment, robust remittance inflows, and continued structural reforms, as Central Asia remains the fastest-growing subregion in Europe and Central Asia. Today, 12:34 3 min read 1 336 views 0 comments 0 Foto: “Daryo” / Farrux Aliyev Uzbekistan’s real GDP growth is projected to accelerate from 7.7% in 2025 to 7.9% in 2026, keeping the country among the fastest-growing economies in Europe and Central Asia, according to the World Bank’s latest regional economic outlook. The World Bank Group’s Europe and Central Asia Economic Update: Making AI Work: Jobs, Firms, and Productivity, released on October 6, projects economic growth across developing countries in Europe and Central Asia to slow to 2.2% in 2026, down from 2.6% in 2025. The slowdown is expected to reflect higher energy prices, geopolitical tensions, and weaker demand from trading partners. Excluding Russia, which accounts for about 40% of the region’s total output, economic growth is projected to decline from 3.7% in 2025 to 3% in 2026. Despite the weaker regional outlook, favorable labor market conditions, rising real wages, higher remittances, increased tourist flows, and public investment are supporting economic activity. Temporary government support measures have also partly cushioned the impact of higher energy prices on households and businesses, although they have added pressure to public finances in some countries. Central Asia remains the fastest-growing subregion Central Asia is projected to remain the fastest-growing subregion in Europe and Central Asia, with growth expected to reach 5.8% in 2026. Robust domestic demand and continued government investment in transport and energy are expected to drive the expansion. Kyrgyzstan’s economy is forecast to grow by 9.6%, while Uzbekistan is projected to expand by 7.9%. In Uzbekistan, growth is expected to be supported by resilient domestic demand, strong real wage growth, rising employment, robust remittance inflows, and continued structural reforms. Remittances to Uzbekistan reached a record $9.2bn in the first half of 2026, up 13% from a year earlier, with Russia accounting for approximately 70% of transfers. Non-gold exports increased by nearly 30%, supported by expanding trade with China and neighboring Central Asian economies. Elsewhere in Europe and Central Asia, growth in the Western Balkans is projected to accelerate from 2.6% in 2025 to 3.1% in 2026. Poland’s economy is expected to grow by 3.6%, while Ukraine’s growth is forecast at 1.2% amid further damage to critical infrastructure and disruptions to exports. AI adoption lags behind exposure The World Bank’s report also examines how artificial intelligence (AI) could help countries increase productivity and create jobs as working-age populations shrink. AI is spreading faster across the region than economies are currently able to absorb it. About one in five workers, predominantly young and highly educated, are employed in occupations meaningfully exposed to AI, while fewer than one in 10 firms currently use the technology, mainly for basic tasks. The report identifies gaps in foundational education and management skills, integrated data systems, and computing infrastructure as barriers to wider AI adoption. “ “Governments can help attract such capital by expanding access to cheap computing power,” the World Bank said, adding that this could enable countries to export computing infrastructure services where sufficient demand exists. In Uzbekistan, clerical workers have the highest AI exposure among occupational groups, while practical use of technology remains limited by gaps in foundational digital skills. With its young and growing population, Uzbekistan is among the countries implementing industry-led skills programs aimed at bridging the gap between basic digital proficiency and an AI-ready workforce. The World Bank noted that the key risk for the region over the next decade may not be excessive AI adoption, but rather insufficient adoption and adaptation to the technology. # Iqtisodiy islohotlar # Iqtisodiy prognozlar # O'zbekiston iqtisodiyoti # economy # employment # gdp # gdp growth uzbekistan # jahon banki # wages # world bank # world bank report # world bank uzbekistan Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan unifies education system under new Ministry of Education and Science Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev reviewed plans to establish an integrated education and science system aimed at improving education quality, strengthening continuity across all levels, and aligning learning and research with labor market needs. Today, 12:00 3 min read 1 744 views 0 comments 0 Source: Presidential Press Service President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev reviewed a presentation on the organization of the Ministry of Education and Science and priority tasks for the country’s education system. The ministry was established following a presidential decree that reorganized the Ministry of Preschool and School Education and the Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovations into a unified Ministry of Education and Science. The reform is intended to create an integrated system covering education, upbringing and science, improve the quality and effectiveness of education, and strengthen human capital development. The new ministry is tasked with ensuring continuity between different stages of education, from preschool to higher education, as well as scientific activity. Its work is to be organized around a unified approach, with priorities including aligning educational content with current requirements and labor market needs, increasing competition, expanding private sector participation and strengthening public accountability. During the presentation, officials discussed organizing the ministry’s operations based on conditions on the ground, eliminating duplicated functions and increasing the responsibilities of regional authorities. Digitalizing management processes and strengthening analytical capabilities were identified as measures to support evidence-based decision-making. In preschool education, attention was given to children’s comprehensive development, updating curricula and teaching methods, and improving the professional skills of educators. Proposals included identifying children’s interests and abilities at an early stage and developing modern facilities within educational institutions. The presentation also covered school education, including the revision of textbooks, consistent development of students’ knowledge and practical skills, and improvements to assessment systems. Among the proposals were using artificial intelligence to provide methodological support to teachers, piloting English-language instruction in selected schools and expanding private sector participation. For vocational education, officials discussed identifying young people’s interests at an early stage and aligning technical college curricula with labor market requirements. The proposals also included improving the material and technical base of colleges, expanding dual education in cooperation with enterprises, and introducing international programs and modern educational materials. In higher education, proposals focused on expanding university autonomy, improving management and strengthening the accountability of university leadership for results. The presentation also addressed partnerships with leading foreign universities, closer alignment between higher education and industry needs, and stronger practical training for students. The development of scientific clusters was also discussed, along with closer cooperation between universities, laboratories and enterprises. Proposals included applying scientific developments in practice and creating new products and enterprises based on research results. Mirziyoyev emphasized that all stages of education, from preschool to university, should operate as a unified vertical system, with particular attention to continuity between schools and universities. He also stressed the need to improve education quality at every stage and ensure that education and scientific activity are based on national and universal values. The president also called for greater practical application of research findings and noted that university rectors should have clear short- and medium-term development plans for their institutions. Relevant officials were instructed to further develop the proposals presented. # Education Reform # Higher Education # Human Capital Development # Ministry of Education and Science # Scientific Research # uzbekistan Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? body: World U.S. provides Tajikistan with six drone systems worth $2.3mn for border security The United States provided Tajikistan’s National Guard with six unmanned aerial systems worth $2.3mn for border surveillance and counter-terrorism operations, adding to more than $600mn in U.S. security assistance provided to the country since 1992. Yesterday, 23:01 2 min read 2 414 views 0 comments 0 Source: U.S. Embassy in Dushanbe The United States has provided six unmanned aerial systems worth a combined $2.3mn to Tajikistan’s National Guard to support border security operations, according to the U.S. Embassy in Dushanbe. The equipment was handed over during a ceremony on October 2 attended by U.S. Chargé d’Affaires in Tajikistan Joel Erdman and First Deputy Commander of the National Guard Major General Bahriddin Azamatzoda. According to the embassy, the unmanned aerial systems will allow Tajikistan’s National Guard to conduct continuous surveillance of designated areas during counter-terrorism operations. The equipment is intended to strengthen monitoring capabilities in areas covered by the National Guard’s security operations. “This equipment represents more than just technical assistance; it reflects the years of trust, cooperation, and shared goals between our countries,” Erdman said during the ceremony. The embassy also said U.S. business representatives are prepared to provide products and services required to support the operation of the drone systems and their continued use. The latest delivery forms part of broader U.S. security assistance to Tajikistan. According to the diplomatic mission, Washington has provided more than $600mn in security-related assistance to the country since 1992. Bilateral cooperation in this area has included military personnel training, equipment deliveries and infrastructure projects. Previous U.S. assistance has included military vehicles for Tajikistan’s border troops and Ministry of Defense, as well as specialized vehicles designed to detect illicit trafficking of nuclear and radioactive materials. The United States has also supplied body armor and equipment intended for operations in mountainous terrain. Infrastructure assistance has included funding for facilities used by Tajik security forces. The United States has also supported the construction or renovation of more than ten border outposts along the Tajikistan–Afghanistan border. The six unmanned aerial systems delivered in October add to these security cooperation programs, with the equipment designated for surveillance and counter-terrorism operations by Tajikistan’s National Guard. # Border Security # Counter-terrorism Operations # Security Cooperation # Unmanned Aerial Systems # tajikistan # united states Reporter Xadicha Abdurashidova All stories Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? body: World Kazakhstan seeks return of citizens recruited by Russia to fight in Ukraine Kazakhstan is negotiating with Russia to return citizens who say they were recruited for the war in Ukraine after traveling to Russia for work, as authorities verify individual cases and prepare a list for the Russian side. Yesterday, 22:01 3 min read 7 593 views 0 comments 0 Source: Screenshot from a video Kazakhstan is negotiating with Russia over the return of Kazakhstani citizens who say they were recruited to fight in the war against Ukraine after initially traveling to Russia for employment, according to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Tengrinews informs. The citizens issued a video appeal requesting assistance with their return to Kazakhstan. The Foreign Ministry said it was taking measures concerning those who appeared in the appeal and continued to receive inquiries through its hotline. “Inquiries continue to be received via the hotline. Information regarding each case is being verified. Once the verification process is complete, the compiled list will be sent to the Russian side,” the ministry said. Kazakh authorities said cooperation with Russia over the cases was taking place at several levels. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Zhanbolat Ussenov said protecting the rights and interests of Kazakhstani citizens abroad remained a priority for the ministry. “The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is treating this issue with the utmost seriousness. Protecting the rights, freedoms, and legitimate interests of Kazakhstani citizens abroad is a priority for the ministry,” Ussenov said. According to the ministry, Kazakhstan has previous experience returning its citizens from conflict zones. On October 2, Kazakhstan’s foreign minister met with Russia’s chargé d’affaires in the country. Kazakhstan’s ambassador in Moscow is also expected to meet with officials from the Russian Foreign Ministry and Ministry of Defense. Kazakhstani citizens who recorded the video appeal say that, they originally traveled to Russia for employment and were offered jobs as security guards. They said they were asked to sign documents carrying the name and logo “BARS.” The citizens alleged that the documents were destroyed the following day and replaced with different contracts. When they refused to sign the replacement documents, they said they were told there was “no turning back” and were threatened with imprisonment. The individuals are believed to be in the Luhansk region. According to their account, the men are being sent to the combat zone on a rotational basis. Qaysar Almaz, who appeared in the appeal, and other citizens requested assistance from Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and the governments of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Separately, data published in April by the Ukrainian project I Want to Live ( Khochu Zhit ) claimed that 12,666 citizens of Central Asian countries were participating in the war on Russia’s side. According to the project’s data, Uzbek citizens represented the largest group, with 4,853 individuals. Tajikistan followed with 3,407, Kazakhstan with 2,389, Kyrgyzstan with 1,439 and Turkmenistan with 578. These figures are attributed to the Ukrainian project and are not independently verified in the information provided. In July, BBC Russian Service and Mediazona reported that at least 3,589 foreign nationals fighting on the Russian side had been killed, including 229 citizens of Uzbekistan. Uzbek legislation provides criminal liability for citizens involved in foreign armed conflicts and military service. Under Article 154 of Uzbekistan’s Criminal Code, being recruited to participate in military hostilities is punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Recruiting, training and deploying individuals for participation in combat operations carries a sentence of up to 12 years. Article 154-1 provides separate liability for Uzbek citizens who enter service in the military, security, police, military justice agencies or similar bodies of foreign states. Such an offense is punishable by up to five years of imprisonment. # Citizen Repatriation Efforts # Deceptive Recruitment Schemes # Foreign Military Service Legal Penalties # Human Rights of Citizens Abroad # Kazakhstan Foreign Policy # Russia-Kazakhstan Relations Reporter Xadicha Abdurashidova All stories Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? body: World Tajikistan, Iran expand visa-free regime to land crossings and third-country travel Tajikistan and Iran expanded their mutual visa-free regime to land crossings and travel through third countries, allowing citizens with valid passports to stay for up to 30 days within a 90-day period. Yesterday, 21:08 2 min read 2 494 views 0 comments 0 Source: iStock A mutual visa-free regime between Tajikistan and Iran came into full effect on October 5, expanding visa-free travel between the two countries beyond direct air routes, according to Saidjon Shafizoda, deputy head of the Information Department at Tajikistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, who spoke to Asia-Plus. Under the memorandum of understanding between the two countries, citizens of Tajikistan and Iran holding valid international passports can enter, transit through and temporarily stay in each other’s territory without obtaining a visa. Travelers are permitted to stay for up to 30 days within any 90-day period. The expanded arrangement applies to both international airports and land border crossings. Citizens can also enter either country by air from third countries without obtaining a visa, subject to the respective national legislation. The visa-free arrangement covers short-term travel and does not automatically provide citizens with the right to work or reside in the other country on a long-term basis. Employment and longer stays remain subject to requirements established under Tajik and Iranian law. Tajikistan and Iran initially introduced their mutual visa-free regime on August 10, 2024. During the first stage, the arrangement applied only to citizens traveling directly between the two capitals on the Dushanbe–Tehran and Tehran–Dushanbe air routes. Travelers entering through land border checkpoints or reaching either country through third countries were previously required to obtain visas. The expansion that took effect on October 5 removes these restrictions for eligible short-term travelers, allowing the visa-free regime to apply regardless of whether they cross by land or through international airports, within the conditions established by the agreement. The expansion follows the resumption of direct air connections between Tajikistan and Iran. Flights to Tehran and Mashhad resumed in the summer of 2025 following a prolonged suspension. The first flight on the Mashhad–Dushanbe–Mashhad route took place on July 4, 2025. Iran’s Varesh Airlines subsequently launched its first Tehran–Dushanbe flight on July 10. Four days later, on July 14, Tajikistan’s Somon Air resumed regular services on the Dushanbe–Tehran–Dushanbe route. Flights between the countries were suspended again in early 2026 due to restrictions affecting the use of Middle Eastern airspace. Following a three-month interruption, air services between Dushanbe and Tehran resumed on May 31. The visa-free arrangement now allows eligible Tajik and Iranian citizens to stay in each other’s countries for up to 30 days within a 90-day period, including when traveling through land crossings or arriving by air from third countries. # Diplomatik kelishuv # Eron # Havo qatnovlari # Xalqaro munosabatlar # tojikiston # vizasiz rejim Reporter Xadicha Abdurashidova All stories Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? body: Kazakhstan Kazakhstan, Oman deepen economic ties as Oman moves to join EDB Kazakhstan and Oman are set to deepen economic cooperation, with Oman moving to become the eighth shareholder of the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) and the bank’s first member from the Gulf region under an agreement signed during Omani Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said’s visit to Kazakhstan. Yesterday, 19:00 3 min read 198 views 0 comments 0 Source: EDB Kazakhstan and Oman are moving to deepen economic ties, with Oman set to join the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) as its eighth shareholder and first member from the Gulf region. The move follows an agreement signed during Omani Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said’s state visit to Kazakhstan. The Agreement on the Terms of the Bank’s Presence in Oman was signed by Omani Finance Minister Sultan bin Salem Al Habsi and EDB Management Board Chairman Nikolai Podguzov in the presence of Sultan Haitham and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. The agreement comes as Kazakhstan and Oman seek to expand cooperation in energy, transportation and logistics, agriculture, financial services, tourism, technology and digitalization. Source: Akorda During talks in Astana, Tokayev described Oman as a reliable partner of Kazakhstan in the Arab world and noted that the two countries will mark 35 years of diplomatic relations next year. He said the agreements reached during the visit could elevate the bilateral strategic partnership to a new level. Oman, meanwhile, sees opportunities to expand investment and cooperation with Kazakhstan in energy and mining, agriculture and food security, transportation and logistics, financial services, tourism, technology and artificial intelligence. The two sides also highlighted the potential of their geographic positions to strengthen trade connectivity. Kazakhstan is located along major trade routes linking Asia and Europe, while Oman provides maritime access to markets across the Gulf, the Indian Ocean, Asia and Africa. Source: Akorda “ “We regard Oman as an important transit and logistics partner for Kazakhstan, given its strategic geographic location, advanced port infrastructure and access to Middle Eastern and African markets,” Tokayev said. The countries are considering cooperation in transportation and logistics, including the development of a trade corridor through Omani ports and stronger air connectivity. Investment cooperation is another focus. Kazakhstan highlighted joint projects involving the Oman Investment Authority and the planned launch of a joint investment structure between Kazakhstan’s Samruk-Kazyna sovereign wealth fund and the Omani sovereign wealth fund. The two countries are also seeking to strengthen direct ties between their business communities through the establishment of a Kazakhstan-Oman Business Council. During the state visit, Tokayev awarded Sultan Haitham the Order of Altyn Qyran, Kazakhstan’s highest state decoration, in recognition of his contribution to strengthening ties between the two countries. In turn, the Omani Sultan awarded Tokayev the Order of Al Said, Oman’s highest state decoration. Oman’s entry into the EDB is expected to provide an additional platform for investment and economic cooperation between the Gulf and Eurasian regions. “ “This Agreement reflects our shared intention to build a bridge between Central Asia and the Gulf region. We see significant potential in this partnership and are committed to deepening our cooperation, which is fully aligned with the Bank’s new strategy,” Podguzov said. The EDB is a multilateral development bank focused on investment and economic integration across Eurasia. As of the end of June 2026, its cumulative portfolio comprised 348 projects with total investments of $22.1bn. Uzbekistan’s Deputy Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade Akram Aliyev recently held talks with Christiane Amari, Head of the Division for Central Asia, Pakistan and Afghanistan at the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. The meeting focused on key areas of the Uzbek-German partnership in social and infrastructure development and prospects for further bilateral cooperation. Particular attention was given to preparations for upcoming Intergovernmental Negotiations on Financial and Technical Cooperation between Uzbekistan and Germany for 2026–2027. As part of the preparations, the sides discussed prospective joint projects covering the green economy, vocational education, energy, quality infrastructure, public administration and social protection. The talks also addressed further coordination between the two countries on the implementation of projects within these areas.
