body: News Zelenskyy Accuses Russia Of Breaking Trump's Cease-Fire On Energy Strikes By Alex Raufoglu October 13, 2026 02:09 CET Updated October 13, 2026 12:58 CET Zelenskyy Accuses Russia Of Breaking Trump's Cease-Fire On Energy Strikes Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russia pounded Ukraine with air strikes overnight on October 12-13, killing at least three people in the city of Kharkiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of failing to adhere to President Donald Trump's cease-fire on air strikes targeting energy infrastructure as officials across Europe looked for clarity on the truce and the US leader's deal with Moscow to allow Russian diesel exports. Trump has maintained that the truce -- which he unilaterally announced on October 11 -- is in place despite a lack of confirmation from either side. Zelenskyy, who was quoted as saying the truce was "news to me," said in a social media post that, over the past two days, Ukraine has held back from striking Russian oil refineries as demanded by Trump. But, he added, Russia has not acted in kind. "During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals ⁠that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine," Zelenskyy wrote on October 13. Embed share Russia Pounds Ukraine In Overnight Missile And Drone Attacks by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:14 0:00 The US leader has in the past declared that the sides had agreed to cease attacks on energy sites, most recently on September 14, only to see Russian President Vladimir Putin continue the attacks, ending any hopes of a lasting truce. Later on October 12, Zelenskyy said Ukraine is willing to halt attacks on Russian refining operations if Moscow agrees to stop its strikes on Ukrainian energy systems. Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn on October 12, Trump told reporters: “They agreed [to the cease-fire]. You know why? Because I said, ‘You agree’ -- that's why. They agreed because I said they agreed, and that thing has to get settled.” SEE ALSO: House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal Asked by RFE/RL about reports of Russian violations of the agreement, Trump said he was “not sure about that,” adding that Zelenskyy and Putin “have to get together and end that ridiculous war.” Kyiv Power Plant Hit Just hours after Trump's announcement, Russian drones hit a power plant in Kyiv and energy facilities in the city of Kharkiv, sowing further confusion on the situation. That prompted Zelenskyy to tell a security conference in Warsaw that "if Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people." Russian air strikes continued on October 13, with Ukrainian authorities saying at least three people were killed and 11 others injured when a Russian missile hit a four-story residential building. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the capital also came under attack. It was not clear if Russia targeted any energy facilities in its attacks. Trump also defended an agreement on allowing diesel exports from Russia, which he first announced after a conversation with Putin on October 9. He argued that Europe had continued buying Russian energy despite the war. While some European countries do still purchase Russian natural gas and crude oil, imports have fallen dramatically as the continent weans itself off Russian supplies. Trump has said that under the deal, the United States would immediately import 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel, with millions more expected to follow. As part of the move, the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a General License 135, authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel, including imports into the United States, through April 7, 2027. Embed share Is Russia Preparing To Attack The Baltics? by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:43 0:00 At a forum in Singapore on October 13, Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen told Reuters that as the leader of ⁠the free world, the United States should stand with Ukraine, which she said has chosen to be free from Russia's oppression. "The rest of the world should be on the side of the victim and certainly those countries who want to still be strong for the concept of freedom," she said. Ahead of November 3 midterm elections, the Trump administration has presented the deal as a response to high fuel costs. But the move has sparked a wave of criticism from Democrats and even some Republican officials, who warned it would embolden Putin to continue his war on Ukraine. Trump dismissed the Republicans who criticized the deal as lawmakers who "can't really be serious.” SEE ALSO: Exclusive: A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine Senators Push Back A bipartisan group of seven senators has urged the administration to reverse its decision, warning that Russian energy revenue helps finance Moscow's war against Ukraine. The US “should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians,” they said. The statement was signed by Republican Senators Susan Collins, Thom Tillis, John Curtis, and Lisa Murkowski, along with Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal, and Ron Wyden. On October 12, another Republican Senator Jerry Moran of Kansas warned that allowing Russian diesel imports risked “erasing our leverage, damaging our credibility with allies, and emboldening our adversaries.” Republican House Majority Whip Tom Emmer defended the president, calling the deal “another example of our president thinking out of the box” and describing it as another step toward resolving the war. Energy analysts who spoke with RFE/RL questioned whether the additional supplies could significantly affect prices before the vote. Mark Temnycky, a nonresident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center, told RFE/RL that the announced 300,000 metric tons of diesel would amount to roughly half a day's US consumption, based on figures from the US Energy Information Administration. SEE ALSO: Former US Diplomat Fried Warns Mixed Signals Could Undercut Russia Sanctions Temnycky questioned whether Russia could deliver the promised volumes, citing restrictions on production and exports following Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. He warned that easing sanctions without securing concessions from Moscow could weaken international pressure on Russia and provide Moscow with potential revenue and a political victory for Putin. Ariel Cohen, managing director of energy, growth, and security at the International Tax and Investment Center, said Trump should use US leverage to secure a cease-fire rather than treat an energy agreement as a substitute for progress toward peace. Cohen added that any energy truce should be reciprocal, covering Ukrainian power-generation facilities and electricity grids as well as Russian energy ports, pipelines, and refineries. “It's either all energy infrastructure, including all the power generation and grid in Ukraine, versus in exchange for energy ports, energy pipelines, energy refineries in Russia,” he said. William Taylor, a former US ambassador to Ukraine who served under President George W. Bush and during Trump's first administration, told RFE/RL that a cease-fire could not take effect without agreement from both sides. Taylor said Zelenskyy had indicated his willingness to participate but that he had seen no evidence Putin had agreed to halt attacks. Zelenskyy Accus
summary: US President Donald Trump, in the face of sharp criticism from officials in Ukraine, Europe, and even his Republican party, defended his decision to allow Russian diesel exports and insisted an energy cease-fire between Kyiv and Moscow is in place despite a lack of confirmation from either side.
title: Zelenskyy Accuses Russia Of Breaking Trump's Cease-Fire On Energy Strikes

body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email When visual journalist Ahmed Chihadeh came under Israeli drone fire in January 2025 while covering the return of displaced residents to the southern Lebanese town of Houla, he removed his press vest and hid his camera. “After what happened to my colleagues, and after seeing that there has still been no justice for those who were killed or injured, I do not feel safe,” the Palestinian-Lebanese freelancer told the Committee to Protect Journalists. Three years after Reuters video journalist Issam Abdallah was killed and six other journalists injured in the first instance CPJ has documented of Israeli forces deliberately targeting journalists following the outbreak of war on October 7, 2023, members of the press in Lebanon say continued attacks, combined with the absence of accountability, have changed how they work. Journalists who have reported from southern Lebanon told CPJ that areas they once covered have become inaccessible due to Israel’s military presence and the risk of being targeted. They said that identifying themselves as press no longer offers them a sense of protection, while mounting risks have forced them to document events from afar they can no longer witness firsthand. Chihadeh and fellow photojournalist Hassan Fneich were among a group of civilians about 150 to 200 meters (490 to 650 feet) from Israeli forces when a drone descended and began firing. Fneich, who was standing beside him, was hit in the leg. “With all the technology and artificial intelligence we have reached, surely whoever is flying in the sky knows they are targeting civilians,” Chihadeh said. A growing record of attacks On October 13, 2023, two Israeli tank shells struck the group of seven journalists reporting near Alma al-Shaab in southern Lebanon, killing Abdallah and injuring six others, including Agence France-Presse photojournalist Christina Assi, who suffered life-altering injuries. At least five independent investigations concluded that the clearly identifiable journalists were deliberately targeted. A screenshot from a mobile phone video shows Agence France-Presse (AFP) photographer Christina Assi working at a site near the village of Alma al-Chaab in Lebanon, close to the Israeli border, October 13, 2023. (Photo: Reuters/ Issam Abdallah) The journalists had been reporting from an open hillside, away from the active exchange of fire, when two 120mm tank rounds struck the group 37 seconds apart. Reuters found that heavy machine-gun fire was likely directed at the journalists for nearly two minutes after the strikes. In 2026, Israel acknowledged that its forces had fired the rounds but described the attack as a mistake. The acknowledgment confirmed who fired the rounds — but did not answer the question: who was responsible for the decision to fire, and have any consequences followed? Lawyers representing Abdallah’s family submitted information about his killing to the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel in 2024. In 2025, they filed a complaint to two UN Special Repertours on the failure of Israeli and Lebanese authorities to conduct a prompt, independent, effective and transparent investigation. No publicly documented criminal prosecution has followed. Neither Lebanon nor Israel are party to the Rome Statute, meaning that the International Criminal Court does not have jurisdiction to prosecute the targeting of civilians or any other war crimes. In 2024, Lebanon approved a special declaration that would have granted the Court jurisdiction to investigate war crimes committed after October 7, 2023. However, a month later the government reversed that decision. Nizar Saghieh, the executive director of Legal Agenda, a Beirut-based nonprofit research and advocacy organization, told CPJ that Lebanon’s reluctance to refer alleged violations to the ICC reflects both domestic and international pressure. The government withdrew its decision in May 2024 “under pressure from both Hezbollah and the US Embassy,” he said, referring to the powerful Lebanese armed group, who could also come under scrutiny by the ICC should it receive jurisdiction. “None of them said that officially.” In June 2026, the U.S.-brokered Lebanon-Israel Framework bound both parties to cease “all hostile or negative actions in international political or legal forums,” prompting warnings from rights groups that it could obstruct efforts to seek accountability for alleged war crimes. Meanwhile, as legal avenues narrowed, attacks on journalists continued. On October 25, 2024 , about a year after Abdallah’s killing, an Israeli airstrike hit a resort in Hasbaya housing at least 18 journalists, killing pro-Hezbollah Al-Mayadeen journalists Ghassan Najjar and Mohammed Reda , and Hezbollah-affiliated Al-Manar journalist Wissam Kassem . Investigations by Human Rights Watch (HRW) and The Guardian found no military activity at the site, and presented evidence that the journalists may have been deliberately targeted. HRW found that U.S.-made weapons were used in the attack. Following renewed hostilities in March 2026, Israeli forces killed three journalists — Al-Manar’s Ali Shoaib, Al-Mayadeen’s Fatima Ftouni and freelance photojournalist Mohammed Ftouni — in Jezzine, southern Lebanon . About a month later, local newspaper Al-Akhbar correspondent Amal Khalil and freelance photojournalist Zeinab Faraj were heading on assignment to document an Israeli incursion in Bint Jbeil when an Israeli airstrike first hit the car in front of them, and then the building where they sought shelter. Israeli forces obstructed medical workers from reaching the site for hours. Khalil was killed and Faraj seriously injured, in an attack CPJ said should be investigated as a war crime . Relatives and friends of Amal Khalil, a veteran correspondent for the daily newspaper Al-Akhbar who was killed in a reported Israeli airstrike in southern Lebanon, mourn at her home in the village of Bisariyeh on April 23, 2026. (Photo: AFP/ Mahmoud Zayyat) Civilians as targets Chihadeh said the change began with basic decisions about where journalists could go. Areas identified as targets by the Israeli or Lebanese armies became off-limits, even for important stories, he said. While journalists can sometimes access occupied villages as embeds in time-controlled UNIFIL tours, entry is not always granted, two journalists told CPJ. The danger has extended beyond locations formally designated as military zones. “Even in places that are supposed to be safe and protected under international law, the risk is there,” said Chihadeh . He recalled covering the aftermath of an Israeli strike in Nabatieh, southern Lebanon, in November 2024 alongside Lebanese Civil Defence and ambulance crews. The first strike had already hit. Chihadeh, a reporter and a producer, ambulance workers, and civil-defence members were attempting to leave when Israeli aircraft returned. “There were people carrying cameras,” he said. “I had a camera, a reporter was with me, my producer was with me, and there were members of the civil defence and paramedics. The place was targeted while we were trying to leave.” Two months later in Houla, it went further: when a drone opened fire and wounded Fneich, Chihadeh hid the equipment that identified him as a journalist. For Chihadeh, he feared the press vest intended to distinguish him as a civilian might put a target on his back. Gear that was used by a media crew of journalists who were killed in an Isareli strike earlier is displayed near the husk of their destroyed vehicle along the side of a road leading to Jezzine in southern Lebanon on March 28, 2026. (Photo: AFP/ Mahm
title: ‘I do not feel safe’: The cost of 3 years of Israeli impunity for journalists in Lebanon

body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Beirut, October 13, 2026 — The Committee to Protect Journalists is deeply alarmed by a recent wave of violations committed by Israeli authorities against the press in Israel and the occupied Palestinian territory. Recent incidents include a local reporter shot with rubber bullets, a Portuguese journalist detained and deported, and the barring of German and British reporters. CPJ demands that Israeli authorities allow the press to operate freely without intimidation or harassment. Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank targeted two journalists documenting the Palestinian olive harvest. On October 8, 2026 , a Portuguese correspondent for the independent outlet Fumaça was arrested in Rantis, northwest of Ramallah, and deported the following day. Ribeiro told CPJ that upon his detention, he identified himself as a journalist, showing his press credentials to the soldiers. He was then taken to a military base where he was threatened with physical assault, and blindfolded. He said that international journalists were removed so that Israeli authorities could continue what he described as an “ethnic cleansing project.” Two days later near Ramallah, Israeli troops fired rubber bullets during clashes involving settlers, striking Palestinian photojournalist Issam al-Rimawi. Al-Rimawi told CPJ that he was wearing an identifiable “Press” vest when the incident occurred. This attack follows similar incidents against Palestinian journalists covering the olive harvest in the West Bank; Israeli settlers attacked Agence France-Presse photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh on October 6, and Israeli authorities detained journalists Mohammad Abed and Mohammad Atiq later that day. On October 11, British journalist Secunder Kermani, working with Channel 4, said he was denied entry into Israel and briefly detained by immigration authorities before the decision was reversed, and he was allowed to enter. Israel also reportedly rejected a work visa application for German journalist Serena Bilanceri, who was set to become Die Tageszeitung’s correspondent there. According to Israeli media , the application was denied due to her “anti-Zionist” views and past reporting calling for sanctions against Israel. Bilanceri told CPJ that the rejection hinders her ability to report from the region. In June, CPJ recorded at least six other cases where journalists were denied entry into Israel, some for expressing opinions critical to the country, and warning of heightened censorship. “Israel’s actions against Palestinian, and foreign journalists are increasing in frequency, demonstrating a clear lack of internal and external accountability,” said Sara Qudah, CPJ regional director. “These repeated incidents of intimidation, detention, deportation, and refusal of entry reveal that Israel continues to operate with complete disregard for international laws preventing retaliation against journalists.” The Israeli Population and Immigration Authority did not immediately respond to CPJ’s request for comment on why the foreign journalists were barred and deported. The Israeli military did not respond toCPJ’s request for comment on the shooting and injury of Issam al-Rimawi. body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email New Delhi, October 12, 2026 — More than three dozen journalists were temporarily detained, and in some cases assaulted , while they were covering protests against the country’s chief election commissioner over allegations of voter-list manipulation in New Delhi, Ahmedabad, and Pune on October 10 and 11. In New Delhi, where the main protests broke out, at least 35 journalists were detained over the course of the next two days, according to CPJ’s review of news reports, direct interviews, and verified social media posts by editors, journalists, and their newsrooms. Two more journalists were detained while covering solidarity protests in other cities on October 10, including Alt News correspondent Kinjal in Ahmedabad and Scroll’s Divya Aslesha in Pune. Police continued detaining journalists even after Supreme Court justices won assurances from Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta on October 11 that lawyers, journalists, and other professionals would not be impeded in their professional duties. The court, which is due to hear the matter again on October 13, also directed that no one be detained except by procedure established by law. “CPJ’s research shows that, on October 10 and 11, Indian police detained at least 37 journalists while they were covering protests against the chief election commissioner — with several also being assaulted, heckled, or obstructed in their work,” said Kunal Majumder, CPJ’s Asia-Pacific program coordinator. “These incidents are deeply troubling and a blot on India’s democratic traditions. They violate international standards on press freedom and journalists’ constitutional rights, and also contradict the government’s assurance to the Supreme Court that journalists would not be impeded in their work. As the world’s largest democracy, India has a special responsibility to uphold press freedom, protect journalists from interference, and hold police officers accountable for assaulting or obstructing them.” The protests were called by the Cockroach Janta Party, a youth-led political movement, together with student groups and opposition parties, to demand the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. Protesters allege that a nationwide revision of voter rolls has wrongly removed eligible voters, allegations that the Election Commission and the government deny. Delhi Police denied permission for the demonstration, citing inadequate notice and law-and-order concerns, and a prohibitory order barred gatherings in central New Delhi. Police also restricted access to dozens of metro stations, canceled some train services, and suspended internet services within about four kilometers (two and a half miles) of the Janpath–Kartavya Path area and around makeshift detention centers. Days before the protest, Delhi Police had issued guidelines for journalists asking them to display press cards prominently. Indian authorities deployed about 23,000 paramilitary personnel for the protests, including forces withdrawn from Jammu and Kashmir, West Bengal, and Chhattisgarh, along with at least 15,000 Delhi Police officers. In addition to detaining journalists, police dragged some reporters by their clothes and shoved others into buses , despite their display of press cards. Authorities also seized at least five phones, pressured at least one journalist to delete footage, and drove some to holding sites up to 65 kilometers (40 miles) away. At least five journalists were struck by police, according to their own accounts or their outlets’. On October 10, prominent Indian journalist Rana Ayyub posted on X that police threatened to detain her when she asked whether they were facilitating a man who was shouting abuse at protesters in their presence. Ayyub, a columnist for The Washington Post, told CPJ that, despite knowing she was a journalist, police beat her with a lathi (baton), resulting in injuries that are still causing her pain. The following journalists were detained over the two days, most while displaying press cards: On October 10, Delhi Police temporarily detained Scroll’s Ayush Tiwari and Shoaib Daniyal ; Business Standard’s Anushka Bhardwaj ; Newslaundry reporters Ashwine Kumar Singh, Astha Savyasachi, and Anmol Pritam and intern Anshu; Reuters’ Saurabh Sharma ; Navbharat Times’ Hritik Joshi and Rahul Charas ; BOOM’s Jagriti Trisha ; Shivang Shukla of Mo , India Today’s digital video platform; Molitics’ Neeraj Jha ; The Quint’s Sarthak Jaiswal ; Reporter TV’s Roshni Rajan and Farza TM ; independent journalists Shrishti Khanna and Prashant Pundir ; No Noise Stories’ Vivek Gupta ; and Alt News intern Agniva Ray . On October 11, police detained Indian Express Hindi reporters Shashwat, Siya, and Vijay ; Hindustan’s Ashish Singh ; Nayab World’s Nitin Katiyar ; Ulta Chasma founder Pragya Mishra ; and independent journalists Nidhi Suresh and M. Rajshekhar . Several journalists also were detained while covering protests at Connaught Place that day . Despite wearing press cards, Peek TV journalists Vedanta Agarwal and Sara Khan were filming police detaining protesters when officers dragged them away and detained them. Khan said that a male police officer grabbed her by the neck and pushed her toward a female officer. Police detained independent journalist Shyam Meera Singh after he was heckled and abused by Hindu rightwing activists. Shortly afterward, Singh’s X account, where he had been posting short videos of the protests, was withheld in India “in response to a legal demand,” according to the platform’s notice. The account remains visible outside India. Police also detained at least three journalists from Malayalam-language news channels on October 11 and released them hours later. Asianet News reporter Sajin A was detained and released after about half an hour, the outlet’s Delhi head, Prashanth Raghuvamsam, confirmed to CPJ. Police grabbed 24 News reporter Suhail Mohammed by the neck and forced him into a police vehicle while he was filming. The outlet reported that its video journalist V.S. Rahul was also detained by police, who snatched his camera and threw away the microphone. That evening, police dragged The Caravan’s assistant multimedia producer Ryan Thomas into a detention bus on Janpath Road as he filmed a detention with his press card visible, hit him repeatedly on the head when he refused to delete his footage, slapped him, and prodded him in the stomach with a gun butt in a police car before letting him go at Connaught Place. CPJ has not yet confirmed the names of several other journalists detained on October 11, including a reporter with The Hindu, who was pushed onto a bus and released after mentioning that she was a reporter, as well as a PTI agency journalist . A news agency photojournalist told the media that police dragged them by the neck into a van. Also that day, a group of men wearing press cards surrounded Maktoob Media reporter Fida Fathima, editorial intern Nada Saeeda, and contributor Aktarista Ansari at Connaught Place in the presence of uniformed police. Maktoob Media editor Aslah Kayyalakkath told CPJ the men accused the journalists of insulting Prime Minister Narendra Modi and hurled Islamophobic slurs at them. When Fathima asked the men to show their own press identification, they refused. A senior Delhi Police officer told The Hindu that some journalists may have been detained because they were working close to protesters and did not move away during detention operations. CPJ emailed Delhi Police for comment but did not immediately receive a response. body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email New York, October 13, 2026—The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Ugandan authorities to locate and ensure the safety of journalist Eria Jengo, who has been missing since he was forced into an unmarked vehicle in the capital Kampala on September 10. “CPJ is increasingly worried about Ugandan journalist Eria Jengo who has not been heard from since he left his office at lunchtime on September 10. His family and colleagues urgently need answers,” said CPJ Africa Program Coordinator Muthoki Mumo. “Ugandan authorities should establish his whereabouts, credibly confirm his safety, and ensure that those responsible for his disappearance are held to account.” Jengo left Baba TV , where he works as a crime reporter, at around midday to buy lunch and was returning to the office in Kampala’s Ntinda suburb when he was intercepted by several people in an unmarked car who forced him into their vehicle, Baba TV’s head of news Joel Kafuko told CPJ. Jengo left his personal belongings, including his cell phone and laptop, at the office, Kafuko said. Baba TV’s program director Phocus Luyobya, told NTV Uganda that Jengo was picked up by two cars, one of which was a Toyota Noah. Ugandans have nicknamed the vehicles “drones” because of the speed with which they drive off with those they have picked up. Uganda’s police and military have long been accused of conducting enforced disappearances. Human Rights Watch has alleged that the Joint Anti-Terrorism Task Force has been involved in the illegal detention of more than 100 people, with some dying as a result of torture. Others remain unaccounted for. The Uganda Journalists Association filed a complaint with the Human Rights Commission over what it described as Jengo’s enforced disappearance by “suspected security operatives.” Jengo has worked for Baba TV for more than four years, largely covering security news, with recent reporting including Uganda’s military cooperation with Rwanda and the defense minister’s presentation to a parliamentary committee. Kafuko said he was unaware of any threats, complaints, or warnings related to Jengo’s journalism. Jengo’s partner Catherine Taidhkwiza told CPJ said that Jengo’s second phone was missing from their shared home but it had been switched off. She said the police had not updated her on their efforts to trace the device. CPJ did not receive responses to its requests for comment, sent via messaging app on October 9, to government spokesperson Alan Kasujja and Kampala metropolitan police spokesperson Rachael Kawala. body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Istanbul, October 12, 2026—Turkey’s ongoing crackdown on independent media is continuing at an alarming pace with four more journalists arrested and placed under house arrest over the weekend on suspicion of publicly spreading disinformation , the Committee to Protect Journalists said Monday. On October 9, Turkish police questioned Mustafa Balcı and İsmail Saymaz from the independent Sözcü media outlet, freelancer Şaban Sevinç, and Murat Ağırel, who works for the independent Cumhuriyet and Onlar news outlets, about their reporting on a recent investment fund scandal . Mustafa Balcı (left) (Screenshot: Sözcü Televisyonu/YouTube) and Şaban Sevinç (Screenshot: Şaban Sevinç/YouTube) Later that same day, an Istanbul court arrested Balcı and Sevinç on suspicion of “publicly spreading disinformation.” Saymaz and Ağırel, who were released after questioning on October 9 under judicial control – meaning a foreign travel ban and regular check-ins with the police – were placed under house arrest on October 10 after the prosecution lodged an objection to their releases. “By arresting Mustafa Balcı and Şaban Sevinç and placing İsmail Saymaz and Murat Ağırel under house arrest on suspicion of publicly spreading disinformation, Turkey continues to erode press freedom at an alarming rate. We are reaching a crisis point with at least 22 journalists arrested or detained under the disinformation law this year alone,” said Özgür Öğret, CPJ’s Turkey representative. “All of the journalists who were either imprisoned or placed under house arrest must be immediately freed and Turkey’s disinformation law should be abolished without delay.” At the time of publishing, CPJ could not determine what content produced by Balcı and Sevinç formed the basis of their arrests. After he was summoned by the police to testify, Balcı said in a post on X that he believed he was going to be questioned about his reporting on the investment fund scandal. İsmail Saymaz (left) and Murat Ağırel (Screenshot: Sözcü Televizyonu/YouTube) Saymaz and Ağırel were questioned about their participation in a live broadcast on Sözcü TV on October 7. Writing in their regular columns in Sözcü and Cumhuriyet on Monday, they denied spreading disinformation. These new arrests come after Faruk Acar, deputy chair of the ruling AKP party in charge of publicity and media, threatened journalists who report so-called false news in comments posted on X on October 8. Turkish authorities have also blocked access to thousands of social media accounts belonging to journalists and rights defenders as part of the media crackdown. CPJ emailed the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office for comment but did not receive a reply. body: Press release OSCE RFoM organized the 26th Central Asia Media Conference in Bishkek, held bilateral meetings with Kyrgyz authorities Date: 13 October 2026 Place: BISHKEK Source: OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media BISHKEK, 13 October 2026 – The OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media, in co-operation with OSCE field operations in the region, organized the 26 th Central Asia Media Conference in Bishkek on 9 and 10 October gathering participants from Central Asia, Mongolia and the broader OSCE region. Interactive discussions focused on information integrity and trusted information landscapes in the region, safety of journalists, legislative and regulatory frameworks, journalism education, and professional standards. The conference was opened by the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media, Ambassador Jan Braathu; Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic Kairat Tursunkulov; Deputy Minister of Culture, Information, and Youth Policy of the Kyrgyz Republic Salkyn Sarnogoeva; and the Head of the OSCE Programme Office in Bishkek, Ambassador Volker Frobarth. “There are multiple challenges journalists face in their work throughout the OSCE region, including Central Asia. However, our responses to these challenges must remain firmly grounded in fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and media freedom. Open discussion about the importance of media freedom and its impact on our common security is crucial,” Ambassador Braathu said in his opening remarks. During his visit to Bishkek, Representative Braathu held bilateral meetings with the Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic, Kairat Tursunkulov; the First Deputy Minister of Justice, Saira Yzakova; and the Chairman of the Service for Regulation and Supervision in the Communication Sector under the Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies, Altynbek Toktorbaev. On 10 and 11 October, the Office of the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media partnered with the Bishkek Academy for the Academy’s annual alumni conference focussing on “Artificial Intelligence, Climate Change and Sustainable Development”. The RFoM Office’s work in the areas of media and AI was discussed at the conference within the Central Asian framework. The Office also laid out strategies to promote stronger climate and environmental journalism, and presented the RFoM/UNESCO joint publication “ Reporting the Environment: A Practical Manual for Journalists ”. Furthermore, the conference provided an opportunity to present the translation of OSCE Ministerial Council Decision No. 3/18 on the Safety of Journalists into five Central Asian languages and Mongolian, and discuss the implementation of the principles included in the Decision. “A commitment adopted at the international level needs to reach the people and institutions that are in a position to give it practical effect. And that means bringing the commitment not only geographically closer, but also linguistically closer, to those stakeholders. This is why translating MC Decision 3/18 into Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tajik, Turkmen, Uzbek and Mongolian is part of the implementation process and a step towards national ownership,” concluded Braathu. The OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media observes media developments in all 57 OSCE participating States. He provides early warning on violations of freedom of expression and media freedom and promotes full compliance with OSCE media freedom commitments. body: News News Item OSCE-supported court simulation strengthens Montenegro’s judicial response to violence against women and girls Issued on: 13 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Montenegro Fields of work: Rule of law , Gender-based violence Strengthening the capacity of judicial professionals to handle cases of violence against women and girls in a victim-centered manner is essential to preventing secondary victimization and ensuring fair trials. As the OSCE Mission to Montenegro marks 20 years of co-operation with national institutions this year, it continues to support joint efforts to strengthen the institutional responses to such violence. In this context, the Mission, in co-operation with the Supreme Court and the Centre for Training in Judiciary and State Prosecution Service, organized a court simulation training in Budva from 9 to 11 October for 15 judicial and prosecutorial advisors on handling cases of violence against women and girls. Now in its fourth consecutive year, the simulation aims to strengthen institutional responses to violence against women and girls. Building on previous simulations on femicide, rape, stalking and marital rape, this year’s exercise focused on the practical application of international and national legal standards through a mock trial involving a case of violence against women and girls. Participants examined the key stages of criminal proceedings, including the assessment of evidence, the preparation of an indictment, the main hearing and the delivery of a judgment. Opening the event, Ms. Ljiljana Perkušić, Democratization Programme Manager of the OSCE Mission, highlighted the relevance of this year’s exercise in translating legal standards into practice, particularly in light of recent amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code, which further strengthen the victim-centered approach. Ms. Gordana Nikolić, Head of the Specialized Training Department at the Centre for Training in Judiciary and State Prosecution Service, expressed her gratitude to the Mission and the Supreme Court for their continued co-operation in organizing the training. She noted that the exercise provided valuable learning opportunities and contributed to reducing the risk of secondary victimization, while strengthening the capacity of the judiciary to address cases involving women who have experienced domestic violence. Ms. Bojana Bandović, advisor to the Supreme Court, noted that the simulation served as a platform for exchanging experiences and good practices, while also raising awareness of the complexity and seriousness of cases involving violence against women and girls. She emphasized the importance of addressing these cases without prejudice or stereotypes, with full respect for the dignity of victims and the principles of a fair trial. body: News News Item Young women from Tajikistan and Afghanistan explore leadership, diplomacy and peace through OSCE course From 5 to 9 October 2026, the OSCE held the second edition of its Advanced Course on Diplomacy, Leadership and Peace for Young Women in Dushanbe, fostering collaboration among 20 young women from Tajikistan and Afghanistan to strengthen their leadership skills and prepare them to contribute to diplomacy and peacebuilding. Issued on: 13 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe Fields of work: Gender equality , Youth From 5 to 9 October 2026, the OSCE held the second edition of its Advanced Course on Diplomacy, Leadership and Peace for Young Women in Dushanbe, fostering collaboration among 20 young women from Tajikistan and Afghanistan to strengthen their leadership skills and prepare them to contribute to diplomacy and peacebuilding. The course aimed to equip participants with the knowledge, practical skills and professional networks needed to take an active role in promoting peace and security across the OSCE region and beyond. Through peer-to-peer learning, intergenerational dialogue and discussions with experienced guest speakers, participants explored a range of issues, including artificial intelligence and diplomacy, peacebuilding, human rights, career development and resilience. They also exchanged experiences and discussed the challenges and opportunities facing young women pursuing careers in these fields. Parvathy Ramaswami (centre), United Nations Resident Coordinator in Tajikistan, leads the “Coffee Talk” session on Diplomacy, Leadership, and the Next Generation as part of the OSCE’s Advanced Course on Diplomacy, Leadership and Peace for Young Women, Dushanbe, 5 October 2026. “Today, Tajik women are not merely participants in political processes, but active, thoughtful and responsible contributors to public life, embodying national values and a culture of peace, dialogue and constructive co-operation,” said Mavsuma Muini, Deputy Chairperson of the Majlisi Namoyandagon, the lower chamber of Tajikistan’s Parliament. “The OSCE School of Diplomacy, Leadership and Peacebuilding for Young Women is a valuable initiative that helps promote women’s participation in diplomacy and public and political life and raise the status of women in society,” Muini added. Fejzo Numanaj, Acting Deputy Head of Office and Officer-in-Charge of the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe, encouraged participants to recognize their leadership potential: “You are not the leaders of tomorrow. You are already leaders today, in your universities, your workplaces, and your communities.” He added: “Together with the Parliament of Tajikistan, the Government, the United Nations and civil society, we remain committed to ensuring that young women’s voices shape dialogue, decisions and solutions.” Group photo marking the launch of the OSCE’s second Advanced Course on Diplomacy, Leadership and Peace for Young Women, featuring 20 young women from Tajikistan and Afghanistan alongside senior women leaders from the Government of Tajikistan and representatives of international organizations, Dushanbe, 5 October 2026. The course concluded with participants expanding their professional networks and reaffirming their commitment to contributing to peace and security. By investing in young women’s leadership and fostering dialogue across generations, the OSCE seeks to promote their meaningful participation in diplomacy and peacebuilding and enable them to contribute to addressing shared security challenges. body: News News Item ODIHR and OSCE PA launch guidelines to strengthen participation of people with disabilities in parliaments Issued on: 12 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights , OSCE Parliamentary Assembly Fields of work: Democratization , Tolerance and non-discrimination The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) and the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly (OSCE PA) launched a new publication in Warsaw on 12 October 2026 to help parliaments identify and remove barriers to the full and effective participation of people with disabilities. People with disabilities remain underrepresented in national parliaments across the OSCE region and continue to face barriers to participation. Addressing these barriers means examining how people can contribute to parliamentary work, influence legislation and hold governments to account, alongside ensuring access to parliamentary buildings and information. “People with disabilities must be able to shape the laws and decisions that affect their lives. Parliaments need to examine their own rules and practices and work with people with disabilities to remove barriers to participation,” said Zaruhi Batoyan, Member of the National Assembly of the Republic of Armenia. Guidelines on Advancing disability-inclusive parliaments: an assessment methodology and insights from the OSCE region draws on a joint ODIHR/OSCE PA survey conducted in 2024. It combines survey findings and examples of good practice with a methodology covering representation, law-making, oversight and access, helping parliaments identify priorities and take practical steps towards reform. “Accessibility is part of everyday parliamentary work, from receiving information to taking part in debates and committee meetings. The test is whether people with disabilities can contribute on equal terms and have their voices reflected in decisions,” said Dastan Bekeshev, Member of the Jogorku Kenesh of the Kyrgyz Republic. Parliamentarians and civil society representatives shared experiences from the OSCE region and discussed how the methodology can be applied in practice. The publication was launched at a side event organized by ODIHR and the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly during the 2026 Warsaw Human Dimension Conference . body: News News Item OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities visits Kosovo Issued on: 12 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Fields of work: Conflict prevention and resolution , Human rights , National minority issues , Tolerance and non-discrimination , Gender equality OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Christophe Kamp visited Kosovo on 9 October 2026 to exchange with central and local authorities on recent developments that affected the situation of non-majority communities. In Prishtinë/Priština, Kamp met with Prime Minister Albin Kurti to continue their conversation on the importance of finding effective modalities to consult non-majority communities on policies and issues affecting them. The High Commissioner also met with the Mayor of North Mitrovica, Milan Radojević, to discuss recent developments in his municipality, particularly related to property rights and dialogue between central and local authorities. Kamp also held an exchange of views with the heads of KFOR, EULEX, the EU Office, and UNMIK. body: 12/10/2026 Impact Impacts en fr Mali International Justice Eva Plevier / ANP MAG / ANP via AFP Summary – In 2012 and 2013, armed groups in northern Mali committed war crimes and crimes against humanity, including gender-based sexual crimes . Among the 15 alleged direct and indirect perpetrators was Al Hassan, the Islamic commissioner for Timbuktu. – In 2018, after years of investigation during which the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) documented cases of serious human rights violations, identified the victims, collected testimonies, and lodged complaints, Al Hassan was arrested in Niger . He could finally be brought to trial. – In 2024, following lengthy proceedings, the International Criminal Court (ICC) rendered justice: Al Hassan was found guilty . However, because the judgement fails to take gender into account, a sense of impunity for sexual crimes lingers. – In 2026, the ICC ordered reparations for 65,202 victims, an unprecedented development. Despite the absence of a conviction, gender-based harm is recognised by the Court. – Mali must now cooperate with the process of providing reparations to survivors, despite its recent decision to withdraw from the Rome Statute. Other alleged perpetrators are still being sought. The FIDH continues to work to ensure that no crime goes unpunished in Mali. The facts: sexual crimes committed in Mali between 2012 and 2013 Between March 2012 and January 2013, armed groups, notably jihadists and rebels [ 1 ] , took control of three regions in northern Mali: Gao, Kidal and Timbuktu. These groups imposed Islamic law, known as Sharia. Under their control, the local population suffered imprisonment, enslavement, flogging, torture, forced conscription, and sexual crimes, all of which constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity. As of 2012, in the midst of the conflict, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) started to investigate the crimes: gathering evidence, identifying and meeting with victims, and collecting testimonies. The investigations meticulously documented the crimes with a view to bringing them before the courts. A report published in July 2012 documented, inter alia, the " campaign of rape " targeting women and girls in Gao and Timbuktu. [ 2 ] The investigation revealed that sexual crimes " appear to have mainly targeted women from the region’s Black communities " and were coupled with " insults and racially based comments ", which suggests " targeted attacks against a section of the civilian population which constitute war crimes ". Gender and intersectionality guided the FIDH’s 14-year legal action for the recognition of survivors. In 2015 and again in 2017, the FIDH documented ongoing sexual crimes in northern Mali, perpetrated by armed groups, the Malian armed forces, and by international military and peacekeeping forces (MINUSMA and Operation Barkhane). " The FIDH fact-finding missions will prove to be decisive in securing recognition for victims of sexual crimes by the international justice system in 2026, " explained Drissa Traoré, Secretary-General of FIDH. The mobilisation: From Malian courts to the International Criminal Court Where war crimes and crimes against humanity are concerned, the course of justice is a long, and often very long, process. The protracted campaign aimed at Malian and international judicial sys-tems began in 2012. In July 2012, Mali referred the situation to the International Criminal Court (ICC) . Because Mali had ratified the Rome Statute, the Court was able to exercise jurisdiction. As soon as the investigation opened in January 2013, the report produced by the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICC indicated that there was a " reasonable basis " to believe that war crimes had been committed in Mali, including cruel treatment, torture, murder and rape. The FIDH collaborates with the ICC’s international missions. The FIDH has travelled to The Hague on numerous occasions to request the opening or continuation of investigations, meet with the Office of the Prosecutor, attend hearings, promote the participation of victims, and advocate for a gender-sensitive approach. The matter was also brought before Malian courts. The FIDH lodged two complaints which subsequently contributed to the ICC’s investigations. – In November 2014, the FIDH and six Malian partner organisations lodged a complaint with partie civile for crimes against humanity and war crimes, before the senior investigating judge of the Court of First Instance of Commune III in Bamako, on behalf of 80 women and girls who were vic-tims of rape and other forms of sexual violence committed in northern Mali by armed groups in 2012 and 2013. – In March 2015, the FIDH, six Malian partner organisations [ 3 ] and 33 victims lodged a complaint with the High Court of Bamako’s Commune III against 15 alleged perpetrators of crimes against humanity and war crimes, including dozens of acts of rape and other forms of sexual violence against women and girls in Timbuktu. Among the alleged perpetrators : Al Hassan , also known as Al Hassan Ag Abdoul Aziz Ag Mohamed Ag Mahmoud, who was the Islamic commissioner of Timbuktu at the time the crimes were committed and was be-lieved to be a member of Ansar Dine, a group linked to Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM). The obstacles: the Malian justice system overwhelmed and suspects on the run Up until 2019, the justice system struggled to bring to trial the alleged perpetrators of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in northern Mali. In Mali, legal proceedings had ground to a halt. Complaints lodged by the FIDH and other partner organisations were not spared. Investigations were stalling, despite testimony facilitated by the or-ganisations and submitted to the investigating judge and which were subsequently taken up by the ICC. The Malian justice system was overwhelmed by the scale and gravity of the crimes. As far back as 2014, the FIDH recommended strengthening the Malian judicial system and ensuring the protection and safety of witnesses and parties civiles . In 2019, the call was heeded: the National Assembly of Mali expanded the jurisdiction of the specialised judicial unit in charge of combating terrorism and organised crime and provided it with the powers and investigative resources deemed necessary for war crimes and crimes against humanity. The political and security context also slowed down investigations, because of a lack of cooperation or willingness on the part of the authorities who were occupied with reconciliation and resolving the political crisis. The Commission Vérité, justice et réconciliation (CVJR) [Truth, Justice and Reconcil-iation Commission] was struggling to fulfil its mandate, which it would finally complete on 31 December 2021, having heard 20,000 victims. In 2017, the FIDH raised the alarm over a draft bill on national reconciliation which raised fears of amnesty for the perpetrators of crimes. The bill was passed in 2019 but the comments provided by organisations were only partially taken into account. For the international justice system, the absence of perpetrators constitutes a major obstacle. Some suspects cannot be found or are dead and the ICC does not try cases in absentia. Consequently, many cases are at a standstill, despite the issuance of arrest warrants, such as that for Iyad Ag Ghaly , whose crimes were documented by the FIDH. In 2016, only Ahmad Al Faqi Al Mahdi was arrested and sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment for physical damage to cultural heritage, offenc-es which do not reflect the gravity of the crimes committed in Timbuktu and are unrelated to the crimes against humanity committed against individuals. Other suspects were released, sometimes in disregard of the legal framework. The FIDH estimates that in Mali, in 2018, " at least fifty alleged perpetrators of crimes against humanity or war crimes, who had been arrested, were released for political reasons or as part of negotiations
title: The Al Hassan Case: 14 years of mobilisation by the FIDH for the recognition of gender-based crimes in Mali

body: 12/10/2026 Statement Morocco en es fr Human Rights Defenders © Miquel Garcia The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), within the framework of the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, together with the undersigned human rights organisations and partners in the SOS-Defenders project, are following the developments of the open hunger strike undertaken by a number of Sahrawi political prisoners from the Gdeim Izik group since 23 September 2026, in Moroccan prisons. 12 October 2026 . This strike is in protest against their continued detention and the conditions of their imprisonment, and to demand the implementation of the opinions and recommendations of the United Nations human rights mechanisms, in particular those issued by the Special Rapporteurs, the Committee Against Torture, and the Working Group on Arbitrary Detention regarding their case. They also demand their transfer to prisons located in Western Sahara, to ensure proximity to their families. The following individuals continue their hunger strike: Naama Asfari , Ahmed Sbaai , Hassan Dah , El Houssein Ezzaoui , Mohamed Bani , Mohamed Lamine Haddi , Mohamed El Bachir Boutenguiza , and Abdallah Abbahah . In a new development, El Bachir Khadda was transferred to the local prison in the city of El Aaiún in Western Sahara, where he suspended his hunger strike. Furthermore, Naama Asfari was transferred to Loudaya prison in Marrakech, Morocco, and Hassan Dah to Ben Guerir prison in Morocco, while they both continue their open hunger strike alongside their comrades. This strike comes after more than sixteen years since the arrest of the Gdeim Izik group, and in light of their ongoing suffering within Moroccan prisons and the suffering of their families. The undersigned organisations follow with great concern the health condition of the prisoners on hunger strike, renewing their demand for the immediate release of all Saharawi political prisoners. body: Facebook Twitter Вконтакте A roundup of news from the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group (KHPG), one of the oldest human rights organizations in Ukraine. Since 2014, KHPG has been documenting war crimes in eastern Ukraine, and since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it has been documenting events that show signs of crimes under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes) across all regions of Ukraine. KHPG is one of the founders of the T4P (Tribunal for Putin) initiative, which brings together more than two dozen organizations with the aim of holding Russia accountable for the crimes committed. Russian Education as a Tool for Militarization In occupied Crimea, discussions are underway about the operation of cadet and “Cossack” classes for schoolchildren, the expansion of the “Little Cadets and Cossacks” project for preschoolers, the role of military training camps, and cooperation between Crimean schools and the Russian occupation security agencies. Thirteen kindergartens, with groups of children aged five to seven, are participating in the propaganda project “Little Cadets and Cossacks.” In the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk Oblast, Russian paratroopers have organized an event where they demonstrated military equipment to minors. In occupied Skadovsk, cadets at School No. 1 were provided with uniforms for classes operating under the patronage of Rosgvardiya (the Russian National Guard). In effect, schoolchildren will be wearing uniforms resembling those of Russian security forces. “The problem is not only that military culture is being imposed on children. The use of uniforms closely resembling those worn by Russian security forces creates a dangerous situation under conditions of occupation and hostilities: it becomes significantly more difficult to distinguish civilian children from members of Russian security forces,” the Ukrainian National Resistance Center notes. In an overview article, KHPG examines the ongoing militarization and indoctrination of Ukrainian children by the occupying power. Read in Ukrainian: Російська освіта як плацдарм для мілітаризації A Family Affair: Russia Persecutes Entire Families in Occupied Territories Russian authorities widely employ the practice of detaining entire families in occupied territories. This makes it easier for Russian security services to exert pressure on those who oppose the regime. When charges are based on self-incriminating statements, detainees can be forced to sign virtually any testimony if their mother, son, or daughter is being held in a neighboring cell. KHPG recounts the persecution of seven families: Valentyn Maliar and his sister Tetiana Behei (Maliar), together with their children Anatolii Rossikhin and Olha Behei; married couple Serhii Kozlov and Yevheniia Samoilova; Viktoriia Strilets and her daughter Oleksandra Strilets; Oleksii Demianenko and his daughter Anzhelika Demianenko; Anna Murdidi, her son Artem Murdidi and his wife Anna Voshkoder; married couple Oleh Platonov and Nataliia Poliukh; and Volodymyr Perzhynskyi and his son Mark Perzhynskyi. Read in Ukrainian: Справи сімейні: росіяни переслідують на окупованих територіях цілі родини Detention Extended for Women Charged in the “First Female Hizb ut-Tahrir Case” Four Crimean Tatar women arrested a year ago, on October 15, 2025—Esma Nimetullaeva, Nasibe Saidova, Elviza Alieva, and Fevzie Osmanova—have had their pre-trial detention extended. It was previously reported that FSB officers had completed the “preliminary investigation” into the case of the Crimean detainees. According to sources, in addition to Article 205.5 of the Russian Criminal Code (concerning involvement in the activities of Hizb ut-Tahrir), the Crimean Tatar women are charged with preparing to seize power by force under Article 278 of the Russian Criminal Code. Esma Nimetullaeva , who lived in Bakhchysarai, worked as a pastry chef and was raising five underage daughters. Her husband, Crimea Solidarity activist Remzi Nimetullaev, was first detained in November 2021 in Sevastopol, when he came to meet a lawyer outside a detention center following the lawyer’s release from administrative detention. Remzi Nimetullaev was detained for a second time in August 2023, following a wave of mass searches. This time, he and five other Crimea Solidarity activists were accused of organizing the activities of Hizb ut-Tahrir. Elviza Alieva worked as a cashier at a bakery in Simferopol. She was also a fourth-year Management student at the so-called Crimean Federal University. Nasibe Saidova , the daughter of a well-known imam in Crimea, was in her final year of college, studying education, and worked with a nursery group at a kindergarten. Fevzie Osmanova worked in the family business, a shop. According to the Crimean Tatar Resource Center, as of March 2026, at least 52 women were known to have been subjected to political persecution by the Russian authorities and were being held in pre-trial detention centers or penal colonies. More details are available in the KHPG article. Read in English: Russia’s ‘trial’ begins of Crimean Tatar mother of five and three young women for ‘trying to violently seize power’ Analytical report within the framework of the KHPG project ‘Strengthening Public Oversight and Accountability of State Institutions in Ukraine’, 2025–2026 KHPG has published three sections of a comprehensive study on the human rights situation in Ukraine in 2025–2026, covering trends under wartime conditions, challenges in combating corruption, and the protection of the rights of vulnerable groups. The study traces developments in human rights protection in Ukraine from the beginning of the Russian-Ukrainian war in 2014, examines changes following the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and identifies trends in 2025–2026. Key issues addressed in the report: The report examines the narrowing of the space for civil and political freedoms under the pretext of martial law, the absence of systematic dialogue between the authorities and civil society, pressure on the opposition and attempts to subordinate the judiciary. It analyses the unconstitutional application of National Security and Defence Council (NSDC) sanctions against Ukrainian citizens and cases of unlawful deprivation of citizenship without transparent procedures or judicial oversight. In the sphere of freedom of speech, the report records the growing state monopolisation of the information space through the retention of the ‘United News Telethon’, the removal of patriotic opposition TV channels ( Espreso, Priamyi, Channel 5 ) from digital broadcasting, and pressure by law enforcement and security agencies (the SBU and the SBI) on investigative journalists and bloggers (the cases of Bihus.Info, Yu. Butusov, B. Bereza and Slidstvo.Info ). At the same time, it emphasises that society has retained its capacity for peaceful resistance (the ‘cardboard protests’ of 2025–2026). The third section of the report, “Human Rights in Ukraine 2025 and the First Half of 2026. Rights of Vulnerable Groups”, analyzes the situation of vulnerable groups in Ukraine during the war in 2025–2026, including sex workers, people who use drugs, women living with HIV, and LGBTIQ+ people. It highlights systemic discrimination, barriers to healthcare, legal challenges and recommendations. Monitoring networks continue to document hate speech, discrimination, harassment, and intolerance-motivated offences against LGBTIQ+ people based on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, and sex characteristics (SOGIESC). At the same time, significant progress has been made in recognizing the situation and needs of LGBTIQ+ people as a social group in legislation and public policy. The number of legal and regulatory acts explicitly prohibiting discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and/or gender identity has been steadily increasing.
title: KHPG News Digest: Militarization of Preschool Children, Persecution of Families in Occupied Territories, and a Report on the Human Rights Situation in Ukraine During Wartime

body: Photo: Unsplash, photo editor: Dastan Shanay Kyrgyzstan has refused to cooperate with an unidentified European country on a workforce deal, saying it won’t accept migrants from Afghanistan and Africa, 24.kg reported, citing Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev . The minister made the statement during a meeting of the parliamentary committee on international affairs, defense, security and migration. At the meeting, MPs asked what the cabinet is doing to help Kyrgyz citizens find jobs abroad. According to Kulubaev, the government doesn’t mind people working anywhere they want but won’t negotiate with European nations, as the conditions they’re proposing are unacceptable. «Our fellow citizens are free to travel and work [abroad] when they have a chance. However, we will not intentionally negotiate the terms we were offered,» the minister said, referring to the proposal. Which countries do Kyrgyzstanis choose to work in? According to the minister, the geography of labor migration is gradually changing. More and more Kyrgyzstanis prefer to work in Turkey and the U.S. Workers from Kyrgyzstan are also in high demand in South Korea and Japan. In particular, they often work in hospitals as caregivers for older people. That said, Kyrgyz authorities have no plans to promote mass emigration of their citizens. As Kulubaev explained, the country itself lacks a workforce, which is why Kyrgyzstan cut state-funded programs aimed at facilitating employment abroad. Seasonal worker programs remain in place, though. According to Kyrgyzstan’s Ministry of Labour, Social Security and Migration, 736,600 people are working abroad this year. In 2025, 789,400 people worked abroad. Russia remains the top destination for labor migration from Kyrgyzstan. In March, 474,000 Kyrgyz citizens worked there, followed by 70,000 in Kazakhstan, 60,000 in the U.S., 35,000 in Turkey and 20,000 in Germany. body: A “procedural error” sparked an explosion at a major gas pipeline between Russia and Central Asia, causing it to be temporarily shut down, local authorities in Russia’s Penza region reported on October 13. The Soviet-era Central Asia-Center gas pipeline, historically used to pump natural gas from Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan to Russia, has primarily been used in recent years to pump gas in the opposite direction due to shortages in Central Asia. Following an explosion that caused a column of fire nearly 70 meters high, the pipeline was shut off near the village of Volchkovo, in western Penza, Russian breaking news Telegram channel Mash reported . According to local authorities, dozens of emergency workers were deployed to respond to the accident, which they say resulted in no casualties. At present, it is not yet known when gas flows will resume. Previously, the Central Asia-Center pipeline primarily transported natural gas from Turkmenistan north to Russia for domestic consumption and onward export to Europe. Since the early 2010s, however, Turkmen-Russian gas relations have soured and supplies have been intermittent. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion, European markets gradually reduced their imports of Russian gas, making Central Asian supplies redundant. At the same time, domestic consumption in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan increased to the point that they started importing gas from Russia via the Central Asia-Center pipeline. A pipeline shutdown may be particularly disruptive in Kazakhstan, whose deputy energy minister Kairkhan Tutkyshbayev announced last month that the country expected to import 11 billion cubic meters this year, up from 4 bcm in 2025.
