body: «هنوز هم گاهی آدمها ما را موقع رانندگی با موتور مسخره میکنند. بعضی از رانندههای مرد هم شروع به اذیتکردن میکنند تا شاید مثلا دستفرمان ما را بسنجند که چطور وقتی استرس میگیریم موتور را مدیریت میکنیم.» پ ، پـ تبلیغات تبلیغات «به سمتم آمد، آنقدر نزدیک شد تا تعادلم را از دست دادم و تصادف کردم. بعد بدون هیچ مکثی گاز داد و رفت». این جملات مشابه بسیاری از دختران موتورسوار است که آزارهای خیابانی را تجربه کردهاند. بسیاری از آنها به دلیل نداشتن گواهینامه حتی اقدام قانونی برای شکایت از آزارگرها نکردهاند. حتی طی ماههای اخیر ویدئوهای مختلفی از آزار زنان موتورسوار در سطح شهر منتشر شد که در بسیاری موارد منجر به تصادف یا زمینخوردن این زنان شده است. این موارد نشان میدهد، بخشی از جامعه در برابر هر تغییر اجتماعی مخصوصا در حوزه زنان همیشه با واکنشهایی همراه میشود. به گزارش شرق، همانطورکه بسیاری از زنان که با خودرو شخصی رانندگی میکنند، پس از چند دهه همچنان شاهد آزارهای کلامی در خیابانها هستند. حقوقدانان و فعالان حوزه زنان تأکید دارند که باید از آزارگران شکایت قانونی شود، حتی اگر این پروندهها پیگیری نشود، به مرور و با افزایش شکایتها، برای سیستم حقوقی هم این موضوع بااهمیت میشود. زن را چه به موتورسواری! از آزارهایی که موقع رانندگی با موتور در خیابان تجربه کرده، روایت میکند. خودش مربی موتورسواری است و بیشتر زمانش را در پیستهای موتورسواری میگذراند. «فهیمه جلیلی»، زن جوانی است که از تجربههای خود و شاگردانش از رانندگی در شهر میگوید: «هنوز هم گاهی آدمها ما را موقع رانندگی با موتور مسخره میکنند. بعضی از رانندههای مرد هم شروع به اذیتکردن میکنند تا شاید مثلا دستفرمان ما را بسنجند که چطور وقتی استرس میگیریم موتور را مدیریت میکنیم. برای همین بهترین راه مراقبت این است که ما زنان، مهارتهای موتورسواریمان را قویتر کنیم و از وسایل ایمنی استفاده کنیم تا موقع آزارهای فیزیکی آسیب کمتری ببینیم. راستش هنوز هم این جملات را میشنویم که برو بشین پشت ماشین لباسشویی، زن را چه به موتورسواری و بسیاری دیگر هم که این کار را منافی عفت میدانند». این مربی موتورسواری از بعضی شاگردان زن میگوید که بهدلیل مخالفت خانوادهها بدون اطلاع آنها آموزش میبینند و در مسابقات شرکت میکنند: «با اینکه در مسابقات شرکت میکنم و کارت مربیگری دارم اما هنوز هم وقتی میخواهم با موتور از خانه بیرون بروم، از واکنشهای احتمالی که در خیابان خواهم دید استرس میگیرم. مثلا در ترافیک به موتورم نزدیک میشوند و از این تجربه آزارها شاگردانم هم تعریف میکنند. بنابراین وقتی در شرایط روحی خوبی نباشم و توان مدیریت روانی این آزارها را نداشته باشم با موتور رانندگی نمیکنم چون فشار روانی زیادی به من وارد میشود. واقعیت این است که خیلی وقتها آدمها به قصد اذیتکردن جلو میآیند و زن موتورسوار برای رانندگی در خیابان باید خودش را برای همهچیز آماده کند. حتی اگر اتفاقی افتاد، چون گواهینامه نداریم نباید ترسید، ماههای قبل یکی از دوستانم با موتور تصادف کرد و الان حتی دیه هم گرفت، پس در این شرایط کسی نترسد و حتما شکایت کند». عمدا به ما نزدیک میشوند تا تصادف کنیم تصادف، تجربه تلخ ماههای اخیرش شده است، «سمیه»، دختر جوانی که با وجود شوق خرید موتور حالا از ترس رانندگی مدتی است از موتورش استفاده نمیکند و توضیح میدهد: «کمتر از یک سال است که موتور خریدم و اوایل کارهای کوچک مثل خرید خانه را در محل نزدیک خانه انجام میدادم، بعد کمکم ترسم که کم شد تا محل کارم که مرکز شهر است میرفتم و تجربه کمی از تیکهانداختن دیگر رانندهها داشتم. شاید حتی بیشتر تشویقم میکردند. ولی چند ماه قبل وقتی در حال حرکت بودم پرایدی به قصد به من نزدیک شد و من نتوانستم تعادلم را حفظ کنم و زمین خوردم. پای راستم به زمین کشیده شد و موتورم هم آسیب دید. جالب آنکه این ماشین در شلوغی خیابان رفت و حتی مکثی نکرد ببیند چه بلایی سرم آورده. از آن روز ترسی را تجربه میکنم که باعث شد موتورم را در پارکینگ پارک کنم و تا الان از آن استفاده نکردهام». بعضی موتوریها به عمد ما را میترسانند حالا شش ماه شده که «سارا» با موتورش در خیابانهای شهر رفتوآمد میکند و از تجربه این مدتش میگوید: «چند باری از خانه که سعادتآباد است تا محل کارم در خیابان مطهری را با موتور رفتم. در این مدت بیشتر آدمها با دیدنم، شروع به تشویقم کردند یا مثلا با خوشحالی دست تکان میدهند. حتی برایم بسیار پیش آمده که زنان درباره اینکه چطور موتور خریدم و سند زدم، یا از کجا راندن موتور را یاد گرفتم، سؤال میکنند. در تمام این چند ماه آزار خیابانی تجربه نکردهام. فقط چند روز قبل وقتی با سرعت کم در خیابان رانندگی میکردم، یک خودرو شخصی کنارم آمد و زمانی که باید در پیچ دور میزدیم یکدفعه ترمز کرد و من با موتور زمین خوردم، اصلا دلیلی نداشت در آن موقعیت و مسیر پیچ ترمز کند. دستم زخم شد و بخشی از رنگ موتور رفت. آن راننده بدون اینکه پیاده شود و ببیند من حالم خوب است یا نه، گاز داد و رفت. ولی پسر جوانی از ماشین پیاده شد، کمکم کرد بلند شوم و موتور را چک کرد که آسیب ندیده باشد و بعد آرامآرام موتور را روشن کردم و به خانه رفتم». «عارفه» پنج سال است که موتورسواری میکند، خودش میگوید از همان ابتدا برادرانش موتورسواری را به او آموزش دادهاند و حالا با موتورهای دندهای در سطح شهر تردد میکند: «اوایل زنان موتورسوار خیلی در خیابان دیده نمیشدند و برای همین رهگذران با تعجب من را نگاه میکردند. از همان موقع تا الان که رفتوآمد زنها با موتور عادی شده، بعضی رانندههای پیک همچنان هنگام رانندگی اذیت میکنند. مثلا یکدفعه و بیدلیل جلوی من میپیچند یا به شکلی از کنارم با سرعت عبور میکنند تا بترسم یا مثلا چک کنند چقدر رانندگی با موتور را بلدم. هنوز هم موقع موتورسواری سعی میکنم لباسهایی بپوشم که جنسیتم مشخص نباشد ولی با این حال اگر متوجه شوند، احتمال این رفتارها وجود دارد. اما در کل چون معمولا با برادرهایم موتورسواری میکنیم کسی جرئت نمیکند اذیت کند». در بین زنان موتورسوار، روایتهای بسیاری وجود دارد که زنان از حس همدلی رهگذران در خیابان میگویند، مثل «هانیه» ساکن لواسان که در یک سالی که موتورسواری میکند، چندان تجربه آزار نداشته و میگوید: «محله ما بسیار آرام است و چون تعداد زنان موتورسوار اطرافم کم است، آدم‎ها با حس همدلی با من رفتار میکنند». زنان موتورسوار باید در برابر آزار، اقدام قانونی کنند آزار خیابانی، به هر شکلی که باشد باید با شکایت قانونی همراه شود؛ موضوعی که وکلا بر آن تأکید جدی دارند. ابوذر نصرالهی، وکیل پایه یک دادگستری، درباره آزار خیابانی، توضیح میدهد: «صرف اینکه فردی با موتور تردد میکند، حتی اگر خود این عمل هنوز غیرقانونی تلقی شود، باعث نمیشود شخص دیگری برخلاف قانون، موتورسوار را مورد آزار و توهین قرار دهد؛ بنابراین عملی که شخص آزارگر انجام میدهد، مجرمانه است و این زنان نباید این هراس را داشته باشند که بهدلیل نداشتن گواهینامه ممکن است مورد تعقیب قرار بگیرند و از اعتراض و شکایت چشمپوشی کنند. صرف رانندگی بدون گواهینامه، حتی اگر سیستم قضائی بخواهد آن را پیگیری کند، نهایتا ممکن است به صدور حکم جزای نقدی از سوی قاضی برای آن خانم منجر شود؛ درحالیکه آزارگری مجازاتی بهمراتب سنگینتر دارد. اگر سیستم قضائی بخواهد در راستای تأمین امنیت عمومی اقدام کند، مجازات سختی شامل حال مزاحمان خواهد شد». این وکیل در بین صحبتهایش میگوید: «نیروی انتظامی و وزارت کشور، با توجه به اینکه قوانین ما برای صدور گواهینامه بانوان کفایت میکند، لازم است برای پیشگیری از عوارضی که ممکن است در آینده به تأثیرگذاری بر وجدان جامعه منجر شود، هرچه سریعتر مسئله گواهینامه زنان را جدیتر بگیرند. برای مثال، ممکن است زنی آسیب ببیند و این اتفاق احساسات جامعه را درگیر کند. برای جلوگیری از چنین اتفاقاتی، باید هرچه سریعتر به این موضوع رسیدگی شود. وقتی مجالی برای دریافت گواهینامه ایجاد نمیکنیم، این مسئله خود باعث تقویت بیقانونی در میان شهروندان میشود و با این کار، به افراد آموزش میدهیم که مجاز به قانونشکنی هستند؛ در حالی که اگر مقررات را اجرائی کنیم، این مسئله ضابطهمند خواهد شد. با این حال در حال حاضر، هیچ ممنوعیتی برای صدور گواهینامه زنان وجود ندارد و بحث صرفا بر سر صدور آن است. دولت باید با توجه به تعداد بالای درخواستهای زنان، این موضوع را عملی کند». همیشه مقاومت وجود دارد نگاه بخشی از جامعه به تغییرات، همیشه با واکنشهایی همراه است، ثریا عزیزپناه، جامعهشناس، درباره موتورسواری زنان و واکنشهای اجتماعی به این موضوع توضیح میدهد: «موتورسواری تاکنون بهصورت عادتی در حوزه مردانه قرار داشته و طی چندین سال، این موضوع جا افتاده است. زمانی که این تغییرات به شکلی پیش میرود که یک وسیله نقلیه، فارغ از جنسیت، مورد استفاده همه افراد قرار بگیرد و زنان از آن استفاده کنند، این تغییر برای همه به شکل یکسان پذیرفته نمیشود. باید در نظر داشته باشیم که هر تغییر اجتماعی، واکنشهایی را به همراه دارد. تاریخ تغییرات جامعه ما همواره با واکنش بخشی از جامعه همراه بوده است. حتی زمانی نسبت به اتفاقی مانند درسخواندن زنان شاهد واکنشهایی بودیم؛ زیرا این موضوع برهمزننده روال معمول جامعه در آن زمان بود». عزیزپناه درباره آزارهای خیابانی میگوید: «هر عملی که حریم خصوصی را بشکند و موجب آسیب روانی و جسمی شود، نوعی آزار است. به نظر body: News Analysis Rubio Trip Highlights US Push For Deeper Ties With Central Asia By Alex Raufoglu October 20, 2026 12:54 CET Rubio Trip Highlights US Push For Deeper Ties With Central Asia Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (right) waves next to his wife, Jeanette Dousdebes Rubio, as they board a plane to leave Samarkand on October 20. SAMARKAND, Uzbekistan -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio departed Uzbekistan on October 20 for India after meetings with all five Central Asian countries, wrapping up a visit aimed at expanding Washington’s economic and diplomatic engagement with a region increasingly intent on shaping its own international partnerships. Rubio’s visit to the historic Silk Road city of Samarkand brought together the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. He also met Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoev and attended a US-Uzbekistan business council event alongside a delegation of nearly 300 American business leaders. The visit produced several concrete initiatives, including Uzbekistan’s signing of the US-led Artemis Accords on peaceful space exploration and a bilateral investment agreement that the parties said would total $12 billion when implemented. Ambassador To Uzbekistan Says Washington Supports 'Sovereignty' For Central Asia by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:04 0:00 But the broader significance of Rubio’s trip may lie less in the immediate announcements than in Washington’s renewed attention to Central Asia -- and its stated willingness to pursue closer ties without demanding that regional governments choose between the US, Russia, and China. “This is not simply a contest between outside powers,” US Ambassador to Uzbekistan Jonathan Henick told RFE/RL in an interview as Rubio departed Samarkand. Henick said Central Asian countries had demonstrated their independence and their ability to determine the terms of their own international relationships over the 35 years since the collapse of the Soviet Union. The United States, he said, wants to offer them additional options, both politically and economically, that would help them preserve their independence and expand their room for maneuver. A Renewed Place On Washington’s Strategic Map Henick said Rubio’s visit represented a historic expansion of American engagement, with growing economic and commercial ties accompanying closer political contacts. But he also stressed that American interests were coinciding with changes already underway in Central Asia, rather than creating them from scratch. SEE ALSO: 'We're Never Going To Be The Major Player': Former Diplomat's Reality Check On US Ambitions In Central Asia Uzbekistan, he said, was in the midst of a historic period of economic reform under Mirziyoev, whose government has sought to create a more business-friendly environment and attract foreign investment. “The coincidence of the attention from Washington with the opportunities that we’re seeing here,” Henick said, was helping drive the transformation. Luke Coffey, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, offered a more measured assessment of the immediate diplomatic results. Speaking to RFE/RL, Coffey described Rubio’s visit as largely a maintenance exercise intended to keep agreements reached during last year’s White House summit on track. He considered that earlier gathering more consequential than the Samarkand meetings themselves. SEE ALSO: Trump And Central Asia Reach Critical Minerals Deal At Washington Summit Nevertheless, he said, the Trump administration’s broader actions during its second term had collectively returned Central Asia to Washington’s strategic map -- a development he welcomed. All five Central Asian states retain significant commercial and diplomatic links with Russia, while China remains a major regional economic power. Their relationships with Iran also vary. Rubio acknowledged that reality during his visit, saying countries wanted as many international relationships as possible. Uzbekistan, he noted, had made clear that it wanted to be friends with everybody. No Demand To Choose Between Washington, Moscow, Beijing The question of whether Washington can expand its influence without pressuring Central Asian governments to distance themselves from Russia and China emerged as a central theme of the visit. Henick rejected the notion that the region should be viewed primarily through the lens of competition among outside powers. “For too long we’ve been characterizing this region as, you know, as sometimes they call it the Great Game,” he said. “It’s outside powers competing in the region. Honestly, I think that completely mischaracterizes what’s happening here.” Coffey agreed that the US should not seek to force regional governments to choose Washington over Moscow or Beijing. SEE ALSO: China Looks To Shore Up Influence In Central Asia After US Minerals Diplomacy Geography, economic ties, history, and cultural connections make such a choice unrealistic, he said. Instead, Washington should remain actively engaged and help its partners balance their relationships with major powers. Angela Howard, a research analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ Center on Economic and Financial Power, said Rubio’s approach could make it easier for Washington to establish partnerships that might otherwise be blocked by an insistence on choosing sides. The administration is signaling that it is interested in the region, prepared to compete with Russia and China, and prioritizing economic statecraft, Howard said. An approach that avoids an “us-versus-them” framework could allow the United States to provide alternatives to Russia, China, and Iran incrementally, she added. Howard argued that Washington would make more progress in limiting its competitors’ influence by pursuing specific policy changes -- including action against sanctions-evasion networks -- than by issuing ultimatums that Central Asian governments would be unlikely to accept. Investment Remains The Real Test The visit’s economic agenda was underscored by the large business delegation accompanying Rubio, as the administration seeks greater access to Central Asia’s markets and natural resources, including critical minerals. During his visit, Rubio defended the commercial dimension of American diplomacy, saying the United States wanted fair competition and an opportunity for its companies. At a business council event, he also argued that US foreign policy should not focus so heavily on immediate crises that it neglects long-term opportunities. “Our focus on a problem region or a problem country or a problem issue in the world still has to be there, but it cannot come at the expense of embracing opportunities,” Rubio said. “You have to be able to do both.” Henick said the visit had helped businesses already working on deals make progress in their relationships and introduced other American companies to opportunities in Uzbekistan for the first time. He expected many of those first-time visitors to return. Uzbekistan’s signature on the Artemis Accords could also open new avenues for cooperation in space exploration, the ambassador said. SEE ALSO: Kazakh Plan To Join Chinese-Led Moon Base Would Strengthen Space Partnership Washington and Tashkent are continuing to work on other projects that Henick hopes will be ready in time for Mirziyoev’s planned trip to the United States to attend the G20 summit in Florida as an official observer. Another issue on the bilateral agenda is the Jackson-Vanik amendment, a Cold War-era US trade provision that continues to apply to Uzbekistan and several other countries. Henick said the provisions were routinely waived and did not significantly affect the embassy’s day-to-day work, but acknowledged their symbolic importance to the countries still covered by the measure. Preside
summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio departed Uzbekistan on October 20 for India after meetings with all five Central Asian countries, wrapping up a visit aimed at expanding Washington’s economic and diplomatic engagement with a region increasingly intent on shaping its own international partnerships.
title: Rubio Trip Highlights US Push For Deeper Ties With Central Asia

body: News US Citizen Accused By Moscow Of Fighting For Ukraine Released From Russian Prison By RFE/RL October 21, 2026 11:53 CET Updated October 21, 2026 12:57 CET US Citizen Accused By Moscow Of Fighting For Ukraine Released From Russian Prison Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google In this screen shot from handout footage taken and released by the Moscow City Court press service, US citizen Stephen Hubbard attends his verdict hearing in the Russian capital on October 7, 2024. Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired US schoolteacher from Michigan who was accused of joining the Ukrainian armed forces and had been held by Russia since the beginning of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has been freed in what is being framed as a goodwill gesture from the Kremlin. Russian President Vladimir Putin announced Hubbard's release on October 21 as be began his latest round of talks -- their ninth meeting -- with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg, which focused on negotiating an end to the war in Ukraine. Putin said Hubbard, the only US prisoner held by Russia with the designation by Washington as "wrongfully detained," was at St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport, where he will fly back to the United States with Witkoff. SEE ALSO: US Envoy Witkoff Begins Meeting With Putin After Zelenskyy Talks On Ukraine Peace Shortly afterward, US President Donald Trump confirmed Hubbard's release, saying he would soon be reunited with his family. "Welcome home, Stephen. It's great to have you back," he wrote on Truth Social. Trump said he had "requested" Hubbard's release during a phone call with Putin last week and that Washington "was not required to give anything in return," describing the Kremlin's move as "unprecedented." Following the latest call between the US and Russian presidents, Trump announced a deal to encourage Russian diesel exports and waived sanctions that were due to be imposed under a law he signed last month. Kyiv and its Western allies had warned that these developments could further fuel Moscow's war machine. Hubbard was detained by Russian forces in April 2022. He was later sentenced by the Moscow City Court in October 2024 to six years and 10 months in prison on charges of being a mercenary. Russian prosecutors claimed that he had fought for Ukraine's territorial defense forces in the northeastern Kharkiv region, which was then heavily occupied by Russian forces, under a contract worth $1,000 per month. Hubbard's family, particularly his sister Patricia Fox, had previously expressed doubts about the accusations, stating that Hubbard had long been sympathetic to Russia and had moved to Ukraine in 2014. Fox revealed that Hubbard had lived in the city of Izyum after splitting up with his Ukrainian girlfriend and was there when the war broke out. She also pointed to a video released in May 2022, in which Hubbard was seen commenting on the war. In the video, he claimed to have witnessed Ukrainian forces shelling Izyum for "propaganda purposes," and expressed understanding for Putin's decision to invade Ukraine. It remains unclear under what circumstances the video was made, raising questions about whether Hubbard was coerced into making the statements. There were no reports or official statements about his arrest or how he ended up in Moscow. SEE ALSO: 'They Remain In Torturous Conditions': The Prisoners Left Behind In Russia After Historic Exchange The subject of US citizens being held in Russian prisons has become a prominent political issue in recent years, with many viewing their cases as part of a broader pattern of Americans being used as leverage in wider geopolitical disputes. Hubbard's release came ahead of November's US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress, and amid protracted negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv to end Russia's full-scale invasion. The two sides remain far apart on the terms of a potential settlement, with the Kremlin offering no concessions and sticking to its hard-line demands. Under Trump, as well as his predecessor, Joe Biden, Moscow and Washington conducted several major swaps of prisoners held in US and Russian prisons. But Moscow still holds several US citizens, whose cases have yet to be resolved. According to Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer at Global Reach, an advocacy group, who spoke with RFE/RL earlier this year, at least five Americans remain in Russian detention. Other reports put the number as high as 10. summary: Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan held by Russia since 2022 on accusations of joining Ukraine's armed forces, has been freed in what is being framed as a goodwill gesture by the Kremlin.
title: US Citizen Accused By Moscow Of Fighting For Ukraine Released From Russian Prison

body: News US Envoy Witkoff Begins Meeting With Putin After Zelenskyy Talks On Ukraine Peace By RFE/RL October 21, 2026 09:43 CET Updated October 21, 2026 11:29 CET US Envoy Witkoff Begins Meeting With Putin After Zelenskyy Talks On Ukraine Peace Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US President Donald Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff (left), is greeted by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev upon his arrival in Saint Petersburg on October 21. US envoy Steve Witkoff has begun his meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg, according to news reports, a day after holding talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo. The meeting in St. Petersburg is the ninth to take place between Witkoff and the Russian leader. Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said that Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, would not personally attend proceedings due to illness, and reportedly will join the meeting virtually. "We have some clear ideas on how to get to peace," Zelenskyy told reporters after the talks, which were hosted by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb in Oslo on October 20. "We want the Americans to take these ideas to the Russians," Zelenskyy said, adding that "one of the important ideas is to move to a potential trilateral meeting of the leaders to address the issues that only the leaders can do." Trump commented on the possibility of direct talks between Putin and Zelenskyy, saying the two leaders did not need to meet face-to-face to reach a deal. "They don't have to be in the same room. I guess they can do it another way," Trump told reporters on October 20. Missile Intelligence 'Works Now,' Says Zelenskyy US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is visiting India, described Witkoff's talks with Zelenskyy in Oslo as "positive." "It was positive, nothing unexpected, nothing surprising, and he'll now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side -- and let's see if we can make some progress," Rubio told reporters on October 21. Zelenskyy said he was grateful to the US for providing intelligence on Russian missile strikes, adding that early-warning systems were now working effectively. "We are thankful that intelligence works.... I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles are] coming," Zelenskyy told reporters in the Norwegian capital. Embed share Funeral Held For Five Children From One Ukrainian Family Killed In Russian Strike In July by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:29 0:00 Zelenskyy reiterated that Kyiv had immediately backed the American proposal for an energy cease-fire, but Russia continued its attacks, highlighting the need for strong security guarantees for Ukraine. Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was seeking a lasting peace rather than a cease-fire, in response to Kyiv's call for an energy truce. Stubb said the Oslo talks had yielded "genuine progress" on both the long-term outlook and more immediate issues. He said the participants had identified "some elements of peace" in the broader picture, along with key points concerning security and the economy. Russian Attacks Continue Amid Talks Amid ongoing talks, Moscow continued its attacks on Ukraine, killing at least four people as Russian drone and missile strikes hit several regions overnight. A Russian air strike on Kyiv on October 21 killed two people and injured two others, damaging a 24-story residential building, Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported . Emergency power outages were reported in several parts of the Ukrainian capital following Russian attacks, as energy workers worked to restore electricity, the energy company DTEK reported on October 21. Russian Drone Hits Kyiv Apartment Building, Killing Two by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:34 0:00 In the Kharkiv region, a Russian drone attack killed an 81-year-old woman and an 83-year-old man, according to regional authorities. In the Lviv region, local authorities said Russian drone "attacked an enterprise" overnight, injuring two workers and damaging a nearby private house with falling debris. Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with cruise missiles and 186 attack drones, Ukraine's Air Force reported on October 21. Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces had launched drone strikes against Ukraine’s logistics hubs, port infrastructure, and vessels. It also reported that Russian air defenses had intercepted and destroyed 373 Ukrainian drones across multiple Russian regions. Imprisoned American Released At the Putin-Witkoff meeting, which was being broadcast on a video feed, both men confirmed the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old native of Michigan who was captured by Russian troops in April 2022 and accused of being a mercenary for Ukrainian forces. Putin said Hubbard was at St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport, where he will fly back to the United States with Witkoff. Trump had said on October 20 ahead of Witkoff's visit that he had asked Putin to release Hubbard. "I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump told journalists in Washington. In 2024, a Russian court sentenced Hubbard to seven years in prison. body: China US Grapples With China-Linked Critical Minerals Shortfall Left Unresolved By Trump-Xi Summit By Matthew Fulco October 21, 2026 07:27 CET US Grapples With China-Linked Critical Minerals Shortfall Left Unresolved By Trump-Xi Summit Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A worker drives a skip loader while working at the site of a rare earth metals mine in China. (file photo) WASHINGTON -- When US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping met in Washington last month, they failed to make headway on one of the most contentious issues in the bilateral relationship: Beijing’s sweeping critical minerals export restrictions that have roiled Pentagon and commercial supply chains alike. Trump and Xi agreed to extend a trade truce -- set to expire on November 10 -- by two months. But the extension doesn’t address Washington’s core concerns about inadequate minerals exports from China. During testimony in July before the Senate Finance Committee, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that China’s mineral exports are “not as much as we would want. It’s not at the pace we would want.” SEE ALSO: Trump, Xi Strike Stabilizing Tone At Beijing Summit Shaped By Iran Conflict China dominates global production and refining of critical minerals and rare earth permanent magnets, which retain their magnetic properties indefinitely without the need for external power. Rare earth permanent magnets are essential for the functionality of everything from electrical vehicle motors and wind turbines to fighter jets and missile guidance systems. The International Energy Agency (IEA), an autonomous intergovernmental organization based in Paris, estimates that China is the top refiner for 19 out of 20 key strategic minerals, with an average market share of 70 percent. China has an even tighter grip on permanent magnets with a 94 percent global market share, according to the IEA. Beijing has weaponized its critical minerals dominance to counter US sanctions on its semiconductor sector and the Trump administration’s tariffs. It has calibrated the export controls to inflict maximum pressure on Pentagon supply chains while avoiding large-scale disruption to consumer industries, which would risk escalation with Washington that China’s ruling Communist Party (CCP) does not want. Overall, China exported 512 metric tons of rare-earth permanent magnets to the US in August, down 21 percent from July and 13 percent from a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. Heading into the summit, Xi sought to leverage China’s strategic metals dominance to secure a lasting trade truce with the United States, says Tomasz Nadrowski, portfolio manager at the New York-based Amvest Terraden Critical Minerals Fund. “China has this spigot that it can turn on and off -- which determines the flow of critical minerals to the US and other countries,” he told RFE/RL in an interview. “Extending the trade truce two years would have given this tool additional value,” further locking in US dependency on China’s critical mineral supply chains. The Trump administration was concerned that with a two-year truce, “everyone [both commercial and defense manufacturers] would relax and think, 'We don’t need to build any new capacity,” he says. SEE ALSO: China Looks To Shore Up Influence In Central Asia After US Minerals Diplomacy “The US cannot afford to accept strategic chokepoint dependencies for inputs that are essential to our defense industrial base and foundational industries like automotive,” Mahnaz Khan, vice president of policy for critical supply chains at the Silverado Policy Accelerator in Washington, said in an interview. The two-month truce agreed to by Trump and Xi “buys the United States time, but it doesn’t eliminate the underlying vulnerability,” she said Partnering With Central Asia As it works to reduce critical minerals dependence on China, the Trump administration has cast a wide net. In an August fact sheet , the White House said it has signed or approved more than 160 mineral deals since January 2025, totaling about $40 billion. While the administration prioritizes domestic minerals production, in some cases, overseas projects are more feasible. This holds true for tungsten, which the United States has not produced at home since 2015. Tungsten is a crucial input for military-grade steel, aerospace components, munitions, and ground vehicle armor. Given its high density, the metal is used for stabilization and control in missiles and aircraft. Tungsten’s importance for defense led the Trump administration to throw its support behind a $1.1 billion project in Kazakhstan. Under an agreement signed in November 2025 between US-based Cove Capital (now known as the Cove Kaz Capital Group) and the state-run Kazakh mining company Tau-Ken Samruk, the two parties will jointly develop one of the world’s largest tungsten resources. “Kazakhstan made a conscious political choice to make an award to a US company, though rumor has it that China was also bidding for the same project,” Akbota Karibayeva Meyer, a research fellow at the Caspian Policy Center in Washington, told RFE/RL. The decision exemplifies Kazakhstan’s multi-vector foreign policy, which aims to preserve strategic autonomy by balancing ties with major powers, she explains. SEE ALSO: US Revisits Georgia's Black Sea Port As Strategic Corridors Rise Drilling, feasibility studies, and site preparation began after the agreement’s formal closing. Yet full commercial production is several years away. “Are these projects in Kazakhstan viable? Sure, they’re viable. The economics are very hard to pencil out without a subsidy, though,” Ian Lange, a professor at the Colorado School of Mines and deputy director of its Critical Materials Innovation Hub, said in an interview. “Ideally, I might want to do something [in terms of a mining investment] that limits the government’s expenditure and provides for some competition,” he says. The Trump administration is also working with Uzbekistan to source critical minerals. In February, the US commodities firm Traxys signed a $1 billion deal with the Uzbek government focused on the exploration and extraction of tungsten, molybdenum, and copper. This agreement aligns with a separate critical minerals pact reached between the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and Uzbekistan. Elsewhere in Central Asia, the potential for cooperation with the US exists. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan both have major reserves of antimony, a critical mineral used as a flame retardant, an alloying agent for lead, and a compound in semiconductors. During a September visit to Bishkek, US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor and US Senator Steve Daines, chairman of the Senate Central Asia Caucus, discussed mining cooperation with Kyrgyz officials. SEE ALSO: China Looks To Shore Up Influence In Central Asia After US Minerals Diplomacy During their trip, they also met with the presidents of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikstan. While the US continues to make progress sourcing critical minerals from Central Asia, “it is important to recognize the limiting factor of geography,” Karibayeva Meyer says. Given its proximity to Central Asia, “it is much easier for China to be involved in the region.” Short And Long-Term Challenges In the short term, the US faces a key hurdle in its critical minerals diversification push: from January 1, 2027, the Pentagon will prohibit the use of certain metals sourced from the “foreign adversary countries” of China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran. The ban, outlined in Executive Order 14415 , sharply narrows the possibility of receiving waivers for the use of rare-earth magnets, tungsten, tantalum, and molybdenum from those four nations. Defense firms can no longer be granted a waiver based on cost or convenience reasons. To receive one, they must show that compliant materials
summary: When U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping met last month, they failed to make headway on one of the most contentious issues in the bilateral relationship: Beijing’s sweeping critical minerals export restrictions that have roiled Pentagon and commercial supply chains alike.
title: US Grapples With China-Linked Critical Minerals Shortfall Left Unresolved By Trump-Xi Summit

body: Georgia Georgia Faces New Test As Court Weighs Ban On 5 Opposition Parties By Sandro Jupalakiani and Farangis Najibullah October 20, 2026 17:19 CET Georgia Faces New Test As Court Weighs Ban On 5 Opposition Parties Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Leaders of Georgia's Opposition Alliance, speaking at a briefing on October 15, urged supporters to join a protest campaign against the ban. Listen to this article 7 min This audio is automated Learn more BATUMI, Georgia -- Georgia's Constitutional Court will begin hearings on October 21 that seek an outright ban on the country's largest opposition parties, a move critics say would undermine fundamental democratic freedoms in the Caucasus nation. The court will convene for three days in the Black Sea city of Batumi to consider the case brought by the ruling Georgian Dream party, which has been in power since 2012. A final ruling must be delivered by June 24, 2027. Rights groups, the European Union, and others have criticized the ban, saying it could further fracture Georgian politics and society and hinder the country's ties with the West. An alliance of opposition parties in Georgia has vowed to protest the ban "fearlessly and forcefully" with a monthlong series of major rallies across the country. The opposition has denounced the proceedings, describing them as politically motivated and arguing the ruling party is seeking to eliminate its main competitors. Georgian Dream officials, including the party's founder Bidzina Ivanishvili -- a billionaire businessman who amassed a fortune in Russia before serving as Georgia's prime minister from 2012 to 2013 -- have repeatedly threatened to ban the opposition parties, saying the move protects the constitutional order. "We will initiate a legal process that will result in the banning of the [opposition] United National Movement, as well as all its satellite and successor parties," Ivanishvili said ahead of parliamentary elections in 2024. SEE ALSO: With Georgia Sliding Toward Russia, Former President Appeals For Renewed US Attention Georgian Dream has said it needed a constitutional majority in parliament to ban opposition parties. After failing to secure such a majority in the October 2024 elections, the ruling party turned to the Constitutional Court, with Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze stating these parties are "inherently unconstitutional." The lawsuit initially targeted three opposition groups and was subsequently expanded to include five: the United National Movement (UNM), Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia – Lelo, the Federalists, and For Georgia. The four opposition groups that crossed the electoral threshold in the 2024 elections received nearly 800,000 votes -- more than a third of all ballots -- combined, according to Georgia's Central Election Commission. The Federalists, established shortly before the elections, have not yet contested a parliamentary election. All five parties support closer ties with the West and Georgia's integration with the European Union and NATO. Nika Gvaramia, a leader of the Coalition for Change, said the aim of the ban was not about depriving opposition politicians of their positions but "about depriving the country of democracy." Some opposition groups said they would kick off a series of rallies starting at Tbilisi State University on October 25. They said the protest campaign, called "Georgia Without Ivanishvili," would run through November 28 -- the second anniversary of widespread protests following Georgian Dream's move to halt EU integration. Allegations Of Unconstitutional Activity The plaintiffs in the case argue that the five parties share unconstitutional goals, including seeking to overthrow or violently change Georgia's constitutional order, undermining the country's independence, and violating its territorial integrity. The case also accuses the opposition parties of seeking to escalate tensions with Russia and bring Georgia into confrontation with Moscow. Much of the supporting material comes from the findings of a temporary parliamentary investigative commission led by Georgian Dream lawmaker Tea Tsulukiani. SEE ALSO: Georgia's Iran Embrace Is Costing It Washington The commission examined the period when the UNM was in power, including the August 2008 war with Russia, as well as subsequent political developments. Founded by former President Mikheil Saakashvili, the party governed Georgia from 2003 to 2012. Opposition parties and rights groups have challenged the legal basis of the proceedings and questioned the commission's impartiality. Transparency International called the commission "an illegal mechanism created by Georgian Dream to destroy opposition parties and eliminate pluralistic democracy in the country." The ruling party has defended its initiative as an effort to protect Georgia's constitutional order. It has also indicated that more parties could face similar proceedings in the future, depending on their political influence. Tinatin Khidasheli, a former defense minister who chairs the Georgian civil society think tank Civic IDEA, said the scale of the proposed bans raised fundamental questions about Georgia's democratic system. "Once a country starts banning political parties on such a scale, it becomes difficult to speak of any compatibility with a democratic system," Khidasheli told RFE/RL. The case comes amid worsening relations between Georgia and its Western partners and a growing crackdown on dissent. Protesters in Tbilisi wave flags during a pro-Europe rally ahead of the 2024 parliamentary elections. Georgia received European Union candidate status in 2023, but its accession process has effectively stalled. In November 2024, Georgian Dream announced it would not seek to open membership talks before the end of 2028, triggering large-scale pro-European demonstrations. The authorities' response to the protests has drawn criticism from human rights groups, which have reported arbitrary arrests, police violence, and pressure on independent media and civil society. George Melashvili, a Georgian political scientist and civic activist, said the case was aimed at consolidating the ruling party's power. "Its sole and primary objective is to establish total control and deprive society of the right to choose," he told RFE/RL. The case also raises questions about Georgia's foreign policy direction and Russia's potential gains from the country's growing isolation from the West. Moscow has long opposed Georgia's efforts to integrate with Western institutions. Melashvili argued that outlawing pro-Western opposition groups would serve Russian interests by weakening those forces and reducing the prospects for Western engagement. Covers politics, conflicts, and economic issues. Previously worked for leading Georgian media outlets and television companies. Farangis Najibullah Farangis Najibullah is a senior correspondent for RFE/RL who has reported on a wide range of topics from Central Asia, including the impact of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on the region. She has extensively covered efforts by Central Asian states to repatriate and reintegrate their citizens who joined Islamic State in Syria and Iraq. This item is part of Features Georgia
summary: Georgia’s Constitutional Court will begin hearings on October 21 on a case seeking to ban five opposition parties that together have won hundreds of thousands of votes. The proceedings mark another critical test for the country’s multiparty democracy, with a final ruling potentially to come later.
title: Georgia Faces New Test As Court Weighs Ban On 5 Opposition Parties

body: Features The Landscape Of Militancy In The Iran-Pakistan Border Region By Daud Khattak October 20, 2026 14:04 CET The Landscape Of Militancy In The Iran-Pakistan Border Region Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google People and police officers gather after a blast near a railway track in Quetta, the regional capital of Baluchistan in Pakistan, on May 24. Increasing militant attacks along Iran's border with Pakistan over the past few months by multiple armed groups have stoked fears of further instability in the two countries, both of which are already facing multifaceted threats of sectarian violence in addition to the broader repercussions of the conflict in the Middle East. Widespread poverty, underdevelopment, and religious discrimination are believed to be the main drivers of violence in the roughly 900-kilometer porous border region inhabited on both sides by mostly ethnic Baluch. In Pakistan's restive Balochistan Province, Baluch separatists have ramped up their campaign of sophisticated attacks -- including the hijacking of a passenger train in 2025 and the deployment of suicide bombers, including women -- and in Iran's southeastern Sistan-Baluchistan Province a simmering insurgency has intensified since the start of the US war with Iran in February. Unlike the Iranian Baluch, whose armed struggle is rooted in ethnic and religious discrimination, the insurgency in Pakistan's Balochistan is largely secular and revolves around demands for control over the region's rich natural resources. SEE ALSO: Iran's Security Challenges Compounded By Rising Domestic Insurgency The area is also home to two strategic ports: Gwadar on the Pakistani side and Chahbahar in Iran's Sistan-Baluchistan. Analysts say that militant groups have benefited from the complex nature of Iran-Pakistan relations shaped by sectarian and religious differences, competing foreign policy priorities, and divergent geostrategic interests. In January 2024, Iran carried out missile and drone strikes inside Pakistan, targeting the anti-regime militant group Jaish al-Adl. Pakistan retaliated with air strikes, saying Iran was sheltering the separatist Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and the Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF). Iran-Based Militant Groups The Hong Kong-based Silk Road Economic Development Center (SREDC) documented at least 11 attacks during September in Iran's Sistan-Baluchistan targeting Iranian security personnel. Five more attacks were recorded between October 1 and 8 -- all of which were claimed by the Popular Resistance Front, an anti-regime coalition of Baluch organizations that joined forces in late 2025 comprising Jaish al-Nasr, the Pada Baloch Movement, the Mohammad Rasul Allah Group, and Jaish al-Adl. Jaish al-Adl, or the Army of Justice, is one of the deadliest militant groups based in Iran. It was formed in 2012 following the execution of Abdolmalek Rigi, an ethnic Iranian Baluch who led the Sunni Salafi jihadist organization Jundullah. Both Jandullah and Jaish al-Adl claimed to fight for the religious rights of Iranians in Sistan-Baluchestan Province. Because neither group explicitly sought an independent Baluchistan, however, separatists in Pakistan's Balochistan Province view Jaish al-Adl as a proxy of the Pakistani state. Jaish al-Adl is designated as a terrorist group by Iran and the United States. SEE ALSO: Separatist Group Jaish Al-Adl Rebrands As Wider Iranian Opposition The group is known for its guerilla tactics, including ambushes and the use of remote-controlled explosives targeting the officers and members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC), government figures, as well as Sunni leaders who support the regime. "Jaish al-Adl is adopting more complex attack patterns resembling those of the BLA and fighters from both groups have used the border region for sanctuary or logistics," said Islamabad-based analyst Iftikhar Firdous. Pakistan-Based Militant Groups While religious extremists such as the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP) and the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP) operate in Pakistan's Balochistan Province and account for a number of the 131 attacks recorded in Baluchistan in September, according to the Pakistan Institute for Security Studies, Baluch separatists have gained significant strength in the region over the past few years. The two factions of the Baluchistan Liberation Army (BLA) -- BLA Jeeyand and BLA Azad -- have expanded their operations from local hit-and-runs to setting their sights on high-value targets in cities as far away as Karachi. The BLF is the second most-active group that focuses on guerilla ambushes, attacks on infrastructure, and operating specialized units for more sophisticated attacks. Other smaller separatist groups include the Baluchistan Liberation Guard, the Baluch Republican Army, and the Baluch Nationalist Army. SEE ALSO: Attacks On Chinese Projects Test China-Pakistan 'Iron Brotherhood' In Balochistan Of those, the BLA and BLF are widely involved in attacks on the Pakistani security forces, as well as targeting Chinese-led projects and workers in the region. In 2015, China launched the multibillion-dollar China-Pakistan Economic Corridor Project (CPEC), a key component of Beijing's Belt and Road Initiative that includes rail, road, and infrastructure investment across Pakistan -- with a particular focus on the development of the Gwadar Port and the excavation of mineral resources such as gold, copper and coal in Baluchistan. In November 2018, several separatist groups formed Baluch Raaji Aajoi Sangar to coordinate their attacks against the Pakistani state, which they accused of plundering the region's resources. Since then, the Baluch separatists have not only intensified attacks on Pakistani security agencies but also targeted Chinese nationals in Baluchistan and the neighboring province of Sindh. Cross-Border Connections The Baluch militant groups on either side of the border between Iran and Pakistan have little in common ideologically. "Unlike the Iranian Baluch groups, whose leadership is coming from religious seminaries and hard-liner Sunni Muslims, the leadership of the Baluch groups in Pakistan's Baluchistan Province is mostly university graduates and secular-minded," said Norway-based researcher Kiyya Baloch. "There are no linkages regarding their agendas. Rather, often they accuse each other of being used as proxies by Iran and Pakistan because groups such as Jaish al-Adl have their hiding places on the Pakistani side, while some Baluch groups are said to have their sanctuaries on the Iranian side," he told RFE/RL. Abdul Sayed, a Sweden-based researcher of jihadi movements, said the Iranian and Pakistani Baluch groups may have camps or bases in proximity to one another, but they oppose different states. "Each side accuses the other of acting as a proxy for its respective opponent," he told RFERL, adding that some of these groups have accused one another of killing their members, as has occurred on several occasions between the BLF and Jaish al-Adl. SEE ALSO: What's Behind The Unprecedented Attacks In Pakistan’s Balochistan? Pakistan and Iran have a history of suspicion regarding border management. The most visible demonstration of those differences was seen when Iran and Pakistan each carried out attacks against targets in the other country in January 2024. Iran has long accused Pakistan of supporting militants who oppose the regime in Tehran. Following a suicide attack in Iran's Sistan-Baluchistan that killed 42 people in 2009, a senior Iranian official had asked Islamabad to hand over Jundullah leader Regi. In March 2016, Pakistan announced the arrest of an alleged Indian spy, Kulbhushan Jadhav, from Mashkel area near the Iranian border. The announcement was made just a day before the arrival of the then Iranian President Hassan Rouhani in Islamabad. Pakistani authorities claimed the ag
summary: Increasing militant attacks along Iran's border with Pakistan by multiple armed groups have stoked fears of further instability in the two countries, both of which already face multifaceted threats of sectarian violence in addition to the broader repercussions of the conflict in the Middle East.
title: The Landscape Of Militancy In The Iran-Pakistan Border Region

body: © CABAR - Central Asian Bureau for Analytical Reporting Please make active links to the source, when using materials from this website На русском Қазақша IWPR and the INIDI Public Foundation have completed the “Civil Society for Kazakhstan” project with the final conference event, funded by the European Union, and have taken stock of three years of work. On 24-25 September 2026, the CS4K project’s final conference, “Time to Preserve Meaning,” took place in Almaty. Participants discussed the project’s results and talked about how civil society in Kazakhstan can develop amid today’s challenges. The conference was more than a closing event. It was a space for open dialogue about restoring meaning to civic work, mutual support, solidarity, and finding joint solutions. Representatives of government bodies, civil society organizations, international partners, donors, experts, the media, and activists took part. The central message of the meeting was that even as civic space narrows, real change is possible through professionalism, partnership, solidarity, and dialogue. Day 1: Stories of change and discussions The first day, 24 September, opened with a discussion of the context in which civil society operates today. Participants then heard “stories of change”: ten local advocacy initiatives supported under the project were presented in two blocks of five. A general discussion of all ten initiatives followed. Key results of the initiatives presented: Diabetic Parents’ Committee: insulin pumps for adults. The team drew on data from 465 patients, the opinions of 20 doctors, and a review of 21 international studies. Order No. 57 was signed on 25 May 2026 and will take effect on 1 January 2027. Wings of Liberty PF: personal data protection for NGOs. The first systematic study covered 111 organizations in 17 regions. It found that only 39.6% of organizations have an internal data protection policy, and only 27.9% have appointed a responsible person. Recommendations were prepared in two languages, and a dialogue with the relevant ministry has begun. Just Support PF: protecting children from bullying and violence. The organization’s proposals are reflected in the national plan “Children of Kazakhstan” for 2026-2030, and in June 2026 Just Support joined the ministry’s permanent NGO expert group. Support for the Initiatives PF: rural women’s access to healthcare. The study covered 582 respondents and 27 interviews. Of 24 recommendations, 10 have been implemented or are in progress: a rural outpatient clinic was renovated, specialists’ schedules were expanded, and video monitoring was introduced to prevent fictitious appointment records. Civil Alliance of Pavlodar Region: pasture management. Following a study of 531 households and 11 recommendations, a plan was published and a coordination and oversight body was designated. Meyirim Public Association: workplace harassment. 155 respondents took part in the survey, 64% of whom reported perceiving harassment in the workplace, and 44 stories were collected. The Ministry of Labor reported that the term “sexual harassment” has been included in the draft amendments to the Labor Code. My Home Public Association: reintegration of women after release. Based on a study involving one hundred women, a model for a non-governmental “one-stop-shop” service was developed. 22 women received comprehensive assistance, and 18 of them were provided with temporary housing. Korgan-M Republican Public Association: inclusive emergency preparedness. A survey of more than 430 people showed that over 70% had difficulties during evacuation and 34% would be unable to evacuate on their own. The national Ministry of Emergency Situations circulated the report to its units, and local measures and a request for training followed. Daris-2016 Public Association: education of migrant children. Based on more than twenty resolved cases, 25 recommendations were prepared. Government Resolution No. 56 of 29 January 2026 added a separate section on migrant children to the “Children of Kazakhstan” Concept. Mama Pro PF : psychological support for parents of children with disabilities. 1,119 people took part in the survey: 73% live with constant anxiety, and only 5.7% had used state-provided psychological help. Responses were received from three ministries, and a pilot for ten mothers will launch in autumn 2026. The strongest cases share a common approach: the problem is framed through the concrete experience of a person or community, backed by data, and translated into a specific regulatory, budgetary, or administrative mechanism. Beneficiaries, specialists, and the bodies responsible for implementation were involved, and the result was secured through a document, a designated responsibility, or a working service. Materials and details on each of the ten supported projects are available via the link. In the second half of the day, participants worked in a World Café format. Tables discussed: human rights in everyday life and how to bring change closer to people; the narrowing civic space and ways to preserve freedom of action and NGO resilience; local advocacy and what actually works in the regions; the safety and support of activists, so they are not left to face risks alone; trust in NGOs and talking to society in plain language; financial sustainability and moving beyond grant dependence; state-NGO partnership: where it is possible and where it turns into imitation; business-NGO partnership; the image of civil society in 3-5 years: what to preserve, change, and build together. The evening included an expert lounge in a live podcast format, the close of the first day, and then a group dinner and networking. Speakers Speakers at the conference included Ruslan Zakiev (Director, Diabetic Parents’ Committee DiaRKom Public Foundation), Svetlana Bogatyreva (Executive Director, Just Support private foundation), Irina Zhdanova (Chair, “My Home” Center for Development and Social Assistance to the Population), Sergey Gulyaev (Director, Desenta Foundation), Madina Tulepova (Chair, Support of Initiatives Public Association), Denis Dzhivaga (Director, Kazakhstan International Bureau for Human Rights and Rule of Law), Irina Mednikova (General Director, Youth Information Service of Kazakhstan), Aizhan Alzhanova (President, Mama Pro Foundation), Gulmira Birzhanova (Head of the Legal Service, “Media Qoldau,” Legal Media Center), and Svetlana Mogilyuk (Chair, Civil Alliance of Pavlodar Region Association). Day 2: Results and recognition The second day, 25 September, began with a presentation and discussion of the World Café results. A ceremony recognizing the contributions of project participants followed. The conference concluded with closing remarks and a group lunch. The conference combined three levels of analysis: specific stories of change, a collective diagnosis of the state of civil society, and expert reflection on values and sustainability. This structure made it possible to move from “what worked” to “why it worked,” and then to the question of “what infrastructure is needed for results to be repeatable.” Participants themselves gave the event high marks: “The conference was held at the highest level, creative and interactive.” — conference participant “I really enjoyed taking part in this event and got answers to many of my questions. I would very much like such events to be held regularly.” — conference participant This publication is funded by the European Union. Its contents are the sole responsibility of IWPR and does not necessarily reflect the views of the European Union.

body: Réagissant à l’intensification spectaculaire des hostilités armées entre les autorités houthies de facto , le gouvernement yéménite et l’Arabie saoudite ces dernières semaines, et à l’impact croissant sur les civil·e·s, sur fond d’attaques persistantes, Heba Morayef, directrice régionale pour le Moyen-Orient et l’Afrique du Nord, a déclaré : « Les risques pour les civil·e·s au Yémen et en Arabie saoudite augmentent rapidement, chaque jour que le conflit s’intensifie. Toutes les parties au conflit doivent garantir que les civil·e·s soient protégés, et respecter leurs obligations en vertu du droit international humanitaire. « Au cours de la semaine écoulée, des attaques meurtrières menées par les forces houthies contre des aéroports en Arabie saoudite ont causé d’importants dommages civils, notamment celle du 10 octobre contre l’aéroport international du roi Khalid à Riyad, qui a tué 13 personnes et en a blessé des centaines d’autres – l’attaque la plus meurtrière en Arabie saoudite depuis plus de 10 ans. Elle a été menée dans le contexte de la reprise des hostilités armées de grande ampleur au Yémen, avec des conséquences dévastatrices pour les civil·e·s sur place, en particulier sur la côte et aux alentours de Taïzz, la troisième ville du Yémen. Les civil·e·s ne sont jamais des cibles légitimes. Ils ne doivent pas payer le prix d’une nouvelle escalade Heba Morayef, Amnesty International « Les civil·e·s ne sont jamais des cibles légitimes. Ils ne doivent pas payer le prix d’une nouvelle escalade. Prendre délibérément pour cible des civil·e·s ou des infrastructures civiles, notamment des aéroports civils, est prohibé au titre du droit international humanitaire et peut constituer un crime de guerre. « Toutes les parties au conflit doivent immédiatement s’abstenir de lancer des attaques directes contre des civil·e·s et des infrastructures civiles, ainsi que des attaques sans discernement ou disproportionnées. « Au Yémen, où les civil·e·s sont déjà aux prises avec une grave crise humanitaire et l’impact d’années de combats sporadiques, ce conflit ne fera qu’aggraver les souffrances de la population civile. Il est essentiel que les parties au conflit prennent toutes les précautions envisageables afin d’éviter ou, tout du moins, de réduire le plus possible les dommages aux civil·e·s et aux objets civils, et de fournir un accès sans entrave à l’aide humanitaire pour les civil·e·s en ayant besoin. » Contexte Ces dernières semaines ont été marquées par une forte intensification des hostilités entre les autorités houthies de facto au Yémen, le gouvernement yéménite reconnu sur la scène internationale et l’Arabie saoudite. La reprise des affrontements au Yémen est lié au conflit régional impliquant les États-Unis, Israël et l’Iran. Les houthis sont soutenus par l’Iran et le gouvernement yéménite est soutenu par l’Arabie saoudite. L’escalade au Yémen a fait suite à l’échec du cessez-le-feu conclu sous l’égide des Nations unies en juillet 2026, après les frappes aériennes contre l’aéroport de Sanaa revendiquées par le gouvernement reconnu sur la scène internationale. Entre 2015 et 2022, Amnesty International a recensé des violations flagrantes des droits humains et des atteintes graves au droit international humanitaire, notamment des crimes de guerre probables, commis par les parties au conflit, notamment le groupe armé des houthis et la coalition menée par l’Arabie saoudite. La détérioration de la situation s’est accompagnée d’une intensification des combats au sol entre les houthis et les forces gouvernementales yéménites au Yémen, notamment des attaques meurtrières menées par les forces houthies contre des zones civiles. Si le véritable bilan est beaucoup plus élevé, le Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies aux droits de l’homme a indiqué à la fin septembre qu’il avait établi qu’au moins 32 civil·e·s, parmi lesquels 15 mineur·e·s, avaient été tués depuis le mois d’août. Les forces houthies ont également lancé des attaques contre des aéroports, des structures militaires et des installations pétrolières à travers l’Arabie saoudite, ainsi que contre des navires en mer. Entre les 5 et 11 octobre, les attaques houthies contre des aéroports civils à travers l’Arabie saoudite ont endommagé des terminaux passagers et des avions civils, et fait au moins 20 morts et plus de 350 blessés, selon The National . L’Arabie saoudite a également repris ses frappes aériennes au Yémen. Selon le Yemen Data Project, au moins 66 civil·e·s ont été tués et 90 autres blessés. Cette dernière flambée exacerbe la grave crise humanitaire que connaît déjà le Yémen, où, selon des chiffres des Nations unies, au moins 18,3 millions de personnes font face à une forte insécurité alimentaire et plus d’1,3 million de femmes enceintes et allaitantes sont victimes de malnutrition aiguë. L’accès à la nourriture et aux soins de santé s’est dégradé à plusieurs reprises en raison du conflit, de la conduite des parties au conflit et de la réduction des financements humanitaires .
title: Arabie saoudite/Yémen. Les civil·e·s ne doivent pas payer le prix de l’intensification des hostilités

body: En réaction à la perquisition menée par la police au siège de Halk TV, l’une des rares chaînes télévisées en Turquie à ne pas suivre la ligne du gouvernement, et à la nomination d’un administrateur public chargé de superviser la chaîne dans le cadre d’une enquête sur des faits présumés de corruption, Esther Major, directrice régionale adjointe pour l’Europe à Amnesty International, a déclaré : « Cette mesure porte un coup terrible à la liberté de la presse et ressemble fort à une nouvelle manœuvre des autorités turques pour réduire les voix de l’opposition au silence. « La descente menée à l’aube et la prise de contrôle, par des administrateurs nommés par l’État, de l’une des principales chaînes de télévision d’opposition du pays constituent une atteinte directe au droit à la liberté d’expression. Les autorités turques doivent rétablir sans délai les activités indépendantes de Halk TV et cesser de malmener la liberté de la presse Esther Major, Amnesty International « Elle intervient le jour où Ekrem Imamoğlu, considéré comme le principal rival politique du président Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, doit témoigner dans le cadre d’un procès que Halk TV aurait sans doute largement couvert. En outre, elle survient quelques jours avant le premier anniversaire de la saisie de TELE1, chaîne d’information télévisée favorable à l’opposition. « Les autorités turques doivent rétablir sans délai les activités indépendantes de Halk TV et cesser de malmener la liberté de la presse. » Contexte Halk TV aurait déclaré que ses employé·e·s n’ont pas pu entrer dans le bâtiment à Istanbul mercredi 14 octobre au matin et qu’un nouveau directeur avait été nommé à la tête de la chaîne. Selon les médias, la Brigade de lutte contre les crimes financiers a procédé à une perquisition dans les locaux et 17 mandats d’arrêt ont été décernés, dont 11 à l’encontre de personnes qui ont été placées en garde à vue. Lundi 12 octobre 2026, Amnesty International s’est jointe à 20 organisations de défense de la liberté de la presse et des droits humains afin de demander aux plateformes de réseaux sociaux, notamment X et Meta, de ne pas se conformer aux décisions des tribunaux turcs ordonnant le blocage de centaines de comptes appartenant à des journalistes et à des militant·e·s, et d’exhorter le gouvernement turc à cesser d’émettre des ordonnances de blocage, qui constituent une violation de la liberté d’expression.
title: Turquie. La descente de police et la mainmise de l’État sur une chaîne de télévision d’opposition sont « un coup dur porté à la liberté de la presse »

body: Комментируя сообщения о задержании всё большего числа мирных активистов, протестовавших против запрета на ношение хиджаба в школах, а также исчезновении активиста, который пытался организовать бесплатные онлайн-занятия для девочек, затронутых новыми правилами ношения школьной формы, директор Amnesty International по Восточной Европе и Центральной Азии Мари Стразерс заявила: «Массовые задержания мирных протестующих наряду с участниками насильственных беспорядков, в том числе, по сообщениям, матери, протестовавшей против отстранения дочери от занятий, а также исчезновение активиста, который хотел помочь девочкам, затронутым новыми ограничениями, — характерное проявление насильственного подавления государством законного осуществления права на мирные протесты и преследования за свободу выражения мнений и любое инакомыслие в Азербайджане. Не допускать девочек в классы из-за того, что они носят хиджаб, — дискриминация, нарушающая их право на образование, а также свободу религии и выражения мнений. Светский характер государственного образования не оправдывает всеобщий запрет на религиозную одежду. Не допускать девочек в классы из-за того, что они носят хиджаб, — дискриминация, нарушающая их право на образование, а также свободу религии и выражения мнений Мари Стразерс, директор Amnesty International по Восточной Европе и Центральной Азии Власти Азербайджана должны отменить эти дискриминационные ограничения и обеспечить возвращение в школы затронутых ими учениц и учителей. Они должны немедленно и безоговорочно освободить всех, кого задержали исключительно за мирное осуществление своих прав. Власти обязаны уважать право на мирные протесты и все права человека». Справка Согласно новым правилам о школьной форме, с 12 октября учеников и учителей в хиджабах перестали допускать в школы по всему Азербайджану. Это вызвало массовые протесты и акции гражданского неповиновения, некоторые из которых сопровождались насилием. По данным МВД, в тот день только в Баку задержали 37 человек, тогда как активисты сообщали о более чем 200 задержанных. В то же время пользователи сообщали, что в Азербайджане стали недоступны TikTok и Instagram. Большинство задержанных вскоре отпустили, однако неизвестно, сколько человек остаются под стражей. Среди известных случаев — Гудрат Абдуллаев, которого за публикацию в TikTok подвергли административному аресту на 25 суток, и Рафаэль Гусейнзаде, задержанный на 30 суток после того, как написал на здании школы «Свободу хиджабу!». Тринадцатого октября по подозрению в попытке поджога школы задержали шестерых несовершеннолетних. По статье 233 Уголовного кодекса, предусматривающей ответственность за организацию действий, нарушающих общественный порядок, или активное участие в них, было возбуждено уголовное дело. Официально в связи с этим делом пока никого не арестовали. Четырнадцатого октября мусульманский активист Ага Гусейнов сообщил об аресте своей жены Шахизяр Гусейновой. Днём ранее её задержали после того, как она вышла на протест у школы в Баку: их дочь не допустили к занятиям. По словам Гусейнова, его жена помещена под стражу на срок четыре месяца, однако ему не сообщили, в чём её обвиняют. Илькин Гусейнов, активист, запустивший бесплатную онлайн-платформу, которая связывала учителей-волонтёров с детьми, отстранёнными от занятий, в том числе из-за ношения хиджаба, пропал 14 октября. Перед этим он вышел из дома в Баку в сопровождении неизвестных.
title: Азербайджан: прекратить дискриминационные ограничения, лишающие девочек доступа к образованию из-за ношения хиджаба, и освободить мирных протестующих

Levine was assaulted by masked settlers despite wearing a clearly marked “Press” vest. CPJ’s October 17 letter emphasized the Israeli government’s “obligation to swiftly, thoroughly, and impartially investigate all attacks against journalists, including identifying perpetrators and holding them fully accountable under criminal law.” Such investigations should examine the actions of Israeli military or police personnel, including any failure to intervene or to protect journalists, CPJ said. On October 17, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee posted on X that the U.S. had called for “a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated.” Multiple members of Congress also strongly condemned the assault, calling on Israel to hold the perpetrators to account and end the culture of impunity for attacks on journalists. CPJ’s letter highlighted that Levine’s brutal assault fits a broader pattern of violence against journalists in the West Bank and called on the Israeli government to commit to a clear timeline for investigations, including public updates on their progress, and to cease downplaying such assaults as that contributes to an enabling environment for future attacks against journalists. Journalists and media workers must be able to report breaking news and current affairs independently, free from fear of legal retaliation, and in the public interest. On October 13, the Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) ordered all satellite television channels to refrain from broadcasting, rebroadcasting, or airing live coverage of any “unfortunate” or “unpleasant” incident, including explosions, blasts, shootings, and terrorist attacks, according to a copy of the directive reviewed by CPJ. Warning of legal action against broadcasters that don’t comply, PEMRA said they can only air information that has been verified by the relevant government departments or law enforcement agencies. Broadcasters must also use time delays and maintain independent editorial boards, according to the directive. “Preventing journalists from independent reporting of major security incidents and requiring them to rely on information authorized by state and security agencies risks turning legitimate safety safeguards into a system of official information control and censorship,” said Waliullah Rahmani, CPJ’s Afghanistan and Pakistan representative. “Pakistani authorities must rescind these sweeping restrictions and allow newsrooms to make responsible editorial decisions without fear of regulatory retaliation.” The directive reiterates restrictions on television channels first issued in February 2023 by PEMRA, which accused TV channels of broadcasting unverified and speculative information during militant attacks. In August, Pakistan’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting issued guidelines requiring foreign journalist and their associates in Pakistan, as well as those working with international media, to register with the ministry and obtain a certificate before undertaking reporting assignments outside Islamabad, Lahore, and Karachi. The latest directive comes after heightened political-security instability in Pakistan, including the imposition of emergency rule in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Pakistan’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting did not respond to CPJ’s email seeking comment. Loterte, an anchor at the local “Rabas Cun Rabas” online program on RBN News Television and a freelance broadcaster on DWIZ FM, was shot at about 4:10 p.m. on Monday at his bakery in Barangay San Roque, Daraga, a municipality in the Bicol region’s Albay province, according to a police report . “Authorities must promptly identify, apprehend, and prosecute the perpetrators behind the killing of broadcast journalist Adrian Loterte,” said Shawn Crispin, CPJ’s senior Southeast Asia representative. “Until President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration does more to end impunity in media murder cases, these grotesque attacks on the press will continue.” One of two unidentified suspects opened fire before both escaped on a black-and-white Honda Click motorcycle, according to Bicol police spokesperson Lt. Col. Maria Luisa Calubaquib. Police recovered eight spent shells from a .45-caliber pistol at the crime scene. Loterte sustained four gunshot wounds and was pronounced dead on arrival at Daraga Doctors Hospital. In an October 13 briefing , Police Regional Office 5 Director Randy Glenn Silvio said a special investigation task group was established to identify the suspects and their motive, and that investigators were reviewing CCTV footage to trace the perpetrators’ movements before and after the crime. Silvio said police were examining possible work, personal and business-related motives. The Presidential Task Force on Media Security (PTFOMS), a state body tasked with investigating media murders, said it had also opened an investigation into Loterte’s killing and was coordinating with law enforcement agencies, without speculating on a motive. The Philippine National Police and PTFOMS did not immediately respond to CPJ’s emailed requests for comment. CPJ research shows that the Philippines is consistently among the top nations worldwide where media murders go unresolved. Living in the U.S. since 2016, Jorjandi is the founder of Webamooz, an independent outlet covering cybercrime and online financial fraud for Persian-speaking audiences, with selected investigations in English . His investigations have exposed alleged links between Iranian state-connected entities and illegal payment processing for gambling networks, VPN sales, consumer fraud involving the state telecommunications network and affiliated companies, and cryptocurrency embezzlement. Jorjandi said actors linked to fraud networks he has exposed are behind the attacks and have repeatedly used Iran’s judiciary to target him, alongside direct state pressure. “Mohammad Jorjandi and his family should not face threats and harassment because of his reporting,” said José Zamora, CPJ’s regional director for the Americas. “Iranian authorities must end their persecution of Jorjandi, and social media platforms must act against threats and the publication of his family’s private information.” He also investigated an alleged fake-degree operation involving NIUTM that he reported was used to defraud Canada’s immigration system and sell fraudulent U.S. university degrees in Iran. A plaintiff who sued him for defamation in Virginia over that reporting withdrew the case on the eve of trial, after nearly two years of litigation. Jorjandi’s subsequent lawsuit against the plaintiff remains pending. Jorjandi says the withdrawal of the lawsuit was followed by a coordinated harassment campaign against him and his family on Telegram and Instagram. Attacks across multiple channels, verified accounts, paid articles, and a website bearing his name have accused him of being an intelligence operative, money launderer, and sanctions evader. They have also published photographs of his relatives, including his elderly father. Inside Iran, subjects of Jorjandi’s reporting have brought multiple criminal cases against him. Judicial authorities have blocked websites carrying his investigations, ordered his channel removed from Iranian platforms, barred Iranian media from mentioning him, and characterized his journalism as sedition and incitement. He has also received a two-year prison sentence in absentia and faces a nationwide arrest warrant. Separately, Jorjandi told CPJ that individuals based in Germany, presenting themselves as opponents of Iran’s government, have targeted him since late 2025. In near-daily Clubhouse and Telegram sessions, they have disclosed his family’s address in Iran, published a photograph of his elderly father’s front door, and offered money to anyone willing to act against his father. Criminal and civil proceedings Jorjandi initiated in Germany remain pending. Jorjandi said he has repeatedly reported the Telegram channel to no results. CPJ is investigating these attacks and calls on social media platforms to protect Jorjandi and his family from further harassment.
