body: Russia An Arctic Traffic Jam Highlights Doubts Over Russia's Northern Sea Route To China By Ray Furlong October 23, 2026 14:34 CET An Arctic Traffic Jam Highlights Doubts Over Russia's Northern Sea Route To China Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google An archive shot of Russia's nuclear-powered icebreaker Yamal in the Kara Sea, west of the Vilkitsky Strait. A group of sanctioned Russian tankers dropped anchor some 1,300 kilometers north of the Arctic Circle in July after getting stuck and hunkered down for a long wait in the frozen waters at the top of the world. Help from two nuclear-powered ice breakers was several days' voyage away. The ships were stuck in the Vilkitsky Strait, a 55-kilometer-wide choke point between the coast of northern Siberia and Bolshevik Island, on Russia's Northern Sea Route (NSR) to China. The Kremlin has heavily invested in the promise that retreating Arctic sea ice opens up a previously impassable route -- one that is farther from the reach of Ukrainian drone attacks or European naval interdiction of shadow fleet vessels. The NSR saw Russian exports of crude oil and liquified natural gas (LNG) moving in record volumes this year. But, as the Arctic traffic jam underlines, it isn't always plain sailing. "That is a good example of one of our main messages: that less ice doesn't mean easier navigation," Ksenia Vakhrusheva, head of the Arctic project at Lithuania-based environmental group Bellona, told RFE/RL. Map: Russia's Northern Sea Route "When the ice is melting, some parts are breaking and floating, and sometimes it happens that in certain places, especially in narrow straits, this ice gets packed, and a ship without an ice class cannot go through," she added. Vakhrusheva was referring to a classification for the degree (if any) to which a ship is capable of dealing with sea ice. Russia's lack of such ships is one of several factors holding back development of the NSR, despite bullish rhetoric from President Vladimir Putin and other Russian officials about the route. 'A Safe Path' The NSR "is crucially important in the current challenging international situation -- a reliable and safe path to the world's largest markets," Putin said last month, speaking at the launch of the flagship Vostok Oil project on the Taimyr Peninsula just south of the Vilkitsky Strait. Putin said that 37 million tons of cargo had moved along the route (though not its entire length) in 2025 and predicted this would "almost double" by 2030. In fact, back in 2019, Kremlin officials were chasing Putin's target of 80 million tons by 2024. This is just one way the numbers tell a more nuanced story about the NSR. SEE ALSO: Russia's Big Arctic Oil Bet: Who Benefits? By end of last month, the Norway-funded Center for High North Logistics (CHNL) reported Russia had shipped some 2 million tons of primarily crude-oil cargoes, or about 15 million barrels, along the entire length of the NSR to China and other Asian destinations, mostly departing from the Barents Sea port of Murmansk. By mid-October, the figure had increased to some 20 million barrels, Reuters reported, citing traders and shipping data. This is already a 50 percent increase on 2025. Yet, at the same time, it still represents around just 1 percent of Russia's total seaborne oil exports. "There is definitely a surge of developments there. However, it's from a relatively low base," Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at maritime security consultancy Ambrey, told RFE/RL. "The messaging largely is internal, but also toward India and China. Russia is trying to reassert itself as a reliable partner that can deliver the volumes contracted or projected." SEE ALSO: Rubio In Iceland Signals Deeper NATO Push As Russia, China Challenge Arctic Security Alexa added that while Russia had launched a number of new, Arctic-capable vessels, it's ability to build and maintain these and other infrastructure in the region was seriously hampered by Western sanctions. "Any spare parts, any construction materials often have to go through third parties to avoid the sanctions regimes because they could be only procured from the United States, Japan, South Korea, or Europe," he said, adding that maintenance and repairs had previously been handled by Norwegian, Danish, and Dutch companies that would no longer do so. A New Front Line While the lion's share of shipping along the route is Russian energy exports, other nations are also dipping their toes in the chilly waters. On October 22, the South Korean government reported that the country's first container ship had used the route, praising it as a shortcut to Europe but noting difficult conditions including large ice flows in the Bering and Vilkitsky straits. This year China, for the first time, ran a scheduled container service to Europe along the NSR that completed several voyages. Catherine Sendak, head of the Transatlantic Defense and Security program at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), said there were big questions about how Russia might manage the route. "Russia feels ownership of a lot of the Arctic -- the majority of it -- and feels that...it's an inner waterway," she told RFE/RL. Embed share Frozen Conflict? Russia And The West Go Toe-To-Toe In The Arctic by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:04:17 0:00 "There have been discussions about tolls...about what Russian authorities would provide commercial vessels transiting through the route," she added. "I don't think there are good answers to that right now. I will be interested to see in a year from now if Russia still thinks it's in their best interest to use this route, but perhaps not open it up as much to other actors." A CEPA report in September said "Russia is turning the Arctic into a fortress." Officials in Washington, Brussels, and elsewhere have used similar language. "With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition," European Union foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said while outlining a new EU strategy on the Arctic on October 21. "Access to Arctic sea lanes and natural resources is of strategic interest to the EU." NATO launched its new Arctic Sentry mission to boost its presence in February, and last month the United States announced plans for expanding its military boot-print in Greenland , as part of a deal that also aims to overcome a bruising battle within the alliance over US President Donald Trump's call for US sovereignty of the island. SEE ALSO: Russia Strips Arctic Air Defenses As Ukraine War Strains Military Alongside these security concerns, groups such as Bellona continue to bang the drum about environmental risks from increased shipping in the region, particularly by aging, poorly maintained shadow fleet tankers like some of those that got stuck at the Vilkitsky Strait. Only one made it through, while others eventually found a different route after waiting up to two weeks for the icebreakers and still being unable to navigate the strait. "An oil spill in the Arctic environment is more dangerous for the environment than elsewhere in the world because natural degradation of oil in cold weather is way slower than in warmer regions, and then it also can spill over the ice, which can accelerate climate change effects," said Vakhrusheva. "Russia doesn't publish any information about incidents or accidents along the Northern Sea Route, and the area is so big and remote that there are no independent organizations or activists who can report anything," she warned. But officials are learning that cutting a path through ice isn't easy.

body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Berlin, October 23, 2026—The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Serbian authorities to ensure that journalists can report safely throughout Sunday’s parliamentary election, and the period that follows, after a campaign marked by physical attacks, police obstruction, and threats against reporters. Since CPJ warned a month ago of growing risks for journalists ahead of the vote, reporters have been pushed and hit by police officers, had phones seized or cameras struck , and been prevented from covering campaign events. At some pro-government rallies , police obstructed journalists, used force to remove them or failed to intervene when reporters were attacked. Security personnel also blocked journalists from some of these events. “The attacks we have seen during this election campaign are a warning of what could happen on October 25 and afterwards. Serbian authorities must ensure that police protect journalists rather than obstruct them and that local and international reporters can access election-related events. All reported attacks and irregularities must be promptly investigated,” said Attila Mong, CPJ’s Europe program coordinator. “Serbia’s international partners, election observers, and foreign embassies should closely monitor the safety of journalists on election day, stay in contact with local media and journalist safety groups, and raise attacks or obstruction immediately with Serbian authorities. Journalists must be able to document what happens around the country without fear. Their ability to do so is an essential part of a free and fair election,” Mong said. Recent attacks unfolded amid a broader climate of intimidation and hostility that has become increasingly common under Aleksandar Vučić, the former president who stepped down in September to run for election as prime minister after more than a decade in power. Independent media have faced repeated verbal attacks from public officials and ruling party figures, and there have been political smears against journalists and outlets, and online threats of death, serious physical harm, and sexual violence, including against family members and children . Several journalists had to leave Serbia because of security concerns. Independent media have also reported coordinated bot attacks on their social media accounts. The following cases, confirmed by local press freedom and media groups including the Association of Independent Electronic Media (ANEM), SafeJournalists Network, and the Independent Journalists’ Association of Serbia (NUNS), offer a snapshot of the attacks journalists have endured and the risks they faced during the election campaign: On September 20, a man assaulted Aleksandar Blanuša, editor of local news site Volim Zrenjanin, while he covered an event in Zrenjanin, northern Serbia. The man pushed him over a refrigerator beside a kiosk, injuring his elbow and back; Blanuša sought medical care. On October 3, a man threatened and attempted to physically attack N1 television reporter Mladen Savatović while he and a cameraman filmed a building suspected of being used for fictitious voter registrations in Serbia’s capital, Belgrade. The same day, a man seized local news site Bečejski Mozaik reporter Kristina Demeter Filipčev’s phone, demanded that she delete footage, and warned her not to publish it. Two days later, police prevented her from filming and reporting on Vučić’s visit to a dairy farm in Bečej, northern Serbia. She received rape threats before and after these incidents. Aleksa Nikolić, a correspondent for online outlet ZOOMER, suffered minor head injuries when a man threw an object that hit him in the temple after he filmed a ruling party campaign stand in the southern city of Niš on October 8. Police officers at the scene reportedly refused to intervene, but later took his statement and accompanied him for a medical examination. On October 11, police prevented a three-person KTV crew from covering a ruling-party rally in Zrenjanin for about two hours. Presenter Nemanja Šarović said officers struck him with shields, hands, and feet and pinned him against a pole, while police also interfered with the crew’s filming and equipment. On October 13, security personnel pushed Nova S television reporter Katarina Golubović and online outlet Glas Zaječara journalist Miljko Stojanović and cameraman Đorđe Đorđević, preventing them from covering a ruling party rally in Zaječar, eastern Serbia. They called the journalists a “security threat” and struck the camera. On October 16, security personnel shoved a reporter for online outlet Mašina as she tried to question Vučić at a campaign rally in Novi Sad, northern Serbia; her name was not disclosed. At the same rally, a man confronted Žarko Bogosavljević, editor of online outlet Razglas News, and struck his phone while he was filming. The election comes after years of mounting pressure on Serbia’s independent media. Earlier elections were also marred by violence. During local voting in March, journalists were pursued, brutally beaten , punched , kicked, pepper-sprayed and obstructed from reporting, their equipment was seized or destroyed and reporters were prevented from filming at polling stations. CPJ has published Serbian and English language safety resources for reporters covering the election and its aftermath. body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email The referral of independent outlet Mada Masr’s editor-in-chief Lina Attalah to trial, alongside the recent detention of an entire newsroom and the targeting of independent journalists, signals an escalating campaign to silence Egypt’s remaining independent media. In the space of a single month, Egyptian authorities detained all six journalists at the investigative and fact-checking platform Matsadaash, referred Attalah to trial over Mada Masr’s reporting, and summoned independent journalist Rasha Azab for questioning over her social media posts. Together, the cases reveal a widening assault on the people, practices, and institutions that make independent journalism possible. “We have always worked in difficult conditions, but I have never been as worried about the future of journalism as I am now,” Nora Younis, editor-in-chief of the Cairo-based independent outlet Al-Manassa, told CPJ. “Independent journalism in Egypt has moved from facing restrictions and threats to facing an existential danger.” The intensified crackdown began in late September, when security forces arrested the Matsadaash journalists. For days they were held in secret locations, with authorities withholding their whereabouts from both their families and their lawyers. After five days , they appeared before the Supreme State Security Prosecution, where they detailed alleged abuses, including being beaten and electrocuted which they described as torture, and said they had been forced to record fabricated confessions. Within weeks, prosecutors also summoned Azab and Attalah . Azab was questioned over her tweets, while Attalah was questioned about a recent Mada Masr report on a wave of protests in prisons across the country. Both were released on bail, but Attalah was referred to trial. Azab, who described the recent crackdown as unprecedented and systematic, said “its timing is no accident.” According to her, the arrests are clearing the ground for major political decisions that authorities want made without independent journalists asking questions — including who will succeed Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi after 2030 , and whether Egypt will join Saudi Arabia’s war against the Houthi rebels in Yemen . “The authorities are using Matsadaash, Attalah and Azab as a message to frighten Egypt’s entire journalism community,” she told CPJ. “Egyptian authorities are moving on multiple fronts to dismantle independent journalism: detaining an entire newsroom, putting one of the country’s most prominent independent journalists, Lina Attalah, on trial, and intimidating journalists who dare to hold power to account. The message is clear: no journalist is safe,” said CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah. This is a coordinated assault on the press, with 25 journalists behind bars, the highest number since 2021, the question is no longer whether Egypt’s independent press is under attack, but who’s next?” Egypt’s Public Prosecutor’s Office did not respond to CPJ’s emailed requests for comment on the recent arrests and summonses, the journalists’ allegations of mistreatment or the legal basis for referring Attalah to trial. Journalism on trial On October 7, prosecutors extended the detention of the Matsadaash journalists by 15 days, and issued a public statement saying the journalists face charges of joining and funding terrorism, spreading false news, and receiving monthly funding in foreign currency through bank transfers. The statement made plain that the case rests on journalism itself . They accused the six journalists of “highlighting shortcomings in state institutions to the exclusion of all else, downplaying the roles and performance of their officials, escalating sectoral grievances, highlighting and exaggerating obstacles related to the country’s internal affairs, publishing negative coverage of various sectors and highlighting officials’ failures in dealing with them.” In other words, the prosecution took the core work of accountability journalism, scrutinizing the state, giving voice to people’s grievances and exposing official failure, and recast it as evidence in a terrorism case. Though Egypt’s constitution explicitly prohibits prison sentences for publication offenses, authorities bypassed this protection by using the 2015 Anti-Terrorism Law, and holding the six journalists for days under an exceptional provision reserved for imminent terrorist threats. When prosecutors finally questioned the journalists, they asked about their journalism, their past employers and Matsadaash’s editorial policy, but did not accuse them of publishing any false or fabricated stories, their lawyers said. The statement also cited “periodic transfers in foreign currency” from a company registered abroad. “This is an empty accusation. There is nothing incriminating about our journalists working for an organization whose funding is well known and publicly disclosed, and was never hidden from the authorities in Egypt,” Abdelrahman Mansour, co-founder of Matsadaash, told CPJ. According to the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, whose lawyers represent the journalists, the company that owns Matsadaash contracted its Egypt-based staff years ago, submitted copies to the Egyptian banks, and received their monthly salaries for years without issue, a fact the prosecution itself acknowledged. State-controlled media amplified the narrative of foreign influence, with talk show host Ahmed Moussa claiming on the pro-government channel Sada El-Balad that the platform had received more than US$3 million from international donors. Fact-check outlet Tafnied revealed that the figure represented the total seven-year revenue of the platform’s parent U.S. nonprofit, not money sent to the Egyptian platform. The same donors, Tafnied found, have also funded Egyptian state universities and an NGO that works on state-backed initiatives, and one of them has an 11-project cooperation portfolio with Egypt’s Ministry of Planning. Pro-government commentator and former parliament member Abdel Rahim Ali portrayed the open-source investigation tools that Matsadaash uses as espionage on pro-government television. He singled out widely-used services such as the ship tracker MarineTraffic and the flight tracker Flightradar24, accusing their use of passing information to Israel’s Mossad spy agency. The licensing trap Shortly after Mada Masr joined other Egyptian and regional outlets in standing in solidarity with Matsadaash, its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, was referred to trial on charges of establishing and managing a website without a license. Under Article 105 of the media law, a conviction carries a fine of 1 million to 3 million Egyptian pounds (US$19,600 to 58,800), and the court can order Mada Masr closed and its equipment confiscated. Mada Masr has applied for a license from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council twice since the media law was enacted in 2018, but received no response . In 2022, the outlet learned of the council’s rejection when Attalah was questioned in a separate case on the same charge she now faces. A lawsuit challenging the council’s failure to notify the outlet was rejected in 2023. “Unfortunately, the charge of running a website without a license is a sword hanging over the neck of every independent platform in Egypt. None of us has been granted a license,” said Mohamed Salah, publisher of Fakar Tany, an independent Egyptian outlet whose own license application was rejected and whose appeal has gone unanswered. “It could be used against Fakar Tany, against Al-Manassa and against dozens of other websites. The rejection decision sits in an office drawer and comes out at the prosecution the moment it is needed to prove
title: Features & Analysis ‘Who’s next?’: Inside Egypt’s unprecedented crackdown on the press

body: Alors que les journalistes sont incarcérés et la presse muselée, Abdel Fattah Al-Sissi exploite le Forum Égypte pour menacer la presse Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Alors que le Forum Égypte, une conférence nationale destinée à mettre en avant les exploits du président Abdel Fattah al-Sissi, entamait sa troisième journée, ce 21 octobre, la rédactrice en chef du site d’information indépendant Mada Masr, Lina Atallah, subissait un interrogatoire en raison de son travail. Cela moins d’un mois après que la police a arrêté l'ensemble de la rédaction du média d’investigation indépendant Matsada2sh, fin septembre. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) dénonce une répression inédite et demande la libération des 26 journalistes détenus en Égypte. Trois semaines après que ses services de sécurité ont arrêté l'ensemble de la rédaction spécialisée en fact-checking de Matsada2sh , dont les six journalistes sont toujours détenus, le président Abdel Fattah al-Sissi a adressé un nouveau message sinistre aux journalistes du pays. Celui-ci a été diffusé sous la forme d’une vidéo gouvernementale lors de la cérémonie d'ouverture du Forum Égypte, la conférence nationale tenue en grande pompe dans la nouvelle capitale administrative, près du Caire, entre le 19 et le 24 octobre, pour présenter les accomplissements du président. Un homme dans une pièce sombre, entouré de graphiques numériques, alerte alors sur le danger d’un site de fact-checking fictif qui, selon lui, manipule l’information. “Partager une vidéo, ce n'est pas seulement cliquer sur un bouton” , estime-t-il, pointant du doigt le site fictif. “Partager, c'est y croire [...]” , ajoute-t-il. Si la référence au site Matsada2sh, un mot qui signifie “N’y croyez pas” , était déjà flagrante, le slogan à la fin de la vidéo, “Matshayyarsh” , qui signifie “Ne partagez pas”, rimait parfaitement avec le nom du site, dont la rédaction entière croupit en prison pour avoir simplement fait son travail. Installé au premier rang dans le public, le président a salué la vidéo : “Certains , dit-il sans préciser qui, sont capables de cerner et d’isoler les utilisateurs [des réseaux sociaux]. En manipulant une personne, ils peuvent manipuler l’opinion publique entière [...] et détruire un pays.” C'est ainsi que, dans son discours improvisé, le maréchal Sissi a de nouveau présenté ses prétextes aux insinuations complotistes pour justifier sa politique de répression. Depuis son arrivée au pouvoir en 2013, celle-ci a fait de l'Égypte l'une des plus grandes prisons du monde pour les journalistes. Au moment même où il prononçait ce discours, ses services de sécurité remettaient une convocation à la journaliste Lina Atallah . La rédactrice en chef de Mada Masr a ensuite subi quatre heures d’interrogatoire le 21 octobre avant d’être libérée sous caution. Son dossier a été transmis au tribunal, avec une audience “d'urgence” fixée au 27 octobre. Elle est accusée de gérer un site web sans licence. Pourtant, Mada Masr avait bien effectué les démarches, mais n’avait pas été informé du refus, en 2018, de délivrance d’une licence d’exploitation, décision que le média conteste en justice depuis 2022, mais qui reste sans réponse. Les reporters de Matsada2sh , eux, sont accusés de diffusion “de fausses informations”, d’“utilisation abusive des réseaux sociaux” et d’“appartenance à une organisation terroriste” à la suite d’aveux extorqués sous la torture, selon leurs avocats. Ces accusations erronées, selon le média, sont celles portées contre la plupart des journalistes détenus dans le pays. “En détenant 26 journalistes de son pays, dont les six journalistes de Matsada2sh, Abdel Fattah al-Sissi compromet la légitimité de toutes les réussites qu'il souhaite présenter au public égyptien lors de son forum. Alors qu’il incarcère des vérificateurs de faits, l’assurance avec laquelle il affirme la véracité des données présentées lors de la conférence relève d’une absurdité violente. Le droit à l’information ne détruit pas les pays, comme le prétend le président : il les renforce. Nous demandons la libération immédiate des six reporters de Matsada2sh , ainsi que celle de leurs 20 confrères. Nous réaffirmons notre soutien et notre solidarité à Lina Atallah : l’accusation portée contre elle doit être immédiatement levée. Elle ne devrait pas être traduite en justice pour avoir exercé son métier de journaliste.” Jonathan Dagher Responsable du bureau Moyen-Orient de RSF Une coalition de fact-checking sur le Forum pour défendre la liberté de la presse Malgré la détention de 26 journalistes et une presse muselée, Abdel Fattah al-Sissi rassure son public lors du festival : “Aucune des données qui vous seront communiquées n'est incomplète, erronée ou douteuse . ” Le public n’a d’autre choix que de le croire sur parole. En réponse à la répression et aux allégations du président, une coalition regroupant huit rédactions basées dans quatre pays, l’Égypte, le Liban, la Syrie, et la Tunisie, s'est constituée afin de poursuivre le travail de Matsada2sh à distance et vérifier les faits présentés lors de la conférence. “Nous suivons ces sessions en ligne, elles semblent très scénarisées” , estime le rédacteur en chef adjoint du site d’information Megaphone News au Liban, Samir Skayni. “Nous avons rejoint cette initiative pour défendre la liberté de la presse et manifester notre solidarité avec nos confrères d'autres rédactions de la région qui luttent, comme nous, contre des régimes autoritaires . ” Selon lui, travailler pour un média libanais permet une couverture plus libre : “Nous pouvons tirer parti de la liberté relative dont nous jouissons au Liban pour repousser les limites de ce qui peut être dit en Égypte et soutenir nos confrères égyptiens.” Selon lui, si les atteintes contre Matsadda2sh et Lina Attala ne suscitent pas de réactions adéquates de la part des journalistes dans les pays voisins, cela pourrait renforcer d’avantage la répression du journalisme indépendant en Égypte. L’absence du site de fact-checking égyptien laisse un vide dans la presse indépendante. Et la situation reste préoccupante pour les journalistes de Matsada2sh : malgré les révélations de leurs avocats, le gouvernement egyptien nie avoir torturé les six journalistes. L’ Égypte occupe le 169e rang sur 180 pays et territoires dans le Classement mondial de la liberté de la presse établi en 2026 par RSF. body: Libye : RSF condamne l’enlèvement d’un journaliste menacé de mort pour avoir enquêté sur la corruption Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Reporters sans frontières (RSF) condamne avec la plus grande fermeté l’enlèvement et les violences subis par Hassan Bakir. Le journaliste de l’Agence de presse libyenne (LANA), enlevé le 20 octobre dans le nord-ouest de la Libye, a été torturé, interrogé et menacé de mort s’il ne cessait pas ses enquêtes sur la corruption, avant d’être abandonné sur l’autoroute. RSF appelle les autorités libyennes à mener une enquête approfondie et transparente afin d’identifier et de traduire en justice les responsables au plus vite, ainsi qu’à assurer la protection du journaliste et de sa famille. Selon les informations recueillies par RSF, Hassan Bakir a été enlevé par un groupe armé devant les locaux de sa rédaction à Misrata , le 20 octobre. Les ravisseurs l’ont emmené à bord d’un véhicule aux vitres teintées de Misrata jusqu’à Tripoli, soit à plus de 200 kilomètres. Après l’avoir séquestré, ils l’ont finalement abandonné gisant sur le bord de la route, où des unités de sécurité relevant du gouvernement de l’Ouest l’ont retrouvé dans la nuit du 20 au 21 octobre. Hassan Bakir est depuis hospitalisé à l’hôpital spécialisé Iwan de Misrata. Hassan Bakir a témoigné auprès de RSF avoir été battu et torturé au cours de sa captivité. Il a expliqué que ses agresseurs l’ont longuement interrogé sur son travail journalistique, et en particulier sur les enquêtes qu’il publie régulièrement sur ses comptes de réseaux sociaux sur la corruption et les détournements de fonds dans l’attribution de contrats et de projets publics. Le journaliste a témoigné, en outre, avoir été menacé de mort s’il ne cessait pas de traiter ces sujets. “Cet enlèvement, mené en plein jour devant une rédaction, puis les tortures infligées pour faire taire un journaliste qui enquête sur la corruption, illustrent à la fois le niveau de dangerosité de l’exercice du métier de journaliste et le niveau d’impunité dont jouissent les groupes armés en Libye. Cibler les journalistes, c’est cibler le droit des Libyens à savoir ce qui se passe dans leur pays. Hassan Bakir a eu la vie sauve, mais ses ravisseurs sont toujours en liberté et lui et ses confrères restent exposés. Nous appelons les autorités libyennes à identifier et poursuivre les auteurs et les commanditaires de cette agression au plus vite, et à garantir la protection du journaliste et de sa famille. Nous appelons également plus largement les autorités de l’ensemble du pays à garantir la sécurité des professionnels des médias et à mettre fin à l’impunité des crimes commis contre eux.” Oussama Bouagila Directeur du bureau RSF en Afrique du Nord Les journalistes libyens, et tout particulièrement ceux qui s’intéressent à la corruption, aux financements publics ou aux groupes armés, travaillent dans un climat de peur permanent , exposés aux enlèvements, aux détentions arbitraires et aux violences, le plus souvent sans que leurs agresseurs aient à répondre de leurs actes. La Libye est placée 138e sur 180 pays au Classement mondial de la liberté de la presse établi par RSF en 202 6. Publié le 23.10.2026 Maghreb - Moyen-Orient Libye Violences contre les journalistes Actualité Dénonciation Liberté de la presse
title: Libye : RSF condamne l’enlèvement d’un journaliste menacé de mort pour avoir enquêté sur la corruption 23.10.2026

body: Recul inédit de la liberté de la presse au Burkina Faso : jusqu’à 30 ans de prison pour des délits de presse Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Alors que les peines privatives de liberté pour des délits de presse avaient été supprimées en 2015 au Burkina Faso, l’Assemblée législative a adopté à l’unanimité, le 20 octobre, un nouveau Code pénal qui les réintroduit. Pour des faits qualifiés d’apologie du terrorisme, dont la définition est vague, les journalistes peuvent désormais risquer jusqu’à 30 ans de prison. Reporters sans frontières (RSF) dénonce une régression alarmante pour la liberté de la presse et appelle les autorités burkinabè à ne pas promulguer le texte. La “repénalisation des délits de presse” est présentée par l’Assemblée législative du peuple (ALP), le Parlement de transition du Burkina Faso, comme l’une des “ innovations majeures ” du nouveau Code pénal. Elle constitue, en réalité, un grave retour en arrière. Plébiscité par l’ensemble des 71 députés le 20 octobre, le projet de loi avait été adopté en Conseil des ministres le 4 décembre 2025. Le texte, dont RSF a obtenu une copie, prévoit de sanctionner une entreprise de presse reconnue coupable d’“apologie de terrorisme” par une amende allant de 500 millions à un milliard de francs CFA (environ 762 000 à 1,52 million d’euros), une fermeture temporaire ou définitive et la confiscation de son matériel. Son dirigeant s’expose à 20 ans de prison et à une amende de 20 millions de francs CFA (environ 30 500 euros). Pire, la définition d’“apologie de terrorisme” reste vague : en est coupable “quiconque présente ou commente favorablement et publiquement, le terrorisme en général, les actes de terrorisme déjà commis et les auteurs de tels actes”, ce qui pourrait alors exposer les journalistes couvrant ou commentant la situation sécuritaire. Toute personne reconnue coupable lorsque les faits sont commis par voie de presse ou en ligne encourt en effet une peine de 21 à 30 ans de prison et une amende de 50 à 100 millions de francs CFA (environ 76 000 à 152 000 euros). Le Code pénal de 2018 , qui avait introduit l’infraction, prévoyait une peine maximale de 21 ans de prison et une amende de 10 millions de francs CFA (environ 15 200 euros). “C’est un coup de tonnerre pour la presse burkinabè. Onze ans après la fin des peines privatives de liberté pour des délits de presse, le Parlement opère un retour en arrière d’une extrême gravité. En criminalisant des contenus journalistiques susceptibles d’être interprétés comme favorables au terrorisme, les autorités risquent de transformer la couverture de la situation sécuritaire en mission impossible. RSF dénonce une grave menace pour le droit à l’information, qui risque d’encourager l’autocensure et d’étouffer les dernières voix indépendantes. La lutte contre le terrorisme ne peut justifier la criminalisation du journalisme. RSF appelle les autorités à ne pas promulguer ce texte et à renoncer à toute disposition qui sacrifie la liberté d’informer au nom de la sécurité nationale. Jeanne Lagarde Responsable plaidoyer du bureau Afrique subsaharienne de RSF Un arsenal répressif qui s’alourdit Le texte reconduit par ailleurs d’autres infractions introduites par la révision en 2019 du Code pénal de 2018 : la diffusion d’informations jugées fausses et susceptibles de faire croire à des atteintes aux personnes ou aux biens, ainsi que la diffusion d’informations relatives aux opérations antiterroristes, aux positions et aux équipements des forces de sécurité. Les sanctions atteignent jusqu’à dix ans de prison et dix millions de francs CFA d’amende (environ 15 200 euros). Il alourdit aussi les sanctions pécuniaires de certaines infractions, comme la participation à une “entreprise de démoralisation des forces” ou la divulgation d’informations sensibles liées à la défense nationale. Certaines amendes doublent et s’ajoutent à des peines pouvant aller jusqu’à dix ans de prison. Depuis l’arrivée au pouvoir du capitaine Ibrahim Traoré en septembre 2022, les pressions contre la presse burkinabè se sont multipliées : menaces de mort , arrestations , enlèvements de journalistes, fermetures de médias, expulsions de journalistes étrangers... Ces restrictions renforcent l’autocensure et poussent de nombreux professionnels des médias à l’exil. Les journalistes Atiana Serge Oulon et Moussa Sareba , enlevés respectivement en juin 2024 et en août 2025, sont toujours portés disparus. title: Recul inédit de la liberté de la presse au Burkina Faso : jusqu’à 30 ans de prison pour des délits de presse 23.10.2026

body: Inde : près de six mois après l'arrivée au pouvoir du BJP dans le Bengale-Occidental, des pressions contre les journalistes se multiplient Organisation : RSF_fr Partager facebook twitter linkedin Courriel Depuis l’arrivée au pouvoir au Bengale-Occidental le 9 mai 2026 d’un gouvernement issu du Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) – parti nationaliste hindou dont est issu le Premier ministre Narendra Modi –, soit en moins de six mois, plusieurs journalistes et médias ont été confrontés à des poursuites judiciaires abusives, à des attaques et à du cyberharcèlement émanant de militants du BJP. Face à ce climat hostile pour la presse, Reporters sans frontières (RSF) appelle le ministre en chef de l’État, Suvendu Adhikari, à engager des mesures fortes pour protéger l’information et le journalisme Quelques jours seulement après son arrivée au pouvoir en mai 2026, le nouveau gouvernement de l’État, dirigé par le Bharatiya Janata Party (“parti du peuple indien” ou BJP), a donné le ton en interdisant aux fonctionnaires, via une circulaire interne du 20 mai 2026, de s’exprimer dans la presse. Deux mois plus tard, pour un titre d’article, la police a ouvert une procédure pénale contre deux journalistes d’ Anandabazar Patrika , le plus grand quotidien en langue bengalie du pays, qui a également vu les murs de ses locaux vandalisés et ses journalistes harcelés en ligne. Le média indépendant Maktoob Media , fait lui aussi l’objet de poursuites pour six chefs d’accusation pour avoir simplement relayé les propos d’une femme politique. “La dégradation des locaux du quotidien Anandabazar Patrika et le cyberharcèlement visant ses journalistes , les restrictions imposées aux fonctionnaires sur le partage d’informations à la presse et les poursuites abusives contre des médias sont autant d’actes d’intimidation, visant à faire taire la presse, et d’entrave au droit à l’information. L’avenir de la liberté de la presse s’annonce sombre sous le nouveau gouvernement du BJP au Bengale-Occidental, qui n’est au pouvoir que depuis près de six mois. Condamnant ces attaques contre le journalisme, RSF appelle les autorités du Bengale-Occidental à mettre un terme aux procédures abusives visant les médias, à garantir la sécurité des journalistes ainsi que leur accès à l’information publique et à mener une enquête sur les responsables du vandalisme et du harcèlement visant Anandabazar Patrika . Célia Mercier Responsable du bureau Asie du Sud de RSF L'information coupée à la source Le gouvernement de l'État du Bengale-Occidental a publié une circulaire , datée du 19 mai, imposant aux fonctionnaires une “interdiction formelle, en l’absence d’une autorisation officielle du gouvernement, de communiquer directement ou indirectement à la presse tout document ou toute information”. Tout agent a également l’interdiction de “participer à un programme médiatique produit par une entité privée”, sans autorisation préalable. Présentée comme un simple rappel des règles existantes, la circulaire va pourtant au-delà de celles-ci, avec des restrictions générales et disproportionnées, selon l'association indienne de défense des droits numériques Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF). Plainte, harcèlement et attaque contre une rédaction Le 21 août, au lendemain d’affrontements entre des groupes d’étudiants dans une université de Calcutta, le quotidien local en bengali Anandabazar Patrika a publié en une un titre qualifiant ces violences de “ hooliganisme safran ” – le safran désignant les nationalistes hindous. Une semaine plus tard, le ministre en chef Suvendu Adhikari a exigé des excuses de la part du journal et la police a ouvert une procédure d’enquête ( First Information Report ou FIR) pénale, à la suite de la plainte d’un particulier, contre la rédactrice en chef Ishani Dutta Ray et la chef du service reportage Soma Mukherjee , qui ont ensuite été également victimes de cyberharcèlement en particulier de la part de partisans du BJP. Alors que les accusations formulées dans la plainte pourraient conduire à une arrestation, la haute cour de Calcutta a ordonné aux autorités policières, fin septembre, de ne prendre aucune mesure coercitive contre les deux femmes journalistes, et ce jusqu’au 15 décembre. Autre acte de représailles, le 1er septembre, des hommes portant des vêtements de couleur safran se sont rassemblés devant les locaux du journal à Calcutta, ont scandé des slogans hostiles au journal et ont peint certaines parties du bâtiment en safran sous le regard de la police. Alors que le gouvernement BJP, nouvellement élu, a nié toute implication, le média en ligne Alt News a révélé que plusieurs manifestants étaient des militants du parti, dont un responsable de la section jeunesse. Un média visé pour avoir rapporté les propos d’une députée La police du Bengale-Occidental a par ailleurs enregistré , le 19 septembre, une plainte contre Maktoob Media , site d’information lancé en 2014, qui couvre en particulier les droits humains, les minorités, l’exclusion sociale et la liberté religieuse. Les poursuites concernent leurs publications sur X et YouTube rapportant les allégations d’une députée de l’opposition. Celle-ci avait dénoncé le fait que trois hauts fonctionnaires musulmans auraient été exclus de réunions de sécurité cruciales lors de la visite dans l'État du ministre de l'Intérieur, Amit Shah. Dans une lettre adressée à X , la police a qualifié le contenu de “purement inventé” et de “malveillant” . Elle a demandé à la plateforme de lui fournir les données relatives au compte du média, à la connexion et à l’appareil informatique concerné pour la période du 1er au 5 février 2026, c’est-à-dire plusieurs mois avant les événements rapportés et la plainte elle-même. Maktoob Media n’a eu connaissance de l’affaire que lorsque X l’en a informé. Quatre des six chefs d'accusation portés contre le média – “incitation à l’hostilité entre communautés”, “atteinte délibérée aux sentiments religieux”, “diffusion d’informations trompeuses susceptibles d’attiser la haine, les tensions entre communautés et les troubles à l’ordre public” et “incitation d’une communauté à commettre des infractions contre une autre”– excluent toute possibilité de libération sous caution. Le BJP a remporté les élections législatives du Bengale-Occidental qui se sont tenues les 23 et 29 avril 2026. Sa victoire a mis fin à 15 ans de règne du Trinamool Congress (TMC), un parti de centre-gauche. RSF avait alors appelé le nouveau gouvernement de l’État à garantir aux journalistes le droit d’informer, sans violences, sans censure et sans intimidation. Publié le 23.10.2026 Asie - Pacifique Inde Violences contre les journalistes Actualité
title: Inde : près de six mois après l'arrivée au pouvoir du BJP dans le Bengale-Occidental, des pressions contre les journalistes se multiplient 23.10.2026

body: News News Item OSCE participating States and Asian Partners share regional experiences in conflict prevention to strengthen responses to today’s interconnected security challenges Issued on: 23 October 2026 Issued by: Asian Partners for Co-operation , OSCE Secretariat Fields of work: Conflict prevention and resolution The OSCE Security Committee and the Asian Partners for Co-operation Group (APCG) held a joint meeting today in Vienna under the theme “Conflict Prevention and Preventive Diplomacy: A Comparative Regional Dialogue”. The meeting offered an opportunity to share regional experiences and explore opportunities to further strengthen dialogue and co-operation across both regions, particularly relevant in today’s volatile security environment. It was co-chaired by the United Kingdom, in its capacity as Chair of the OSCE Security Committee, and Finland, as Chair of the APCG, and co-organized with Australia. The meeting provided a first opportunity for an even broader and inclusive discussion among the two regions, with Qatar recently joining the five APCG members (Afghanistan, Australia, Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Thailand), following a consensus Ministerial Council decision by all 57 OSCE participating States. In his keynote video address, OSCE Secretary General Feridun H. Sinirlioğlu highlighted that “at a time of intense geopolitical polarization, placing huge strain on multilateralism and international security and stability, structured political dialogue between regions is a diplomatic necessity.” “The OSCE continues to have a unique role to play in conflict and crisis situations through its conflict-cycle toolbox, but even the best tools alone are not enough, if there is a lack of political will and trust among states. Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is the starkest possible reminder of this. No region or organization can address the challenges of conflict prevention alone, making cooperation and the exchange of experiences across regions important,” said Ambassador Outi Hyvärinen, Permanent Representative of Finland to the OSCE and Chair of the OSCE Asian Partners for Co-operation Group. “Today’s exchange has underlined that preventive diplomacy is not one instrument or one moment. It requires credible early warning, open communication, engagement and the political will to act before positions harden and risks escalate. It has also shown the value of comparing regional experience and learning lessons between regions. I hope this can be the basis for continued, practical exchange between the OSCE and ASEAN on conflict prevention and preventive diplomacy,” said James Ford, Chargé d'affaires, United Kingdom Delegation to the OSCE on behalf of the Security Committee. Ambassador I Gusti Agung Wesaka Puja, Executive Director of the ASEAN Institute for Peace and Reconciliation (ASEAN-IPR), stressed that “in this current global fragmentation, the region needs to develop regional crisis management capacity and to strengthen its resilience against sudden conflicts and geopolitical surprise by developing an early warning mechanism and multi stakeholder preventive diplomacy ecosystem.” Contributions from the co-organizers highlighted the importance of sustained diplomatic engagement, political will, trust, confidence-building and early warning in preventing tensions from escalating into conflict.
title: OSCE participating States and Asian Partners share regional experiences in conflict prevention to strengthen responses to today’s interconnected security challenges

body: News News Item OSCE workshop in Turkmenistan promotes best practices in preventing and responding to gender-based violence Issued on: 23 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Centre in Ashgabat Fields of work: Gender-based violence Representatives from state institutions, municipal bodies and civil society organizations in the Ahal velayat (province) discussed practical experiences in preventing and responding to gender-based violence (GBV), including domestic violence (DV) at the local level during an OSCE-organized workshop that took place on 22 and 23 October 2026 in Ashgabat. The OSCE Centre in Ashgabat organized the workshop to enhance capacities of different stakeholders in preventing and responding to gender-based violence, including domestic violence, and provide a platform for exchanging practical approaches and good practices, including lessons learned from the preceding study visit to the Republic of Tajikistan. International experts presented facts and figures on gender-based violence, including domestic violence, in the world and Central Asian region, and elaborated on the existing mechanisms for GBV prevention and response in Turkmenistan and the Ahal velayat. Discussions focused on multi-agency response to gender-based violence, and national priorities for the prevention and response to GBV. “Addressing gender-based violence requires a comprehensive, co-ordinated and survivor-centred approach, involving state institutions, law-enforcement bodies, social and healthcare services and civil society organizations,” said Olivera Zurovac-Kuzman, Economic and Environmental Officer and Gender Focal Point at the OSCE Centre in Ashgabat. The workshop presented essential services to victims of DV/GBV, such as specialized police units, one-stop centers and short-term transit shelters, as well as specialized services, including helplines, women’s resource centers and crisis centers. Behavior-change programs for perpetrators of domestic violence were also discussed. During discussions, participants shared their views on possibilities of introducing GBV prevention strategies and tailored services to victims of DV/GBV in the Ahal velayat. The workshop was organized as part of the OSCE extra-budgetary project on preventing and combating GBV funded by the Governments of Norway, Germany, the United States and Finland. body: News News Item OSCE Mission to Montenegro initiates co-operation to strengthen practice-oriented journalism education Issued on: 23 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Montenegro Fields of work: Media freedom and development The OSCE Mission to Montenegro brought the Faculty of Political Science’s Department for Media Studies and Journalism and student radio Radio Krš together, to introduce “Production Days”, a practice-oriented learning initiative enabling journalism students to produce their own radio programmes. The initiative aims to bridge the gap between academic learning and professional practice, helping future journalists develop the editorial, technical and ethical skills needed for accurate, public-interest and responsible reporting. This initiative responds to the 2025 Media Training Needs Assessment, supported by the Mission, which identified a demand for more structured hands-on learning and stronger links between journalism education and hands-on practice. In response to these recommendations, the Mission initiated and facilitated dialogue between the Department and Radio Krš to create opportunities for students accordingly. Another step took place this week, when second- and third-year students met with Radio Krš representatives to learn about the station’s operations and opportunities to contribute to its programming. Through Production Days, students will work in mixed groups of five to select topics, develop stories, and produce their own programmes. Radio Krš will provide technical assistance and broadcast the programmes, with the Department’s teaching staff supporting students’ assignments. This approach will enable future journalists to apply their academic knowledge, develop editorial judgement, and gain experience in teamwork and radio production. Head of the Journalism Department, Nataša Ružić, stated that, in addition to theoretical knowledge, the Department wants to provide future journalists with as much practical experience as possible in various media. “That is why we continuously expand the network of media that we co-operate with. Co-operation with Radio Krš will give students the opportunity to learn new skills and get to know work in the radio medium, in order to more easily develop their professional interests,” said Ružić. The co-operation builds on the Mission’s longstanding support to both partners. The Mission has assisted the Department in strengthening practice-oriented teaching and student production, including through donations of technical equipment. It has also supported Radio Krš in producing content of public interest and donated equipment to strengthen the station’s production capacity. body: Share H.E. Hun Manet Prime Minister Royal Government of Cambodia Phnom Penh, Cambodia October 12, 2026 Re: Follow-up to the Urgent Appeal to Free the Five Imprisoned Mother Nature Cambodia Activists Dear Prime Minister Hun Manet, We are writing to follow up on our previous letter to you on June 4, 2026, in which 74 organizations from Europe, Asia, Africa, Latin America, and North America urged you to release the five young leaders from the group Mother Nature Cambodia (MNC). Unfortunately, to date, we have received no reply or even acknowledgement from your office to that urgent correspondence. A copy of that June 4, 2026, letter is attached. Those five leaders, popularly known as the Mother Nature Cambodia 5 (MNC5), are Long Kunthea, Yim Leanghy, Thun Ratha, Phuon Keoraksmey, and Ly Chandaravuth. They were unjustly convicted and imprisoned in July 2024 in a trial that violated fair trial and due process requirements, and are currently serving six to eight year prison terms. Since their imprisonment, their applications for bail have been repeatedly rejected. Their lawyer filed an appeal against their conviction in July 2024, and has repeatedly raised this appeal request, but more than two years later, the Ministry of Justice and the courts have failed to move forward with an appeals court trial. In addition to the matters set out in our previous letter, we consider it important to draw your attention to the fact that the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD) investigated the case of the MNC5 and rendered a clear determination that their detention is arbitrary and unjust on multiple grounds, and stated that “the appropriate remedy would be to release Mr. Ly, Ms. Long, Ms. Phuon, Mr. Thun and Mr. Yim immediately and accord them an enforceable right to compensation and other reparations, in accordance with international law.” The WGAD found that the Cambodian authorities’ actions in the criminal case and court proceedings against the MNC5 included instances of judicial bias and violated multiple civil and political rights guaranteed by international law in treaties ratified by Cambodia, such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The Cambodian government failed to even provide a response to the WGAD’s communications requesting information about the MNC5 case. It is very important that the WGAD found no evidence that the MNC5 defendants had engaged in or advocated violence, which calls into question the basis for their conviction on charges of “plotting” against the government. It further noted that the lèse-majesté law cannot justify a restriction on freedom of expression or be invoked as a legal basis for detention. The WGAD concluded that the MNC5 were denied a fair trial and effective appeal – and called on the Cambodian government to immediately release the five activists. The full UN WGAD decision 67/2025, dated February 5, 2026, can be accessed online here: www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/issues/detention-wg/opinions/sessions104/a-hrc-wgad-2025-67-cambodia-advance-edited.pdf Since 2012, the award-winning Mother Nature Cambodia has led peaceful environmental conservation campaigns reaching millions, creatively using social media to effectively raise public awareness about issues threatening Cambodia’s fragile environment. The five activists have peacefully advocated for environmental protection in Cambodia by expressing their views and exercising their rights to peaceful public assembly in line with UN human rights conventions ratified by Cambodia. As Cambodia is preparing to host the 20th Francophonie Summit in Phnom Penh on November 15-16, 2026, the international spotlight will naturally be focused on your country’s actions as the host nation. Francophonie nations and observer states around the world will have strong expectations that Cambodia should live up to its international commitments, including upholding its international human rights law obligations. Whether or not Cambodia complies with the decision of the WGAD about the MNC5 will be a prominent issue that will likely be raised with you. In this context, we urge you to recognize that civil and political rights, environmental protection, and climate action are central to the global challenges addressed at the summit, and releasing the MNC5 from their arbitrary and unjust imprisonment would be an important signal for Cambodia to send to visiting Francophonie leaders. In this spirit, we strongly urge you to comply with the decision of the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention and take immediate, proactive steps to release these five young environmental leaders ahead of the Francophonie Summit, if not earlier. We thank you for your consideration of our views and look forward to hearing from you. To convey your response, please contact Ines Gavrilut of the Bruno Manser Fonds at email: ines.gavrilut@bmf.ch Sincerely, Agent Green, Romania Asian Forum for Human Rights and Development (FORUM-ASIA) Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates (AHRLA) Bruno Manser Fonds CIVICUS: World Alliance for Citizen Participation Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) International FERN: Making Europe Work for People & Forests Human Rights Watch International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), within the framework of the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders Mother Nature Cambodia Platforma Pentru Adaptare Climatică (PAC), Romania Right Livelihood World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), within the framework of the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders Copies to: Louise Mushikiwabo, Secretary-General of the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) Emmanuel Macron, President of France Mark Carney, Prime Minister of Canada Ignazio Cassis, Swiss Federal Councilor Bart De Wever, Prime Minister of Belgium Luc Frieden, Prime Minister of Luxemburg Tags Justice system Arbitrary detention Related resources Cambodia 13.10.26 Urgent Interventions Vietnam/Cambodia: Human rights defenders Nguyen Duc Thuan, Hiep Tran and Thai Cong Truong Son charged with terrorism in Vietnam after their enforced disappearance in Cambodia Read more Cambodia 04.06.26 Statements Cambodia/Thailand: Six years on, authorities must act on the enforced disappearance of Wanchalearm Satsaksit Read more Cambodia 02.06.26 Statements Cambodia: Appeal to free the five imprisoned Mother Nature Cambodia activists Read more

body: Share VNM 001 / 1026 / OBS 050 Enforced disappearance / Arbitrary detention / Transnational repression / Vietnam/Cambodia 13 October 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT) and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Vietnam and Cambodia . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed about the enforced disappearance in Cambodia of Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan , Mr Hiep Tran and Mr Thai Cong Truong Son and their subsequent arbitrary detention and prosecution on terrorism-related charges in Vietnam. Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan is a Vietnamese-Norwegian human rights defender based in Oslo, who campaigns for the release of political prisoners and for freedom of religion or belief in Vietnam. Mr Hiep Tran, also known as Ho Pham Hiep Huy, is a Vietnamese-Australian human rights defender based in Melbourne, known for his work against human trafficking. On 28 September 2026, the Vietnamese Ministry of Public Security announced that Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan, Mr Hiep Tran, and a third person, Mr Thai Cong Truong Son, a Vietnamese national, had been arrested on 18 September 2026 at 9:50 pm at the My Quy Tay border gate in Vietnam’s Tay Ninh Province. The Ministry alleged that the three men had entered Vietnam illegally from Cambodia using forged documents to carry out “terrorist” activities. According to the Ministry, Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan, Mr Hiep Tran and Mr Thai Cong Truong Son “confessed” to being members of Viet Tan, a pro-democracy political party that authorities designated as a “terrorist organisation” in 2016. On the same day, the Supreme People’s Procuracy approved the decision to prosecute and detain the three men. They were charged with “terrorism” under Article 299(2) of the Criminal Code, which prescribes a sentence of five to 15 years’ imprisonment, and with “forging seals and documents of agencies or organisations” under Article 341(2), which prescribes a sentence of two to five years’ imprisonment. According to information obtained from Norwegian and Australian embassies, the HRDs are being detained at Chi Hoa Prison in Ho Chi Minh City. On 15 September 2026, Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan and Mr Hiep Tran travelled from Bangkok, Thailand, to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with Vietnamese human rights activists. They were due to return to Bangkok on 19 September 2026. Their last known communication took place on the morning of 18 September 2026, while they were in Kaoh Andaet District, Takeo Province, near Cambodia’s southern border with Vietnam. Their relatives and colleagues lost all contact with them thereafter, and their fate and whereabouts remained unknown for 10 days. The Observatory notes that Kaoh Andaet District, where Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan and Mr Hiep Tran were last known to be, is located more than 250 kilometres from the My Quy Tay border gate, on a different section of the Cambodia-Vietnam border. This discrepancy casts serious doubts on the Cambodian and Vietnamese official accounts and raises serious concerns that the two defenders were abducted on Cambodian territory and forcibly transferred to Vietnam outside of any legal procedure. The Observatory recalls that the deprivation of liberty of Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan, Mr Hiep Tran and Mr Thai Cong Truong Son, followed by the refusal of the Vietnamese authorities to acknowledge it or to disclose their fate and whereabouts for 10 days, thereby placing them outside the protection of the law, constitutes an enforced disappearance under international law. The Observatory further recalls that Cambodia, as a State party to the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance, is bound to investigate any disappearance committed on its territory. Cambodia is also prohibited from transferring any person to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that they would be in danger of being subjected to enforced disappearance or torture. The Observatory expresses serious concerns that the alleged “confessions” of Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan, Mr Hiep Tran and Mr Thai Cong Truong Son were obtained while they were held incommunicado, without access to lawyers, their families or consular representatives, placing them at heightened risk of torture and other ill-treatment. This is all the more worrying as the use of torture and ill-treatment to extract confessions from human rights defenders and dissidents in Vietnam has been repeatedly documented by civil society organisations and denounced by UN human rights mechanisms . The Observatory recalls that, pursuant to Article 15 of the UN Convention against Torture, ratified by Vietnam in 2015, any statement established to have been made as a result of torture shall not be invoked as evidence in any proceedings. The Observatory is also deeply concerned about the health of Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan, who reportedly requires daily insulin, and stresses the urgent need to guarantee him immediate and unhindered access to appropriate medical care. The Observatory expresses its deep concern that the enforced disappearance and arbitrary detention of Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan, Mr Hiep Tran and Mr Thai Cong Truong Son appear to be part of a broader and systematic pattern of transnational repression by the Vietnamese authorities, aimed at silencing and punishing human rights defenders and dissidents abroad for their legitimate human rights activities. Such practices include abductions, forced returns, threats and the misuse of extradition procedures, often carried out with the cooperation or acquiescence of authorities in neighbouring countries and frequently under the guise of counter-terrorism legislation. The Observatory recalls the case of Mr Y Quynh Bdap , a Montagnard human rights defender who was sentenced in absentia to 10 years' imprisonment on "terrorism" charges in Vietnam in January 2024 and extradited from Thailand to Vietnam on 28 November 2025 despite the serious risks of torture, ill-treatment and enforced disappearance he faced there. Other emblematic cases include those of blogger Duong Van Thai, abducted in Thailand in April 2023 and later sentenced in Vietnam to 12 years' imprisonment, and journalist Truong Duy Nhat , abducted in Bangkok in January 2019 and sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment. The Observatory also recalls that UN human rights mechanisms have repeatedly expressed concern over these practices. In July 2025, the UN Human Rights Committee expressed concern about allegations of extraterritorial enforced disappearances and other forms of transnational repression by Vietnamese officials as well as the use of politically motivated extradition processes and counter-terrorism laws to target dissenting voices. In joint communications made public in November 2025, including to Vietnam and Cambodia , UN Special Procedures warned of a surge in human rights violations of a transnational nature across Southeast Asia, and recalled that States are obliged to prevent violations committed by foreign States on their territory. The Observatory therefore calls on the Cambodian authorities to clarify the circumstances in which the three defenders left Cambodian territory and to investigate and prosecute any involvement or acquiescence of Cambodian officials in their abduction and transfer. The Observatory strongly condemns the enforced disappearance, arbitrary detention, and judicial harassment of Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan, Mr Hiep Tran and Mr Thai Cong Truong Son, as well as the misuse of counter-terrorism legislation to criminalise human rights defenders and the transnational repression targeting Vietnamese human rights defenders abroad. The Observatory calls on the Vietnamese authorities to immediately and unconditionally release Mr Nguyen Duc Thuan, Mr Hiep Tran and Mr Thai Cong Truong Son and to drop all charges against them. Finally, the Observatory urges the Government
title: Vietnam/Cambodia: Human rights defenders Nguyen Duc Thuan, Hiep Tran and Thai Cong Truong Son charged with terrorism in Vietnam after their enforced disappearance in Cambodia Read more

body: Share IND 002 / 1026 / OBS 049 Arbitrary detention / Judicial harassment / Deterioration of health condition while in detention India 8 October 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in India . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed about the arbitrary detention and further deterioration of the health of Mr Vishal Singh , an Indian documentary filmmaker and human rights defender, in connection with the so-called “Lucknow Conspiracy Case”. His work focuses on marginalised communities, including migrant workers and tribal communities, as well as issues relating to social justice. Detained since 29 June 2025, Mr Vishal Singh's health condition has severely deteriorated during his arbitrary detention. He requires dialysis three times a week, while also suffering from severe migraines, vomiting, difficulties retaining food and water, extreme weakness, impaired vision, and difficulty walking. He was first admitted to Balrampur Hospital in Lucknow on 14 August 2026 and was subsequently referred and transferred to King George Medical University (KGMU) Hospital in Lucknow, Utter Pradesh State, and discharged on 5 September 2026 before returning to Lucknow District Jail from where he is currently taken to KGMU three times a week for dialysis. On 4 October 2026, Mr Singh also experienced breathing difficulties and was taken to the KGMU Trauma Centre before being discharged and returned to Lucknow District Jail. His next hearing on the evidence of the proceedings is scheduled on 13 October 2026. On 29 June 2025, the National Investigation Agency (NIA) arrested Mr Singh in Delhi in connection with the “Lucknow Conspiracy Case” (RC-01/2023/NIA/Lucknow), concerning alleged attempts to revive the activities of the banned Communist Party of India Maoist (CPI Maoist) in northern India. The NIA filed a chargesheet against him on 29 November 2025 under Section 121A of the Indian Penal Code and Sections 18, 20, 38, and 39 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA). The first hearing in the case took place on 11 December 2025, after which a series of hearings were regularly postponed. The proceedings subsequently moved from the appearance stage to the framing of charges and then to the evidence stage in February 2026. According to the NIA, Mr Singh participated in efforts to revive the CPI, supplied a drone to members of the organisation and trained cadres in its use. Mr Singh's health had already seriously deteriorated since July 2026. On 30 July 2026, an application was filed before the NIA Special Court in Lucknow seeking for an appropriate medical treatment for Mr Singh. The Court authorised his transfer to a hospital. However, the prison authorities delayed his transfer for approximately 15 days. During this period, Mr Singh's health further deteriorated. The Observatory recalls that the “ Lucknow Conspiracy Case ” was initiated by the NIA in September 2023 to investigate alleged attempts to revive Maoist activities in northern India. The case has involved i nvestigations and arrests of human rights defenders, labour rights activists, students, and lawyers across several Indian states. The Observatory also recalls that persons deprived of their liberty must be treated with humanity and with respect for their inherent dignity, in accordance with Article 10 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which India is a state party. The Observatory is gravely concerned by the severe deterioration of Mr Singh's health in detention and by the fact that he continues to be deprived of his liberty while requiring dialysis three times a week. The Observatory is particularly concerned that his continued arbitrary detention may hinder him from receiving the specialised and continuous medical care required by his health condition. The Observatory urges the Indian authorities to take all necessary measures to protect Mr Singh's life and physical integrity, ensure that he has immediate and continuous access to appropriate specialised medical care, and unconditionally release him for his next hearing on 13 October. Actions requested: Please write to the authorities of India urging them to: Guarantee in all circumstances the physical integrity and psychological well-being of Vishal Singh and all human rights defenders in India; Immediately ensure that Vishal Singh receives adequate and specialised medical care, including regular dialysis, and that his health condition is assessed; Put an immediate end to all acts of judicial harassment against Vishal Singh and all human rights defenders in India; Guarantee in all circumstances that human rights defenders, journalists, filmmakers and activists in India can carry out their legitimate activities freely and safely, without fear of judicial harassment, intimidation or reprisals. body: Share THA 002/ 1026 / OBS 048 Criminalisation Judicial harassment 8 October 2026 Thailand The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Thailand . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed that a criminal defamation complaint has been filed by Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul against Mr. Yingcheep Atchanont , director of the Thai non-governmental organisation Internet Law Reform Dialogue (iLaw), an FIDH member organisation, in connection with his legitimate work of monitoring public affairs and promoting democratic accountability. On 15 September 2026, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul filed a criminal defamation complaint against Yingcheep under Article 326 (“defamation”) and 328 (“libel”) of Thailand’s Criminal Code with the Bangkok Criminal Court. The court has scheduled a preliminary hearing on 14 December 2026. If found guilty, Yingcheep could face up to two years in prison and a fine of up to 200,000 Thai baht (approximately 5,300 Euros). This development follows the announcement made by the Prime Minister on 22 July 2026 that he would take legal action against Yingcheep. The Prime Minister’s criminal defamation complaint stems from Yingcheep Atchanont’s submission of a petition to the opposition coalition in the House of Representatives on 21 July 2026, seeking a parliamentary examination of allegations that nine politicians from the ruling Bhumjaithai Party, including Prime Minister Anutin, five cabinet ministers, and three senior figures, were involved in vote manipulation during the June 2024 Senate election. According to iLaw’s investigation, evidence and witness statements suggested irregularities including candidate arrangements, the distribution of voting instructions, and the provision of financial incentives to candidates by networks linked to the Bhumjaithai Party, across different stages of the election process, which raised serious concerns over the integrity and transparency of the polls. The Observatory recalls that since its founding in 2009, iLaw has played a prominent role in advancing democratic participation, freedom of expression, and a fair justice system in Thailand. The organisation has documented the impact of repressive laws and decrees adopted following the 2006 and 2014 military coups d’état and campaigned for their reform through public engagement and online advocacy. It has also worked to support citizen participation in legislative and constitutional reform processes, particularly through campaigns to collect signatures for proposed legislation and initiatives to amend Thailand’s military-backed 2017 Constitution. In addition, iLaw has contributed to strengthening electoral transparency by systematically documenting voting irregularities and mobilising citizens to participate in election observation. The June 2024 Senate election gave rise to allegations of systemic fraud and vote-buying. Under a new selection system, more than 40,000 candidates voted among themselves through multiple rounds of selection at the district, provincial, and national levels to determine the 200-member Senate. The results led to public scrutiny particularly due to the disproportionately high number of successful candidates from provinces where the Bhumjaithai Party enjoyed strong electoral support. A separate investigation conducted jointly by the Election Commission (EC) and the Department of Special Investigation (DSI) was concluded in July 2025. The investigation found sufficient evidence to prosecute 229 individuals, including 138 senators and 91 political figures associated with the Bhumjaithai Party, in connection with fraudulent practices during the June 2024 Senate election, in violation of the 2018 Organic Act on the Acquisition of Senators. However, in March 2026, an EC subcommittee voted to overturn the earlier finding. The conflicting recommendations were subsequently submitted to the EC for a final decision. On 14 September 2026, the EC decided to refer 77 individuals to the Supreme Court to initiate criminal proceedings against them for alleged collusion in the 2024 Senate election. Among the 77 individuals are 26 sitting senators. No political party executives or other political office holders were among the 77. The Observatory denounces the criminal lawsuits against Yingcheep, which appear to be in retaliation against the peaceful exercise of his right to freedom of expression, as enshrined in international human rights law, in particular in Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which Thailand is a state party. The Observatory calls upon the Thai authorities to ensure that all complaints are dropped and urges them to take concrete steps towards the decriminalisation of defamation under Articles 326 and 328 of the Criminal Code, which are used to intimidate, silence, and harass human rights defenders in Thailand. Actions requested: Please write to the Thai authorities urging them to: Guarantee in all circumstances the physical and psychological integrity of Yingcheep Atchanont and of all iLaw staff, and put an end to all forms of harassment, including judicial harassment, against them; Dismiss the criminal defamation complaint filed on 15 September 2026 before the Bangkok Criminal Court, and ensure that all other complaints against Yingcheep Atchanont are dropped; Take concrete steps towards the decriminalisation of defamation by repealing or amending Articles 326 and 328 of the Criminal Code, and adopt effective safeguards against SLAPPs; Guarantee in all circumstances the rights to freedom of expression, as enshrined in international human rights law, and particularly in Article 19 of the ICCPR, to which Thailand is a state party; Addresses: Mr. Anutin Charnvirakul, Prime Minister of Thailand, Email: spmwebsite@thaigov.go.th Mr. Sihasak Phuangketkeow, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of Thailand, Email: minister@mfa.go.th Police Lieutenant General Rutthaphon Naowarat, Minister of Justice, Email: complainingcenter@moj.go.th National Human Rights Commission of Thailand, Email: help@nhrc.or.th H.E. Ambassador Usana Berananda, Permanent Mission of Thailand to the United Nations in Geneva, Switzerland, Email: thaimission.GVA@mfa.mail.go.th H.E. Kanchana Patarachoke, Embassy of Thailand to Belgium and Luxembourg, and Head of Mission of Thailand to the European Union, Email: thaibxl@thaiembassy.be Please also write to the diplomatic representations of Thailand in your respective countries. *** Paris-Geneva, 8 October 2026 Kindly inform us of any action undertaken quoting the code of this appeal in your reply.
